0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
The message. Acts is not first the story of the early church but the story of the risen Christ continuing his work by the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke opens with a deliberate hinge: his “first book” told “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (1:1). Acts tells what he went on to do, no longer on earth in the body but from heaven, by his Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses. His own word sets the programme: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8). In about thirty years the good news travels from a frightened upper room to the capital of the empire, and nothing can stop it.

Background: the writer. Acts is the second volume of a two-part work: both books are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts refers back to “the first book”, the Gospel of Luke. Neither names its author, but in several passages the story moves from “they” to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), so the writer travelled with Paul, even on the voyage to Rome. The early church agreed that he was Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), Paul’s fellow worker (Philemon 24) and the friend who stayed to the end (2 Timothy 4:11). He was probably a Gentile. Where he was not an eyewitness he could ask those who were, such as Philip the evangelist in Caesarea (21:8), during Paul’s two years in custody there (24:27).

When, and for whom. Many scholars date Acts in the 80s or later, and some doubt that a companion of Paul wrote it, setting the Paul of Acts against the Paul of the letters. But a friend telling a story will sound different from a man writing to churches, and Luke’s exact details of places, titles and sea travel fit an eyewitness. The book ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after “two whole years” (28:30), about AD 62, and says nothing of his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Luke could hardly have left out had they happened. So this commentary takes Acts as probably written in the early 60s. Theophilus, “most excellent” in Luke 1:3, was probably a man of rank already taught the faith, and Luke writes to make him sure of it. Along the way he shows that the gospel is no threat to Roman order: official after official finds these Christians guilty of no crime (18:14–15; 23:29; 26:31–32).

The world of Acts. The story runs along the Roman Empire’s roads and sea lanes, in a common Greek tongue. Jews lived in every city, and their synagogues gave Paul his first hearing wherever he went, with Gentile God-fearers at their edge, often the first to believe. In Jerusalem the Sanhedrin and the priestly Sadducees opposed the apostles from the start. Rulers known from other sources appear in their places: Herod Agrippa I, who killed James and was struck down by God in AD 44 (12:1–23); the emperor Claudius, who expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2); Gallio, proconsul in Corinth about AD 51–52 (18:12); the governors Felix and Festus. Paul’s Roman citizenship protects him (16:37; 22:25) and carries him to Rome by his appeal to Caesar (25:11).

How the book makes its case. The movement follows 1:8. Chapters 1–7 are in Jerusalem: the ascension, the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (chapter 2), the church’s common life, arrests, the Seven and the death of Stephen. Chapters 8–12 carry the word into Judea and Samaria and beyond: “those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (8:4), Philip reaches Samaria and an Ethiopian official, Saul the persecutor meets the risen Christ (chapter 9), Peter is sent to the centurion Cornelius (chapters 10–11), and at Antioch “the disciples were first called Christians” (11:26). Chapters 13–28, with Paul at the centre, go “to the end of the earth”: his first journey (13–14); the Jerusalem council, which settles that Gentiles are saved “through the grace of the Lord Jesus” without becoming Jews (15:1–35); the second journey into Europe, to Philippi, Athens and Corinth (15:36–18:22); the third, centred on Ephesus (18:23–21:16); arrest in Jerusalem and trials before the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus and Agrippa (21:17–26:32); and the voyage to Rome (27–28). Short reports mark the stages: “the word of God increased and multiplied” (12:24; also 6:7; 9:31; 16:5; 19:20).

The Spirit and the sovereign Lord. The Holy Spirit drives the action, sending Philip to a desert road, setting apart Barnabas and Saul (13:2), forbidding Paul to speak in Asia (16:6) and binding him to go to Jerusalem though chains await (20:22–23): not a vague force but a Person with a will, sent by the risen Son from the Father. Over every step stands God’s plan. The cross came “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (2:23), and “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (13:48). Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment gives prisoners kings to preach to. Shipwreck lands an apostle on Malta, with not one life lost (27:24, 44). The book ends with Paul under guard in Rome, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (28:31). Its last words are without hindrance: the empire could chain the man, but not the word.

Should churches copy everything in Acts? What Acts describes is not automatically a command. A pattern binds us when the rest of the New Testament teaches it, or when Luke shows it as God’s settled way: preaching Christ, baptising those who believe, appointing elders, devotion “to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (2:42). But the casting of lots (1:26), the signs that marked the apostles (2:43; 5:12) and the outpouring of the Spirit at each new crossing of the gospel, to Samaria, to Gentiles and to John’s disciples (8:14–17; 10:44–48; 19:1–7), belonged to that unrepeatable time. The sharing of goods (4:32–35) was free love, not a system: Ananias’ land was his to keep (5:4).

Where it leads: to Christ. Acts is full of sermons, and they all preach one person. Jesus, crucified by men and raised by God, is exalted to God’s right hand and made “both Lord and Christ” (2:36); he reigns now, pouring out the Spirit, and “there is salvation in no one else” (4:12). In him the promise to Abraham reaches the nations, “in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed” (3:25), and the hope of Israel is fulfilled: Paul says “nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: that the Christ must suffer” and rise (26:22–23). The risen Lord is so joined to his people that to persecute them is to persecute him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). The same Jesus who was taken up “will come in the same way” (1:11), when God will judge the world “by a man whom he has appointed” (17:31).

For us. We are the fruit of the mission to “the end of the earth”, and Acts calls us to the same message, Christ crucified and risen, and the same means: the word, prayer, baptism, the Lord’s Supper and a church that shares its life. It promises no easy road, for “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (14:22), but it shows the Lord turning every opposition into an open door. Read it with your eyes open to the God who is always working: in the upper room, the council chamber, the storm and the jail at midnight. He is the same God today, and his word still runs without hindrance.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
Where we are. Acts opens where Luke’s Gospel closed, with the risen Jesus and his disciples near Jerusalem. Chapter 1 is the hinge between the two volumes: the forty days after Easter, the ascension, and the days of waiting before Pentecost.

The message. The risen Jesus has not finished his work: from heaven, by his Spirit, he will carry it on through ordinary witnesses. He has not gone away but been enthroned, and he will come back as he went. Until then his people neither set dates nor rush ahead in their own strength: they wait for his Spirit, pray, take Scripture as their guide, and go to the whole world as his witnesses.

Why it was said. Theophilus and the churches of his day needed certainty (Luke 1:4) about a movement spoken against everywhere, whose best-known preacher was a Roman prisoner (see the introduction). Luke shows that it began not in human ambition but in the commands of the risen Lord, and that its apostles were his own choice.

How the chapter makes its case. Luke links his two volumes and sums up the forty days (vv. 1–3). Jesus commands the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Spirit (vv. 4–5), turns their question about the timing of the kingdom into a commission that maps the whole book (vv. 6–8), and is taken up in the cloud, with the angels’ promise that he will return in the same way (vv. 9–11). Back in the city the believers pray with one accord (vv. 12–15). Peter finds Judas’s treachery in the Psalms (vv. 16–20) and sets out what an apostle must be (vv. 21–22). After prayer to the Lord who knows every heart, the lot falls on Matthias, and the Twelve stand complete for Pentecost (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. The chapter is about Christ from first to last. The cloud that takes him is the cloud of God’s glory, and Daniel had seen the other side of it: one like a son of man brought before the Ancient of Days and given a kingdom that will never pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). He reigns now in our nature at the Father’s right hand, and will come again still bearing the marks of the nails. Even the betrayal and the empty seat lie inside his plan, and he keeps his number of twelve.

For us. We live in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that will bring him back. The cure for restless speculation and anxious self-reliance is the same: depend on his Spirit, pray together, and tell what he has done, beginning with the people near us and the ones we would rather skip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Lord who began his work on earth now sends his church to carry it on, by his Spirit and under his reign. Luke links his two volumes and shows Jesus proving himself alive over forty days and teaching about the kingdom of God (vv. 1–3). He commands the apostles to wait for the promised Spirit (vv. 4–5), turns their question about dates into a commission that maps the whole book, from Jerusalem to the end of the earth (vv. 6–8), and is taken up into the cloud of glory to his throne (vv. 9–10). The angels’ promise closes the section: this same Jesus will come back as they saw him go (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but his exaltation. The church acts under the authority of its enthroned King. The cloud that received him is the glory cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had seen the same moment from heaven’s side (Daniel 7:13-14; see the note on vv. 9–10). The ascension belongs to the gospel itself: through it Christ sends the Spirit (John 16:7), intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and carries our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations are unchanged: to work out timetables the Father has kept to himself, or to rush at the work in our own strength. The command is the same as it was on the hillside: receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story of Jesus did not end at the ascension: in this second volume the same Lord goes on working from heaven, by his Spirit, through the apostles he chose. Acts covers about thirty years, from the ascension (around AD 30) to Paul under house arrest in Rome (around AD 62), and its hero is not Peter or Paul but the risen Christ.

In the first book, O Theophilus. The first book is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4), whose name means friend of God. There he is “most excellent Theophilus” (Luke 1:3), a courtesy Luke gives elsewhere only to the governors Felix and Festus (23:26; 26:25), so he was probably a real man of rank; here the formal title has quietly gone, as between friends. Luke wrote “that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4), and Acts carries that purpose on. For a reader who knew that of this sect it was said that “everywhere it is spoken against” (28:22), and that its best-known preacher was a Roman prisoner, Luke shows step by step that the movement was God’s own work and no danger to public order. The writer is Luke the doctor, Paul’s travelling companion (Colossians 4:14; see the introduction).

All that Jesus began to do and teach. This sentence gives the whole book its shape: the story did not finish at the tomb or at the cloud, and in volume two it is still Jesus who is at work. It is the Lord who adds to the church (2:47), pours out the Spirit (2:33), asks Saul, “why are you persecuting me?” (9:4–5), and opens Lydia’s heart (16:14). The apostles are the instruments. He who healed lepers and forgave sinners in Galilee did not retire when he ascended.

A book with no last page. Luke leaves Paul in a rented house in Rome, preaching to whoever comes, and simply stops: no verdict, no farewell. The simplest explanation is that a book about what Jesus continues to do has no natural last page, because the work has not stopped. If you want to know what the risen Christ is doing this morning, this book shows you.

Until the day when he was taken up. The ascension is where the two books meet. Luke’s Gospel ends with it (Luke 24:50–51) and Acts begins with it: once as the close of the earthly ministry and once as the launch of the heavenly one. What looks like an ending from the ground is, from the throne, a beginning.

Commands through the Holy Spirit. The risen Son still speaks and acts by the Spirit, as his whole ministry had been carried out in that power (Luke 4:18). So the Spirit about to come at Pentecost is not a replacement brought in to cover an absence. He is the Spirit by whom Jesus was conceived and anointed, and when he lives in a believer, Jesus himself is present, not a deputy standing in while he is away. Paul can say in one breath that a Christian has the Spirit of Christ and that Christ is in him (Romans 8:9–10).

To the apostles whom he had chosen. They did not apply. He chose them after a night of prayer on a mountain (Luke 6:12–13), and their authority in the rest of this book is never their own: everything they will say with such boldness rests on their having been picked and sent.

Did Luke contradict himself about the ascension? A reader closing Luke 24 can easily come away thinking that Jesus went up on Easter evening, since the chapter runs from the empty tomb to the ascension in one unbroken stretch, while Acts 1 says forty days. But it is the same man writing, with his first volume at his elbow, quoting its opening line in his second sentence. He is not correcting himself; he is filling in. Luke 24 names events in order without dating them, as compressed endings do: the close of one scroll contracts and the opening of the sequel expands.

So how is Jesus still working today? Chiefly where he promised to: through the gospel preached and believed, through his Spirit giving new birth, through the Scriptures read and obeyed, through prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and through ordinary believers caring for one another. When a hardened man is converted, when a believer endures grief without letting go of God, when a small church keeps preaching Christ for decades, Jesus is acting from heaven. His promise is enough: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack the words “and was carried up into heaven” at Luke 24:51; most include them, and the ESV prints them with a note.
verseByVerse.note: “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus. “Began” implies that Acts records what Jesus continued to do through his Spirit and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For forty days the risen Jesus gave his apostles proof that he was alive and taught them about God’s kingdom; then he told them not to begin the mission until the Father’s promised Spirit had come.

By many proofs. The word (tekmēria) means evidence that settles a matter, a law-court and medical term found nowhere else in the New Testament. And Luke says what it consisted of: not one apparition in a dim room, but appearances spread across forty days, to individuals and to crowds, on roads, beside a lake and behind locked doors, with conversation and with food. Jesus let them touch him and showed them his wounds (Luke 24:39; John 20:27), and Paul could list more than five hundred witnesses, most of them still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The Lord of glory spent his first six weeks of resurrection life eating fish with fishermen, letting doubters touch his scars, and teaching slow men about his kingdom.

Ghosts do not get hungry. Luke has shown the risen Jesus eating broiled fish while they watched (Luke 24:41–43), and “staying with them” in verse 4 may mean eating with them (see the note on the wording at the end). Visions do not chew. The men about to be flogged for saying he rose had eaten breakfast with the evidence.

Forty days. Scripture uses forty for seasons of preparation before a new stage: Moses forty days on the mountain before the law was given (Exodus 24:18), Elijah forty days on the road to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Jesus forty days in the wilderness before his ministry began (Luke 4:2). Now forty days of the risen Lord, before the church is sent.

Speaking about the kingdom of God. Luke records not one sentence of the forty days’ teaching, because the rest of the book shows what it was. What the apostles preach from Pentecost on, that the crucified Nazarene is Lord and Christ and the door stands open to Gentiles, is not something they pieced together afterwards in committee; it is what he told them (28:31).

What the kingdom of God is. We tend to hear “kingdom” as a place, heaven after death. The word means first a reign, a king actually ruling, so the question is not where but who. Left to ourselves we each run a small kingdom of our own, and it is an anxious throne to keep. Jesus had just won his kingdom, not by seizing power but by dying under judgment and rising again. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Jesus’ miracles, and above all his resurrection, were not breaks in the natural order but foretastes of its restoration: the world as it will be when the King has finished. God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). Before the next decision about money, a grudge or a free evening, ask what your King wants, and trust him to rule you well. See Kingdom of God in the Theological Dictionary.

Wait for the promise of the Father. A man with a message that will remake the world tells eleven men to go nowhere. Waiting costs a willing person more than any other command, because it looks like doing nothing. But the promise had to arrive before the mission did. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, promised through the prophets (Joel 2:28) and by Jesus himself (Luke 24:49; John 14:16–17); they must not begin in their own strength.

Why Jerusalem. He made them wait in the city where they had failed, where Peter had sworn he had never met the man. He kept them still until what they needed was inside them, so that the church’s first sermon would be preached in the city where its preacher had collapsed.

Evidence and surrender. They are not the same thing. In this book men will hear the apostolic testimony, find nothing in it they can refute, and stroll away amused (17:32); others will tremble and still only postpone (24:25). Good evidence removes an excuse; it does not make a man willing. Tell the friend who would believe if only the case were stronger that it is already stronger than he thinks, and that for many of us the deepest obstacle lies in the will.

If the resurrection is so well proved, why do I still have doubts? Because doubt is not only a matter of evidence. Fear, grief, tiredness, temperament and a world that assumes the dead stay dead all press on the mind. Even some who saw the risen Jesus doubted at first (Matthew 28:17; Luke 24:41), and he did not throw them out; he showed them his hands and ate in front of them. So do not pretend your doubt is not there, and do not treat it as proof that you have no faith. Go back to the evidence the Spirit has preserved for you, the Gospels and 1 Corinthians 15, and pray with the father in Mark 9:24: “I believe; help my unbelief!” Faith that has looked honestly at its doubts and is still holding on is not weak faith.

Does this mean I should wait for a feeling before I serve God? No. This waiting was unique: the Spirit had not yet been poured out, and the apostles had to stay put until a once-for-all event arrived, and it has happened. Every believer now has the Spirit (Romans 8:9), and nobody needs to wait for an experience before obeying a clear command, such as loving a neighbour, confessing sin or telling a friend about Christ. What carries over is the attitude: depend on God before you act. Pray before you plan, because the work of God is never done in human strength.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “staying with them” (v. 4) is rare. It may come from a verb meaning to eat salt with someone, that is, to share a meal, hence the alternative “eating with them”; or from a very similar verb meaning to stay together. Both fit, and Luke elsewhere shows the risen Jesus eating with his disciples (Luke 24:42–43; and in this book, 10:41).
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s baptism in water was only a picture; within days Jesus would plunge his people into the reality it pictured, the Holy Spirit himself. It is the risen Jesus who gives him.

For John baptized with water. John the Baptist had drawn this contrast himself: “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming … He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16). John’s baptism was outward, a sign of repentance. Water was the picture; the Spirit is the thing pictured. Water goes over a man; the Spirit goes into him.

Baptized with the Holy Spirit. To baptize (baptizō) is to immerse, to plunge, to drench. They are about to be overwhelmed by the Spirit as a man is overwhelmed by water: God himself taking up residence in people who a few weeks earlier had scattered like birds. That the Holy One should choose such lodgings is staggering, and stranger still that he calls it a gift he is glad to give, when for him it is a great stooping down.

Not many days from now. It turned out to mean about ten; they knew only that it was near. This is often the shape of Christian waiting: a certain promise, a real nearness, a withheld date.

The one who holds the Spirit. John could pour a river over a man; he could not pour God into him. Only God gives God. In the Old Testament it is always the LORD who promises his own Spirit: “I will pour out my Spirit” (Joel 2:28); “I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27). Here the risen Jesus speaks of God’s own Spirit as his to send, something no prophet, priest or angel ever dared to say, and Peter will say that he has poured him out (2:33).

Why the phrase is contested. A large and sincere part of the church teaches that baptism with the Holy Spirit is a second work of grace after conversion, usually with tongues as the sign. The case is built almost entirely from Acts, where the Spirit does sometimes come visibly and later. But Acts is narrative, and narrative tells you what happened, not always what must happen. When the letters take up the phrase directly, they define it the other way: “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). All, not only the advanced; and it makes us members of the body, not a higher rank within it.

The four doors. The four occasions in Acts where the Spirit comes with visible drama are the four boundary-crossings of the mission: Jews (chapter 2), Samaritans (chapter 8), Gentiles (chapter 10), and disciples who knew only John’s baptism (chapter 19). Each is a first, with apostles present as witnesses. Luke is recording not a pattern for private experience but how the door was opened, one hinge at a time, and certified by heaven in public, so that nobody could later say the wrong people had been let in.

Not second-class, and not content. If the Spirit is what makes a person belong to Christ at all (Romans 8:9), then a believer who trusts Christ, hates his sin and loves the brethren has the Spirit, whatever his emotional weather and whether or not he has an experience to point to. Yet this same book shows men filled at Pentecost being filled again in a shaken room (4:31), so fresh fillings with the Spirit are biblical, not an embarrassment, and to want more of God is right. The label “second baptism” may be wrong; the hunger is not.

Then what does being filled with the Spirit mean? Being baptised with the Spirit is the once-for-all beginning: God joins you to Christ and comes to live in you. Being filled is the ongoing, renewable condition of a life increasingly yielded to the Spirit. Paul’s command is in the present tense, keep on being filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he describes what it looks like: singing to the Lord, giving thanks always, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:19–21); the parallel passage puts the word of Christ dwelling richly in you in the same place (Colossians 3:16). So seek the Spirit’s fullness by staying close to Scripture, confessing sin quickly, praying, and obeying what you already know. And ask: the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Where Christians differ: Spirit baptism. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching holds that Spirit baptism is a second blessing after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and that every believer should seek it. This commentary’s view: Pentecost was a unique, unrepeatable event in the history of salvation: the Spirit poured out on the church once for all, as the cross and resurrection happened once for all. For believers since, Spirit baptism happens at conversion: all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). We are to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), but there is no second-class Christian waiting for a second baptism. Brothers and sisters who hold the other view love Christ and often shame the rest of us by their prayerfulness and zeal, and the difference should be argued from Scripture with warmth, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not scold the apostles for hoping in Israel’s kingdom, but he corrects them on two points: the timing belongs to the Father alone, and the kingdom is far larger than the one they had in mind.

Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? This is the last question Luke records the apostles putting to Jesus on earth, and it is about politics. After a crucifixion, a resurrection and six weeks on the kingdom of God, they want to know whether the occupation is about to end. The two on the Emmaus road had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). Think what they lived with: a foreign garrison in the temple city, a governor who had executed their master to keep the peace, taxes flowing to a Caesar hailed as the son of a god. Their Scriptures had promised a son of David on a real throne. They were not inventing the expectation; they were asking when the book would come true.

He does not call the question foolish. Nor does he say the hope is wrong. He corrects two things only: the timing, and their assumed right to know it.

Times or seasons. Times (chronous) are stretches of time; seasons (kairous) are appointed moments. The Father has fixed both by his own authority, and they are not the apostles’ to know. Jesus had said the same of the day of his return: “concerning that day or that hour, no one knows” (Mark 13:32). Date-setting for the end is forbidden ground.

A secret, not an evasion. Jesus did not say there is no date. He said the date is not yours. It is certain, and kept from them for their good. A man who knew it would spend his life either presuming on the time remaining or paralysed by its shortness; not knowing, he is left to do the only sane thing, which is to be found faithful whenever it comes. And wanting the date is very often wanting control: managing the future instead of trusting the one who holds it.

The Father kept every appointment. The Son himself lived by the Father’s calendar. John’s Gospel tells us again and again that “his hour had not yet come” (John 7:30), and then, on the night of the supper, that it had (John 13:1); he walked into it without flinching, because the hour of his death was a season the Father had fixed. The Father who kept every appointment he made with his Son, the day of the cross and the morning of the empty tomb, will keep the last one.

A throne higher than the one they asked for. The answer arrived within a fortnight and was larger than the question. At Pentecost Peter will tell this city that God has seated David’s son on his throne: Jesus, raised from the dead and exalted to God’s right hand, is the one David called Lord (2:30–36). The kingdom was not postponed on the Mount of Olives. They asked whether the King would take back the land. He was about to take the world.

The cost of the calendar. Hardly a decade has passed without someone announcing the date; farms have been sold and careers abandoned, and the morning after has always come, with the faithful poorer and the watching world confirmed in its suspicion. When a teacher claims to have worked out what the Father reserved to his own authority, you need not examine his arithmetic.

Is it wrong to think about the end times at all? No. The New Testament speaks of the last things constantly, to give hope to the suffering, to warn the careless, and to keep believers awake and faithful (1 Thessalonians 4:18; 2 Peter 3:11–14). What Jesus forbids is trying to fix the date and read the calendar out of the newspapers. So study what Scripture plainly teaches: Christ will come personally and visibly, the dead will be raised, all will be judged, and God will make all things new. Hold the details loosely where good Christians differ. And if a book or a preacher leaves you more fascinated by charts than eager to love Christ and your neighbour, put it down.

What does amillennial mean? The word comes from Revelation 20, where Christ reigns for a thousand years. Amillennialists understand that thousand years not as a future golden age on earth after Christ returns, but as his present reign from heaven between his first and second comings, while the gospel goes to the nations and the saints who have died reign with him. On this view there is one return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, the world is judged and the new creation begins (John 5:28–29). The kingdom is already here, because the King is on his throne; and it is not yet complete, because his enemies are still being made his footstool (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25).

Other views. Premillennial believers, many faithful and learned, see a further earthly reign after his return; the difference is real, but it is not a difference about whether Jesus is coming. Dispensational believers, many of whom expect Christ to remove his church before a great tribulation and later to reign from Jerusalem, are brothers and sisters too, often with a deep love for Scripture and for the Jewish people.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and Israel. Dispensationalists (who see God’s purposes for Israel and for the church as two distinct tracks) read this to mean that a political kingdom will be restored to national Israel in a future millennium, and that Jesus only postponed it. This commentary’s view: Jesus redirects their question from a political kingdom to a worldwide mission: his next sentence begins with but (v. 8). The kingdom is restored to Israel as the Messiah reigns from heaven (2:30–36) and gathers a renewed Israel of Jewish and Gentile believers (15:16–17; Galatians 6:16). The Old Testament promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, and will be completed in the new creation. This is the amillennial view. It does not follow that God is finished with the Jewish people, and the New Testament will not let that conclusion stand (Romans 11:1): on the most natural reading of Romans 11:25–26, held here with humility, Paul still hopes for a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ. A reader can hold the mission of verse 8 with both hands and still expect God to keep every promise he ever made, without needing a chart to show him how.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of a date, Jesus gives a gift and a map: the Spirit’s power, so that his followers will be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the end of the earth. It is the programme of the whole book (see the introduction).

You will receive power. He answers a question about the calendar with a map, and begins not with an instruction but a gift: not summon power, but receive it. The word (dynamis) means ability, strength, the capacity to do what you could not otherwise do. It is given not for politics or private experience but for witness.

What the power turned out to be. Within three chapters these men are in custody; within seven, Stephen is dead under a pile of stones. The power did not make them untouchable; it made them unstoppable. What Luke records after Pentecost is boldness where there had been hiding, clarity where there had been confusion, and joy where joy has no business being: a flogging that ends in rejoicing (5:41), a midnight hymn from a prison floor (16:25). A Christian waiting for power to feel like invincibility may miss it when it comes as the ability to speak where speaking costs him something.

My witnesses. Not preachers or strategists, but witnesses, who tell what they have seen and heard: “we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (4:20). The word is martyres, and English took it over as martyr, not because the word means dying, but because of what kept happening to the people it described; Luke shows the change beginning when Paul speaks of “the blood of Stephen your witness” (22:20). But keep the courtroom sense first, because it sets a nervous believer free. A witness is not the barrister. He is not asked to win the case, only to say what he saw. Cleverer people may cross-examine him; it does not touch his qualification, because he was there and they were not. Anyone who has been dealt with by Jesus Christ has standing in that witness box, and every believer who has stammered out the name of Jesus to a friend has been a fulfilment of this sentence.

To the end of the earth. The geography doubles as the table of contents: Jerusalem fills chapters 1 to 7; Judea and Samaria, chapters 8 to 12; the end of the earth, chapters 13 to 28, ending in Rome, the centre of the known world. Samaria, whose people a Judean might cross the Jordan to avoid, sits not last but second, so that no one could reach the ends of the earth while stepping over the neighbours he despised. And the phrase “the end of the earth” comes from Isaiah, where the Servant of the LORD is made “a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6), words Paul will apply to his own mission (13:47).

The Servant’s light in his witnesses’ hands. Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, has already said who the Servant is: “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). So the end of the earth is not a target the church set itself but the Servant’s own commission, the reach God promised his Son, and Jesus hands it to his witnesses because the light they carry is himself. He spoke of it to eleven provincials with no money and no standing as already settled: the confidence of a King who has bought what he is about to claim. The nations were his inheritance before a single witness set out (Psalm 2:8), and his Spirit has carried his name into languages Luke never heard of and as far as the reader of this page.

What it does not mean. This verse is often turned into a method (reach your Jerusalem first, then your Judea, then the world), as though local outreach must be completed before anyone may go abroad. But it is Luke’s map of one historical expansion, not a sequence of permissions, and the book itself refuses that reading: the gospel reaches Samaria because a persecution scattered people who had no strategy at all (8:1–4), and Antioch is evangelised by men whose names Luke does not record (11:20). God has never waited for one city to be finished before starting on another.

Is this command to every believer, or a promise to the apostles? It was spoken first to the apostles, eyewitnesses of the resurrection in a unique sense (v. 22). But Acts goes on to show ordinary believers telling the good news wherever they went (8:1–4), and Peter tells every Christian to be ready to give a reason for his hope (1 Peter 3:15). The apostles’ eyewitness testimony is now written down; the witness to it belongs to all.

Does power mean I should expect miracles? The Spirit’s power is promised to every believer, but its main form in this verse is witness: courage, clarity and endurance in speaking of Christ. The signs and wonders in Acts cluster around the apostles and those closely linked to them, and the New Testament calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), given to confirm the message when it was first delivered (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation laid and the Scriptures complete, we hold that those gifts of new revelation and of miraculous signs have ceased, though many fine Christians disagree. This view, called cessationism, rests on the link the New Testament makes between such signs and the apostles’ foundational witness (Ephesians 2:20); continuationist brothers and sisters, Reformed believers among them, read 1 Corinthians 12–14 as describing gifts for the whole church age, and their case deserves a respectful hearing. But God has not stopped acting. He answers prayer, he heals when he pleases, and he does the greatest miracle of all every time a dead heart is made alive. Expect that power, and pray for it.

So what do I actually do? Start with the people already in your life and with what Christ has done for you. You need no speech, only honesty when someone asks why you go to church or how you got through the year. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ, ask for one opportunity this week, and when it comes, say one true thing about Jesus and leave the results with him. And ask honestly whether there is a Samaria in your life, a person or a kind of person you would quietly prefer the gospel to skip. The map Jesus drew went straight through the people his disciples least wanted to meet, and he has not redrawn it for you. None of us witnesses as faithfully as we should; the Servant obeyed the Father perfectly in our place, so failure here does not undo your standing, and his Spirit sends you out again.
verseByVerse.note: This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the end of the earth (13–28).

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was taken up bodily before their eyes into the cloud of God’s glory: not a departure into absence but his enthronement at the Father’s right hand.

As they were looking on. Luke the reporter is careful: they did not infer it from an empty hillside; they watched it happen. It was not a fading or a dissolving. He was lifted, a cloud came between, and the hillside was one man emptier. The ascension was a real, bodily event, and it marks his exaltation to the Father’s right hand, where he reigns over all things (2:33; Ephesians 1:20–22).

A cloud took him. The cloud is the detail everything turns on, and it is not weather. All through Israel’s Scriptures the cloud is the sign of God’s presence, showing that he is there while hiding him from sight. It leads Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), wraps Sinai (Exodus 19:16), fills the tabernacle and the temple so that no one can stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11), and overshadows the mount of transfiguration (Luke 9:34–35). When a cloud takes a man out of sight in the Bible, he has gone inside the glory.

Received as into his own home. That presence was never safe for sinners to approach (Exodus 19:12). Jesus is received into it as into his own home, and he enters as our representative, carrying our nature where no sinner could stand. The one by whom all things were made had been spat at by soldiers, and had let them; now the glory that Moses was not permitted to see opens to receive him. The marks in his hands went in with him and are there still.

The underside of a coronation. From the hillside it is a departure, and looks like loss. From the other side of the cloud it is an arrival, and Daniel had described it centuries before: one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before the Ancient of Days, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). In Daniel he is not coming down to earth but up to the throne; the disciples are watching the underside of a coronation. And the psalm the apostles quote more than any other says what happens when he gets there: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1). Peter will preach it within a fortnight (2:34–35).

Two men stood by them in white robes. Angels, as at the tomb (Luke 24:4): the same kind of messengers explain the empty grave and the empty sky.

He took his body with him. At this moment, in the presence of God, there is a human being, with hands, with a voice, with a memory of Nazareth and of nails, and he is not visiting. The nature he assumed in the womb of a Galilean girl he has never laid down and never will. The Reformed churches have insisted on care here: a real body is somewhere, and being somewhere means not being everywhere, so when Christ promises to be with his people always he is with them as God and by his Spirit, not by his body being spread thin across the world. Lutheran Christians take a different line on that point, but the disagreement is not about whether Christ is truly present with his church. The comfort belongs to all: our nature is not a costume he wore for thirty years; it has been carried into the immediate presence of God and seated there.

What it does not mean. Not that heaven is a distance measurable in miles above Jerusalem, as if Jesus flew upward through space. That mistakes a sign for a map. He went up because a body must leave visibly if witnesses are to testify that it left, and because upward is what exaltation looks like to creatures who walk on the ground. The direction was for their eyes; the destination was the throne.

Why did Jesus have to leave? Jesus himself said it was better: “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7). In Galilee he could be in only one village at a time; now, by his Spirit, he is present with every believer in every place at once. You are not worse off than the disciples who could see him; in one way you are better placed, because the Spirit they had to wait ten days for has been given to you.

What is Jesus doing now? He is reigning, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), working all things toward the day his enemies are put under his feet. He is interceding: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), so that at this moment a man who knows your name is praying for you in the presence of God. He is preparing a place for his people (John 14:2–3) and building his church through the gospel. And he is waiting, with perfect patience, for the day the Father has fixed, when he will come back. So when you pray, remember who is on the other end: a man in our nature at the Father’s right hand, who knows tiredness, hunger and grief from the inside. Bring him the small things as well as the large.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence.

parallels.desc: two men in dazzling apparel

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels send the disciples back to work with a certain hope: the same Jesus who was taken up will come again in the same way, personally, bodily and visibly.

Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? Angels have a way of asking questions that are really instructions. The men are doing nothing wrong; they are lingering over something that is finished. The sky has nothing further to show them, and the next thing God has for them is at the bottom of the hill. And men of Galilee is no compliment in Jerusalem: it is the label that will be thrown at Peter beside a fire and at the whole company at Pentecost (2:7). Provincials with an accent. Heaven uses the word without apology, and then tells these provincials that the next act of world history runs through them.

This Jesus. The same Jesus, personally: not a successor or a spirit distinct from the man. The one they had walked the roads with is the one who will return.

In the same way. The anchor of Christian hope: the return will match the ascension. He left personally, and a person will come back: not an influence, not a movement, not an era of improved conditions. He left bodily, and the same body, the same face, the same scarred hands that blessed his disciples as he left, will return. He left visibly, watched by eleven men; the whole world will not be informed of the return but will see it, every eye (Revelation 1:7). And he left in a cloud, where Daniel had said the Son of Man belonged, and where Jesus said he would be seen coming with power and great glory (Matthew 24:30).

What the phrase rules out. It rules out the teaching that Christ has already returned invisibly, whether in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or at some private date since. Something did happen in AD 70, as Jesus said it would; but the angels say “in the same way”: seen, and in the body. It equally rules out treating the second coming as a figure of speech for death, or for the gradual improvement of the human race. The Christian expectation is not that things will get better. It is that a particular man will arrive.

A record that has been kept. Many Christians have died holding this sentence. Measure it against what is actually wrong with the world. Someone harmed as a child has watched the man who did it live comfortably into old age and die unaccused. Whole categories of injustice are now unrecoverable, the witnesses dead, the record lost. To all of it this sentence says: there is a date, and on that date the one who was in the room the whole time will come back in the open, and nothing will be left buried. Every tear will be answered by a face, every hidden wrong by the one who saw it, every grave by the voice that raised Lazarus. That is not a poetic way of saying things will feel better eventually; it is a man on a cloud, and a record of every wrong that has been kept.

But doesn’t 1 Thessalonians 4 speak of being caught up? It does, and it is anything but secret: a cry of command, the voice of an archangel, the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and the word for meet was used of citizens going out of a city to greet an arriving king and escort him back in. The picture is not of the church taken away while the world carries on, but of his people going out to welcome him, and the chapter flows straight on into the day of the Lord (5:1–3). One coming, seen by all, with his people gathered to him. Many faithful Christians were taught to expect a rapture before a great tribulation, and they often long for his appearing more eagerly than the rest of us; the disagreement is over how to read these texts, not over whether he is coming.

It has been two thousand years. Is he really coming? Yes, and the delay is not forgetfulness. Peter met this very objection in his own lifetime, from scoffers who said that everything goes on as it always has. His answer was that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and that the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:3–9). Every year since Olivet has been a year of mercy, in which more people have been brought to repentance. The waiting is long by our clocks, not by his, and it is not empty.

How do I live ready without being anxious? Readiness in the New Testament is not nervous watching of the sky; it is faithful work and trust in Christ. The servants in Jesus’ parables are ready because they are doing what their master told them, not because they have guessed the hour (Luke 12:42–43). If you belong to Christ, his coming is not a threat hanging over you but the arrival of your Saviour, and no condemnation waits for you (Romans 8:1). So keep short accounts with God, love the people around you, do your ordinary work well, and say each night, as the church has said from the beginning, “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

Where Christians differ: a secret rapture? Some teach that Christ will return secretly to remove believers before a tribulation (a time of great distress before the end), then visibly later. This commentary’s view: the angels promise one return, in the same way he went: visible and bodily. The New Testament knows one second coming, at which believers are gathered, the dead raised, and the world judged (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). No secret rapture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Between the ascension and Pentecost the church does two things: it prays, and it obeys Scripture. About a hundred and twenty believers, the eleven, the women, Mary and Jesus’ once unbelieving brothers, devote themselves to prayer with one accord (vv. 12–15). Peter explains from the Psalms that Judas’s treachery was foretold and that his office must be filled (vv. 16–20). The new apostle must be an eyewitness of the whole ministry and of the resurrection (vv. 21–22). The church puts forward two qualified men and prays to the Lord who knows every heart, and the lot falls on Matthias, so that the Twelve stand complete before the Spirit comes (vv. 23–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Twelve and Their Significance

Filling the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and stand for the restored people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30; see v. 26). The qualifications Peter states (vv. 21–22) could be met only by men who had been there, so the apostles are a closed group, the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Judas stands as the sober warning at the door of the book (see vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no standing prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church still prepares for what God intends to do in the same way: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles obey at once and go back into the city where their Master was killed: eleven named men in a borrowed room, with nothing yet but a promise.

They returned to Jerusalem. An act of obedience with a cost: Jerusalem was the most dangerous place on earth for a follower of the executed Nazarene. Jesus had told them to stay there (v. 4), and Luke’s Gospel adds that they went with great joy (Luke 24:52).

From the mount called Olivet. The Mount of Olives rises east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley; Luke 24:50 places the ascension near Bethany, on its eastern slope. Zechariah had foretold the day when the LORD’s feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and the King left the world from that same hill.

A Sabbath day’s journey away. A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the rabbis permitted on the day of rest, about two thousand cubits, roughly a kilometre (compare Exodus 16:29).

The eleven by name. Luke writes out every name, matching the list in his Gospel (Luke 6:14–16), minus Judas Iscariot. A movement staking everything on the claim that certain men saw a dead man alive has to be able to say who they were, and Luke names them in a city where they could be found and questioned. John has moved up beside Peter, because those two are about to work as a pair through the opening chapters (3:1; 4:13; 8:14). Judas the son of James is not Iscariot, as Luke makes clear by naming the father; he is probably Thaddaeus in the other lists, and a church inventing its own records would hardly saddle itself with a second Judas.

Simon the Zealot and Matthew. Simon’s title points to zeal for the law, and possibly to the movement that believed the answer to Rome was a knife (see the note on the wording at the end). Sitting in the same small room is Matthew, who had made his living collecting Rome’s money from his own people. If Simon’s zeal was of that fiercer kind, the two were natural enemies: the collaborator and the man who thought collaborators traitors to God. Now they are praying together. What held them was not a compromise between their causes but a Lord who had died for them both, and who had shown them that the sin he saved them from was a far greater enemy than the one they had quarrelled over.

The upper room. Probably a borrowed space up the stairs of a Jerusalem house, perhaps the room of the last supper, or the house of Mary the mother of John Mark (12:12). What matters is the scale. The risen Lord of heaven and earth has been enthroned at the right hand of God, and all there is to see of his kingdom in Jerusalem is a borrowed room upstairs with about a hundred and twenty people in it, most of them without money, and one of them, Peter, still living down the worst night of his life. Everything in this book grows from that room.

What if my church contains people whose politics I find hard to bear? Then you are in the church Jesus built. He deliberately put a tax collector and a zealot in the same company, not by asking them to stop caring about the world but by giving them a Lord who mattered more than their causes. You may still hold your convictions, and some political questions are moral questions on which Scripture speaks. But the person across the aisle who votes differently is, if he trusts Christ, your brother for eternity, and the election will be forgotten long before he is. Pray with him. Eat with him. Let the gospel be louder in your conversation than the news, and you will find, as Matthew and Simon did, that you have more in common than you had in conflict.

Uncertain wording. “The Zealot” may describe Simon’s character, zealous for God’s law, or mean that he had belonged to the Zealots, the nationalists who later led the revolt against Rome. How organised that movement was in Jesus’ day is uncertain, so we cannot be sure which is meant. (In Matthew and Mark his title in Greek is “the Cananaean”, from the Aramaic word for zealot.)
verseByVerse.note: A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed on the Sabbath, a little over half a mile. The list of eleven matches the Gospels’ lists; Judas the son of James is probably Thaddaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church’s first act after the ascension is to pray together, and the room holds a surprising company: the eleven, the faithful women, Jesus’ mother, and the brothers who had once thought him mad.

With one accord. Luke’s favourite word for the early church: homothymadon, of one mind and one impulse together (2:46; 4:24; 5:12). The verb (proskarterountes) describes something kept up: they were devoting themselves to prayer, the way a man keeps at something he cannot do without. They had been given a promise with no date attached, and the only work available to them was asking.

Together with the women. These are probably the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee, supported him from their own means and witnessed the cross and the empty tomb (Luke 8:2–3; 23:49; 24:10). Women, whose word carried little weight in court, were last at the cross and first at the tomb, and are now in the founding prayer meeting of the Christian church. Someone constructing a respectable origin story in the first century would hardly have arranged it that way.

And Mary the mother of Jesus. This is the last time Mary is named in the New Testament. Scripture leaves her not on a platform, and not being asked for anything, but praying in a crowded room with a hundred and nineteen other people, waiting for the Holy Spirit like everyone else. She is blessed among women, and the church should not be so nervous of the wrong honour paid to her that it forgets what the text says; but she is honoured as one of the redeemed, not as a channel of redemption. When a woman in a crowd blessed the womb that bore him, her son answered, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” (Luke 11:27–28). Here she is doing exactly that, which is an honourable place to leave her.

And his brothers. These are the men who had come to collect him because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), who did not believe in him (John 7:5). Now they are in the prayer meeting. One of them, James, will be leading the Jerusalem church within a few years, giving the decisive judgment at the council that settles the Gentile question (15:13–19). His letter calls his own elder brother Lord and himself his servant, as Jude’s does. Whatever else happened in the forty days, this happened: “Then he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). As for who these brothers were, the natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus (Matthew 13:55–56).

That house turned the right way up. The boy Jesus was once submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51); now the order of that house has been turned the right way up. The mother is a disciple on her knees, the brothers are servants waiting on his word, and the son who once did as he was told in a carpenter’s home is the Lord of heaven about to pour out what he promised. The grace that reached into that household does not stop at the door of ours.

About a hundred and twenty. A strikingly modest number set against the end of the earth: ten times twelve, perhaps a quiet hint of a renewed Israel. Within a chapter three thousand more will be added.

Should Christians pray to Mary? No. Scripture never shows a believer praying to Mary or to any departed saint, and it gives a reason why we need not: “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Mary herself called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47), which means she needed saving like the rest of us. Honour her as the Bible does: call her blessed, imitate her faith and humility, “let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38), and do what she told the servants at Cana, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). Her last recorded words in the Gospels turn every eye to her Son, and so should ours.

For the one praying for an unbelieving relative. There is no formula here, only this: it took years. Mary lived in a house where her other sons thought her firstborn was mad, with no promise that they would change; what she was given, eventually, was a room with all of them in it. The case is never closed while a man is alive, and the risen Christ went looking for one of them personally. That is not a promise that every son and every brother will come. It is a plain fact that the hardest cases in the New Testament include the ones who had shared a childhood with him, and they came.

Why pray, if God has already promised? Because the promise is the reason to pray, not a reason to stop. The disciples knew the Spirit was coming, and they spent the ten days asking for exactly that. Daniel did the same when he read in Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years: he turned to God in prayer (Daniel 9:2–3). God has chosen to bring about his purposes through the prayers of his people, so that when the answer comes they know it came from him. Pray most confidently for what God has promised: the spread of the gospel, the holiness of his church, the coming of his kingdom. And go to your church’s prayer meeting, however small, unglamorous and easy to skip; the promised Spirit came on a church that was praying.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry, are now among the believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, restored after his denials, shows the church from Scripture that God had foretold even Judas’s betrayal, while Judas remained wholly guilty for it.

The Scripture had to be fulfilled. The last time Luke showed Peter speaking about Jesus in Jerusalem, he was beside a fire, swearing that he had never met the man. Now he opens the Scriptures on the young church’s hardest subject, the treachery of one of their own. This is what restoration looks like a few weeks later (John 21:15–19): not a man excused, but a man working. “Had to” (edei) means that God had determined it, the word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 24:26). Even the betrayal had been foretold; God was not surprised.

In the flow. Peter’s speech (vv. 16–22), the only scene between the ascension and Pentecost, answers one question: what is to be done about the hole Judas left? Before the witness begins (v. 8), the Twelve must be twelve again, because they stand for the renewed Israel the Messiah is gathering (Luke 22:30). The speech moves from Scripture fulfilled (v. 16) to Scripture obeyed (vv. 20–22).

By the mouth of David. The double authorship is stated without any awkwardness: the Spirit spoke, by the mouth of David. Not as through a hollow pipe: the grief at a friend who turned on him was David’s own, and the Holy Spirit was speaking in all of it. Scripture has a divine author and a human author (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), which is why Peter can treat a thousand-year-old lament as an instruction for a decision this week.

A guide. The man who knew the garden because he had prayed in it with Jesus led the soldiers there with torches.

Numbered among us. Judas was not an outsider who got in. He was on the list, sent out to preach with the rest and trusted with the money. When Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, the eleven did not turn on Judas; each asked, “Is it I?” (Mark 14:19). Three years closer to Jesus than almost anyone has ever been did not save him. Outwardly a real apostle, he was never truly Christ’s (John 6:70; 17:12). Office and outward service are not proof of salvation: on that day many will say, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and he will say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Being near Christ is not the same as belonging to him.

If God planned it, was Judas to blame? “Had to be fulfilled” raises a question that has troubled thoughtful readers ever since: was Judas ever free to do otherwise, and is God then the author of the worst act in human history? Luke states both halves of the answer twice more, very starkly. At Pentecost Peter says Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same breath says “you crucified and killed” him (2:23). A few weeks later the church prays that Herod and Pilate and the nations gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (4:27–28). The Bible never treats these as two positions to choose between. It puts them in one sentence.

God did not put the greed there. Scripture never says that God implanted the sin. Judas was not overpowered. He was a thief with his hand in the common purse long before he went to the priests (John 12:6), and in the end he did what he had been doing in small amounts for years: he turned Jesus into money. He was not a man forced into a role but a man who found a buyer. God wove a free and filthy act into a purpose its doer knew nothing about. That is not tyranny. It is something more frightening and more reassuring: no evil is so deliberate that it can get outside the plan of God, and none so useful to that plan that the man doing it is thereby excused. The Westminster Confession says it with care: God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet so that he is not the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creature, that is, no one’s will is forced (Westminster 3.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1 says the same).

Mercy held out to the last. No one may say that Judas was never given a chance. He had three years of it. His feet were washed by the man he had already agreed to sell. He was warned in a way that let him withdraw without public exposure, and was called friend in the garden with the kiss still wet on the face. Whatever mystery lies behind the word predestined, God’s plan never kept Judas from a repentance he wanted.

Judas is not your mirror. The warning of “numbered among us” has frightened tender consciences, so one thing must be added. Judas is not a mirror for the believer who is afraid he loves Christ too little. Judas was never afraid of that for a moment. He did not want Christ and fear he was failing him; he wanted what Christ could be turned into, and when the exchange rate disappointed him he cashed out. Someone anxious because he longs to love Jesus more than he does has already given the evidence that Judas never gave in all his years of standing closer than anyone. The Saviour who was betrayed by a friend is the friend who will never betray you.

How do I examine myself without falling into despair? Scripture tells us to examine ourselves (2 Corinthians 13:5), but never to look only at ourselves. Ask simple questions. Am I trusting Christ, not my record, for my acceptance with God? Do I hate my sin and want to be rid of it, even when I fail? Do I love God’s word and God’s people, however weakly? Those are the marks of the Spirit’s work. Then look away from yourself to Christ, because assurance grows by looking at him, not by staring at your own pulse. If you find no faith at all, do not despair but come to him now: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke steps out of Peter’s speech to tell how Judas died, and how the field bought with his blood money became known to all Jerusalem as the Field of Blood. The traitor’s reward became his grave.

This man acquired a field. These two verses are most likely Luke speaking, not Peter: Peter would not have told people in Jerusalem that the name was “in their own language”. Luke has stepped out of the speech, and many English Bibles rightly put the verses in brackets.

Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. A story invented at a distance would hardly preserve the local Aramaic name of a piece of ground still in use, which any reader in Jerusalem could go and look at. Legends do not usually give an address. It was called Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money, and because of the bloody death that took place there. Tradition places it in the Hinnom valley south of Jerusalem, the valley whose name became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell.

Who bought the field? Two apparent collisions with Matthew’s account have to be faced, and they come apart more easily than their reputation suggests, though what follows is a likely harmonisation rather than a proof. The first is the purchase. Matthew says the chief priests took the returned silver and bought the field, because it was blood money and could not go into the treasury (Matthew 27:3–8); Luke says Judas acquired it “with the reward of his wickedness”. That is natural speech about a dead man’s money. The silver was legally his; the priests would not touch it for sacred use and could not simply return it to a corpse, so it was spent on his account, and the ground was counted as his. Luke is not picturing a man house-hunting between the betrayal and the rope; he is telling you whose money paid for it, which is why the city tied his crime to the land.

Falling headlong. The second is the death itself. Matthew says he hanged himself; Luke says he fell headlong and burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. Read as two claims about the same instant they are irreconcilable; read as two moments in one afternoon they are not. A body left hanging does not stay hanging indefinitely, and the ravine country south of Jerusalem is rock. The rope or the branch gives, or the corpse comes down of its own weight in the heat, and what is found at the bottom is what Luke describes, with a doctor’s plainness. Matthew tells you what Judas did; Luke tells you what was found, and why the field got the name it kept. On this reading neither writer contradicts the other: they stand at different ends of the same terrible day. Not every detail can be recovered now, and believers hold both accounts true while admitting that some questions remain open.

The blood the field was named for. Matthew records that Judas came back to the priests saying he had betrayed innocent blood, and that they counted the silver as the price of blood (Matthew 27:4–6). So the blood in Akeldama is first of all the blood of Jesus, priced and sold. The blood that could buy a traitor only a field of shame is the blood with which God obtained the church (20:28). The one innocent man in the whole transaction was led outside the city walls and paid in full the wages of sin, such as Judas earned, for everyone who will come to him. The field of blood is a grave; the blood of Christ is a purchase.

What it does not mean. This passage is read by people carrying something heavy. Judas is not in Scripture as a case study in suicide, and he must not be used as one. What is said about him is said about a man who sold the Son of God for money and never once repented of the wanting, only of the outcome. The manner of his death is reported; it is not what he is condemned for. A reader who has buried someone who took their own life, a son, a wife, a friend who was in agony and could not see a morning, is not looking at that person’s portrait in these verses, and anyone who hands it to them as one has badly misread the passage. Despair and treachery are not the same sin, and the God who reads hearts has never confused them.

Can a Christian who takes his own life be saved? Suicide is a grave sin, the taking of a life God gave, and no one should ever think of it as a way out. But Scripture nowhere calls it the unforgivable sin, and salvation does not depend on a person’s state of mind in his last moment. It depends on Christ, who saves to the uttermost those who come to God through him, and from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28). A true believer overwhelmed by illness or despair is still covered by the blood that covered all his sins. If you are grieving such a loss, bring your grief and your questions to God and to your pastor. If you are thinking of ending your own life, please tell someone today, a pastor, a doctor, a friend, and let them help you carry what you cannot carry alone.

In everyday life. Ask what you are tempted to trade Christ for: a promotion, a relationship, a reputation, a comfortable silence when you should speak. You were bought with blood worth more than all of them.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “falling headlong” normally means falling flat on one’s face. A few scholars suggest that here it means “swelling up”, but that sense is poorly attested, and the usual meaning is more likely.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; the two accounts are often harmonised as a hanging followed by a fall. Akeldama is Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter finds both Judas’s ruin and the duty to replace him in the Psalms, because the righteous sufferer of those psalms is finally Christ, and his chief enemy is the man who betrayed him.

Written in the Book of Psalms. Peter’s authority for acting is two lines of Hebrew poetry, and his use of them shows how the first Christians read their Bible. Psalm 69 is David hunted and hated, drowning in trouble, with the scorn of those who reproach God falling on him; it is among the psalms most often applied to Jesus (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3).
