Psalm 109 is David betrayed by a man he had loved, who repaid friendship with accusation. Neither psalm names Judas; both are the cry of the Lord’s anointed under treachery. David’s sufferings were a shadow cast ahead of time by those of his greater Son, who was betrayed by a table companion. The Holy Spirit wrote the story of Christ into David’s tears a thousand years before Bethlehem, so that the betrayal of the Son of God was already in Israel’s hymnbook when it happened.

May his camp become desolate. Peter alters one thing, openly. The psalm has their camp and their tents, plural, a whole party of enemies (Psalm 69:25); Peter makes it singular, his camp. He is not misquoting: he applies a judgment on a whole group of enemies to the one man who led them. The word (epaulis) means a homestead. The field of blood is that camp, and no one would ever live there.

Let another take his office. The second citation, Psalm 109:8, is the one Peter acts on. The word behind office (episkopē) means oversight, a position of responsibility, and it would later give the church its term for an overseer, or bishop. Peter reads it as a command to carry out, not a comment. The man who disgraced the seat did not abolish it; he vacated it, and it is to be filled.

The office outlived the man. This steadies people who have watched a leader fall. When someone trusted proves a fraud, the temptation is to conclude that the whole thing was a fraud, or to leave the position quietly empty. Peter’s answer is to open the Scriptures and appoint a successor. The work is bigger than the worst man who ever did it.

One office will never fall vacant. Judas left his post, and another had to take it; but the Righteous Sufferer of the Psalms holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever (Hebrews 7:24). No one will ever have to stand up in a room and propose his successor.

Does this mean every psalm is about Jesus? Not in the sense that every line is a coded prediction. Read each psalm first as what it is: a real prayer of a real believer, often David, in a real situation. Then ask how it fits into the larger story. Some psalms speak directly of the coming King (Psalms 2 and 110). Many are the prayers of the anointed king, and Christ is the King who prays them most truly. Others are the prayers of God’s people, and we pray them in Christ, with him as our representative. Some lines, such as David’s confessions of sin in Psalm 51, Jesus could not pray of himself, though he bore those sins for us. Following the apostles, you will find the Psalms leading you to Christ again and again.

The prayers that ask God to ruin somebody. These are the imprecatory psalms, prayers that call down God’s judgment on an enemy. Anyone who looks up Psalm 109 will find that the line right after the one Peter quotes asks that the man’s children be fatherless and his wife a widow. How is a Christian, told to pray for those who persecute him, to hold a book that contains prayers like that?

Three things that make it bearable. First, an imprecation is the opposite of vengeance, not an instance of it. A man who prays that God will judge his enemy has handed the matter to a court and taken his own hands off it, as Paul says: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Forbid such prayers, and wronged people do not turn gentle; they reach for the knife. Second, the enemies in view are not personal irritants but the settled adversaries of God’s anointed and God’s purpose, which is why Peter can apply the psalm to a man who sold the Son of God, not to a neighbour who is difficult about the boundary hedge. Third, these prayers are finally in the mouth of Christ himself, the righteous sufferer the psalms were describing all along: he has the right to ask for judgment, and on the cross he asked instead that his killers be forgiven (Luke 23:34).

A caution and a permission. The caution is that no Christian may use these psalms as ammunition for a grudge; the moment a man prays desolation on someone who has merely wounded his pride, he has stopped praying and started cursing. The permission is for the other reader, the one who has been truly and terribly wronged, who wants justice with an intensity that frightens him, and who has concluded that wanting it makes him a bad Christian. It does not. Scripture has given him words for it, and the words are prayers: the fiercest thing in him is to be neither turned on the offender nor politely pushed down, but taken to God.

parallels.desc: may their camp be a desolation
may another take his office

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An apostle had to be an eyewitness of Jesus’ whole ministry and of his resurrection, so the office belonged to one generation only, and its authority lives on in what the apostles wrote.

One of the men who have accompanied us. Peter’s job description is remarkably narrow: the man must have been with them from John’s baptism to the ascension, and must have seen the risen Lord. Nothing about gifting or eloquence. An apostle is defined not by his abilities but by where he had been and what he had seen.

The ones who stayed. Peter assumes there is more than one such man, and two are produced. For three years there had been people following Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through the crowds, the opposition and the night of the arrest, whose names appear in no Gospel. They were there when almost everyone walked away (John 6:66). The qualification for the highest office the church would ever have turned out to be exactly what they had been doing unnoticed the whole time: staying.

A witness to his resurrection. The office in one phrase: not a visionary or the holder of a private revelation, but a man under oath about an event. Paul argues his own apostleship the same way: “Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” (1 Corinthians 9:1). Everything the church has to say begins with a factual claim about a particular Sunday, and the Twelve exist to say they were there.

A foundation is laid once. The office is closed by the very terms Peter has just read out: nobody alive has accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension. The apostles are defined entirely by his life, and their office closed because his work on earth was finished. He died once for sins, was raised never to die again (Romans 6:9), and ascended once to the right hand of God; there is nothing more to see, and so no more need of eyewitnesses. A builder who keeps returning to lay more foundation has stopped building, and this foundation will never need relaying, because the stone at its corner is Christ himself, alive for evermore. Nobody will arrive with a revelation that changes the terms, because nobody will arrive with a further work of Christ to report.

Are there apostles today? In the wider sense of a sent one, a pioneering missionary, the New Testament allows the word (14:14; 2 Corinthians 8:23), and that ministry is badly needed; in the sense of the office Peter is filling here, no. This gives an ordinary Christian a workable test for anyone called an apostle today: not what he calls himself, but what he claims the title entitles him to. If he means he plants churches, no harm is done. If he means that his word carries the weight the apostles’ words carried, that he may add to Scripture, or bind a conscience where Scripture has not, or require obedience that is not accountable to the text, he is claiming something Peter’s own criteria exclude him from, and the humblest believer in the room may say so with a Bible open at this page. When you open the New Testament, you are hearing the apostles; before you take up a confident new teaching, ask whether it agrees with what the eyewitnesses wrote.

So do pastors and elders have any authority today? Yes, but a derived and limited authority, not an apostolic one. Elders are given by Christ to shepherd and oversee his flock (20:28; 1 Peter 5:1–3), and believers are told to obey their leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17). But their authority is the authority of the word they teach. They may not invent doctrine, bind consciences beyond Scripture, or lord it over the flock. Christians differ on the best form of church government, with elders, bishops or congregations holding different roles, and each tradition makes its case from Scripture. All agree that every leader is under the word, accountable for how he handles it, and answerable to the Chief Shepherd.

Where Christians differ: apostolic succession. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican teaching hold that bishops today are successors of the apostles, with their authority passed down. This commentary’s view: by these qualifications, no one after the first generation could be an apostle in this sense. Paul was the exception, as one who saw the risen Lord, as to one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Their authority continues today not in successors but in their writings, the New Testament. When James was killed (12:2), no replacement was chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church puts forward two men who both meet the standard; one will be chosen and one will not, and Scripture tells the story of the man passed over with remarkable honesty.

They put forward two. The church does its part, choosing qualified candidates. Joseph carries three names, Hebrew, family and Latin: the mark of a Jew at home in the wider world of the empire. Both men clear the bar Peter has just set. Of Matthias nothing more is known from Scripture, and later traditions about where he preached are unreliable.

Then one of them is not chosen. Barsabbas was not passed over for a defect or a sin. He was found fit, publicly, and then lost, in front of a hundred and twenty people, and had to walk home through Jerusalem knowing that the man beside him was now one of the Twelve and he was not.

The taste of being passed over. It is not failure, which at least gives you something to work on. It is being good enough, being told so, and watching the place go to someone else: the post you had trained for and he had not; the ministry you would plainly have done well, handed to someone whose only advantage was that God chose him. It is a lonely grief, because there is nobody to blame and so nothing to do with it. And Scripture offers no cheap comfort. It does not say that God had something better in mind for Barsabbas, or that everything worked out. It says he was not chosen, and then it never mentions him again. Sometimes faithfulness has to be carried on without an explanation, and pretending otherwise only adds a lie to a disappointment.

He stayed. There is no schism and no faction of the aggrieved. The natural reading is that he was still among the believers all together in one place when the Spirit fell a few days later (2:1). Whatever it cost him, nothing suggests he walked away. What qualified him was years with Jesus and the risen Lord seen with his own eyes; the lot decided an office, and it could not touch that. Jesus had once told disciples returning elated from a mission not to rejoice that the spirits were subject to them, but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Barsabbas walked home without the apostleship. He did not walk home without Christ.

The one man the world refused to choose. Our Lord knows this taste from the inside. A few weeks earlier, in the same city, a crowd was offered a choice between two men; it asked for Barabbas and shouted that Jesus should be crucified (Luke 23:18–21). He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3). So there is no believer who has watched the honour go elsewhere whom he cannot understand, and none whom he will ever pass over. The one man the world refused to choose is the one who chose us, and his choosing never falls on anyone by accident.

Is it wrong to want a position of service, or to put myself forward? No. Paul says that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1), and both these men allowed their names to go forward. Wanting to serve Christ in a particular way is not pride, provided the desire is held open-handed. Test it: would you be glad to see someone else chosen, and keep serving gladly in the background? Are you willing for the church to say no? Let others weigh your gifts and character, pray, and accept the outcome as from the Lord. The aim is not the title but the glory of Christ, and he can be glorified as much by the one who was not chosen as by the one who was.

parallels.desc: Judas called Barsabbas

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church prays to the Lord who reads every heart, most likely the risen Jesus himself, asking him to show which man he has already chosen to fill the place Judas abandoned.

They prayed. The prayer is short, with no preamble: they tell God what they cannot do, ask him to do it, and stop.

Who know the hearts of all. Heart-knower (kardiognōstēs) appears only here and at 15:8, and both times the church is trying to decide who truly belongs: here two candidates identical from the outside, there a house full of Gentiles nobody expected God to accept. Both times the church has run out of evidence it can see, and turns to the one who reads what no one else can. Knowing the heart belongs to God: “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

Praying to Jesus. They say Lord, and the most natural reading takes that to be the one who chose the original apostles (v. 2): Jesus, who knew what was in man (John 2:24–25). Some take the Lord here to be the Father, and the prayer would still be remarkable; but Luke has just reminded us that Jesus did the first choosing, and later in this book a dying believer calls on him by name, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (7:59). So within weeks of the ascension, before any council, creed or doctrinal controversy, a room full of Jewish monotheists is praying to a man they had eaten breakfast with, addressing him by a title that in their Scriptures belongs to God, and attributing to him the knowledge of every human heart. Nobody argues for it; they simply do it. Even if this prayer is to the Father, Stephen’s cry shows that the deity of Christ was not voted in at a later council; it was already the posture of the church.

Show which one you have chosen. Not help us choose, but show us whom you have already chosen. And they did the work first: they set out the qualifications from Scripture, applied them honestly, narrowed the field to two men who truly met them, and only then said, show us. Guidance in the Bible often comes after the homework has been done.

His own place. The word for the place he leaves (topos) is used again of where he goes: the darkest clause in the chapter, which the church neither enlarges on nor softens. It says only that he arrived somewhere that fitted him, a destination matched to a direction he had been travelling for years. Where Scripture draws a line and stops, it is safest to stop there too, and it is telling that the men who had most cause to be bitter about Judas said less about his end than almost any preacher since.

A searching mercy. He is not taken in by anyone’s best behaviour. Your church’s estimate of you is assembled from what you have let it see; his is not. That cuts first the way most people fear: he has read the thing you would resign over if it were known. It also cuts the other way, the side worth resting on. He has read the part of you that nobody has ever believed: the repentance that was real even though nothing changed for months, the love for him that survives in someone whose life makes it look implausible, the reason you did the thing everyone misread. There is one person in the universe who has never once misunderstood you, and he went to a cross knowing all of it in advance. So pray to him honestly: you cannot impress him, and you need not perform.

Does his own place mean Judas is lost? That is the most natural reading, and the rest of Scripture supports it. Jesus said of his betrayer, “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Mark 14:21), and called him “the son of destruction” (John 17:12). Those words could not be said of anyone who would finally be saved. Scripture teaches that those who die without Christ face conscious, eternal punishment, and Judas, who stood closest to the light and turned from it, is its most solemn example. But mark the church’s restraint, and copy it. We are not told to speculate about the eternal state of people we have known; we are told to warn the living and to flee to Christ ourselves.

parallels.desc: God, who knows the heart

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord himself chose Matthias through the lot, and the Twelve stand complete for Pentecost, just as Jesus had promised.

They cast lots. Luke does not say how; perhaps two marked stones were shaken until one fell out. A modern reader is right to find it startling, but it was not superstition. Casting lots was a means God had himself appointed in Israel: it divided the land, chose the goat for the Day of Atonement and arranged the priests’ duties (Joshua 18:6; Leviticus 16:8; Luke 1:9). The proverb that governs the practice says exactly what the eleven were counting on: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

The lot fell on Matthias. Then the lot disappears from the New Testament, because within days the Spirit came. The Lord who governed the falling of a stone in an upper room governs every detail of his church’s life, and rules your life with the same care.

The King keeps his number. Behind the lot stands a promise of Jesus. At the last supper he told the Twelve that they would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30), and that same night one of them led the arresting party to him. Judas’s treachery tore a hole in that promise, and the risen Lord fills it. The number Jesus set at the beginning stands whole on the morning of Pentecost. He keeps his promises down to the arithmetic.

Did they get it wrong? A good many teachers have said the eleven acted in their own wisdom, using lots before the Spirit had come and jumping ahead of God, and that the real twelfth apostle was Paul, whom the Lord would choose himself a few chapters later. The case is usually pressed by noting that Matthias is never mentioned again.

The evidence does not support it. Luke records the episode without a breath of disapproval, and he does not hide the church’s failures: he tells of Ananias lying to the Spirit, of the Greek-speaking widows neglected, of Paul and Barnabas quarrelling so sharply that they parted company. Here there is no such note. When the Spirit falls in the next chapter Peter stands up with the eleven (2:14), which makes twelve, and Luke gives no hint that the number is wrong. Nor were they improvising: Peter was following the text he had quoted, “Let another take his office” (v. 20; Psalm 109:8). They prayed before they drew, and they used the means God himself had appointed for exactly this purpose (Proverbs 16:33).

Why not Paul. The later silence about Matthias proves nothing, because Acts is silent about nearly all of them. Ten of the Twelve are never heard from again in this book as actors in the story; only Peter and John, with a brief mention of James’s death, get a narrative. By that test nearly all the Twelve were a mistake. And Paul cannot have been the man in view, because he fails the stated qualification in the plainest way: he had not accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension. He is not the twelfth apostle to Israel; he is the apostle to the Gentiles, which is a different thing and no smaller. The Twelve had to be twelve because they answer to the twelve tribes, and the gap had to be closed before Pentecost.

So how does God guide you today, if not by lots? Not by dice, omens, opening the Bible at random or putting out a fleece, but by the settled means he has since given in fuller measure: his completed word, “a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105), the indwelling Spirit, prayer, sanctified wisdom, and the counsel of godly friends. The lot belonged to the brief gap before Pentecost and before the New Testament was written; we stand on the far side of both, and are the richer for it.

How do I make a big decision, then, practically? First, settle what Scripture commands or forbids; God will never lead you against his word. Second, if more than one path is right, pray, and ask God for wisdom, which he promises to give generously (James 1:5). Third, gather the facts honestly and think, because a renewed mind is meant to be used (Romans 12:2). Fourth, ask mature Christians who know you, and listen especially if they all say the same thing. Fifth, weigh your gifts, your responsibilities to family and church, and the opportunities actually in front of you. Then decide, and do not torment yourself afterwards about whether you missed a hidden signal. Within the bounds of his word, God is glad for his children to choose, and he rules over the outcome either way.

Where Christians differ: should we cast lots today? Some say the apostles were wrong to do this, and should have waited for Paul. Others use lots or similar methods for guidance today. This commentary’s view: Luke records no disapproval, and the choice was valid. But after Pentecost the church never cast lots again. With the Spirit given and the Scriptures complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel and the judgment of the church (15:28; Romans 12:2). We don’t need dice.
verseByVerse.note: Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after the Spirit is given.

parallels.desc: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is easily overlooked, yet it is not simply that Jesus left; he was enthroned. Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand (Psalm 110:1; see vv. 9–10), over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). His kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church, and every soul converted is the work of the reigning Christ.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples, staring at the sky and confused about timing and the kingdom, learned that faithfulness between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness.

Now: We live in the same interval, between the first coming and the second (on its temptations, see vv. 6–7 and 11). He is coming; in the meantime, there is work.

keyVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
keyVerse.note: This is the risen Lord’s answer to every question about timing, and the table of contents of the whole book: Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the end of the earth. It puts the gift before the task, for the power is received, not produced, and it defines the church’s work as witness to Christ. Everything in Acts, and in the church’s life since, is this sentence being kept.

1.reflection:
Jesus told the apostles to wait for the Spirit before they began (vv. 4–5), and they spent the waiting in prayer (v. 14). Where are you tempted to run ahead of God in your own strength, and what would depending on him first look like this week?

The disciples asked about dates, and Jesus answered with a mission (vv. 6–8). Why do you think he redirected them? Who is your “Samaria”, the person or kind of person you would rather the gospel skipped?

The angels promised that “this Jesus” will come in the same way as he went (v. 11). How does knowing that a real man reigns now in our nature, and will return in person, change the way you pray, grieve and work?

Judas was numbered among the Twelve yet never belonged to Christ, while Barsabbas met every qualification and was not chosen (vv. 17, 23). What do these two men teach about the difference between position and belonging, and how can we care for someone in our church who has been passed over?

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. <sup>2</sup>And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. <sup>3</sup>And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. <sup>4</sup>And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. <sup>5</sup>Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. <sup>6</sup>And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. <sup>7</sup>And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? <sup>8</sup>And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? <sup>9</sup>Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, <sup>10</sup>Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, <sup>11</sup>both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.” <sup>12</sup>And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” <sup>13</sup>But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. <sup>15</sup>For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. <sup>16</sup>But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: <sup>17</sup>‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; <sup>18</sup>even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy. <sup>19</sup>And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; <sup>20</sup>the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day. <sup>21</sup>And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’ <sup>22</sup>“Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know— <sup>23</sup>this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; <sup>26</sup>therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. <sup>27</sup>For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. <sup>28</sup>You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ <sup>29</sup>“Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. <sup>30</sup>Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, <sup>31</sup>he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. <sup>32</sup>This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. <sup>33</sup>Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. <sup>34</sup>For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>35</sup>until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>36</sup>Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” <sup>37</sup>Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” <sup>38</sup>And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. <sup>39</sup>For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” <sup>40</sup>And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” <sup>41</sup>So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. <sup>42</sup>And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. <sup>43</sup>And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. <sup>44</sup>And all who believed were together and had all things in common. <sup>45</sup>And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. <sup>46</sup>And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 left the hundred and twenty praying in Jerusalem, the Twelve made whole again, waiting as ordered for the Spirit (1:4–8, 14–26). Fifty days after Passover, on the harvest feast of Pentecost, the waiting ends.

The message. The crucified Jesus is alive and reigning at God’s right hand, and he has proved it by pouring out the Spirit God promised for the last days. So the last days have begun: the Spirit is for all God’s people, whatever their age, sex or rank, and forgiveness is offered to everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, even in the city that killed him.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus, and every reader after him, may be certain of what he has been taught (see the introduction). This chapter shows where the church came from: not from human enthusiasm, but from the risen Christ giving his Spirit, as the Scriptures and Jesus himself had said.

How the chapter makes its case. The Spirit comes with wind and fire, and pilgrims from across the Jewish world hear God’s mighty works in their own languages; some ask what it means, others mock (vv. 1–13). Peter answers from Scripture: this is Joel’s promise of the last days (vv. 14–21). Then he proclaims Jesus, handed over by God’s plan and killed by lawless hands (vv. 22–23), raised because death could not hold him, as David foresaw (vv. 24–32), and exalted to pour out the Spirit, so that God has made him both Lord and Christ (vv. 33–36). Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do; Peter calls them to repent and be baptised, and about three thousand receive the word (vv. 37–41). The new community devotes itself to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, and the Lord adds to it daily (vv. 42–47).

Where it leads. The whole chapter is about Christ. The harvest feast counted from Passover week brings in the first harvest of his death and rising; the fire he longed to cast on the earth (Luke 12:49) falls from his throne; the Spirit who rested on him at the Jordan flows from him to all his people. Peter’s sermon has one subject, “this Jesus”, and its climax gives the name of the LORD to the man the city crucified, who then offers his murderers forgiveness.

For us. The Spirit is not a reward for advanced Christians; he is the risen Lord’s gift to everyone who repents and believes, whatever their past. No sin, not even the murder of the Son of God, lies beyond the forgiveness offered here. The life the Spirit produces is not chiefly spectacular but steady: teaching, fellowship, the Lord’s table and prayer, with glad and generous hearts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the harvest feast of Pentecost the risen Christ sends the promised Spirit, and the church begins with the nations listening. The Spirit comes with a sound from heaven like a mighty wind and with tongues as of fire resting on each believer, and all are filled and speak in other languages (vv. 1–4). Devout Jews from every part of the scattered people hear Galileans declaring the mighty works of God in their own native tongues: Babel reversed, and a first gathering of the nations (vv. 5–11). The crowd divides, some asking what it means and others mocking (vv. 12–13), and the question opens the way for Peter’s sermon.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a few officeholders but on all his people (Joel 2; Ezekiel 36–37; Jeremiah 31), as Moses had once wished aloud (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day. The Spirit’s coming is not a reward for people who prayed hard enough but a once-for-all act in the history of salvation (see vv. 1–2); what is repeated afterwards is the filling (see vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first names on Luke’s list are the lands Israel and Judah were exiled to (see vv. 9–10). Now: The same thing happens whenever the Bible is put into a language that has never had it (see the note on vv. 5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the very day God had set, the risen Christ sends the Spirit he promised, and the place where his waiting people sat is filled with the sound of heaven’s breath.

When the day of Pentecost arrived. Pentecost means fiftieth: it was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). Observant Jews everywhere had counted off seven full weeks, and God, who had kept that calendar for fifteen centuries, kept his promise on the very morning he had set.

All together. Probably the hundred and twenty (1:15), in the upper room or perhaps in the temple courts, where a crowd could gather quickly. Luke does not say; the point is not the building but the company: all of them, together, where obedience had put them.

A sound like wind. Not a wind, but a sound like one. In both Hebrew (ruach) and Greek (pneuma) the same word can mean wind, breath and spirit, and Jesus had compared the Spirit to the wind that blows where it wishes (John 3:8). The word Luke chooses here, pnoē, is the one the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7 for the breath God breathed into a figure of dust until it became a living man. Ezekiel saw the breath enter a valley of bones until they stood up, “an exceedingly great army” (Ezekiel 37:9–14). The same breath is in this room, and what is about to stand up is the church.

The entire house. It filled the house, and then, in the next verse, the people. The glory cloud had once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11); now God’s presence fills his new temple, which is his people.

The feast of firstfruits. At Passover a farmer waved the first sheaf of barley before the LORD. Fifty days later, at Weeks, he brought two loaves baked from the new wheat, unusually among Israel’s offerings baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17). The whole feast was firstfruits: a handful brought in early as the guarantee that the fields were coming. By evening three thousand will be brought in, firstfruits of a harvest still coming. Later Jewish tradition also linked the feast with the giving of the law at Sinai; if that link was already known, the fit is exact: on the day Israel remembered the law written on stone, the Spirit came to write it on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3).

In the flow. The book has been heading here since its first paragraph: the disciples were to stay in the city until they were “clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49), and the Spirit would make them witnesses to the end of the earth (1:4–8). All that follows in Acts is his work.

Counted from an empty tomb. The fifty days ran from the waving of that first sheaf in Passover week (Leviticus 23:10–16), and that year Passover week was the week of the cross and the empty tomb. Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the harvest feast fifty days later is the day his harvest begins to come in. The Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified (John 7:39), and Peter will say that the exalted Jesus has poured him out (2:33). Pentecost is counted from Easter, because it is the risen Lord’s gift.

The breath comes from his throne. The first Adam received the breath of God into his dust, and lost the life it gave him. The last Adam went down into death for those who had lost it, and rose to become a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). On this morning the breath comes from his throne, and a room of frightened disciples stands up alive.

Received, not produced. When it happened, they were sitting. They had been told to wait (1:4), and they had done that and nothing else: no campaign, no technique, no working up of atmosphere. If you have been told the Spirit’s work can be triggered by enough intensity, have tried, and concluded the failure must be yours, take heart: it cannot be triggered, only received, in the place obedience has put you.

Should my church pray for another Pentecost? Not for a repeat of this day. Pentecost was the once-for-all arrival of the Spirit to dwell in the church; like Calvary, it needs no repeating. The Spirit came and has never left. But pray, expectantly, for what Acts goes on to show: that the Spirit already given would fill his people afresh, make them bold and bring many to Christ (4:29–31), as he has done in many seasons of revival through the ordinary preaching of the gospel. Just do not imagine the Spirit is absent until something dramatic happens.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest. Wind and breath picture the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Weeks

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy fire of God comes to rest on every believer without consuming them, and the Spirit’s first work is to fill their mouths with God’s praise in languages they had never learned.

Tongues as of fire. Fire in Scripture is where God is and where God may not be touched: the bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), the mountain wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the fire that fell on Carmel, the coal from the altar at Isaiah’s mouth. Nearly every one is kept at a distance. Here it settles on people’s heads, and nobody dies. John the Baptist had promised that the coming one would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). And it is shaped like tongues, because it is given for speaking.

Divided … on each one. Fire can be shared without being lessened: light a hundred candles from one flame and the first is no smaller. The Spirit is not rationed, a larger share for apostles and a thinner one for everyone else. And it rests on “each one of them”. In the old covenant the Spirit came on particular leaders and craftsmen for particular tasks; now the flame settles on a fisherman, on Mary, on brothers who had once thought Jesus out of his mind, on many whose names Luke does not record. Moses had wished aloud that it were so: “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). Every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38).

Filled with the Holy Spirit. Filled means controlled and empowered, and Luke uses the word again and again for being empowered to speak (4:8, 31; 13:9). It is not a quantity poured into a container but a Person taking hold of a person for the work in front of him, which is why Peter, filled here, is filled afresh before the council (4:8).

Other tongues. Tongues (glōssai) is the word just used for the tongues of fire: the sign was shaped like the gift. In this chapter the gift is unambiguous: other tongues (heterais glōssais) are real human languages, which the crowd identifies three times (vv. 6, 8, 11). Here is the reversal of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9). There God confused the languages and scattered people in judgment; here he gives languages to gather the nations in grace.

The fire he longed to cast. Luke has already recorded Jesus speaking of this fire, and of what it would cost him: “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:49–50). The baptism he meant was his death. Seven weeks after the cross the fire falls, and it falls from him (2:33). The holy fire came down and rested gently on sinners, and did not consume them, because the one who was consumed for them had already risen.

What the fire was for. Not the experience for its own sake. The Spirit’s first act in the church is to make ordinary people talk about God to strangers, in words the strangers understand. The Spirit who filled the mouths of fishermen is in every believer: ask him to fill yours with the gospel.

A test Scripture will not carry. This verse is regularly held over believers as the test of whether the Spirit is truly in them. But Paul asks a church that prized the gift above everything, in a run of questions expecting the answer no: “Do all speak with tongues?” (1 Corinthians 12:30). A Christian who has never spoken a syllable of another language lacks nothing of the Spirit. And the same chapter forbids contempt in either direction: no member may say to another, “I have no need of you.” Beneath the demand for a sign is often the wish for something we can feel, so that we need not simply trust what God has said. But the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children comes as we cry, “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15–16), and its ground is Christ’s finished work, not the intensity of any experience.

Is this the gift Paul discusses at Corinth? The two are not obviously identical. What happens here is understood instantly by native speakers; what happens at Corinth needs an interpreter and is unintelligible without one (1 Corinthians 14:2). Some conclude they are two gifts sharing a name. More probably they are one gift in two settings: a real language is clear to its native speakers and noise to everyone else, and Corinth, it seems, had no native speakers present. The text does not settle it, and a reader may leave it unsettled.

Is this the baptism in the Spirit that Pentecostal Christians teach? Pentecostal teaching describes a second experience after conversion, marked by tongues. But Pentecost was the once-for-all outpouring of the Spirit on the church, promised by Jesus (1:5). From now on every believer receives the Spirit when he believes: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Those added later this same day received the gift of the Spirit on repentance and faith (v. 38), and Luke records no tongues among the three thousand. Pentecostal believers’ longing for more of the Spirit is right; the difference is over how Scripture describes his coming, not over whether we need him.

What do I say to a Christian friend who speaks in tongues? Remember that he is your brother, and what you share, Christ crucified and risen, the authority of Scripture, salvation by grace, is far greater than this difference. Tell him honestly why you believe the sign gifts served the founding of the church and have ceased, and point him to what Acts 2 shows: known languages, declaring God’s mighty works, understood by hearers. But do not mock him or question his faith. Ask what the experience means to him, and listen. Agree together that every gift must build up others and point to Christ (1 Corinthians 14:12), and that love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13). Then pray together.

Where Christians differ: tongues today. Pentecostals and charismatics teach that tongues continue today, often as a prayer language, and some that it is the sign of Spirit baptism. This commentary’s view: the tongues of Pentecost were known languages, a sign that the gospel was for every nation. Tongues and other sign gifts served to confirm the apostolic message in the founding era (Hebrews 2:3–4; 1 Corinthians 14:22), and the church’s historic testimony is that they ceased. This is the cessationist position (that these sign gifts ceased with the apostles), held charitably: we gladly acknowledge that many charismatic believers love Christ deeply. Continuationists answer that no text ends the gifts before Christ returns, reading 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 that way; this is a difference among faithful believers about the Spirit’s gifts, never about his gospel. The Spirit himself, and his saving and sanctifying work, continue in full.
verseByVerse.note: Fire often signals God’s presence.

parallels.desc: the LORD descended on it in fire

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God draws devout Jews from every nation into one street and lets each of them hear his own native language: Babel is reversed, and God shows himself as the one who comes to people and speaks as they speak.

Dwelling in Jerusalem. Luke’s word means residents, not visitors; he has a separate word for visitors and uses it five verses later of the Romans. These are Jews born in Parthia or Egypt or Cappadocia who had come back to settle, some probably to die in the land; the Dispersion may have numbered several million across the Roman and Parthian empires.

Devout men. Devout (eulabeis) is Luke’s word for a certain kind of serious Israelite: God-fearing, careful, pious. He uses it of old Simeon waiting in the temple for “the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25), and later of the men brave enough to bury Stephen (8:2). Not sightseers, but people who had been waiting.

Bewildered. This is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses at Babel, where “the LORD confused the language of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9). At Babel men were thrown into confusion because they suddenly could not understand one another. Here they are thrown into confusion because they suddenly can.

His own language. What staggers them is that each man hears his own dialektos, his native speech. The miracle was in the mouths, not the ears (v. 4): God gave a hundred and twenty Galileans the speech of fifteen nations.

God crosses the room. He could have required every nation to learn Hebrew, the language of the covenant. He did the opposite. The first sermon of the Christian era was given in the languages people count money in, swear in when they drop something, and sing over their children at night. He had already done it once, at far greater cost: the eternal Word took flesh, learned to talk at his mother’s knee, and spoke the Aramaic of Galilean villages. At Pentecost he does the same in every tongue. From the first morning of the church, God has been the one who crosses the room.

Why does God care which language people hear him in? Because he wants to be understood, not merely obeyed, and a message in your mother tongue reaches the heart. God means to gather worshippers from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9), and he does not ask them to become culturally Jewish, or English, or anything else first. That is why the church translates the Scriptures rather than requiring a sacred language, and why missionaries spend decades learning languages with a few thousand speakers. Every translation is a small Pentecost.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came as pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd cannot get past the fact that the speakers are provincial Galileans, yet each hears them in his own mother tongue: God has chosen the despised accent to carry his word.

Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? The crowd’s objection is an accent. The northern pronunciation was easy to mock; later rabbinic stories laugh at Galileans for swallowing their gutturals so badly that a hearer could not tell which word was meant. It was the accent of the provinces: fishing villages, small farms, no great rabbinic schools within a day’s walk.

Each of us in his own native language. Literally, the language in which we were born. Most of these men could trade in Greek or Aramaic, but they hear the gospel in their mother tongue, the language of the heart (see the note on vv. 5–6).

Amazed and astonished. The first verb is the one Luke uses of Jairus and his wife when their dead daughter sat up (Luke 8:56). Several thousand sober, widely travelled men have no category left for the thing: the right condition in which to hear a sermon.

The accent that once betrayed him. Some fifty days earlier, in a high priest’s courtyard, a bystander told Peter that his accent betrayed him (Matthew 26:73), and Peter swore that he did not know Jesus. God did not give Peter a new voice; he gave him a new message, and sent the voice that had denied his Lord back into the same city to proclaim the resurrection.

The first Galilean. The accent was not only Peter’s. Jesus grew up in Nazareth, and the Pharisees were sure that “no prophet arises from Galilee” (John 7:52). Yet Isaiah had said that the LORD would make glorious Galilee of the nations, and that the people who walked in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2). The scorn the crowd aimed at the disciples had first been aimed at him. He is not ashamed of Galilean accents, of stammering tongues, of the people the world dismisses.

The disqualifications we hold against ourselves. The disqualifications believers privately hold against themselves are often of just this kind: not enough education, the wrong background, a stammer, a criminal record, a voice that goes thin exactly when it matters. The council will make the same complaint a few weeks later, that these are “uneducated, common men”, and stumble on the answer without meaning to: they recognised that they had been with Jesus (4:13).

Should I support Bible translation, if most people speak a trade language? Yes. People can do business in a second language and still hear God as a foreigner, and hundreds of millions still have no complete Bible in the language they think and pray in. Supporting translation, by prayer, giving or going, is joining the work God began on this morning. And at home it means explaining the gospel in everyday speech, not church jargon, to people who do not share your background.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke’s roll-call of nations maps the whole scattered Jewish world, from Parthia to Rome, and on this morning God begins to gather what exile had scattered.

Parthians and Medes. The list runs roughly east to west. It opens outside the empire, in Parthia beyond the Euphrates, the one great power Rome never conquered. Then Media, Elam and Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers that had been Babylon: the places Israel was exiled to. Assyria settled the northern tribes “in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes” (2 Kings 17:6), and Babylon later took Judah. On this morning God begins to gather a scattering that history never repaired.

Judea. Strange in a roll-call of foreign parts: most likely Judea lies on the arc Luke is tracing, or he means that even the locals heard their own speech.

Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia. The list sweeps north and west through Asia Minor, very nearly the route Paul will spend the second half of this book walking. Years later Peter writes to the exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1); some of them may first have heard the gospel in this street.

Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene. Then south to Egypt, whose Jewish community at Alexandria was large enough to have produced its own Greek translation of the Scriptures, and along the North African coast to Cyrene, whose Jews turn up again in this book both as opponents (6:9) and as the men who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (11:20). One of them had carried a cross up a hill outside this city only weeks earlier: Simon of Cyrene (Luke 23:26).

And visitors from Rome. The list ends at Rome, where Luke’s second volume ends (28:16). These visitors may well have been among the beginnings of the church in Rome, to which Paul later wrote.

A promise kept in the wrong order. The witness was to go from Jerusalem to the end of the earth (1:8). On the first morning the end of the earth has come to Jerusalem, and before a missionary has packed a bag, the gospel is heard by men who will carry it home.

Gathered to the root of Jesse. Behind those names of exile stands a promise about the Messiah. Isaiah said that the root of Jesse would stand as a signal for the peoples, and that the Lord would recover the remnant of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Elam and from Shinar, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:10–12). John tells us why Jesus died: “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52). This morning the scattered stand in one street, gathered to a crucified and risen son of David, who is himself the signal raised for the nations.

Why does a list of places matter to me? It is a map of God’s faithfulness and a preview of his plan: from every place where his people had been scattered, some are gathered to hear of Christ. If you are a Gentile believer, your own people are on the long extension of this list. And the gospel is owned by no one culture. It belonged to Parthians and Libyans before it belonged to Europeans, and it belongs today to the churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America as much as to anyone.

In everyday life. Pray for the nations by name. Choose one of the places in this list, find out what the church there is facing now, and pray for it. Many of these lands, once full of churches, now have very few believers; the God who gathered them once can do it again.
verseByVerse.note: The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome): the whole Jewish world scattered among the nations.

parallels.desc: the table of nations
Babel, where languages were confused

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews, converts and the far margins of the map all hear the same message, and it is not advice or religious feeling but the mighty works of God.

Both Jews and proselytes. Two words that widen the list past nationality. Proselytes were Gentiles who had gone the whole distance into Judaism: renouncing their family gods, circumcised as adults, probably immersed, bringing an offering. Even then, in many eyes, they were second-class members of the covenant people. Such men hear the wonders of God here, and within twenty years the church will meet in this same city to decide whether Gentiles need any of that at all (15:1–11). The door they crawled through is about to be taken off its hinges.

Cretans and Arabians. Island and desert, west and east, the far margins added as if to say the list could go on. Paul would later leave Titus in Crete (Titus 1:5) and spend time himself in Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

The mighty works of God. Ta megaleia, the great things God has done: the Old Testament speaks this way of what he did in bringing Israel out of Egypt: his mighty hand, the signs, the sea (Deuteronomy 11:2–4). The first Christian speech was not moral instruction or religious feeling but a recital of God’s acts, in the language of the exodus, now used of an empty tomb. God introduces himself to the nations by reciting his acts of rescue, in fifteen languages at once, to men who had crossed an empire to worship him at a distance and had no idea he had come out into the street to meet them.

The exodus he accomplished at Jerusalem. Luke has prepared us for this. On the mountain of transfiguration, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31), and the word for departure is exodos. Moses led Israel out through the sea; Jesus led his people out through death itself, out of the bondage of sin and the grip of the grave, and came up on the other side alive.

News before advice. Christianity is first news and only afterwards advice; if nothing had happened in Jerusalem that spring, all that would be left is a philosophy of life. A believer’s own story matters, but on the first morning the street was filled not with what had happened to a hundred and twenty people, but with what God had done.

What are the mighty works of God I should be telling? God created the world and made us for himself. We turned away and came under his judgment. God sent his Son, who lived the life we should have lived, died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing their punishment, and rose bodily from the dead. He has ascended and reigns, and he has poured out his Spirit. He will come again to judge the living and the dead. Everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven and made new. Your own story fits inside that one: tell what God has done for you, but make sure the cross and the empty tomb are in it.
verseByVerse.note: Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

parallels.desc: Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with what God has done, the crowd divides: some admit they have no explanation and ask what it means, while others reach for a sneer. Every crowd that has ever heard the gospel is inside these two sentences.

What does this mean? A real question, and the right one: these men admit they have no explanation, and so hold a door open. Peter answers it in the next verse, and the rest of the book is an answer to it.

Filled with new wine. A poor explanation. The word is gleukos, sweet new wine, an odd charge in late spring with the grape harvest months away, even if some sweet wine had been kept from the year before. And nine in the morning on a feast day is no hour for drinking, as Peter points out in his first breath. Perhaps those who heard only languages they did not know took it for babble (compare 1 Corinthians 14:23). But the mockers were not weighing evidence; they grabbed the nearest insult.

What the sneer concedes. Drunkenness was the closest thing they could find to what they were watching: people who seemed no longer in control of themselves. Paul turns the comparison into a contrast: “do not get drunk with wine … but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).

Called a drunkard before them. The sneer had been used on their Master. Jesus said what his generation made of him: “The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard’” (Luke 7:34). The world dismisses his Spirit-filled people with the same joke, as he told them to expect: “A servant is not greater than his master” (John 15:20). There is an honour hidden in it: the life in the church is unmistakably his.

The mercy that prayed on the cross. On the cross, with the mocking going on around him, Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). That prayer did not end at Golgotha. Seven weeks later his Spirit is poured out, the world calls it drunkenness, and the answer from heaven is not fire but a sermon, an offer of pardon to everyone standing there, scoffers included. Peter preaches to both halves of the crowd without distinguishing between them, and by evening three thousand have been baptised; some of the men shouting about new wine at nine in the morning may well have been in the water before dark. The gospel has a long history of being sneered at by people who go on to preach it.

What should I do when someone mocks my faith? Do not answer mockery with mockery, or take it as the last word. Peter corrected the misunderstanding in a sentence and then told them about Jesus. A light, honest reply, a question back, or a simple statement of what you believe and why often does more than a long argument. Be gentle and respectful (1 Peter 3:15–16). The mocker may be closer to faith than he looks, so keep praying for him by name. And if the mockery hurts, remember that your Lord was mocked first, and bore it for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The meaning of Pentecost is Jesus: the Spirit poured out is the proof that the man the city crucified is now Lord and Christ. Peter first answers the mockers from Scripture: this is what Joel promised for the last days, the Spirit on all kinds of people and salvation for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord (vv. 14–21). Then he proclaims Jesus, attested by God, handed over by God’s plan and killed by lawless hands (vv. 22–23); raised because death could not hold him, as David foresaw in Psalm 16 and the apostles witnessed (vv. 24–32); and exalted to God’s right hand, from where he has poured out the Spirit, as Psalm 110 foretold (vv. 33–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's use of Psalm 16 is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption; David died and was buried, and his tomb was a short walk away. So the words say more than David's own life could bear, and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. Psalm 110 is read the same way: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which he hears the LORD speak to my Lord is about someone greater. The risen Christ had taught them to read like this (Luke 24:27, 44). It is not squeezing Christ out of texts but recognising that the Spirit who wrote the Scriptures knew where the story was going and left its shape in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated, this Jesus whom you crucified, and said it to their faces seven weeks after they had done it. He did not soften the charge to get a hearing, and three thousand were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer has nothing to forgive him for. This crowd asked what shall we do because Peter had left them with something that needed doing; preaching about sin in general, committed by people in general, will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, standing for all twelve apostles, brushes aside the charge of drunkenness and begins to explain the morning: the man who denied Jesus is now the first preacher of his resurrection.

Standing with the eleven. Eleven beside him makes twelve, the number restored at the end of chapter 1 (1:26): the apostolic band stands complete on its first working day. What follows is the witness of them all, not one man’s opinion.

Lifted up his voice and addressed them. Lifting up the voice is Old Testament language for a solemn public declaration (Judges 9:7). And addressed (apephthenxato) is the same word as utterance in verse 4: Peter speaks out boldly, moved by the Spirit.

Men of Judea. The settled residents of verse 5, the Dispersion come home, alongside the people of the city: people who had spent their lives waiting, now told that the waiting is over.

Only the third hour. The defence is brief. The third hour was about nine in the morning, and, as later Jewish sources describe the custom, devout Jews ate and drank nothing on a feast day until the morning prayer was over. He disposes of the charge in a sentence; it is only the door the mockers held open for him.

In the flow. The first Christian sermon moves in three steps: Scripture explains what the crowd has seen (vv. 16–21); Jesus, crucified, risen and exalted, explains Scripture (vv. 22–36); and then comes the call to repent and be baptised (vv. 38–40). Nearly every later sermon in Acts comes to the same point: the risen Jesus and what a hearer must do about him.

He makes weak men strong. This is the voice that, not two months before, in this city, said “I do not know the man” (see the note on vv. 7–8). Between those two mornings Peter attended no course; what came between was the risen Christ, and then Pentecost. On the night of the denials the Lord turned and looked at Peter across the courtyard (Luke 22:61). That look did not end the friendship; it began the restoration. He did not replace the apostle who denied him. He kept him, filled him, and made him the first preacher of the resurrection. Our Lord does not need strong men. He makes weak men strong, and the glory is his.

Not more determination. The usual advice to a frightened Christian is to try harder. Peter had plenty of determination, and at the point of testing it was worth nothing. What he lacked was the Spirit, and when the Spirit came, courage came with him: not a technique to be mastered but a Person to be received.

I am timid by nature: can the Spirit really make me bold? Yes, though boldness may not look like Peter shouting to thousands. In Acts it usually means speaking plainly about Jesus when it would be easier to stay silent, and the Spirit gives it to quiet people as well as loud ones. Ask for it directly; the church prayed exactly this, “grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness” (4:29), and God answered. Then take one small step, a sentence, an invitation, an honest answer, and expect his help in the step rather than before it. Peter’s past did not disqualify him, and yours does not disqualify you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m., far too early for drunkenness.

parallels.desc: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter explains the morning by opening the Scriptures: what the crowd is seeing is not new but promised, the coming true of Joel’s word.

This is what was uttered. Peter’s first move is to say that it was on the schedule: nothing new has happened; something promised has. That is the first principle of all true spiritual experience: the Spirit’s work is always in line with Scripture, because he is its author.

Through the prophet Joel. An unexpected text for a morning of glory: Joel is about locusts, a real swarm that stripped a real country, wave after wave, until the grain offering was cut off from the house of the LORD and the cattle groaned for want of pasture. Out of that ruin God makes the promise everybody knows: “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (Joel 2:25). Immediately after it comes the promise of the Spirit.

A fisherman reading the prophets. A fisherman tells scholars what their own Scriptures are about, and he is not guessing. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, the risen Jesus had interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). So “this is what was uttered” is finally a sentence about Christ: Joel’s promise has come true because the one it waited for has died, risen and been exalted, and has poured out the Spirit (2:33).

The years the locust has eaten. The outpouring is the sequel to a promise made to people who had lost everything, the sign that God means to put the years back. Anyone who has lost years, to an illness, a marriage that came apart, a decade of his own folly, is reading a promise addressed to exactly that condition. The Spirit is not given first to the flourishing. He is promised to a field eaten bare, as the down payment on a harvest that is coming back.

How do I test a spiritual experience by Scripture? Ask whether it matches what God has said. Does it exalt Jesus Christ as Scripture presents him, crucified, risen and Lord (1 John 4:2–3; John 16:14)? Does it agree with the plain teaching of the Bible, or add to it or contradict it? Does it lead to holiness, love and humility, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), or to pride and division? An experience can be intense and still mistaken. And if something is not taught in Scripture, you are not bound to seek it, however many people around you claim it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Pentecost the last days have begun: the Spirit once given to a few leaders is now poured out on all God’s people, without regard to age, sex or rank, so that all of them know God and speak his word.

In the last days. Joel 2:28 has “afterward”; Peter, by the Spirit, interprets it as “the last days”, and declares them arrived. They are not only a short window before the end but the whole gospel age, from Christ’s first coming to his return. In these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:2); “it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). Scripture does speak of the days growing harder as the end nears (2 Timothy 3:1), but the era as a whole is already under way. The effect is urgency, not date-setting: we live in the final act, awaiting the King’s return.

God declares. Peter makes two more such changes. He inserts “God declares”, so that the promise carries God’s own signature. And where Joel’s line about the male and female servants ends, he adds “and they shall prophesy”: an apostle saying what the text turned out to mean, and refusing to let the slaves be dropped from the promise on the way past.

On all flesh. Not every individual without exception, but all kinds of people without distinction: sons and daughters, young men and old men, and then male servants and female servants, a word that means slaves. The lowest person in the household, with no property and no standing, is written into a promise about the Spirit of God. No social barrier keeps anyone from the Spirit (Galatians 3:28), and before long the promise will reach the Gentiles too (10:45).

Prophesy … visions … dreams. Prophecy, rare in the Old Testament, here means speaking God’s word, declaring his mighty works (v. 11), and the gift is now spread among all his people. The visions and dreams are Hebrew poetry saying the same thing in other words: all will know God, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34). Under the old covenant Israel gathered round one Spirit-filled man to hear what God had said; under the new, God has moved into the whole house: the daughters, the old men who thought their useful years were over, the slave girl in the kitchen.

Your daughters. Luke shows us four of them: the unmarried daughters of Philip the evangelist, prophesying at Caesarea (21:9). Whatever prophecy is in Acts, it plainly includes women.

The roll of the Spirit-bearers. Who had the Spirit under the old covenant? A very short roll, nearly every name on it holding an office: Moses and the seventy elders, Bezalel, Gideon and Samson, Saul and David, the prophets. The Spirit came upon them for the work and could depart again, which is what David is terrified of when he begs God not to take his Holy Spirit from him (Psalm 51:11).

The last name on the roll. The roll ends with one more name, and it changes all the rest. At the Jordan the Spirit came down on Jesus (Luke 3:22) and remained on him (John 1:32); in Nazareth he read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:18). David feared losing the Spirit; the Son never could. Pentecost is what happens when the anointed one is exalted: the Spirit given to him without measure (John 3:34) flows from him, the head, to all his people.

In everyday life. If you are old and think your usefulness is over, or young and inexperienced, or in a humble job, read the list again: old men, young men, servants. The Spirit poured out on them has been poured out on you; speak of God’s mighty works to someone today.

Do women, and men, still prophesy today? Whether prophecy as new revelation continues is weighed in the box on prophecy today below. What certainly continues is the Spirit empowering every believer to speak of Christ (1:8): the mother teaching her children, the old man telling his grandson what God has done, the young woman explaining the gospel to a friend at work.

So what may a woman do with this gift? A great deal: she is filled with the same Spirit as any apostle. She may pray and speak God’s truth, tell the gospel to anyone, teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), explain the way of God more accurately, as Priscilla did with her husband to Apollos (18:26), counsel, encourage, serve and lead in many ministries. The New Testament restricts one thing: the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church belong to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). That restriction is about order in God’s household, not about worth or gifting, and it is never a licence for men to belittle or silence women. Paul grounds it in creation, not in the customs of his day (1 Timothy 2:13), and Christians who read these passages differently are to be heard with respect. The Spirit came on the daughters as fully as on the sons.

Where Christians differ: when are the last days? Dispensational teaching usually places the last days chiefly in a future period connected with a restored national Israel, a seven-year tribulation and an earthly millennium, with the church age as a parenthesis. This commentary’s view: Peter says the last days began at Pentecost, and the New Testament consistently treats the whole time between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days. This is the amillennial reading (the view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign from heaven, not a future earthly kingdom): Christ reigns now from heaven, the Spirit has been poured out, the gospel goes to the nations, and the next great event on God’s calendar is the return of Christ, the resurrection and the judgment. Faithful brothers, including some in the Reformed tradition who expect an earthly reign of Christ after his return, read the prophetic timetable differently, and the difference should be held with patience.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Charismatic Christians see ongoing prophecy as new words from God. This commentary’s view: Joel’s promise is fulfilled in the Spirit given to all believers, who all know God and declare his word. In the apostolic era this included revelatory prophecy, which laid the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). With the canon complete, the prophetic word continues in the Spirit-empowered proclamation of Scripture. Women as well as men proclaim God’s mighty works, while the office of elder and preaching in the gathered church belong to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Continuationist brothers, who believe prophecy continues and must always be weighed by Scripture, are fellow believers, and the difference is held in love.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!
Philip’s four daughters prophesied

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joel’s darkened sun and blood-red moon are the prophets’ way of announcing the end of a world: the day of the Lord has begun with Christ, and it will be complete when he returns. The whole age of the church lies between.

Wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below. None of the blood, fire and darkened sun had happened that morning. Peter adds three words to Joel, “above”, “below” and “signs”, linking the passage to the signs Jesus did (v. 22). Three things resolve the difficulty.

The language of a world ending. First, this is how the prophets speak of the fall of a power. When Isaiah announces the end of Babylon, “the sun will be dark at its rising” (Isaiah 13:10); when Ezekiel announces the end of Egypt, God covers the sun with a cloud (Ezekiel 32:7). Babylon fell, Egypt was humbled, and the sun came up throughout: not failed prediction, but Scripture’s settled idiom for the end of a world. Jesus used the same kind of language of the fall of Jerusalem and of his own coming (Luke 21:20–28), and the fall of Jerusalem arrived within the lifetime of some of the men standing in that street.
