The sun shall be turned to darkness. Second, a piece of it had happened. Weeks earlier, at midday, the sun’s light failed for three hours while a man died on a hill outside the wall (Luke 23:44–45). Peter quotes a prophecy about a darkened sun to people who had stood under one.

The great and magnificent day. Third, the shape of the whole promise. The day of the Lord, the day of God’s judgment and salvation, began with Christ’s first coming and will be complete at his return. Peter is opening an era, not closing one. The signs belong to it, and so does the sentence he is driving towards: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.

Judged in their place. Amos warned an Israel that longed for the day of the LORD what was in it: “It is darkness, and not light” (Amos 5:18). At midday on a Friday the darkness of that day came down on one man. The Son of God stood under the judgment the great day will bring and took its night into himself, so that for everyone who calls on him the day will dawn as light. The judge on the throne of that day will be the one who was judged in their place.

Should I be worried when I hear about blood moons or world events as signs of the end? No. Wars, earthquakes, eclipses and disasters have filled every century, and Jesus said such things must take place, but the end is not yet (Matthew 24:6). They remind us that this world is passing, but they are not a code, and no one can read the date from them. The right response to any sign is the one Peter draws: call on the Lord, live faithfully, and tell others. A believer who knows Christ need not fear the day of the Lord, because the judge is his Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: darkness at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who calls on the Lord for rescue will be saved, and the Lord on whom they call is Jesus. The whole citation has been climbing to this line, and Peter stops here; the end of Joel’s verse, about those whom the LORD calls, he picks up at the close (v. 39).

Everyone. No qualifier of nation, class, sex, age or record, spoken in the city that had killed the Son of God.

Who calls upon the name of the Lord. The single condition is not a work or a standard of behaviour but the cry of someone with nothing left to offer. To call on the Lord’s name is to appeal to him, trusting him for rescue. It is faith expressed in prayer.

Shall be saved. Not “may be”, not “stands a better chance”. Peter is quoting a promise, not proposing a scheme.

The name of the LORD, given to Jesus. In Joel it is the LORD in small capitals, the ESV’s sign for the covenant name of God, Yahweh, the name Israel would not say aloud. Fifteen verses later Peter tells the same crowd who the Lord is: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (v. 36). To call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh. The name the crowd shouted down before Pilate is the name by which many of them, that same day, were saved.

Not a slip. Nor is it a slip in the excitement of a first sermon. Peter will say there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12); “all who call on your name” is soon the ordinary description of Christians (9:14); Paul quotes this very line of Joel and applies it to Jesus without pausing to justify himself (Romans 10:9–13). And Stephen dies praying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”: a Jewish monotheist praying to Jesus with his last breath (7:59).

How the deity of Christ entered the church. Not by committee, vote or slow promotion of a teacher into a god over three centuries, as is often claimed, but by Jewish monotheists, who would sooner have died than pray to a creature, praying to Jesus within weeks of the resurrection. And if it is objected that Luke wrote these speeches down decades later, Paul’s letters, written within about twenty-five years of the cross, show the same worship, including an Aramaic prayer that must go back to the earliest Jewish believers: Maranatha, Our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22).

What does calling on the name actually look like? Not a formula or a technique, but what the tax collector did at the back of the temple when he would not even lift up his eyes, but beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” No preparation, no cleaning himself up first, no promise of improvement, and he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). Justified means declared right with God by the Judge himself: not made perfect on the spot, but acquitted and accepted, on the ground not of his record but of God’s mercy, a mercy the cross shows to rest on Christ (Romans 3:24–26). Calling is what the unrepaired do. If you have never called on Christ, you can do it now, in your own words: “Lord Jesus, I have sinned; you died and rose again; save me.”

But if salvation is for everyone who calls, how does that fit with God’s choosing? Peter holds both together in this sermon: the promise is for everyone, and for everyone whom the Lord our God calls (v. 39). The invitation is genuinely universal, and no one who calls on Christ is turned away. Yet no one calls on him unless God first opens his heart (16:14). The two do not compete. God’s choosing is the reason anyone calls at all, and it never makes the offer insincere. You do not need to know whether you are chosen before you call. Call, and your calling will be the evidence that he chose you.
verseByVerse.note: In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD; Peter applies the name to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus of Nazareth, whom God publicly accredited, was handed over by God’s fixed plan and killed by men who were fully guilty: the worst crime in history is the means God planned to save the world. Now the sermon turns from explaining the morning to announcing the man.

Attested to you by God. A real man from a real town, accredited by God in public, as credentials are produced in court.

As you yourselves know. Jesus had worked in public, in their own country, within the last few years, and even his enemies did not deny the miracles; they put them down to Beelzebul (Luke 11:15). Peter appeals to the memory of a hostile crowd, a dangerous way to preach unless it is true (see vv. 29–30).

The definite plan and foreknowledge of God. Two claims about one event are welded together, neither softened. Definite plan (hōrismenē boulē) is a fixed purpose; the word is built on the verb for marking out a boundary, the root of our word horizon. The cross was not an accident or a tragedy that took God by surprise; it lay inside a line drawn before the world was made (4:27–28; 1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8). And foreknowledge (prognōsis) here is not God peering ahead to see what people would decide; his foreknowing carries his settled purpose.

You crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. The second claim is as sharp: not circumstances, but “you”. The lawless men, without God’s law, are the Romans: the Jerusalem crowd wanted it done, the empire’s soldiers did it, and nobody involved is a mere tool or has clean hands. They did it freely and wickedly; God planned it for good. As Joseph said to his brothers, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

Hold the two together. Take away the plan and the cross becomes a tragedy God salvaged, a very thin comfort. Take away the guilt and the cross becomes theatre in which nobody is responsible, and there is nothing left for it to forgive. Scripture has kept them in one sentence since Isaiah, who watched God send Assyria as the rod of his anger, though the Assyrian did not so intend, and then punish the king of Assyria for the arrogance of his heart (Isaiah 10:5–12).

There has never been a plan B. If the murder of the Son of God did not fall outside the plan, nothing does. Whatever you have done that seems to put you beyond reach, and whatever has been done to you that looks like the end of every good purpose, is smaller than this and stands inside the same sovereignty. Not one nail was outside his plan, and not one drop of that blood was wasted.

What it does not mean. This verse does not make God the author of sin or say that he forced anyone to sin: Peter charges his hearers with murder in the same breath in which he says it was planned, and no preacher could do that if the real agent of the crime were God. Nor does it make the Jews uniquely guilty. All of us, by our sins, put Christ there, and Gentiles and Jews together crucified him (4:27). The long and wicked history of Christians blaming the Jewish people for the death of Christ has no ground here; Peter speaks as a Jew to his own people, and offers them pardon within the hour. Nor is this a tidy explanation to hand a suffering person: Peter is not explaining a tragedy; he is announcing that the worst thing the human race has ever done is the thing God used to save it.

If God planned the cross, why did Jesus have to die at all? Because there was no other way to save sinners justly. Our sin deserved God’s judgment, and he could not simply overlook it without ceasing to be just. So in love he planned that his own Son would bear our sin and its punishment in our place, that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). It was the plan of a God who loved sinners enough to give his Son, and is holy enough that only such a sacrifice would do. That is why the cross is both the greatest crime and the greatest gift.
verseByVerse.note: Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reversed the world’s verdict by raising Jesus, because death had neither the right nor the power to hold him. This is the heart of the apostolic preaching: you killed him; God raised him.

Loosing the pangs of death. Pangs (ōdinas) are labour pains: death is in labour, and it cannot keep what it is carrying. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and fittingly, because on one Sunday a tomb behaved like a womb.

Not possible. Not unlikely, not difficult: not possible. The New Testament gives several reasons why.

Because of who he is. Jerusalem killed the Author of life (3:15), and life does not stay dead any more than fire stays cold.

Because of what he had not done. Death in Scripture is not a natural process; it is a wage, paid to those who have earned it (Romans 6:23). Jesus had earned nothing; the ruler of this world had no claim on him (John 14:30). He went in voluntarily, carrying other men’s debts, and once they were discharged there was no ground in law to hold him another hour. The stone was not rolled back to let him out. It was rolled back to let the world in to look.

Because God had promised it. In Psalm 16, which Peter goes straight on to quote, God had said that his Holy One would not see corruption.

What it does not mean. “Not possible for him to be held” does not mean that he could not die. He really died: the body went cold, friends made the arrangements, and women prepared spices for a job that genuinely needed doing (Luke 23:56). Anything less than a real death would leave the human race exactly where it was.

What does Christ’s resurrection mean for my own death? Not the end for anyone who belongs to him. Because he was raised, those united to him will be raised too, bodily, at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests until the resurrection. There is no soul sleep and no purgatory in between; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So you may grieve at a Christian’s graveside, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

In everyday life. Most of us carry one grave we cannot think about calmly: our own, or that of someone we love. This verse does not ask you to stop grieving; it tells you that death has met a man it could not hold, and if you belong to him it cannot hold you either. A believer at a graveside is not looking at a permanent arrangement. He is looking at a room death has already been made to give up once, by a man who walked out of it and took the keys with him.

Uncertain wording. Pangs of death is the Greek Old Testament’s phrase in Psalm 18:4–5 and 116:3, but the Hebrew word behind it can mean either cords or birth pains, and the ESV of the Psalms reads “The cords of death encompassed me”. So the picture may be death in labour, unable to keep what it carries, or death’s ropes untied, unable to hold its prisoner. Luke’s word is pangs; loosing and holding suit either picture, and the point is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Psalm 16 David speaks of unbroken trust in God and of a body that rests in hope; the words were true of David in part, but fully true only of Christ, whose voice Peter hears in them.

For David says concerning him. Peter settles a question about a man who died seven weeks ago by quoting a poem a thousand years old, Psalm 16:8–11. It is a psalm of trust, genuinely David’s: he meant every word about himself. David could say “my flesh also will dwell in hope” and mean that God would bring him through the present trouble alive. He could not make the sentence come true in the full sense the words will bear, and Peter is about to point at his grave to prove it. The words fit the writer, then overflow him.

I saw the Lord always before me. The psalm reads “I have set the LORD always before me”: a deliberate act of keeping God in view, not a feeling that he is near. It describes perfect trust in God, never broken, true of David in part but fully true only of Christ. Even on the cross, when he bore the judgment our sins deserved and felt himself forsaken, he did not let go: his cry was still “My God” (Mark 15:34).

He is at my right hand. A soldier’s shield hung on his left arm, so his right side was exposed, and what he wanted above everything was someone he trusted at his right, covering the side he could not cover himself. That is where the psalm puts God.

My heart … my tongue … my flesh. The gladness works outwards until even the flesh is included, the part of a man that knows it is going to die. Not stoicism, which expects nothing and so cannot be disappointed, but a man expecting his own body to have a future, even as it is laid in the grave.

What held the Son of God steady. Peter puts these words into the mouth of Christ, so we are being told what held the Son of God steady on the road to the cross: not the absence of dread, for in Gethsemane he was “greatly distressed and troubled” (Mark 14:33–34), but the Father in view. The same is asked of anyone walking into something he cannot get out of: a diagnosis, a court date, a conversation dreaded for a month. The Lord who was at Christ’s right hand in the valley of death is at the right hand of every believer, and the hope that held his flesh holds ours.

My flesh also will dwell in hope. Most of us use “hope” for things we are not sure of: I hope the scan is clear. That hope is anxious, because it rests on things that may give way, and underneath we all lean on such things: the career, the children turning out well, a comfortable retirement, a body that keeps going. Timothy Keller often pointed out that how we live now depends on what we believe about our future; when that future is fragile, so are we. To dwell in hope is to live in it, like a house, with the grave in full view, and it is safe for one reason: Christ’s flesh went into the tomb and did not see corruption (v. 31). His hope came true, and he shares it with all who are his: we are “born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). The next time you notice your body failing, a stiff knee, a tired heart, a name you cannot remember, say the verse over it: “my flesh also will dwell in hope.” See also Hope in the Theological Dictionary.

How do I set the Lord always before me when I cannot feel him near? By deliberate attention, not by feeling. Start the day with a few verses turned into prayer, so that the first voice you hear is his. Through the day, bring your thoughts back to him: before a hard conversation, in the car, at the hospital bed. Remind yourself of what is true whether you feel it or not: that he is at your right hand, that he is for you, that he has promised never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5). Feelings of his nearness come and go, even for mature believers; setting him before you is something you do, and he honours it.

parallels.desc: I have set the LORD always before me

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God would not leave his Holy One among the dead or let his body decay, but would lead him by the paths of life into the gladness of his presence.

You will not abandon my soul to Hades. Hades here is not hell. It is the realm of the dead; the psalm Peter is quoting says Sheol (Psalm 16:10), the place where the dead simply are. God would not leave him there.

Or let your Holy One see corruption. To see corruption (diaphthora) is to undergo decay: not that he would not die, but that his body would not decay. The dead were laid on a shelf in a rock tomb for a year until the bones could be gathered into a box. Martha warned Jesus that by the fourth day there would be an odour (John 11:39), and the women went out on the Sunday morning carrying spices (Luke 24:1). Jesus was raised on the third day, before decay could set in.

The paths of life. Paths, in the plural: a whole country to walk in, not bare survival, opened by Christ’s resurrection and ascension.

Full of gladness with your presence. The phrase is literally “with your face”. Suppose the resurrection delivered everything but that: a body that never failed, a world with no funerals, and God himself somewhere else, benevolent and absent. It would not be enough. The psalm describes the joy of the risen Christ as a presence, and whatever else the life to come is, it is the end of God being somewhere else. The risen Christ has walked the road through death and out the other side into the gladness of the Father’s face, and he has opened that road for all who are his.

Why does the Creed say he descended into hell? This verse lies behind that uneasy line in the Apostles’ Creed. Nobody in the mainstream of the church has taught that Jesus went somewhere to be punished further after the cross; the punishment was finished there, and he said so: “It is finished” (John 19:30). Some read the phrase as meaning simply that he was truly dead and went where the dead go. Others, in the Reformed tradition especially, take it to describe the God-forsakenness of the cross itself, when he bore the wrath of God in our place. Others again have held that he went to announce his victory among the dead, drawing on 1 Peter 3:19, a passage read in several ways. And the psalm claims only that he would not be abandoned there.

Where did Jesus go between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb. His human soul went, as he promised the thief, to paradise: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not go to further suffering, or to give the dead a second chance, which Scripture never offers (Hebrews 9:27). His death was real, body and soul truly separated, as ours will be. And because he has walked that road and come back, a believer facing death walks a road with his Lord’s footprints on it.
verseByVerse.note: Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s occupied tomb proves that he was not speaking of himself: as a prophet who held God’s sworn promise of an everlasting heir, he was speaking of the Messiah.

His tomb is with us to this day. The boldest move in the sermon: an appeal to a landmark. David’s tomb was a real building on the southern ridge of the city, known to everybody in that street (Nehemiah 3:16); Peter could have raised his arm and pointed at it.

Two graves in one city. He stakes the argument on a grave anyone could visit that afternoon: David’s tomb is occupied. His argument needs the tomb of Jesus to be empty, and the earliest counter-story we know of, that the disciples stole the body, quietly admits that it was (Matthew 28:11–15). Legends need distance and time; this claim was made in the town where it happened, within weeks, before the people best placed to demolish it.

Being therefore a prophet. David was not merely a poet who wrote more than he knew, but a prophet, speaking by the Spirit (1:16); “The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me,” he said at the end of his life (2 Samuel 23:2). He knew, at least in part, what he was doing.

God had sworn with an oath to him. He had been given a promise on oath: that God would set one of his own offspring on his throne, and that the throne would have no end (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11). Such a promise cannot be kept unless somebody in that family stops dying.

The hidden child. Look at what God steered to keep that oath. The royal line ran through adultery and murder in its first generation, through kings who burned their own children as offerings, and through exile, when the throne stood empty for centuries and the family ended up as village carpenters. At one point the whole line came down to a single infant, hidden in the house of the LORD for six years while the queen who had killed every royal child she could reach ruled the country (2 Kings 11:1–3). The oath God swore to David hung on whether a hidden child would cry at the wrong moment.

David’s Son will call David out. David’s tomb is still sealed, and his greater Son’s is open, but the story does not leave David there. The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come out (John 5:28–29), and on that day David’s Son will call David out of his grave, glad at last in the presence he sang about.

Waiting on a promise that looks lost. Anyone waiting on a promise of God that looks impossible may take heart. This one did not fail in exile, or while the throne stood empty, or while the last heir was a toddler hidden in the temple; it was kept in the end by a man from Nazareth whom this crowd had watched die.

What promises of God can I rely on in my own waiting? On what God has actually promised in Scripture, not what you wish he had. He has promised to forgive all who confess their sins (1 John 1:9), never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), to work all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), to give wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), to complete the work he began in you (Philippians 1:6), and to raise you on the last day (John 6:40). He has not promised every outcome you pray for, such as a particular healing or marriage. But every promise he has made is yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the story of David’s line shows how far he will go to keep them.

Where Christians differ: is Christ on David’s throne now? Dispensational and other premillennial teaching holds that the promise of David’s throne will be fulfilled chiefly in a future earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem during a millennium after his return. This commentary’s view: Peter says the oath to set David’s descendant on his throne was what David foresaw when he spoke of the resurrection (vv. 30–31), and that Jesus, raised and exalted to God’s right hand, now reigns (vv. 33–36). The throne of David is fulfilled in Christ’s present heavenly reign, which the New Testament calls the kingdom already come (Luke 1:32–33; Colossians 1:13; Hebrews 1:8–13). This is the amillennial reading (defined at vv. 17–18). Christ reigns now, until his enemies are made his footstool, and his reign will be seen by all at his return, in the new creation. Brothers who expect a future millennium love the same King and await the same return, and the difference is held in charity.
verseByVerse.note: David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: the LORD swore to David a sure oath

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David foresaw the Messiah’s resurrection, and the apostles saw it: Scripture foretold it, and eyewitnesses confirm that it happened to Jesus.

He foresaw and spoke. The psalm does not merely happen to fit. David looked ahead and wrote of the Messiah’s resurrection, so the resurrection was not the salvage of a wrecked plan; it was announced in Israel’s hymnbook centuries before there was a tomb for it to empty. Jesus had taught the apostles to read the Old Testament this way: “that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead” (Luke 24:44–47). It is fulfilled in Jesus, and in no one else: every other son of David lies on the ridge.

Of that we all are witnesses. Then Peter argues from the eleven men beside him: “we all”, not “I”, and not a report that reached him. The qualification for the vacancy in chapter 1 was exactly this: a man who had been with them the whole time and had seen the risen Lord (1:21–22). Named men, open to cross-examination by a crowd that may have included friends of those who arranged the execution.

Men in a position to know. People say that nobody dies for a lie. In fact the world is full of sincere martyrs for untrue things. The real point is narrower and harder to get round: these men were in a position to know whether it was a lie. A man may die for a doctrine he cannot check; he does not ordinarily die for a resurrection story when he hid the body himself. Floggings, prisons and, for many of them by early tradition, execution are not the record of men who had the option of quietly correcting themselves.

An inheritance and a limit. The inheritance: Christian faith is not a philosophy that would survive the disproof of its history; it rests on something that either happened outside a wall in Jerusalem or did not, and Peter is content for it to be tested. The limit: nobody today is a witness in Peter’s sense. What the church holds is the testimony of the men who were, written down while people who could have contradicted them were still alive. That is enough to build a life on, but the honest name for it is trusting their testimony, and no believer need feel awkward saying so.

If I did not see it, how can my faith be certain? God has given you something better than a private sighting: the public testimony of chosen eyewitnesses, preserved by the Spirit in Scripture, and the Spirit himself bearing witness in your heart that it is true. Jesus told Thomas that those who have not seen and yet have believed are blessed (John 20:29), and John wrote his Gospel so that you may believe (John 20:31). Your faith rests on the same event the apostles saw, through their words. That is not a weaker faith; it is the faith God intended for every generation after the first.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit the crowd can hear is the proof of a throne they cannot see: the exalted Jesus has received the Spirit from the Father and poured him out, as only God can.

Exalted at the right hand of God. The place of highest honour and power, which nobody in that street could see. How can a crowd know it?

This that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. Peter points at the noise. You cannot see a throne in heaven; you can hear a hundred and twenty Galileans speaking Parthian, the sound of a coronation that has already taken place where no one can look. And only God pours out God’s Spirit: in Joel it was the LORD who would pour it out (Joel 2:28), and here it is Jesus.

Having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit. Three persons are named in this one sentence, doing three different things: Jesus is exalted at the right hand of God, receives the promised Spirit from the Father, and pours out the Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God, existing eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, distinct but never divided: not three gods, and not one person taking turns in three roles. It is not a later theory laid over the gospel. It is the shape of the gospel’s first sermon.

David did not ascend into the heavens. The same logic as before: David’s body is on the ridge, so the psalm is not about him but about the one he calls his Lord.

The Lord said to my Lord. This is Psalm 110:1, often said to be the Old Testament text most quoted in the New, and Jesus used it himself (Luke 20:41–44). In the psalm the ESV prints the first in small capitals, “The LORD says to my Lord”: the first is the covenant name of God, the second a title for a master. So David, the king, with nobody above him in Israel, overhears God addressing someone David himself must call his master. Jesus had put that puzzle to the scholars weeks earlier: if the Christ is David’s son, how does David call him Lord? The son of David turns out to be the master of David.

The coronation gift. A king’s accession was marked by generous giving: gifts scattered, debts remitted, prisoners released. Psalm 68, which Paul applies to the ascension, pictures the conqueror going up on high and receiving gifts among men (Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8). The first recorded act of Jesus after his enthronement is to give, and what he gives is not a benefit but a Person: the coronation gift of a King who had nothing left to prove and gave anyway.

A receipt from the throne. When a believer understands a verse that was closed to him a year ago, or wants to pray when he does not feel like it, or finds that a sin which used to own him has loosened its grip, he holds evidence of where Jesus is. Peter’s argument did not stop working when the languages did. The Spirit’s presence in an ordinary life is a receipt, and the transaction it records took place at the right hand of God.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Look for the evidence Peter points to: the things only the Spirit produces. Do you confess that Jesus is Lord and mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3)? Do you, however weakly, love God and want to obey him? Do you call God Father with trust (Romans 8:15–16)? Is there some growth, however slow, in love, joy, patience and self-control? Do you love other Christians? These are not achievements that earn the Spirit; they are the fruit of his presence. If they are there, even in seed form, the King has given you his gift. If you ask anxiously, the anxiety is itself a good sign: a heart dead to God does not worry whether it is alive to him. And when you feel far from God, remember that the Spirit was a King’s gift, not a wage; he has not been withdrawn because you had a bad week.

parallels.desc: “Sit at my right hand”

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus now reigns until every enemy is beneath his feet, and God has installed the man Jerusalem crucified as Lord and Messiah. This is the conclusion of the sermon, and Peter states it as a fact to be known for certain.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The picture is not gentle. Ancient kings put their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24), and footstools were carved with bound captives: not a negotiated settlement with the powers that oppose God, but their subjugation under the feet of a man who is sitting still. Christ reigns now, until every enemy is subdued, the last being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

The King who sits. The sitting matters. The priests in the temple across the city never sat down at their work, because it was never finished: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices”, but Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down (Hebrews 10:11–12). Nor does “until” mean that the reign expires when the job is done; it means the reign is what does the job.

Know for certain. For certain (asphalōs) means beyond doubt, securely, from the root Luke used when he told Theophilus he was writing so that he might have certainty (Luke 1:4). Peter is announcing a fact.

Both Lord and Christ. Lord was the Greek Old Testament’s word for the divine name; Christ is the Messiah, the anointed king. Read carelessly, the sentence sounds as though a good man was handed a divine job at Easter, and it is quoted today by those who say the church made Jesus God. The sentence cannot bear that meaning, and three things show why.

The verb. First, “made”, in a sentence of this kind, is the language of appointing someone to an office, and Greek uses it that way constantly. The Greek Old Testament says the LORD made Moses and Aaron (1 Samuel 12:6), which English Bibles render appointed. The Gospels say Jesus made twelve, meaning he appointed them (Mark 3:14). To be made Lord in this sense is to be installed in an office, not brought into existence.

The man writing it down. Second, Luke has already told us, in the first volume of this same work, what an angel said over a newborn at Bethlehem: “unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Whatever Luke meant here, he cannot have meant that Jesus acquired those two titles that spring, because he had already used both of them of a baby in a manger.

Declared, not created. Third, the resurrection is said to declare, not to create. Paul puts it precisely: Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4), with a verb built on the same root as the definite plan in verse 23. What is new at Easter is not who he is but the office he publicly takes up. The eternal Son, who humbled himself, is exalted in his human nature to the highest place and given the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). A king’s son is royal from birth and may be crowned years later; nobody at the coronation supposes the crown created the man.

This Jesus whom you crucified. The closing move of a prosecution. A court in this city condemned a man and had him put to death; heaven has reviewed the case, overturned the verdict, and seated the condemned man as Judge. Yet he does not settle accounts. The crowd that hears what it has done is told that it may repent, be forgiven, and receive the very Spirit it jeered at an hour before. The first thing he does as Lord is offer his murderers himself.

What does it mean for me that Jesus is Lord? That he has the right to rule every part of your life, and the power to. Lordship is not a title you confer on him when you are ready; it is the office God has given him, and the only question is whether you will bow now, gladly, or later, unwillingly (Philippians 2:10–11). In practice it means bringing your money, your sexuality, your time, your work, your plans and your fears under his word. But the one who rules you is the one who died for you. His lordship is not a tyrant’s; it is the rule of the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep. To call him Lord is to be safe. Is there an area of your life where Jesus is Saviour but not yet Lord? Name it, and bow to him there today: the hand that claims it was pierced for you, and his Spirit is in you to make the yielding real.
verseByVerse.note: “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God’s name; “Christ” means the Messiah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel creates a people. Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do, and Peter calls them to repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, promising the gift of the Spirit to them, to their children and to all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord calls (vv. 37–40). About three thousand receive the word and are baptised (v. 41). Luke then shows what the Spirit builds: a church devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, filled with awe, sharing with any in need, meeting in the temple and in homes with glad hearts, while the Lord adds to it daily those who are being saved (vv. 42–47).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 names four practices, the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers (each is treated in the note on v. 42), and the church has rightly read them as the lasting shape of its life. The fellowship is a shared life the Spirit creates. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. The prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation that quietly lets one of the four go will be the poorer for it, often without noticing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The immersion pools were standing ready on the morning three thousand needed baptising (see vv. 40–41). Now: God does not wait for ideal conditions. He uses what is already to hand: a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Convicted by the Spirit, the crowd asks what it must do, and Peter offers full forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit himself to every one of them who turns to Christ and is baptised in his name.

Cut to the heart. Pierced, stabbed (katenygēsan): the blade is the Spirit’s. When he comes, Jesus had said, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8). The crowd recognises its city’s guilt and its own share in it.

Brothers, what shall we do? The right response to the gospel: people taking it seriously enough to ask what it demands. They call the apostles brothers, as Peter had called them (v. 29); an hour earlier some in this crowd were calling these men drunk.

Repent. Repent (metanoēsate) means to change your mind and turn around: about Jesus and about sin, leading to a change of life. It is not penance, a payment made in tears, but a turning of the whole self, from sin to God, from trusting yourself to trusting Christ.

And be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ. Baptism publicly marks the turn and identifies the believer with Jesus: his death, his burial, his rising (Romans 6:3–4). “In the name of Jesus Christ” means by his authority, into union with him and under his ownership. “Every one of you”: each person who repents, individually. Nobody is baptised by proxy or comes in by belonging to a nation. Nor does the phrase contradict the threefold name of Matthew 28:19; it says whose disciple one becomes: to be baptised into Jesus is to be baptised into the God who raised him, the Spirit he poured out and the Father who sent him. The earliest manual of church practice outside the New Testament prescribes the threefold name (Didache 7), and this chapter, where Jesus receives the Spirit from the Father and pours him out (v. 33), shows why.

For the forgiveness of your sins. All of them, even crucifying the Messiah, offered in full in the same breath in which Peter charges them. There is no blood on any hand that his blood cannot wash away. If there is something you have never believed God could forgive, bring it to him today, by name.

You will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Not the gifts of the Spirit but the gift who is the Spirit, the same Spirit poured out on the apostles that morning. The three thousand did not wait ten days; he was given as they repented and believed.

They looked on him whom they had pierced. Luke does not cite it, but the scene fits Zechariah closely. God promised to pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem “a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy”, so that “when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). John applies it to the spear at the cross (John 19:37). Here it comes true in order: the Spirit is poured out on Jerusalem, the city is shown the one it pierced, and the piercing turns on the hearers’ own hearts. The pierced one has sent the Spirit to wound them in order to heal them.

Repentance for the religious. Those told to repent are not pagans but devout men, many of whom had crossed the world to keep this feast. It is possible to keep every festival and say every prayer and still have rejected God’s Christ, trusting your religion to do what only he can do. The moralist and the rebel stand in the same line here, and both are offered the same pardon.

How do I actually repent? Repentance is not a one-off ceremony but the way a forgiven person keeps walking, and it always starts from the promise in this verse, forgiveness held out before anything has been put right, never from a hope of earning it. In practice it looks like this. Name it. Tell God the particular thing, not “nobody’s perfect” but what you did, said or wanted, and call it what he calls it. Lean on Christ, not on your tears. What matters is not how bad you feel but where you put your weight: on the one who bore exactly this in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Turn round. Decide what the opposite looks like this week, and cut off what feeds the sin: the phone app, the bottle, the company, the habit of the tongue. Put it right. Where someone else was wronged, apologise plainly and, where you can, make it good, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8). Come back again. You will fall again. Repentance is proved not by never needing it but by returning quickly, because the welcome has not changed. Luther began his Ninety-five Theses by saying that when Jesus said “Repent”, he meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance.

Does the water wash sins away? No. Forgiveness is by grace through faith in the blood of Christ (see the box at the end of this note), which is why the dying thief was saved with no baptism at all (Luke 23:43). We rest our hope not in the water but in Christ, to whom it points. To call baptism a sign, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession does (1689 29.1), is to say that it points to something real beyond itself, as a wedding ring points to a marriage: it does not make the thing it marks, but assures us that it is ours. Paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers, also call it a seal, as the Westminster Confession does (Westminster 28.1), drawing on Romans 4:11, as a wax seal marks a letter as the king’s.

I trusted Christ years ago but was never baptised as a believer: what should I do? Be baptised. You are not less saved for having waited, but the Lord commands it, and in the New Testament it is every believer’s normal first step (8:36–38; 16:33). Speak to your pastor or elders. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to personal faith, weigh this carefully and humbly: we would encourage baptism as a believer, for the reasons given at v. 39, and you should act on your own conscience before God, from Scripture.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read this to mean that baptism itself brings forgiveness (baptismal regeneration), so that forgiveness depends on baptism. This commentary’s view: the preposition for (eis) can mean with a view to or in connection with. Throughout Acts forgiveness is received by faith (10:43; 13:38–39; 26:18), and Cornelius received the Spirit before baptism (10:44–48). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness; baptism is the God-given sign of it, closely linked, normally following at once. It is commanded, and no believer should neglect it, but it is not the cause of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise of forgiveness and the Spirit reaches the hearers, their children and those far off: everyone whom God calls to himself.

For you and for your children. You: people of the city that called for his death. Your children: the next generation. The promise is the one Peter has just named, forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit.

And for all who are far off. This came to include the Gentiles, though it takes a vision and a centurion’s house to show Peter how far (10:28, 34; see Cornelius). Paul takes the phrase from Isaiah 57:19 and tells us what closed the distance: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

Everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself. The promise’s boundary is not ethnic or geographic but the call of God, which is more than an invitation: through the preached word the Spirit opens the heart and makes a sinner willing to come, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14). Peter commands all to repent (v. 38) and assures them that the promise rests on God’s call (see v. 21 on how the two fit).

“They will listen to my voice.” Jesus once said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, and that he must bring them also, and “they will listen to my voice” (John 10:16). The call in this verse is that voice. The promise travels outward from Jerusalem because the one who made peace by his cross is doing the preaching, through every mouth that carries it. It went from the men who crucified him to peoples Peter had never seen, and it has never once failed to reach the sheep it was sent for.

What does this mean for my children? That you may pray for them with confidence and raise them with hope. They are not saved by being born to you, and must repent and believe for themselves. But they live near the promise every day, hearing the gospel at your table, seeing it in your life, and sitting under it in church. God very often calls the children of believers, sometimes so early that they cannot remember not trusting Christ. So tell them plainly that the promise is for them, teach them the Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15), pray with them and for them, and welcome every sign of real faith. When they profess it credibly, rejoice to see them baptised.

Where Christians differ: baptism and children. Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) read for you and your children as a covenant promise to believers’ infants: an unbroken covenant pattern, the sign given to believers’ children then in circumcision (Genesis 17) and now in baptism. Baptists baptise those who profess faith, and the difference turns on how much the old covenant sign carries into the new. This commentary’s view: the promise is to children as to everyone, whom the Lord calls: it is received by those who repent (v. 38), and those baptised were those who received the word (v. 41). Believer’s baptism is the New Testament pattern. Children of believers are in a place of great privilege, and the promise is for them as they come to faith. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters hold their view in good conscience, and we hold ours charitably. On this both sides agree: the promise is sheer grace, and it is offered to you and yours.
verseByVerse.note: “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter urges his hearers to let God rescue them from a generation heading for judgment, and about three thousand receive the word and are baptised.

With many other words. A digest: what survives takes three minutes to read aloud. He kept going.

Save yourselves. In English this sounds like a call to perform a rescue, but the Greek verb is passive: “be saved”. Peter tells them to stop resisting a rescue being carried out on them. A man in a burning building is not told to put the fire out but to stop arguing and be carried down the stairs. And the one doing the carrying is Jesus, made Lord and Christ (vv. 21, 36). The difference between grace and self-rescue sits inside a verse often quoted to prove the opposite.

From this crooked generation. Crooked (skolias) means twisted, perverse, and the phrase comes from the Song of Moses, where God calls his own covenant people a crooked and twisted generation (Deuteronomy 32:5). For Peter’s hearers the phrase also carried a warning they had heard from Jesus himself: the blood of the prophets would be charged against this generation, and Jerusalem would be surrounded by armies and trampled underfoot (Luke 11:50–51; 21:20–24). Within forty years it was. To be saved from this crooked generation was to stop sharing its verdict on Jesus before its judgment fell. Nobody chooses his decade or the assumptions he absorbed before he could examine them; a generation cannot be resigned from, only escaped by being taken out.

Those who received his word were baptized. Receiving the word, then baptism: faith first, the order Luke gives throughout Acts (on children, see v. 39).

Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was built for it. The southern approach to the temple was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; many have been excavated and can still be walked into today, and the great pools of Siloam and Bethesda lay within the city. The plumbing of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it.

About three thousand souls. When Moses came down from Sinai and found the nation dancing round a calf, about three thousand men fell that day (Exodus 32:28). The law came, and three thousand died. Here the Spirit comes, and three thousand live, because between the two mountains stood a cross where the Son of God took the death the law demanded. Paul puts the principle in a sentence: “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

The harvest of one death. Pentecost was the feast of the wheat harvest, and Jesus had told his disciples what kind of harvest he meant to bring in: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Seven weeks after the grain went into the ground, three thousand are gathered in a single day. Every one of them is fruit of his dying, and the harvest of that one death is still coming in.

What it does not mean. Three thousand in a day is not the measure of a ministry, and this verse has bruised many faithful people. The same Spirit produced this and produced Jeremiah, who preached for forty years to a nation that would not turn, and was right the whole time. Numbers are God’s business, not a report card. What is asked of a preacher is what Peter did here: bear witness, keep exhorting, and leave the cutting of hearts to the Spirit.

How do I know whether I have truly received the word? Not by remembering a moment, though some do, but by what the word is doing in you. Do you believe that Jesus died for sinners and rose again, and are you trusting him rather than yourself? Have you turned, however imperfectly, from the life you lived without him? Do you want to keep hearing and obeying his word? Those who received the word that day went straight on to devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching (v. 42). The best evidence that the seed has taken root is that it keeps growing.
verseByVerse.note: Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai; now three thousand receive life.

parallels.desc: a crooked and twisted generation

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit’s first lasting work is a people who hold fast to the apostles’ teaching, to a shared life, to the Lord’s table and to prayer. The wind and fire lasted a morning; what remained was a people.

They devoted themselves. To devote oneself is to stick at a thing, to hold on (proskarterountes, Luke’s word); it is used of the apostles refusing to be pulled away from prayer and the word (6:4), and of Simon the magician attaching himself to Philip (8:13). It is the vocabulary not of attendance but of someone who will not be prised off what he has got hold of, and the tense means they kept at it. Each of the four things has its definite article: the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. Not four qualities to aspire to, but four things you could have been taken to and shown.

The apostles’ teaching. First, because everything else is measured against it. Three thousand new believers had just witnessed wind, fire and a miracle of languages, and what they were given next was teaching: what an overwhelming experience needs is not more experience but more truth. What the apostles taught is preserved for us in the New Testament, so there is no way to be devoted to the apostles’ teaching and casual about Scripture.

The fellowship. Fellowship (koinōnia) is a word worn thin by use; in this chapter it costs money within three verses. It means sharing, partnership, common life: not the conversation over coffee afterwards but a shared life in Christ, in which what belongs to one is genuinely available to another (v. 44).

The breaking of bread. Almost certainly both ordinary meals and the Lord’s Supper, which in this period were not separated: the table where the bread was broken in remembrance was the table where supper was eaten (20:7; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26). Luke has used the phrase before: at Emmaus the risen Lord was known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35). Christ’s chosen memorial of himself is not a monument or a pilgrimage but the most ordinary act of a human day, and at that table he still makes himself known.

The prayers. Plural and definite, very likely including the set hours of prayer at the temple, which the apostles were still keeping a chapter later (3:1), as well as their own gatherings. The first Christians did not invent a devotional life from nothing. They took the one they already had and prayed it to a Lord they could now name.

In the flow. This is the first of several short summaries in Acts (4:32–35; 5:12–16) showing that the Spirit builds a community around the apostles’ word.

Not a test to pass. This describes what the Spirit produced, not hoops to clear for approval. Nobody here is doing these things to be accepted; they had been forgiven that morning, and this is what forgiven people turned out to want. Christ feeds his people through these things still, and he has never needed anything more spectacular to keep his church alive.

Believing without belonging. The sociologist Grace Davie used that phrase of modern Britain: many still believe something, but belong nowhere. Most of us assume this is progress: faith is private, assembled to suit ourselves. Yet the culture that freed the individual from every unchosen bond now worries openly about loneliness; in 2018 Britain appointed a government minister for it. And a faith of my own design can never contradict me: it agrees with me about money, sex and my enemies, because I made it. Luke shows something more radical than the old religion of the tribe or the new religion of the self. These people did not belong because they were born to it or had found others like themselves, but because they had been forgiven on the same morning by the same Lord. The church is not a club for the like-minded. It is “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (20:28). Christ did not die to produce solitary believers. He died to make a people, and he still meets us among them.

What if my church is weak in one of these? Most churches are stronger in some than others. Do not leave at once, and do not grumble. Start by being devoted yourself where your church is weak: come to the prayer meeting, open your home, take the Supper seriously, read the Scriptures with others. Speak graciously to your elders about what you long to see, and pray for your church. But if a church has abandoned the apostles’ teaching itself, denying the gospel or the authority of Scripture, it has lost the first mark, and you should find a church that holds it.
verseByVerse.note: “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s nearness filled the church with awe, signs marked the apostles as Christ’s messengers, and believers held their possessions open to one another.

Awe came upon every soul. Awe is literally fear (phobos), as again in chapter 5 on a far darker morning. Not the dread of a prisoner before a hostile judge, for these people had just been forgiven, but the trembling of people who have realised that the holy God is really among them, and has come near not to consume them but to save them.

Many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. “Were being done”: a season rather than a single burst. And through the apostles specifically: the signs marked them as Christ’s authorised messengers (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

All things in common. Shared (koina): they treated their possessions as available to one another. Three things need saying.

It was not compulsory. Peter says so outright a few chapters on, when Ananias sells a field and lies about the price: “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?” (5:4). Luke is describing not a system imposed on a community but something a community did.

It did not abolish ownership. They still had homes to break bread in (v. 46), and Mary the mother of John Mark still has a house with a gate and a servant girl in chapter 12. This is selling as needs arose, not the founding of a commune.

None of that lets the reader off. Still, these people held what they owned so loosely that men sold land to feed fellow believers they had met that month, and that in consequence “there was not a needy person among them” (4:34). A church can be perfectly orthodox about private property and completely unlike this.

Jesus Christ heals you. The apostles knew whose power it was. A chapter later Peter tells the staring crowd not to look at him as though he had healed the lame man: the name of Jesus, by faith in that name, has made this man strong (3:12, 16); at Lydda he says, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you” (9:34). The wonders are the risen Lord’s own works, continued from heaven, and the awe that fell on every soul was awe at him.

Joy and fear together. The first church was joyful (v. 46) and also afraid, and did not find the two competing. Any picture of God that has to shed one in order to keep the other has quietly lost him. The God before whom the first church trembled made them so glad that they held their goods loosely and their brothers tightly.

Would anyone know? The uncomfortable question is not whether a Christian would give if asked, but whether he would know anyone was in need. In a congregation of any size, is anyone quietly going without whom nobody has noticed? The Jerusalem church knew, which means somebody had asked, and the asking is where the whole thing begins.

Do such signs continue? Luke ties them to the apostles (5:12), and Paul calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Whether they continue is treated at vv. 3–4 (tongues) and vv. 17–18 (prophecy). God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills, and we should pray for the sick with faith (James 5:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again and again, as needs arose, believers sold what they had to provide for one another: generosity flowing from grace received, not a system imposed.

They were selling. The tenses are continuous: they kept selling and distributing as needs came up. One grand gesture is at least soon over; what Luke describes costs more: staying ready to give, again and again.

As any had need. Not equally, not by formula: the measure is need, which means somebody had to know what the needs were, in a community close enough that a widow’s circumstances are not a private matter she has to raise herself.

The arrangement was not perfect. Within four chapters the distribution has broken down along language lines, the Greek-speaking widows overlooked, and the apostles have to restructure the leadership to put it right (6:1). Even a loving church needs good organisation, and those who complained were right to.

Generosity as a symptom. Preached as a scolding, this verse produces unease and no actual giving. These people did not resolve to become generous. They had been forgiven an unpayable debt by the man their city killed, and given the Spirit when what they had coming was judgment. Money went out of their hands because something enormous had come into them. Generosity here is a symptom of grace received, and nobody produces a symptom by being scolded for lacking it.

In everyday life. Is anyone in your church in need? A meal, a lift, an evening’s help or a spare room may meet it as well as money. Look at your diary and bank statement this week, and ask the Spirit to make you more available. Your giving will never be perfect; only Christ’s was, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours, so ask this in gratitude, not as a test of your standing.

How much should I give, then? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage; it sets the bar by grace, not law. Give regularly, as the Lord has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give proportionately, more as you have more. Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to your own church family and its ministry, then more widely. Many find a tenth a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. Keep some margin in your life so that you can respond when a real need appears, as the Jerusalem church did. Above all, look at the cross first: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Where Christians differ: was this communism? Some have seen here a model for Christian communism, or a rule that all Christians must give up private property. This commentary’s view: it was a spontaneous, voluntary expression of love, not a compulsory system imposed by any authority. It met real needs, perhaps of pilgrims who stayed on in Jerusalem. The abiding principle is generous, sacrificial sharing with fellow believers in need (2 Corinthians 8:13–15; 1 John 3:17), not a particular economic model.
verseByVerse.note: Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of property.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new church worships gladly in the temple and in homes, enjoys the people’s favour for a season, and grows every day, because the risen Lord himself keeps adding those he is saving.

Day by day. The phrase appears twice, of their meeting and of the Lord’s adding. It describes what they did, not a rule for a modern week: nobody told them to meet daily; they wanted to.

Attending the temple together. Two settings, and the church has needed both ever since. In the temple, some thirty-five acres of stone, a man is one voice among thousands; they met in Solomon’s Portico (5:12). They have not walked out of Israel’s worship; they are Jews who have found in the Messiah what the temple was for, and the break, when it comes, is forced on them. Jesus himself had taught there every day in his last week (Luke 19:47), and Luke’s Gospel ends with the disciples continually in the temple blessing God (Luke 24:53). Now the church is back in those courts, because the Lord who taught there is still teaching, through them.

Breaking bread in their homes. A room where the loaf is passed from hand to hand and everybody present is known by name. Nothing the temple does can be done in the kitchen, and nothing the kitchen does can be done in the temple. Congregations tend to be strong in one and thin in the other, and to make a virtue of whichever they happen to have.

Glad and generous hearts. Glad (agalliasis) is exultant joy, the leaping kind. The second word describes a table at which nobody is angling for anything, and anyone who has sat at the other kind of table will recognise that as rarer than it sounds.

Having favor with all the people. It does not last. Within two chapters the apostles are under arrest; within five, Stephen is dead; within six, persecution has scattered the church. Luke is describing a season, not issuing a promise.

The Lord added. Not the apostles or the preaching: the Lord added, and in this chapter the Lord is the one God has made both Lord and Christ (v. 36). Peter had preached the sermon of his life, and when Luke summarises, the credit goes elsewhere. Church growth is the risen Jesus’ own work, and being saved is in the present tense: day by day he kept on doing it.

He has not missed a morning since. Everything in this chapter comes down from above: wind, fire, languages, three thousand hearts cut, and now the daily arrival of people being saved. The church did not launch itself and has never grown itself. He was adding on its first morning, and he has not missed a morning since.

What it does not mean. It is a mistake to think a faithful church will always be liked, and an equal mistake to treat unpopularity as evidence of faithfulness: sometimes a church is disliked because it is faithful and sometimes because it is unpleasant. For a church, the wish to be liked is a quiet idol. The first church enjoyed the people’s favour without living for it, and when the favour turned to flogging, the apostles went out rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (5:41).

If the Lord adds, what part do we play? The part he has given us, done faithfully: preaching the gospel, praying, welcoming, loving, and living in a way that commends Christ. He usually saves people through the words and lives of ordinary believers. But we cannot make anyone a Christian; only he can open a heart. That frees us from two errors. One is laziness, as if God’s sovereignty meant we need do nothing; the Jerusalem church did a great deal. The other is anxiety and manipulation, as if growth depended on our technique. Plant and water faithfully, and pray for the Lord of the harvest to do what only he can do.

Uncertain wording. The word the ESV renders generous (aphelotēs) is found nowhere else in the New Testament. Related words describe ground that is smooth, free of stones, and so something simple and uncomplicated. It probably means singleness or simplicity of heart: sincerity, with no hidden agenda. Generous is a fair rendering if it is heard in that sense, open-handed because single-minded, but the word itself is more about an undivided heart than about giving.
verseByVerse.note: The believers still worshipped at the temple while meeting in homes.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 holds two truths in one sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”: God’s settled purpose, formed before the world began (1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8), not God merely looking ahead to see what people would choose. Yet the guilt is wholly human: lawless hands did it, and Peter charges his hearers with it (both truths are treated fully at vv. 22–23). The worst thing people have ever done became the means of the greatest gift God has ever given.
2.examples:
Then: A harvest feast became the birthday of the church. Three thousand were gathered in.

Now: The same Spirit, the same word and the same call to repentance are at work every Lord’s Day, and the same Lord still adds to his church. The question for each congregation is whether it holds to the four things that first church did; the power behind them has not diminished.

keyVerse.quote: Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.
keyVerse.note: This is where Peter’s sermon, and the whole chapter, has been heading. The wind, the fire and the languages are explained by it: the Spirit poured out is the evidence that the crucified Jesus has been raised and enthroned (v. 33). The sentence that convicts the crowd of the worst crime in history is also the one that brings them to ask what they must do, and to find that the Lord they crucified offers them pardon.

2.reflection:
When the Spirit came, the hundred and twenty were simply sitting together where Jesus had told them to wait (vv. 1–2), and the first thing the Spirit did was fill their mouths with God’s mighty works (v. 11). What does this teach us about where spiritual power comes from and what it is for?

Peter, who had denied Jesus beside a fire some seven weeks earlier, now stands up to preach him to thousands (vv. 14–15). What in your own past or personality do you feel disqualifies you from speaking about Christ, and how does Peter’s story answer it?

Peter says both that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and that his hearers killed him by lawless hands (v. 23). Why do we need both truths, and how do they help us when we face suffering, or our own guilt?

Look at the four things the first believers devoted themselves to and at the way they shared what they had (vv. 42–47). Which is strongest in your church, which is weakest, and what is one step you could take this month to strengthen it?

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with the new church in Jerusalem, the apostles doing many “wonders and signs” and the Lord adding to their number day by day (2:43–47). Luke now shows one of those signs in full, and the sermon that explained it.

The message. The Jesus whom Jerusalem disowned and killed is alive, glorified by the God of Abraham, and still at work: his name makes a man lame from birth walk into God’s house. What he did for one man’s feet he offers his whole people: to blot out their sins and bless them by turning them from their wickedness. To refuse him is to be cut off from God’s people.

Why it was said. Peter’s hearers were worshippers at the afternoon prayer, in the city that had called for the crucifixion only weeks before (on Luke’s purpose, see the introduction). They needed to know who had really healed the man, what they had done to Jesus, and whether there was any way back.

How the chapter makes its case. A beggar at the Beautiful Gate is healed in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth and enters the temple praising God (vv. 1–8), and the crowd, recognising him, runs together (vv. 9–11). Peter refuses the credit (v. 12): the God of their fathers has glorified his servant Jesus, whom they denied and killed and God raised, and his name, through faith, made the man strong (vv. 13–16). Then the sermon turns: they acted in ignorance, and God fulfilled his word through it (vv. 17–18), so they must repent and turn back, that their sins may be blotted out, before Christ returns to restore all things (vv. 19–21). Whoever will not listen to the Prophet Moses promised will be cut off (vv. 22–24); but they are heirs of Abraham’s covenant, and the blessing comes to them first (vv. 25–26).

Where it leads. The man raised up by the hand in Jesus’ name is a small picture of the Servant God raised from the dead, and his leaping is a first taste of the restoration Isaiah promised, when the lame would leap like a deer. Jesus is Isaiah’s Servant, the Prophet like Moses and Abraham’s offspring, and the city that killed him is the first to be offered his blessing.

For us. We come to God as that man did: with nothing, outside the gate, asking for far too little. In Jesus’ name the way in is open, every sin can be wiped off the page, and the blessing he gives is greater than health or money: to be turned from our sin to God. When he has done it, the right response is the man’s: walking and leaping and praising God, not the people he used.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the name of Jesus a man lame from birth is made whole and walks into God’s house praising him: a sign that the crucified Jesus is alive and still at work. At the hour of prayer Peter and John meet a beggar who has sat for years outside the Beautiful Gate, asking for coins (vv. 1–3). Peter looks him in the eye, admits he has no money, and gives him instead the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, taking him by the hand and raising him up (vv. 4–7). The man leaps, walks and enters the temple praising God, as Isaiah had promised the lame would leap (v. 8), and the whole crowd recognises him and is filled with wonder (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Signs, and What They Are Signs Of

The healings in Acts are called signs, and a sign is not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination's name on it. They are not the working of an impersonal force but the personal act of a risen King through men he has authorised, and they point to the repair of a world broken since Eden: a man's ankles made whole in Jerusalem are a down payment on a whole creation put right. They also confirmed the apostles' message, which is why Scripture ties them so closely to the apostles, and why the debate over whether such signs continue is about their purpose, never about whether God is able.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The man asked for alms and got his legs, and more: he went into the temple (see v. 8). Now: The church still meets people asking for the small thing because it is the only thing they know to ask for, and it still has no silver worth mentioning. What it has is a name.
