verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the hour of the evening sacrifice, two apostles on their way to pray meet a man who has spent his whole life outside the gate of God’s house, unable to go in. What follows is a sign: those who could never walk into God’s presence are made whole and brought in.

Peter and John. Luke keeps putting Peter and John together: partners in fishing (Luke 5:10), sent to prepare the Passover (Luke 22:8), later sent together to Samaria (8:14). The loud one and, as far as we can tell, the quieter one: the church is not an arrangement in which everybody has to be the same shape.

The ninth hour. About three in the afternoon (see hours of the day), when the evening lamb was offered and the incense went up. It is also the hour at which Jesus died (Luke 23:44–46). Peter and John go up to pray at the hour of the sacrifice, not long after the real Lamb died at that same hour. Luke makes nothing of it. He simply tells us the time.

A man lame from birth. Not an accident or an illness he might recover from: he had never taken a step, and he was over forty (4:22). Somebody carried him to the gate every day: years of lifting that nobody recorded.

The Beautiful Gate. Most likely the great doorway of Corinthian bronze into the inner courts; Josephus says it took twenty men to close it. People on their way to pray are at their most generous, so here he was set down, at the most magnificent doorway in the Jewish world, where he could see in without going in. The law barred a lame priest from the altar (Leviticus 21:18), and an old saying kept the blind and the lame out of the house (2 Samuel 5:8). Whether or not any rule formally shut this man out, everyone knew where he belonged: outside, at the door, with his hand out.

Outside the gate. The one who will open this gate was himself put outside one. As the bodies of the sacrifices were burned outside the camp, so Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The lame man sat at the edge of the holy place because the system, with nothing to offer him but the small change of passers-by, had no room for him; the Son of God was led out to the edge of the city to make room for people like him. In his last week the blind and the lame came to him in the temple and he healed them (Matthew 21:14); this afternoon he does it again, from heaven. Every one of us was lame at the gate until he took us by the hand.

What it does not mean. Nothing here suggests the man’s condition was a punishment, and Jesus had already refused that way of thinking: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:3). The exclusion at the gate exposes not a defect in the man but the limit of the temple system, which could not make him whole.

Why were Peter and John still going to the temple? The first Jewish believers kept its hours of prayer, from habit and to reach their people: they had not left the faith of Israel but found its fulfilment. The break came gradually, through Stephen’s preaching, persecution and the temple’s destruction in AD 70; Hebrews explains that the old system is ready to vanish away (Hebrews 8:13), because Christ is the true temple, priest and sacrifice. Christians are not bound to Jewish worship practices, though there is wisdom in keeping regular times of prayer.

Who are the people at the gate today? Those near the church who cannot get in: the disabled person who cannot climb the steps, the visitor who does not know the songs, the mentally ill man who makes people uncomfortable, the single mother alone in the pew with the children, the widow nobody visits. A church that loves Christ will notice them, make room for them, and above all bring them the gospel, the one thing that gets anyone through the gate.

Uncertain wording. No other ancient writer uses the name “Beautiful Gate”, so we cannot be sure which gate Luke means. Most identify it with the bronze gate Josephus describes, into the inner courts; some suggest a gate in the outer eastern wall. The point does not depend on the answer.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer. The Beautiful Gate is not named elsewhere; it was probably a great bronze gate into the temple courts.

parallels.desc: the evening offering

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beggar asks for what forty years have taught him to expect, a coin, and God is about to give him far more than he knew to ask for.

He asked to receive alms. Giving alms was a religious duty, especially on the way to prayer (Matthew 6:2). He has asked ten thousand times, and the words are out before he has properly looked at the two men. Healing does not occur to him; nothing in forty years has suggested it. The request is entirely reasonable and enormously too small.

Our prayers are not the ceiling. This is not an argument that God is obliged to produce whatever larger things we ask, a teaching that has hurt a great many people. The point is quieter. “We do not know what to pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26), which is not a rebuke but a mercy: our prayers are not the ceiling. God is able to do “far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). This man was still expecting coins when Peter took hold of his hand.

Isn’t religion a way of wanting less? The beggar points to the opposite diagnosis. His trouble was not that he wanted too much but that he had learned to want so little. C. S. Lewis made the point in his sermon “The Weight of Glory”: our desires are not too strong but too weak, like a child who wants to go on making mud pies in a slum because he cannot imagine what is meant by the offer of a holiday at the sea. “We are far too easily pleased.” The moralist’s answer is to want less; the pleasure-seeker’s is to want more of the same small things. The gospel offers what we had not thought to ask for: not coins at the gate, but a Lord who takes us by the hand and brings us inside, into the presence where there are “pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11).

Why was he still lame? A harder question sits in this verse, and a suffering reader will find it whether or not anyone points to it. Jesus went in and out of that temple, feast after feast, for about three years, and may well have passed this man. Yet he was still lame on the afternoon Peter came by. There is no making that comfortable, but Scripture never presents God’s healing as a service delivered evenly. At a pool in this same city a multitude of sick people lay in five colonnades, and Jesus healed one man and left (John 5:2–9). Elisha cleansed a foreign general and left many lepers in Israel uncleansed, and Jesus said so in his first sermon, to a congregation that tried to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:27).

Kept for an afternoon. Forty years of lameness looked, from inside, like forty years of nothing happening. It turns out to have been a life kept for an afternoon when his healing would be seen by the whole city, admitted as undeniable by the highest court in the nation, and followed by a sermon after which the men alone numbered about five thousand (4:4). He had not been overlooked. That is said of this man, not laid as a formula over anyone else’s forty years; but this delay had a purpose, though from inside it none could be seen.

Healed by a living Lord. Had he been healed on a day Jesus taught in the temple, it would have been one more wonder in a ministry that ended on a cross. Done weeks after the crucifixion, by two men with nothing but a name, it could mean only one thing, and Peter draws it out at once: the Jesus they killed is alive, and his name has made this man strong (vv. 15–16). The beggar’s new legs became a witness to an empty tomb.

Should I keep praying for a healing that has not come? Yes, unless God has made it plain that the answer is no, as he did to Paul about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8–9); Jesus taught us always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). But pray as a child, not as a negotiator: ask for healing, and ask also for what God may be giving instead, endurance, his nearness, a deeper trust. And hold on to the certain promise behind all the uncertain ones: every believer will be healed completely at the resurrection, when he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Peter gives the man anything, he looks him in the eye and makes him look back, turning his hope toward the messengers of Jesus.

Peter directed his gaze. A fixed, deliberate stare (atenisas), the word used of Stephen gazing into heaven (7:55). A beggar’s pitch is arranged so that nobody has to look at anybody: the hand goes out, the eyes go down, the coin drops from above. It protects both, the giver from facing the person and the beggar from the humiliation of being seen. Peter dismantles it before any healing is on offer.

Look at us. Not a request to be admired. It turns the man’s hope toward the two men who are about to give him the name of Jesus. He is wrong about what he will receive and entirely right about whom to look to, and God has a long record of meeting people exactly there.

Looked at by the Lord. Peter had learned this look somewhere. On the night of his denial, as the rooster crowed, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61), and Peter went out and wept bitterly. The man who now fixes his eyes on a beggar has himself been looked at by Jesus at his worst and not discarded. And the look serves a name: Peter draws the man’s eyes to himself only so that, a moment later, he can turn them past himself to Jesus of Nazareth.

Attention before help. This is not a method to be copied for results, but the order holds everywhere. The church cannot do anything for people it will not look at, and every person at the gate is made in the image of God. The Lord of glory looked at us when no one else would, and saw not a nuisance but a person he would die for. Before he gave us anything, he gave us his attention.

Should I give money to people who beg? Scripture commands generosity to the poor (Proverbs 19:17; Galatians 2:10), and also calls for wisdom, because some gifts help and some harm. There is no single rule: sometimes a little money is right; sometimes food, a meal, or help through a church mercy ministry, shelter or organisation that knows the person does more good. What is never right is contempt, or walking past as if the person were not there. Whatever you give, look him in the eye, speak kindly, and if you can, ask his name.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter has no money, but in the name of the crucified and risen Jesus he gives the man what money could never buy: feet and ankles made strong in an instant.

I have no silver and gold. The leading apostle, in the church’s days of greatest power, stands at the temple gate without money; what was given went to the needy (2:45; 4:35). Yet he does not brush the man’s need aside. He gives what he has, and it is far more than was asked for.

In the name of Jesus Christ. A name stood for the person and his authority, as a king’s officer acted in the name of the king. Peter recites no incantation; he has no power of his own, and he will say so (v. 12). He acts on his master’s authority, in public. Jesus is the healer, from heaven.

Of Nazareth. The address, the sneer, the words on the board over the cross for the whole city to read on its way past (John 19:19). The name used to dismiss and execute Jesus puts a lame man on his feet. The despised man from the despised town is the Lord of all.

Raised him up. Peter does what he had watched Jesus do, taking Peter’s own mother-in-law and Jairus’s daughter by the hand (Mark 1:31; 5:41). And raised him up (ēgeiren) is the word this chapter uses of the resurrection (v. 15). The gesture acts out in small what is being announced: a man who cannot get up is pulled upright by somebody who has met the one God raised.

Feet and ankles. Luke the physician (Colossians 4:14) uses a term for the ankle bones found nowhere else in the New Testament: instant and complete healing of a condition from birth.

Answered from the throne of God. A man asked two strangers for the price of a meal, and was answered from the throne of God. The power that raised Christ from the dead came down to a pair of ankle bones at three in the afternoon. That is how low the risen Lord’s reign stoops. What he gives the poor is not silver or gold but his own strength, put into their feet.

Silver and gold have I none. An old story tells of a medieval pope showing a visitor the treasures of Rome and remarking that the church could no longer say “silver and gold have I none”, and being answered, “Neither can she now say ‘rise up and walk’.” Whether it happened or not, the point stands. Power in the church has never been carried in its purse.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s favour shows itself in wealth: the man through whom this miracle came has nothing in his pockets. Nor that poverty is holiness; this same church will handle money carefully. But what Peter had to give was not for sale.

The name is not a lever. Luke supplies the warning himself: men at Ephesus tried to work the name as a formula, adjuring evil spirits by “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims”, and it went badly for them (19:13–16). The name works here because Peter belongs to the one who owns it. It has never worked for anybody who wanted the effect without the allegiance.

Do healings like this still happen, and should churches have healing ministries? God still heals, in answer to prayer and through ordinary means such as medicine, as he wills. But this healing was a sign confirming the apostles’ message. Many Christians believe such gifts continue; the more likely reading is that healings of this apostolic kind, instant, complete, at a word, belonged to the foundational age, and that position, cessationism, is held charitably toward those who see it differently. The church today prays for the sick (James 5:14–15) and expects God to answer; but no one holds the apostles’ gift.

What does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? Not a password added at the end. It means coming to God on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, not your worthiness; asking for things that fit his character and purposes; and trusting his authority, not your technique. So Jesus promised, “Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:13). A prayer truly in his name is one he would sign, and you can pray it with great boldness.
verseByVerse.note: “In the name of” means by his authority and power.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who had never walked leaps into the temple praising God: a living picture of Isaiah’s promise that the lame will leap when God comes to save, and of every sinner Christ brings near to God.

Leaping up. Luke piles up seven verbs in one sentence, and the pile is the point. A man lame from birth has never learned the balance infants learn over months of falling down. He does not fall down. He is given the legs and the use of them in the same instant, and his first instinct with a working body is to jump.

Walking and leaping and praising God. Never once through that gate, he now walks in on his own feet, making a scene, and goes not home but into the house of God to praise, which Luke says twice (vv. 8–9). Not praising Peter, but God.

Then shall the lame man leap like a deer. Isaiah had used that very picture: “then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy” (Isaiah 35:6), in a poem about a desert that blossoms and the ransomed of the LORD coming home to Zion with everlasting joy. The leaping man is one line in a song about the end of exile.

The lame walk. Jesus had already claimed that song as his own. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether he was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with Isaiah’s list: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk” (Luke 7:22). So when a lame man leaps in the temple courts weeks after the crucifixion, the sign adds one thing: the one who was to come has not stopped coming. What breaks out at the Beautiful Gate is a fragment of Isaiah’s homecoming arriving early, under the name of the King who leads it.

Brought near. His walk through the gate is a picture of salvation: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ”, and through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:13, 18). A believer may come to God at any hour, as a child to his father, with no gate, priest or animal sacrifice in between, because Christ’s blood has opened the way (Hebrews 10:19–22).

Why don’t I feel like leaping any more? Because joy fades when memory fades, and familiarity dulls even the greatest gifts. The answer is not to manufacture excitement but to remember. Go back over what you were without Christ: guilty, far off, without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Recall specific mercies: the answered prayer, the sin forgiven, the dark year he carried you through. Sing truths, not just feelings. And sit near those who have just come to faith; their wonder is contagious. Joy in God is not always loud, but it grows wherever grace is remembered.

parallels.desc: then shall the lame man leap like a deer

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole crowd sees the man walking and knows exactly who he is, so the miracle cannot be denied; but wonder is not yet faith, and the sign still needs explaining.

They recognised him. A public miracle at the busiest hour in the busiest place, and this word is the chapter’s key evidence. He had sat at that gate day after day; every worshipper had stepped round him. There was no room for substitution or mistaken identity. The council runs into this the next morning. Hostile, with every motive to find a hole in the story, it concludes that a notable sign has been done, that all Jerusalem knows it, and that “we cannot deny it” (4:16). It then forbids the apostles to speak, which is not what men do when they have exposed a fraud.

Wonder and amazement. Amazement (ekstasis) is being beside oneself with astonishment. Neither it nor wonder is faith, and Luke never confuses them: a crowd can be amazed at an act of God and still need telling what it means. Which is why the miracle takes ten verses and the sermon fifteen.

The same Jesus, still at work. Luke called his Gospel an account of “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (1:1), and here is what he meant. The scene has happened before: when Jesus healed a man born blind, his neighbours said, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” (John 9:8). The hands are different now, but the work is the same, because the worker is the same. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8), and the risen Lord is still straightening legs from the right hand of God.

A changed life. The people who knew you before Christ are best placed to notice what he has done, and they are also the ones you are most tempted to hide it from. Do not hide it.

Why doesn’t God do public miracles today to convince sceptics? Partly because miracles do not by themselves produce faith: the council admitted this one and still refused to believe. Jesus said that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And partly because the great public signs have already been given and written down, above all the resurrection, so that you may believe (John 20:31). God now works chiefly through his word and Spirit, and his most persuasive evidence today is often a changed life: a man who was known for one thing and is now known for Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter explains the sign: the Jesus whom Jerusalem killed is glorified and alive, and through him God offers his people forgiveness and blessing. Peter refuses the credit for the healing (vv. 11–12) and names the one who did it: the Servant of the God of their fathers, the Holy and Righteous One whom they denied and God raised, whose name through faith has made the man whole (vv. 13–16). Their ignorance and God’s plan are both true, so the door is open: they must repent and turn back, that their sins may be blotted out, until Christ returns to restore all things (vv. 17–21). Refusing him means being cut off (vv. 22–24); but they are heirs of Abraham’s covenant, and the blessing comes to them first (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfilment of the Covenant with Abraham

Peter closes on the promise to Abraham, in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed (v. 25; cf. Genesis 22:18; 28:14). The gospel is not God abandoning his promises to Israel but their arrival: the first plan reaching its appointed date. One covenant of grace runs from Genesis to Revelation and finds its full form in Christ, which is why Peter can preach this to Jews in the temple courts without once suggesting that they should change religion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who bore the most direct responsibility there was, you denied the Holy and Righteous One, then called them brothers three verses later and told them the blessing was coming to them first. Now: A gospel that cannot name what a man has done has nothing to forgive him for; a gospel that names it and leaves him standing there is not the gospel at all. Peter does both in one sermon, and the second half is longer than the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter turns the crowd’s stare away from himself and John: the miracle came neither from their power nor from their godliness, and the rest of the sermon names the one whose power it was.

While he clung to Peter and John. The first thing Luke tells us about the healed man is that he would not let go. A man dependent his whole life has just been made independent, and his instinct is to hang on to the two people through whom it happened.

Solomon’s Portico. The long covered colonnade on the eastern side of the temple courts, where Jesus was walking at the Feast of Dedication when the crowd demanded that he tell them plainly whether he was the Christ, and picked up stones for the answer (John 10:23–31). Peter is preaching Christ on the very stones where Christ was nearly stoned for preaching himself. As at Pentecost, the sign draws the crowd and the word explains it: who did this (vv. 13–16), what they had done and what God did with it (vv. 17–18), and what they must now do (vv. 19–26).

Our own power or piety. Peter disclaims two things. The power, anybody would expect. The piety, godliness or personal devotion, is the harder disclaimer, because it is the flattering one. A crowd watching a miracle concludes that the men involved must be unusually holy, and that is extremely pleasant to leave uncorrected. But miracles were not rewards for holiness.

A matter of fact. Remember who is speaking: the man who, a short walk from here, told a servant girl that he did not know Jesus (Luke 22:57). If any man in Jerusalem knew that his own godliness was not what made anything happen, it was Peter. He is not being modest; he is stating a fact. The Lord Jesus does his mighty works through weak and failed servants precisely so that no one can mistake whose power it is.

Because he went to the Father. Peter can deflect so completely because he knows where the power came from. Jesus had said that whoever believes in him will do the works he does, and greater works than these, because I am going to the Father (John 14:12). The healing at the gate is that promise beginning to be kept: the work of a Lord who acts from the Father’s side through the men he left behind.

Who are people looking at? There is a counterfeit of this deflection that achieves the opposite. Peter does not say “it was nothing”, or perform the shuffling embarrassment that draws as much attention as accepting the credit. He names somebody else, immediately and at length, and the crowd’s attention goes where he sends it. False modesty keeps the light on the man by making him interesting; genuine deflection moves it. The test of true ministry is simple: when the sentence is finished, whom has it made much of?

How do I accept thanks without stealing glory? Simply and honestly. You need not deny that you did anything; say thank you, and where it is true and natural, say who really did it: “I am so glad God used it,” or “The Lord was kind to us.” Do not fish for more praise, and do not perform humility. Then, privately, hand the compliment straight on to God in prayer. And watch your heart when you are not thanked: if that stings badly, you were collecting the glory for yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s portico was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God Israel had always worshipped has glorified Jesus as his Servant, the very man this crowd handed over and disowned before Pilate.

The God of our fathers. Peter opens with the oldest name in Israel’s vocabulary, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15). He is not announcing a new God or a new religion; he is telling a Jewish crowd in the Jewish temple that the God they have worshipped all their lives has just acted in Jesus.

Glorified his servant Jesus. Servant (pais) echoes the opening of the last of Isaiah’s Servant Songs in the Greek Old Testament: “Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted” (Isaiah 52:13). That sentence runs straight on into Isaiah 53: the wounds, the silence before the shearers, the Servant bearing the sin of many. One word brought it all to mind: Jesus is the Suffering Servant, now glorified by God in his resurrection and in the healing done in his name.

In the presence of Pilate. God glorified him; you denied him. And the comparison with Pilate is deliberate and brutal. A pagan governor with no covenant, no Scriptures and no particular appetite for justice had worked out that the prisoner ought to be let go (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 22). The covenant people insisted otherwise, and many listening remembered it.

Denied. This word changes the temperature of the whole sermon. Luke used it of Peter himself in the high priest’s courtyard: “But he denied it, saying, ‘Woman, I do not know him’” (Luke 22:57). Peter is accusing a crowd of the very sin he had committed, and he has been forgiven for it by the man he is now preaching, which is why he can say this to their faces and call them brothers four verses later.

Is the God of the Old Testament the same as the Father of Jesus? Yes, and this verse says so as plainly as anything in Scripture. Some, from the ancient heretic Marcion to modern writers, have set an angry Old Testament God against a loving New Testament Jesus. Peter knows nothing of it. The same God shows mercy and judgment in both testaments: the Old is full of his steadfast love, and the New speaks of his wrath as plainly as the Old. Jesus himself said the Scriptures bear witness about me (John 5:39). Read your whole Bible as one story, told by one God, about one Saviour. If you have been avoiding the Old Testament, start this week with Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, and read it with the cross in view.
verseByVerse.note: “His servant” echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who would be “lifted up” and glorified.

parallels.desc: my servant shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd chose a murderer over the Holy and Righteous One and put to death the very source of life; but God raised him, and the apostles have seen him alive.

The Holy and Righteous One. The Holy One (Psalm 16:10; Mark 1:24) and the Righteous One (Isaiah 53:11; Acts 7:52; 22:14) were both used of the Messiah, and both are the opposite of what a court is supposed to condemn. The Holy One is the very name of Israel’s God in Isaiah (Isaiah 1:4), and that holiness was in the man they handed over, the only sinless man who ever lived. “Denied” comes twice in two verses: it was a choice, made out loud, in daylight.

A murderer granted to you. That is Barabbas (Luke 23:18–19, 25), and nobody needed reminding. A guilty man was released and an innocent man executed in his place, at the crowd’s request. What the crowd arranged as a miscarriage of justice turned out to be a working picture of the atonement, Christ putting sinners right with God by taking their place, and they built it without the faintest idea what they were making.

The Author of life. The founder and source, the one who goes first and opens a way (archēgos). Peter sets it directly against “killed”: life itself put to death. They spared the murderer and killed the life-giver. The source of all life lay in a tomb so that dead sinners could rise. Then God’s reversal, “whom God raised from the dead”, and the apostles’ testimony: to this we are witnesses; we saw him alive.

What it does not mean. These verses have done enormous harm. Sentences like “you denied” and “you killed” have been read out from pulpits in Christian Europe and followed within days by violence against Jewish neighbours. Read their paragraph. Speaker, audience and setting are all Jewish. Peter calls them brothers; he says in the next breath that they acted in ignorance; he tells them God sent his servant “to you first”; and the entire sermon is a plea that they should be blessed. This is a prophet of Israel addressing Israel, as Isaiah called its rulers the rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10), and nobody has ever thought Isaiah an enemy of the Jews. Peter is not indicting a people across the centuries. He is telling the men in front of him what they did, in order to tell them what may now be done about it.

Am I like Barabbas? In the way that matters most, yes. Every believer is a guilty person set free because an innocent one took his place. Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18); God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). He bore the wrath of God our sins deserved, so that we never will. Barabbas was the first to say, literally, that Jesus died in his place, and walked out of prison with nothing to do but go home. You walk out with everything to live for, and a Saviour to thank.

Uncertain wording. “Author” translates a word with a range of meaning (archēgos): founder or originator, but also leader, prince, the champion who goes ahead and opens the way. Acts uses it again of the exalted Jesus as Leader (5:31), and Hebrews calls him the founder of salvation (2:10) and of our faith (12:2). Set against “killed”, the likely sense holds both: the one from whom life comes, and who leads his people into it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the name of Jesus, his own person and power, that made the man strong, and faith in that name, itself given through Jesus, was the means by which it reached him.

Whose faith? Peter gets the name in twice and faith in twice, in his hurry to make sure the credit lands in the right place: the power is Christ’s; faith is the hand that receives it. Underneath lies a pastoral question of the first order. It cannot straightforwardly be the man’s faith, at least not before the healing. Look back at verse 5: he was expecting a coin. He had not asked for healing, did not know it was available, and had, as far as Luke tells us, no opinion whatever about Jesus of Nazareth. He was not healed because he believed hard enough. The faith in view is most probably the apostles’, and perhaps the man’s as he responded when Peter took his hand.

Through Jesus. Even the faith is Christ’s gift: “by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). That does not mean God believes for us. It means he opens our eyes to see Christ as he is, so that we trust him, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14).

Perfect health. Wholeness (holoklēria, found nowhere else in the New Testament): sound in every part. Not managed or improved: whole, and in the presence of you all, public and checkable.

Not patching, but making new. The name of Jesus took a man who had never stood and made him sound in every part. That is how our Lord saves: not by patching, but by making new. What he did for one man’s ankles he will do for the whole body of every believer on the day of resurrection.

What it does not mean. A whole style of teaching is built on the opposite reading, and it wounds people badly. It tells the sick that they are not healed because their faith was insufficient, and sends them home worse off than they came, carrying the illness and an accusation on top of it. This verse cannot be used that way: Peter credits the healing in so many words to faith in the name of Jesus, and an hour earlier the man had shown no interest in the name at all.

What part does faith play when I pray for healing? Pray in faith, trusting that God is able and good (James 5:15). But faith is trust in God, not a force that guarantees a result. Paul had great faith and prayed three times, and his thorn was not removed; Timothy was told to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23); Trophimus was left ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). So never conclude, or say, that someone remains ill because they did not believe enough. Ask boldly, submit humbly, and keep trusting God whatever the answer, because his love is proved at the cross, not by the outcome of a particular prayer.

Uncertain wording. This is one of the most tangled sentences in Acts, and a reader who finds it hard to follow is not being slow. Word for word the Greek runs something like and on the faith of his name, this man whom you see and know, his name made strong; English versions punctuate it in different ways. The main claim is clear: the name of Jesus did it, and faith was the channel. Less clear is how “by faith in his name” fits the grammar, and whose faith is meant (see above).

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now calls his hearers brothers: they did not know what they were doing, and God used even their sin to fulfil what all the prophets foretold, that his Christ would suffer; so the door of mercy stands open.

And now, brothers. The sermon turns on one word. Two verses ago they were the people who denied the Holy One and killed the Author of life. Now they are family. The facts have not changed; Peter has reached the reason he recited them.

You acted in ignorance. Not an acquittal; Peter has just spent three verses establishing what they did. It means they did not know who Jesus truly was, and its force lies in how Israel’s law treated sins done in ignorance. For sin committed unintentionally there was a sacrifice: the offender brought his offering and was forgiven. For sin committed with a high hand, in open defiance, the law made no provision; that man was to be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:27–31). So Peter is telling a crowd who have just realised they killed the Messiah which side of that line they stand on, and handing them the only door the law of Moses ever left open.

What God foretold. All the prophets point to a suffering Messiah (Luke 24:25–27; 1 Peter 1:10–11). God fulfilled his own word through their ignorant wickedness. Both are true at once, and Peter does not choose between them.

Father, forgive them. Paul makes the same judgment: “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). And Luke alone records the prayer from the cross that says it first: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Some early copies lack the sentence, but it is very old and it is what the rest of the New Testament assumes. The Lord Jesus prayed for his murderers while the nails were in his hands, and the Father answered at Pentecost and in Solomon’s Portico, by turning those very men into brothers.

Ignorance is not innocence. Paul says he received mercy because he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13), a sentence about mercy, not acquittal; he still called himself the foremost of sinners. And Scripture can condemn sincere ignorance: “they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10:2). Ignorance opens a door. It does not walk anybody through it.

The man who fears he cannot be forgiven. Look hard at who is being addressed. These people had shared in the judicial murder of the Son of God and chosen a murderer over him, and they are being called brothers and offered forgiveness, weeks later, by one of his friends. Whatever the unforgivable sin may be, it is evidently not this.

What is the unforgivable sin, then? Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30), when religious leaders, faced with his plain works of power, attributed them to Satan. Not a careless word or a terrible deed done in weakness, but a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, until the heart no longer wants forgiveness: unforgivable not because Christ’s blood is too weak, but because the only remedy is refused. If you are worried that you have committed it, your worry is itself strong evidence that you have not. Come to Christ: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

In everyday life. When someone wrongs you, consider whether they truly knew what they were doing, and pray for them as Jesus prayed for his executioners.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the Servant they killed is alive, the way back is open: they must change their minds about him and turn round to God, and their sins will be wiped clean away.

Repent therefore, and turn back. “Therefore” ties the command to all that precedes it: because the Servant they killed is alive and his name has made this man strong, the door is open, as at Pentecost (2:38). And it is two commands, not one said twice. Repent (metanoēsate) names what happens in the mind: a reversal of judgment. Turn back (epistrepsate) names what happens to the feet: what a man does in a street when he realises he has been walking the wrong way. The mind changes, and then the body goes somewhere different, away from sin and towards God in Christ. A repentance that never reaches the feet has stopped halfway; a change of direction with no change of mind will not last the winter.

What it does not mean. Neither word means feeling bad. Sorrow often comes with repentance, rightly, but a man can be extremely sorry and turn round nothing at all, and Scripture has a name for that: “worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Nor is this penance: Peter is not asking them to pay for the crucifixion, but to change their minds about the man they crucified and walk the other way.

Blotted out. Wiped away (exaleiphthēnai), and the picture is exact. Ancient ink sat on the surface of papyrus, and a wet sponge took it off and left the sheet clean. Not the debt reduced, not the file put in a drawer: wiped off. David prayed for it: “blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1, 9). God promised it: “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake” (Isaiah 43:25). And at the cross he did it, cancelling the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14).

Wiped by the death they demanded. That cross was the one their own city had shouted for in front of Pilate (Luke 23:21). The death they caused is the death that cleans their page. Their sin is not overlooked; Jesus himself, crucified at their demand, is the way it is removed. There is no rejection of him so complete that his blood cannot wipe it out.

The private file. Ask a man at eleven in the morning whether his sins are forgiven and he will say yes. Ask him what happens at three in the morning, when a particular memory arrives, the thing he said, the person he damaged, the year he does not talk about, and a different answer comes out. He agrees that God wiped the record, goes on consulting a copy he keeps privately, and calls it humility. It is a quiet insistence that the sponge did not work. God keeps no private copy. If the record can come off the page for a crowd whose city murdered the Son of God, it can come off yours. If you still struggle, that does not mean you are unforgiven; it is a weak faith wrestling with a strong memory, and Christ does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20).

How do I stop keeping my own copy? Name the thing to God plainly, once more if you need to, and thank him that it is gone: “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Where you can, put right what you damaged, because restitution is part of repentance. When the memory comes at three in the morning, answer it with Scripture rather than argument: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). Your accuser is not God; his verdict on you in Christ is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). If the memory still crushes you, speak to a pastor or a mature friend. You were not meant to carry it alone.

Is it fair that men who called for the cross could be wiped clean so quickly? It was not cheap: God did not lower his standard to forgive them; he met it himself, in his Son. And the objection often hides another: that the person raising it needs the sponge less. But the respectable worshipper on his way to the three o’clock prayers needed the same blotting out as the man who shouted at Pilate, for there is no distinction: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:22–23). Grace is not unfair to the good. It is the only hope of anyone.

In everyday life. Is there something you have repented of in your mind but not yet with your feet: a habit, a relationship, a way of speaking? The record against you was nailed to Christ’s cross; turn today, leaning on the Spirit he has given rather than on fresh resolutions.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who turn will know refreshment from the Lord’s own presence, and Jesus, who must remain in heaven for the time God has fixed, will return to put right everything the prophets promised.

Times of refreshing. The word (anapsyxis) means a breathing space, relief from pressure; the Greek Old Testament uses it when the plague of frogs stopped and Pharaoh saw that there was a respite (Exodus 8:15). And the relief comes not from a change in circumstances but from the presence of the Lord, which is the difference between a man whose troubles have lifted and a man who has stopped being alone inside them.

Whom heaven must receive. The one appointed beforehand as their Messiah will be sent from heaven again. Until then, “must”: God has determined it, the same sort of “must” that stood over the cross. There is an appointed span and Jesus is keeping it, which settles every claim that he has quietly returned already. Then comes the restoring of all things (apokatastasis): the renewal of all creation, which Jesus called the new world (Matthew 19:28) and John the making of all things new (Revelation 21:5).

Spoken by the prophets. Isaiah, among many: “behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The God who spoke by them long ago will finish what he began: every ruined thing that belongs to him will be put right, and we will see his face.

The not-yet. The restoration is certain, its date is fixed, and it has not yet come. The refreshing is available now, and it is not the same thing: a breathing space in a world still broken. Anybody told that the Christian life ought to feel like the new creation already has been sold something Peter did not offer. What he offers is enough air to keep going, and the certainty that the one who fixed the date is coming back.

What will the restoration of all things look like? Scripture gives glimpses, not a map. A renewed creation, not an escape from it: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Resurrection bodies like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21). No more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), no curse (Revelation 22:3), no sin. And at its centre God himself: the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). Everything good in this world, healed, and far more besides.

Will everyone be saved in the end? “Restoring all things” is the anchor text of those who teach that hell will finally empty; the Greek word gave the doctrine its historic name, from Origen’s day to our own. The hope is understandable, but Peter defines his own term two verses later and leaves no room for it: “every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people” (v. 23). The restoration he means is the healing of the world, not the reversal of the judgment; and this whole sermon is a plea to repent precisely because that judgment is real.

Does Christ’s return depend on Israel’s repentance? Dispensational Christians read Peter as offering the kingdom to Israel, postponed when they refused. But the day of Christ’s return is fixed by the Father (1:7), and does not wait on any nation’s response. What depends on their repentance is whether they will be ready.

Where Christians differ: restoration of all things. Some (universalists) take restoring all things to mean that every person will eventually be saved. Others (dispensationalists) take it as an earthly millennial kingdom for Israel. This commentary’s view: the restoration is of all things about which God spoke by the prophets, the renewal of creation, which the prophets also say includes judgment on the wicked (Isaiah 66:24). And the next verses warn that those who refuse Christ will be destroyed (v. 23). It is the new creation at Christ’s single return, not the salvation of all, nor an interim kingdom. Dispensational believers share the same hope of Christ’s return, and the difference with them is held in charity.

Uncertain wording. The noun for “refreshing” occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and Peter’s sentence is compressed. It is not certain whether the times of refreshing are the final restoration at Christ’s return, or a refreshing that comes now, from the Lord’s presence, to those who repent. The likely meaning is both: they begin now, in measure, and come in full when he returns.

parallels.desc: new heavens and a new earth

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the prophet like Moses whom Moses himself promised, God’s final spokesman, and whatever he says must be heard and obeyed.

Moses said. Peter reaches for the promise in the books of Moses that another prophet like Moses is coming (Deuteronomy 18:15–19). Israel waited for that prophet; crowds would later ask whether Jesus was the one (John 1:21; 6:14; 7:40). Peter says he is.

A voice they could live through. At the foot of the mountain the people heard God speak out of the fire, and begged Moses: “Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.” God said they were right, and made the promise Peter is quoting: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth” (Deuteronomy 18:16–18). What he finally sent was his Son, who could be listened to by fishermen on a hillside without anybody dying of it.

A prophet like me. Moses spoke with God face to face, mediated a covenant, did signs, brought a people out of slavery and gave them God’s word. All are true of Jesus, and truer: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6).

Listen to him. Not consider him, not weigh him against other authorities: listen. The Father said the same at the transfiguration, with Moses himself standing there: “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” (Luke 9:35). The obligation to obey Jesus does not originate with Christians; it was laid on Israel by Moses, in the law they revere.

He bore what they could never have borne. Moses once begged to be blotted out of God’s book for his sinning people, and God would not take him in their place (Exodus 32:32–33). The prophet like Moses gave himself for his people, and the Father accepted the offering. He is not only the voice they could bear to hear; he bore what they could never have borne, and rose to speak peace to them.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Chiefly by listening to Scripture, because the Prophet speaks there: in his words in the Gospels, the teaching of the apostles he sent, and the Old Testament he said testified about him. Read the Bible as his word to you, all of it, not only the parts you like: “whatever he tells you”. Do not look for him in inner impressions that go beyond or against what he has said in Scripture. And listening always means obeying: “be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22). You will never obey him perfectly; he obeyed the Father perfectly in your place, and that obedience is counted as yours, so you can open his commands without dread. Is there one you have been politely ignoring? Ask his Spirit for strength to do it today.

Does this verse point to Muhammad? Many Muslim teachers claim it for Muhammad, on the ground that he came from among the brothers of Israel, from Ishmael’s line. The text will not carry it. In Deuteronomy “from among your brothers” is used repeatedly of a fellow Israelite and set directly against the foreigner: Israel’s king must be one from among your brothers; you may not put a foreigner over you (Deuteronomy 17:15). The prophet is promised from inside Israel, as the answer to Israel’s own request at Israel’s own mountain; and Peter is settling a question his hearers already had (John 1:21; 7:40), not inventing one.

parallels.desc: a prophet like me from among you

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To refuse the Prophet God has sent is to be cut off from God’s people, and all the prophets since Samuel have been pointing to these very days.

Destroyed from the people. The hardest sentence in the chapter. In Deuteronomy God says of the man who will not listen, “I myself will require it of him” (Deuteronomy 18:19). Peter finishes the sentence with Leviticus in mind: “shall be cut off from his people”, the fate of anyone who will not humble himself in repentance on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:29). To refuse the Prophet is like standing outside on the one day in the year when the nation’s sin was dealt with. That sacrifice has now been offered once for all in Jesus (Hebrews 9:11–12), so to refuse him is to refuse the only atonement there is. From now on, belonging to God’s people turns on one’s response to Jesus.

From Samuel. With Samuel the line of the prophets properly begins after Moses, and Samuel anointed David, so the prophetic succession and the royal line start on the same page. The whole tradition, prophets and kings together, has been pointing toward these days.

These days. An ordinary afternoon at the three o’clock prayers. A Christian in a life that feels entirely unremarkable is living inside the period the prophets strained forward to see; they searched and inquired carefully about this grace, and angels long to look into it (1 Peter 1:10–12).

Why the warning is not cruel. A warning is cruel if it is false, or too late to act on, or if there is no way out. This one is true, it is early, and Peter has just described the way out. And a reader who fears he has not listened well enough is already listening: the warning is for those who will not hear, not for those anxious that they hear too faintly. If someone you love has heard the gospel and is still refusing it, do not stop warning them, and do not stop loving them. Warn with tears, not with triumph, and point to the way out in the same breath.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse speaks of those who hear the Prophet and refuse him, and they carry the greater guilt (Luke 12:47–48). But Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12), and how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (Romans 10:14). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a gospel they never knew, but for their sin against the light God gave them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and God judges them justly. We hold, with many in the Reformed tradition, that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession both say (1689 10.3; Westminster 10.3). Grieving parents may take real comfort: Scripture shows a God tender toward little ones (2 Samuel 12:23; Mark 10:14), and many Reformed pastors have believed that all who die in infancy are among his elect. The answer to this question is not speculation but mission: it is why the church sends and goes.

parallels.desc: Nathan’s prophecy in Samuel’s days

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s hearers are heirs of God’s promise to Abraham, and God has sent his risen Servant to them first, to give them the blessing promised to all nations: being turned from their wickedness.

Sons of the covenant. Peter ends by telling them who they are: not late arrivals to a religion, but heirs. Everything he has been quoting at them is family property.

In your offspring. Then the covenant text itself (Genesis 22:18; 12:3), the promise to Abraham of blessing for all nations through his offspring. Paul says the offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The gospel to the Gentiles is no departure from the Old Testament; it is its fulfilment.

To you first. To Israel first, then to the nations (13:46; Romans 1:16). In the city that killed him, to the crowd that asked for a murderer instead, the offer arrives before it goes anywhere else in the world. That is the pattern of the whole book, and a window onto the character of God, who deals with the people who have wronged him worst by putting them at the front of the queue.

To bless you. Not what we usually mean by the word: health, safety, a scan that came back clear. Peter defines the blessing promised to Abraham for the whole world as being turned away from your own wickedness: not first prosperity but forgiveness and transformation. Jesus saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), not in them. The man at the gate asked for a coin and was given his legs. Israel wanted a Messiah who would deal with the Romans and was offered something worth incalculably more: to be turned out of their own wickedness by the one they had nailed to a cross.

On the mountain of the substitute. The promise is repeated in Genesis 22, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in a thicket. The blessing of the whole world through Abraham’s line is promised at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no ram was found, and the knife was not stopped. Abraham got his boy back down the mountain. God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

The blessing has reached even us. God sent his Servant not to buy off the people who had killed him, nor to excuse them and leave them as they were, but to take hold of them one at a time and turn every one of them from their wickedness. The Son who was not spared comes carrying the blessing he bought with his blood. In Abraham’s offspring all the families of the earth are blessed, and the blessing has reached even us.

Two lives. Suppose a man were given a long, easy life, with everyone he loves kept safe, and arrived at the end exactly as he began, still governed by the temper, the appetite, the coldness or the dishonesty he had at twenty. By this verse’s definition he was never blessed at all. And suppose another man loses most of what he owned and half of what he hoped for, and is prised loose over thirty years from the thing that was quietly destroying him. Peter says God blessed the second one.

So is it wrong to pray for health and provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and God delights to give good gifts to his children (Matthew 7:11). Health, work, safety and family are real blessings; ask for them and thank him for them. But they are not the greatest blessing, nor the measure of God’s favour. Pray more for the blessing Peter names: that God would turn you, and those you love, from sin and toward himself. If he grants the lesser gifts, receive them gladly. If he withholds them, he has not withheld the greater one.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. Peter credits the healing to the name of Jesus and to faith in that name (v. 16), and he means a person, not a formula (see vv. 6–7). Faith is the hand that receives what the name offers, and what it offers is the power of the one who conquered death, for a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth sat daily at the gate of a temple he could not enter, with an empty hand held out. In the name of Jesus he walked in.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. Programmes, therapy and public help have real worth, but they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

keyVerse.quote: God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.
keyVerse.note: The last sentence of Peter’s sermon gathers up the whole chapter. The Servant God raised from the dead is the one whose name raised the lame man, and he comes first to the very people who killed him. The blessing he brings, promised to Abraham for all the families of the earth, is not first health or wealth but being turned from our wickedness.

3.reflection:
The lame man asked for a coin and was given his legs (vv. 3–8). In what ways do we ask God for too little, and what does this chapter suggest about what he wants to give?

Peter refused the credit both for power and for piety (v. 12). Where are you tempted to let people think well of you for what God has done, and how can you turn their attention to Jesus instead?

Peter tells the crowd plainly that they killed the Author of life, then calls them brothers and offers them forgiveness (vv. 14–19). What does this teach us about how to speak about sin, and how does it answer someone who fears they are beyond forgiveness?

Peter defines God’s blessing as being turned from our wickedness (v. 26). How would your prayers for yourself and for others change if you believed that this is the greatest blessing?

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 3 Peter and John healed a man lame from birth at the temple gate, and Peter told the crowd that the Jesus they had denied was the Author of life, raised by God. Chapter 4 opens while he is still speaking.

The message. The name of the crucified and risen Jesus cannot be silenced, because it is the only name by which anyone is saved, and the God who rules even the worst deeds of his enemies gives his people boldness to keep speaking it. Opposition does not stop the word; it drives the church to prayer, and prayer sends it out again with fresh courage and open hands.

Why it was said. Luke writes to make Theophilus sure of what he was taught (see the introduction). Here he shows that the very council that condemned Jesus opposed the gospel from the start, and could not refute it, only forbid it.

How the chapter makes its case. Peter and John are arrested for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus, yet the believers grow to about five thousand men (vv. 1–4). Before the Sanhedrin, Peter, filled with the Spirit, names the crucified and risen Jesus as the power behind the healing, the rejected stone made the cornerstone, and the only name by which we must be saved (vv. 5–12). The council cannot deny the sign but forbids the name, and the apostles answer that they cannot stop speaking (vv. 13–22). Back with the church, they pray Psalm 2, and ask not for safety but for boldness; God shakes the place and fills them all with the Spirit (vv. 23–31). The same Spirit opens their hands, so that no one is in need, and Barnabas gives a field (vv. 32–37).

Where it leads. The chapter is a trial about one name. The council that tried Jesus now tries his servants, and Peter finishes his master’s own sentence to them: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Luke 20:17). The church prays about “your holy servant Jesus”, whose suffering God planned and whose name he honours with healing, and the Spirit Jesus poured out from his throne fills the room. Even the closing generosity is his: he became poor so that his people could open their hands.

For us. We are not asked to be naturally brave, only to stay near Jesus, to pray when we are threatened, and to keep saying what we have seen and heard of him. The God who turned the murder of his Son into the world’s salvation holds every threat we face, and he still gives boldness, and open hands, to those who ask.

keyVerse.quote: And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the name of Jesus: the council asks by what name, then forbids the name, and the church prays for healing through the name. This verse says why the name cannot be silenced: it is the only one God has given for the rescue of the world. Spoken by a prisoner to the court that condemned Jesus, it is both the narrowest claim in the chapter and its widest invitation.

4.reflection:
The council could not deny the healed man standing in front of it, yet it ordered silence (vv. 14–18). Why is unbelief so often a matter of the will rather than the evidence, and how should that shape the way we pray for, and speak to, friends who do not believe?

Peter tells the court that “there is salvation in no one else” (v. 12). Why do many people find this offensive, and how can we hold it with both conviction and humility, as Peter did when he included himself in “we must be saved”?

Under threat, the church began its prayer with God as the Maker and Ruler of everything, and asked not for safety but for boldness (vv. 24–30). What do your own prayers under pressure reveal about what you most want to keep safe?

The Spirit who filled their mouths also opened their hands, so that no one among them was in need (vv. 31–37). Who in your church is overlooked, in need or easily written off, and what would it look like to be a Barnabas to them?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Opposition cannot stop the name of Jesus, because it is God’s only way of salvation and he has already vindicated it. The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection, yet the church grows to about five thousand men (vv. 1–4). Before the very council that condemned Jesus, Peter, filled with the Spirit, explains the healing by the name of the crucified and risen Jesus, the rejected stone God has made the cornerstone, and declares that there is salvation in no one else (vv. 5–12). The judges cannot deny the sign standing in front of them, so they forbid the name (vv. 13–18). The apostles reply that they must obey God and cannot stop speaking (vv. 19–20), and the council can only threaten and release them (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The exclusivity of Christ

Verse 12 is among the clearest statements in Scripture that salvation is found in Christ alone, and it is spoken in a courtroom, to men who could imprison Peter for it. Why the claim is exclusive, and why the one door stands open to all, is treated in the note on v. 12.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Two laymen without rabbinic training stood in the middle of Israel’s supreme court, and their boldness astonished the men trying them. Now: The same Spirit is given to every believer. Boldness in the New Testament is not a temperament but a gift, asked for and granted, and it is perfectly compatible with being frightened.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple authorities come down on Peter and John because they are teaching the people without anyone’s permission and proclaiming that the resurrection of the dead has begun in Jesus.

As they were speaking. They do not wait for the sermon to finish. The priests were the men on duty; the captain of the temple commanded the temple police, with the power of arrest; the Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and cooperated with Rome. They gave the five books of Moses a unique authority and denied that there is any resurrection, or angel, or spirit (23:8). Their whole position rested on the temple continuing as it was.

Greatly annoyed. Luke names two causes. The first is that the apostles were teaching the people: two laymen with no standing, instructing a crowd on the priests’ own premises without anybody’s permission.

In Jesus the resurrection. The second is what they taught. Men who had built a career on denying that the dead rise heard that one man already had, and heard him named. “In Jesus” means that his resurrection is the proof and guarantee that the dead will be raised: he is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20–23), the first of a sure harvest, and every believer’s grave will one day be emptied by the power that emptied his. Weeks earlier these officials had thought the matter closed with a sealed and guarded tomb (Matthew 27:62–66). Now it is back in their own courtyard, with a healed man standing next to it.

The third irritant. Luke need not state a third, because the previous chapter supplied it: the apostles were telling Jerusalem that its rulers had handed the Messiah to Pilate and killed him (3:13–15).

He had answered them once already. When the Sadducees tried a riddle against the resurrection on Jesus himself, in these same courts, he answered from the books of Moses they accepted, where God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: “he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him” (Luke 20:27–38). They had no reply. Now the argument has been settled in a way no riddle could answer: the man who told them that God is the God of the living is alive himself, and his name has just made a lame man walk.

Should I expect opposition if I speak about Jesus? Some, though not always and not usually in this form. Jesus said, “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20), and Paul that “all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). In some places that means prison or death; in others mockery, exclusion, a lost promotion or a cold family. Do not go looking for it or provoke it by being needlessly offensive. But do not be surprised by it, or take it as a sign that you have done wrong. Often it means the gospel has touched something people would rather not have touched.
verseByVerse.note: The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest. The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The authorities can lock up the preachers but not what they have preached: while the apostles spend the night in custody, the number of believing men grows to about five thousand.

Until the next day. By the rules later written down in the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, capital cases were not to be tried at night, which makes the night hearing of Jesus all the more irregular. So the two men spend the night in custody: the first Christian imprisonment. By the end of the book it will be so routine that Luke barely comments on it.

But many believed. They took the preachers into custody and left the sermon at large, as Paul would write from his own chains: “I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!” (2 Timothy 2:9).

About five thousand. The word means adult males (andrōn), perhaps heads of households. Add wives and households, and the community may already be well past ten thousand: from a hundred and twenty, to three thousand, to this. No wonder the authorities were alarmed.

Along the master’s road. Jesus too was seized at night by the temple authorities and led before the council at daybreak (Luke 22:54, 66), and he had told his disciples that being delivered up for his name would be their opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). But the roads part in the morning. His night ended at a cross; theirs ends in release and a sermon, and the master who walked the road first walks it now beside them.

In everyday life. Perhaps you once spoke to someone about Christ and saw nothing come of it. That conversation is in God’s hands now, and it may still be working in a heart you cannot see.

My church is small and getting smaller. Has God failed? No. He has promised to build his church, and “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), but not that every congregation will grow, or grow now. Ask honestly whether your church is faithful to the gospel, prayerful, loving and outward-looking, and repent of anything that is not. Then keep sowing and leave the harvest to the Lord. He asks faithfulness, not size, and a small faithful church is precious to him.
verseByVerse.note: Hearings were not normally held at night.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The supreme council of Israel, led by the high-priestly family that had condemned Jesus, assembles in full to try two fishermen.

Rulers and elders and scribes. Luke’s shorthand for the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council (by later Jewish tradition seventy-one men), with authority over religious law, the temple and, within the limits Rome allowed, life and death. This body had condemned Jesus a few months earlier. The room and most of the faces are the same; only the defendants have changed.

With Annas the high priest and Caiaphas. Caiaphas held the office, from about AD 18 to 36, so “Annas the high priest” has been produced as evidence that Luke did not know Jerusalem. But Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until a Roman prefect removed him, and by the law of Moses the high priesthood was for life. Five of his sons held the office after him, and so did his son-in-law Caiaphas.
