Annas ran the family firm, out of the chair but still in charge, which is why the arrested Jesus was taken to him first (John 18:13, 24). Luke, who dates John the Baptist’s ministry to Annas and Caiaphas together (Luke 3:2), is not confused: he names both the office-holder and the power.

John and Alexander. Probably members of the family; a Jonathan son of Annas later became high priest, and some manuscripts read Jonathan here. Names like these, which lead nowhere in the story, suggest Luke was drawing on people who remembered who was in the room.

The arithmetic of the morning. On one side, the dynasty that controlled the temple, its treasury, its police and its courts; on the other, two fishermen fresh from a cell, with no lawyer and no allies in the building. By the end of the session it will be the judges who cannot think what to do.

Seated at the right hand. The last time Jesus stood before this council they asked whether he was the Christ, and he told them: “from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke 22:69). The prisoner of that morning has taken his seat, and this morning’s session, with a man standing on his own feet by his name, is held in his sight.

How should I think about powerful people who oppose the faith? Neither with fear nor with hatred. Not with fear, because the Lord laughs at the rulers who take counsel against him (Psalm 2:4); their power is real but borrowed and temporary. Not with hatred, because Jesus told us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and because some of them will be converted: soon “a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith” (6:7), and Saul of Tarsus had been trained by a member of this council, Gamaliel (5:34; 22:3). Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honour their office where you can, and keep speaking the truth.
verseByVerse.note: The rulers, elders and scribes made up the Sanhedrin. Annas had been high priest earlier and remained head of the family; Caiaphas was the serving high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council does not deny the miracle; it asks by what power and in whose name it was done, a question that hides a trap and is, without their meaning it, exactly the right question.

In the midst. According to later Jewish tradition the Sanhedrin sat in a semicircle, every member able to see every other, with the accused in the open space at the centre: a room designed to make a man feel the weight of the institution before a word is spoken.

By what power or by what name? It sounds neutral and is not. Asking a man to name the power and the name behind a wonder is the language of magic and exorcism, where everything depended on which being you had invoked. And there is a trap under it. Israel’s law prescribed death for a man who worked a sign or wonder to draw the people after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Give the wrong answer, and the charge need not be disorderly preaching. It could be capital.

The small contempt. They do not ask how he healed this man, but by what power “did you do this”: an unnamed “this”, as if it were a mere incident. And the “you” is emphatic in the Greek, probably scornful: people like you?

The old move. When Jesus cast out demons, the accusation was not that nothing had happened but that he did it by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Luke 11:15). It is a durable tactic: concede the event and poison the source.

The right question. Without meaning to, the council has asked the right question, and asked it before. In these same courts the chief priests, scribes and elders had said to Jesus, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority” (Luke 20:2). Now they ask his servants, and this time they get a straight answer. By what power and by what name: the whole book of Acts exists to answer that question, and its one answer is the name of the man they asked first.

How do I answer when someone asks why I believe? Be ready, as Peter tells every Christian, “to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you”, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). You need not be an expert. Start with Jesus: who he is, what he did, and that God raised him from the dead. Then say honestly what he has done for you. If you cannot answer a hard question, say so and offer to find out. Think through, before you are asked, three or four sentences that explain the gospel and why you trust it.

parallels.desc: by what authority?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled with the Spirit, as Jesus had promised his witnesses in the hour of trial, Peter answers the court with courtesy and shows what it is really examining: a kindness done to a crippled man.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. Luke has said it of Peter before, and will say it of the whole church before the chapter is out (2:4; 4:31). Pentecost has not worn off (on repeated filling, see v. 31). A man about to speak for his life is given what he needs at the hour he needs it, and not before.

Rulers of the people and elders. Peter begins courteously. Boldness in this chapter never once shades into rudeness; being obnoxious is not being faithful.

A good deed. He takes the vague “this” of their question and names it. “Examined” is courtroom language, and he reads the charge sheet aloud in words nobody would want in the minutes: we are on trial for making a cripple walk. Without raising his voice, he has made the court’s position sound absurd, which it was.

Has been healed. One word carries the whole speech, and English hides it. The verb (sesōstai) is the ordinary Greek word for saved. Peter uses it here of a man’s ankles; three verses later, of the whole world’s only hope (v. 12). The council asked about a body, and he will answer about a soul with the same word.

The promise kept. Jesus had promised exactly this: “when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say” (Luke 12:11–12; 21:12–15). In the high priest’s court it came true to the letter. The Lord does not send his people into the dock and leave them there; he puts into weak mouths the calm and courage he himself showed before the same judges.

What it does not mean. The promise is no licence to go into the pulpit unprepared and call it faith. Jesus specified the courtroom, not the study, and the same New Testament tells a teacher to be “a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). What is promised is that a believer put on the spot for Christ, in a courtroom, a hostile family or an interview, will not be left to improvise alone.

What if I freeze when I am put on the spot? Most of us have, and Peter himself once did, beside a fire, in front of a servant girl. The promise is not that you will never feel fear, but that you are not alone in it. Pray before hard conversations, even a sentence under your breath. One true, kind sentence about Jesus is better than a flustered argument. If you fail, do what Peter did after the courtyard: go back to the Lord, receive his forgiveness, and try again. The Spirit who filled Peter in the council lives in you, and he delights to help weak people speak.

parallels.desc: I will give you a mouth and wisdom

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter gives the council the name it asked for: the healed man stands there by the power of Jesus, whom they crucified and God raised, the stone they rejected and God has made the cornerstone.

Let it be known. They asked for a name; they get it, with the crucifixion and the resurrection attached, and without a syllable of diplomacy. “Whom you crucified, whom God raised”: what you did, and what God did about it. It is the gospel in one sentence, said to the men who had done the crucifying.

Standing before you well. Peter can point as he says it, because the healed man is in the chamber (v. 14). All his life he had been carried to the temple gate and no further; this morning the court’s exhibit has walked into the supreme court of Israel on his own feet.

The stone that was rejected. Peter quotes Psalm 118:22, from the last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, whose lines about the one who comes in the name of the Lord a crowd had shouted as Jesus rode into the city a few months before. He adjusts the psalm deliberately, putting in “by you”, so that the builders are the men in front of him: not guilty of a technical mistake, but of looking at Jesus and judging him worthless.

Finishing his master’s sentence. Jesus had quoted this very verse to these same men, in the temple, after the parable of the tenants who killed the owner’s son, and “they perceived that he had told this parable against them” (Luke 20:17–19). Peter is finishing his master’s sentence before the same audience.

The spoil heap and the corner. Judging which block goes where is the whole of a builder’s competence. These men examined this stone with the best professional judgment in the nation and threw it on the spoil heap. God took it off the heap and set it at the corner, where every line in the building is measured from. Jesus is the cornerstone of the new temple, the church, “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8). Every living stone in every age rests on the one the world despised: “This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvelous in our eyes” (Psalm 118:23).

Wrong about the most important thing. The most qualified people in the nation, with every appearance of due process, were wrong about the most important thing that has ever happened. It is a caution against being impressed by consensus, and a comfort to anyone weighed by people with every right to weigh him and found to be of no value.

What does it mean to build my life on the cornerstone? Taking your measurements from Jesus rather than anyone else. Your worth is set by what he says about you, not by the verdict of employers, family or friends; your choices are lined up with his word; your hope rests on his promises, not your plans. Return to him daily in Scripture and prayer, and ask of each decision: does this fit the line of the cornerstone?

parallels.desc: the stone the builders rejected

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is not one Saviour among many but the only one: God has given his name, and no other, for the rescue of the whole world. Peter includes himself in that “we”, and holds the door open to the very judges who condemned his Lord.

Salvation in no one else. The sentence the chapter is famous for answers a question about a pair of ankles. The word for saved that described the healing in verse 9 now runs into its largest meaning. Saved here means rescued from the guilt of sin, from the just anger of a holy God and from death itself, and brought whole into his presence, of which the man’s new legs were a small picture.

No other name under heaven. Every clause tightens it. No other name: no other person, no other way. Under heaven: anywhere in the world, not merely in Israel. The name is given, by God, a gift handed down rather than a prize achieved. And the last phrase carries a quiet necessity: “by which we must be saved”. This is the exclusive claim of the gospel, spoken to the highest religious court of the only nation that knew the true God.

In the flow. The name is the thread of the whole episode: the healing was done in the name (3:6), the council asked by what name (4:7), and it will soon forbid the name (4:17–18). At Pentecost Peter quoted Joel’s promise that “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (2:21); now he says whose name that is. And if there is only one name, every nation must hear it (1:8).

Said by a prisoner. Peter says it under arrest, before a court that could flog him and had recently arranged an execution, answering a question that could have trapped him into a capital charge. He had every incentive to find a broader formula, Jesus as one road among several; instead he tells them that the man they threw away is the only name there is. The narrowness people object to was spoken by a prisoner who gained nothing by it, and it included an invitation to his judges.

His name over the only door. God did not leave the world to find its own way back to him; he came himself, in his Son, and wrote his name over the only door. The name Jesus means “the LORD saves”, and he has never failed to save anyone who called on it.

How can Jesus be the only way? It is called narrow and arrogant, but three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation is found in him and nowhere else, not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way, infinitely wide in the welcome, for “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save. A man can be sincerely wrong, like one who drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Reason for God, that the story of the blind men and the elephant gives itself away: the teller can say that each blind man grasps only part of the truth only because he claims to see the whole elephant himself, so the belief that no religion has the whole truth is just as exclusive a claim as the one it rejects.

Could people be saved through Christ without ever knowing him? Inclusivist Christians think so, pointing to Old Testament believers, to Cornelius before Peter arrived (10:1–4), and to Romans 2:14–16. But Old Testament saints trusted God’s promise of the coming Saviour; Cornelius was told to send for Peter, who would declare “a message by which you will be saved” (11:14); and Romans 2 is about how all are judged, not how any are saved. The plain reading is the likelier one: there is salvation in no one else. As for those who never hear, Scripture’s answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Romans 1:20), none seek God on their own (Romans 3:11), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. And therefore we must go and tell (Romans 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deuteronomy 29:29).

How do I say this to friends of other faiths without arrogance? By remembering that you stand where the lame man stood, with nothing to boast of except what was done for you. Listen first, and understand what your friend actually believes; respect his sincerity and the good in his life. Speak of Jesus himself, not of your religion’s superiority, and admit your own sin and need. Be honest that you believe Jesus is the only Saviour because he said so (John 14:6), and explain why that is good news: God has provided the way himself. Live the love you speak of, and pray, for only God can open a heart.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways of salvation? Pluralists hold that all religions lead to God; inclusivists that people may be saved by Christ through other religions, without knowing him. This commentary’s view: “no other name” is unmistakable. Even Israel’s religion, without Christ, could not save. Salvation is found in Jesus alone, through faith in him (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). This is why the gospel must be preached to every nation (Romans 10:13–15), not with arrogance, but with urgency and love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court is astonished at the free, bold speech of two untrained laymen and recognises where it came from: they had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing beside them, it has nothing to say.

The boldness. The word (parrēsia), boldness or frankness, carried weight in the Greek world: in classical Athens it named the citizen’s freedom to speak his mind in the assembly, which a slave or a foreigner did not have. Two prisoners fetched up from a cell are talking like free men. It is a fair candidate for the theme word of Acts: the church prays for it (v. 29) and receives it (v. 31), and the book’s last line leaves Paul under house arrest, proclaiming the kingdom “with all boldness” (28:31). It is the Spirit’s gift.

Uneducated, common men. Not illiterate, but without formal training in the rabbinic schools: no letters after the name. Common men (idiōtai) means laymen, amateurs as opposed to professionals. They had not sat at the feet of a Gamaliel, as the young Saul of Tarsus had, yet Galilean fishermen are arguing from Scripture with the scholars of Israel.

They had been with Jesus. Recognised is the word Luke used of the crowd recognising the beggar (3:10): not a guess but an identification. Something in these two men made a hostile court think of the prisoner it had condemned, who had also astonished them without formal training: “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?” (John 7:15). Time spent with Jesus leaves a residue which outlasts any argument, and those who dislike him are often the first to spot it. He gives his own freedom to those who have no right to it, his own boldness to those who once ran, and his own likeness to those who stay near him, until the world looks at ordinary believers and sees their Lord.

Nothing to say in opposition. You cannot argue with a walking man, and Luke gives the healed man not one line of dialogue. He stood where everybody could see him, which is very largely what the church has been asked to do ever since.

Do I need training before I can speak for Jesus? Not to be a witness. Peter and John spoke of what they had seen and heard (v. 20), and every believer can say who Christ is and what he has done. But they were not untaught: they had spent about three years with the best teacher who ever lived, and Peter’s answer is full of Scripture. So learn all you can, but do not wait until you feel qualified: the fear of not being impressive is usually a love of being approved.

How do I spend time with Jesus, now that he is in heaven? We meet him now by his Spirit through his word. Read the Gospels slowly and often, watching how he speaks, treats people and prays. Pray to him, not only in emergencies. Meet him at the Lord’s Table. Obey him, for “whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me”, and to such a person Jesus promises to show himself (John 14:21). Keep company with others who love him. The residue the council noticed was not produced in a weekend; it grows by daily nearness.
verseByVerse.note: “Uneducated, common men” means they had no formal training in the law under a rabbi — not that they were illiterate.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In private the council admits that the sign cannot be denied, and in the same breath looks for a way to suppress it: their problem was never the evidence but their will.

They conferred with one another. How does Luke know what was said in a closed session? The council was not sealed: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were members (John 3:1–2; Luke 23:50–51), soon a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7), and Saul worked closely with the council’s leaders (9:1–2). Men who had sat in that room, or near it, changed sides.

What shall we do with these men? The council had asked the same about Jesus. After the raising of Lazarus they said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs” (John 11:47). That meeting ended with Caiaphas advising that one man should die for the people, and John adds that he spoke better than he knew: Jesus would die for the nation, and “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:50–52). Their worst decision became the means of the world’s salvation. Now the same men meet over the same problem, and the problem is still Jesus.

With these men. At Pentecost a crowd told it had crucified the Messiah cried out, “Brothers, what shall we do?” (2:37). This council, told the same, asks what to do with these men. One is asking to be changed; the other, how to make the problem go away.

We cannot deny it. This is a hostile court in closed session, with no audience to perform for and every motive to find a flaw. They examine the case intending to destroy it, find that denial is not open to them, and in the next breath resolve to shut it down. Anyone who thinks unbelief is at bottom an information problem should read this: a case conceded in private by qualified, hostile investigators, and at once suppressed. Their problem was not proof, but unwillingness.

What it does not mean. That does not make evidence worthless. Peter’s speech is an appeal to evidence, the healed man is in the room as evidence, and Luke wrote so that his reader might have certainty (Luke 1:4). Facts are needed, but not enough: a man may be convinced in his mind and unwilling in his heart, and it is the heart that decides.

Only God can change a will like that. And he does. The risen Lord condemned in that chamber went on to win men from its own circle, including a young Pharisee who would call himself the foremost of sinners. No heart is so closed that Christ cannot open it, and every believer is someone whose unwillingness he overcame.

In everyday life. Ask yourself the council’s question, and Pentecost’s. When God’s word confronts you with something uncomfortable, are you asking what shall I do, or what shall I do with this? The first leads to life; the second to the closed door of verse 17.

Why won’t my friend believe when the evidence seems so clear? Because unbelief is not only in the head. Pride, fear of others, love of a way of life, or simple unwillingness to bow to God can hold a person back when the arguments are answered; “people loved the darkness rather than the light” (John 3:19). So keep giving reasons, patiently and kindly, because God uses them, but do not expect the right argument to do what only God can do. Pray for your friend’s heart, not only his mind, that the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness”, would shine in his heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). And keep loving him, whatever he decides.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having lost the argument but still holding the power, the council bans the one thing that matters most: speaking in the name of Jesus.

That it may spread no further. No rival account, no enquiry into fraud: straight to damage control. They answer a question about God with a regulation, which is what institutions reach for when they have lost the argument but still hold the power. The measure meant to stop the name travelling is recorded in a book that carried it to Rome.

In this name. They do not prohibit healing, gathering, charity or prayer, but a name. Jesus had said it would come to this: “You will be hated by all for my name’s sake” (Luke 21:17). The council grasped the essential point better than some of the church’s friends since: everything in this movement depends on one person. And in private they say only “this name”, never once pronouncing the name of Jesus. The Lord whose name his enemies would not even say has been given the name above every name, and every tongue will one day confess it (Philippians 2:9–11).

Not to speak or teach at all. A direct order from the highest religious authority in Israel: the first ban on evangelism. Many have followed.

Soup without the sentence. Christian activity of most kinds is welcome nearly everywhere: the food bank, the night shelter, the hospice. It is the speech that draws objection, the claim that this particular man is Lord. Institutions happy to fund the soup often ask that his name not be mentioned: the council’s exact position. The church’s answer is in the next verse.

In everyday life. The world often says: believe what you like, but don’t speak in Jesus’ name. Notice whether you have already given in without anyone asking, doing the good works and quietly leaving out the name. If you have, the name you left out belongs to the one who forgives; take it up again.

What it does not mean. Comfortable Western Christians most of all should admit the enormous distance between being thought awkward at work and a night in a cell, let alone the flogging these apostles get in the next chapter or what believers in many countries will face this week. A man who finds a conversation uncomfortable and calls it persecution has not read the passage he is quoting.

My employer has told me not to talk about my faith at work. What should I do? Think carefully about what is being asked. A reasonable rule about working time, or a ban on pressuring colleagues or customers, is not a command to deny Christ; obey it gladly, while answering honestly when someone asks a direct question in a break or outside work. Be a diligent, kind and truthful worker; that itself speaks. But if you are told to lie, to affirm what Scripture calls sin, or never to admit that you are a Christian, you have reached the line in the next verse: obey God, respectfully, and accept the cost. Seek advice from your pastor and, where needed, from Christian legal organisations.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and John leave it to the court to judge whether God or men should be obeyed, and say plainly that they cannot stop speaking of what they have seen and heard.

You must judge. What is usually missed is the form: Peter asks the court a question and leaves it with them. They cannot deliver the verdict, because the only possible answer, that God must be obeyed, cancels the order they have just given. A body whose authority rests on representing God has been asked, on the record, whether God ought to be obeyed.

We cannot but speak. Not that they refuse to stop, but that they cannot: the position of a man who has seen something and cannot un-see it. Jeremiah knew it: “there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in” (Jeremiah 20:9). Paul knew it: “necessity is laid upon me” (1 Corinthians 9:16). A witness can be silenced, but what he has seen cannot be undone, and that is the whole of Peter’s case.

What we have seen and heard. The claim is also modest. They do not claim to be brave by nature, only to have seen that a man they watched die was afterwards alive in front of them, and that they ate with him. Everything the church has ever said stands or falls with whether that is true. They feared God more than men because they had seen the risen Christ, and the fear of him made them free.

The smaller room. Most Christians meet this verse in a much smaller room than a Sanhedrin. A conversation turns, and there is a sentence that would be honest and a silence that would be easier. The issue is the one Peter names: a believer must not pretend he has not seen what he has seen. And when he takes the easier silence, as every believer has, the way back is the one Peter took after he denied Jesus beside the fire: to the Lord who never once kept back the true word before his judges, whose perfect faithfulness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and whose Spirit gives the next sentence.

When may a Christian disobey the authorities? Human authority is real and must normally be obeyed (Romans 13:1–7); only where it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, as here, must we obey God rather than men (5:29; see the box at the end of this note). Soon these two, with the other apostles, gave the same answer to the same court and were flogged for it (5:29, 40).

Does this mean I may break any law I think is unjust? No. The apostles did not refuse a law because it was inconvenient, unfair or badly made; they refused one command that required them to disobey God. Paul told Christians under Nero to pay taxes and give honour to whom honour is owed (Romans 13:7), and Peter told slaves to be subject even to unjust masters (1 Peter 2:18). Christians may work to change bad laws by lawful means. But disobedience is reserved for the narrow case where obeying man means disobeying God, and even then it is open, peaceful and willing to bear the penalty.

Where Christians differ: civil disobedience. Some say Christians must always obey the government; others that they may resist any unjust law. This commentary’s view: Christians are to submit to governing authorities and pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honouring even unjust rulers (1 Peter 2:13–17). But where the state commands sin or forbids obedience to God, as in forbidding the gospel, we must obey God, openly and peacefully, and accept the consequences, as the apostles did. This is not rebellion but faithfulness.

parallels.desc: we must obey God rather than men

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council can only threaten and release them, held back not by conscience but by a city praising God for a man healed after more than forty years.

They let them go. Threats, but no punishment. Yet.

Because of the people. Not persuaded, and not troubled by scruples, the council has weighed public opinion. Men whose position depends on the people putting up with them cannot afford to flog the heroes of the hour. So public opinion had protected Jesus for a time (Luke 20:19; 22:2).

Praising God. Not the apostles. Peter had spent the previous chapter pushing attention off himself and onto a name, and this is Luke’s quiet note that it worked.

More than forty years old. Luke has held this back until it serves as evidence, the kind of fact a court enters in a record: no passing complaint or good day, but a lifetime of public disability ended in an afternoon. The supreme council has established exactly two things: that it happened, and that nothing can be done about it. The first recorded attempt by human authority to stop the gospel is on file, and so is its result.

A gauge that moves. A few months earlier a crowd in this city had asked a Roman governor for a murderer instead of Jesus. Public opinion killed the Master and is now shielding the servants, and it will swing again: by chapter 7 a crowd is stoning Stephen, and by chapter 8 persecution has scattered the church. A church that reads its safety off the public mood is watching a gauge that moves.

He did not entrust himself to them. Jesus had read this crowd long before: when many in Jerusalem believed at the sight of his signs, “Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people” (John 2:23–25). His apostles now learn the same freedom. Their safety rests not on the crowd’s mood but on the Lord who knows every heart in that city, governs it, and will still be governing it when the crowd turns.

Should Christians care about public opinion? Care about it, but do not live by it. Scripture wants believers to be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7) and to live so honourably that slander falls flat (1 Peter 2:12). But public opinion is not the measure of faithfulness. Aim to please God, do good to all, and leave your reputation in his hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A threatened church prays, and God answers with boldness and generosity. Peter and John report to their friends, who lift their voices together to the Sovereign Lord, Maker of all (vv. 23–24). They read their own week in Psalm 2: the rulers gathered against God’s Anointed, Herod and Pilate with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, did only what his hand and plan had predestined (vv. 25–28). So they ask not for safety but for boldness, and for healing in the name of Jesus (vv. 29–30), and God shakes the place and fills them all with the Spirit (v. 31). The same Spirit makes them one heart and soul: the apostles testify to the resurrection with power, and no one is in need, as Barnabas’s gift shows (vv. 32–37).
verseByVerse.theology:
The sovereignty of God and human responsibility

Verses 27 and 28 hold together real human guilt and a real divine purpose: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel acted freely and wickedly, and did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. This prayer shows what holding the two together is for (see the note on vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luke’s there was not a needy person among them echoes Deuteronomy 15:4 (see vv. 34–35). Now: Selling land and pooling the money belonged to that moment; open-handed generosity belongs to every age. And Luke sets the giving beside the preaching in one paragraph, so that the church’s life and the apostles’ message are not two subjects but one.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Released under threat, the apostles go straight back to the church, and the whole church takes the threat to God, beginning not with the danger but with the Sovereign Lord who made everything.

In the flow. Verses 23–31 are the church’s answer to verses 1–22: the council has ordered silence, so the church goes to a higher court. The prayer moves from who God is (v. 24), to what Scripture foretold and has now happened (vv. 25–28), to what they ask (vv. 29–30); then God answers (v. 31).

To their friends. Literally, to their own. Nobody treats them as dangerous company, though with a formal warning hanging over them they now were. They tell everything, with no shrinking of the threat and no heroics, and the church takes the facts straight to God.

Together. The word (homothymadon) means with one accord, all facing the same way, a favourite of Luke’s for the early church (1:14; 2:46). Whether they spoke in unison or one man led, Luke describes a room in which nobody is a spectator.

Sovereign Lord. They call God Despota: not the ordinary word for Lord, but an absolute master, the owner of a household with total authority over everyone in it. Simeon used it holding the infant Christ: “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace” (Luke 2:29). They begin not with their problem, but with God’s sovereignty.

Who made the heaven and the earth. Before a word about the council comes creation, in a line from the Ten Commandments and the Psalms (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6). In a real emergency they open with doctrine, not to avoid the subject but to get it into proportion. The Sanhedrin controls the temple, the treasury and the police. It did not make the sea. No council is above him, and no threat is outside his house.

Even winds and water. Peter and John were very probably in the boat when Jesus rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and the disciples asked, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” (Luke 8:22–25). This prayer stands on the answer: the Son who calmed that storm now sits at the Father’s right hand, and a council is a smaller thing than a storm. Prayer under pressure tends to begin at the pressure and stay there. By the time this church raises the threat in verse 29, it has been set inside a universe that has a Maker, and has shrunk to its actual size.

Why does it matter that they went back to the church? Because Christians were never meant to face pressure alone. In trouble the instinct is often to withdraw; Peter and John went to their own people, told them everything, and prayed together. That is what the church is for. If you are under pressure, at work, at home, from illness or from opposition, tell some trusted believers and ask them to pray with you. And if you are part of a church, be the kind of friend a frightened brother can come back to.

parallels.desc: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church finds its own week already written in Psalm 2, where God spoke by his Spirit through David of the nations raging against the Lord and his Anointed, and called all such raging futile.

Through the mouth of David. Dropped in without fuss is a sentence about how Scripture came to exist. God is the speaker; the Holy Spirit is the speaker; David’s mouth is the instrument (as at 1:16). These believers held without difficulty that David composed the poem from his own heart and that God said it. (Psalm 2 has no title in the Hebrew Bible, but the church, like many Jews of the day, received it as David’s.) One of the clearest statements of inspiration in Acts comes in a prayer, where nobody was trying to prove anything: what Scripture says, God says (2 Timothy 3:16), and a frightened church can stand on it.

Why did the Gentiles rage? Psalm 2:1–2 is a royal psalm, written for the day the LORD’s king was crowned in Zion, when subject nations weighed their chances against a new king. In vain means empty, to no purpose. The opposition it describes is not feeble but furious and well-resourced, and it calls it empty.

Against his Anointed. His Anointed is his Christ, his Messiah, and opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God. The church is not hunting for a verse to suit its mood; it finds its own week already written down. The Sanhedrin met that very morning, and Psalm 2 has the minutes.

He who sits in the heavens laughs. They stop the quotation just before the line everyone in the room had known since childhood: “He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (Psalm 2:4). It lies underneath the prayer and accounts for the confidence of what they ask. Not that opposition to God is comic, to be laughed off. Two of the men praying had been in custody overnight, and within a few years Herod would put one of the apostles to the sword (12:2). But seen from God’s throne, the only viewpoint that finally matters, the raging is futile: not harmless, not painless, but futile. Kings have set themselves against the Lord’s Anointed for three thousand years, and the psalm has never needed rewriting.

You are my Son. The psalm does not end with the laughter. The Lord goes on to speak of his King, “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill”, and then, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:6–7). Paul, preaching later in this book, reads that line as fulfilled when God raised Jesus from the dead (13:33). The Anointed against whom the rulers gathered has already been enthroned, not by a coronation in Jerusalem but by an empty tomb. He let them do their worst, because their worst was the road to his throne. Every throne that has risen against him has fallen, his throne stands, and those who take refuge in his Son are as safe as his throne (Psalm 2:12).

How can I pray Scripture like this? Read a passage, especially a psalm, slowly, asking what it says about God and what situation it describes. Then bring your own situation into it, as this church did, and pray its truths over the people and pressures you name. Psalm 2 for opposition, Psalm 23 for fear, Psalm 51 for guilt, Psalm 46 for upheaval, Psalm 121 for travel, Psalm 139 for feeling unseen. Over time it will give you words when you have none, and change what you ask for.

In everyday life. Read Psalm 2 today, the whole of it, aloud. Then think of what most frightens you about the future of the church, and read verse 4 again.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verse 25 is famously awkward, and exactly how its phrases fit together is uncertain. The KJV follows later manuscripts that leave out the Holy Spirit here, while the earliest include him. The sense is not in doubt: God spoke, by the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of David.

parallels.desc: why do the nations rage?

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel gathered freely and wickedly against Jesus, yet did only what God’s hand and plan had decided beforehand, and that is the floor the church stands on to pray.

Your holy servant Jesus. Now the church puts names into the psalm: the gathering happened here, in this very city. (Where the KJV has thy holy child Jesus, it translates the same word, pais, which can mean child or servant; here it recalls the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah.)

Herod and Pontius Pilate. Psalm 2 lists four parties, and the prayer supplies the roster: the kings, Herod Antipas; the rulers, Pontius Pilate; the nations, the Romans; the peoples, the peoples of Israel. All four met on one Friday morning: Jew and Gentile together crucified him, and all humanity is implicated. Luke’s Gospel alone records the meeting of Herod and Pilate over Jesus, and that the two enemies became friends that day (Luke 23:6–12).

Your hand and your plan. Predestined (proōrisen) means decided beforehand; it is the word used of election in Romans 8:29–30 and Ephesians 1:5, 11. They did what they wanted, wickedly, and exactly what God had determined; he rules even over evil deeds, yet never does the evil and is never to blame for it (2:23).

The floor they stand on. Predestination is usually met as a controversy. Here frightened people put their weight on it in prayer, and it holds. If the worst single act in the history of the world, carried out freely and wickedly by a coalition of everybody, was inside the hand and plan of God, then what happened in a council chamber that morning is inside it too. Verse 28 runs straight into verse 29: the sovereignty is not the conclusion they work towards but the floor they stand on to ask. No power in heaven or on earth can get outside the hand of the God who turned the murder of his Son into the salvation of his people.

If God predestined the cross, how were Herod and Pilate guilty? Both are true: God ordained the event, and the men who carried it out chose freely and wickedly, from their own motives, and were fully responsible. So it was with Joseph, whose brothers meant harm while God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God is never the author of sin; he governs even sin for good, and holds sinners accountable. The cross is the clearest proof that both truths stand together.

How does God’s sovereignty help me when I am suffering? It rarely tells you why. But it tells you that what is happening to you is not random, not out of control, and not outside the care of a Father who did not spare his own Son. If God could take the worst thing ever done and make it the salvation of the world, he can work your trouble together for good, as he has promised to those who love him (Romans 8:28). The pain is no less real, and you may weep and ask him to take it away. But you weep inside a plan, held by a hand that was pierced for you.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under threat, the church asks not for safety but for boldness to go on speaking, and for God to go on healing in the name of Jesus: the very things it has been forbidden to do.

Look upon their threats. Now, at last, the problem. They do not ask for the threats to be withdrawn, for the council to be judged, for protection, or for wisdom about proceeding more discreetly: all reasonable prayers, and none of them here.

Your servants. Having called God Sovereign Lord, master of the household (v. 24), they call themselves your servants (doulois), the ordinary word for slaves. It is not a negotiation. A slave does not ask his master to arrange easier work; he asks for what he needs to do the work he has been given.

With all boldness. Not safety, but courage to keep doing what they were forbidden to do, and the word is the very one the council had noticed in them at verse 13. They already had it, and they come back for more the same day.

Stretch out your hand. They ask for more healings, the very thing that started the trouble: the council forbade the name, and the church asks God to make it more conspicuous, as he did (5:12).

Your hand, twice. Two sentences earlier the church confessed that Herod and Pilate did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (v. 28). Now it asks the same hand to stretch out and heal through the name of “your holy servant Jesus”. The hand that ordained the Servant’s suffering is the hand that now heals in the Servant’s name, and the healing flows from the suffering.

What a prayer reveals. What we pray for under pressure shows what we most want to keep safe, and the Master is glad to change what we want most when we ask him.

What it does not mean. It would be a serious mistake to conclude that praying for safety is unspiritual. Paul asks the Romans to pray that he may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea (Romans 15:31); the church in chapter 12 prays earnestly for Peter in prison; Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). A parent praying for a sick child need not be told his prayer is insufficiently missionary.

How should I pray for persecuted Christians? Very often as they ask to be prayed for, like this church: that they would stand firm, speak boldly and love their persecutors, as well as for their protection and release (Hebrews 13:3).

Should we pray for signs and wonders today? Continuationist Christians see this prayer as a model for every church. The more likely reading is that the signs accompanying the apostles’ witness belonged to that founding period and are not promised as normal church life; that is the cessationist view, held charitably, because the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles in particular (5:12; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, and whole churches that love the gospel, read these chapters differently, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters, not dismissed. What we may always pray for is what this church asked first, boldness to speak God’s word, and God’s help for the sick and suffering, as he wills. And God still heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15).

parallels.desc: pray that words may be given me to open my mouth boldly

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers at once, shaking the place and filling them all with the Spirit, and the proof that he has answered is that they go on speaking his word with boldness.

The place was shaken. God does not reply in words. He moves the building. In Scripture shaking marks God’s arrival: Sinai trembling (Exodus 19:18), the thresholds shaking when Isaiah saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:4). That should sober as well as cheer: the Father who answers his children is never to be prayed to as if he were small.

All filled with the Holy Spirit. All of them, not the apostles only. And filled once again: the same word used of these same people at Pentecost (2:4), and of Peter twenty-three verses ago. Not a second Pentecost, for the Spirit has never left. It is a fresh supply for a fresh need. Believers who already have the Spirit can be filled again and again for new tasks (Ephesians 5:18).

Continued to speak. This is the real answer to the prayer. Luke does not say they felt bold; he says they spoke, and went on speaking, which is the only form of courage that can actually be measured. The answer is exactly what was asked for and not one item more. The council was not struck down, the prohibition was not lifted, and the danger did not decrease: by the next chapter these men are arrested again and flogged. God supplied nerve and left every circumstance standing, re-equipping the people inside the situation instead of removing it.

Poured out from the throne. Peter had already told Jerusalem where this filling comes from: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (2:33). The council banned the name; the one who bears it answered by filling every person in the house. The church does not receive courage in the abstract. It receives the Spirit of Jesus, and the courage is his.

What it does not mean. A shaking like this comes only rarely in Acts (compare 16:25–26), and nobody in the New Testament goes looking for it or suggests that a prayer without a physical sign has gone unheard. Luke’s evidence that God had answered is not that the walls moved but that they spoke.

Is being filled with the Spirit a feeling? Not essentially. It may come with deep joy, peace or courage. Luke measures it by what it produces: here bold speaking; elsewhere wisdom, faith, joy and love (6:3, 5; 13:52); for Paul, worship, gratitude and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:18–21). So do not judge it by the temperature of your emotions on a given day. Ask whether you are yielding to his word and leading, and whether Christlikeness and courage are growing. Ask God to fill you, and then obey him; the filling is often recognised afterwards, in what you found you were able to do.

parallels.desc: the whole mountain trembled

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit who filled their mouths also opened their hands: thousands of believers became one heart and soul and held their possessions loosely, while the apostles proclaimed the risen Lord with power.

In the flow. This is Luke’s second summary of the church’s life (the first is 2:42–47). It prepares the next scene, where one man’s gift shows the real thing and another’s the counterfeit (4:36 to 5:11).

One heart and soul. Luke’s Greek readers would have stopped here. A well-worn saying called a friend a single soul in two bodies, and an older proverb said friends hold all things in common: ideals thought out of reach except between two rare individuals. Luke uses both of several thousand people, most of whom had met only months before. This is unity, not uniformity: the answer to Jesus’ prayer “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).

No one said. It does not say that nobody owned anything; Luke uses the language of possession, and ownership remained. What they dropped was the insistence on it: they held their things loosely, as belonging to God and available to others. Luke reports not a scheme but people who still held the deeds and had stopped speaking as though the deeds settled anything.

With great power. In the middle of all this comes verse 33: Luke puts the preaching inside the paragraph about the money. The community that had stopped saying “mine” is the community in which the resurrection was announced with power. People who know that Jesus is risen know that their future is secure, and people whose future is secure can afford to open their hands. The empty tomb had loosened their grip on their fields. The ancient dream of friendship came true among thousands of strangers who had nothing in common except the risen Lord.

How can a large church be of one heart and soul? Not by everyone becoming the same, but by sharing one Lord, one gospel and one love; the risen Christ mattered more to them than their differences or possessions. In practice, unity grows when believers keep the gospel at the centre, pray together, deal quickly and honestly with offences (Matthew 18:15), refuse gossip, bear with one another in love (Ephesians 4:2–3), and share life in homes and service, so that a large church becomes a family of families. It is the Spirit’s work, and he loves to give it to those who ask.

Uncertain wording. “Great grace was upon them all” can be read two ways, and probably means both: the favour of God resting on the whole company, and the goodwill of a watching city, which is how Luke used a related phrase two chapters earlier (2:47).

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one in the church was left in need, because owners of property sold it freely and laid the money at the apostles’ feet to be shared as anyone had need: the Spirit doing what the law had hoped for.

Not a needy person. Luke is echoing the law. Deuteronomy promises, “there will be no poor among you … if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God”, and a few verses later says flatly, “there will never cease to be poor in the land” (Deuteronomy 15:4–5, 11). The Old Testament never once reports that it came true. Luke reports it as plain fact: the new covenant community did, by the Spirit, what Israel was meant to do.

The year of release. That promise belonged to the year of release, when debts were cancelled and the poor given a fresh start (Deuteronomy 15:1–2). Jesus opened his ministry at Nazareth by reading from Isaiah that he was anointed to proclaim good news to the poor, liberty to the captives and the year of the Lord’s favour, fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18–21). A church with no needy person in it is what his release looks like when it reaches people’s purses: debtors he has set free, setting others free.

At the apostles’ feet. Not handed to the apostles but laid at their feet, which placed the gifts under their authority to distribute; the apostles managed the fund until the Seven took over the daily distribution (6:1–6). It also kept the giver out of sight: the widow eating that week need not know whose field paid for it, and no giver gained a hold over those he helped, a danger that has dogged religious giving ever since. Need, not equality, was the principle.

He became poor for our sake. The Lord of glory was rich and became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and in Jerusalem his riches showed up as fields sold and widows fed. Whenever a believer’s need is met in secret by a brother’s gift, the generosity is finally Christ’s, running down through his people to the poor.

Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? That is a sharper test than whether you would give if asked: not merely your name left off a list, but the person helped never knowing it was you, never grateful, never owing you anything. That is the arrangement Luke describes. The money went on the floor at the apostles’ feet, and after that it was nobody’s.

In everyday life. Somewhere in your church there is probably a need nobody has mentioned out loud: a bill, a broken boiler, a cupboard running low. Begin by asking the deacons whether there is a family they are quietly worried about.

Was this Christian communism? It is sometimes called that and pressed into political service, but it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary: Peter tells Ananias that the land remained his own while it was unsold, and the money was at his disposal after it was sold (5:4), so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was Spirit-prompted love from hearts made one, not enforced by any state, and it met need rather than equalising. This is the opposite of coercive collectivism: the glad open-handedness of people the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment’s response.

Did this sharing make the Jerusalem church poor? Scripture never calls it a mistake, but neither does it repeat or command it. The Jerusalem church later needed help from the Gentile churches (Romans 15:26), probably because of the famine (11:28–30) and persecution.

Should all my giving be anonymous? Not necessarily, but much of it can be, and the motive always should be. Jesus said, “when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret” (Matthew 6:3–4). The danger he names is giving in order to be seen. Sometimes it is right for a gift to be known: Barnabas’s gift is recorded in the next verse, and Paul publicly praised the Macedonians’ generosity to stir others (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). But it is wise to give much of it quietly or through the church, so that the glory goes to God and the receiver is beholden to no one but him.
verseByVerse.note: Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke gives the pattern a face: Barnabas, son of encouragement, sells a field and lays the money down, the genuine gift that Ananias will soon counterfeit.

Son of encouragement. The man’s name is Joseph, but the apostles’ nickname, Barnabas, stuck so completely that the New Testament uses it more than twenty times. Son of, in Hebrew idiom, means characterised by. The word behind encouragement (paraklēsis) is related to the Spirit’s own title, the Helper, the one called alongside (John 14:16): the apostles named this man after something the Holy Spirit does.

A Levite, a native of Cyprus. Cyprus had a large Jewish community, and he would later preach there (13:4). Some readers have thought a Levite should not have owned a field at all (Numbers 18:20). There is probably no problem: the rule concerned the tribe’s share when the land was divided, not private purchase, and the priest Jeremiah bought a field long before (Jeremiah 32:6–9).

Sold a field. Before a single word he ever said, the first fact on file about Barnabas is that he sold a field, put the money down, and made no speech about it.

A Levite with a better portion. The Levites were given no share of the land because the LORD was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 18:2), and that was always meant to be enough. Barnabas, a Levite who owned a field after all, sells it and lays it down, and lives out the old promise in its new form: whoever has Christ has “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven” (1 Peter 1:4). At Antioch the whole content of his encouragement was Christ: he “exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose” (11:23).

Three things to come. He is about to do three things on which much of Acts turns. When every Christian was too frightened to go near the converted Saul, Barnabas brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (9:26–27). When the gospel broke out among Greeks at Antioch, he rejoiced at the grace of God and fetched Saul from Tarsus into the work (11:22–26). And when Paul refused to take John Mark again, Barnabas took him anyway and lost his partnership with Paul over it (15:37–39). He was proved right: years later Paul writes asking for Mark, “for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11).

The real thing and the imitation. The chapter break hides it, but the next sentence in Luke’s narrative begins, “But a man named Ananias”. Barnabas and Ananias are two halves of one paragraph, the real thing and the imitation, both selling property and laying money at the apostles’ feet, and one of them dead the day he brought it (5:1–11). Luke has put the genuine article first so that the reader knows exactly what the counterfeit was copying.

How can I be a Barnabas? Look for the people others are wary of, overlooking or giving up on: the new believer with a bad past, the young person who failed, the newcomer nobody has spoken to. Go and stand beside them. Tell them honestly what God is doing in them; Barnabas “saw the grace of God” and was glad (11:23). Vouch for people when it costs you something, and give practically. And be patient with those who have let you down; Mark is in the New Testament partly because Barnabas would not write him off. You will rarely be thanked, but you may be helping to raise the next Paul.

Uncertain wording. Scholars debate which Aramaic words lie behind the name Barnabas, but Luke tells us what it meant to the church.
verseByVerse.note: Cyprus was a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community.

4.theology: The sovereignty of God and mission. The prayer of verses 24 to 30 addresses God as Sovereign Lord, the Maker of everything, and confesses that Herod, Pilate and the nations did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. This is not fatalism (the idea that nothing we do matters) but God’s rule over the darkest day in history, and it leads not to passivity but to boldness (see vv. 27–28). The church does not need favourable conditions to advance. It needs the Spirit and the word, and God gives both.
4.examples:
Then: A church a few weeks old, with two of its leaders just out of custody and no legal protection or political allies, prayed for boldness and was given it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same choice between silence and speech. The God who shook that room still gives boldness to those who ask.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 ended with the church of one heart and soul, sharing its goods so that no one was in need, and with Barnabas laying the price of his field at the apostles’ feet (4:32–37). The council has already forbidden the apostles to speak in Jesus’ name (4:18).

The message. The church belongs to a holy God who lives among his people and will not be played with, and to a risen Lord whose word no power on earth can stop. God guards his church from within by purifying it and from without by preserving it. The right response to him is fear: not the fear of men, which makes people lie and makes rulers helpless, but the fear of God, which makes people honest and makes them free.

Why it was said. Luke is showing Theophilus how the risen Christ built his church (see the introduction). The first believers needed to know that the Spirit among them was God himself and that persecution could not undo what God had begun.

How the chapter makes its case. Ananias and Sapphira copy Barnabas’s gift while secretly keeping back part of the price, lie to the Holy Spirit and die, and great fear comes on the whole church (vv. 1–11). That holiness fills the church rather than emptying it: signs are done, multitudes are added to the Lord, and the sick of the region are healed (vv. 12–16). The jealous high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the prison and sends them back to the temple (vv. 17–26). Before the court they answer that they must obey God rather than men, and preach the Jesus whom God exalted as Leader and Saviour (vv. 27–32). Gamaliel talks the enraged council out of killing them (vv. 33–39), and they are flogged and leave rejoicing, still teaching every day (vv. 40–42).

Where it leads. The God whose holiness struck down two hypocrites is the God whose holiness fell in full on his Son at the cross, so that sinners may come near him with confidence. The Jesus whom the council hanged on a tree under the curse now reigns at God’s right hand, giving repentance and forgiveness even to the men who killed him, and the name the high priest would not say is the name the apostles count it an honour to be shamed for.

For us. No one is right with God by looking devoted; only Christ’s perfect obedience covers ours, and the honest word to God is always welcome. Because the Spirit among us is holy, we come with reverence and confidence together. And because Christ reigns, we can obey God rather than men, quietly and at cost, and count it joy to be shamed for his name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Inside the church, God guards its holiness; outside, his holiness draws the needy in. Ananias and Sapphira copy Barnabas’s gift while secretly keeping back part of the price, and Peter exposes it as a lie told to the Holy Spirit, who is God (vv. 1–4). God strikes both down, three hours apart, and great fear falls on the whole church, now named as the church for the first time (vv. 5–11). That holiness does not empty the church but fills it: signs are done through the apostles, outsiders keep a respectful distance, multitudes of men and women are added to the Lord, and the sick of the whole region are brought and healed (vv. 12–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The holiness of God and the danger of hypocrisy

When God begins something holy, the first sin against it is often judged with startling swiftness: Nadab and Abihu, Achan, Uzzah, and here the first hypocrisy in the church. Why God was so severe, and why such judgments are the exception and not the rule, is treated fully at vv. 5–6. The gospel does not lower that holiness but satisfies it: Christ bore the judgment our sin deserved, so that those in Christ may come near with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: Now: Two cautions belong with this passage: it is not a lever for extracting money (see the note on vv. 1–2), and it gives leaders no licence to make a congregation afraid of them (see v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two people copy Barnabas’s gift on the outside while secretly keeping back part of the price: the first serious danger to the church comes not from its enemies but from inside, in a devotion that is performed rather than real.

But a man named Ananias. Everything hangs on the opening word. The paragraph before introduced Barnabas, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet (4:36–37). Luke now sets beside him two people who did the identical thing and were not the same at all: the same land sold, the same money on the same floor. Even the names carry a sad irony. Ananias means the Lord is gracious; Sapphira means beautiful.

He kept back. A rare word (nosphizomai): elsewhere in the New Testament it describes slaves pilfering from their masters (Titus 2:10), and in the Greek Old Testament it appears at one unforgettable place, Joshua 7:1, where Achan takes for himself some of what had been devoted to God at Jericho, hides it in his tent, and stands in the assembly as though nothing had happened. Luke has reached for Achan’s own word. The first sin inside Israel’s new life in the land was a private theft hidden behind a public show of innocence, and the church’s new life meets the same sin.

With his wife’s knowledge. It was not a moment’s weakness. Two people sat down together, settled a figure, agreed what they would say, and rehearsed it well enough that she could still deliver it three hours after he was dead. Every private sin has a moment where one person saying no could have stopped it. This one had two people in the room, and neither said it. The marriage that should have been the safest place for an honest word became the place where the lie was made airtight.

What they were really buying. It was not money they were after. They could have kept the whole field and sinned in nothing, or sold it and given part openly and been thanked. What they wanted was something the honest options could not supply: the reputation of total surrender, at a price negotiated down in private. Barnabas’s gift had just been noticed and named, and it is easy to want that kind of name cheaply.

Great grace was upon them all. Luke has set the whole scene of sharing around that sentence (4:33). That is where Barnabas’s gift came from: people who had been given everything in a risen Saviour found that land was easy to let go (2 Corinthians 8:9). Ananias and Sapphira turned the same act into a purchase, trying to buy with a field what Christ gives for nothing, a name and a place among his people. Over against them stands the one Man whose outward life and inward heart were the same at every moment. Jesus never performed a devotion he did not have. When he gave, he gave the whole: not a portion of a field laid at men’s feet, but himself laid down for his people (Galatians 2:20).

The ordinary version. Before anyone comforts himself that this is an extreme case, measure it against the everyday form: the testimony allowed to sound a little better than the facts; the prayer that lengthens and warms when others are listening; “we’ve been praying about that”, when the last time was in March; the struggle described in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. None of that is on the scale of what Ananias did, but it is the same kind of act: buying a reputation for a devotion you have not got. If you recognise yourself here, that is a mercy, not a sentence. The way out is the honest word to God, who already knows and receives the honest gladly (Psalm 32:5).

What it does not mean. This chapter has been misused for money more often than almost any other. It is not a warning about giving too little: the sin was not withholding but pretending (see vv. 3–4). Pressure to look generous is nearer to their sin than keeping money back ever was.

Why would Luke put such an ugly story in the church’s golden age? Because he is an honest historian and a pastor. He has just painted the church at its most beautiful, one heart and soul, with no needy person among them (4:32–35), and he could have stopped there and left us a legend. Instead he shows that the first serious danger came not from Rome or the Sanhedrin but from people who sat in the meetings and handled holy things. That is a mercy. It tells us not to be shocked when a church we love proves to have hypocrites in it, not to imagine that any golden age was free of them, and where to look first for the danger: in our own hearts.

parallels.desc: Achan keeps back what was devoted to God

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter exposes the sin for what it is: not keeping money, which was Ananias’s right, but a lie told to the Holy Spirit, and so to God himself. Satan prompted it, yet Ananias planned it, and both are true.

Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? Given discernment by the Spirit, Peter names the sin precisely. It was not keeping the money; it was presenting part as the whole, a generosity they were not practising. And Peter means it literally: Satan, a real person, prompted it. Being filled by Satan is the dark opposite of being filled with the Spirit (2:4; 4:8, 31; Ephesians 5:18).
