To be filled with the Spirit is to be so taken up and governed by God that his presence controls one’s words and courage; here Satan floods and masters a heart, so that tongue and deed are ruled toward a lie. The whole church had just been filled with the Spirit (4:31); one man in it had let another tenant in. This sets Ananias beside Judas, into whom Satan entered to betray Jesus for money (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). Having failed from outside with threats (4:21), the adversary tried from inside with a lie.

Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? Yet Satan’s hand is no excuse. In the same breath Peter asks why Ananias planned it. Satan filled his heart, and Ananias schemed it in his own: Scripture holds these together everywhere (Luke 22:3 beside 22:22; Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). The tempter does not override the will; he inflames a heart already willing, for each person is tempted “when he is lured and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14). The verb means to set or lay down: the deed was put in place in the heart before it was done in the room. It was premeditated.

While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, the money was still at his disposal. They were free to keep the land, or the money. Giving was voluntary and private property was not abolished (2:45): the church in Jerusalem was not a commune with compulsory pooling but a family in which people sold things as needs arose and gave freely. Peter’s two questions protect every Christian’s freedom to own and to give as he decides before God (2 Corinthians 9:7). God loves a cheerful giver, and he has no use for a pretended one.

You have not lied to man but to God. In verse 3 Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit; here he lied to God. So the Holy Spirit is God: this is one of the clearest statements of the Spirit’s deity and personhood in Scripture. You cannot lie to a force or an influence; you lie to a person. The Spirit dwelling in the church is the living God (1 Corinthians 3:16), who searches the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10) and our hearts too, and “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7).

The promise of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit Ananias lied to is the one Peter had said the exalted Jesus poured out from the right hand of God (2:33): the risen Christ’s own gift, his way of keeping his promise not to leave his people as orphans (John 14:16–18). So the lie was told in the presence of the ascended Lord of the church, and the adversary behind it is the one Jesus had already met and beaten, refusing his offers in the wilderness and disarming the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Satan could fill one man’s heart; he could not take the church out of Christ’s hands. And this holy, all-seeing Spirit has chosen to make his home in sinners washed by Christ’s blood, to be grieved by them and yet never to leave them (Ephesians 4:30).

Is every sin a work of Satan like this? Lying bears his family likeness, for Jesus calls him the father of lies (John 8:44). But the ordinary spring of sin is the human heart itself (Mark 7:21–23), not a direct filling by Satan as here and with Judas. Paul names three sources together (Ephesians 2:2–3): the course of this world, human life organised against God; the prince of the power of the air; and the passions of our flesh, the fallen self we carry from Adam. So we neither blame every sin on demons nor pretend Satan has no hand in sin.

Can a true Christian be filled by Satan like this? Scripture never speaks of a believer, in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, being owned or possessed by Satan (1 John 4:4). But believers can be deceived, tempted and used by him for a moment: Peter himself heard “Get behind me, Satan!” soon after his great confession (Matthew 16:23), and Paul warns Christians not to give the devil an opportunity through unresolved anger (Ephesians 4:26–27). (Whether Ananias was a true believer is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: was Ananias saved?” at the end of the note on vv. 5–6.) So do not leave a door open. Unconfessed resentment, a secret love of praise, a hidden sin being managed rather than fought: these are footholds. Close them by bringing them into the light.
verseByVerse.note: Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, not Peter, strikes Ananias dead, and the church suddenly grasps whom it is dealing with: the Spirit among them is the holy God, who will not be played with.

He fell down and breathed his last. Luke does not linger. Peter pronounces no sentence and calls down no curse; he only exposes the sin. The death is God’s act. The Spirit among them is no benevolent force that winks at religious play-acting but the holy God himself. Holy means more than good: utterly set apart, pure light with no darkness in it, so far above sin that the seraphim, who have never sinned, cover their faces before him and cry holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:2–3). Ananias had treated that God as someone who would not notice.

Wrapped him up. Four verbs, no pause, and no funeral. A Jewish death normally set in motion days of formal mourning; none of that happens, and he is in the ground within hours (on burial the same day, see burial customs). Luke reports it without comment, which is itself a comment. The men who carried him out came back and, three hours later, had to do it a second time.

Why so severe? Nearly every liar walks away still breathing. Why this one? Because Scripture shows a pattern: when God begins something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire at the dawn of the priesthood and died (Leviticus 10:1–2); Achan died at Israel’s entry into the land (Joshua 7); Uzzah was struck as the ark came home (2 Samuel 6:6–7); and here is the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgments: one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once to stamp God’s holiness on his people and keep a young church from being poisoned at its core. Over Nadab and Abihu God said, “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified” (Leviticus 10:3). Nearness to God raises the demand for reverence; it never lowers it.

Then why do the rest of us not fall dead at every lie? Because these are the exception, not the rule. God’s ordinary way is patient kindness, meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4; Psalm 130:3). The lightning flashes once to light up the whole landscape. And the deepest answer is the cross. The holiness that struck Ananias down is the holiness that met our sin at Calvary, and there it did not flash once; it fell in full on the Son. The judgment every hypocrite deserves was borne by the one Man who was never a hypocrite. So the fear Luke records is not the terror that drives us from God but the awe that keeps us from trifling with him.

Does God still strike people dead for sin today? He is free to, and Scripture shows he has done it more than once (Acts 12:23; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But the New Testament never teaches us to expect it, and we must never read a particular death, illness or accident as God’s verdict on someone’s hidden sin. Jesus forbade that reasoning about the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by the tower in Siloam; his conclusion was not that they were worse sinners but “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:1–5). That is the right use of Acts 5 too. It is not for diagnosing other people’s funerals but for searching your own heart while there is time.

Where Christians differ: was Ananias saved? Some think this proves he was never a believer, a false professor exposed like Achan; they point out that Satan had filled his heart (v. 3) and that his sin was a deliberate attempt to deceive the Holy Spirit. Others think a true believer can be disciplined by death without losing salvation, as Paul says of some at Corinth who were sick or had died, judged by the Lord so that they would not be condemned along with the world (1 Corinthians 11:30–32; 5:5). This commentary’s view: Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. What is clear is that God takes sin in his church seriously, especially hypocrisy, and may discipline severely. It is not a pattern to expect in every case; it is a warning written at the church’s beginning.
verseByVerse.note: Burial usually took place the same day.

parallels.desc: Nadab and Abihu struck down

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sapphira is given three hours and an open question, a real chance to tell the truth, and she chooses the lie freely, for herself.

About three hours. Luke times it, and the interval is a mercy: three more hours in which she could have come and told the truth. Somewhere in the city she is going about her day, her husband dead and nobody telling her. Then she walks into a room where everyone knows what has happened, and what she is about to say.

Tell me. Peter does not accuse her or tell her that her husband is dead. He asks a question as easy to answer truthfully as a question can be made: a door held open. The God of this scene is the God who waits three hours, and three years, and thirty, holding the door open with a question, “not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

Yes, for so much. She keeps to the lie: two words in the Greek, the sound of a rehearsed line. And she was under no pressure. Her husband was not beside her, and no one was watching to see whether she held the line. She kept it anyway, alone and freely, which is why Peter’s next words treat her as a full partner in the deed and not a wife who was dragged along.

Peter knew what a question can do. He had once been asked one himself. On a beach in Galilee the risen Jesus faced the disciple who had denied him three times and asked him three times, “do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). No recital of the charge: a question, held open until Peter could answer it truly, and on the other side of the answer, a commission. That is the way of Christ with sinners, and through his apostle the Lord who restored Peter with a question offered Sapphira the same road back. The difference between the two scenes is not in the Lord who asked but in the answer that was given.

A wife and her husband’s sin. On this, women have been badly counselled. Scripture nowhere requires a wife to follow her husband into sin, and a husband’s headship has never included authority to make a liar of her. Headship is self-giving love modelled on Christ’s love for the church (Ephesians 5:25), and Christ never asks his bride to sin. The principle is the one the apostles will state to the highest court in the land later in this chapter: “We must obey God rather than men” (v. 29). If that holds against a Sanhedrin, it holds against a husband, and in a kitchen. Abigail went round her husband’s ruinous folly, acted without his knowledge to stop it, and is commended for it in the text and by David himself (1 Samuel 25). Sapphira had the same road open. Her tragedy is not that she submitted; it is that she agreed.

What if refusing my husband would put me in danger? Then the issue is no longer submission at all but safety, and Scripture never asks a wife to stay in harm’s way. A husband who threatens, intimidates or harms his wife has abandoned the Christ-like headship Scripture describes; abuse is never to be tolerated or covered by a church. If you are afraid of what will happen if you say no, tell someone you trust today, a pastor or elder or a wise friend, and if you are in danger, call the police. Getting safe is not rebellion: Abigail acted to save lives, and was praised for it. In ordinary disagreements, a godly wife can refuse to sin respectfully and gently, as Sapphira could have done, and leave the rest with God.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husband and wife had agreed together to put the Spirit to the test, daring him not to notice; he did, and she falls dead on the very spot where they had wanted to be seen giving.

How is it that you have agreed together? Peter names it as a partnership. The verb is symphōneō, to sound together, the word behind our symphony. It is one of marriage’s good gifts that two people can come to one mind, and here it is, working perfectly, in the service of a lie. A spouse’s calling is to help the other toward God, never away from him.

To test the Spirit of the Lord. Testing (peirazō) means putting God to the proof: presuming on him, daring him, finding out whether he is really watching and will really act. Israel did it at Massah, asking, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7; Psalm 95:9). Ananias and Sapphira had in effect wagered that the Spirit would not notice, or would notice and not mind. They had watched the Spirit fall; they simply did not believe he was paying attention to them. He was. That is a terror to the hypocrite and the deepest comfort to the believer, because the Spirit who saw through Sapphira’s rehearsed line also sees every secret prayer, every hidden tear and every unseen act of faithfulness.

The feet at the door. In one sentence she learns that she is a widow and about to follow him. Peter passes no sentence and claims no power to strike; he knows by the Spirit what is about to happen and says so. The judgment in this chapter is God’s, twice.

At his feet. Eight verses earlier her husband laid the money at the apostles’ feet (v. 2). To be seen laying money on that square of floor, before that watching room, was the whole point of their plan, and it is the exact spot where she falls. The place they had wanted to be seen is the place she is carried from.

Beside her husband. The young men come back and do again what they did three hours earlier. Together in the planning, together in the rehearsing, together in the ground.

Terrible but not arbitrary. God was not defending his dignity against an insult; he was defending a very young church against the one thing that kills churches from inside: people who have learned to perform a devotion they do not have and to be admired for it. Everything the early chapters describe, the one heart and soul, the goods held loosely, the apostles’ teaching received as the word of God, depends on the assumption that when a Christian says a thing, it is so. Two people set out to show that the assumption could be exploited, and the Lord of the church answered in a way the church would never forget.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. Set the scenes side by side. On the pinnacle of the temple the devil invited Jesus to presume on his Father, and the Son refused to stage a display to make God prove himself (Matthew 4:5–7). Ananias and Sapphira, with Satan filling their hearts, staged one before the church and dared the Spirit not to notice. Israel failed that test at Massah, and these two failed it in the church. One Man passed it on our behalf, trusting his Father all the way to a cross where no angel caught him, and the obedience they lacked is the obedience he offers to everyone who takes refuge in him.

What does testing God look like today? Usually it is quiet: sinning on purpose because you are sure of forgiveness afterwards; taking a risk God has warned against and daring him to protect you; living as though he does not see what happens on a phone at midnight, in the accounts, or in a marriage behind closed doors. At the other end, it is demanding that God prove himself on your terms before you will trust him. The cure is the one Jesus used: answer the temptation with the word of God, and remember that the Lord who sees in secret is the Lord who loves you. You do not need to test a Father you can trust.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD your God to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose of the two deaths was fear: the whole church, now named as the church for the first time, learns the reverent awe that belongs to a people with the holy God living among them.

Great fear. For the second time (see v. 5) Luke dwells not on the death but on its effect: this is what the episode was for. And it did not stay indoors. Jerusalem heard, outsiders as well as believers, and drew its own conclusions about what sort of company this was.

The whole church. This is the first time Acts calls the believers the church (ekklēsia), the assembly, the called-out people (some later manuscripts already have the word at 2:47). In the Greek Old Testament the word was used of Israel assembled before God at Sinai and in the temple; now it is the people of the Messiah. The God before whom Israel trembled at Sinai has come nearer than Sinai ever allowed, to dwell in his church by his Spirit. Luke does not use the word at Pentecost, nor in the golden paragraph about sharing, but here, in the silence after two funerals. To be the church is, before anything else, to reckon with the holiness of the God who has moved in.

The man at the hearth. This is not cringing terror but reverent awe that draws near in love and will not trifle: “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:1). Picture a man at his hearth on a winter night. He loves the fire, pulls his chair as close as he can bear, and would not dream of putting his hand into it, because he knows what it is. He is nearer to it than anyone else in the house. That is the fear of the Lord, and Luke will later name it as the mark of a healthy church, “walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit” (9:31): both, in one sentence.

The soil of the church’s life. This fear is not the enemy of the church’s life but its soil. Watch what grows in the next three verses: signs and wonders, a people all together in Solomon’s Portico, and more believers than ever added to the Lord. The awe did not freeze the church; it purified it and then filled it. A church without the fear of God is not a happier church, but a weaker one.

In everyday life. Before you next walk into a church service, pause at the door for ten seconds and remember whose house you are entering and who is present among his people. Then go in glad and careful. Let the same awareness follow you home on Monday: the God present in the assembly is present at your desk.

If God is this holy, how can I come near him at all? Only through Christ, and through Christ with confidence. The fire is not safe because you keep your distance; it is safe because someone has made a way to sit beside it. By his blood Jesus has opened “the new and living way”, so that we may “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22). Hebrews puts the two together just as Luke does: worship “with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (12:28–29), and “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (4:16). Reverence and confidence are not opposites. They are the two hands with which a forgiven sinner holds on to a holy God.

Am I Ananias, if I know I am not what I appear to be? Some read Acts 5 and lie awake: they know they are not what they appear to be in their church, they can name the exaggeration and the unconfessed thing, and they half expect the floor to open. That fear deserves a straight answer. Ananias was not caught out by a God waiting to pounce. He engineered a lie in advance, with a partner, in the presence of God, and she was given three hours and an open question and still kept to it. Both wanted to be admired more than they wanted to be true. A man trembling because he longs to be genuine and knows he is not yet is in an entirely different condition, and the trembling itself is the evidence. The Spirit does not produce that ache in people he is about to strike down; he produces it in people he is not going to leave alone. The door out has always been open: say the true thing, to God first and then to whoever needs to hear it, and the whole weight of it goes. No one who confesses his sin and trusts Christ is in their position.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Acts uses the word “church.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the church’s prayer for boldness with many signs done through the apostles, his seal on their message, while the believers gather openly in the most public space in the temple.

Many signs and wonders. God answers the prayer of 4:30. A sign points beyond itself; a wonder astonishes. They authenticated the message and its messengers: the Lord “bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands” (14:3). The wonder was the wrapping; the word was the gift. That is why Jesus rebuked those who craved signs for their own sake (Matthew 12:39).

By the hands of the apostles. Luke is careful about whose hands. The signs in these chapters are done by the apostles, and Paul could call them “the signs of a true apostle” (2 Corinthians 12:12) because they marked out the men Christ had sent. The church prayed, the apostles’ hands were the instruments, and the risen Christ was the healer (3:6, 16; 9:34).

Solomon’s Portico. A roofed colonnade along the east side of the temple’s outer court, where Peter had preached after healing the lame man (3:11). The believers were not huddled in hiding but gathered openly in the most public religious space in Jerusalem.

The works bear witness. The Portico had heard this before. There, in winter, Jesus was pressed to say plainly whether he was the Christ, and answered that his works bore witness about him (John 10:24–25). Now the same colonnade sees the same kind of works, done by other hands in his name (3:6, 16) and pointing to the same Person. The rulers who rejected his works then are watching them go on, because he is not absent. He is reigning, and his hand is stretched out through theirs.

Two honest qualifications. First, no verse says outright that miracles will cease when the apostles die. The certain ground is the purpose of the signs; the timing of their ceasing is a strong inference from that purpose, joined to the close of the apostolic age and the completed canon of Scripture, not a single proof text. Paul says that tongues and prophecy will pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8–10), though believers differ over when “the perfect” comes. Second, God has not stopped working wonders. He remains free to heal and to act in answer to prayer, and he often does. What ceased is the apostolic sign gift as a standing credential of new revelation, not God’s power or his nearness.

Does that mean I should not pray for healing? Not at all. Pray, and pray boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, anointing with oil, and promises that “the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick” (James 5:14–15). God answers such prayers, sometimes with healing doctors cannot explain, sometimes through medicine, sometimes by giving grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The cessationist conviction is not that God has stopped healing, but that no one today holds an apostle’s gift to heal at will, and that no new revelation is being added to Scripture. Ask your Father freely, and trust his answer.

Where Christians differ: have the sign gifts ceased? Many Christians, called continuationists, believe that healing, tongues and prophecy continue in the church today. They point out that 1 Corinthians 12–14 was written to an ordinary church, that Paul urges believers to “earnestly desire the spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 14:1), and that no verse says plainly the gifts would cease before Christ returns. The historic Reformed church has held that these apostolic sign gifts have ceased, and its case is drawn from Scripture, not mere observation. The signs marked out the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12), and the apostles were a foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid only once. Their office could not be handed on, for its holders had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, and Paul calls himself “last of all” (1 Corinthians 15:8). The revelation the signs authenticated is complete: “the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3). Once the foundation was laid and the message set down in Scripture, the credentials of the foundation-layers had served their purpose, like scaffolding taken down once the building stands. This commentary’s view: the cessationist reading is the more likely one: the apostolic sign gifts, as standing credentials of new revelation, belonged to the foundation age and have ceased. This is held charitably. Our continuationist brothers love the same Christ and the same Bible, and many are at least as zealous for Scripture’s sufficiency as we are.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Ananias and Sapphira, nobody attached himself to the church lightly any more, yet the ordinary people held the believers in high regard.

None of the rest dared join them. The word join (kollasthai) means to throw in one’s lot with someone. The rest are most naturally the fringe: the curious and the would-be hangers-on who might have attached themselves to so admired a movement for the prestige or the perks (see the box below). After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared. The holiness that had struck fear into everyone (vv. 5, 11) made plain that you do not join this people with mixed motives.

Held them in high esteem. They respected them from a distance. The church’s public welcome runs hot and cold through Acts: esteemed here, arrested a few verses on (vv. 17–18), and soon Stephen stoned amid great persecution (chapters 7–8). Both come from God’s hand. He grants seasons of favour to open doors (2:47) and permits persecution to scatter the seed (8:1–4).

The road their Lord had walked. Luke’s Gospel showed the same pattern around Jesus: the people hung on his words while the chief priests and scribes sought to destroy him (Luke 19:47–48). Jesus received the people’s favour without ever leaning on it, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24–25), and he did not lose his way when it vanished. The apostles walk the road their Master walked, as he told them to expect (John 15:20). So the believer should be neither intoxicated by esteem nor crushed by opposition. Esteem is a gift to be spent for Christ; opposition is what faithful witnesses must expect in the long run (2 Timothy 3:12).

Is it wrong to want my church to be well thought of? No, as long as you want it on the right terms. Paul wanted elders to be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Peter wanted unbelievers to see Christians’ good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). What is wrong is buying respect by hiding what is distinctive: softening the gospel, dropping holiness, or becoming so like the world that nobody could be offended. The esteem in this verse came to a church that was holy, honest and unashamed of Christ. That is the only good reputation worth having, and God may give or withhold it as he pleases.

Uncertain wording. Who “the rest” are is not certain. Luke can hardly mean the believers, who are being added in multitudes (v. 14), and open opponents had no wish to join. Most take the rest as outsiders who admired the church but would not commit to it; some think of the people generally, set against the apostles who were gathering in the Portico (v. 12). Whichever is right, the sense is the same: outsiders kept a respectful distance, while those whom God was drawing came in.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Holiness did not shrink the church; more believers than ever, men and women alike, were joined not to a movement but to the risen Lord himself.

More than ever. Two people have dropped dead in the meeting and nobody dares attach himself casually any more (v. 13), and the result is not decline but more believers than before. We assume a church grows by being easier to belong to, less demanding, more like the surrounding culture with a religious accent. Luke reports the opposite. When it became unmistakable that the God in that room was real, the pretenders stopped coming and everyone else started. Verses 13 and 14 are one movement: the same holiness keeping the casual away and drawing the needy in.

Added to the Lord. Not to a movement or a register. In Acts the Lord is the risen Jesus, whom God made “both Lord and Christ” (2:36). Conversion joins a person to him, united to the living Christ by faith, and membership among his people follows because they belong to him too. Union with Christ means being bound to him so closely that what is his becomes yours: his death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness is counted as yours, and his life flows into you as sap flows from the vine into the branch (Romans 6:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21; John 15:5). Anyone who wonders whether he truly belongs because he signed something or attends something has the answer here: the attachment that counts was made to the Lord himself, and it will outlast every congregation any of us belongs to. And God did the adding: “the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved” (2:47). The church grows by his gathering, not by its marketing.

Multitudes of both men and women. Luke counts the women, in a world where a crowd was ordinarily numbered by its men, and he does it repeatedly (8:12; 16:13–15; 17:4, 12). Joel’s promise of the Spirit on sons and daughters alike (2:17–18) is showing in the arithmetic.

Not one of them came by accident. The Lord who added them is the Lord to whom they were added: he gathers, and he is the home of the gathered. Every man and woman in that crowd was a sheep the Good Shepherd had laid down his life for and now called by name (John 10:11, 16). Not one came by accident, and not one would be lost (John 6:37–39). The Shepherd of multitudes counts his flock one by one.

Not a licence for severity. This has been abused. The fear in Acts 5 came from something God did, not from something the leaders did. Peter struck no one, threatened no one and ran no campaign of discipline; he asked two honest questions and God did the rest. A church where people are frightened of the elders, watch their words in the foyer, and cannot admit a struggle without consequences has not reproduced this chapter. It has produced the very thing this chapter killed: a community where everyone performs. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

So will a strict church always grow? No, and this verse does not promise it. Churches have been holy and small for generations, and faithful churches have shrunk under persecution. Numbers are in God’s hands: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). What this verse forbids is the opposite assumption, that holiness hinders growth and must be traded away for it. Our task is to be faithful, honest and unashamed of Christ, and to leave the arithmetic to the Lord who adds.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ heals all who are brought, from the city and the towns around, a foretaste of the new creation; the power was his, not Peter’s shadow.

At least his shadow. The healing has reached a scale that draws the whole region. Many ancient people believed that a person’s shadow carried something of his power. Luke does not say the shadow healed anyone; he reports what people hoped. This is the faith of ordinary people mixed with the popular beliefs of their day, and God was gracious to that imperfect faith, as with the woman who touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment (Luke 8:44) and the handkerchiefs carried from Paul (19:11–12). The power was God’s.

From the towns around Jerusalem. The word begins to spread beyond the city, as Jesus said it would (1:8).

Unclean spirits. Here we say only what Scripture tells us. Unclean spirits are real, personal, evil beings, what the Gospels also call demons (Mark 5:2, 12–15; 7:25–26): not symbols, nor an ancient label for illness. The New Testament treats them as intelligent beings with will and speech, part of Satan’s kingdom (Matthew 12:24–26), commonly understood as fallen angels (Revelation 12:9). Unclean marks their nature: defiling, the opposite of God’s holiness. They can oppress and torment, and at times control a person, with effects both physical (Mark 5:3–4; 9:18) and inward (Mark 5:5). But Scripture does not blame every sickness on demons: it lists the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits as two groups, here and in Mark 1:32–34. So we neither deny the demonic nor see a demon behind every illness.

All healed. All, as in Jesus’ own ministry (Luke 4:40; 6:19). It was an extraordinary season: the kingdom had arrived, and a preview of the new creation was visible in the streets of Jerusalem. Verses 12–16 are Luke’s third summary picture of the church (2:42–47; 4:32–35). The holiness that struck down two pretenders drew a whole region to the risen Christ, and this success is what fills the high priest with jealousy (v. 17).

Their relation to Christ. What Scripture stresses above all is how the spirits stand before Jesus. They recognise him and tremble (Mark 1:24; James 2:19). They are subject to his authority and to his name on the lips of his servants (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18), and they flee before the advancing kingdom (Matthew 12:28). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). On how exactly a spirit afflicts, or why some and not others, Scripture says little, and so do we. It gives us enough to take the reality seriously, never to fear it, and to look only to the Conqueror: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4).

Should we expect healing through objects or special people today? No. Peter’s shadow describes a unique moment, not a method. Prayer cloths sent in the post, anointed water, a celebrity healer whose touch is said to carry power: none has a promise behind it, and the danger of superstition, and of desperate people being exploited, is real. God still heals in answer to prayer, and the ordinary means he has given are prayer, the elders of the church, and medicine received with thanks (James 5:14–15; 1 Timothy 5:23). Bring your sick to Christ directly. You do not need anyone’s shadow.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? A true Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Scripture nowhere describes a believer being owned or controlled by a demon, and it assures us that the evil one does not touch the one born of God (1 John 5:18). But believers are attacked: tempted, accused and oppressed in their minds, which is why we are told to put on the whole armour of God and to resist the devil, who will flee (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). If you are troubled by dark fears, do not go looking for a specialist in exorcism. Go to Christ in prayer, fill your mind with Scripture, tell your pastor, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up, because much that feels spiritual is also bodily, and God uses both kinds of help.

Where Christians differ: relics and holy objects. Some have used verses like this to support venerating relics or objects linked with saints. This commentary’s view: Luke reports; he does not prescribe. The healing came from the risen Christ, confirming his apostles’ message. The New Testament never teaches believers to seek power through objects, shadows or relics, and the apostles would have been horrified to be venerated (14:14–15). Look to Christ, not to his servants or their belongings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No prison, court or whip can stop the word of the risen Christ. Jealous, the high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors and sends them back to the temple at dawn, while the whole council gathers to fetch men already free (vv. 17–26). Before the council they answer that they must obey God rather than men, and Peter preaches the crucified Jesus as exalted Leader and Saviour, offering repentance even to his judges (vv. 27–32). Enraged, the council wants them dead, but Gamaliel persuades it to wait, warning that it might be fighting God (vv. 33–39). They are flogged, leave rejoicing to have suffered for the name, and go on teaching every day that the Christ is Jesus (vv. 40–42).
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God rather than men

God used Gamaliel’s advice to restrain the council, but it is not a theological authority (see vv. 35–36). The apostles stand on something else: an order of obedience, with God first. How that order fits with submission to rulers, and why the apostles took the flogging rather than resist, is set out at vv. 29–30.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The man leading the apostles out of the council, rejoicing, was the one who months earlier had denied knowing Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire (see vv. 41–42).

Now: Joy in suffering for the name is given, not manufactured, and it is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person (see vv. 41–42); nor is obeying God rather than men a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes (see vv. 29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second attack comes from outside: the temple’s ruling party, burning with jealousy at the gospel’s success, throws all the apostles into the common jail.

The high priest and the party of the Sadducees. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem, the wealthy families who controlled the temple, with the high priest at their head. They profited from the status quo and cooperated closely with Rome to keep their power. They held to the written law of Moses, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions, and, crucially here, denied the resurrection of the dead, along with angels and spirits (23:8). The apostles were proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead (4:2) and drawing the people’s allegiance away from the temple establishment: the gospel struck at both their theology and their power.

Filled with jealousy. Jealousy (zēlos) here is not petty envy but hot zeal: the burning of men who believe something precious is being taken from them, as any religious establishment feels when the people begin listening to someone else. It is the motive that handed Jesus over: Pilate “perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up” (Mark 15:10). Again and again in Acts, attempts to shut the church down are provoked by the gospel’s advance. But the Lord they envied envied no one. He emptied himself, and the glory he could have grasped he gave away (Philippians 2:6–7).

The public prison. All the apostles this time, and in the common lock-up. It was meant to be seen and to be degrading: the men Jerusalem had begun to admire were walked through the streets and put in with ordinary criminals.

They never investigate the claim. The men running the case against the resurrection are the party whose theology depends on there being no such thing. From the guards’ report at the tomb (Matthew 28:11–15) to this morning’s empty cell, not one of them is recorded as asking the only question that matters: is it true? They investigate the preachers, never the claim. It is possible to hold the highest office in the religion of the living God and have no interest whatever in whether he has done something.

How do I fight envy when God blesses someone else? Name it first, because envy rarely calls itself by its name; it calls itself concern, or discernment, or a sense that something is not quite right about that ministry. Then bring it to God as sin, not as an assessment. Pray by name for the person or church whose blessing stings, and ask God to bless them more, until your heart catches up with your prayer. Remember that everything anyone has is a gift (1 Corinthians 4:7), and that the master of the vineyard is free to be generous to whom he will (Matthew 20:15). And “rejoice with those who rejoice” (Romans 12:15), even if at first it is obedience rather than feeling.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens the prison, not to send the apostles to safety, but straight back to the temple to speak the whole message of the risen Christ’s life.

An angel of the Lord. Luke spends one clause on the miracle; the escape is not the story. And the humour is not lost: the Sadducees, who denied angels (23:8), are thwarted by one. Angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14), and here one of them serves with a key.

Go and stand in the temple. What the angel says is the story. Not go home, not leave Jerusalem: go straight back to the building owned and policed by the men who locked you up, and do precisely what you were arrested for. They were not rescued to safety; they were sent back to the front line.

All the words of this Life. Not eternal life in the abstract, but this Life: the life that came out of a sealed tomb and is now visibly loose in Jerusalem, healing people in the street and putting courage into fishermen. Speak all of it, the angel says, not only the parts the council will tolerate.

Why does God open this door and not others? A suffering reader will ask, and Acts itself refuses to duck it. Seven chapters on, Luke tells of another night, another angel, another set of chains falling off Peter; and in the same paragraph James the brother of John is killed with the sword, and no angel comes (12:1–11). Luke sets them side by side without explanation, and he could have left the beheading out. Later Paul sits in custody for two years while a governor hopes for a bribe (24:26–27), and no angel comes for him either, yet the gospel goes on regardless, to a governor and a king (24:24–25; 26:1–29). So this passage must never be turned into a promise that the door opens for the faithful. The doors that stayed shut in this book were shut on better men than most of us, and it was never a question of whether they had believed hard enough. What Acts teaches is narrower and steadier: God opens what he needs opened for the gospel to go where he intends, and he owes no one an explanation of his choices. If a door in your life has stayed shut, it is not because you believed too little.

What have you been let out for? That gives an ordinary Christian a better question than why his door has not opened. Every deliverance in Acts is for the mission, never for the comfort of the delivered, and this one lasted a few hours before the same men were arrested again and flogged. Anyone who has been brought out of something, a diagnosis, a debt, a marriage that nearly ended, has a plainer thing to ask than why it happened to him and not to someone else. He can ask what he has been let out for. In this chapter the answer came with the door.

Do angels still rescue people today? God still sends his angels to serve his people; Hebrews speaks of them in the present tense, and some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). But Scripture never tells us to seek angelic visits, pray to angels, or expect to see them, and it warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). Most of their work is unseen, and most of God’s deliverances come through ordinary means: a doctor, a friend, a changed decision. Thank God for his unseen care, and keep your eyes on the Lord of the angels.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles obey at once and are teaching in the temple at dawn, while the whole supreme council solemnly gathers to fetch prisoners God has already set free.

At daybreak. They heard, they went, they taught. There is no interval in the sentence for asking whether it might be wiser to let a day pass. A great deal of what passes for seeking God’s will is really the search for a delay he has not granted. These men had every reason to want one, and did not take it.

All the senate. The council is the Sanhedrin, the supreme court of the Jewish nation, presided over by the high priest; under Rome a death sentence needed the governor’s ratification (John 18:31). The senate (gerousia) is the council of elders. Luke piles term upon term to stress that the entire body convened in its most solemn session.

Sent to the prison. Here the comedy begins. The grandest court in Israel grinds into motion to fetch men who are at that very hour teaching in the temple. All its dignity could not keep pace with the word of the risen Christ.

Early in the morning in the temple. In his last week Jesus taught daily in the temple, and “early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him” (Luke 21:38). On the morning of his trial, “when day came”, the elders gathered and led him away to their council (Luke 22:66). Now both happen again at the same hour. The difference is the empty tomb. Then the council had the Teacher in its hands; now it cannot even find his messengers. The Lord they condemned at dawn sends his servants out at dawn.

But shouldn’t I pray before I act? Yes, about the things God has not already told you. Prayer for guidance is right where Scripture leaves a real choice open: which job, which city, whom to marry among believers. But when God has already spoken, praying about it can become a pious way of not doing it. The apostles did not need to pray about whether to preach; they had been told. You do not need to pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, or to be kind to the colleague who wronged you. Pray for strength to obey, and then obey, today.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prison is found locked, guarded and empty: a quiet miracle that leaves the authorities facing, in their own jail, the same shape as the empty tomb.

No one inside. Luke lets the officers’ report stand without comment. Every part of the system worked perfectly, the men are gone, and nobody in the room can account for it. Nothing was broken and nobody was hurt. This is not power straining against resistance; it is power to which locked doors are no obstacle worth damaging.

The same shape as the tomb. A sealed place, guards posted, an occupant certainly there last night; and in the morning everything secure, the place empty, and nobody able to explain it. Jerusalem had heard that story once already, about a tomb with guards and a seal (Matthew 27:62–66; 28:11–15), and this council had done its best to keep the lid on it. Now the same shape has turned up in its own jail, before Sadducees who say there is no resurrection, nor angel (23:8).

Without breaking anything. Locked doors have never been an obstacle to this Lord. On the evening of his rising, “the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you’” (John 20:19). The same quiet power that walked his apostles out of a bolted prison walks into rooms bolted by fear, and into hearts bolted against him, and opens them without breaking anything.

Could someone inside simply have let them out? It is the sceptic’s obvious question, and the officers’ report goes a long way toward answering it. A friendly jailer who freed twelve prisoners would hardly lock the doors behind them and leave the guards at their posts, guards who, as Acts later shows, could pay with their lives for an escape (12:19). Nor would men who had slipped out by a bribe walk straight into the temple at dawn, the one place the authorities were sure to look. Luke, who tells us he investigated everything carefully (Luke 1:3), says plainly that an angel opened the doors. The council itself never offered a natural explanation; it simply ordered the men to stop talking.

How should I speak to someone whose mind is already closed? Patiently, honestly and with prayer, because the problem is not finally in the evidence but in the heart, and only God can open a heart (16:14). Give the reasons for your hope when asked (1 Peter 3:15), but do not imagine a cleverer argument will do what only the Spirit can do. Ask gentle questions that help a person notice what he has ruled out in advance: what would you accept as evidence? Live so that your faith is hard to dismiss, and keep praying for him. Saul of Tarsus had his mind closed tighter than anyone in this council, and the risen Christ opened it on a road.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who run the temple are left at a loss, and then hear that their prisoners are standing in the temple doing exactly what they were arrested for: God is laughing at the rulers who set themselves against his Christ.

The captain of the temple and the chief priests. The captain of the temple ranked next to the high priest: a senior priest who commanded the Levitical temple guard, kept order in the precincts and held the power of arrest. His office helped seize Jesus (Luke 22:4, 52) and the apostles (4:1). With the chief priests, here is the temple’s whole ruling establishment, its head of security and its senior clergy, standing helpless before an empty cell.

Greatly perplexed. At a complete loss, out of explanations (diēporoun). They are not asking what has happened but where it will end. It is a more honest reaction than anything they will say for the rest of the day: they have lost control, and they know it.

Standing in the temple. Then the anticlimax: “Look!” Not fled or hiding, but standing in the establishment’s own building, doing the very thing they were arrested for, while the establishment holds an emergency session about where they might have gone.

Why does Luke make the authorities look so foolish? Not to mock them for sport, but to show the truth about every power that sets itself against Christ. Psalm 2 had described it: the rulers take counsel together “against the LORD and against his Anointed”, and “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:2, 4). The church had prayed that very psalm not long before (4:25–28), and Luke lets us see the answer in the form of a farce. When Christians feel small before powerful opponents, this is the scene to remember. The opponents are not in control, and the comedy is God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council fears the crowd, while the apostles, who fear God, walk back quietly to stand before the court: the fear of God sets people free from every other fear.

But not by force. The head of temple security, in his own precinct, arresting men he has the legal right to arrest, does it carefully, almost politely, because he is frightened of the crowd. The men who hold every instrument of power in Jerusalem cannot use any of it.

Before the council. The apostles, standing in a temple full of people who admire them, could slip away or let the crowd do what the officers fear. Instead they walk back with the officers and stand before the council. They submit to arrest, and then refuse to submit on the question of preaching. The one group in Jerusalem with real reason to be afraid behaves as though there were nothing to fear.

Two kinds of fear. Luke has built this chapter around one word. Great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5); great fear came upon the whole church (v. 11); and now fear again, in the other party, with a different object. The church is afraid of God. The council is afraid of the public. Nobody in the Sanhedrin appears to be afraid of God at all, and that is exactly why they are afraid of everybody else. A man who truly fears God has one thing to be afraid of and is free of nearly everything else; a man who does not ends up with a long and growing list. The council cannot act on its convictions, because it has to keep watching the temple courts to see how the crowd is taking it. That is the price of replacing conscience with reputation, and anyone who has softened a conviction because of what a room would think has felt the same rope round the same neck. “The fear of man lays a snare” (Proverbs 29:25).

Put your sword into its sheath. Peter had been at an arrest before. In Gethsemane, when the temple officers came for Jesus with lanterns and weapons, Peter drew a sword, and Jesus told him, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (John 18:3–11). Jesus went out to meet the men who came for him and gave himself up. Now Peter has learned what his Lord was doing that night. He does not reach for the crowd as he once reached for the sword; he walks back as quietly as Jesus did, because he serves a King who conquered by being handed over. When they struck Jesus, he did not strike back, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Jesus feared God perfectly, and so he feared no one else.

How do I get free of the fear of what people think? Not by caring less about people, but by fearing God more. The fear of man shrinks when God grows large in your sight. Jesus put it with startling directness: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28), and in the next breath, you are of more value than many sparrows. Fear God, and know that God loves you. Begin small: say the true thing in the next meeting where you would usually stay quiet, and notice that you survive it. Ask what you would do if only God were watching, and do that. He is the only one who always is.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest, who will not even say Jesus’ name, complains that the city is full of the apostles’ teaching and that they are laying Jesus’ blood at the council’s door; yet that blood is being offered to them as their cleansing.

Not to teach in this name. The high priest avoids saying the name of Jesus: “this man”, he will say in a moment. It is one more failed attempt to suppress him by silence.

You have filled Jerusalem. An unintended compliment. The council complains, in open session, that the gospel is unstoppable: the prosecution has entered the defence’s best evidence into the record. It is the third filling in twenty-eight verses. Satan filled Ananias’s heart (v. 3); the high priest’s party was filled with jealousy (v. 17); now the city is filled with the message they forbade. Everything in the chapter that sets itself against the Spirit is full of something, and none of it holds its ground. A heart full of the adversary lasted a morning; a council full of envy could reach no further than a whip; the teaching filled a capital city and has not stopped.

This man’s blood. An old biblical idiom for bloodguilt: to hold someone responsible for a death, to lay its guilt at his door (Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16). The council fears that the apostles are publicly fastening on them the charge of murdering Jesus, and they are right, for that is exactly what the apostles have been doing (2:23, 36; 3:15; 5:30). The irony is bitter. At Jesus’ trial the crowd stirred up by this same leadership had cried, “His blood be on us and on our children!” (Matthew 27:25). They once called the bloodguilt down on themselves; now they are terrified of being held to it.

The accusation and the cure. They want to silence the accusation rather than be cleansed of the blood. Yet there was a way to be rid of this man’s blood: not to muzzle the preachers but to be washed in the very blood they had shed. The blood that lay on them as guilt was held out to them as atonement: repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of your sins (2:36–38). Christ bore the penalty in the sinner’s place (Isaiah 53:5–6), and his is “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for vengeance; the blood of Jesus cries for pardon. The risen Lord had told his apostles that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, “beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47): beginning in the city that shed his blood, with the men who called for it. There is no guilt so close to the cross that the cross cannot reach it.

Were the Jewish people as a whole guilty of Christ’s death? No, not in the way that has so often been claimed. The apostles charge the particular leaders and crowds of Jerusalem who handed Jesus over, and they do it to call them to repentance and forgiveness, not to curse a nation. The church in Acts prayed that Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against Jesus to do what God’s hand had predestined (4:27–28). Jew and Gentile together crucified him, and the deeper truth is that our sins put him there. The centuries in which Christians used Matthew 27:25 to persecute Jewish people were a grievous sin against Christ, himself a Jew, and against the apostles, who were all Jews. The right response to this verse is not to point at anyone, but to plead the blood for ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a ruler forbids what God commands, God must be obeyed; and having said so, Peter at once preaches to his judges the Jesus they killed under the curse and God raised.

We must obey God rather than men. No preamble and no apology. The verb (dei) means it is necessary, binding: Peter is not claiming a right but describing an obligation he has no power to set aside. The first time they said it to this court, it was a question for the council to answer (4:19); now it is a statement. Christian conscience does not usually start by shouting. It asks first, and only hardens when the asking has been refused. The sentence has been the motto of martyrs through the centuries.

Putting the frame back. Without its frame, the rest of what the New Testament says about rulers, this sentence becomes a slogan for whatever a believer wants to defy. The New Testament’s ordinary teaching about government is not resistance but submission, stated most strongly by men living under an empire that, by early Christian tradition, would execute both of them. “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God”, Paul wrote to Christians in Nero’s capital (Romans 13:1). “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution”, writes Peter (1 Peter 2:13), the man speaking these very words. Both regarded submission to rulers as part of obeying God.

Real and derived. So how do the two fit? A government’s authority is real, but on loan from God. A ruler holds office by God’s appointment, which is why a Christian obeys him in the ordinary run of things without needing to agree with him. But a ruler who commands what God forbids has, at that point and only there, gone beyond the authority God lent him. Scripture supplies the pattern before Acts does: midwives who would not kill the boys (Exodus 1:17); three men who would not bow to a statue, not knowing whether they would be spared (Daniel 3:16–18); an old official, Daniel, who kept his windows open toward Jerusalem when prayer had been made a capital offence (Daniel 6:10). God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2).

The test. The test is narrower than most people who quote this verse would like. The question is not whether a law is unwise, unfair, expensive or offensive to me, but whether I am commanded to do what God forbids, or forbidden to do what God commands. The apostles are in the second case: God had told them, that very night, to go and speak (v. 20). A tax I resent, a policy I judge foolish, a regulation that inconveniences my church: none of these is Acts 5, and dressing them in this verse cheapens it for the day it is genuinely needed.

The half that is always dropped. These men do not resist arrest, summon the crowd or flee the city. They walk in, state their position, take a flogging for it, and go back to work. Biblical civil disobedience is open and peaceful, and joined to a willingness to bear the penalty, not to a search for an escape clause. Anyone appealing to this verse who is unwilling to pay the fine, take the sentence or lose the position is appealing to something other than what Peter is doing here.

The God of our fathers raised Jesus. Having refused the court’s authority on this point, Peter preaches to it on the spot. The God of our fathers claims continuity: not a foreign God or a new religion beside Israel’s, but the God of Abraham keeping his word; it is the council, not the apostles, who have departed from him. “Whom you killed” is said to their faces, in their own chamber, by a man with no legal standing whatsoever.

Hanging him on a tree. Peter could have said crucified. Instead he reaches for Deuteronomy, where a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God, his body to be taken down before nightfall so that the land is not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The leaders very probably meant the cross to show that Jesus was cursed by God. Peter chooses the description most offensive to every man listening, because it is true. The curse was real, and it fell on him; but it was not his own. He hung there in the place of people who had earned it and could not carry it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). To redeem is to buy out of slavery, and the price was the Son himself; and God raised him to show the account was settled. There is no gospel that does not go through that sentence, and Peter puts it before his judges within a minute of being told to be silent.

Obedient to the point of death. Before Peter said it, one Man lived it. Jesus obeyed his Father rather than men at every step, when crowds wanted to make him king and when rulers wanted him silent, “becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). That obedience is the whole of our righteousness: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). The perfect obedience of the faithful Son covers the faltering obedience of all his people.

What if I am not sure whether a command crosses the line? Then go slowly, and go with others. Ask the test plainly: am I being made to sin, or kept from a clear duty? Search the Scriptures, not your preferences. Seek the counsel of your elders and of mature Christians who will tell you the truth, because one person’s conscience can be too tender or too hard. Where the matter is genuinely unclear, lean toward submission and courtesy, for Scripture’s default is honour for those in authority. Where it is clear, be respectful in manner and firm in substance, and ready to bear the cost without bitterness. Daniel served a pagan king faithfully for decades, and still knew exactly where the line was when it came.

In everyday life. At work and at home this week, be the most willing, cheerful and law-abiding person in the room, so that if the day comes when you must say no for Christ’s sake, it is plain that you are not saying it from a rebellious spirit. And if that day has come, say it calmly, take what follows, and keep speaking of him.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jesus the council killed now reigns at God’s right hand as Leader and Saviour, giving repentance and forgiveness even to Israel’s rulers, and both the apostles and the Holy Spirit bear witness to it.

God exalted him at his right hand. The seat at a king’s right hand belonged to the one who shared his honour and wielded his power. Jesus is not resting in heaven; he is ruling, with authority over every power and “as head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:20–22).

Leader and Saviour. Leader (archēgos, 3:15) can mean the pioneer who cuts the track others will walk (see the box below). Jesus did not arrange a rescue from a safe distance; he went through death first, and the road exists because he made it. No one who follows him into that country goes anywhere he has not already been. Saviour (sōtēr), rescuer, is a title the Old Testament gives to God himself (Isaiah 43:11), and Peter gives it to Jesus without hesitation, before the very court that condemned him for blasphemy.

To give repentance. Here is a phrase to stop anyone who has tried and failed to repent: repentance itself is something Christ gives, not something we achieve (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). Repentance is a change of mind that becomes a change of direction: seeing sin as God sees it, hating it, and turning from it to him (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Forgiveness is God cancelling the debt (Colossians 2:13–14). Most people hear the command as though God stood at a distance requiring a change of heart we must manufacture before he will look at us. Anyone who has wanted to be sorry for something and found he could only regret the consequences knows the difference between working up remorse and being given a new mind about a thing. The second is a gift, from the one exalted to give it. The hands that were pierced are now full of gifts for the men who pierced them. Yet we are commanded to repent (3:19). Both are true: God commands what he gives, and gives what he commands.

And so is the Holy Spirit. Two witnesses, as the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the very pairing Jesus had promised: the Spirit of truth will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness (John 15:26–27). The apostles are human eyewitnesses of the resurrection. The Spirit testifies by his outpouring, which only the exalted Christ could send (2:33), by speaking through the witnesses (4:8, 31), and inwardly by convicting the world (John 16:8–11). So the council faces not the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself, a witness they can no more imprison than they could keep the prison shut.

A sermon in four sentences. Peter’s reply holds the principle (v. 29), the cross (v. 30), the exaltation and the offer (v. 31), and the witnesses (v. 32), with repentance offered to the very men who killed Jesus.

Whom God has given to those who obey him. Read carelessly, this turns the Spirit into a wage. But the obedience Peter means is not a record of performance. It is the word he used three verses earlier, “We must obey God”, and what he meant there was believing God’s word about his Son and acting on it: what the New Testament calls obeying the gospel, or “the obedience of faith” (6:7; Romans 1:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8). The Spirit is not the prize for a life already put right; he is the one who puts it right, and he comes to people who have answered the message about Jesus by surrendering to him.

If repentance is a gift, do I just wait for it? No. You ask for it, and act on the light you have. God’s gifts come through the means he has appointed: hearing his word, praying, and turning toward him even when the turning feels weak. Ask Christ plainly for a true sorrow for this sin, a hatred of it, and the strength to leave it. Then take the next step you can see: confess it, put it right, remove the occasion. If you find any desire at all to repent, that desire is already the gift beginning. The man who would like to repent but cannot feel it is not far from the kingdom; he is being drawn.

How can I know I have the Holy Spirit? Not mainly by dramatic experiences, but by what the Spirit always does. He makes Jesus precious to you, so that you confess him as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He bears witness with your spirit that you are a child of God, so that you call God Father (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate your sin and fight it (Galatians 5:17). And he grows his fruit in you, slowly, over years (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit has been given to you (Ephesians 1:13). You do not have to earn a second blessing (a later, separate experience some teach every believer must seek); you have to walk in the one you have been given.

Uncertain wording. The Greek word behind “Leader” (archēgos) has a range of meanings: leader or ruler, founder or originator, and pioneer, the one who goes first and opens the way. English Bibles render it variously; the ESV has “Author” of life at 3:15 and “founder” in Hebrews 2:10 and 12:2. Which shade Peter means here is not certain. Beside “Saviour” and at God’s right hand, a ruling Leader is likely, but the pioneer sense, the one who went through death first, fits the context of resurrection well, and the ideas overlap.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same message that cut three thousand to the heart at Pentecost enrages the council to the point of murder, and God rescues the apostles this time not by an angel but by a respected Pharisee.

Enraged. Rage, not refutation. The verb (dieprionto) is used literally of sawing: they were cut to the quick. Set that beside Pentecost, when those who heard the same message “were cut to the heart” and asked, “Brothers, what shall we do?” (2:37). Here the same message produces a decision to kill. Luke uses this word of the same council when it hears Stephen, and that time the rage ends in the killing it wanted here (7:54).

The gospel is never neutral. It either breaks a man open or hardens him, and at first the wound feels much the same from inside. Three thousand went one way in chapter 2; this council went the other. We are the aroma of Christ, “to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life” (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). Often what decides it is what a man is holding on to. These men had the temple, the people’s deference and the last word in Jerusalem, and a risen Christ threatened all three. Rage is what control sounds like when it is slipping.

A Pharisee named Gamaliel. With murder openly proposed, God sends not an angel but a Pharisee. A respected old teacher stands and asks for the room to be cleared, and the apostles live. Providence sometimes arrives as the one person present whose opinion the others cannot afford to dismiss. The Pharisees were a minority in the council but popular with the people, and they had less reason than the Sadducees to want these men silenced: they believed in the resurrection and in angels (23:8), and years later Pharisees in this same council would stand up for Paul (23:9).

Who was Gamaliel? Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about him, best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by tradition, a descendant (commonly said to be the grandson) of the famous Hillel and a leader of Hillel’s school. He is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the title Rabban, our master, a rank above Rabbi. The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic law, pays him a striking tribute: when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the law ceased, and purity and abstinence died (Sotah 9:15). Tradition credits him with rulings for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce. And the young Saul of Tarsus was educated at his feet (22:3). A much later Christian legend that Gamaliel secretly became a believer has no historical foundation.

Outside for a little while. The apostles were outside, yet Luke knows what was said; perhaps Saul himself, Gamaliel’s pupil, later told him.

Appointed for the fall and rising of many. The dividing line runs through a Person. Simeon told Jesus’ mother that “this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel”, a sign opposed, so that the thoughts of many hearts would be revealed (Luke 2:34–35). At Pentecost many rose; in this council many fall. No one meets him and stays the same, because he is not an idea to be weighed but the Lord, and every heart is laid bare before him.

Why does the same message soften some and harden others? Because the difference is not finally in the message or the messenger but in God’s work in the hearer. Faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8), and it is the Lord who opens hearts to pay attention to what is said (16:14). Luke says it plainly later: “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (13:48). Scripture’s word for this is election: God chose a people for himself in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything he foresaw in them, and in his time he opens each of their hearts (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). Many Christians understand election instead as God choosing those he foresaw would believe; Reformed Christians read it as the cause of faith rather than its reward, because Paul says the choice was made before either child had done anything good or bad.

What this does and does not mean. It does not make the hardened man a puppet; he chooses his rage freely and is responsible for it. But it should humble every Christian: if you were cut to the heart rather than sawn through, it was grace, not your superior openness. And it should free every preacher and every ordinary witness. Our task is to speak Christ faithfully; the opening of hearts belongs to God.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel warns the council to be careful, citing failed movements that collapsed when their leaders died: shrewd advice that God used, but a way of waiting that avoids the one question that matters.

Take care. To a court that has just proposed killing the apostles without a trial, he says be careful. He is the only man in the chamber who says anything of the kind.

Claiming to be somebody. Judea in living memory had produced a run of men who gathered a following, claimed to be somebody, and came to nothing when they were killed; Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, says the land was full of them. Gamaliel’s reasoning is simple: movements of that kind collapse when their leader dies, so let time do the work and keep the council’s hands clean.

Came to nothing. As practical advice, Gamaliel’s case is shrewd, and God used it. As a way of settling what is true, it is worthless, and the same reasoning is offered constantly today. Lasting a long time does not prove a thing true: plenty of false things last for centuries, and Gamaliel was speaking inside a temple that had stood a long time and would be rubble within forty years. Plenty of true things are crushed early and stay crushed for a generation. Applied consistently, his rule would have condemned nearly every prophet Israel ever had.

A decision not to look. The deeper problem is that the rule avoids the only question in the room. The apostles had made a factual claim: God raised Jesus from the dead, and we saw him. That claim has witnesses, a date, and a tomb nobody in that chamber claimed was still occupied. Gamaliel proposes that they wait and see, which is a decision not to look. The posture is common, and presented as open-mindedness. It sounds humble, and it is the one position that cannot be held. A man deciding whether Jesus rose from the dead is not an observer of the case but a party to it. Waiting to see how it turns out is itself an answer.

I will strike the shepherd. Gamaliel’s pattern, a leader killed and his followers scattered, had already happened once more. On the night of his arrest Jesus quoted Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). Within hours the Shepherd was struck and his followers ran. By Gamaliel’s rule that should have been the end. But in the same breath Jesus had added, “after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee” (Mark 14:28). The flock in Solomon’s Portico is a scattered flock gathered again by a living Shepherd.

Uncertain wording. Who this Theudas was is not known. The only Theudas Josephus records led a crowd to the Jordan about AD 44 to 46, a decade after Gamaliel is speaking, whereas Gamaliel places his Theudas before Judas the Galilean (AD 6). The likeliest answer is an otherwise unrecorded rebel who shared the name, one of the many who rose in the unsettled years after Herod the Great’s death in 4 BC.
