(On whether Luke has erred, see the note on vv. 37–38.)
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel’s second example, Judas the Galilean, makes his rule plain: what is merely of man will fail, so leave these men alone. The comparison also shows how unlike these rebels Jesus was.

Judas the Galilean. He led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6, under Quirinius, as Josephus confirms. He taught that paying taxes to Rome was slavery and that God alone was king, and his movement is often thought to have fed the later Zealots.

If this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail. Gamaliel’s conclusion is the first half of a two-sided rule, and the second half, in the next verse, is the one that matters: “if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them” (v. 39).

The King came without a sword. Luke tells of another census, a decree from Caesar Augustus that sent a carpenter and his betrothed to Bethlehem, where the true King was born and laid in a manger (Luke 2:1–7). God did not fight the empire to bring his Son into the world; he used its paperwork to keep his promise about the city of David. The King came without a sword, and his kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).

Was Jesus a political rebel like these men? No, and the comparison shows the difference. Judas the Galilean said that paying taxes to Caesar was treason against God; Jesus said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Mark 12:17). Theudas and Judas raised armed followings; Jesus told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52) and said to Pilate, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). The would-be messiahs wanted a throne in Jerusalem; Jesus took a cross outside it. His kingdom does come, and in the end it overturns every power, but it comes by the word and the Spirit, not the sword. Christians who try to advance it by force or political domination have misunderstood their King.

Did Luke get his history wrong? These two names carry a well-known objection, and since Luke’s standing as a historian matters to this whole book, it should be met. Josephus describes a Theudas whose rising came about AD 44 to 46, a decade or more after Gamaliel spoke, and Gamaliel places Judas (AD 6) after Theudas; so Luke is said to have the order backwards and to have invented the speech. Two things need saying. First, a country full of failed insurgents could easily produce two rebels of the same name decades apart (see the box at vv. 35–36). Josephus himself says there were countless disturbances in Judea after Herod the Great died, and Gamaliel’s Theudas had about four hundred men, while Josephus’s drew a great crowd to the Jordan. No reconciliation can be proved, and it is honest to say so, but this is a reasonable answer, not a desperate one. Second, the objection assumes that where Luke and Josephus differ, Josephus is the standard, yet Josephus is careless in places. Luke was long said to have blundered over the titles of local officials, the city authorities of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the chief man of Malta, and inscriptions have since shown him right, in details easy to get wrong. A writer with that record has earned the benefit of the doubt about a rebel’s name.
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel warns that if this work is of God it cannot be overthrown, and that the council might find itself fighting God: the truest sentence spoken that day, and the theme of the whole book, from a man who did not believe it.

If it is of God. Gamaliel’s last sentence is the sharpest thing said in the chamber all day, and he almost certainly did not know how sharp it was.

You might even be found opposing God! God-fighters (theomachoi) is a word found nowhere else in the New Testament. It belongs above all to Greek tragedy, where the man who sets himself against heaven is destroyed by the attempt, usually while believing he is defending something. Gamaliel raises it as a remote hazard worth insuring against. It is the actual position of every man he is speaking to. The wisest man in the room got nearer the truth than anyone else present and still kept it at arm’s length. It is possible to say “if it is of God” and never get as far as admitting that it is.

Delivered by an argument they did not make. Twelve men who could not defend themselves, in the hands of a court that wanted them dead, were delivered by an argument they did not make, from a man who was not on their side, for reasons that were not the right ones. The church’s survival did not depend on its enemies being reasonable. It never has. What Gamaliel offered as a warning against a possibility, the apostles could have offered as a statement of fact: nothing that is of God will be overthrown.

The theme of the book. Gamaliel’s “if” states the theme of Acts. The Sanhedrin, Herod, mobs and a shipwreck all try to overthrow the work, and “the word of God increased and multiplied” (12:24). The book ends with Paul under guard in Rome, proclaiming the kingdom “with all boldness and without hindrance” (28:31). Luke lets an unbeliever ask the question in chapter 5 and spends the rest of the book answering it.

His most famous student. Two chapters on, a young man stands at a stoning, holding the coats and approving, and he tells us himself that he was brought up in this city “at the feet of Gamaliel” (22:3). Saul of Tarsus had this exact warning from his own teacher and went out and did what it warned against, until a voice on the Damascus road said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads” (26:14). Gamaliel’s word proved a prophecy about his most famous student. Saul fought God, and was thrown to the ground and raised up an apostle. The Lord does not only defeat his enemies; sometimes he turns them into his servants.

That is how this God wins. No one has ever fought against God and won. Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his chariots. But the fiercest battle ever fought against God was fought at a cross, and there the One under attack prayed for his attackers: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). That is how this God wins: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).

Will history be the judge? Gamaliel’s rule has a modern descendant. We rarely say “if it is of God”; we say history will judge, or that someone is on the wrong side of it. It sounds modest, but it quietly gives history the throne, assuming that whatever wins was right, and that the future, which happens to agree with us, will vindicate us. History has a long record of siding with the strong. By every measure available in the year Jesus died, the cross was the wrong side of history: a Galilean preacher executed under a curse, his followers flogged. Christians do not trust the drift of history; they trust its Lord. And the one place where God has already announced his verdict is an empty tomb, where he overturned the decision of every court that mattered (17:31). That frees us from two anxieties at once: the fear of being left behind, and the need to win in order to be right.

So how do I test a movement or a teacher? By Scripture first, with Christ at the centre. Does it confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, crucified and risen (1 John 4:1–3)? Does it agree with what the apostles taught, as the Bereans checked even Paul against the Scriptures (17:11)? Does it make much of Christ, or of a leader, a method or an experience? And what fruit grows in its leaders and followers over time: humility, holiness and love, or pride, money and control (Matthew 7:15–20)? Size and success are not on the list, nor how moving the meetings are. A small, faithful church preaching Christ crucified passes the test that a famous movement may fail.

Where Christians differ: is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some treat it as a sure rule: if something succeeds, it is from God. This commentary’s view: it is wise caution, and true in the long run, but not a full test. False religions have lasted centuries, and God’s work can look as if it is failing for a time. The true test is Scripture and Christ (1 John 4:1–3). Gamaliel’s advice was sensible, but it was neutrality, not faith, and neutrality towards Christ is not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council accepts Gamaliel’s warning and then flogs the apostles anyway, forbidding them again to speak in Jesus’ name: they cannot kill the message, so they punish its messengers.

They beat them. Probably the synagogue flogging, forty strokes less one: the law permitted forty, and the practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break it (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The strokes were laid on with a leather strap across the bared chest and back, and men were carried away from it. Paul received it five times and listed it among the things that nearly killed him (2 Corinthians 11:24). Jesus had warned them that they would be flogged in the synagogues (Matthew 10:17).

The incoherence of it. Minutes earlier the council was warned by its most honoured member that it might be found fighting God, and it accepted the advice. Then it had the men beaten and told them again to stop speaking. They kept the verdict and lowered the sentence, which is what men do when they have decided the question already and are only negotiating the cost.

In the name of Jesus. In the Bible a name stands for the whole person: his identity, his character and above all his authority. To speak in someone’s name is to act as his representative, by his authority, as an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king’s. So when the apostles spoke in the name of Jesus, they were not merely mentioning him. They were proclaiming who he is, the crucified and risen Lord, and calling people to trust and obey him, as his authorised messengers (3:6; 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

Scourged first. The backs of the apostles were laid open for the name, and the name was worth it, because the one who bears it was scourged first, and “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

And what does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? The same thing, turned toward heaven. It is not adding a formula to the end of a prayer. It is coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, not of our own worthiness, and asking for what he would want, as people who belong to him (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). We come with confidence, because his name opens the door, and with humility, because we are asking for his glory and not merely our wishes. When you end a prayer “in Jesus’ name”, you are saying: I have no standing of my own here; I come in his.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flogged and forbidden, the apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy of shame for Jesus’ name, and go on every day, in public and in homes, announcing that the Christ is Jesus.

Rejoicing. The apostles walk out with their backs opened, and Luke says they were rejoicing: not resigned, not bearing it well. Not because pain is good, but because suffering for Christ is an honour (Matthew 5:11–12; 1 Peter 4:13–16; Philippians 1:29).

Counted worthy to suffer dishonour. The two halves of the phrase ought to contradict each other. To be counted worthy is to be honoured, judged fit for something valuable; dishonour is public shame, the thing every man in that culture organised his life to avoid. Not long before, this same group had argued on a road about which of them was the greatest (Mark 9:33–34). The prize turned out to be a flogging. Honour was the currency of their world, as approval is of ours, and these men had found an approval that outweighed the whole city’s contempt: Christ’s.

For the name. Luke does not say whose name. In Jewish speech the Name was how one referred to the God of Israel without pronouncing the divine name itself. Luke uses it, with nothing added, of a carpenter executed outside the city wall, and among these people there was no confusion; John could later write simply of believers who “have gone out for the sake of the name” (3 John 7). The council in this chapter refused to say the name at all, calling him “this man” (v. 28). The apostles can leave it unsaid for the opposite reason: for them there is no other name it could be.

He counted it worth it. The Name they carried out of that chamber belongs to the Christ “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), and his joy is the joy that filled them on the road home. He counted it worth it to be shamed for them; they counted it worth it to be shamed for him.

In the temple and from house to house. Every day, from that day. In the temple, the most dangerous place in the city; and from house to house, at kitchen tables, where the church has always done most of its real work. Public and private together, the pattern Paul would describe to the Ephesian elders: “teaching you in public and from house to house” (20:20).

That the Christ is Jesus. Preaching (euangelizomenoi) is announcing good news, and its heart is one sentence: the Messiah is Jesus. All Israel’s hopes have a name and a face, the man the council would not name. Arrest, prison, trial, flogging and a court order had been brought to bear on twelve provincials, and the only measurable result was that the message was preached in more houses than before. He is worth this, was the verdict of the men with the wounds. Two thousand years later the name they would not stop saying is spoken every hour in thousands of languages, and of the men on the council that day hardly anyone is remembered, except the high priest and the one who argued for leaving them alone.

In the flow. With verse 42 the first great movement of Acts comes to rest. The chapter began with a threat from inside and ends with a threat from outside, and both have failed: nothing can stop his name being spoken.

What it does not mean. This verse has been laid on suffering people as a demand, and it is not one. Three things keep it honest. First, they are not rejoicing in the pain but in what it meant: that the Lord they had abandoned in a garden had now counted them fit to be shamed on his account. Nobody is asked to enjoy a scourge. Second, this is a specific kind of suffering: dishonour incurred for Christ, in the course of obeying him. A diagnosis is not dishonour for the name; neither is a bereavement, a betrayal, or a depression that will not lift. Those are real, and Scripture speaks to them elsewhere and at length; this verse is not the text to beat a grieving person with. Third, this joy is given, not manufactured. It arrived in them on the way out of that building. It is not a mood a Christian owes in advance and is failing to produce.

I could never do that. To anyone who quietly concludes that if it cost him his job, his family’s standing or a beating, he would fold: look at who is walking out of that chamber. The man in front is Peter. A short while ago, with nothing at stake but a servant girl’s opinion beside a fire, he said he did not know Jesus, and then went out and wept. What changed was not his temperament. Something was given to him that had not been there in the courtyard, and it is given when it is needed and not before. The measure of what you could bear today is not the measure of what you would be carried through tomorrow.

Is it right to want to suffer for Christ? Not to seek it. The apostles did not court the flogging; they obeyed and accepted what came. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next when persecuted (Matthew 10:23), and Paul used his Roman citizenship to escape unjust punishment (22:25). Some in the early church rushed to martyrdom, and wise pastors rebuked them. What is right is to be willing: to love Christ more than comfort or reputation, so that when faithfulness costs something, you pay it gladly. Do not go looking for the cross; do not run from it when it is laid on you for his sake.

Must I go house to house? Not necessarily door to door with leaflets, though some are called to that. But every Christian has a house, and the house is where the gospel has always travelled furthest. Open your home: a meal with a neighbour, a Bible read with your children, a conversation over coffee with a friend who is struggling. Speak of Christ where you already are, naturally and honestly, and support the public preaching of your church with your presence and prayers. The temple and the house belong together: your pastor preaches in the one; you are sent into the other.

5.theology: The holiness of God in the new covenant community. As Nadab and Abihu died at the founding of the tabernacle worship (Leviticus 10), so at the birth of the church God makes his holiness unmistakable. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than in the old. It is that the church lives closer to the Holy Spirit than any generation before it, and nearness to holiness calls for honesty and purity.
5.examples:
Then: A church a few weeks old learned that the Spirit who fills it also searches it, and that the God of grace is the God of holiness. The fear did not empty the church: within a few verses believers were added to the Lord in multitudes.

Now: We speak, rightly, of grace, love and welcome. But grace is not tame, and Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled and that our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29).

keyVerse.quote: We must obey God rather than men.
keyVerse.note: Peter’s answer to the council joins the two halves of the chapter. Ananias and Sapphira feared what people thought more than they feared God, and lied; the apostles feared God, and so feared no one else, even under the lash. The sentence is not a licence to defy any law we dislike, but the settled loyalty of people whose Lord is the risen Jesus, the one Man who obeyed his Father perfectly, to the point of death.

5.reflection:
Ananias and Sapphira wanted the reputation of total devotion without paying its price (vv. 1–4). What are the everyday forms of that temptation in a church like ours, and what would it look like to be honest instead?

Luke says great fear came on the whole church (v. 11), yet the church went on to grow (v. 14). How can the fear of the Lord and confidence in his love belong together, and which of the two do you find harder?

The apostles said they must obey God rather than men (v. 29), yet they did not resist arrest and they accepted the flogging. Where is the line between submitting to authorities and refusing them, and how should a Christian behave on either side of it?

The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (v. 41). What makes that joy possible, and what small cost of following Christ might you be facing this week?

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 4 and 5 showed the young church threatened from outside by the council and from inside by the lie of Ananias and Sapphira. Now a third danger appears, a quarrel that could split the church along a line of language and culture, and with Stephen Luke begins the story that carries the gospel out of Jerusalem.

The message. The risen Christ cares for his people’s bodies and souls, and orders his church so that neither is neglected: the overlooked are fed, the word is preached, and the word keeps growing. A man appointed to wait on tables can be filled with his Master’s Spirit, wisdom and grace, and when he is falsely accused, God himself answers for him.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). He shows a church that was honest rather than perfect, which failed some widows, owned it and mended it; and he shows that the charge of being against Moses, the temple and the law was first laid by false witnesses against a man whose face shone like Moses’ own.

How the chapter makes its case. Growth exposes a failure: Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily distribution (v. 1). The Twelve ask the whole church for seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom, so that they can keep to prayer and the word (vv. 2–4); the church chooses seven, all with Greek names, and the apostles commission them (vv. 5–6), and the word spreads, even among the priests (v. 7). Then Stephen, full of grace and power, wins the argument in the Greek-speaking synagogues (vv. 8–10), so his opponents plant false witnesses, turn the people against the church and bring him before the council for blasphemy against Moses, the temple and the law (vv. 11–14). The court sees the face of an angel (v. 15).

Where it leads. Stephen’s story follows his Lord’s step by step: full of the Spirit, gracious words in a synagogue, false witnesses, a charge about destroying the temple, a hearing before the council. Behind it stands Christ, who was among his disciples “as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27), the true temple and the one Moses wrote about; the light on Stephen’s face is borrowed from his.

For us. No one in Christ’s church is too small to be seen, and no task too ordinary to be done in the fullness of his Spirit. Ask who is being looked past in your church, and serve them. And when you are misrepresented for Christ, remember that he went that way first, and does not leave his servants alone in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the church failed some of its most vulnerable members, it did not hide the failure but mended it in a way that kept both the tables and the word in their place. Growth exposed a blind spot: the Greek-speaking widows were being missed in the daily food distribution (v. 1). The Twelve brought it before the whole church, refused to leave the word for the tables, and asked for seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom (vv. 2–4). The church chose seven, all with Greek names, and the apostles prayed and laid their hands on them (vv. 5–6). The result was more than peace: the word of God kept growing, even among the priests (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and service in the church

The apostles’ refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about calling, not dignity (see the note on vv. 1–2), and waiting on widows and preaching are two forms of one service (see vv. 3–4). What the passage protects is the church’s food supply in both senses: a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked is contradicting what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows had no land and no clan to fall back on. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone, but who is currently being looked past (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Growth brought a real injustice to light: Greek-speaking widows were being missed when the food was shared out, and the apostles took it seriously without abandoning the work of the word.

When the disciples were increasing. The church had outgrown arrangements that once kept everyone in view. Growth brings new problems, and a church never troubled by them is usually not growing.

Hellenists and Hebrews. Both groups in this quarrel are Jews, and both are Christians. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, mostly born in the Jewish communities scattered across the empire and now settled in Jerusalem; the Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews native to the land. The line between them is language and culture, not theology.

A complaint. The word is grumbling (gongysmos), the word the Greek Old Testament uses again and again for Israel muttering in the wilderness. Yet neither Luke nor the apostles rebuke the complainers. The grievance was true, and it was acted on. Sometimes the murmuring is right.

The daily distribution. Widows then had no pension or state support, and the church fed them daily. Some Jews of the dispersion came to Jerusalem in old age to be buried near the temple, and their widows were left in a city where they owned no land, had no clan to fall back on and could not always follow what was said around them. Nobody had decided they should go without. In the press of a distribution serving thousands, run by men who spoke a different language at home, the women without a voice were simply not seen. That is how this kind of injustice nearly always happens: by oversight, not malice.

The full number of the disciples. The Twelve could have quietly adjusted the rota. Instead the failure is put in public, before the very people who had been neglected.

To serve tables. Not a clergyman declining a menial job: the men chosen for it must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom (v. 3). Serving tables is not beneath the apostles; their calling is the word, and if they did everything, the word would suffer. A congregation whose teachers disappear into administration will be starved of the word within a generation, and the widows will still not be fed.

He looked up and saw a poor widow. The church that missed these women belonged to a Lord who never missed one. At the gate of Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s bier, had compassion on her, and gave the boy back to his mother (Luke 7:11–15). In the temple, among the rich with their large gifts, he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins, and said she had given more than all of them (Luke 21:1–4). His Father is “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5), who upholds the widow and the fatherless (Psalm 146:9). And when the Son hung dying, carrying the sin of the world, he still looked down, saw his mother standing by the cross, and gave her into the keeping of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). His eyes find the one at the edge of the crowd, even from a cross; to overlook a widow was to forget whose table they were serving at.

Who is being looked past? That is sharper than the usual question, would we turn anybody away? Almost nobody would. But who is in the building and in nobody’s line of sight, because they were never in the middle of the room and nobody has gone over to ask? The widow who comes alone, the international student, the family whose English is halting, the man with a disability who leaves before the coffee.

If this church was full of the Spirit, how could it fail its widows? Being filled with the Spirit does not make a church sinless or all-seeing. Luke does not hide the failure, and that honesty is part of why his account can be trusted: he is not selling a perfect church. The test of a Spirit-filled church is what it does when its failure is pointed out. This one listened, owned it, and put it right in a single meeting.

What should I do if I feel overlooked in my church? Say so, gently and to the right people, as the Hellenists did. Go to an elder or deacon, describe what happened without accusing anyone of motives, assume, as is usually true, oversight rather than contempt, and give the leaders time to act. Avoid the wilderness kind of grumbling, which talks to everyone except the people who can help. And because you know what it is to be overlooked, become the person who notices others who are.

Uncertain wording. “Hellenists” (Hellēnistai) is not found in any surviving Greek writing before Acts, so its meaning has to be worked out from how Luke uses it. Most take it to mean Jews whose language was Greek, as against the Aramaic-speaking “Hebrews”; some think it marks a Greek way of life as much as a language. At 9:29 the Hellenists are Jews who oppose Paul, so the word names a group within Judaism, not a church party. The likely meaning is Greek-speaking Jews.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside the land; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic. Widows without family depended on the community’s daily food distribution.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles ask the church to choose seven men of proven character and Spirit-given wisdom to care for the widows, so that they themselves can keep to prayer and the word.

Seven men of good repute. For men who are to hand out food, the apostles ask three qualifications, none of them administrative: a good name, the fullness of the Spirit, and wisdom. Handling money and caring for vulnerable people requires character before skill, as Paul’s later qualifications for deacons agree (1 Timothy 3:8–13).

Wisdom. Not intelligence or education, but the skill of living well in God’s world: seeing a situation as God sees it, and knowing what to do next. This task needed exactly that, for no law of Moses said how to share a food budget between two language groups who distrusted each other. Timothy Keller often pointed out that most of the decisions we face are not settled by a plain command, and that wisdom is knowing the right thing to do where the rules run out. It begins with the fear of the LORD (Proverbs 9:10), and it has a face: Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). How do you grow in it? Ask, for God “gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5). Fill your mind with his word, and take counsel from people wiser than you (Proverbs 15:22). Test it by its fruit: “the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason” (James 3:17). The widows needed men who were not merely capable but gentle.

The congregation chooses. The apostles set the standard, the congregation chooses with no slate presented, and the apostles appoint. The word for “duty” (chreia) means “need”: the office exists because of a need, not a need because of an office.

Prayer and the ministry of the word. To devote oneself is to stick at a thing and refuse to be prised off it, the verb Luke used of the whole church at 2:42. Prayer is named first: the one thing nobody would have noticed them dropping. Both are labour (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:2), and a minister who neglects them for administration fails his flock, however busy he looks.

Service of tables, service of the word. “Ministry” here is diakonia, service, from the same root as the verb for serving tables. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not a menial category and a spiritual one, but two forms of one service.

Not an administrative committee. Stephen is arguing in synagogues within a paragraph and is dead within a chapter. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, baptises an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and is still called an evangelist twenty years later (21:8). Neither of them stayed at the tables. Whatever the church later made of the office, it began with men so full of the Spirit that the job could not hold them.

I am among you as the one who serves. The Twelve had learned that word at a table. At the Last Supper, while they argued about which of them was the greatest, Jesus said: “I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:24–27). Their Lord had waited on them. So when they hand the tables to the seven, they are not stepping up out of service into something grander; they are keeping to the service he gave them, and giving his other service to men fit to do it. He fed multitudes and spent whole nights in prayer; both kinds of service meet perfectly in him, and he gives both to his body.

How can I help my pastors keep to prayer and the word? By taking up the tasks that do not need them: the rota, the accounts, the building, the visits, the meals for the new mother, the lifts for the elderly. Doing one well, without being asked twice, is not lesser than preaching; it serves the word by clearing room for it. Pray that their study would be fruitful and their prayers persevering, and guard their time kindly: not every question needs the pastor.

Does this mean only men may serve as deacons? Luke uses the word for men here. Christians differ on whether women may hold the office of deacon. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church at Cenchreae, using the same word (Romans 16:1), and 1 Timothy 3:11 may speak of women deacons or of deacons’ wives. Many complementarian churches appoint women as deacons, since the office is one of service, not of teaching and ruling, which belong to the elders; others reserve it for men. Plainly, women served the early church in many ways, and every church needs their gifts.

Where Christians differ: were the seven the first deacons? Luke uses the verb serve (diakonein) and the noun (diakonia), but he never calls these men deacons, here or anywhere; later he simply calls Philip one of the seven (21:8). This commentary’s view: many rightly see here the pattern for the office of deacon, which appears formally later (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13): men set apart to oversee practical care so that elders can give themselves to the word and prayer. The two offices, elders and deacons, are the New Testament pattern for church leadership.

parallels.desc: Jethro advises Moses to share the load

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole church agrees and chooses seven Spirit-filled men, all apparently from the side that complained, and the apostles commission them with prayer and the laying on of hands. A church with money, a grievance and an ethnic fault line running through it settles the matter in one meeting, by giving the power away.

They chose Stephen. Stephen will be the first martyr (chapter 7). But how could anyone tell that a man was full of the Spirit? The church was told to pick out such men (v. 3), so the fullness was something a congregation could recognise: in character, the fruit the Spirit grows (Galatians 5:22–23), steady enough to earn a good name; in wisdom, which Stephen’s opponents could not withstand (v. 10); and in faith, a settled trust and boldness. They knew the tree by its fruit (Matthew 7:16). And these Spirit-filled men were chosen to wait on tables. The Spirit who raised Christ from the dead does not save his power for platforms; his fullness is proved first in humble, everyday service.

Philip. Later Philip the evangelist (21:8), who takes the gospel to Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (chapter 8).

Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Parmenas. Four men named once in Scripture and never again, trusted with widows’ bread and forgotten by history. They are remembered by God.

Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. A Gentile convert to Judaism, and then to Christ, now helping to run the welfare of the Jerusalem church. Antioch will become the great centre of the Gentile mission (11:19–26).

All seven have Greek names. Aramaic-speaking Jews sometimes bore Greek names (the apostles Andrew and Philip did), so this is not proof, but it strongly suggests that the seven came from the Hellenists. The majority could have appointed four Hebrews and three Hellenists, which would have been fair and would have left the Hebrews in control of the money. Instead, it seems, they handed the whole operation to the people who had raised the complaint.

They laid their hands on them. Scripture uses this gesture for blessing (Mark 10:16), for identifying with a sacrifice (Leviticus 1:4) and, closest here, for commissioning to an office. The pattern is Moses and Joshua. God told Moses to take Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit”, and lay his hand on him and commission him (Numbers 27:18–23), and afterwards Joshua was “full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him” (Deuteronomy 34:9). So the seven are publicly set apart, with prayer that God would equip them, and the New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry (13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6).

Not magic. The hands do not transfer power. The act is always joined to prayer, and the prayer asks God to act. It is a public recognition, and Scripture warns against doing it lightly: “Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands” (1 Timothy 5:22).

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke first used those words of Jesus, returning from the Jordan to face the devil in the wilderness (Luke 4:1). He chooses them for Stephen with care, because Stephen’s story will follow his Lord’s step by step: false witnesses, a charge about the temple, a hearing before the council, a death outside the city with a prayer committing his spirit and a prayer for his killers (6:11–14; 7:59–60). The Spirit who filled Jesus is the Spirit the exalted Jesus has poured out on his people, forming them in their Master’s likeness. Stephen will shine because Christ is shining through him.

How do we heal division in a church? The way this church did. Take the complaint seriously. Bring it into the open rather than handling it in corners. Look for godly people from the group that feels unheard and give them real responsibility, not a token seat. Pray over the solution together. And keep the gospel at the centre, because the deepest unity in a church is not a compromise between groups but a shared belonging to Christ, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). Division grows where people feel unseen, and shrinks when they are seen and trusted.

Was this Nicolaus the founder of the Nicolaitans? Revelation condemns a group called the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2:6, 15), and some early writers, from Irenaeus on, linked them with this man. Scripture does not. Luke presents him as a man of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the whole church; the name was not rare, and the link is uncertain at best. It is wise not to blacken a man whom the Bible honours on the strength of a later guess.
verseByVerse.note: All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. Laying on hands marked commissioning for a task.

parallels.desc: Moses lays hands on Joshua

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the church’s unity restored, the word of God keeps spreading, and even many of the temple’s own priests submit to Christ.

The word of God continued to increase. Luke closes sections with a formula of this shape (9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20); here it closes the church’s Jerusalem years, and what follows is Stephen, persecution, Samaria, then the world. Notice what increased: not the church, but “the word of God”. The message is the living thing, and the congregation its visible result; God’s word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:10–11).

A great many of the priests. Not the high-priestly families, who appear in this book only as opponents. The ordinary priesthood was an enormous body, by Josephus’s reckoning some twenty thousand, divided into courses that served at the temple for a week or two each year and spent the rest at home in the villages of Judea (Luke 1:8–9). Zechariah, John the Baptist’s father, was one of them: the temple’s rank and file, often poor.

Obedient to the faith. Not only persuaded: obedient. The faith is something a person obeys, and Paul speaks of “the obedience of faith” at the beginning and end of his letter to Rome (Romans 1:5; 16:26). In the New Testament, to believe is to act on the truth, not only to agree with it.

The quiet argument of the chapter. Luke reports a row about widows and bread, and in the next sentence the word spreads and the priests begin coming. He does not say the one caused the other, and it would be crude to pretend that sorting out administration produces revival. But he has put the two side by side. A church whose Greek-speaking widows go hungry while it preaches that the risen Christ has made one people out of many is making an argument against itself. Remove the contradiction, and the message can be heard for what it is.

The cost of their faith. A priest who confessed Jesus was saying that the sacrifice he assisted at, the altar his family existed to serve and that fed his household, had done its work: the shadow had given way to the substance. The morning lamb was only an outline thrown ahead of someone coming, and Christ is the one who cast it (Hebrews 10:1). Some may have been on duty at the Passover when Jesus died outside the wall, on the day, as John’s Gospel sets it, that the Passover lambs were killed (John 19:14). Hebrews would later explain what they had grasped: Christ “had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12).

He has never been off duty. These priests, serving in courses a week or two a year, found a High Priest whose course never ends. He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever, and he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25). He has never once been off duty for his people.

Can people still come to Christ from the heart of another religion? Yes, and this verse is a great encouragement to pray for them. These priests had more invested in the old system than anyone: training, income, family identity and the respect of their village. God brought them to Christ anyway. He still calls imams, monks, rabbis and convinced atheists, often at great personal cost. Do not write anyone off as too committed elsewhere to be reached. The Spirit who opened the hearts of temple priests can open any heart.
verseByVerse.note: There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A servant of Christ may win the argument and still be dragged into court, but God does not leave him without witness. Stephen, one of the seven, full of grace and power, works great signs (v. 8). Greek-speaking Jews from the synagogue of the Freedmen dispute with him and cannot withstand his Spirit-given wisdom, just as Jesus had promised (vv. 9–10). So they plant men to accuse him of blasphemy, turn the people against the church for the first time, and bring him before the council (vv. 11–12), where false witnesses twist his teaching about the temple and the law into an attack on both (vv. 13–14). Then the court looks at the accused and sees the face of an angel (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost of witness

Stephen’s arrest follows the shape of his Master’s (traced in the note on vv. 5–6). The servant is handed his Master’s charge sheet (Mark 14:58). Where the gospel threatens entrenched religious power it often meets resistance of the same kind, because in the end the objection is not to the argument (Stephen’s opponents lost that at verse 10) but to what admitting it would cost them. Stephen won the argument and still lost his life (see v. 10), and Luke did not think his death undid his victory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen’s opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they found men who would swear to blasphemy. Now: A believer put on the spot for Christ is promised a mouth, not a result (see the note on v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen, chosen to see that widows were fed, is so full of God’s grace and power that he works great signs among the people.

Full of grace and power. Three verses ago this man was chosen to see that the widows got their bread; now he is working great wonders. Luke praises him more warmly than most of the Twelve, yet gives no home town, trade or family: two chapters, one sermon and a shining face. Four times he is called full: of the Spirit and of wisdom (v. 3, the standard he was chosen to meet), of faith and of the Holy Spirit (v. 5), of grace and power (here), and of the Holy Spirit as he dies (7:55). Grace is both God’s unearned favour resting on him and the winsome graciousness it produces; power is the Spirit’s enabling might, which Jesus promised (1:8).

Great wonders and signs. Stephen is the first in Acts outside the apostles to do signs, and it comes after the apostles laid their hands on him (v. 6). In these chapters signs go with the apostles and with men closely linked to them, such as Philip (8:6).

Grace first, then power. Power flows out of a life already full of grace. Power without grace is dangerous, and the church has seen enough gifted men without grace to know it. Luke has shown that order before. Of the boy Jesus he wrote that the favour, the grace, of God was upon him (Luke 2:40); of the grown man, that he “returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee” (Luke 4:14). Peter would later sum up that whole life in a sentence: “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (10:38). Stephen’s grace and power are his Master’s, shared with a servant: rays from the One full of grace and truth, from whose “fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16). Stephen was full because Christ is fuller.

Stephen was not an apostle, so how does this fit the view that signs belonged to the apostles? Stephen and Philip were among the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands, and their signs belong to the same foundational ministry, given not to every believer but to those closely tied to the apostles as the gospel first spread. On the cessationist reading (that these sign gifts ceased with the apostles’ generation), which is the more likely one and should be held charitably, they did not continue as standing gifts, because their purpose was to confirm the apostles’ founding message. Christians who believe they continue read these chapters as a pattern for every age; they love the same Lord, and the question deserves patient study, not scorn. What did continue, and continues today, is what Stephen had first: grace, faith, wisdom and the Spirit. Those are for every believer.

Textual note. The KJV, following later manuscripts, reads full of faith and power here; the earliest manuscripts have grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen takes the gospel into the Greek-speaking synagogues he knew best, and Jews from across the empire rise up to argue with him.

The synagogue of the Freedmen. The first mention of a synagogue in Acts: the local Jewish assembly and meeting house for reading Scripture, prayer and teaching, found in every town where Jews lived. Jerusalem held many, often grouped by homeland or language. The Freedmen were freed slaves and their descendants, most likely Jews, or the children of Jews, taken captive when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC, carried to Rome as slaves and later set free; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. An inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built by one Theodotus, with lodging for those coming from abroad, a vivid picture of exactly this kind of community. The God who scattered his people to Rome as slaves gathered their children back to Jerusalem to hear the gospel. Nothing in their history was wasted.

Cyrenians and Alexandrians. Greek-speaking Jews from North Africa (Cyrene), Egypt (Alexandria) and Asia Minor (Cilicia and Asia): all Hellenists, the group Stephen very probably belonged to (v. 1). This first great clash is Hellenist against Hellenist; Stephen seems to have gone to those he knew best.

Cilicia. Its capital was Tarsus, the home city of Saul (21:39), who at the end of the next chapter stands by approving Stephen’s death (7:58; 8:1). Scripture does not say Saul was among these disputants, but the synagogue debate may well be where the future apostle Paul first set himself against the name of Jesus.

As was his custom, in the synagogue. Luke has told this story before. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah, spoke such gracious words that all marvelled, and then, when his words cut too close, they rose up, drove him out of the town and tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:16–30). Stephen’s story runs along the same line: a synagogue, gracious and unanswerable words, men rising up, and in the end a man driven out of the city to die (7:58). The servant walks where the Master walked, and the hostility he meets is hostility to the One he speaks of.

How do I start speaking about Christ to people I know? Begin where Stephen did, with your own circle: people who share your language, background and world. You understand their questions, and they know you well enough to see whether your faith is real. You need not win debates. Ask what they believe and why, listen properly, and say honestly what Christ means to you and why you believe he rose from the dead. Pray before and after, expect some to argue and some to listen, and remember that the man arguing hardest may, like Saul, be closer to the kingdom than anyone would guess.

Uncertain wording. The Greek does not make clear how many synagogues Luke means. It can be read as one synagogue drawing on all these places, as two (the Freedmen with the Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and another for Cilicia and Asia), or as several; the number is not the point. “Freedmen” (Libertinoi) is a Latin word in Greek letters meaning freed slaves; exactly who they were is not certain, though the account above is the likeliest.
verseByVerse.note: The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps taken captive to Rome. Cilicia, in south-east Asia Minor, was Paul’s home province.

parallels.desc: Tarsus in Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who waited on tables out-argues trained debaters, because Christ is keeping his promise to give his witnesses a wisdom no opponent can withstand.

They could not withstand. A promise is kept word for word. Not long before, in the temple, Jesus had told his disciples what would happen when they were dragged before synagogues and rulers: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict” (Luke 21:15). A mouth means words to say. Luke records the fulfilment with the same verb and the same word for wisdom: first the promise, then the proof that it was kept.

The wisdom and the Spirit. Stephen has no training that Luke mentions and a job seeing that widows are fed. The men across the room were literate, argumentative and at home in Greek, men who had spent their lives in exactly this kind of dispute. They lost. Here is the promised mouth and wisdom, in a table-servant before the scholars of the dispersion. He is the Wisdom of God in person (1 Corinthians 1:24), and his Spirit speaks through his servants still.

What it does not mean. The verse does not say Stephen’s opponents were persuaded. He won the argument and was dead within a chapter. What is promised is both better than a debating record and more limited. When a Christian is put on the spot for Christ, he will not be left with nothing to say; he is not promised that he will be believed, or that he will be safe. At the family lunch where your faith suddenly comes up, most people fear not being argued into a corner but standing there empty, and this verse speaks to that fear exactly. The mouth is promised; the outcome is not.

Does this mean I need not prepare to explain my faith? No. Peter tells every Christian to be prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for the reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Stephen’s wisdom came from the Spirit, but the Spirit had a man soaked in Scripture to work with, as the next chapter shows. So read your Bible, learn the reasons for the resurrection, and think through the questions your friends actually ask. Then, when the moment comes and your preparation feels thin, trust the promise. The Spirit brings to mind what you have learned (John 14:26).

parallels.desc: a mouth and wisdom none can withstand

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to answer Stephen, his opponents plant false witnesses, turn the people against him and drag him before the council on a capital charge.

Secretly instigated. Luke’s word (hypoballō, found nowhere else in the New Testament) means to put a man up to something underhand, to plant him. They did not find witnesses but planted them, as false witnesses had been found against Jesus (Mark 14:55–59). Someone had to find men willing to swear a false oath in a capital case, and brief them: not a crowd losing its temper but a considered operation, undertaken by religious men against someone they had failed to answer in open debate.

Against Moses and God. To blaspheme is to speak of God in a way that insults him, the gravest crime of speech in Israel, and the charge carried the death penalty (Leviticus 24:16). And Moses comes first. In an accusation drafted to secure a conviction, the name placed first is probably the one expected to do the work, and here it is not God’s. What they had heard Stephen discuss was the law and the temple, and they knew that a charge of insulting Moses would move a room most.

They stirred up the people. The turning point of the narrative, easily read past. When Peter and John were arrested, the council could find no way to punish them because of the people (4:21). When the apostles were seized the second time, the captain brought them in without force, “for they were afraid of being stoned by the people” (5:26). Twice the crowd has protected the church. Here, for the first time, it is turned against the church, and the moment it turns, the church has its first martyr. Peter walked out of that chamber alive. Stephen will not.

When a man cannot be answered, he is re-described. It is the oldest trick there is: a false account of what he says, so the argument never has to be had again. It works because a crowd cannot check, and a short summary always travels faster than the words it claims to sum up.

Against us the charges are true. Every charge against Stephen was false, and so was every charge against his Lord, who stood silent like a lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). Against us the charges are true. Yet the innocent One, condemned on false testimony, carried our true guilt, and so the question rings out: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.” Christ Jesus is the one who died, who was raised, and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Two warnings for Christians. First, this describes what was done to a man who was genuinely innocent; it is not a licence to file every criticism under persecution. Some criticism of Christians is accurate, and reaching for Acts 6 is an efficient way of never having to look at it. Second, and harder, the church has over the centuries done exactly this to others: the misquoted opponent, the summarised heretic, the man whose actual words nobody troubled to read. Luke is describing a human technique, and the people using it here were the religious ones.

Why would devout men lie to defend God? Because their religion had become their own possession. The law and the temple were not only how they served God but how they stood before him and before everyone else, the proof that they were in the right. A message that the temple and its sacrifices had done their work threatened the self they had built, and when a man’s standing rests on his religious record, he will defend the record even at the cost of the truth. Yet grace reached this very circle: one of the men nearest the scene was Saul, who later wrote that he had acted ignorantly in unbelief and received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13).

What should I do if I am falsely accused? First take it to God, as Jesus did, who when he was reviled did not revile in return, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Then ask honestly whether there is any truth in it, and own whatever there is. Where a false accusation does real harm, correct it calmly through proper channels, as Paul repeatedly did in Acts. But do not retaliate, do not slander back, and do not let it make you bitter. God sees, and he will vindicate his servants, sometimes in this life and always on the last day.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: false witnesses against Naboth

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false witnesses twist what Stephen really taught, that Jesus fulfils the temple and the law, into an attack on both.

Against this holy place and the law. Luke gives the verdict before the evidence: false witnesses. Yet the charge was built from things Stephen really taught. “Never ceases” paints him as an obsessive, and “this holy place”, said inside the building to the men who ran it, makes the offence personal.

Will destroy this place. Jesus had spoken of this temple being thrown down, not one stone left on another (Luke 21:6). He had also spoken of destroying a temple and raising it in three days, which his hearers misunderstood and which John tells us was about his body (John 2:19–21; Mark 14:58). Stephen probably taught that Jesus is the true temple, and that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as he will say in the next chapter (7:48).

Will change the customs. The customs of Moses were indeed going to change, as Hebrews argues at length. Stephen probably taught that the law is fulfilled in Christ (Matthew 5:17), and that its ceremonies were “a shadow of the good things to come” (Hebrews 10:1). That is not speaking against the law but following it to the Christ it pictured. Jesus did not destroy the law; he kept it perfectly and bore its curse.

They kept the topic and removed the reason. Subtler than invention, they said “destroy” where Stephen meant fulfil, and “change” where he meant complete. They said nothing about a new covenant, nothing about a temple that had finished the work it was built for, nothing about the one in whom God had come to live among his people. It is like describing a surgeon as a man who cuts people open with a knife. Every word is true. The account is a lie.

In the flow. These two charges set the agenda for the longest speech in Acts. Stephen answers by retelling Israel’s story: God met his people far from this holy place, and it was Israel, not Stephen, who refused Moses and did not keep the law (7:35–39, 53). If God is not tied to one building, the gospel can go to Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and two chapters later it does.

Something worth distorting. Misrepresented Christians reach for this passage naturally, but first ask a hard question: is the thing being distorted actually something I said? Stephen was not misquoted about his views; he was misrepresented about his reasons. If a man is going to be misrepresented, let it be because he said something worth distorting.

Did Christianity abolish the law of Moses? It fulfilled it. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows God’s holy will and guides the Christian life, though it no longer condemns those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1; 13:8–10). The ceremonial law, the sacrifices, priesthood, food laws and temple rituals, pointed forward to Christ and has been fulfilled in him, so we no longer keep it (Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though their general principles of justice remain wise (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5; the Westminster Confession 19.3–5). This threefold division is the classic Reformed way of reading the law; some Christians draw the lines differently, but nearly all agree that Christ fulfils it. So Stephen did not speak against Moses. He spoke of the one Moses wrote about (John 5:46).

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Stephen says a word in his defence, God answers the charge that he has blasphemed Moses: the whole court sees his face like the face of an angel.

Gazing at him. The verb (atenizō) is a fixed gaze, and it is the whole court of Israel looking at the same face. Luke closes the chapter on a sentence he never explains.

The face of Moses. Luke very probably means more than that Stephen looked calm. He is on trial for blasphemy against Moses, and there is exactly one man in the Old Testament whose face is described as altered by nearness to God: Moses, when “the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God” (Exodus 34:29–35). The court assembled to try a man for defaming Moses looks up and sees the one face in Jerusalem that looks as Moses’ did. They have the charge sheet and the answer to it in front of them at the same moment, and they proceed with the trial.

They knew what they were looking at. Two chapters ago the same council recognised that two uneducated men had been with Jesus (4:13). Now, before Stephen speaks a word, God shows them whose side he is on.

The appearance of his face was altered. Luke’s reader has seen a shining face before, with Moses present. On the mountain, as Jesus prayed, “the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white”, and Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with him about the departure he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:29–31). Moses’ face shone because he had been with God, and the shining faded (2 Corinthians 3:7); Jesus’ face shone with a glory of his own. Now a servant of Jesus stands before the court of Moses with that light on him, borrowed light whose source is the face of Jesus Christ, in whom God has shone the light of the knowledge of his glory into our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6). Moses saw that glory from behind; Stephen will see it in Jesus, standing at God’s right hand; every believer will see it face to face.

What kind of God does this? He does not deliver Stephen. There is no earthquake, no angel opening a prison door as there had been for Peter, no crowd too dangerous to defy. Soon he will be dragged outside the wall and stoned by people who have just heard him preach. What God gives him instead is a face. He is not spared, and he is not left alone. The glory that met Moses on the mountain comes to rest on a man about to be executed for allegedly slandering him, in the last hour of his life, where every one of his judges can see it. This is not the conduct of a God who has lost control of the proceedings. Then Luke lets the sentence hang, and the next thing that happens is that the high priest turns to the shining man and asks him whether these things are so.

What it does not mean. This verse is easily turned into a burden. It does not establish that a faithful Christian will look radiant under pressure. A great many faithful people have gone to prison, to a diagnosis or to their deaths looking precisely as frightened as they were, and Scripture nowhere treats that as a failure of faith. The Lord himself was greatly distressed in a garden and asked for the cup to be taken away (Mark 14:33–36). It is a gift given once, to one man, not a standard anyone is asked to meet, and Luke reports it as something the observers saw, not something Stephen felt.

Will God give me peace when I face my worst moment? He promises to be with you, and he promises a peace that surpasses understanding to those who bring their requests to him (Philippians 4:6–7). He does not promise that you will feel calm or look radiant. Sometimes his peace is a deep stillness; sometimes it is simply the strength to keep going, one step at a time, while afraid. Both are his gift. And we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). That transformation is going on in every believer now, mostly unseen. One day it will be seen in full.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

6.theology: Word and deed, order and Spirit. The body has different members with different callings; no one person can or should do everything; the qualification for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and when ministry is rightly ordered, it is the word, not the institution or its ministers, that grows.
6.examples:
Then: A fast-growing church learned that love without structure lets real women go hungry, and that structure without love is dead religion. The seven brought both.

Now: Every growing church faces the same tension: how to care well for people without its leaders becoming so busy with management that the word is starved. The answer is to raise up people of Spirit and wisdom to share the load.

keyVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
keyVerse.note: Luke’s summary shows what the whole chapter serves. When the church fed its overlooked widows and kept its apostles at prayer and the word, what grew was not the institution but the word of God, until even priests whose lives were built around the temple bowed to Christ. The rest of the chapter shows that word advancing again, through a servant’s grace, wisdom and suffering.

6.reflection:
The church failed its Greek-speaking widows through oversight, not malice (v. 1). Who might be in your church but out of everyone’s line of sight, and what could you do this month to see them?

The apostles treat waiting on tables and preaching the word as two forms of the same service (vv. 2–4). How does this change the way you think about the practical jobs in your church, and about your pastors’ need for time to pray and study?

The church seems to have handed the care of the widows to men from the very group that had complained (vv. 5–6). What does this teach about healing division and sharing responsibility in a church?

Stephen’s words were twisted into blasphemy, yet God gave him a face like an angel’s before his accusers (vv. 11–15). How should we respond when we are misrepresented for Christ, and what comfort is there in knowing that Jesus was falsely accused before us?

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built a house for him. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Where we are. Stephen, one of the Seven chosen to care for the widows, has done great wonders among the people and out-argued opponents from the synagogue of the Freedmen. They have brought him before the council on false charges of speaking against the temple and the law, and the court has seen his face like the face of an angel (6:8–15). Chapter 7 is his answer, and his death.

The message. God has never been confined to a land or a building, and his people have always rejected the deliverers he sent, until they rejected the last and greatest of them, Jesus the Righteous One.
