Yet the rejected one is the one God vindicates: Stephen sees him standing at God’s right hand, and dies in his likeness, forgiving his killers. The true dwelling of God is not a house of stone but the risen Christ, and he does not abandon those who confess him.

Why it was said. The charges (6:13–14) raised the question every Jewish hearer of the gospel had to face: does following Jesus mean abandoning Moses and the temple? Luke records the answer at length because it explains why the word was about to leave Jerusalem for Samaria and the nations (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Asked whether the charges are true (v. 1), Stephen tells Israel’s story. God appears to Abraham in Mesopotamia and gives him a promise, but not a foot of land (vv. 2–8). The brothers sell Joseph, yet God is with him in Egypt and makes him their saviour (vv. 9–16). Moses, rejected at his first coming, meets God at a bush in the desert and is sent back as ruler and redeemer, promising a prophet like himself (vv. 17–38). Israel thrusts him aside for a calf and the star gods (vv. 39–43). God gave a tent and Solomon built a house, but the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (vv. 44–50). Then the defence becomes a charge: they resist the Spirit as their fathers did, and have murdered the Righteous One (vv. 51–53). Enraged, they rush on him; he sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, and dies commending his spirit to him and praying for them, while a young man named Saul looks on (vv. 54–60).

Where it leads. Every thread ends in Christ. Joseph and Moses are deliverers rejected and then raised up by God, and Jesus is the one they pictured; the prophet like Moses has come; the tent and the temple give way to the Son in whom God dwells, the temple not made with hands. Stephen never names Jesus in the speech, yet the whole story points to him, and at the end heaven opens to show him standing at God’s right hand, the Son of Man of Daniel’s vision. His servant dies as he died, and the prayer for the killers is answered in Saul.

For us. God is not tied to our buildings, routines or places; he meets his people wherever they are taken. Our hearts, like Israel’s, can stop their ears against him, and we need his Spirit to soften them. And whoever confesses Jesus before others, even to death, has a Lord who stands for him in heaven, and can die, as Stephen did, forgiving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has never been confined to one land or one building, and Israel has always resisted the deliverers he sends. Asked whether the charges are true, Stephen answers with Israel’s own history. God appears to Abraham in Mesopotamia and promises a land he never gives him in his lifetime (vv. 2–8). He is with Joseph in Egypt, where the brother the patriarchs sold becomes their saviour (vv. 9–16). He calls a patch of Sinai desert holy ground, and sends back as ruler and redeemer the Moses whom Israel had thrust aside (vv. 17–38). Israel rejects Moses again for a golden calf (vv. 39–43). God gave a tent and Solomon built a house, but as Isaiah asks, what house could hold the Maker of heaven and earth (vv. 44–50)?
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple and the greatness of God

Stephen’s climax, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48), is not an outsider’s attack on the temple: Solomon and Isaiah said it first (see vv. 46–49). The problem was never the temple but the shrinking of God to a location: the belief that having the building meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Where God now dwells is treated at vv. 48–49.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is whether it could lose its building, its tradition or its structures and still know where to find God (see the note on vv. 44–45).

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest opens Stephen’s trial with a formal question, and Stephen answers it with Israel’s whole history: not a denial but a carefully built defence.

Are these things so? Four words, and they hand Stephen the longest speech in the book. The high priest, probably Caiaphas, is following procedure: the charges have been read (6:13–14), and the accused is invited to answer them. It is the formal opening of a trial before the Sanhedrin.

Not a history lesson but a defence. A man asked a direct question answers with fifty verses of history and not one word of denial. Hold the two charges in mind, speaking against this holy place and saying that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered, and the history turns out to answer both.

The temple charge answered by geography. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, called a patch of desert holy ground, designed his own sanctuary as a tent with carrying poles, and told David he had never asked for a building; and Isaiah asked what house anyone imagined could hold him. Stephen does not argue that the temple is bad. He lets his accusers see from their own Scriptures that God has spent the whole story refusing to be tied to one place.

The Moses charge turned round. Stephen honours Moses extravagantly, and in the middle of the tribute points out that Israel rejected him twice, and made a golden calf while he was on the mountain receiving the law. By verse 53 the man accused of despising the law is telling the court that they received it from angels and did not keep it. Through famines and slavery, deserts and rebellions, the God of this speech has worked one plan from Abraham to Jesus, and has woven every rejection of his messengers into the rescue of his people.

He never asks to be let off. He produces no character witnesses and does not show that the testimony was perjured, which it was. Given the last opportunity of his life to save it, he spends it trying to reach the people who are going to take it.

Why does Stephen hardly mention Jesus until the end? Because he lets the story do the work. He never names Jesus in the speech; he calls him the Righteous One in verse 52, and names him only in his dying prayer. But Jesus is everywhere in it: Joseph, rejected by his brothers and raised up to save them; Moses, thrust aside and sent back as ruler and redeemer; the prophet like Moses; the true dwelling of God that no hands built. When Stephen finally says that they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, every man in the room knows whom he means. It is a lesson in reading the Old Testament: it is Christ’s story from the beginning (Luke 24:27).

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen begins where Israel began, with the God of glory appearing to Abraham in a pagan land, long before there was a temple, or even a promised land to stand in.

Brothers and fathers, hear me. He calls the court that will kill him his family, with the respect owed to elders; there is no defiance until verse 51. Paul uses the same opening years later before a mob in this city (22:1): this is an argument inside the house, not an attack from outside it.

The God of glory. The title is the psalmist’s (Psalm 29:3), and glory is the temple word: it filled the tabernacle when it was finished and the house when Solomon dedicated it, until the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). (The Hebrew word suggests weight: the greatness of God, shining out.) If anything belongs to their building, these men believe, it is the glory. Stephen attaches it to an event before Israel existed, in what is now southern Iraq, roughly six hundred miles from the room they are sitting in.

Ur or Haran? “Before he lived in Haran”: Genesis 12:1 records the call in Haran, but Stephen follows the earlier summons in Ur, which Scripture itself records: “I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7). Either God called him twice, or the call begun in Ur was renewed in Haran. So God first appeared to the founder of the covenant people in a pagan city, to a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2). God came looking for an idolater in Ur and made him his friend (James 2:23). That is how grace has always worked, and it is how it reached you.

Go out from your land. In that world land and kindred were survival, not sentiment (Genesis 12:1): your kindred fed you in famine and avenged you if wronged, and to leave both was to leave all protection. And God tells Abraham in full what to leave, and nothing about where he will arrive.

From the God of glory to the glory of God. The speech opens with the God of glory appearing to Abraham, and the chapter closes with Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazing into heaven and seeing the glory of God, and Jesus standing at his right hand (7:55). The glory that met an idolater in Mesopotamia now has a face: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). Abraham rejoiced that he would see Jesus’ day (John 8:56): the man who left everything for a land he had not been shown was walking toward the Son in whom that glory would dwell among us (John 1:14).

The ordinary shape of obedience. Anyone asked to obey without being shown the destination, in a move, a resignation, a relationship ended, stands where Abraham stood. Scripture holds up the man who managed it as the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11; Hebrews 11:8).

Does God still speak to people as he spoke to Abraham? God spoke to Abraham directly because there was as yet no written word. Now he has spoken to us finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and that word is recorded for us, complete and sufficient, in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17). So do not wait for a voice before you obey: the commands and promises you need are already written. God still guides his people through his word, wisdom given in prayer, the counsel of mature believers and his providence opening and shutting doors. And the voice that called Abraham is heard whenever the Bible is opened, calling us, as it called him, to trust and go.

Where Christians differ: does God still give personal words? Many sincere believers, especially in charismatic churches, expect God still to give personal words of guidance or prophecy. This commentary’s view: such direct revelation ended with the apostles, because Scripture is now complete. All agree that any impression must be tested by the written word.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building, and that Israel repeatedly rejected his messengers.

parallels.desc: go to the land that I will show you

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham came into the land, yet died owning none of it but a grave: from the start God’s people lived on his promise, not on property.

Did Terah die before Abraham left? A reader with Genesis open will find a difficulty in “after his father died”. Genesis appears to say that Terah was seventy when he fathered Abram (Genesis 11:26), died at two hundred and five (11:32), and that Abram left Haran, a stopping place on the road west in northern Mesopotamia, at seventy-five (12:4). That would leave Terah alive for another sixty years.

How Genesis counts. “When Terah had lived 70 years, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran” does not mean all three arrived that year; it marks when he began having sons. Genesis uses the same formula of Noah and his three sons (Genesis 5:32), and nobody imagines triplets there; in both lists the sons come by prominence, not birth order. Put Abram’s birth in Terah’s hundred and thirtieth year and every number falls into line: Terah dies at two hundred and five, Abram is seventy-five, and he leaves exactly as Stephen says. Ancient readers noticed the question too: the Samaritan copies of the law give Terah’s age at death as a hundred and forty-five, and Philo agrees with Stephen. Some suggest instead that Stephen means Terah, an idolater (Joshua 24:2), was spiritually dead. This fits the passages together rather than proving it, but strongly, and it does not affect Stephen’s point.

Not even a foot’s length. The man to whom the whole country was promised died holding title to one thing in it: a cave with his wife buried in it, bought from a Hittite (Genesis 23). He lived in tents, a stranger in a land his by promise and other men’s by law (Hebrews 11:9). Stephen says this to men whose case rests on a plot of land and a building on it. Abraham died owning a grave, and died rich, because he had God’s word.

Though he had no child. No land and no child, only God’s word: and he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

The heir who owned nothing. Paul points out that the promised offspring is one person, Christ (Galatians 3:16), and the strange shape of Abraham’s life is repeated in him. The Son whom God appointed heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2) had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and died owning the clothes the soldiers divided. Then God raised him and gave him the nations for his inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Those who belong to Christ are “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29).

Where Christians differ: is the land of Israel still promised to the Jewish people? Some believe God’s promise of the land to Abraham’s physical descendants still stands and will have a future fulfilment, pointing to the promise’s unconditional language and to Romans 11. Others believe the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs themselves were looking for a better country, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). This commentary’s view: the second; the land promise was fulfilled in Joshua’s day and points on to the whole new earth that Christ’s people will inherit. All agree on what Stephen shows here: Abraham’s true hope was never a piece of real estate but God himself and the city he has prepared, and every Christian shares that hope with him.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Abraham in advance of four hundred years of slavery, and of the rescue that would end it: the long affliction was inside the plan, not a failure of it.

Four hundred years. The promise as God gave it (Genesis 15:13–14) contained four centuries of slavery, announced beforehand. Anyone who concludes from four months of silence that God has changed his mind should remember that Abraham was told of four hundred years, and still believed.

I will judge the nation. The plagues on Egypt were foretold centuries before Pharaoh was born. The oppressor is never out of God’s reach, even when he is out of the oppressed people’s sight. He named the slavery and the rescue before either came, having set his love on a people who did not yet exist.

Worship me in this place. Stephen blends Genesis 15:14 with Exodus 3:12, where the place meant is the mountain in the desert. The first national worship God promised his rescued people was at Sinai, hundreds of miles from the building these men are prosecuting Stephen to protect. Worship, not land, was the goal of the exodus.

Something greater than the temple. The place of worship was first a mountain, then a tent, then a house, and Stephen’s accusers thought the line ended at the house. Jesus said it ends in him: “something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6), and he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with him about the exodus he would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). That greater exodus brings a people out of a worse slavery than Egypt’s, and the place where they come to worship God is Christ himself.

How do I keep trusting when God’s promise seems delayed? Remember that delay is not denial: God told Abraham about the four hundred years in advance so that later generations would not mistake the waiting for abandonment. Fill the waiting with what you know of his character and promises, and keep obeying. Bring your impatience honestly to him, as the psalmists did: “How long, O LORD?” (Psalm 13:1). And remember that the longest wait in history, for the Messiah, ended exactly on time, “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4). He is not late with you either.

Four hundred or four hundred and thirty? Stephen is quoting God’s word to Abraham, which says four hundred. Exodus gives the sojourn as four hundred and thirty years (Exodus 12:40), and Paul uses that figure too (Galatians 3:17). Four hundred is the round number for the affliction, as suits a promise rather than an account book; four hundred and thirty is the precise span, counted from a different starting point.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Abraham the covenant sign of circumcision, and the covenant family grew to twelve patriarchs, all before there was a land to own or a temple to worship in.

The covenant of circumcision. The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant was God’s promise to Abraham of a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12; 15; 17), and circumcision was its token: “This is my covenant … Every male among you shall be circumcised … and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Genesis 17:10–11). The sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous before he was ever circumcised (Genesis 15:6; 17), so circumcision was “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11). The mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it.

A sign that travels. Stephen honours the sign, and notes that it came while Abraham had no land and no son of the promise (Genesis 17:9–14). Put on the flesh, not on a plot of ground, it travelled into Egypt and out again, and through seventy years in Babylon with no temple.

The twelve patriarchs. Three generations in a sentence, and a nation exists: everything essential to being the people of God was in place generations before there was a land to live in or a house to worship in.

The son circumcised on the eighth day. The sign Abraham gave Isaac on the eighth day was given to another son of Abraham (Luke 2:21). The Son of God took the covenant mark in his own flesh, born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). He kept the covenant his people had broken, so that the blessing promised through Abraham could flow out to the nations.

Always too large for one family. The covenant God gave Abraham always reached toward the blessing of all the nations (Galatians 3:8). Men and women who never bore the old mark, from places Abraham never heard of, have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13), and given the circumcision that was always the point, of the heart, by the Spirit.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Our paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) in the Presbyterian and Reformed churches see baptism as the new covenant sign that takes the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and so give it to the infant children of believers, as circumcision was given to Isaac on the eighth day. They act from a sincere conviction about God’s faithfulness to families, and we honour them for it. Credobaptists (those who baptise only on profession of faith) answer that the new covenant differs in its membership: all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and its true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). In Colossians 2 the circumcision that answers to baptism is the one made without hands, the new birth, and in Acts baptism follows repentance and faith (2:38, 41; 8:12). This commentary’s view: baptism is for those who profess faith in Christ (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2). Circumcision marked out a physical family through whom Christ would come; baptism marks out those who have been united to Christ by faith. Both sides agree on what matters most here: the sign never saves, and the promise is received by faith alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The patriarchs rejected Joseph out of jealousy, but God was with him in every affliction and raised him to rule Egypt: the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers, and a picture of Christ.

Jealous of Joseph. The names of these twelve patriarchs were engraved on the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:21), worn over the heart of the man presiding at this trial. Stephen says without softening that they sold their brother into slavery. The fathers of Israel rejected the one God had chosen to save them, out of jealousy, the same motive as the leaders who handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10; Acts 5:17).

But God was with him. Not in the promised land, but in a slave caravan, in an Egyptian official’s household, and in a prison cell on a false accusation, for some thirteen years between the pit and the palace. Joseph had no priest and no place of worship, and God was with him.

Out of all his afflictions. God’s presence did not keep him out of prison: he was rescued out of his afflictions, so he was in them first. The rescue ran through the trouble, not round it. Then God exalted the rejected one, and the man his brothers got rid of became the man they could not live without: he went down into Egypt in a slave train and came up as the only source of food in the world, the saviour of the brothers who sold him. “God sent me before you to preserve life”, he told them; “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 45:5; 50:20).

The greater Joseph went further down. God was with Joseph in the pit, the caravan and the cell. The greater Joseph went further down, to the one place where even that comfort was withdrawn, and cried out that God had forsaken him (Matthew 27:46). He was abandoned so that his brothers never will be, and now he is Immanuel, God with us, in every Egypt they are carried to. Raised to the right hand of the Majesty on high, he feeds the people who sold him, forgives with tears, and calls them to come near.

What it does not promise. This story is sometimes preached as a guarantee that your Egypt is preparing you for a throne. Scripture does not promise that: many faithful people are not rewarded visibly in this life, and Hebrews says plainly that a long list of them died still waiting. What the passage does establish is what Stephen needs, and it is enough to build a life on: there is no place a believer can be taken, sold, imprisoned, deported, forgotten or simply stuck, where God is not already there ahead of him, and no institution whose absence can put him out of reach.

Is it right to see Joseph as a picture of Jesus? Yes, because Stephen does, and because the shape is unmistakable: the beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, falsely accused, brought down into the depths, then raised to the right hand of the throne, and from there giving bread to the very people who betrayed him. The New Testament calls such patterns types: real events and people that God shaped to point forward to Christ (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 10:1). We should not invent fanciful links, but where Scripture itself draws the line, as here, we should follow it with joy.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When famine struck, the covenant family could find no food in the promised land, and the only bread was in Egypt, in the hands of the brother they had sold.

A famine. In the ancient world a household in famine ate its stores, then its animals, then its seed corn, and then it moved, or it died (Genesis 41:54–57). The chosen family, in the land of promise, could find no food; the grain was in the pagan empire down the road. Stephen’s accusers tie God’s favour to God’s land; the covenant family’s first great crisis was solved by leaving. And God was ahead of the hunger by seven years, storing grain in Egypt through the son the brothers thought was dead.

Grain in Egypt. A rumour reaches an old man in Hebron that there is wheat for sale in the south, and he sends his sons to buy some. No vision, no word from God: a man acts sensibly on market news, and sets in motion the descent into Egypt, the exodus, Sinai and the whole national life of Israel. And on that first visit they did not recognise Joseph (Genesis 42:8).

Bread only in the hands of the rejected. The only bread in the world is in the hands of the brother they sold, though they do not know it. Stephen’s hearers stand in the same place. The Jesus they handed over is the one through whom alone God gives life: “there is salvation in no one else” (4:12). Jesus called himself the bread of life, and promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35). Every sinner who comes to Christ comes as Jacob’s sons came to Egypt: hungry, empty-handed and unaware, to find that the one they wronged has been ready for them all along.

How providence usually works. Very little of what God does in a life arrives labelled. It arrives as the price of wheat, a job that fell through, a piece of news somebody happened to mention. Jacob was being practical, not spiritual, and without the faintest suspicion of it he was delivering his household into the hands of the son he had mourned for twenty years. That is not fatalism: Jacob still had to weigh the risk and send the boys. But a man doing the sensible next thing, with no sense of destiny about it, may be doing something talked about for thousands of years.

Does God send famines and disasters? Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including famines, storms and pandemics, and that nothing happens outside his wise and holy providence (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1 and the Westminster Confession 5.1; Amos 3:6). Genesis says plainly that God sent the famine as part of his plan to save many lives (Genesis 45:5–7). But he is never the author of sin, and his purposes in a disaster are usually hidden. Jesus forbade us to read a disaster as proof that its victims were worse sinners (Luke 13:1–5). The right response is not to explain other people’s suffering, but to humble ourselves, help the hungry, and trust that the God who governed Joseph’s famine is governing ours for the good of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the second visit Joseph revealed himself to the brothers who had sold him and brought the whole family down to safety: the wronged one made himself known in order to save.

The second visit. Everything turns on it (Genesis 45:1–4), though Stephen needs only its outline. The brothers had assumed for twenty years that they had got away with it, and the man they had wronged had meanwhile been put in charge of the only food in the world, and could have done anything he liked with them.

Recognised the second time. Many see a hint Stephen means his hearers to catch: Moses too is not understood when he first comes to his brothers (7:25), and returns as ruler and redeemer. Israel did not recognise Jesus when he came, and acted in ignorance, as Peter told them (3:17). Now, risen and exalted, he is making himself known through the preaching of men like Stephen. Joseph weeping and telling the men who sold him that he is their brother is the gospel in miniature.

Known to Pharaoh. Israel came to Egypt by royal invitation, given the best of the land in Goshen under the protection of the second man in the kingdom. That is why the new king of verse 18 is such a catastrophe: everything had rested on one man’s standing at court, and courts forget.

Christ has a face like that. The brothers dreaded for twenty years the face of the man they had wronged, and when they saw it, it was wet with tears and turned toward them in welcome. Christ has a face like that. The one with every right to condemn us is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he gives his people more than Goshen: “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4).

Seventy or seventy-five? Genesis puts the number at seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, widely used in his day, which reads seventy-five, counting several more of Joseph’s descendants. It is a difference in counting, not an error; a Hebrew copy of Exodus found among the Dead Sea Scrolls also reads seventy-five. Either way Stephen’s point holds.

Where Christians differ: will Israel recognise Jesus at a second visit? Many believe Romans 11 foretells a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in through the gospel age. This commentary’s view: held with humility, that Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God. All agree that God has not cast away his people, and that the church should pray for Jewish people to see in Jesus the brother they did not recognise.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob and his sons died in Egypt, yet were carried back to be buried in the land they never owned: their graves were a confession of faith in God’s promise.

He died, he and our fathers. One clause for the death of a generation, but Stephen stops for the burial: men who died outside the land were carried back to lie in ground they had never owned. Joseph made his brothers swear to it on his deathbed, and four hundred years later a nation leaving Egypt in a hurry took his coffin with them (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19).

A tomb as evidence. The only property any of the patriarchs held in the promised land was a tomb and a field, and they arranged their own funerals around the promise. Stephen’s accusers hold the land, the city and the temple, and are about to kill a man over a building. The founding fathers held a tomb, and held on to God.

Two purchases in one clause. Genesis records two separate transactions: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and Jacob bought the plot at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah (Genesis 50:13); Joseph’s bones were laid at Shechem, in Jacob’s plot (Joshua 24:32). Stephen has folded two purchases and two burial grounds into a single clause.

Joseph’s field and Jacob’s well. The patriarchs lie at Shechem, in despised Samaria. There Jesus sat by Jacob’s well at Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph (John 4:5–6), and told a Samaritan woman that he was the Messiah (John 4:26). In the next chapter Philip preaches Christ in Samaria (8:5–12). The fathers were buried in Samaritan ground in hope, and their hope came and sat down beside them.

If Stephen compressed the history, can I trust the Bible? Yes. Racing through a thousand years on trial for his life, Stephen compresses the burials into one summary phrase, as speakers often did; he is not filing a title deed. His hearers knew the law better than we do, and as far as Luke records they do not challenge his history: they rage at his conclusion, not his facts. A few have suggested Abraham made a further, unrecorded purchase at Shechem, where he built his first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7): possible, but speculative. And Luke’s task is to report the sermon faithfully, which he has; inspiration guarantees a true record of what Stephen said, as it guarantees a true record of what Job’s friends said. Nothing hangs on the detail; believers can hold Scripture true while admitting that no explanation here is certain, and Stephen’s point stands untouched.

Why did the patriarchs care so much where they were buried? Because their burial was an act of faith in God’s promise and, at its deepest, in the resurrection. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus and gave directions concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22). Christians bury their dead with the same hope: not because the place saves, but because the body matters to God and will be raised. Christ lay in a borrowed grave and then left it empty, and because he lives, those who sleep in him will live also.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As God’s appointed time drew near, Israel multiplied in Egypt, and a new king who had forgotten Joseph turned their blessing into persecution. With verse 17 Stephen moves to Moses, the very man the charge sheet named (6:11), and his two threads run on: God at work outside the land, and Israel refusing the deliverer God sends.

The time of the promise. The four hundred years of verse 6 are nearly up, and Israel’s circumstances harden rather than soften.

Another king who did not know Joseph. Blessing and persecution arrive in the same sentence (Exodus 1:7–8), and the second follows from the first: a fast-growing foreign population in the delta is exactly what alarms a new regime. A man had saved the country from starvation, and within a few generations the palace had no idea who he was. Nations forget their benefactors fast.

When the fullness of time had come. Stephen’s phrase, “the time of the promise drew near”, is the language of the whole Bible’s waiting. The first deliverance came when God’s appointed years ran out in Egypt. The greater one came the same way: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4), into a land ruled by a foreign emperor whose census decided where he was born (Luke 2:1–7). Every promise that drew near in Egypt was drawing near to him.

The whip and the promise. Before this king, Israel in Egypt was doing well: land in Goshen, growing numbers, standing because of Joseph, and no recorded wish to leave. The promise required them to go, and what finally made them willing was the whip. God’s people can prosper quietly for a long time in a place they were never meant to settle. Christians are sojourners and exiles (1 Peter 2:11), and the danger of comfort is that we forget it.

What it does not mean. It does not follow that every hardship is God prising somebody loose from a comfort, and that is never a thing to say to a person in the middle of one; a friend who explains your suffering to you has stopped being a friend. What can be said is only what the text says: this affliction fell inside a promise made four hundred years before, and the people groaning under it could not see that, and found out afterwards.

How do I wait for God’s timing without becoming passive? Waiting on God in Scripture is never idleness. Israel waited in Egypt by working, raising children and keeping the promise alive; Joseph’s unburied bones told every generation they were not home. Do your work well, raise your children in the faith, pray for what God has promised, and hold your present comforts loosely, ready to move when he moves you.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s calculated cruelty set out to destroy Israel’s baby boys, and into the middle of it God sent a child, Moses, the deliverer the decree was designed to kill.

He dealt shrewdly. The persecution was policy, escalated by stages (Exodus 1:10, 22): forced labour, then the midwives, then the decree that every son be thrown into the Nile. Stephen puts the horror where it belongs: Pharaoh forced our fathers to expose their infants. To expose a baby was to abandon it to die, a common practice in the ancient world, and early Christians became known for taking such babies in.

Beautiful in God’s sight. God’s answer to the machinery of a superpower is very small: a baby, born to slaves, in the middle of the programme designed to kill precisely him (Exodus 2:2).

Three months. Hidden where one cry would have finished the whole family. Hebrews picks up the detail: “By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict” (Hebrews 11:23). The first act of faith in Israel’s deliverance was performed by a mother and a father with a basket.

Another child under a king’s decree. Matthew tells Jesus’ birth to recall this one: a king orders the boys of a district killed, the child is carried to safety, and the angel tells Joseph to return, “for those who sought the child’s life are dead” (Matthew 2:16, 20), almost the words God spoke to Moses in Midian (Exodus 4:19). The greater deliverer did more than escape the decree as a baby. At the end he walked into the death sentence on purpose, so that it would fall on him and not on his people.

The other babies. Rescues are not universal. The other babies died, and for their households the deliverer born down the street was, at the time, no help at all. Scripture neither explains them nor pretends they were not there, and no one should read this passage as a promise that God protects the children of the faithful as a rule. What the passage does say is that a state which had decided to end a people could not kill one particular child, and ended up paying for his upbringing. That does not explain the others. It says who was in charge of the outcome, to a court that thought it was.

What does this say about the value of unborn and newborn children? That every child is precious to God, including the ones the powerful find inconvenient. Each is made in his image and known by him before birth (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139:13–16). God condemned Pharaoh’s policy, and he condemns every modern equivalent, including abortion and the abandonment of the unwanted. Christians should speak for the voiceless (Proverbs 31:8), and care practically for mothers and children, as the early church did. To anyone carrying the grief or guilt of an ended pregnancy: there is full forgiveness in Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and the church is meant to be a place of refuge for you, not judgment. And Scripture gives grieving parents real hope: we believe that God in his mercy saves the elect infants who die in infancy (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3 and the Westminster Confession 10.3; 2 Samuel 12:23). If you have lost a little one, you may rest that child in the hands of a Father who is kinder than we are, and who knew and loved your baby before you did.

Uncertain wording. “Beautiful in God’s sight” is literally “beautiful to God”. It may mean that God looked on the child with favour, or it may be a Hebrew way of making a superlative with God’s name, as Jonah 3:3 calls Nineveh “an exceedingly great city”, literally a city great to God. Either way Moses was an exceptionally fine child (Exodus 2:2), and God’s hand was on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daughter of the king who ordered his death adopted Moses, and Egypt itself educated the man God would use to bring Egypt down.

Pharaoh’s daughter. The rescue is arranged by the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant (Exodus 2:5–10). Stephen does not need to comment on the irony.

All the wisdom of the Egyptians. Egypt was the great seat of ancient learning; even Solomon’s wisdom is measured against it (1 Kings 4:30). Exodus does not say Moses received a prince’s education; it is the natural inference, preserved in Jewish tradition. Stephen’s point is aimed at the temple charge again: God’s man was formed in a pagan palace, at the pagan state’s expense.

Mighty in his words and deeds. Moses would later say he was not eloquent (Exodus 4:10), but his words carried power.

A prophet mighty in deed and word. On the Emmaus road two disciples described Jesus of Nazareth as “a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people” (Luke 24:19), and the risen Jesus then showed them from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (24:27). Moses was a son adopted into a palace that was not his; Jesus is the Son who came from the Father into a world he had made. Moses learned all the wisdom of Egypt; in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

Egypt paid for the deliverer’s schooling. The Lord used Pharaoh’s own daughter to raise the man who would bring Pharaoh down, and Egypt’s treasury to pay for the schooling of Israel’s deliverer. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10). He did it again, on a scale that dwarfs Egypt, at the cross: the rulers who gathered against his Son did only what his hand and his plan had predestined to take place (4:28), and their worst became the rescue of the world.

Equipped, but not the deliverer. Yet Moses’ first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29). The world’s finest wisdom equipped him; it did not make him the deliverer. God did.

Should Christians pursue a secular education? Yes, with open eyes. Moses learned the wisdom of Egypt, Daniel the literature of Babylon (Daniel 1:4, 17), and Paul quoted pagan poets (17:28). All truth is God’s truth, and learning is a gift to be used for his glory and our neighbour’s good. But neither Moses nor Daniel let the school decide who they were: Daniel resolved not to defile himself, and Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24). So study hard, take your faith into the classroom, and let God’s word judge all you learn.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At forty Moses chose his oppressed people over the palace and struck down an Egyptian: right about the cause, wrong about the method, and not yet sent by God.

It came into his heart. A man raised as an Egyptian must settle which of his two peoples he belongs to. Hebrews describes the moment as a refusal: he “refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin” (Hebrews 11:24–25). He chose to identify with his oppressed people, and it cost him a kingdom.

He defended the oppressed man. And then he kills a man (Exodus 2:11–12). Exodus settles the moral question: Moses “looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand”. Those are the movements of a man who knows exactly what he has done.

Right about the cause, wrong about the method. His loyalty was right, but he acted on his own: God had not sent him, and there is no word from God anywhere in these verses. The deliverer who eventually stands before Pharaoh will come with a staff and a message and no violence of his own. The pattern is common and does not look like sin from the inside: being right about the cause, a man assumes it authorises whatever gets it done.

The reproach of Christ. Hebrews adds a startling phrase: Moses “considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt” (Hebrews 11:26), the scorn that falls on God’s Anointed and on those who side with him. His choice had the shape of Christ’s before Christ came, and the contrast tells as much as the likeness. Moses left a palace and took a life; the Son left glory and gave his. He too saw his brothers wronged, by sin and death and the devil, and came down to defend them, but he struck down no one. He let himself be struck, and by his wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24).

Never wrong in his method. Moses looked this way and that before he struck; the Son of God did his saving work in full view, lifted up outside the city, with no blood on his hands but his own. One blow cost Moses forty years in the desert; one offering of Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). This deliverer was never too early, never too late, and never wrong in his method.

Forgiven, but not spared. God did not discard Moses. The man who buried an Egyptian at forty was standing before a burning bush at eighty, and the decades between turned out to be preparation rather than punishment. But they were real: Israel’s slavery went on, and being forgiven was never the same as being spared the consequences.

When should a Christian step in to defend someone being wronged? Often, and gladly, by right means. Scripture commands us to open our mouths for the mute and defend the rights of the poor and needy (Proverbs 31:8–9), and Moses’ instinct to stand with the oppressed was right. But we act within the law: we report abuse to the authorities, give evidence, support the vulnerable, and in an emergency protect life. What we do not do is take private vengeance; vengeance belongs to God and to the authorities he has appointed (Romans 12:19; 13:4). Care deeply, act wisely, and do not let zeal for justice become an excuse for sin.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God was giving Israel salvation by Moses’ hand, but his own people did not understand, and when he tried to reconcile two quarrelling Hebrews, they turned on him.

He supposed. Verse 25 is not in Exodus: Stephen interprets, and the interpretation unlocks the speech. God was giving Israel salvation (sōtēria) by Moses’ hand, and Moses supposed they would grasp it. They saw a palace-raised Egyptian who had killed a man. The failure was not in the sending but in the seeing, and “they did not understand” hangs over everything that follows.

The following day. Yesterday he stepped between an oppressor and a victim; today between two Hebrews, both with a grievance and neither wanting him. Anyone who has made peace in a family or a congregation knows which day is harder, and what tends to happen next: two parties who agree about nothing else unite against the man who came to help.

Men, you are brothers. “Why do you wrong each other?” A plea for unity: true, and exactly what neither of them wished to hear.

Salvation by an unrecognised hand. God giving salvation by the hand of a deliverer his people did not recognise is the story of Jesus before it is the story of Moses. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11); the rulers acted in ignorance (3:17); and God was giving salvation by his hand all the same. The cross they did not understand was the salvation itself.

How should I try to make peace between two people? Carefully, prayerfully and humbly. Pray for both. Go to each privately before bringing them together, and listen far more than you speak. Remind them, as Moses did, of what they share: if they are believers, they are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died. Do not take sides before you understand, and do not carry tales between them. Be ready to be resented; peacemakers often are. And know your limits: serious conflict, especially where there is abuse or law-breaking, belongs with elders and sometimes with the authorities. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wrongdoer thrust Moses aside and mocked his authority, a rejection Stephen will soon turn round: the man they refused as ruler, God sent as ruler and redeemer.

Thrust him aside. A key word (apōtheō): Israel will thrust Moses away again (v. 39).

Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? The answer comes eight verses later: “This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ … this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer” (v. 35). The answer to “who made you?”, forty years in becoming visible, was God (Exodus 2:14).

Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? The second half of the taunt is the sting, and a threat. Moses had looked round and seen nobody. Somebody had seen, and the man who tells him so is one of the two he has just tried to reconcile: the secret is out, through the very people he was trying to help.

Israel had some reason. Consider how it looked from the labour camp. A palace man who has never carried a brick kills an Egyptian and expects to be hailed as deliverer, while the reprisals fall on them. Their failure was real, but it was not stupidity. It was the ordinary difficulty of recognising a deliverer who does not look like one, the very difficulty the men listening had lately failed to overcome with a carpenter from Nazareth.

The question asked again. Stephen leaves unspoken that men of this same council had put the same question to Jesus in the temple courts: “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority” (Luke 20:2). God has since answered it, in Peter’s words at Pentecost: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (2:36).

How do I respond when my help is thrown back at me? Do not be surprised; Moses was rejected for trying to make peace, and Jesus for far more. Ask honestly whether your manner or method made the help hard to receive. Do not retaliate or become bitter; commit the matter to God, who sees. And do not conclude that you must never help again. Moses was rejected at forty and sent back at eighty; sometimes the timing was wrong, not the love. Keep your heart soft, and wait to see whether God reopens the door.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected, Moses fled and spent forty years as an exile in Midian, where God turned a confident prince into a humble shepherd fit to carry his name.

Moses fled. Forty years disappear into one sentence. The word for exile (paroikos) means a foreigner living in a land not his own, as Abraham was.

Three forties. Only this speech gives Moses’ age when he fled, setting his hundred and twenty years in three forties: Egypt (v. 23), Midian (v. 30; Exodus 7:7), the wilderness (v. 36). Two-thirds of his life was over before God spoke to him.

What the middle forty contained. He kept another man’s sheep in another man’s country, and named his first son Gershom, which Exodus explains as “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land” (Exodus 2:22). A man who names his child after his own homelessness is telling you how the years were going, and nothing in the record suggests he expected to go back.

God waited for the second man. At forty he was a prince with an education and a plan. At eighty he was a shepherd before a burning bush, producing five separate excuses why God ought to send somebody else. God waited for the second man. He takes proud princes into the desert and brings out humble shepherds fit to carry his name.

The rejected one who went away. The deliverer is refused, goes away into a far country, and comes back with God’s authority to the people who refused him. It is the shape of what Peter had preached in the temple: the Jesus they denied, God has raised, and heaven must receive him until the time for restoring all things (3:13–15, 21). In the long middle the deliverer is not idle. Christ, risen and ascended, is gathering his flock from every nation, and he will come back.

The fallow years. This is a passage for anyone in a long fallow stretch, after the plan that came to nothing. But the pattern is easily turned into a promise it does not make. Not every fallow decade is preparation for something visible, and telling somebody in year twelve that God is getting them ready is a guess dressed up as a word from the Lord. Moses did not know. What can be said is that the desert was not wasted and God had not finished, and nobody in Midian could have told you either thing at the time.

Is it wrong to run from danger? No. Moses fled for his life, and so did David, Elijah, Joseph and Mary with the infant Jesus, and Paul over the Damascus wall. Jesus told his disciples, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” (Matthew 10:23). Fleeing is not cowardice when it preserves life without denying Christ; what a Christian must not do is run from a clear duty. Where faithfulness and safety can go together, take the safe road with a clear conscience. Where they cannot, stand.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After forty silent years God met Moses in the Sinai desert, in a bush that burned without burning up, far from any temple.

When forty years had passed. Stephen puts the silence first: four decades without a word from God to the man he meant to use (Exodus 3:1–2).

In the wilderness. Stephen’s real interest: not Egypt nor Canaan, but desert belonging to nobody, with a flock of sheep for a congregation.

He was amazed at the sight. Among the bare rock and thorn scrub of Sinai, a dry bush that caught fire would be a handful of ash a minute later. What arrested Moses was not the fire but that it kept burning: “I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned” (Exodus 3:3).

As he drew near to look. Exodus gives the order: “When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush” (Exodus 3:4). God spoke to a man who had stopped. That is not a technique, but much of what God does is open to anybody prepared to stop and look twice, and a life can be spent walking briskly past.

He called it twice. The bush was not consumed, because the God in it needs nothing to keep him burning. After forty years of silence he still knew the name of a fugitive shepherd, and he called it twice (Exodus 3:4). The God who spoke from that fire came nearer still in his Son, and the sinners he came among were not consumed: he ate with them, touched them, and gave himself for them.

Was it an angel or God himself in the bush? Exodus says the angel of the LORD appeared, and then that God spoke from the bush, saying, “I am the God of your father” (Exodus 3:2–6). The angel of the LORD speaks as God and is called God. Many Christians, from the early church onward, have understood him as the Son of God appearing before his incarnation, and this commentary takes him so, though some see a created angel speaking for God. What is certain is that Moses met the living God himself, and that the God who spoke from the bush is the God revealed in Jesus Christ (John 8:58).

Should I expect God to speak to me in a burning bush? No; the bush was a unique moment in the history of redemption, when God was giving new revelation (on how God speaks now, see the note on vv. 2–3). But the lesson of turning aside still holds. God speaks whenever we stop and attend to his word, and he often draws our attention through ordinary things: a verse that will not let go, a sermon that lands, a providence that makes us look twice. Make room to stop, read and listen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God named himself the unchanging God of the patriarchs, and called a patch of foreign desert holy ground, for no other reason than that he was there.

The God of your fathers. The first thing God says is that he is the same (Exodus 3:6). No explanation of the delay: he names himself by three men dead for centuries, and so tells Moses that nothing has been dropped: the promise made in Mesopotamia to a childless man is being kept this morning in a desert. Jesus would later draw from this very sentence the proof of the resurrection: “he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him” (Luke 20:37–38).

Moses trembled. At forty he was ready to take on Egypt single-handed; at eighty he cannot raise his eyes to a bush. This is the man God has decided to send.

Holy ground. This (Exodus 3:5) is the first time the Bible calls any ground holy, and it is a patch of dirt in a foreign desert with a thorn bush on it: no altar, no priest, no temple. What made it holy was that God was there, and nothing else has ever made any place holy. He makes ground holy by standing on it, and he makes sinners holy by dwelling in them.

Take off the sandals. In that world a man took off his sandals at the door of a house, and by long tradition the priests served barefoot in the sanctuary. God is telling Moses that this hillside is his house.

Where God now stands. If ground is holy only because God is there, the holiest place on earth in Stephen’s lifetime was wherever Jesus stood, for “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). This council had condemned the one who was God with us, after witnesses accused him of saying he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands (Mark 14:58). Within minutes Stephen will see where Jesus stands now, at the right hand of God (7:56).

Is my church building holy ground? Not in itself. Under the new covenant no place is holier than another; Jesus said that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). A church building is a useful room, not a temple. What is holy is the presence of God among his gathered people, and that is why worship should be reverent: not because of the bricks, but because the Lord is among them (Matthew 18:20). Wherever God’s people meet in his name, whether a cathedral, a school hall or a living room, take off your sandals in your heart.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had seen his people’s misery and heard their groaning, and he came down to rescue them, by sending Moses.

I have surely seen. Seen, heard, come down (Exodus 3:7). The first is doubled in the Hebrew: seeing I have seen, steadily, every year of it.

And have heard their groaning. Exodus, describing the same moment, does not say that Israel prayed. They groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help, their cry rose up to God, and God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant (Exodus 2:23–24). No petition properly worded, only the noise of people at the end of their strength, and God treats it as prayer: worth knowing for anyone whose words will not come. Paul says that when we do not know what to pray for as we ought, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). What reaches God is not the wording.

I have come down to deliver them. God does not explain the timing. Israel received a rescue and never an explanation; what was given instead was God himself, in motion, on the way.

I will send you. The last clause is a surprise. God has come down to deliver them, and he sends a man: he comes down by sending. The men listening to this speech had lately seen God come down in the fullest way of all, in his own Son, and they had killed him. They are about to kill the next messenger too.

How can God come down, if he is everywhere already? God is everywhere present, filling heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24). When Scripture says he came down, it means he drew near in saving power to a particular people in a particular place: language suited to us, describing something real. It reaches its full meaning in the incarnation, when the eternal Son came down from heaven and became flesh (John 6:38; 1:14). The God who said, I have come down, in Exodus said it again in Bethlehem, and this time he stayed.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Moses whom Israel rejected is the very one God sent as ruler and redeemer, attested by signs: Stephen is drawing the portrait of Jesus without yet naming him.

This Moses, whom they rejected. Stephen begins hammering the same words: “this Moses”, “this man”, “this is the one” (vv. 35–38). He has stopped narrating and is pointing.

Both ruler and redeemer. Israel demanded to know who had made Moses a ruler and a judge; God made him a ruler and a redeemer. The office they refused him is the office he was given. So with Jesus (see the note on vv. 27–28): the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (4:11). Redeemer (lytrōtēs), found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the one who buys a man out of slavery or debt: a word his hearers cannot keep at a comfortable distance.

Wonders and signs. Signs confirmed Moses, as they confirmed Jesus (2:22), and Luke uses the phrase of the apostles (5:12) and of Stephen himself (6:8). Moses, the Twelve and the man now on trial are set in a single line: all sent, all attested, and all disbelieved by the same institution.

The pattern fully drawn. Stephen still does not name the one it points to. Joseph, sold by his brothers, fed them. Moses, thrust aside by his people, brought them out. Twice God sent Israel a deliverer, twice Israel refused him at first sight, and twice God sent him anyway.

What does it mean that Jesus is my redeemer? That you were a slave, and he paid to set you free: not with silver or gold, Peter says, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). You were in bondage to sin, under the law’s curse and the fear of death (Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 2:15), and could not buy yourself out. Christ had the right, as your kinsman in our flesh, and the resources, as the Son of God, and he paid it all. So you belong to him now, not as a slave in fear but as a ransomed child, and your life is no longer yours to spend as you please, because it was paid for (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses himself promised a greater prophet to come and received living words from God for Israel: far from despising Moses, Stephen claims him, and Moses points to Jesus.

A prophet like me. The promise (Deuteronomy 18:15) is the text Peter preached from in the temple courts (3:22), and Stephen means Jesus, as Peter did. It answers the second charge: Moses himself told Israel to listen to somebody else. To honour Moses is to listen to Jesus.

The congregation in the wilderness. The congregation (ekklēsia) is the Old Testament’s term for the assembly of Israel and the New Testament’s word for the church. Israel in the wilderness was God’s assembly, the church of the old covenant.

With the angel. The law came through angels (v. 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2): not a slight on the law, but an honour that makes breaking it worse.

He received living oracles to give to us. An oracle is a message from God, and these are living: not a dead code or an antique, but words of God with life still in them, still speaking. It is said by the man on trial for despising the law. And not “to you” but “to us”: he claims the law as his own inheritance, in a hearing convened on the charge that he has thrown it away. Rather than deny the charge, Stephen states what he believes in terms so high that it collapses: the best answer to being misrepresented is usually not a correction but a demonstration.

Through one of our own brothers. The living oracles given at the mountain were never meant to stay on stone. The God who spoke through angels and through Moses has now spoken in a Son, who is himself the Word, full of grace and truth, and whose words are spirit and life (John 6:63). At Sinai the congregation begged not to hear the voice again (Deuteronomy 18:16), and the promise of a prophet like Moses was God’s answer: he now speaks through one of our own brothers.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians? Entirely. It is the Bible Jesus read, quoted and called the word of God, and he said it bears witness about him (John 5:39). Paul says these Scriptures are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable (2 Timothy 3:15–16). We read it through Christ, so that its sacrifices point us to his cross and its ceremonies are fulfilled in him rather than kept by us. But its stories, laws, psalms and prophets remain living oracles for us. If you have neglected it, start with Genesis, the Psalms or Isaiah, looking for Christ.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts read “to you” here; most modern Bibles, like the KJV, read “to us”.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after the exodus Israel pushed Moses aside, longed in their hearts for Egypt and demanded gods they could see: the deliverer rejected again, this time by the people he had rescued.

Our fathers refused to obey him. “Thrust him aside” is the word of verse 27. Even the rescue at the sea did not change their instinct to reject him.

In their hearts they turned to Egypt. Within weeks of the sea they were longing for Egypt (Exodus 16:3), and they still wanted to go back at the edge of the land (Numbers 14:3–4), because it was familiar and the food arrived. Numbers records what they missed: the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic (Numbers 11:5). They remembered the menu and forgot the whips. The heart turned back before the feet did.

Make for us gods. They gave Moses about forty days on the mountain before asking Aaron to replace him (Exodus 32:1). Idolatry is wanting a god you can see and control, one who goes where you want to go. And their words are full of contempt: “this Moses … we do not know what has become of him.”

The mediator out of sight. The calf was made while Moses was out of sight, doing for the people what they could not do for themselves. Our mediator has gone up, out of sight, and the world asks what has become of him. He is not idle: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When Moses came down he offered to be blotted out of God’s book for the people’s sin, and God would not accept the offer (Exodus 32:30–33). Christ’s offering was accepted. He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and bore the sin of the very people who were so quick to replace him.

The homesickness of the redeemed. A man truly delivered, who would not go back if asked outright, can still be homesick for the country he was rescued from: not for its misery but for its familiarity, the not having to trust anybody for tomorrow. Egypt fed you every day and asked nothing of you except your life. Yet God did not give up on a people whose hearts went back to Egypt. He fed them, forgave them and brought their children into the land; his patience outlasts our homesickness for sin.

A trap closing. These people had eaten manna that morning; miracles do not make anybody faithful, and a Christian who assumes he would have done better is just the sort of man Stephen has in front of him. Every man on that council would have agreed that their ancestors were a disgrace. That is the trap, and it closes in twelve verses: “As your fathers did, so do you” (v. 51).

What do I do with the longing for my old life? Name it honestly, without shock; most believers feel it at some point. Then remember accurately: Egypt was not garlic and melons but whips and dead babies. Feed on what he has given now: his word, his people, the manna of each day’s grace. Remove what makes the road back easy. And look forward, as Moses did, to the reward (Hebrews 11:26). The longing for Egypt fades fastest when the heart is fixed on the promised land.

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel worshipped a calf of their own making, so God gave them over to the star worship they wanted; and even their many wilderness sacrifices, Amos says, never truly reached him.

The works of their hands. This phrase helps explain why Stephen dies (Exodus 32:4–6). Its twin arrives at verse 48: “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands”. In the Greek Old Testament, “made by hands” is very largely a word for idols, the contemptuous term for things people carve and then bow down to (Isaiah 46:6). So when Stephen applies it to the temple, a Jewish ear does not hear a remark about architecture. It hears the temple put into the same category as the golden calf. That is the offence. Even a God-given building can become an idol when it takes God’s place.

God turned away and gave them over. He did not strike them; he let them have what they wanted. Paul uses the language three times in Romans 1 (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). From the inside it feels like nothing at all: a man insists on his idol, and God stops arguing.

Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices? Stephen quotes Amos (Amos 5:25), and it is an extraordinary question, because of course they did. The wilderness generation sacrificed constantly; Leviticus is the paperwork for it. Amos is not denying that the ritual happened. He is denying that it ever reached God. This is religion as a bargain: doing the right things in God’s direction, so that God will owe us and leave us alone, while the heart stays with the calf. Before the men who run the sacrificial system, Stephen puts the offerings themselves in question, and the question reaches anyone who does religious things: is it brought to God, or merely performed in his vicinity?

The calf and the temple. Stephen has put the irreligious idol and the religious one in the same sentence. The calf was a god of appetite and freedom; the temple, as the council used it, had become a god of respectability and control. Both are made by hands, and both are ways of being our own saviour. Our world keeps the same two shrines: the career, the body, the self we have built; and the moral record, the right views, a clean reputation, a church attended. The psalmist noticed what such gods do to their makers: “Those who make them become like them” (Psalm 115:8). The man who lives for his work slowly becomes a function; the man who lives for his rectitude becomes as hard as stone. Jesus was accused of threatening the temple made with hands because he meant to raise “another, not made with hands” (Mark 14:58), and that temple was himself: the one sanctuary neither the libertine nor the moralist could ever have built.

The one offering that arrived. The New Testament answers Amos’s question: “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). But one offering did arrive. Christ, through the eternal Spirit, offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14), and God accepted it, as the empty tomb and the ascension declare. The men who run the altar have condemned the one sacrifice to which every altar pointed. And if the most terrible judgment is to be handed over to what we wanted, the wonder of the gospel is that God handed someone else over: he “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), so that people who had rejoiced in the works of their own hands might rejoice for ever in the work of his.

Could God give me over like that? If you are worried that he might, that worry is good evidence he has not. Those whom God gives over do not tremble about it; they rejoice in the works of their hands and want nothing more. The grieving believer who wants to be rid of his idol is being pursued by God, not abandoned. God disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and his discipline hurts precisely because he has not let go. The danger is not the struggle but the settled, contented refusal to be turned. If you can still hear his objection to your idol, thank him, and listen.

parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Amos, Stephen shows that the very generation which carried God’s tent also carried the shrines of pagan gods, and that exile was the sentence that followed.

The tent of Moloch. Amos (5:26) means that Israel in the wilderness had two tents: the tent of witness, and the tent of Moloch, carried through the same camp by the same people. From the first generation the sanctuary had a rival in the baggage. And note again: “the images that you made”.

Who were Moloch and Rephan? Moloch (or Molech) was a pagan god, named as the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice: children were made to pass through the fire to him (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). The tent of Moloch is a portable idol shrine carried in procession, a grim parody of the tabernacle. Rephan, “the star of your god”, was a star god, probably the planet Saturn worshipped as a god: the bowing to the host of heaven that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

Beyond Babylon. Amos wrote “beyond Damascus”; Stephen carries the prophecy on to the exile that actually came, in Babylon. Having the land did not protect them, and the same sentence hangs over this court.

Exile borne for us. The prophets also promised a return from exile, and the New Testament shows how God brings home a people who deserve to be sent away. Christ was “cut off out of the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8), carrying the banishment that idolatry earns, so that those whose fathers had carried Moloch’s tent could be brought near.

Do people still worship Moloch and the stars? In other forms, yes. Moloch was the god to whom children were sacrificed for the sake of prosperity and security, and every age finds its own ways of sacrificing children to adult comfort, career or convenience. The star of Rephan is the ancestor of astrology, the belief that our lives are ruled by the heavens rather than by the God who made them. Scripture treats looking to the stars for guidance as turning from God (Isaiah 47:13–14). The Christian looks past the stars to their Maker, who calls them all by name (Isaiah 40:26), and who holds our times in his hand.

Uncertain wording. Stephen quotes the Greek Old Testament of Amos 5:25–27, whose wording differs from the Hebrew, and the Hebrew at this point is genuinely obscure. Where it has Sikkuth and Kiyyun, probably names or titles of Mesopotamian star gods (Kiyyun perhaps Saturn again), the Greek rendered them Moloch and Rephan.
