The exact identifications are the best reconstruction, not certainty, but the sense, and Stephen’s point, is plain.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself gave Israel a sanctuary, but it was a tent, made to a heavenly pattern and carried from place to place, until the days of David.

The tent of witness. Stephen first defends the sanctuary: God ordered it. The tent of witness is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the law, the testimony (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). The fathers carried the tent of Moloch; God gave them the tent of witness.

A tent, not a house. Taken down in a morning and standing again by evening, the one dwelling God designed for himself was portable, its furniture fitted with rings for carrying poles. He did not wait for his people to build him a house before he came to live with them. And the God who travelled with his people in a tent later pitched his tent among us in the flesh of his Son: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally tabernacled, among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

According to the pattern. Even the tent was a copy of what Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), a shadow of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5). Christ is “a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man” (Hebrews 8:2). He entered through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:11–12).

With Joshua. And it kept moving, to Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon. For Greek readers there is a glint of something more: the name Joshua in Greek is Jesus (Iēsous), which is why the KJV prints Jesus in this verse. The first Jesus brought the tent into the land; the second would bring the true dwelling of God among men.

Until the days of David. The turning point: everything after it concerns what happened when somebody decided God ought to have a permanent house.

Then should churches not own buildings? They may, and many should; a building is a tool, and a good one. The question is not whether a church has a building but whether it could lose one and still be a church. The early Christians met in homes, in rented halls (19:9) and in the open air, and the church grew. A congregation that would collapse if its building were taken away has put its weight on the wrong thing. Use your building gladly, and keep your heart in the people and the word.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David, who pleased God, longed to build him a dwelling, but it was Solomon who built the house, and God answered David by promising to build him a house that would last for ever.

A dwelling place for the God of Jacob. David comes off well (Psalm 132:5). He wanted to build God a house, having noticed that he lived in a house of cedar while the ark sat in a tent (2 Samuel 7:2), and Scripture never suggests the motive was wrong.

But it was Solomon. The little word “but” carries what God said through Nathan: “Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt … but I have been moving about in a tent” (2 Samuel 7:5–6). None of this makes the temple illegitimate: God filled it with his glory, and Jesus called it his Father’s house. And the man who built it said at the dedication, before the whole nation, “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built” (1 Kings 8:27). Even the builder knew.

I will build you a house. God turned the offer round: David would not build God a house; God would build David a “house”, a dynasty, a line of kings descended from him, with a son whose throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:11–13). Solomon’s kingdom split soon after he died; the promise was waiting for a greater Son. The angel told Mary that the Lord God would give her child the throne of his father David, “and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). The house he builds is not cedar but living stones, his people (1 Peter 2:5). And the heir of that dynasty is the one these men had lately helped to nail to a cross outside the city wall.

A house for ever. God answered David’s offer with a gift that made it look small: not a building for a season but a house for ever, and every believer gathered into the house of David’s Son is part of the overflow.

A short and nearly invisible step. David’s desire was good. But there is a step from “I want to honour God with this” to “God requires this, and must be honoured here”, and the step is short and very nearly invisible. A thousand years after Solomon, a man is on trial for his life because a building God never asked for had become the thing his people could not imagine him without.

How do I know whether my good plan for God is what he wants? Hold it with open hands, as David did. When God said no, he did not sulk; he sat before the LORD and gave thanks for what God would do instead (2 Samuel 7:18–29). Test your plan by Scripture, prayer and godly counsel, and watch how God opens or closes the way. Above all, notice if you can no longer imagine God without it: then a good desire is turning into an idol. God may give you something better than you asked: not the house you wanted to build him, but the house he builds you.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “house of Jacob” where most Bibles have “God of Jacob”: David asked to find a dwelling place for the house of Jacob. The sense is close either way, since the dwelling was for God among his people (Psalm 132:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Most High does not live in buildings made by human hands: as Isaiah says, heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so no house can hold him.

Houses made by hands. “Made by hands” (cheiropoiētos) is the word used of idols, and Stephen used its twin of the golden calf (v. 41). Now he fastens it onto the temple. His point is not that the temple was wrong, but that treating it as the place where God was contained was idolatry. Paul says the same in Athens (17:24).

The Most High. A title outsiders often use, from Melchizedek to a fortune-telling slave girl (Genesis 14:18–20; Acts 16:17): the God of Israel described from beyond the boundary, and exactly the right title for a speech about a God who declines to be kept inside one.

Heaven is my throne. So that nobody can accuse him of inventing the idea, he quotes Isaiah (Isaiah 66:1): God seated with the sky for a chair and the planet under his feet for a stool. Then the prophet asks for the plans: describe the building, give the dimensions, say where the resting place is to go. It is God asking a builder for a specification, and the question answers itself the moment anybody tries. No house can hold him. Now he dwells in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), and in his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

The line he leaves out. His hearers knew the passage well enough to supply Isaiah’s very next sentence: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2). So Isaiah does say where God dwells: not in a structure but in a certain sort of person. Stephen stops one line short, and the line describes exactly what the men in front of him are not. Supplying it themselves would cut deeper than hearing it.

The throne Stephen is about to see. Within minutes Stephen will see the man they condemned for threatening their temple at the right hand of the only throne Isaiah says God has (7:55–56). No house can hold the Most High; but the Most High has a Son, and in him God came close enough to be crucified and has been raised high enough to rule.

If God is everywhere, why should I go to church? Because the church is not a building but a people, and God has promised to be present among his gathered people in a special way (Matthew 18:20; 1 Corinthians 14:25). Scripture commands us not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), because we need the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, the prayers and the fellowship of the saints. You can pray alone anywhere; but the living stones are meant to be built together into one house, not scattered across the field. Going to church is not visiting God’s building; it is joining God’s temple.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made everything, the temple’s stone and the hands that cut it included, so no one can house his Maker in what his Maker supplied.

Did not my hand make all these things? Eight words close the argument (Isaiah 66:2). The temple was built by human hands, and human hands were made by God. The stone came from ground he made, cut by men whose lungs he kept breathing. A man cannot house his maker in materials his maker supplied.

A question to end on. The last thing the council hears before Stephen turns to face them is God’s own voice asking whether they had ever stopped to consider who made the quarry.

The hand that made all things. That hand was pierced with nails, and by it the true temple was raised on the third day. God, who needs nothing from us, gave everything for us.

A question to put to oneself. It is possible to know perfectly well that God is not contained in a building and to have quietly relocated him somewhere just as manageable: a style of service, an hour of the week, a way of feeling when the music is right. The test is what a man would have left if the thing were taken away.

What does it mean to tremble at God’s word? Not to be terrified of the Bible, but to take it with utter seriousness, as the voice of the living God. The one who trembles at God’s word lets it correct him rather than correcting it. He reads it expecting to be addressed, obeys it even when it costs, and is moved by its promises as well as its warnings. Josiah tore his clothes when he heard the law read (2 Kings 22:11–19), and God looked on him with favour. Trembling at the word is the opposite of the council’s stopped ears: a soft heart that hears God speaking and bows.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The defence becomes a charge, and the man who preached the rejected Righteous One dies like him. In the prophets’ own words Stephen tells the council that they resist the Holy Spirit as their fathers did, and have betrayed and murdered the one the prophets foretold, though they received the law from angels (vv. 51–53). They grind their teeth in fury, but Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees heaven opened and Jesus standing at God’s right hand (vv. 54–56). They stop their ears, drive him out of the city and stone him, laying their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul (vv. 57–58). Stephen commits his spirit to Jesus, prays for his killers and falls asleep (vv. 59–60).
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the pattern of martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it came to mean someone killed for the faith only after enough witnesses had been killed. Stephen’s death has the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Such a death earns nothing: the courage, the vision and the forgiveness were all given (see vv. 54–55 and vv. 59–60). And martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for it. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The defence becomes a charge: in the words of Moses and the prophets, Stephen tells the council that, like their fathers, they always resist the Holy Spirit.

You stiff-necked people. The turn lies in a single pronoun. Stephen has said “our fathers”, as one of the household; now he says “your fathers”, twice. The defence has become a prosecution, and each charge is a quotation. Stiff-necked describes an ox that sets its neck against the driver’s hand: not bolting, simply refusing. It is the word God himself used of Israel at Sinai after the golden calf (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5).

Uncircumcised in heart and ears. A cutting insult to circumcised men: the mark in their bodies never reached the place it pointed to. Moses and Jeremiah said it first (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 9:26), so the Scriptures do the accusing. They bore the sign of belonging to God, but their hearts had never been given to him, and their ears took in his words without letting them in. Yet he is the God who circumcises hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6), who takes out the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh.

You always resist the Holy Spirit. To resist is to shove back against something coming toward you. The Spirit is the one who spoke through the prophets, and Isaiah says that Israel “rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10). “Always” is the sting: a habit running from the wilderness into this room.

The Spirit of Christ in the prophets. Peter says that the Spirit who spoke through the prophets was the Spirit of Christ in them, predicting the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow (1 Peter 1:10–11). So to resist the Spirit in Moses and the prophets was already to resist Christ, and when the Son came, anointed with that same Spirit (Luke 4:18), the old resistance reached its height against him.

A word of care. Sentences like this have been used as a weapon against Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years, and that must be named. This is a Jew, in the Jewish council, quoting Moses and the prophets, saying to the leaders of his own nation what Isaiah and Jeremiah had said to the leaders of theirs. It is prophetic speech inside a family, and no one may borrow Stephen’s sentence unless he is standing where Stephen stood, and almost nobody who has quoted it has been.

How do I know if I am resisting the Spirit? Resistance rarely looks like open rebellion; usually it looks like being busy, or being reasonable. There is a part of the Bible you avoid, or explain away before you have let it speak. A sermon puts its finger on something specific, and by lunch you are discussing the preacher’s manner instead. You keep saying “not yet” to a step you know you should take: a confession, an apology, a habit to give up. When you hear a hard word, your first thought is of someone else who needs it. And what once troubled you no longer does. The Spirit you are pushing against is the Spirit of Christ, and he presses on you not to crush you but to bring you to the one who bore on the cross the judgment every stiff neck deserves. So stop pushing back: name the thing to God, ask the Spirit who raised Jesus to soften your neck, and do today the small obedience you have been putting off. And if the question troubles you, take heart: the trouble is itself the Spirit at work, for a hardened neck does not worry about being stiff.

If the Spirit can be resisted, is grace not irresistible after all? Both truths are taught in Scripture, and they fit. The Spirit’s outward call through preaching comes to many, and hearts left to themselves always resist it. But when God effectually calls his elect, he does not merely invite; he gives a new heart that gladly comes (Ezekiel 36:26; John 6:44; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1 and the Westminster Confession 10.1). An effectual call does what it says, as the voice of Jesus at the tomb brought Lazarus out alive (John 11:43–44). The resistance is real, and God overcomes it, not by forcing an unwilling man but by making him willing. The proof is standing at the edge of this very scene, holding coats. Saul resisted the Spirit as hard as any man in Jerusalem, until the risen Christ called him by name, and he could resist no longer.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel always persecuted the prophets who foretold the Righteous One, and now this council has betrayed and murdered him, and broken the very law it claims to defend.

Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? A question with no available answer. Jeremiah was imprisoned and dropped into a cistern; Isaiah, by tradition, was sawn in two; Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:21). Jesus had said the same (Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 11:47–51).

The Righteous One. The title Peter used in the temple courts (3:14), and the one Paul will hear applied to Jesus at his conversion (22:14); it reaches back to the righteous Servant of Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11). The supreme court of the nation is told that it condemned the one truly innocent man in its history. Betrayers and murderers, the Greek calls them: not only what they did, but what they now are.

Received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it. On trial for speaking against the law, Stephen closes by honouring it, as he did at verse 38, and saying that they broke it. He does not deny the charge or say the law is finished; he says they had it and did not do it: the most conservative accusation available, because it takes the law at its word, and the hardest to answer.

Was Stephen being unloving? No. Love sometimes has to say the hardest thing, and Stephen said it as a member of the family, in the words of the family’s own prophets, to people he wanted to see saved. His last breath proves it: he prayed for these very men. The prophets spoke like this because they loved Israel, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same week he pronounced its judgment (Luke 19:41–44). We should be slow to imitate Stephen’s sharpness, because we rarely have his clarity, his Spirit-filled courage or his love. But when the truth must be spoken, it is not unloving to speak it plainly, as long as we would gladly die for the people we are speaking to.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the council grinds its teeth in fury, Stephen, full of the Spirit, looks into heaven and sees the glory of God, and Jesus standing at his right hand.

They ground their teeth. Enraged is the word Luke used at 5:33 of this same body hearing Peter: cut to the quick, sawn through. Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury (Psalm 35:16; 37:12), and Jesus uses the phrase of the lost in outer darkness (Matthew 8:12).

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke has used the phrase of Stephen before (6:3, 5), and at this moment it brings two things. First, sight: the Spirit gives eyes for the unseen, for “the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). Second, strength for the supreme test, so that he dies like his Lord, committing his spirit to Jesus and forgiving his killers. It is what Jesus promised witnesses dragged before councils: “the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say” (Luke 12:11–12). Luke does not say Stephen was filled afresh (as Peter in 4:8) but that he was full: the settled state carries him through.

He gazed into heaven. While they glare at him, he looks up with the fixed gaze (atenizō) the council had turned on him in 6:15, and what he is looking at is not in the room.

The glory of God. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia (v. 2) now appears to the first martyr in Jerusalem, and in the middle of the glory stands a man, Jesus, at God’s right hand, the place of honour and power. While men grind their teeth on earth, heaven is open, and the glory of God rests on the face of the crucified and risen Jesus. He is not absent from his suffering people; he is enthroned above them and watching over them.

Can I be filled with the Spirit? Yes; every Christian is commanded to be: “do not get drunk with wine … but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). The form of the Greek verb suggests “keep on being filled”. It is not a one-off experience for a spiritual elite but the ordinary Christian life lived under the Spirit’s control, and its truest evidence is not ecstatic feeling but a person who sees Christ clearly and, like Christ, lives and dies graciously (Ephesians 5:19–21). So ask God for it daily, feed on his word, confess sin quickly, and obey what you know. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones. He filled him to face them.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen declares that he sees heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand: the one the council condemned reigns, and has risen to his feet for his servant.

Behold, I see the heavens opened. As at Jesus’ baptism (Luke 3:21), the barrier is drawn back, and a dying man is allowed to see.

The Son of Man. Outside the Gospels, where it is Jesus’ own name for himself, the title almost never appears. Stephen calls Jesus what Jesus called himself, before the very council to which Jesus had said: “from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke 22:69). Stephen says: I see him. The council has now heard the claim twice, and the second time it does not wait for a verdict. The title carries Daniel’s vision: the Son of Man to whom the Ancient of Days gives dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, with a dominion that will never pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). The council had the last word on earth for about an hour.

Standing. Elsewhere Christ at the Father’s right hand is seated. Psalm 110 says sit, and Hebrews builds an argument on the fact that this priest sat down, because his work was finished (Hebrews 10:12). Stephen sees him standing. Perhaps to welcome his servant home; or as a witness standing to testify for him in the heavenly court, as Stephen testifies for him on earth; or as a judge rising to pass sentence. All may be true.

Two courts. Two courts are sitting that day. In the lower one a man is tried on the evidence of witnesses put up to lie, the outcome settled before he opened his mouth. In the higher one, as the accused is about to be condemned, his advocate rises to his feet. Jesus had promised it: “everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God” (Luke 12:8). The King of the everlasting kingdom is on his feet for one servant about to die outside Jerusalem, because no one who confesses him is too small for him to rise for.

The court at three in the morning. Most Christians will never stand before a council, and will nevertheless be judged: by an employer, a family, a country, or their own conscience convening a court at three in the morning with the evidence stacked and no defence prepared. This verse says another court is in session. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. … Christ Jesus is the one … who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:33–34). To justify is a courtroom word: God the Judge declares the sinner righteous, because Christ has borne his sin and Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Will I see heaven opened when I die? Scripture does not promise every believer a vision like Stephen’s, and many faithful Christians die without one, some peacefully and some in confusion or pain. What it promises is better than a vision: presence (see the note on vv. 59–60). Whether your eyes see anything at the end or not, the Lord Jesus will be there to receive you. Stephen was allowed to see beforehand what every believer will see immediately afterwards.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.

parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing to hear, the council rushes on Stephen, drives him out of the city and stones him, and the witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

They stopped their ears. The most dignified men in the nation, fingers in their ears, shouting so as not to hear: the exact fulfilment of Stephen’s charge six verses earlier. He said they were uncircumcised in their ears, and they stopped them with their hands.

Rushed together. “Together” means with one accord (homothymadon), the word Luke used of the church’s unity in prayer and in the temple (1:14; 2:46). Now it describes a mob’s rage. There is a unity of the Spirit and a unity of the mob, and for a moment, from a distance, they look alike.

They cast him out of the city. No verdict, no sentence, no vote; they simply rushed at him. Rome kept the death penalty in its own hands (John 18:31), so this was probably a lynching, not a lawful execution. Yet they took him out of the city, because the law required a stoning to take place outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). They keep the geography of Leviticus and abandon everything else in it.

The witnesses laid down their garments. The law of Moses required the witnesses to throw first in a stoning (Deuteronomy 17:7), so that any man who had sworn a life away had to be the one to take it. These are the planted witnesses of chapter 6: the men who lied about Stephen killed him with their own hands, and took their coats off to do it properly.

At the feet of a young man named Saul. With no introduction, Luke brings in the most important man of the second half of his book. A young man (neanias), minding the coats: the respectable part, the part that gets no blood on it, the part a man can afterwards tell himself was not really participation. Paul never let it go (22:20; 26:10). On the very day the church lost its first martyr, God had already marked the man who would carry the gospel to the nations.

Outside the gate with his Lord. Jesus had been led out of Jerusalem to die, suffering “outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12), and false witnesses had stood up at his trial too (Mark 14:56–57). Stephen’s death has the shape of his Master’s because he belongs to him. But the likeness stops at the decisive point. Stephen’s blood cleanses no one from sin. He goes outside the camp bearing the reproach that Christ endured (Hebrews 13:13), because Christ had already gone there bearing his sin.

Why would learned men refuse even to listen? Because to listen was to lose too much. Their standing, their power and their whole religious identity rested on being right about God, and to hear Stephen out was to admit that they had handed God’s Messiah to death. Every heart has the same reflex when the truth threatens what it lives for. Yet the grace of this chapter reaches even here: the young man holding the coats had his ears stopped as firmly as any, and Christ opened them.

Is holding the coats really so bad? Yes, and that is why Paul never forgot it. Most of us have never thrown a stone but have held a coat: laughed at the cruel joke, stayed silent at slander, approved in our hearts what we would never have done with our hands. Scripture treats approval as participation; Paul says those who give approval to evil share in its guilt (Romans 1:32). The good news is in this same verse of Acts, in the name Saul. The man who held the coats became the apostle who wrote, “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15). There is forgiveness for the coat-holders too.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen dies as his Lord died, commending his spirit to Jesus and praying for his killers, and for him death is falling asleep.

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. The first of two prayers is for himself, and it is a quotation. Psalm 31:5 says “Into your hand I commit my spirit”, addressed to God. Jesus prayed it from the cross to the Father: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays it to Jesus.

Dying in the certainty that Jesus is God. A Jewish man, killed for blasphemy by the highest religious authority in Israel, spends the last moments of his life praying a psalm addressed to the God of Israel, and addresses it to Jesus of Nazareth. He does not argue that Christ is God; he dies certain of it. Scripture says “the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7). No faithful Jew would commend his soul to a mere creature.

Falling to his knees. A man under a hail of stones does not kneel by accident. He knelt because he was going to pray.

Lord, do not hold this sin against them. The request for his own soul was spoken; the request for his murderers was shouted. It is Jesus again: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). (Those words of Jesus are missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but many scholars judge them genuine and most Bibles print them.) Jesus prayed first for his killers and then committed his spirit; Stephen reverses the order. The first Christian death is shaped like Christ’s, with the sequence turned round.

He fell asleep. A gentle verb for a violent death, but not a way of softening the facts. It is the New Testament’s word for the death of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20): sleep, from which the body will wake in resurrection, because Christ has taken death’s sting.

The prayer answered. A few feet away, holding the coats and approving, stood a young man who would be struck down on the road to Damascus, would one day call himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and would write more of the New Testament’s letters than any other man. Augustine is said to have put it this way: if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. The prayer was answered first in the man who would have been the last to expect it.

In the flow. Stephen’s death closes the Jerusalem chapters of Acts, and Luke at once shows what God does with it: the persecution that follows scatters the believers, and they preach the word as they go, first in Judea and Samaria (8:1, 4), exactly the next steps Jesus named in 1:8. The stones meant to stop the word are the means of its spread.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to lay a burden Scripture does not lay. It is not a rule that a Christian must feel forgiving at the moment of injury, or that failure to produce this prayer at the graveside of a murdered child is a failure of faith. Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit: the forgiveness here is a gift being reported, not an achievement to copy by willpower. Ordinary Christians are asked to want to get there, and to be willing to be taken there slowly, which for most is the work of years, not minutes.

In everyday life. Learn to die as Stephen did: each night as you lie down, commend your spirit to the Lord Jesus, so that when the last night comes, the words are already familiar.

Must I forgive someone who is not sorry? Stephen prayed for men who were still throwing stones, so the heart of forgiveness does not wait for an apology. It lets go of revenge, hands the wrong to God, and genuinely desires the other person’s good, even their salvation (Romans 12:17–21). But full reconciliation, restored trust, requires repentance (Luke 17:3–4), and forgiveness never means pretending a wrong was not wrong, staying exposed to someone dangerous, or not reporting a crime. You can forgive an abuser in your heart and still go to the police. Begin, as Stephen did, by praying for them. The feelings often follow the prayers, slowly.

Does fell asleep mean the soul is unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies in the grave and will be woken. Stephen’s spirit did not sleep: he had just prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”, and the Lord did. Jesus promised the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The souls of believers at death are made perfect in holiness and pass immediately into glory, while their bodies rest in their graves until the resurrection (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; Westminster Confession 32.1).
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: Rejected, then vindicated. Stephen’s survey shows a pattern in God’s ways: the one God sends is rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets and at last the Righteous One himself were refused, and each time God vindicated the rejected one and used the rejection to rescue his people. It is the pattern of the cross, and Stephen shares it. He is killed by men and received by Christ, and his prayer is answered in the conversion of the young man who watched him die.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the council in Jerusalem and preaches to them from their own history.

Now: Where Christians cannot be answered by argument, they are sometimes silenced by force. Stephen did not meet that day in his own strength. Full of the Holy Spirit, he looked up, saw Christ, commended his spirit to him and prayed for his killers. The same Spirit is given to every believer, and the same Lord stands at God’s right hand for them.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.
keyVerse.note: The speech argued that no house made by hands can hold God, and that Israel always rejected the one God sent. This verse shows where both threads end: the rejected Righteous One stands in heaven itself, at God’s right hand, the Son of Man whose kingdom will never pass away. And he is on his feet for the servant who confessed him.

7.reflection:
Stephen’s accusers thought God’s presence belonged to their land and their building, yet God met Abraham in Mesopotamia, Joseph in an Egyptian prison and Moses in the desert (vv. 2–34). Where are you tempted to think God can be found, and where might he be meeting you that you have not expected?

Again and again Israel failed to recognise the deliverer God sent: “they did not understand” (v. 25). Why do people, religious people included, so often fail to recognise Jesus, and what keeps our own hearts soft toward him?

The council stopped their ears rather than hear the truth (v. 57). Which truths are you most tempted to stop your ears against, and what helps you listen instead?

Stephen died praying, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (v. 60), while Saul looked on. Who is hardest for you to pray for, and how does the sight of Jesus standing at God’s right hand give strength to forgive?

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Where we are. Stephen has just been stoned, the first Christian to die for Christ (7:54–60). Until now the church has stayed in Jerusalem; with this chapter the second stage of Jesus’ programme begins: “in all Judea and Samaria” (1:8).

The message. Nothing can stop the word of Christ, and nothing can keep out those he means to bring in. A persecution meant to destroy the church only scatters its seed; the good news crosses an ancient hatred into Samaria and reaches a foreigner shut out of the temple, and wherever it comes it brings great joy. But the gift it brings is God’s gift: it is received with empty hands, never bought or used.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). Here he shows that the church’s spread beyond Jerusalem was the risen Lord’s plan, carried out by his Spirit, and that believing Samaritans and Gentiles belong to one church with Jewish believers.

How the chapter makes its case. Saul’s persecution scatters the church (vv. 1–3); the scattered preach as they go, and Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria, where his signs and his message displace a magician’s long hold on the city and bring much joy (vv. 4–13). Peter and John come from Jerusalem, and the Samaritans receive the Spirit through their hands: one Spirit in one church (vv. 14–17). Simon’s offer of money exposes a heart that wanted God’s power without God, and Peter calls him to repent (vv. 18–25). Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where an Ethiopian official, barred from the temple courts, is reading Isaiah 53; Philip tells him the good news about Jesus and baptises him, and the man goes home rejoicing (vv. 26–40).

Where it leads. The chapter turns on one passage: the Lamb led silently to the slaughter, denied justice and cut off from the earth (vv. 32–33). Philip begins there and tells the eunuch about Jesus. The Servant was cut off so that the cut-off could be brought in, and the gift Simon tried to buy is free only because Christ paid for it with his own blood. Behind every scene stands the risen Lord himself, scattering his people, sending his messengers and pouring out his Spirit from heaven.

For us. The disruptions of our lives may be God’s way of scattering us where he wants his word to go, and no office is needed to tell someone about Jesus. No one is too far off or too shut out for Christ, and no one can buy what he gives: come to him with empty hands, and go on your way rejoicing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns a persecution into a mission, and the gospel crosses the oldest hatred in Israel’s world. Saul’s attack scatters the church, but the scattered believers preach the word wherever they go (vv. 1–4). In Samaria Philip proclaims Christ, and his signs and message bring much joy to a city long held by a magician’s amazement; even Simon believes and is baptised (vv. 5–13). Peter and John come down from Jerusalem, pray and lay hands on the Samaritans, who receive the Spirit, so that Jew and Samaritan are one church (vv. 14–17). When Simon tries to buy that power, Peter warns him that God’s gift cannot be bought and calls him to repent, and the apostles go home preaching in many Samaritan villages (vv. 18–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The scattering as mission

God’s purposes are not only unharmed by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go to Judea and Samaria (1:8), and so far the church had stayed in the city. It took a murder and a persecution to send it out. That does not make the suffering less real (see the grief at vv. 1–2). It means that the man leading the destruction was, without knowing it, spreading the gospel across two regions.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding: it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it (see vv. 4–5). The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen’s death sends the church out instead of stopping it: persecution scatters the believers beyond Jerusalem, while devout men mourn the martyr openly.

Saul approved. The chapter division cuts a sentence in half: this line is Luke’s last word on the stoning. The young man holding the coats was no bystander. The word (syneudokōn) means he consented, thought well of it, was pleased; and Paul spent the rest of his life saying so, with shame (22:20).

A great persecution. It began “on that day”, aimed probably at the Hellenists, the Greek-speaking Jewish believers of Stephen’s circle. Once somebody had been killed and nothing happened to the killers, the restraint was gone.

All scattered, except the apostles. The word for scattered (diesparēsan) is built on the verb for sowing: seed thrown across a field. Yet the twelve, already arrested twice and flogged once, stayed. Luke does not say why; probably the fury fell hardest on Stephen’s circle, whose words about the temple had given the offence (6:13–14), while the apostles were still known as men who taught in the temple every day (5:42). Either way, the people who took the gospel to Samaria were not the apostles but the ordinary members who ran.

Devout men buried Stephen. The burial is braver than it looks. Jewish law as later recorded in the Mishnah withheld public mourning from a man executed by the court, and the custom was probably older. These men, believers or devout Jews who would not let him be shovelled away, did the opposite, loudly, on the day a persecution began: people with something to lose, weeping aloud on purpose.

The Lord who stood for Stephen. Stephen’s last sight on earth was the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (7:56), and on the day of the first martyr’s death he begins to send his witnesses out, using the stones as his means. Luke also shapes the burial to recall another, when a good and righteous man laid in a tomb a body the council had condemned (Luke 23:50–53). The servant is buried as his Master was. But the Master’s tomb was empty on the third day, so the loud tears over Stephen are not tears without hope. What Saul meant for the destruction of the church, God meant for the salvation of Samaria and Ethiopia.

Grief is not a lapse. Some Christians think a believer who grasps the resurrection should bury somebody quietly. The first Christian response to the first Christian martyrdom was a great lamentation, and Luke records it without a word of correction. Paul tells a grieving church not that they should not grieve but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and Jesus himself wept at a graveside he was about to empty (John 11:35). Hope does not forbid tears; it gives them a future.

Why does God allow his church to be persecuted? Scripture gives part of the answer, though not all of it. Persecution purifies the church, as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It joins us to Christ, who was persecuted first (John 15:20; Philippians 3:10). And, as here, God uses it to spread the gospel; Tertullian’s old saying, that the blood of the martyrs is seed, could have been written over this verse. None of that makes persecution good, and we should pray for persecuted believers and work for their relief (Hebrews 13:3). But no persecution is outside God’s purpose or beyond his power to turn to good.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul tears the church apart house by house, sure he is serving God, when every door he breaks belongs to Christ.

Ravaging the church. Luke picks a violent word. Ravaging (elymaineto) is the word the Greek translation of the Psalms uses of a wild boar wrecking a vineyard (Psalm 80:13), ruining in an afternoon what took years to grow. Saul later admitted it all, calling himself a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (22:4; 1 Timothy 1:13).

House after house. There were no church buildings; the church met in homes. So persecuting it meant going through front doors, into a kitchen where a family had been praying, and taking people out, women too. “Dragged off” is the word Luke will later use of Paul himself being dragged out of a city and left for dead (14:19).

Every door he broke was Christ’s. Saul thought he was clearing heretics out of Israel’s vineyard. In fact he was laying hands on the Lord himself, who will ask him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). The Lord counts his people’s injuries as his own. And the psalm whose word Luke borrowed already pointed to the remedy: after the boar has ravaged the vine, Israel prays, “let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself” (Psalm 80:17). Stephen had just seen that Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. The vine had a keeper, and the ravager was about to meet him.

Zeal without God. Saul was not irreligious. He did all this out of zeal for God, blameless as to righteousness under the law (Philippians 3:6). Here is the warning for religious people: religion used to prove that we are the righteous ones can make us hard and even cruel, sure we are serving God while we fight him. Saul’s cure was not more zeal but meeting the Lord he was persecuting, and counting his own righteousness as loss compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–9).

Grace did not give him amnesia. The man who went door to door arresting mothers later wrote that love is patient and kind (1 Corinthians 13:4). Some thirty years on he still calls himself the foremost of sinners, in the present tense (1 Timothy 1:15). Grace did not erase the memory; it let him carry it, accurate and unbearable, without despair, which is more remarkable than forgetting.

Not a guarantee. Saul’s story is no pledge that every persecutor will be converted; most died as they had lived. It shows that no one’s past puts him beyond mercy, which is what Paul says his conversion was for: “that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe” (1 Timothy 1:16).

How should I pray for those who persecute Christians today? As Jesus told us: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Pray for their conversion, by name if you know them, remembering Saul. Pray that God would restrain their violence and protect his people (4:29–30), for justice and religious freedom, and for persecuted believers to stand firm and be comforted. It is not wrong to ask God to stop evil men, as the psalmists did. But let the first prayer be Stephen’s: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. God has answered that prayer before.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scattered believers cannot stop talking about Christ, and Philip carries him across the oldest hatred in Israel’s world, into Samaria.

Those who were scattered. The scattering that looked like defeat is the next stage of the plan Jesus gave in 1:8. Stephen had just argued that God was never confined to one building or one land (7:48–50), and the scattered church now proves the point on foot. Luke will open the next great advance with the same words (11:19).

Preaching the word. Luke chooses the word for telling good news (euangelizomenoi), not the herald’s word he uses of Philip in the next verse. The first missionary expansion of the church was carried out by amateurs, under duress, with no strategy, because they could not stop talking about the reason they had been driven out.

Philip went down. This is Philip, one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle: one of the men appointed to see that the widows were fed. In this book the men appointed to serve tables cross the boundaries first, while the apostles stay in Jerusalem.

A feud centuries old. After Assyria deported the northern tribes, it resettled the land with foreign peoples (2 Kings 17:24–41). Their mixed descendants, the Samaritans, claimed the God of Israel, kept only the five books of Moses, and worshipped at a rival temple on Mount Gerizim, which a Jewish army had pulled down about a hundred and fifty years before. Calling a man a Samaritan was an insult (John 8:48).

Proclaimed to them the Christ. Into that, Philip preaches a person, not an argument about which mountain was right or whose copy of the law was correct. The Samaritans expected a Messiah too (John 4:25), and Philip tells them he has come. The quarrel that centuries of argument had not settled was left where it was, and something was announced that made it irrelevant.

Am I meant to share my faith if I am not a pastor? Yes. The people in this verse had no office at all, and they spread the gospel across two regions. Pastors have a particular calling to preach and teach (Ephesians 4:11), but every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done. You do not need to preach a sermon. You need to be ready to give a reason for your hope, gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15), to invite people to hear the word, and to speak naturally of Christ where life has put you. The gospel has always travelled furthest in ordinary conversations.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In despised Samaria the crowds listen to Philip, and the signs Jesus gave as the marks of his own coming are done again in his name. The miracles won Philip a hearing; the message held the crowd.

With one accord. Luke used the phrase of the disciples praying in the upper room (1:14); now it describes a crowd of Samaritans, and he means the reader to feel the shock. In his sentence the message comes first and the signs second.

Unclean spirits. Demons, crying out as they did before Jesus (Mark 1:26). The list ties Samaria to Jerusalem on purpose: spirits coming out, the paralysed and the lame healed, visible ailments a whole town could verify (3:1–10), now in a despised city through a man appointed to hand out bread. There is no reduced edition of the kingdom for people on the wrong side of a border.

Many, not all. A small honesty for anybody who has prayed long and not been healed: even at the height of an outpouring, spirits came out of many, and many were healed, so somebody may still have been left on his mat. Luke neither explains it nor hides it.

The lame walk. These are not random wonders. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus pointed to exactly these things: the lame walk (Luke 7:22), as Isaiah had said that when God came to save, the lame man would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:4–6). When paralysed Samaritans stand up under Philip’s preaching, the answer Jesus gave John is being given again. The healer has gone up to heaven, and his work goes on in his name (1:1).

A city with no sickbed in it. In the city Jerusalem despised, men carried for years on mats walked home, and the demons went out shrieking at the name of Jesus. That name has lost none of its authority. The King who healed many in Samaria has promised a day when those of every century who prayed and still sat on the mat will rise whole, to walk with him in a city with no sickbed in it.

Philip was not an apostle, so why could he do signs? Like Stephen, he was one of the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands (6:6), and his signs belong to the same founding ministry. Even so, the Samaritans received the Spirit only when the apostles came (vv. 14–17), which shows how closely these gifts were tied to the apostles. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, such sign gifts belonged to the foundation age, because the New Testament ties them to the apostles’ founding witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, often called continuationists, believe these gifts continue today, and they are brothers to be loved, not dismissed. God still heals in answer to prayer; what has ceased is the apostolic sign gift attesting new revelation.

Why does God not heal everyone I pray for? Scripture does not fully explain, and we should beware of anyone who claims to. It is not because your faith was too small: Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed, and God said no, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God heals some now as a foretaste of the new creation, and he will heal all his people in the resurrection, when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, keep praying, use the means he gives, doctors and medicine among them, and trust that his no is never a lack of love.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ brings joy to a whole city, and against that joy Luke sets a man whose whole message was himself.

So there was much joy in that city. Not merely in individuals: the atmosphere of a whole city had changed (13:52; 16:34). Luke will sound the same note at the end of the chapter, when a single man goes home rejoicing (v. 39). No magician’s wonder had ever produced it; Christ had come.

A man named Simon. Magic (mageuōn) was not entertainment or conjuring. A practitioner claimed real access to powers, and people paid him for results: a curse on a rival, a charm against illness. Such a man was feared, consulted and rich. Later Christian writers regarded this Simon, often called Simon Magus, as the father of heresies, and Justin Martyr, himself born in Samaria, wrote that the Samaritans honoured him as the first god.

Somebody great. Luke sums up Simon’s message in one line: “he himself was somebody great”. Not a doctrine, not a God, not a promise: a claim about the speaker. Everything Simon offered was ultimately about Simon.

The one who is great. Simon’s claim has an answer in the one Philip preached. An angel had said of Mary’s son, “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32). The one who truly is great said, “I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27), and the next day died for the people he served. Simon took a city’s worship and gave it nothing. Christ takes nothing from us and gives himself.

The test of a ministry. The difference is not power against no power, for Philip has just healed paralytics, but what the power points at. Simon amazed people, and they concluded that Simon was great. Philip did signs, and the crowds ended up listening to a message about somebody else. The test in any century is what the watchers end up attached to. If a ministry produces crowds who know all about the minister and little about Christ, something has gone wrong that no orthodox statement of faith will correct.

The craving underneath. Few of us have claimed to be the power of God, but the craving under Simon’s claim is common: to be admired, to be thought somebody. Christ frees us from it, because the one who matters most has already loved us at our worst, and we have nothing left to prove (Romans 5:8; Galatians 1:10).

Is magic real, and is it harmless to dabble? Scripture treats sorcery and the occult as real and forbidden, not as harmless fun (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Galatians 5:20). Some is trickery and some may involve real spiritual powers: the one deceives, the other enslaves. So a Christian should have nothing to do with fortune-telling, séances, spells, tarot or any attempt to gain hidden knowledge or power apart from God. If you have been involved, confess it, renounce it and get rid of the objects, as the Ephesians burned their magic books (19:19), and rest in Christ, who has disarmed every power (Colossians 2:15). You do not need to be afraid. You need to be finished with it.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A whole city, high and low, had given itself to Simon, held not by truth but by amazement and long habit.

From the least to the greatest. The labourer and the magistrate, the servant girl and her mistress. It is comforting to think only the gullible fall for this. Simon’s hold reached the top.

The power of God that is called Great. The odd, half-technical phrase shows that Simon had supplied the city with a theology: they thought him a divine power flowing out from God. He was a religious institution with a creed. The true power of God is the crucified Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), shown supremely in weakness, at a cross, and in an empty tomb.

For a long time. Luke names what held them, and neither thing is truth: amazement, and long habit. That is how most religious authority that does not come from God keeps its hold. Nobody has to be persuaded, only left unable to explain what is happening for long enough that it becomes normal.

The stronger man. Jesus described his own work in words that fit this city: when one stronger than the armed strong man overcomes him, he takes away the armour he trusted in and divides the spoil (Luke 11:21–22). Samaria had been held a long time by fear and wonder. Jesus does not send a cleverer magician against those powers. He comes in his word, by an ordinary preacher, and takes his spoil: men and women set free and baptised into his name.

How was anyone to tell the difference? From outside, Philip’s ministry looked similar: crowds, signs, amazement. Luke’s answer is not the phenomena but the message: Simon offered an experience and a claim about himself; Philip preached a King, and people believed (v. 12; see “The test of a ministry” at vv. 8–9).

Can Satan really do miracles? Scripture warns that he can produce counterfeit signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13; Matthew 24:24), though his power is limited and always under God’s control (Job 1:12). So a miracle is never enough by itself to prove a message true. Moses told Israel that if a prophet gave a sign that came to pass but led them to other gods, they were not to listen (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Ask of any wonder not merely whether something happened, but what it is being used to teach, and whether it leads you to the Christ of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message of the King sets Samaria free: men and women believe and are baptised, and even Simon believes, though, as the sequel shows, without a changed heart.

When they believed Philip. What displaces Simon is not a stronger performance but a message, given in two phrases: the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ.

What is it to preach the kingdom of God? The kingdom is God’s saving reign, breaking in through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. Philip preached the kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ in one breath, because there is no kingdom without the King. To preach it is to announce that God’s promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe and bow to him as Lord (28:31). The phrase fills the first three Gospels and is rare in John and the letters because the vocabulary shifts, not the truth: Jesus preached the kingdom to hearers steeped in Israel’s hope (Matthew 4:17; Daniel 7:13–14); John speaks of eternal life (John 3:3, 5); the apostles, after the resurrection, proclaim the reigning King: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9). It is the same kingdom throughout.

Both men and women. They believed, then were baptised, the order this commentary follows (see vv. 36–37). And in a world where a woman’s religious standing often travelled through her husband, Luke records the women baptised on their own faith.

Even Simon himself believed. Luke states it without qualification: he believed, was baptised, and attached himself to the preacher. Luke does not say he was play-acting. He is like the seed on rocky ground, which believes for a while (Luke 8:13): he believed something, for a time, but without the new birth, in which God gives a new heart, so that a person loves God instead of using him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26). His belief changed his opinions, not his heart.

He was amazed. The amazer is now amazed. He has changed sides, but not his interest: he was drawn by power, not by Christ, and five verses later he will try to buy it.

Was Simon truly saved? Some take him as a true believer who fell into serious sin. But Peter says his heart was not right before God, that he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, and that he had neither part nor lot in this matter (vv. 20–23). The more likely reading is that his was a faith impressed by miracles that had never turned from self. That fits what Scripture teaches about perseverance: those whom God truly saves, he keeps, and those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

Can I be baptised and still not be a Christian? Yes, sadly; Simon was. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, commanded by him, and believers should be baptised. But the water does not save. What saves is Christ himself, received by the faith the Spirit works in the heart (Ephesians 2:8–9). So the question is not, was I baptised, but, do I trust Christ, love him, and want to turn from my sin? If you find those things in yourself, however weakly, they are the marks of the new birth. If you do not, do not rely on your baptism. Come to Christ today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem welcomes the Samaritans’ faith instead of questioning it, and sends Peter and John to pray that God will give them his Spirit. One of the two had once wanted Samaria burned.

The apostles at Jerusalem heard. Notice what is missing: no debate, no committee, no summons for Philip to explain why a food-distributor was evangelising the other side of an old quarrel. The apostles send two men to pray, and their first act is to ask God to give those people more. It sets a pattern: when Gentiles believe in Antioch, the church again sends someone (11:22–23), and when Peter baptises Cornelius, Jerusalem glorifies God (11:18). One church, not a cluster of rival ones.

Peter and John. John is the best thing in the verse. When a Samaritan village refused Jesus hospitality, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to consume them, and were rebuked (Luke 9:52–55). Now the same man walks into the same territory to lay his hands on Samaritans and ask God to give them the Holy Spirit. What grace had done to John is described nowhere; it is visible in the fact that he made the journey.

Reaping where Jesus sowed. At a well outside Sychar, Jesus had told the disciples that the fields were white for harvest, and that he had sent them to reap that for which they did not labour (John 4:35–38). He had sown in Samaria himself, with one woman. The harvest the apostles came to bless was the Lord’s before it was anyone else’s.

Blessing where there might have been fire. John once asked for fire from heaven on Samaria, and Jesus said no. Now he asks heaven for a gift on Samaria, and what comes down is the Spirit. Between the two prayers stands a cross, where the judgment those villages deserved, and John deserved, fell on the Son of Man himself. That is why heaven can send blessing where it might have sent fire.

How can I lose a prejudice I have had all my life? Probably not by argument. John’s instinct about Samaritans was to incinerate them, and it was replaced, slowly enough that nobody recorded the process, by walking with Jesus. So bring the prejudice to Christ honestly, as sin. Pray for the people you find it hardest to love. Get to know some of them, especially fellow believers from that group, and serve them. Christ died for them as he died for you, and they will share heaven with you (Revelation 7:9). Feelings follow faithfulness, and the Spirit who changed John can change you.
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God held back the Spirit from the Samaritan believers until the apostles came, so that Jew and Samaritan would be one church under one Spirit. It was a once-for-all bridge across an ancient divide, not a pattern every believer must follow.

Not yet fallen on any of them. They had believed and been truly baptised, and the Spirit had not come. Normally the Spirit comes with faith (2:38); in chapter 10 he comes before anybody has been baptised at all (10:44). Here there is a gap.

They laid their hands on them. The reading that best fits Luke’s narrative is that this was a turning point in the history of salvation. After centuries of rival temples there was a real danger of two churches, a Jewish one and a Samaritan one. Instead, centuries of division were healed in public, by Jewish hands on Samaritan heads. Something visible probably happened, since Simon saw it (v. 18).

The great crossings. The pattern across Acts supports this. As the gospel crossed each great barrier, God marked the crossing with a visible coming of the Spirit: on Jews at Pentecost, on Samaritans here, on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10), and on the disciples of John at Ephesus (chapter 19). These were once-for-all moments in the spread of the one church to all peoples (1:8).

The apostles’ hands. No one today should claim to give the Spirit by laying on hands. The gift came through the apostles because it was their foundational work to join each new people into the one church (Ephesians 2:20), and that role was not passed on. The letters teach the regular way: when you believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13).

The gift of the ascended Christ. Whoever lays hands on whom, the giver in this scene is the Lord Jesus, who, exalted at the right hand of God, had poured out the promised Spirit (2:33). The Samaritans had not been baptised into a lesser Lord. The apostles prayed; Christ answered. And receiving the Spirit is not a feeling or an impersonal force, but God himself coming to live in a person: he joins him to Christ, assures him that he is God’s child, and begins to make him holy (John 14:16–17; Romans 8:15–16).

In everyday life. A Samaritan and a Jew under the same apostolic hands: that is what a church is. The believer of another background or style whom you pass in the car park on Sunday has the same Spirit you have, all of him, and God means you to be one.

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit? No. If you belong to Christ, you have the Spirit, all of him, from the moment you believed (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). You are not a half-Christian waiting for a second gift. What you need, every day, is to walk by the Spirit and be filled with the Spirit (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 5:18), yielding more of yourself to the one who already lives in you. Seasons when God makes his presence and love unusually vivid are precious gifts, but they are fresh fillings of the Spirit you have, not the arrival of a Spirit you lacked.

Should I seek to speak in tongues as proof that I have the Spirit? No. Even in the apostolic church Paul asked, do all speak with tongues? and expected the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). The proof of the Spirit’s presence is that you confess Jesus as Lord, cry to God as Father, and bear the Spirit’s fruit (1 Corinthians 12:3; Romans 8:15; Galatians 5:22–23). Many Reformed Christians believe the gift of tongues ceased with the apostolic age; continuationist brothers disagree, and we hold our view charitably. But on any view, no believer should be told that he lacks the Spirit because he has not spoken in tongues.

Where Christians differ: a second blessing, or a sacrament? Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a two-stage pattern, conversion and then a distinct baptism in the Spirit, and read Acts 19 the same way. Roman Catholics and others see the basis for confirmation, a sacrament in which a bishop’s hands confer the Spirit. This commentary’s view: this was a once-for-all bridging as the gospel crossed a great barrier, like chapters 10 and 19, not the normal pattern. Romans 8:9 says anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, without a second stage or an apostle’s hands. This is said with real respect for brothers who differ, many of whom love the Spirit and the Scriptures deeply.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, treating God’s free gift as a commodity he could own and sell.

He offered them money. Simon saw something happen, though Luke does not say what, and made the first attempt in Christian history to purchase a spiritual gift.

Give me this power also. He does not ask to receive the Spirit, but for the power to lay his own hands on others and have the Spirit come. He is not applying for a blessing but for a franchise, the right to hand out the gift himself, and so to be somebody great again (v. 9).

Doing business the only way he knew. In Simon’s old profession names, formulas and techniques were commodities, bought at the going rate, and his request is even courteous. He has not noticed that he has changed worlds: here there is no going rate, for the thing was never for sale, and the men holding it did not buy it either. The Spirit is not a power to be bought and used but God, who gives himself, and no one can buy or control him. Three chapters earlier money and the Holy Spirit had already met, when Ananias and Sapphira lied not to men but to God, and fell dead (5:3–5). Simon is standing nearer to the fire than he knows.

The Spirit for the asking. Simon wanted to buy what Jesus had promised to give for the asking: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). And the one who dispenses the Spirit is the Son, who received him from the Father without measure (John 3:34). Simon wanted to stand where only Christ stands, and Christ gives freely to beggars, never to buyers.

Simony. Simon’s name has been attached to the sin ever since. Simony, the buying and selling of church office and spiritual privilege, became a great scandal of the medieval church. Its quieter modern shapes are everywhere: the giving that expects a return in blessing, the service undertaken with an eye on what it buys, the prayer offered as a lever to move God.
