In each the assumption is Simon’s: that there is a rate, and a man who pays it is entitled to the result. It is how nearly everything else works. It is not how grace works.

When everything has a price. We live inside a market, which assumes that anything worth having can be bought, even a sense of the sacred, sold by subscription. Economists once studied nurseries in Israel that began fining parents who collected their children late. Lateness went up. The fine had turned a duty into a price, and parents who used to feel guilty now felt they had simply paid. A price does not only buy a thing; it changes what the thing is. Had the Spirit been for sale, Simon would have become a customer of God, and never his child. Religious people make Simon’s mistake with good works instead of silver, and secular people with effort, therapy and spending: the same wish to stay the one who pays. The gospel is the one offer in the world made on the opposite terms: “come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). It is free to us only because it was not free to Christ.

Is it wrong to pay ministers, or to give expecting God to bless me? Paying ministers is right: the labourer deserves his wages, and those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). That is support for work, not a purchase of grace. And God does promise to bless generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–11). What is wrong is giving as a transaction to obtain spiritual power or material reward, the seed-faith teaching that a gift to a preacher will make God pay you back with money or healing. That is Simon’s error dressed up as faith. Give because God has given to you, freely and cheerfully, and leave the blessing to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter warns Simon that a man who thinks God’s gift can be bought has no share in it at all, because his heart is not right before God.

May your silver perish with you. Among the harshest things Peter ever says; J. B. Phillips rendered it, “To hell with you and your money!” Yet it is a warning, not a curse: Peter names where the man and his money are heading because he wants it changed, and he goes on to tell Simon to repent.

The gift of God. This clause holds the passage’s theology. It is the word Peter used at Pentecost, the gift of the Holy Spirit (2:38). A gift is not a cheap purchase but a different kind of thing: once a price is paid, it is no longer a gift. Grace is God’s undeserved kindness, and if it could be earned, grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). On Simon’s terms nobody in that room would have had any, Peter included.

Neither part nor lot in this matter. The phrase echoes the law of Moses, where the Levite has no portion or inheritance when the land is divided (Deuteronomy 12:12): when the ground is measured out, Simon’s name is on none of it. Then the diagnosis, “your heart is not right before God”, echoes the psalm, “Their heart was not steadfast toward him” (Psalm 78:37): faith on the outside, a crooked heart within.

Not with silver. Years later the same Peter wrote that we were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). The gift is not free because it is cheap; it is free because the whole price was paid by another. To offer money for it treats the blood of Christ as a deposit that needs topping up. Peter’s horror is that of a man who knows what the Spirit cost.

Simon believed and was baptised, so could that be me? Verse 13 says Simon believed; verse 21 says he has no share at all. Scripture knows the category. The demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19); a crowd believed when they saw the signs, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them, for he knew what was in man (John 2:23–25); and see “Was Simon truly saved?” at vv. 12–13. Some believing is real as far as it goes and never goes as far as Christ. Simon is its portrait: gripped, impressed, attached to the preacher, and interested from first to last in what he could get.

If you are afraid it could be you. The reader who thinks, that could be me, is showing the one symptom Simon never shows. Simon is not worried about his heart; as his reply to Peter shows, he is worried about what might happen to him. Anxiety about whether you truly love Christ is a question that never entered Simon’s head, and is itself evidence of an interest he did not have. God gives his children assurance through his promises, the inner witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of a changed life (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2; Westminster Confession 18.2).

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter shows Simon the way out in the same breath as the diagnosis: repent, and pray to the Lord yourself, for you are poisoned and bound by sin.

Repent and pray. Peter at once tells the man what to do, which is what distinguishes a rebuke from a dismissal. Some say the hard thing and leave the man standing in it; others will not say it at all and call the omission kindness. Peter shows the way out within two sentences, and the way out is the reason he said the hard thing. To repent is a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, turning from sin to God (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

If possible. The phrase does not mean Peter doubted that God would forgive a sin this size. The uncertainty attaches to Simon, not to God’s willingness: the difference between saying, “God may not forgive you”, and saying, “you may not repent”. That distinction matters to anyone carrying something he fears is too large.

Pray to the Lord yourself. Not, ask me to pray. The man who has just tried to buy access through an intermediary is told to go directly and ask for himself. In one sentence Peter refuses both the money and the role of broker.

The gall of bitterness. The diagnosis is built from two Old Testament phrases. The gall of bitterness reaches back to Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deuteronomy 29:18): a thing growing out of sight, exactly right for a man whose problem nobody could see until money was mentioned. The bond of iniquity is the language of chains, from Isaiah’s call to loose the bonds of wickedness (Isaiah 58:6). Simon is not a believer who has slipped but a man still tied up, and a man in chains cannot untie himself.

The chains Jesus came to loose. At Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah a line drawn from this same passage, “to set at liberty those who are oppressed” (Luke 4:18), and said the Scripture was fulfilled that day. So when Peter tells a man bound in iniquity to pray to the Lord, he is sending him to the one person who announced, as the programme of his ministry, that he had come to undo exactly this kind of knot. The chains are real. So is the Liberator.

Is there any sin too big to be forgiven? No sin is too big for the blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Jesus does speak of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as unforgivable (Mark 3:28–30), but that is the settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work the devil’s, not a single terrible act a person regrets. Those who have committed it do not fear they have; they do not care. If you are troubled that your sin may be too great, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Do what Peter told Simon: repent, and pray to the Lord. Whoever comes to Christ, he will never cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon asks to escape the consequences, not to be changed, and Luke leaves his story open as a warning, while the apostles go home preaching through Samaria.

Pray for me. Simon misses the point. Peter had named a crooked heart and a bond of iniquity; Simon asks about the consequences. He is not asking to be changed but not to be hit: the difference between a man who is sorry and a man who is frightened, two states that make very similar noises. It is Pharaoh asking Moses to plead with the LORD to take away the frogs (Exodus 8:8).

Whom he asks. Peter had told him to pray to the Lord himself. Simon replies, you pray for me. He is still in his old trade, assuming that the power belongs to the practitioner. Rebuked for treating the Spirit as a commodity, he now treats Peter as one.

Luke stops. Scripture says no more of Simon; the later legends about Simon Magus are lurid and unreliable. Luke leaves him under a question mark: a warning delivered, a door held open, no answer recorded. A settled ending would let the reader off, either because grace reached even Simon or because we are not like him. Left open, the question passes to the reader: what will you do with the warning?

Many villages of the Samaritans. Sent to look into a revival in one city, the apostles went home seeding a whole region on foot, part of what they came to see; and one of the two had once wanted the place burned to the ground.

The prayer behind Peter. Simon wanted Peter to stand between him and God. Peter knew what he himself stood on: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Peter denied his Lord three times, and his faith did not fail, because the prayer that held him was Christ’s. That intercession is not for hire. The risen Jesus always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the way to be covered by it is to come to him oneself.

In everyday life. Fear of consequences is not repentance. Next time you are sorry for something, ask yourself honestly: am I sorry I did it, or sorry about what it might cost me? Take the real thing to God. Even our best repentance is mixed, and we stand not on its purity but on Christ, who obeyed perfectly in our place (1 John 2:1).

Is it wrong to ask others to pray for me? Not at all. Scripture tells us to pray for one another (James 5:16), and Paul constantly asked churches to pray for him (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19). Simon’s fault was asking for prayer instead of repenting and going to God himself. Ask your friends to pray for you, and pray for them, but never let someone else’s prayers become a substitute for your own coming to Christ. No one can repent for you, and no one needs to stand between you and God: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends his messenger to one seeking man and opens the Scriptures to him, and the man shut out of the temple goes home rejoicing in Christ. An angel sends Philip from a revival to a desert road, where an Ethiopian treasurer, returning from worship in Jerusalem, is reading Isaiah (vv. 26–28). The Spirit sends Philip to the chariot, and the official humbly asks for a guide (vv. 29–31). The passage is the silent Lamb, denied justice and cut off, and Philip begins there and tells him the good news about Jesus (vv. 32–35). At the first water the man asks what prevents his baptism, and nothing does (vv. 36–38). The Spirit takes Philip away; the Ethiopian goes on his way rejoicing, and Philip preaches up the coast (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the Old Testament passage that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. The transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the whole point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering but a substitute, the guiltless one bearing the penalty the guilty deserved, so that the guilty go free. From Isaiah 53 the road to Christ was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation (see the notes on vv. 26–27 and vv. 36–37). Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are often the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes Philip away from a revival and sends him to an empty road, to meet one man from the end of the earth who had travelled to worship God and been kept at the door.

Toward the south. In the middle of perhaps the most fruitful work of his life, Philip is told to leave and stand on a road. The road to Gaza, the last town of any size before Egypt, ran south-west through empty country: no town, no crowd, no synagogue, and no word on how long he is to wait.

He rose and went. There is not a question in it: not what for, nor whether the Samaritan work will survive without him. Everything that follows depended on a man being willing to leave something that was going extremely well.

An Ethiopian, a eunuch. Ethiopia here is the ancient kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt, in modern Sudan, with its capital at Meroë; to Greeks and Romans it lay at the end of the earth. Royal courts employed eunuchs, who posed no dynastic threat, and they often rose to the highest posts of trust. Candace was a title, like Pharaoh, for the queen, or queen mother, who ruled Meroë, and this man is her finance minister: powerful, wealthy, trusted with the treasury of a kingdom.

He had come to Jerusalem to worship. Now the poignancy. The law said that no one whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1). Here, most likely, is a God-fearing Gentile (one who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming a full convert) who has travelled more than a thousand miles to worship, only to be kept at the door. He is a step beyond the Samaritans, who shared Moses with Israel, and a step short of Cornelius (chapter 10): one conversion at a time, Luke shows that no one is too far off for Christ. Yet he is reading Isaiah, the book in which God promised the eunuch who holds fast his covenant a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:3–5).

A house of prayer for all peoples. Two verses later God says his house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7), the verse Jesus quoted when he cleared the outer court where foreigners like this treasurer were allowed to pray (Mark 11:17). That same week he was crucified, the temple of his body destroyed and raised on the third day (John 2:19–21). In him the house Isaiah promised was built. The eunuch had gone to Jerusalem to find it and been held at the door. On the road home, the door came to him.

Was it not cruel of the law to shut a eunuch out? It was hard, and it was meant to teach. Bodily wholeness pictured the wholeness God requires of those who come near him, which is why even a priest with a blemish could not offer the sacrifices (Leviticus 21:17–23). The rule was not a verdict on the man’s worth or sincerity but a lesson in God’s holiness: no one is fit by nature to walk into his presence. And the law was never God’s last word. Isaiah promised its end for eunuchs (Isaiah 56:3–5), and Christ, the only truly unblemished one, was cut off so that the shut-out could be brought in (Hebrews 10:19–22).

Why would God take Philip away from a revival to reach one man? Because God values the one as well as the crowd (Luke 15:4), and sees what we cannot: this man may have been the gospel’s door into Africa. We measure ministry by numbers; God by faithfulness and his own purposes. If you are called from something fruitful to something small and hidden, it is not demotion. It may be the most important work you will ever do.

Why did God guide so directly then but not now? Angelic appearances were never everyday, even in Scripture. They cluster at pivotal moments, the patriarchs, the exodus, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, and most godly saints never saw an angel. Acts is such a moment, the once-for-all launch of the gospel to the end of the earth, and God steered it by angels, visions and the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9). Like the signs that authenticated the apostles, this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Ephesians 2:20).

How God guides today. We are not less supplied but more: the completed Scripture, a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105), able to equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; prayer, wisdom, godly counsel and providence. Scripture even warns against craving angelic encounters (Colossians 2:18; 2 Corinthians 11:14; Galatians 1:8). God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is to ask for something lesser. Two honest qualifications: angels still serve the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen; and no verse says outright that they stopped speaking. That they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a fair inference from the foundational character of Acts and the sufficiency of Scripture, held charitably.

Uncertain wording. Three phrases are uncertain. “Toward the south” (kata mesēmbrian) can also mean “about noon”; either way Philip is sent onto an empty road, and at midday it would be emptier still. “This is a desert place” may describe the road or the town of Gaza, since old Gaza had been destroyed and a new town built nearby; most take it of the road, which ran through lonely country. And “eunuch” could be used loosely as a court title (Genesis 39:1), but here, beside the separate title “court official”, he is most likely a literal eunuch.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long before Philip reached the road, God had been drawing this man, and he is already reading the passage that speaks of Christ; Philip has only to go over to him.

Seated in his chariot. A covered carriage, moving slowly, with a driver, and he was reading aloud, as ancient readers usually did, so that Philip could hear him. A hand-copied scroll of Isaiah was a serious purchase. He has spent real money on the sacred book of a religion that will not fully admit him, probably in Greek, not his own language, and reads it on the way home from a pilgrimage that ended at a barrier. He was seeking because the Spirit had long been at work in a royal court in Africa, drawing a man to Jerusalem and putting Isaiah in his hands. God is always ahead of his messengers.

Go over and join this chariot. The angel sent him to the road; the Spirit sends him to the chariot. The verb (kollaō) means to be glued to something, the word used of Saul later trying to attach himself to the disciples (9:26). Philip is told to fasten on.

The man in the scroll. He had bought a book whose central figure he could not yet name, though Jesus said of the Scriptures, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39). Barred from the temple courts, he was carrying home the Servant whose soul would be made an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:10), in whom every sacrifice in that temple was fulfilled. Philip is sent to supply the name the passage was waiting for.

The division of labour. The work is shared, which lifts a great weight off the messenger. The Spirit arranged the road, the timing, the scroll and the passage; what was left for Philip was to walk over. Few of us will hear an audible sentence like Philip’s, but much of his obedience was doing something small and mildly awkward with a situation already in front of him.

How do I know when God wants me to go over to someone? Usually not by a voice, but by an opportunity you can see and a love you already have. Pray that God would put people in your path and give you courage, then watch for openings: the colleague who mentions a crisis, the neighbour who asks why you go to church, the friend reading something spiritual. Scripture has already told you to love your neighbour and be ready to speak (1 Peter 3:15); you need no special guidance to obey that. If an opportunity is in front of you and nothing forbids it, take it. You may be walking toward someone God has been preparing for years.
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip begins with the book already in the man’s hands, and the man humbly admits he needs a guide. Scripture is for everyone to read, and God gives teachers to open it.

Philip ran to him. A grown man jogging, out of breath, beside a state official’s carriage: eager obedience, not dignity.

Do you understand what you are reading? In Greek a play on words: do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)? It is a light touch, exactly right: not a challenge, not a sermon, not a change of subject. Anyone who dreads these conversations should notice: the dread is usually of introducing a subject out of nothing, and Philip introduces nothing. He notices what is in the man’s hands and asks how he is getting on with it.

How can I, unless someone guides me? The answer is as humble as any sentence in Acts. A man of rank, in his own carriage, replies to a stranger on foot, and does not bluff or claim his own view of the passage. He admits at once that he is out of his depth. The word for guide (hodēgēsei) means to lead on the way, the word Jesus used of the Spirit guiding into all the truth (John 16:13). Then he invites Philip up, to sit beside him, not to stand over him.

Two errors ruled out. First, that Scripture is so plain nobody needs help with it: this intelligent, serious man cannot get through Isaiah 53 alone, and the God who inspired the text also gave the church teachers (Ephesians 4:11; Nehemiah 8:8). Second, that Scripture is so difficult ordinary people should leave it to the qualified: nobody tells the eunuch to stop reading. The answer to his difficulty is not less Bible but a teacher beside him in the carriage.

The key is a person. The passage stays locked until you know whom it describes. The apostles themselves had not understood the suffering Servant until the risen Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45–46). What Philip brings to the carriage is not superior scholarship but the name that turns a riddle about a silent lamb into good news. God did not leave a seeking man alone with a scroll he could not read; he sent a runner along a desert road. He wrote the book, he sends the guide, and by his Spirit he opens the eyes, until the reader sees that the page he has been puzzling over is about the one who loved him.

What if someone asks me a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly; the eunuch’s humility suits the teacher too. Say you do not know but would like to find out together, and then do: ask your pastor, read a good book, and come back. People are not looking for a Christian who knows everything, but for one who is honest. And you can always tell what you do know: who Jesus is, what he did, and what he means to you. Philip did not need to answer every question about Isaiah. He needed to get to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By God’s providence the scroll lies open at Isaiah’s silent, innocent Servant, denied justice and cut off, and the man reading it, himself cut off, is reading his own story.

The passage. It is Isaiah 53:7–8, in the fourth of Isaiah’s Servant Songs, poems about a mysterious Servant of the LORD who will bring God’s salvation to Israel and the nations (Isaiah 42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). The wording differs a little from our Old Testament because the eunuch was reading the Greek translation, but the sense is the same: an innocent sufferer led to death and cut off.

Like a lamb before its shearer. At shearing, the animal is turned over and held, and goes completely still. The Gospels record exactly that: Jesus was silent before his accusers (Mark 14:61), and before Herod he answered nothing (Luke 23:9).

Justice was denied him. Not merely that he suffered, but that the courts failed. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus, and then delivered him over to their will (Luke 23:4, 14, 22, 25).

His own biography. Now picture the man in the carriage. He is a eunuch: no children, no name carried forward, and in the ancient world that was not a private sorrow but the erasure of a man from the future. The law had shut him out of the assembly on precisely that ground. And he is reading aloud about a man whose life is taken away from the earth, who yet, a few lines on, “shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10): dying without descendants, and given countless spiritual children. He was reading his own biography and could not work out whose it was. He asks who this is because whoever it is stands exactly where he stands.

What does Isaiah 53 offer someone who feels cut off? Everything. The Servant was cut off so that the cut-off could be brought in. He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), so he knows from the inside what it is to be excluded, shamed and alone. If you feel shut out, by your body, your past, your singleness or childlessness, your illness or your story, look at him. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (53:4–5). In him you have a family, the church, and a name better than sons and daughters. No one who comes to the Lamb is left outside.

In everyday life. Read Isaiah 53 slowly this week, all twelve verses, and every time it says he, put Jesus’ name; every time it says we or us, put your own.

Uncertain wording. “Who can describe his generation?” is genuinely difficult, in Isaiah’s Hebrew and in the Greek the eunuch read. Readers take it two main ways: that nobody could describe the wickedness of the men among whom he lived, or, more probably, that nobody could number his descendants, which fits the promise of offspring a few lines later.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eunuch asks the question the passage itself raises, whom the prophet is speaking about, and Philip begins from that very Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus.

About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this? It is the right question, not a naive one. The identity of Isaiah’s Servant was genuinely disputed. Interpreters, Jewish and later Christian, have proposed the prophet himself, or Hezekiah, or Israel as a nation, or a faithful remnant within it, or a Messiah still to come. The eunuch has read carefully enough to see that the passage is about a person, and honestly enough to admit that he cannot tell which.

Beginning with this Scripture. “Philip opened his mouth” is a solemn phrase for an important speech (10:34; Matthew 5:2). He does not change the subject or produce an outline. The man had a question about a text; Philip answers it, and keeps going until he arrives at Jesus, as the risen Christ did on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27). We tend to steer such conversations onto ground we know; Philip does the opposite.

He told him the good news about Jesus. Literally, he announced Jesus as good news. Jesus is not a topic within the message. He is the message, and he himself said Isaiah 53 was written of him (Luke 22:37).

Their meaning and their joy. The Lamb opened not his mouth before his shearers, and so Philip could open his. He kept silent under judgment so that good news could be spoken about him on every road on earth. Nor is he one subject among many in the Scriptures: Moses wrote of him, the prophets foretold him, the psalms sang of him. He is their meaning and their joy.

How can I be sure Isaiah 53 is really about Jesus? The eunuch asks the question before Philip says a word: the text raised it by itself, in a foreigner with no Christian instruction. Christ is not imported into Isaiah; he is identified in it. And the fit is exact: a Servant who suffers not for his own sins but for the sins of many, is silent before his accusers, is condemned unjustly, dies, is buried with the rich, and then sees his offspring and is exalted (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). Many Jewish readers today take the Servant to be Israel, but Isaiah’s Servant suffers “for the transgression of my people” (53:8), and is innocent, as no nation is. Nor did Christians write Jesus into the text: the great Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, copied more than a century before he was born, contains this chapter much as we read it. Jesus said it was about him, and the apostles preached it so (1 Peter 2:22–25).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man barred from the temple asks what prevents him from being baptised, and because the Servant was cut off in his place, the answer is nothing.

See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized? A stream or pool in the desert, there by providence. He asks; Philip does not suggest it, though what was said in the carriage evidently included baptism. And “prevents” (kōlyei) is the word he has carried his whole life. He knows what has always prevented him, confirmed at the end of a journey of over a thousand miles: his own body, the plain words of the law, and a temple that would not let him past the outer court. What he is really asking is whether the barrier is still there.

The prophecy of his own gathering. Three chapters on, the book in his hands promises eunuchs a place within God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–5). The Spirit sent Philip not just to the right road but to the right man, reading the right book at the right passage.

The curtain and the water. The temple’s barriers marked a real distance between sinners and a holy God. When Jesus died the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Luke 23:45), and we now enter the holy places “by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). The barriers were not swept aside as though they had never mattered. They taught that sinners cannot walk into God’s presence uncleansed, and Christ has done the cleansing, once for all (Hebrews 10:10). So the honest answer to the eunuch’s question is nothing, any longer, because the Servant was cut off in his place.

Does this show that baptism is for believers? Yes. The order here, as in verse 12, is hearing, believing, then baptism, and that is the order in every baptism in Acts where the order is described. How Christians differ over baptising infants is set out in the box “Where Christians differ: the mode and subjects of baptism” at the end of the note on vv. 38–39.

I was baptised as a baby. Should I be baptised now? On the believer’s baptism view, which this commentary holds, yes, and that is no criticism of your parents, who very likely acted in love and faith; talk with your pastor, with humility and a desire for peace.

In everyday life. If you have believed in Christ and not been baptised, ask the eunuch’s question: what prevents me? Speak to your pastor this week.

Nothing is lost if verse 37 is not original. The eunuch plainly did believe, and every word the verse contains is taught openly elsewhere in Acts (2:38; 8:12; 16:31–33). The words may be a later copyist’s; the practice they describe is apostolic.

Textual note: verse 37. Your Bible may not have it, though the KJV and NKJV print it. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says that if he believes with all his heart he may, and the eunuch confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. It is not in the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added later, perhaps from an early baptismal liturgy. The words are old; Irenaeus quotes them before the end of the second century. It reflects true early practice, since baptism followed faith, but it was likely not part of what Luke wrote.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powerful man stops his chariot to be baptised, Philip is taken away, and the new believer goes home alone yet rejoicing, because he has Christ.

He commanded the chariot to stop. In this whole passage the powerful man gives exactly one order: to halt his own carriage in the middle of a desert so that a stranger can baptise him. They went down into, and came up out of, the water: the language suggests immersion, the ordinary meaning of baptizō, to dip or plunge.

One of the Servant’s offspring. An hour earlier he had been reading about a Servant cut off, who would yet see his offspring (Isaiah 53:8, 10). Now he comes up out of the water as one of them. The burial and rising the water pictures are not his own achievement but Christ’s, shared with him (Romans 6:4). He went down into the water as a man whose line ended with him. He came up in Christ, in a family that will never end.

The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away. Carried away means snatched (harpazō), as of a man caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), a sudden removal like Elijah’s (1 Kings 18:12). Whether by miraculous transport or a sudden leading, Philip’s work there was done.

On his way rejoicing. Stand where the Ethiopian is standing: a Christian for perhaps ten minutes, wet, on a desert road, and the man who explained everything to him has gone without a goodbye. Ahead lie a thousand miles and more, and a court where he may be the only believer, with no church and no Bible in his own language. And he went on his way rejoicing. He did not need Philip; he had Christ. The joy is not bravery under adverse conditions. It is the ordinary result of the gospel.

Toward the end of the earth. Later tradition holds that the Ethiopian church traces itself to this man; Luke does not say so. What can be said is that a man went south that afternoon with the good news about Jesus, toward the end of the earth (1:8).

Not a case against the church. The verse is sometimes used to argue that a Christian does not need the church. Luke has spent seven chapters on a community that ate, prayed and grieved together; the eunuch’s isolation is a circumstance, not a recommendation. What the verse establishes is narrower and more comforting: a believer who has nothing but Christ has enough to be going on with, in a hospital, a prison, or a country where the nearest congregation is far away.

What if I am the only Christian where I am? Then you are in the eunuch’s company, and Christ is enough for you. Hold on to him through his word: read it daily, and memorise some of it. Pray, aloud if you can, as this man read aloud. Find even one other believer to pray with, in person or at a distance, and a church online to listen to while you pray for one nearby. Live your faith openly and kindly among the people around you; you may be the beginning of a church, as he may have been. And you are never really alone: you belong to a body that spans the earth, and the Lord has promised, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

Where Christians differ: the mode and subjects of baptism. Some sprinkle or pour; some baptise infants. The words down into and up out of could, taken alone, describe a man wading into a stream. This commentary’s view: the pattern here, a believer confessing faith and baptised by immersion, is the New Testament norm. Christians who sprinkle or baptise infants hold their views sincerely, and we hold ours with charity, but the credobaptist practice (baptising those who profess faith) best fits passages like this. Immersion shows most clearly what baptism means: dying to the old life, buried with Christ, and rising to walk in newness of life.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip goes on preaching town by town up the coast to Caesarea, and after his famous afternoon come twenty quiet years of ordinary faithfulness.

But Philip found himself at Azotus. Azotus is Ashdod, one of the old Philistine cities, some twenty miles up the coast from Gaza. Without pausing, he does what he has done all chapter: town after town, all the way to Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea.

In the flow. Philip settles in Caesarea, the city where Peter will open the door to the Gentiles (chapter 10). Before that, Luke turns back to Saul, the ravager of verse 3, and shows the risen Lord meeting him on another road.

Twenty years later. Philip reappears once, some twenty years later: “we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him” (21:8). Look at the word we. Luke stayed several days under Philip’s roof, and much of chapters 6 and 8 very likely came to him across a table, from the man it happened to. Philip is still called the evangelist two decades on, and he has four unmarried daughters who prophesied (21:9), fulfilling Joel’s promise that sons and daughters would prophesy (2:17). He settled in a port city, raised a family, and went on being the man who tells people about Jesus.

The king who comes to Ashdod. Zechariah said that God would take the abominations from Philistia’s teeth until it too became a remnant for our God, like a clan in Judah (Zechariah 9:6–7), and then announced the coming king, righteous and having salvation, humble and mounted on a donkey (9:9; Matthew 21:5). Philip, preaching up the coast, is the herald of that King, and Israel’s old enemies are hearing that he has come.

The afternoon and the twenty quiet years. Philistia and Cush were named long ago among the peoples of whom the Lord would one day say, this one was born in Zion (Psalm 87:4–6). In a single chapter a treasurer of Cush is born again on the road south and the towns of Philistia hear the gospel on the road north. The Lord saw Philip’s famous afternoon and his twenty quiet years alike, and he will gather the fruit of both before his throne.

What if my Christian life feels ordinary? It may be exactly what God intends. Most of Scripture’s faithful people spent most of their lives working, raising children, opening their homes and speaking of Christ to whoever was near. Philip’s twenty ordinary years were not the lesser part of his life. God does not grade us by the drama of our stories but by faithfulness (1 Corinthians 4:2). Keep your door open, raise your children in the Lord, speak of him in your town. Nothing done for Christ is ordinary to him.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The gospel crosses its first barriers. In Acts 8 the gospel crosses from Jews to Samaritans, and then to a man from Africa, as Jesus said it would (1:8). The Ethiopian, kept out of the temple’s inner courts, is reached on a desert road through the passage he happened to be reading. Here we watch God’s call, the call that brings a person to faith, at work: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures and draws the seeker. The God who gathers a people from every nation does it through ordinary means: a man, a chariot, a scroll.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop talking about Christ. A table-server taken from a city-wide revival to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and found him on the way home.

Now: In Acts 8 God works through disruption: a persecution that scatters, a command that redirects, a passage that raises exactly the right question. Planning is not wrong, but our plans should be held loosely enough that we will go over to the person God puts in front of us.

keyVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word.
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the whole chapter. The persecution meant to stamp out the church becomes the means of spreading it, and ordinary believers, not apostles, carry the word to Samaria and beyond. What they preached was a person: Philip “proclaimed to them the Christ” (v. 5) and told the Ethiopian “the good news about Jesus” (v. 35).

8.reflection:
Persecution drove the believers out of Jerusalem, and they preached the word wherever they went (vv. 1–4). Has God ever used an unwelcome disruption in your life to put you among people who needed to hear of Christ? Where might he have scattered you now?

Simon amazed people so that they said he was great; Philip’s signs left people listening to a message about Jesus (vv. 9–13). How can we tell whether a ministry, or our own service, is drawing attention to Christ or to ourselves?

Simon wanted to buy what God gives freely (vv. 18–24). In what quieter ways are we tempted to treat God’s blessing as something we can earn or pay for, and what does Peter’s answer say to that?

The Ethiopian, shut out of the temple, was reading about the Servant who was cut off, and asked, “What prevents me from being baptized?” (vv. 32–36). Who in your church or neighbourhood feels shut out, and how could you help them hear that in Christ nothing prevents them from coming?

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
Where we are. Stephen is dead, the church has been scattered, and the gospel has reached Samaria and an Ethiopian on the desert road (chapters 7–8). Saul of Tarsus, the man behind the persecution, now sets out to carry the hunt beyond Judea.

The message. No one is beyond the reach of the risen Christ, not even his fiercest enemy. Jesus is alive, he counts what is done to his people as done to him, and he saves by sovereign grace: he stops Saul on the road, takes him for his own and makes him the chosen instrument to carry his name to the nations. And the same Lord goes on healing and raising the dead through his servants, so that many turn to him.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). The apostle who fills the second half of Acts had been the church’s persecutor, so Luke shows that his conversion and commission came from Christ himself and were accepted by the church, and that the Gentile mission he would lead was the Lord’s plan, not his own.

How the chapter makes its case. Saul sets out for Damascus with warrants (vv. 1–2), and the risen Jesus meets him in blinding light and names himself as the one Saul is persecuting (vv. 3–9). The Lord sends a frightened disciple, Ananias, who calls him brother; Saul sees again, is filled with the Spirit and is baptised (vv. 10–19). At once the persecutor preaches Jesus, and soon he is hunted himself (vv. 19–25). Barnabas brings him to the apostles, the brothers send him to Tarsus, and the church has peace (vv. 26–31). Then through Peter, Jesus Christ heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa, and many believe (vv. 32–43).

Where it leads. The whole chapter turns on the words spoken from heaven: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (v. 5). The crucified man Saul thought accursed is alive and glorified, so joined to his people that their wounds are his, and so gracious that he answers his persecutor’s hatred with his own name and a commission. In Lydda and Joppa the same Lord is at work: “Jesus Christ heals you” (v. 34), and a dead disciple sits up, a sign of the resurrection he will give all his people.

For us. If Christ could stop Saul, he can stop anyone, so pray for the hardest person you know, and be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the time comes. Grace makes us honest about our past and useful in spite of it. And whatever is done to you for his sake, he counts as done to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Jesus turns the church’s fiercest enemy into his chosen messenger, showing that no one is beyond his grace. Saul sets out with warrants for Damascus, but Christ meets him on the road in blinding light and names himself as the one Saul is persecuting (vv. 1–9). The Lord sends Ananias, who calls the persecutor brother; Saul sees again, receives the Spirit and is baptised (vv. 10–19). At once he preaches that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ, and soon he is hunted himself, escaping Damascus in a basket (vv. 19–25). Barnabas brings him to the apostles, the brothers send him away to Tarsus, and the church has peace and grows (vv. 26–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion shows grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians, with an arrest warrant in his bag. Paul never describes his conversion as a search that ended, but as being laid hold of. Reformed theology reads it as the pattern rather than the exception: in every conversion Christ takes the first step (see the box “Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen?” at the end of the note on vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was sent to the man carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He told God plainly what he thought of it, and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul sets out, organised, lawful and utterly sincere, to bring the followers of Jesus back from Damascus in chains. This is the man Christ is about to stop: the most important conversion in church history, which Luke tells three times (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18), begins at the height of his hatred.

Still breathing threats and murder. No passing fit of temper but the settled condition of his life. The word empneōn, breathing in, describes the air he lives in: his very breath is hostility. And murder means murder: when believers were put to death, Paul says years later, he cast his vote against them (26:10). Stephen was not the only one.

Letters to the synagogues. He does not gather a mob; he goes through the proper office. Damascus lay about a hundred and thirty-five miles north-east of Jerusalem, a week on foot, outside Judea altogether, under a different administration. Letters from the high priest carried great weight in the synagogues of the Diaspora (the Jewish communities scattered outside the land), and Rome generally let Jewish authorities deal with their own people in religious matters, though how far such letters could be enforced in a foreign city is uncertain. Saul carries not a licence to riot but paperwork. He was organised, funded and legal, and he believed with his whole heart that he was doing God’s work (22:3; Galatians 1:13–14).

Why Damascus? It had a large and ancient Jewish community, and the believers scattered by the persecution of chapter 8 had gone somewhere. Saul is not opening a new front. He is pursuing refugees he had himself created, to bring them back in chains.

Belonging to the Way. One of the earliest names the Christians had for themselves, which Luke uses half a dozen times (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Not a school, a party or a sect, but a road, hē hodos. Whether the name came from the Lord’s own words, I am the way (John 14:6), or from the prophet’s cry to prepare the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3), or both, it describes a manner of life rather than a set of opinions. Christianity is not first a society you join but a road you walk, behind someone who has gone ahead, and that is precisely the wrong kind of thing to try to stamp out. You can shut a building. A road runs.

Men or women. Luke has said it of Saul before (8:3), and he will not let the reader make it abstract. Whatever else was in those letters, they authorised the arrest of somebody’s mother.

Synagogues and prisons, as he said. None of this took the Lord by surprise. Before his death Jesus warned his disciples: “they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name’s sake” (Luke 21:12). Saul’s letters are addressed to synagogues and his purpose is prisons: the persecutor is fulfilling, item by item, the word of the man he thinks a false prophet. And the last clause holds a further irony. The man carrying these warrants will himself be brought before governors and a king, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, for that same name.

In everyday life. A way is something you are either walking or not. Ask what in this week’s diary is on the road behind Christ and what is simply parked beside it: the conversation you have put off, the generosity you mean to start.

How could a man so devout be so wrong? Because sincerity is not the same as truth, and zeal is only as good as what it is aimed at. Paul later said of his own people what had been true of himself: they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2). Saul knew his Bible, prayed daily and lived strictly. What he did not know was who Jesus was, and that one error turned all his devotion into a weapon against God. Being earnest, disciplined and certain does not make us right; only the truth about Christ does. The safeguard is not less zeal but zeal held open to Scripture, and a readiness to be corrected by it.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus lay about 135 miles north-east of Jerusalem and had a large Jewish community. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the gates of Damascus the risen Jesus confronts his persecutor in the glory of heaven and asks why Saul is persecuting him. The question reveals that Christ is alive, and so united to his people that every blow against them lands on him.

He approached Damascus. The city was in sight, the arrests perhaps a few hours away. God sometimes lets men reach the very edge of what they meant to do. He had set this man apart before he was born and called him by his grace (Galatians 1:15), and he waited until the persecutor was at the height of his fury and nearly at the gate. That is the patience of the Son of God with his enemies: not indifference, but a purpose that had already chosen the day.

A light from heaven. It flashed and enveloped him: the verb is built on the word for lightning. Paul later adds that it was midday, and the light was brighter than the sun (22:6; 26:13). A Syrian noon, and something outshone it: the glory of the risen Christ, the glory Isaiah saw in the temple, which John says was Christ’s (John 12:41).

Falling to the ground. The man who had been dragging others to the floor of their own houses is on the floor of the road. When the glory of God comes near, men do not stand and assess it; they go down, as Ezekiel did by the river Chebar and John on Patmos.

Saul, Saul. Scripture repeats a name sparingly, usually at a hinge: Abraham with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11), Jacob on the way down to Egypt (Genesis 46:2), Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:4), Samuel in the dark (1 Samuel 3:10), Martha in her busy kitchen (Luke 10:41), Simon on the last night (Luke 22:31). It is the address of someone who knows the person and is about to change his life. And it came in the Hebrew language (26:14): the glorified Christ speaks to Saul in his mother tongue and uses his Hebrew name, not the Greek one the world would come to know.

Why are you persecuting me? Saul had never met Jesus of Nazareth; he had dragged Christians out of houses. Yet the voice does not say my people, or my church. It says me. Everything Paul later wrote about the church as the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 1:22–23) lies in that pronoun, and he heard it before he had a theology to put it in. The Lord had taught it on the Mount of Olives: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40).

He called the wound his own. The Lord of glory looked down on a road in Syria, saw his people being hunted, and called the wound his own; and he stopped the man doing the striking, not with a thunderbolt that ended him but with a question that saved him. It cuts two ways. The way a Christian treats another Christian is not a matter of church politics: Christ files it under his own name. And whatever has been done to a believer, the exclusion, the cruelty, the years of it, the thing nobody else noticed, has not gone unrecorded, because it was not finally done to him alone.

In everyday life. Think of the Christian you find hardest to bear. The way you speak about that person this week, and to him, Christ files under his own name.

Does this mean Jesus is still suffering in heaven? No. He is risen and glorified, beyond the reach of any persecutor; death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9). The word me teaches union, not fresh suffering. Christ is so joined to his people, the Head to the body, that what is done to them is counted as done to him, and he feels it with them in sympathy, a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). So when you are wronged for his sake, you are not suffering in a corner of the universe he has forgotten. He will answer for it.

Three tellings of one event. Sceptics point to differences between Luke’s three accounts. Here the men stood speechless (v. 7); before Agrippa, Paul says we had all fallen to the ground (26:14): most likely everyone went down, and the escort got up while Saul stayed where he was. More striking, here the commission comes later through Ananias; before Agrippa it is spoken by Christ on the road. But Paul is then in the dock before a king and a Roman governor, to whom a Jewish disciple’s testimony from a back street in Damascus is worth nothing, so he joins what Ananias told him to the meeting on the road, since both came from Christ. Before a Jerusalem crowd, by contrast, Ananias is the point, “a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews” (22:12), exactly the credential that mattered there. The three are one event told to three audiences, which is how truthful people ordinarily retell things.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice names himself: the crucified Jesus is alive, he is Lord, and he has been the target of all Saul’s zeal. Yet he answers his enemy not with revenge but with a summons into his service.

Who are you, Lord? He says Lord before he knows who is speaking. Kyrios could mean no more than sir, but Saul knows he is facing a divine being. By the end of the answer the word will mean everything it can mean.

I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Six words in Greek, which cost Saul everything he had, and each half is a demolition. I am Jesus: so the body is not in the tomb, the disciples were not lying, and the man Saul thought a deceiver justly hanged on a tree and cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23) is alive, glorified and speaking from heaven. Gamaliel, his own teacher, had warned the council that they might be found opposing God (5:39); Saul had been doing exactly that to the Messiah of Israel. Whom you are persecuting: present tense, as of this morning. He is not being told about a past mistake but interrupted in the middle of it, with the warrants still in his luggage.

Rise and enter the city. Not a word of rebuke, nothing about Stephen. He is told to get up and wait for instructions, like a man just taken into someone’s service, which is exactly what has happened. His first act of obedience is to be led somewhere he did not choose.

He said his own name. The whole Christian faith turns on this: the Crucified is not dead but speaking, and he speaks first. Saul did not find Christ; Christ found Saul, and answered his hatred not with revenge but with his own name and something to do.

In everyday life. Think of the person you consider least likely ever to become a Christian, and bring that name to God, not vaguely, and not with your expectations already lowered. If Christ could stop Saul, he can stop anyone.

Must every Christian have a dramatic conversion like this? No. Saul’s experience was unusual in form, because he was being called as an apostle. But its substance is the same for every believer: Christ seizes a sinner by grace. Many come gradually, like Timothy, who knew the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15), and cannot name a day. What matters is not the drama but whether one now trusts Christ.

Does God force people to believe against their will? No. He does not drag an unwilling man into the kingdom kicking and screaming; he changes the will itself, so that the man who would not come now wants to come. Saul was not overpowered into a faith he resented; he got up from that road asking what his new Lord wanted of him. As the Westminster Confession puts it, God draws his people to Jesus Christ, yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace (Westminster 10.1; so too the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1). Grace does not cancel our freedom but rescues it from bondage to sin, so those called this way speak of it afterwards as release, not captivity.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Many earnest Christians in the Arminian tradition (which holds that God’s grace enables everyone who hears, but each person’s free choice decides whether he believes) see Saul’s conversion as untypical, and they rightly insist that people must truly repent and believe. This commentary’s view: the details were unique, but in every believer Christ takes the initiative, overcomes the sinner’s resistance and makes him willing (Galatians 1:15–16); every conversion is a Damascus road, whether quiet or dramatic.

Textual note. The King James adds a sentence here: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks, with Saul’s trembling question about what the Lord would have him do. Jesus really did say the words about the goads, as Paul recalls before Agrippa (26:14), but they are not in the Greek manuscripts at this point; copyists of the Latin Bible filled them in from chapter 26. Nothing has been lost from Scripture. And the image is worth keeping: an ox that kicked at the farmer’s spiked goad only drove the point deeper. Stephen’s face and Stephen’s prayer may have been such goads, at work on Saul’s conscience long before the light.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s companions share the event but not the revelation, and the man who set out to bind others is led into Damascus blind and helpless.

Stood speechless. They came out of Jerusalem as an armed escort; they go into the city with nothing to say, leading a blind man by the hand.

Hearing the voice but seeing no one. They saw the light but not the person who spoke, and heard a sound but could not make out the words (see the box below). The event was real and public. The revelation was for Saul.

Eyes opened and seeing nothing. A man who had never doubted what he was looking at opens his eyes and sees nothing, and Paul would spend his life writing about veils, blindness and light shining into hearts (2 Corinthians 3:14–16; 4:4–6).

Led by the hand. He meant to lead prisoners out of Damascus; he is led into it, helpless, in the position of the people he came to arrest.

That those who see may become blind. Jesus had said it to Pharisees: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). Saul, a Pharisee and a son of Pharisees (23:6), as sure of his sight as any man in Jerusalem, feels that word come true in his own body. But the same Lord came to make the blind see, so the darkness is the first stage of the miracle.

He shone on him. Christ did not argue Saul out of his blindness; he shone on him. That is how the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). It is hard to believe Paul wrote that without remembering this road.

Being near is not the same as hearing. The men beside him went away from the identical event with a story about strange weather; Saul went away with a Lord. People can sit under the same sermon for years, a pew apart, and one hears a noise and the other hears the voice of Christ.

In everyday life. Pride is the feeling of seeing perfectly well. If there is a subject on which you are completely certain and have stopped listening to anyone, ask God whether that is where you are blind, and ask without dread: the Lord who opened Saul’s eyes gives sight as a gift.

Was the blindness a punishment? More a mercy and a sign than a penalty; nothing in this chapter is made to fit his crimes. It was the natural effect of the glory he had seen, and gave him three days in which the whole world he had lived in could be taken down. It was also a living picture: the spiritually blind man was made to feel his blindness, so that he would know his sight was a gift. Contrast the sorcerer Elymas, struck blind for a time as a judgment for opposing the gospel (13:11). Saul was blinded on the way into the gospel, and his sight was given back with the Spirit.

Uncertain wording. Luke says the men were “hearing the voice” (v. 7); Paul later says they “did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me” (22:9), which the King James renders as not hearing it, and sceptics call this a contradiction. The Greek verb can mean either to hear a sound or to hear with understanding, and the word for voice can also mean simply a sound. The likely meaning is that the men heard a noise but could not make out the words, as when the Father spoke from heaven and the crowd said it had thundered (John 12:29). Exactly what they heard cannot be known, but the accounts need not clash.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three days Saul sits in darkness, neither eating nor drinking: the old Saul is dying, and in the dark he prays.

Three days without sight. No sight, no food, and, the detail people skim, no water. In that climate three days without drinking is the edge of what a body will take. This is not a fast but a man who has stopped functioning, in shock, in repentance and, as the Lord will tell Ananias, in prayer.

The room in the dark. A strange city, a borrowed house, warrants nobody is going to use. Every certainty he had is gone, and the one thing he now knows is that the people he set out to imprison were right about everything, and that he has spent his best years and considerable gifts hunting the Messiah of Israel. And he prayed, not in the well-formed manner of a lifelong Pharisee, one imagines, but in the dark, with no idea what to say. The God who brought Jonah up from the deep and raised his own Son on the third day was at work in that silent room, taking a man apart in order to make him new.

A death and a rising. Luke does not press the number, and we should not build on it. But the shape is unmistakable: he goes into darkness, everything he was dies there, and then a man comes and he is raised up and washed. It is the shape of the gospel, the death and resurrection of the Lord into which every believer is baptised. Paul would write of being buried and raised with Christ (Romans 6:4), of the old self crucified, and of a new creation in which the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17); he lived it on the floor of somebody’s guest room before he wrote a word of it. Christ died and rose as the representative of his people, so God counts the believer as having died to his old life in Christ’s death and as living a new one by his life (Romans 6:4–11): I have been crucified with Christ, yet Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

For anyone in a collapse of certainty. Here is something for the person whose faith has come apart in his hands, or who has seen something about himself he cannot unsee. Saul’s three days were not the end of him, though they cannot have felt like anything else. Scripture’s most spectacular conversion has a dark room in the middle of it.

In everyday life. If you are in a dark room of your own just now, do what Saul did: pray, even if the prayer has no shape. And if you know someone in that room, do not rush him out of it with explanations. Be the person who brings food on the third day.

Does God always bring people through darkness before conversion? No. Some are broken before they are healed; others are drawn quietly: of Lydia Luke says simply that the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (16:14), and the Ethiopian went on his way rejoicing the day he met Philip (8:39). Nobody should think his conversion suspect because it lacked a dark room. What every conversion shares is that the old self is put to death and a new one raised by Christ. In some lives that takes three days on a floor; in others it happens over a cup of coffee and an open Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord sends an ordinary disciple to an exact address, to the man who came to arrest him, and gives a single credential: he is praying.

A disciple named Ananias. No office, no title: a Christian who lives in the city, handed one of the most consequential errands of the first century. (He is not the Ananias of chapter 5; the name was common.) Paul adds that Ananias was a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews there (22:12): a man with a good name to lose by this errand.

Here I am, Lord. The answer of Abraham, of Samuel and of Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8). Ananias has not been told what the thing is, and he will argue once he hears. It is the reply of a man available before he knows the assignment, which is rarer than being willing once the details are known.

The street called Straight. The ordinariness is the point. It was a real road, the long thoroughfare through Roman Damascus, and it runs through the old city to this day. A street, a householder, a name and a home town, Tarsus, a proud city of learning (21:39): God’s guidance here has an address on it.

For behold, he is praying. The single credential given for the most dangerous man in the province is that he is praying, which, said by anybody else, would prove nothing. Said by the Lord, it settles the matter. A man who has begun to pray to Christ is a man Christ has already taken hold of.

In everyday life. God uses ordinary believers for extraordinary tasks, and almost always the task is a person at an address: the neighbour who has just lost her husband, the colleague who asked about church and was never followed up, the young man at the back who has stopped coming. The Shepherd who sends you already knows the door.

Does God still guide his people by visions like this? God is free to do as he pleases, and Christians who believe he still sometimes speaks in dreams and visions are our brothers. But even in Acts such visions were rare, coming at turning points in the founding of the church, and the more likely reading is that this kind of direct revelation belonged to the apostolic age. We are guided by Scripture, which is sufficient for everything we need for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and by prayer, wise counsel and the ordinary providences that open and close doors. Any impression that pulls against the plain teaching of Scripture is to be refused, however vivid. And we need no vision to obey: Ananias’s great act was going to a house and loving a man, guidance anyone can follow today.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has been at work at both ends: before Ananias sets out, Saul has already seen him coming.

He has seen in a vision. While Ananias is being given a street name, Saul has already been shown a man called Ananias coming through a door. Neither arranged it, and the blind man will be expecting him by name, as God will prepare both Peter and Cornelius in the next chapter. The one who sits at the Father’s right hand is Lord of every appointment, and he loves to bring his enemies and his friends into the same room and make them brothers.

The door opened from the inside. The Lord reasons with a frightened man: the door has already been opened from the inside. The same is often true of the conversation a Christian quietly dreads, the apology owed, the subject that has to be raised. That is no guarantee that obedience will be safer than it looked; Ananias’s errand was genuinely dangerous, and he was right to say so. But the God who sends people is already at work on the far side, and the messenger is very rarely the first one there.

Why did the Lord not simply heal Saul himself? He could have, on the spot. But Christ chose to give Saul his sight, his welcome and his baptism through a member of the church he had been persecuting. Saul needed to receive mercy from the hands of the people he had hunted, and to be taken into their family, not merely converted on his own. That is how the Lord ordinarily works still. He alone saves, but he brings people to faith through the word spoken by other believers (Romans 10:14), and gathers them into a church. Nobody is meant to be a Christian by himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
