Ananias tells the Lord honestly why the errand looks like madness: Saul has come with authority to arrest everyone who calls on Jesus’ name, Ananias included.

I have heard from many. Ananias argues with God, and Luke reports it without a syllable of disapproval. Some of the refugees who had fled to Damascus were sitting in his own meetings, and Saul’s reputation had arrived well before Saul.

Your saints. The first time in Acts that Christians are called hagioi, holy ones set apart for God: not a special class but the ordinary name for all of them (Romans 1:7). Your saints: they belong to Jesus, which is why harming them is harming him (v. 4). And he calls them that while they are still frightened, still arguing and far from finished. The man Ananias is sent to will later use the word of ordinary congregations of fishermen and slaves, and of himself, the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8).

All who call on your name. All: Ananias is describing a warrant with his own name inside it, and he is being asked to identify himself, as a Christian, to the officer sent to arrest him. Calling on his name was the mark of a Christian from the beginning (1 Corinthians 1:2). The phrase comes from Joel, everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved (Joel 2:32), and Peter and Paul both apply it to Jesus (2:21; Romans 10:9–13). The name on which Israel called for salvation is now the name of Jesus.

Arguing with God. Moses produced five objections at the bush, and God dealt with each; Jeremiah said he was too young. What distinguishes Ananias from Jonah, who objected and ran, is not that he kept his doubts to himself but that he raised them in God’s presence and then did what he was told. To swallow an objection and call the silence faith is usually only fear, dressed up to look better.

In everyday life. If you belong to Christ, you are a saint, not because you feel holy but because he has set you apart for himself. Live like one, in the ordinary places where nobody calls you anything.

Is it right to pray to Jesus himself? Yes. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18), as Jesus taught us. But the first Christians also called directly on Jesus, as Stephen did while the stones were falling: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (7:59), and Ananias is talking to Jesus in this very verse. It is one of the clearest signs that the church worshipped Jesus as God, for a devout Jew would never pray to anyone less. So you may speak to the Lord Jesus freely, as to the Father: the three persons are one God, and every prayer offered in Christ’s name reaches him.

Where Christians differ: who are the saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches use “saints” mainly for specially holy people, canonised after death, whose prayers are sought. This commentary’s view: in the New Testament every believer is a saint, set apart by God in Christ (Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Holiness of life should follow, but the title is given by grace, not earned. We pray to God alone, through Christ alone.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people: all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord answers the objection with his own choice: Saul is his chosen instrument to carry the name of Jesus to the nations, and he will suffer for it.

Chosen. The answer is not reassurance but information. The word, eklogē, is the word of election: God’s choosing of particular people to belong to him and serve him, out of his free love and not for anything he saw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). Saul was chosen before he was born, and long before he deserved anything but judgment: by the grace of God I am what I am, he would write (1 Corinthians 15:10).

A chosen vessel. Instrument is the ordinary word for a container (skeuos): a jar, a pot, a word from an inventory. Not a hero but a receptacle picked out, whose value lies in what it is for and who chose it. Paul never forgot it: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Gentiles and kings. The destinations are the contents page of the rest of the book: the Gentiles, named first, an extraordinary thing to say in those early years (13:46–48); kings, Agrippa and, in prospect, Caesar (27:24); and the synagogue in every city. And he is to carry the name, as one carries something precious through a crowd: the name, not his own.

A share in the Servant’s work. Isaiah’s Servant was to be a light for the nations, that God’s salvation might reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6); Simeon called the infant Jesus exactly that (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas quoted the verse to explain their turning to the Gentiles (13:47). Saul is not sent on an errand of his own but drawn into the Servant’s mission, a vessel through which the light of the nations will shine.

How much he must suffer. This passage cannot be preached as a success story. The calling and the cost arrive in the same breath, joined by “For”, and spoken to a third party before the man himself has been told anything. Must, dei, is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 9:22). And there is an exchange in it: Saul had spent months making people suffer on account of that name, and the first thing said about his future is how much he will suffer for it. Not as punishment, for he was forgiven, but as the cost of carrying the name of a crucified Lord. Christ chose the man who had shed his people’s blood to herald his name, and to walk the road he himself had walked first, all the way to the cross.

What that meant in practice. Paul eventually listed it (2 Corinthians 11:23–28): five times thirty-nine lashes, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea, and the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. That is the career being announced here.

What it does not mean. Not every calling carries this measure of suffering, and a Christian whose life has been comparatively gentle has not been given a second-rate commission; Scripture nowhere makes hardship the proof of authenticity. But the verse permanently corrects any preaching that offers Christ as the way to a better, smoother, more successful version of the life one already has.

In everyday life. If following Christ is costing you something this week, a friendship, a promotion, a reputation, do not conclude that you have taken a wrong turning. The cost was in the calling from the start, and your Lord said so.

Was Saul chosen only for service, or for salvation too? Both, and they cannot be pulled apart. Here the emphasis falls on service, an instrument for a task. But Paul traced his salvation to the same choosing grace, which set him apart before he was born (Galatians 1:15) and showed him mercy as an example to others (1 Timothy 1:16). So with every believer: chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), and created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). You were not chosen because you were useful. You were chosen in love, and then made useful.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias goes, calls the persecutor brother, and through him Christ gives Saul his sight, his Spirit and his baptism. The man who came to bind the church is welcomed into its family.

Ananias departed. A plain sentence for the bravest act in the chapter: he had said what he thought, been answered, and gone.

Brother Saul. Ananias lays his hands on him, and his first word is brother. The blind man in the room arrived with a warrant covering Ananias and everyone like him, and Ananias’s congregation is swollen with refugees who ran from him, some of whom may have lost somebody. He has every reason to open with a question, a condition or a wary silence. He opens with a family word, before Saul has said anything at all.

On the road by which you came. Ananias names the road and the one who met him there, so Saul knows he is not being humoured.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. No apostle does this, but a disciple in a provincial city about whom nothing else is known, who very probably baptises him too (22:12). Paul would insist that he had not received his gospel from any man (Galatians 1:11–12), and that is consistent: what Ananias gave him was not a gospel but his eyes, a welcome and water.

Something like scales. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14) marks it as a comparison: something like. We still say the scales fell from my eyes. At Nazareth Jesus had read out his own programme, including recovering of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18); here the risen Lord keeps that word for the man who had fought him hardest.

Then he rose and was baptized. No interval, no probation: baptism follows faith, at once.

Forgiven before a single apology. In the two words Brother Saul the whole gospel stands in a doorway. The Lord Jesus had forgiven his persecutor before a single apology was offered, and sent one of the persecuted to say so. Ananias could say brother because Christ had said it first: he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The blood that cleanses the sinner makes him a son, and every son a brother. That is what the risen Christ does with his enemies: he gives them eyes, his Spirit and a family.

In everyday life. Is there someone you find it hard to call brother or sister: a person who hurt you, a new convert with an ugly past? Grace calls you to say the family word first. That does not mean pretending nothing happened or setting aside wise safeguards. It means meeting a person Christ has received as Christ received you.

How could God forgive a man like this? Many quietly wonder whether some sins are too great. Paul answered himself: though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent, I received mercy, and Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:13–15); and he was shown mercy as an example, so that no one would ever think himself beyond it (1:16). The blood of Christ is enough for the worst thing you have done. The only sin that is never forgiven is the one never brought to him.

Was Saul converted on the road, or at his baptism? He was Christ’s from the road: he called Jesus Lord, he prayed, and Ananias greets him as brother (v. 17). Baptism was the outward sign and public confession. When Ananias later says be baptized and wash away your sins (22:16), he joins the sign to what it signifies, as Scripture often does; the washing is by faith in Christ, calling on his name.

Was this a second blessing after conversion? No. The filling came as part of Saul’s conversion, within days of the road, with his sight and his baptism, not as a later stage every Christian must seek. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so every believer has the Spirit from the first day; what Christians rightly go on seeking is to be filled with the Spirit more and more (Ephesians 5:18). Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach a later baptism in the Spirit, and their hunger for more of God is right; we differ from them, as brothers, on whether Scripture makes it a second stage.

Should we baptise people as quickly today? In Acts those who professed faith were baptised promptly, usually the same day (2:41; 8:38; 16:33): baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, not as a reward at the end of a long course. We hold, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, because in the New Testament it is those who hear, repent and believe who are baptised (2:38, 41; 8:12); so a church rightly asks for a credible profession first and takes time to hear it. Our paedobaptist brothers also baptise the children of believers, and we honour them while we differ. If you were baptised as a baby, talk it over with your pastor without fear, and without contempt for the church that baptised you. But no one should be kept waiting years to prove himself. If you trust Christ and have not been baptised, speak to your pastor this week.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fed and strengthened among the disciples he came to arrest, Saul at once preaches in the synagogues the very thing he came to stamp out: Jesus is the Son of God.

Taking food. The Lord who restored his eyes also cared that he had not eaten for three days. Before the theology there is a meal, and the people he came to arrest became his family: he sat at their tables and slept under their roofs, perhaps among the very refugees he had hunted.

In the synagogues. The very synagogues his letters authorised him to search.

He is the Son of God. Not that this man was a prophet or a teacher, or even the Messiah; that comes two verses later. Paul’s first recorded sermon, preached within days of his baptism by a man who had spent his life defending the oneness of God, is that Jesus of Nazareth is God’s Son. It is the only time in Acts the title is used in preaching like this (but compare 13:33), and it is exactly the claim for which the council had condemned Jesus (Luke 22:70–71). He did not work his way toward it gradually; he had met the person, and drawn the only possible inference on the road (compare Galatians 1:16; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

What “Son of God” means. The title gathers two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it claims full deity. To call Jesus God’s own Son in the unique sense is to say he shares the very nature of God, and so his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with “making himself equal with God” because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). “Son” speaks not of a beginning or a lesser rank but of sameness of nature: as an earthly son shares his father’s humanity, the divine Son shares the Father’s deity, eternally, “begotten, not made.” Second, it is a royal title: the promised king of David’s line was called God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), so the Son of God is also the Christ, the anointed King, where Saul’s preaching goes next (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers “sons of God” (Job 1:6; John 1:12), but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the only Son (monogenēs, John 3:16, which older Bibles render only begotten), Son by nature and eternal right, not made or adopted; we become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the crucified and risen Jesus is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust and worship. It is the confession that saves, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31; compare 1 John 4:15).

In everyday life. If someone asked you today who Jesus is, what would your first sentence be? Saul’s was not about himself or what Jesus could do for his listeners, but about the person. Practise saying it plainly, in your own words.

Should a new believer start speaking about Christ straight away? Yes, in the sense Saul did: telling people who Jesus is and what he has done. No theology degree is needed for that; the man born blind in John 9 had known Jesus for less than a day when he said, I was blind, now I see. What a new believer should not do is rush into teaching or leading others (see “Able at once, but not sent at once” at vv. 21–22). Speak of Christ freely and early. Take on responsibility slowly.

Textual note. The King James reads that he preached Christ; the earliest manuscripts have Jesus. The King James also puts the title Son of God on the Ethiopian’s lips at 8:37, a verse missing from the earliest manuscripts and so given only in a footnote in most modern Bibles.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The persecutor is now the preacher, growing in strength and proving from the Scriptures that the crucified Jesus is the Christ. His hearers can hardly believe it is the same man; it is, and grace has made him able to say so.

Is not this the man who made havoc? The synagogue’s amazement is understandable. The letters had been announced and arrangements presumably made, and here he is in the speaker’s seat, saying the opposite of what he was sent to say. Their word, porthēsas, made havoc, is the language of sacking a city, and Paul uses it of himself, twice, writing to the Galatians (Galatians 1:13, 23). He never softened the vocabulary. A man trying to justify himself has to manage his record. A man justified by God, declared righteous for Christ’s sake and not for his own deeds, can tell the truth about his past, because his standing no longer rests on it (Philippians 3:9).

Increased in strength. The verb is the one behind I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13). This was not natural confidence coming back; strength was being given to him.

Proving that Jesus was the Christ. Proving (symbibazōn) means bringing things together, knitting or joining them: laying two things side by side until the fit is obvious. That is what Paul does in every letter and sermon recorded of him: the promise beside the fulfilment, until the listener can see they belong together. And the hardest piece he now fitted was the one that had kept him from Christ: a Messiah hanged on a tree, under the curse of the law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He had thought the cross disproved Jesus. He came to preach that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Every text he had memorised as a boy lit up with the face of Jesus, and his first-class training now pointed to Jesus instead of away from him. God does not throw away the gifts and training of the people he converts. He turns them round.

Able at once, but not sent at once. Saul is formidable immediately, yet within a few years he is sent quietly home to Tarsus for a long, largely unrecorded season. The New Testament warns against putting a recent convert into leadership, lest he become puffed up with conceit (1 Timothy 3:6), and even this gifted convert waited years.

A world that never forgets. Ours is a culture with a long memory and very little absolution: an old post is found, and a person is defined for good by the worst thing anyone can find. The historian Wilfred McClay has argued that guilt has not faded from modern life at all; what has faded is any way of being rid of it. So we handle it in the ways that are left: we deny it, we load it on to others, or we claim the one innocence still on offer, the innocence of the victim. Saul, with more to answer for than anyone in that synagogue, told his record in the harshest word available, because it had been dealt with. The gospel does not tell you that your past was not so bad. It tells you it was worse than you feared, and paid for in full. Only forgiven people can afford to be that honest, and only a church that knows it has been forgiven can open its doors to a man like Saul.

In everyday life. God can use your training, your mind and your past for his glory, including the parts of your past you are ashamed of. Somewhere in what you know and what you have lived is something that could serve Christ’s people, and he does not waste it.

How can I show someone that Jesus is the Christ? Do what Saul did, on a smaller scale: lay the Scriptures and the facts side by side. Read Isaiah 53 with a friend and ask whom it describes; read Psalm 22 beside the crucifixion. Show how the promises to Abraham and David land on Jesus, and how the empty tomb holds it all together (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You need not win every argument, and cleverness converts no one, for only the Spirit opens blind eyes. But God uses honest explanation of his word, and it is far better to open the Bible with someone than to argue round it.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After about three years the hunter becomes the hunted: Saul’s opponents plot his death and watch the gates day and night, but God lets him learn of it.

When many days had passed. Set beside Paul’s own account, those days include a departure into Arabia and a return to Damascus, about three years in all (Galatians 1:17–18). Luke, telling the story of the church rather than of Paul, passes over them in a phrase.

The Jews plotted to kill him. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas, the Nabataean king, was guarding the city in order to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Why a Nabataean official should want him is not said; the likeliest explanation is that Saul’s preaching in Arabia, Aretas’s own kingdom (Galatians 1:17), had already made him enemies there. Religious objection supplied the charge and the state supplied the soldiers, as with Jesus before Pilate and later at Thessalonica (17:5–9).

Watching the gates. Three years earlier Saul had the authority, the letters and the men; now he cannot use the gates, and depends on a handful of disciples to get him out alive. For the next thirty years Paul is on the receiving end of precisely what he used to administer.

In everyday life. If you are opposed for your faith this week, do not take it as proof that you have failed. Ask instead whether you have given offence by Christ or only by your manner. If it is by Christ, rejoice quietly. You are in good company.

Why did God let his new servant be hunted so soon? Because the Lord had said it would happen (v. 16), and because the servant is not above his master (John 15:20). Persecution was a sign not that his conversion had gone wrong but that it was real. And the plot became known to Saul: God did not prevent the danger, but kept his man in the middle of it. That is how he usually protects his people: not always from trouble, but always through it, and never one day beyond his appointed time.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The future apostle to kings escapes in a basket over the wall, and he will later count that night of weakness as his boast.

Lowering him in a basket. Perhaps the best-known escape in the New Testament, and entirely undignified. The man who will stand before kings is folded into a large woven hamper and let down over a wall in the dark by people hoping the rope holds, like the spies Rahab let down at Jericho (Joshua 2:15).

His disciples. He has been a Christian for perhaps three years, and already there are people in Damascus who are his. They held the rope.

The boast of a basket. He never forgot it. Writing to Corinth against men boasting of their credentials, he says he will boast of the things that show his weakness, lists labours, imprisonments, beatings and shipwrecks, and ends the catalogue on the basket (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). Of everything in a life that included being caught up into the third heaven, he chose as his boast the night he was lowered out of a window like a sack of figs.

Strength in weakness. That is not false modesty. He had understood something his rivals had not: my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Those words were the risen Christ’s, and they describe Christ before they describe Paul: he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). The basket was where the servant began to learn that his Master’s glory comes through weakness.

Christ held the man. The Lord who would send Paul before Caesar first sent him over a wall in a basket; both journeys were in his hand. The disciples held the rope; Christ held the man.

Is it cowardly to run? Saying this plainly releases many people from an unnecessary burden. Saul ran away, over the wall at night, with no hint of reproach in the text; the Lord himself had told his disciples that when persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Courage in Scripture is not the refusal to leave. Paul stood his ground on plenty of occasions and left quietly on others. As a rough guide, it is right to flee when staying would achieve nothing but your death or imprisonment and the work can go on elsewhere, as here, and as when Jesus himself withdrew from those who sought to kill him before his hour had come (John 8:59; 10:39). It is right to stay when leaving would mean denying Christ, or abandoning people in your care who cannot leave with you; a shepherd who runs and leaves the sheep is a hired hand (John 10:12–13). Between those two, pray, take counsel from your church, and do not despise yourself for choosing life. The Lord wants living witnesses as well as faithful martyrs.

Textual note. Most modern Bibles follow the earliest manuscripts in reading his disciples; the King James has the disciples.

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church in Jerusalem is afraid of Saul until Barnabas takes hold of him, vouches for him and brings him to the apostles.

All afraid of him. The loneliest sentence in the chapter. The people shutting their doors are the ones who got away, or whose relatives did not, and their fear is plain reasoning: a man with his record claiming to be one of them is exactly what a spy would do. That they were still unsure three years on is less strange than it sounds: Damascus was a week’s journey away, Saul had spent part of the time out of sight in Arabia (Galatians 1:17), and he had left Damascus in secret, over a wall at night, so he very probably arrived with no one to vouch for him. Unwelcome in the synagogue and not admitted by the church, a man once advanced beyond his contemporaries (Galatians 1:14) learned the hard way that his standing now came not from any room in Jerusalem but from the Lord who had received him.

Barnabas took him. Then one man crosses the room. Took him means took hold of him: he laid hands on the man everybody else was backing away from, walked him in and vouched for him out loud. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus whose name meant son of encouragement (4:36), had once laid down the price of a field without a speech; now he puts his reputation at risk for somebody with none. Had he been wrong, he had introduced an assassin to the whole leadership of the church. Years later he would take the same kind of risk on John Mark (15:37–39), and be proved right again (2 Timothy 4:11).

He had seen the Lord. Barnabas tells the two things that mattered: that Saul had met the risen Lord, and that his life since had matched his claim. Paul would later rest his whole apostleship on that sight (1 Corinthians 9:1).

The apostles, or two of them? Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that on this visit he saw Cephas, stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:18–19). The accounts fit once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul’s reception by the church’s leadership, and uses the collective term for that body, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when only two directors were in the office that week. Paul, arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, counts heads with deliberate precision: his case depends on the visit having been short and limited; Luke’s, on its having happened at all. And Paul’s two names are exactly the two who mattered for the introduction: Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas got him in front of the men whose word would settle it.

The door the Gentile mission came through. One man with no office beyond a nickname believed a story everybody else found incredible, and Paul’s whole mission to the Gentiles came through that door. Barnabas walked Saul into a room of frightened apostles; Jesus Christ brings us into the presence of the holy God and says, this one is mine. Every Barnabas in the church is a small picture of him.

In everyday life. You were brought into God’s house because Christ vouched for you, so be a Barnabas. Think of the newcomer at church whom nobody quite knows what to do with, the person with the awkward history. Find out his story, sit with him, introduce him to someone.

How can I be a Barnabas without being naive? Barnabas did not simply feel generous; he knew the facts. He seems to have heard Saul’s story and judged it true before he put his name to it. So take time to listen to the person others are wary of, find out what has actually changed, and then speak up for him. At the same time, welcoming a repentant sinner never means ignoring real dangers. Where someone has abused or harmed others, a church must keep proper safeguards in place and protect the vulnerable, while still offering the gospel and fellowship. Grace and wisdom are not opposites. Barnabas had both, and the church was safer for it, not less safe.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Received at last, Saul preaches boldly in Jerusalem and takes up Stephen’s argument with Stephen’s opponents, until they too seek to kill him.

In and out among them. An Old Testament way of describing ordinary comings and goings (1 Samuel 18:16): he was part of the household now, no longer at the door. And he spoke boldly, with parrēsia, plain and fearless speech, Luke’s mark of the Spirit-filled witness (4:13, 31).

Disputed against the Hellenists. The term (the King James has Grecians) names language and culture, not faith: Greek-speaking Jews of the diaspora, with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem, whose circle included men from Cilicia (6:9), Saul’s own world. In 6:1 it labels believers; here, unbelievers, the circle Stephen had argued with, who could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke and had him killed. Saul had held the coats (7:58). Now he has walked back into the room where it happened and taken up Stephen’s argument, on Stephen’s side.

Seeking to kill him. The second organised attempt on Saul’s life in one chapter, and he has been a Christian for about three years.

In everyday life. Is there a place, a family, an old circle of friends, where you used to stand on the other side? That may be exactly where God wants you to speak now, not with superiority, but as one who knows from the inside what they believe and why.

Was Stephen’s death wasted, then? It looked like it: a brilliant preacher silenced in his first public season, and the church scattered. But Stephen died praying for the men who stoned him, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), and one of those men is now preaching Stephen’s message in Stephen’s synagogue. Augustine is often quoted as saying that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. Whether or not one can draw the line so straight, the pattern is plain: no faithful witness for Christ is ever wasted, even when it seems to end in failure. God answers prayers in ways the one who prayed may never see this side of glory.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers send Saul away to safety in Tarsus, as Christ himself had told him to go, and years of hidden preparation begin.

Sent him off to Tarsus. The church takes him down to Caesarea and home to Cilicia, and he goes where the brothers put him. Paul later adds that the Lord himself had told him in a vision in the temple to leave Jerusalem quickly (22:17–21). The church’s decision and Christ’s command pointed the same way.

The hidden years. Then Luke’s story leaves him. Saul does not appear again until Barnabas travels to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26), a gap of something like eight to ten years, depending on how they are counted. Luke covers a decade of Paul’s life with half a sentence.

What was he doing? Not nothing. Paul says he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, and that the churches of Judea kept hearing that the man who used to persecute them was now preaching the faith he had once tried to destroy (Galatians 1:21–23). Several beatings in his later catalogue probably fall in these years, and very likely the vision he dates fourteen years before he wrote (2 Corinthians 12:2). He was working. Nobody was writing it down.

Thirty years in Nazareth. Saul’s hidden decade follows the shape of his Lord’s life. Of Jesus’ first thirty years the Gospels tell us almost nothing (Luke 3:23), yet at the end of them, before he had preached a sermon, the Father said: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22). The years nobody wrote down had pleased God. For anyone who measures his worth by being seen to be useful, that is a quiet rebuke: Christ valued the servant long before anyone valued his work.

In everyday life. If you are in a season where nothing you do seems to be noticed, do the work in front of you as though Christ were watching. He is. What you do for him unseen is not lost; he receives it, flawed as it is, for the sake of his own perfect obedience.

Was the church wrong to send its best preacher away? No. They were protecting his life, and the Lord himself had told him to go (22:18). Sometimes the wisest thing a church can do for a gifted and endangered young man is to take him out of the spotlight. And if you have been moved on, out of a role, a city or a ministry you loved, it may not be a demotion but the Lord’s way of preparing you for the work he actually has in mind.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With its persecutor converted, the church throughout the land has peace, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it is built up and multiplies.

The church had peace. One of Luke’s summary sentences, which close one part of the story and open the next (see the introduction). Church is singular: one people across three regions under one Lord.

A target hit. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria: the first stages of the commission (1:8) are done, not by any plan of the church but through a persecution nobody wanted. Only the end of the earth remains, and the man who will take it there has just gone home to Tarsus to wait.

The fear of the Lord. The reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness, like a man who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it.

The comfort of the Holy Spirit. Paraklēsis belongs to the same family as paraklētos, the name Jesus gave the Spirit: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). It means coming alongside to help, and sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted and, as our word comfort reminds us (from the Latin for “with strength”), to make strong.

The peace Christ made. The peace comes in the paragraph after the chief persecutor has been converted and shipped home, not from a change of policy in the council: the risen Lord had gone out to meet the man driving the persecution and made him his own. The enemy was not pacified but converted. And the building that follows is the work of the same hands: I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

Fear and comfort together. The God who is a consuming fire is also the God of all comfort, and he gives his church both at once. Out of the two together the church was built up and multiplied (Ephesians 4:12–16). A church with fear and no comfort becomes harsh and anxious. A church with comfort and no fear becomes careless and soft.

In everyday life. Take the two phrases as a check on your own walk this week. Where have you been treating God casually? Where have you been carrying anxiety alone, as if there were no Helper beside you? Neither lack is mended by trying harder: the Helper is already given to every believer, and his power, not your resolve, makes a holy and unafraid walk possible.

Does a church grow only when there is no persecution? No. It had grown explosively under persecution too (8:4). God uses both seasons: persecution scatters the seed; peace lets it root and be built up. In a quiet season the question is whether you are using the peace to be built up in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit, or simply to rest.

Textual note. The King James, following later manuscripts, reads churches; the singular, church, is the earlier reading.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Lord is still at work through his apostle, giving life where there was none, and the signs bring many to faith. Visiting the churches of the coastal plain, Peter finds Aeneas, paralysed for eight years, and tells him that Jesus Christ heals him; the whole region turns to the Lord (vv. 32–35). At Joppa the much-loved Tabitha dies, and Peter, sent for urgently, puts the mourners out, kneels to pray and calls her to rise (vv. 36–41). Many believe, and Peter stays on with a tanner, in the house where the door to the Gentiles is about to open (vv. 42–43).
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter, and Peter kneels first because the authority is borrowed (see vv. 39–40). Every healing and raising in Acts is a sign rather than a policy: a small sample, given in advance, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right for good (see v. 41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and dresses she had made while she was with them (see vv. 39–40). Now: It is worth asking what would be held up for you (see “In everyday life” at vv. 36–37). And whatever it is, Christ counts the smallest of it as done for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, travelling among the churches of the coastal plain, finds at Lydda a man who has lain paralysed for eight years. The risen Lord has not forgotten him.

Here and there among them all. Luke leaves Saul in Tarsus and takes up Peter, last seen in 8:25, who goes from congregation to congregation on the coastal plain, from Lydda to Joppa, where chapter 10 opens: the first glimpse in this book of what most Christian ministry consists of, visiting believers in unremarkable towns. Peter the fisherman has become Peter the shepherd: feed my sheep (John 21:17). And he did not plant these churches. Philip had preached his way through this plain (8:40), and these saints are the fruit of a persecution and of refugees who could not stop talking.

The saints at Lydda. Lydda is the old town of Lod, about twenty-five miles north-west of Jerusalem, a market town on the main road down to the sea, where whatever happened would be discussed by travellers within a day.

Bedridden for eight years. Peter found him, as you find somebody you were not looking for. In eight years everybody in a town that size knows the house and has stopped expecting anything. Somebody had been washing and turning him all that time, and had long since stopped mentioning it.

He went about doing good. Peter’s circuit has a model, which he would soon describe in Cornelius’s house: Jesus went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him (10:38). The healing in Lydda is the same Jesus still doing good, now from heaven: the ministry of Acts is not Peter’s replacing Christ’s, but Christ’s, continued. The Lord of glory sends his apostle down the road to find a man on a mat: the Good Shepherd goes after the one, and he knows how long each of his creatures has been waiting.

Mercy before confession. Aeneas matters because of where this book is going. Luke says nothing of his faith: he is not called a disciple, not said to have believed, not recorded as speaking. The healing will arrive before he has confessed any faith, and in the next chapter Peter will watch the same thing happen, on a much larger scale, in a Gentile house.

In everyday life. Christ had not forgotten Aeneas. Somewhere in your church or street is someone who has been housebound so long that people have stopped calling; go this week. And remember the carers, who have been doing the lifting and washing for years without anyone mentioning it.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter heals in Jesus’ name, not his own: Jesus Christ makes the paralysed man whole, and the whole region turns to the Lord.

Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. The tense is present: is healing you, now. Not I heal you, but Jesus Christ heals you. Peter had learned at a temple gate to tell a staring crowd that it was not by his own power or piety that the lame man walked (3:12–16), and he does not wait to be misunderstood a second time.

Rise and make your bed. The first command to a man who has not stood for eight years: do for yourself what others have done for you all this time (see the box below), the ordinary domestic gesture that signals the illness is over.

Lydda and Sharon. Sharon is the fertile coastal plain. Luke’s “all” describes a movement across a region, not a head count, and it is easy to see how it spread: everybody had known about Aeneas for eight years, and now he was standing in the street. The sign led to faith, and the faith was in the Lord, not in Peter.

In everyday life. When something good happens to you, a recovery, an answered prayer, a crisis averted, say out loud whose doing it was, as Peter did. Jesus Christ did this.

Does Christ still heal like this through his ministers? Christ still heals as he wills. But healings like that of Aeneas and the raising of Dorcas at Joppa were apostolic signs confirming the gospel as it spread. Many Christians believe such gifts continue, and they are our brothers; the more likely reading is that they belonged to the apostolic age, and that no minister today may claim them. The question between us is not whether Christ heals today, which he plainly does, but whether he now gives anyone the power to heal at will, as he gave it to the apostles as the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12).

A word to the reader still on the mat. A passage like this can be quietly cruel if left to speak alone. Aeneas was healed after eight years; a great many faithful people are not healed after eighty. Paul left a colleague ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and carried a thorn that was never removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Nothing suggests that Aeneas had more faith than anybody else on the plain. What the passage shows is not a method for getting healed but who has the authority to heal, and his authority has not diminished. The timing is in his hands, not ours, and the day is coming when the whole plain of Sharon gets up.

Then should I still pray for healing? Yes, and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them (James 5:14–15), and God often heals in answer to prayer, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. What we may not do is claim a guarantee, or tell a sick believer his illness continues because his faith is weak. Pray as Jesus did in the garden: ask plainly for what you want, and add, not my will, but yours, be done. If healing comes, give Christ the glory. If it does not, he has promised grace sufficient for the weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and a resurrection body that will never be ill again.

Uncertain wording. Peter’s command, strōson seautō, means literally spread for yourself, with no object stated. Most translations supply bed, the mat he has lain on. But the same verb is used of preparing a room for a meal (Mark 14:15), so some take it as spread your own table, get yourself a meal. Either way the sense is the same: the man who has been served for eight years now does it himself.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Joppa a much-loved disciple, whose faith showed in good works for the poor, falls ill and dies, and her friends wash her body and wait.

A disciple named Tabitha. Luke calls her a disciple using the feminine form of the word, mathētria, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean gazelle: a woman known in both halves of a mixed port town.

Full of good works. Luke used the phrase of Stephen: full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (6:5). He now uses it of a woman whose recorded output is coats, and did not rank the one below the other: both are faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

In those days she became ill and died. In half a sentence she is gone, in a chapter full of healings, with an apostle eleven miles away, and Luke does not soften it.

Laid her in an upper room. The last detail matters most. In that climate burial usually followed death within the day: washing the body came first, and interment ordinarily next. They did the first and stopped, put her upstairs, and sent two men down the road. Nobody says why, but it is not hard to guess. They were hoping.

Her Lord’s compassion, stitched. Tabitha’s needle was doing in Joppa what her Lord had done in Galilee. Luke’s Gospel is full of Jesus’ care for widows (Luke 21:1–4; 20:47), and the God of Israel had always called himself protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). Her coats were not a side-activity of discipleship but the likeness of Christ, made in cloth. And the Lord who will judge the world by what was done for the least of his brothers counted every garment she stitched as made for him; he names a seamstress in a port town in the same breath as the first martyr.

In everyday life. Be full of good works: not famous ones, but the kind that can be held up in a room after you are gone, the meal, the coat, the visit, the note. Ask what one thing you could make or do this week for someone who has no one to provide for them.

Why does God take his most useful servants? Scripture does not give the reason in Tabitha’s case, and it would be presumption to invent one. It does tell us that our days are written in God’s book before one of them comes to be (Psalm 139:16), and that usefulness is not a shield against death. The comfort is not that we can explain it but that the one who holds the days is good, and that for the believer, to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). The church in Joppa grieved as people who loved her, and rightly; but they did not grieve as those who have no hope.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples send for Peter with an urgent plea that cannot bring itself to name what they want. They had heard of Aeneas, and they hoped.

Please come to us without delay. Eleven miles, a long day’s round trip, with a body upstairs in a warm climate. The message does not say what for, does not ask Peter to raise her, does not even name the woman. They have washed a corpse, declined to bury it, and sent for an apostle with a request that cannot say what they want.

Joppa again. Joppa is the port where the prophet Jonah, ordered to preach to the Gentiles of Nineveh, took ship in the opposite direction (Jonah 1:3). On a roof in this town Peter will be told three times to kill and eat what he has spent his life refusing, and will then go to a Gentile house. The call to the nations comes a second time at Joppa, and this time the man goes.

Something greater than Jonah. The difference is not that Peter is braver than Jonah, but that the greater Jonah has come. Jesus called himself the sign of Jonah to his generation and said, something greater than Jonah is here (Luke 11:29–32). The prophet who sailed from Joppa went down into the deep against his will, came up, and preached to Gentiles grudgingly. The Son of Man went down into death willingly, rose on the third day, and sent his own message to the nations with joy. The second call from Joppa is his, and he has already been to the depths and back for the people he is calling.

In everyday life. In your grief, send for help. Do not wait until you can pray properly or explain what you need. Call a friend, call your pastor, call on the Lord with the six words you have.

How do people pray at the worst moments? Not with a petition properly framed, but with a half-formed sentence that cannot ask for what it wants, because the thing is too large to say out loud. Come quickly is often the whole of it, and God is not put off by a badly drafted request. He heard the groaning of his people in Egypt before they had managed to compose a prayer at all (Exodus 2:23–25), and the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). These disciples had a dead friend, a road, and a conviction they could not articulate that it was worth fetching the man who knew Jesus. It was enough.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter does what he had seen his Lord do: he clears the room, kneels to pray and calls the dead woman to rise, and she does. The words echo Jesus’ words; the power is borrowed from him.

Showing tunics and other garments. Upstairs they hold up the clothes, one after another, while they cry, a detail that reads like the memory of somebody in that room (Luke 1:2). Her love had been made visible in cloth.

All the widows. A widow without a son often had nothing but charity between her and destitution, and the neglect of widows had caused an early dispute in the church (6:1). Luke recorded the failure; he records the remedy too, and it has a name: Tabitha.

Put them all outside. Peter has seen every move before. His Lord had cleared a house in Galilee where a twelve-year-old girl lay dead (Mark 5:40), and Peter was one of only three disciples allowed in.

Knelt down and prayed. But one thing he does that his Lord did not. Jesus took the child’s hand and told her to get up, with no need to pray. Peter kneels beside a dead woman and asks for something he has no power to perform, and only then speaks.

Tabitha, arise. What he said, very likely in Aramaic, was Tabitha, koum, one letter away from Talitha koum, the words Jesus had said to Jairus’s daughter with Peter in the room (Mark 5:41). He reaches for the only precedent he has, because he was there when it worked. And Luke tells what follows through her eyes: she opens them, sees Peter, and sits up.

Borrowed authority. The words are nearly identical; the authority is entirely borrowed, from the one who said to a dead girl, “Child, arise”, to a widow’s son at Nain, “Young man, I say to you, arise”, and to a friend four days in the tomb, “Lazarus, come out.” When Peter knelt in Joppa he was kneeling before that Lord.

In everyday life. Before you try to help anyone in a crisis, kneel. Whatever room you are walking into this week, a hospital ward, a grieving home, pray first and speak second, and remember that every good thing you bring is borrowed.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter raises Tabitha by the hand and presents her alive: a sign, given in one upper room, of the resurrection Christ will give all his people.

He gave her his hand. The most ordinary gesture, as for the lame man at the temple gate (3:7), and as Jesus did for Peter’s mother-in-law (Mark 1:31).

Presented her alive. Minutes earlier they had been put outside in tears with an armful of clothes. Presented her alive is the language Luke used of Jesus presenting himself alive to his apostles after his suffering (1:3): a picture of resurrection, and of whose resurrection lies behind this one.

A greater hand. Peter’s hand was a picture of a greater one, the pierced hand of the Son of God, which will reach into every grave where his people lie and raise them up. On that morning he will call the saints and widows of every age and present them alive, all of them together, for ever.

The hard thing. Something has to be said, or the passage becomes an instrument of cruelty. Tabitha was raised; every other Christian who died in Joppa that year stayed dead. Luke records two such raisings in the whole of Acts (here and Eutychus, 20:9–12) and the deaths of many believers, including James, one of the Twelve, executed by Herod with no rescue, in the same chapter in which prayer brought Peter out of prison (12:1–11). Whatever this passage is, it is not a description of what God routinely does when his people ask, and no one should be handed it as though it were.

A sign, not the destination. It is a board at the roadside with the destination’s name on it. Tabitha herself proves it, for she died again, and at her second funeral nobody sent to Lydda. She was given not immortality but a few more years of making coats. The comfort lies not in the hope that God might do this again for the person you have lost, but in what he announced in that upper room before witnesses: what he means to do for all his people, all at once. The widows got their friend back for a while. They will get her back for good.

In everyday life. If you are grieving a believer who has died, do not let this story become a reproach, as though you had not prayed hard enough. Let it become a promise. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 aloud this week, and say the name of the one you have lost alongside it.

Will we know our loved ones again? Scripture gives good reason to think so. Paul comforts grieving Christians not with a vague hope but with a reunion: the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be caught up together with them, and so we will always be with the Lord; therefore encourage one another (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). That comfort would mean little if we did not know each other. Moses and Elijah were known on the mount of transfiguration, and the risen Jesus was recognised by his friends. We will be changed, made like Christ, but not made into strangers. The widows of Joppa will hold Dorcas’s hands again, and they will know whose hands they are.

Can a modern person really believe this happened? Everyone in Joppa knew that dead people do not normally get up; that is why they wept and washed the body. The real question is whether God exists and whether he raised Jesus. If the tomb in Jerusalem was empty, as the first witnesses insisted at the cost of their lives (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), then the raising of a seamstress in Joppa is not a strange exception to how the world works but a small sign from the One who made the world and has already begun to remake it. Luke, a careful historian who checked his sources (Luke 1:1–4), names the town, the woman and the house, and says all Joppa knew; he wrote within living memory, about a place where people could still ask, not of a legend grown in the retelling.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign brings many to faith in the Lord, and Peter stays on in the house of a tanner, a man whose trade made him unclean, where God is about to open the door to the Gentiles.

Many believed in the Lord. The pattern of the whole section: the sign is not the point; it gets a hearing, and what people believe in is the Lord rather than the apostle.

Simon, a tanner. A tanner turned the hides of dead animals into leather, in solutions that included urine and dung. It meant constant contact with carcasses, which under the law made a man unclean (Leviticus 11:39–40), and later Jewish law required tanneries to stand well outside the town (Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:9). And Peter, who will shortly say he has never eaten anything common or unclean (10:14), moves in and stays for weeks.

The touch that cleanses. Jesus touched a leper (Luke 5:13) and the bier of a dead young man (Luke 7:14), and the uncleanness did not pass to him; his cleanness passed to them. Peter, lodging among carcasses, is following the Holy One who came to the unclean, and who is about to send him into a Gentile house to do the same.

Outside the gate. The bodies of the animals whose blood was brought into the holy place were burned outside the camp, and so Jesus also suffered outside the gate, to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The Son of God went to the place where the town ended, the place of carcasses and shame, and made it the door into the household of God. Blessed be the one who went outside so that outsiders could be brought in.

Whose house would you not stay in? Not in theory, where everybody is generous, but in practice: the address that would need explaining, the household whose habits or history or trade would make it awkward. Peter had not yet worked out his theology of clean and unclean; he had merely accepted an invitation from a man who worked with dead animals. The theology came later, on the roof of that house, over that smell, when the sheet was let down (10:6, 11): the vision that opened the door to the Gentile world was given to a man already sleeping in a house no strict Pharisee would have entered.

Does this mean every scruple is just prejudice? No. Some lines are drawn by God’s word, and those we must keep whatever it costs: Christians may not join in idolatry or sexual sin, however welcoming the house. But many of our lines are drawn by custom, class, culture or temperament, and Christ is constantly stepping over them. Ask, honestly and with an open Bible, whether a thing you avoid is forbidden by God or merely unfamiliar to you (Romans 14:1–4, 14). Peter’s food laws had once been God’s command, and in Christ they had been fulfilled and set aside (Mark 7:19). How much more should we hold loosely the barriers that were never commanded at all.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean: a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest picture of unconditional election (God choosing people freely, not for anything in them) and effectual calling (his call that actually brings them to faith). There was nothing in Saul to attract God’s grace (Philippians 3:4–6); God chose him according to his own purpose. Paul later wrote that his conversion was meant as a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. Election is not a closed door; it is the ground of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother, and they were afraid. It took Barnabas, the son of encouragement, to vouch for him.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person most openly opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to stop. That is a reason for prayer, and for being ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

keyVerse.quote: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter flows from this answer. It tells Saul that the crucified Jesus is alive and Lord, that he counts his people’s sufferings as his own, and that the persecutor has been fighting God himself; and Jesus says it not to destroy his enemy but to make him his servant. The rest of Saul’s life, and the mission to the nations, grew from these words.

9.reflection:
Jesus asks Saul, “why are you persecuting me?” (v. 4), though Saul had only attacked Christians. What does it mean for you that Christ counts what is done to his people as done to him, both in how you treat other believers and in what you suffer for him?

Ananias objected honestly and then went, and his first word was “Brother” (vv. 13–17). Whom do you find it hardest to welcome as a brother or sister in Christ, and what would it look like to say the family word first, while still being wise?

Saul never softened the truth about his past (Galatians 1:13), and he was then sent home for years of unrecorded work (vv. 21–30). How does being forgiven free you to be honest about your past, and to serve faithfully when no one is watching?

Peter told Aeneas, “Jesus Christ heals you” (v. 34), and knelt to pray before he spoke over Tabitha (v. 40). How should these scenes shape the way we pray for the sick, and the way we grieve for believers who have died?

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
Where we are. The gospel has reached Samaria and an Ethiopian (chapter 8), Saul the persecutor has become a preacher (chapter 9), and Peter is lodging with a tanner at Joppa (9:43). Now comes one of the great turning points of the book, so important that Peter tells it again in chapter 11 and at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11).

The message. Jesus Christ is Lord of all, so there are no outsiders to his welcome and no insiders who can do without him. God shows no partiality: a Gentile is received exactly as a Jew is, by believing in Jesus, without first becoming a Jew. And the best of men, devout and generous as Cornelius was, needs Christ as much as the worst.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). A church more and more Gentile needed to know that their welcome was no human compromise but God’s own doing, prepared from heaven at both ends and sealed by the Spirit.

How the chapter makes its case. An angel tells Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion, to send for Peter (vv. 1–8), and a vision three times repeated tells Peter not to call common what God has made clean (vv. 9–16). The Spirit sends him with the messengers, and he takes Gentiles into his lodging (vv. 17–23). In Caesarea Peter refuses worship, names the wall between Jew and Gentile and says God has shown him to call no person unclean (vv. 24–33). Peter preaches Jesus: anointed, crucified, risen, appointed Judge, the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness (vv. 34–43). While he is still speaking the Spirit falls on the Gentiles as at Pentecost, and they are baptised (vv. 44–48).

Where it leads. The chapter turns on the bracket in Peter’s sermon: “he is Lord of all” (v. 36). The wall the food laws guarded was not worn away by time but taken down by his death, when the one hanged on a tree bore the curse for Jew and Gentile alike (v. 39). The Judge of the living and the dead offers forgiveness now (vv. 42–43), and the risen Lord pours out his Spirit to seal his own gospel. In one Roman house the promise to Abraham, that all the nations would be blessed in his offspring, begins to be kept in Abraham’s greater Son.

For us. No one is too far off for Christ, and no one too good to need him. Do not call common anyone God has made clean: cross the walls you were raised behind, open your home, and speak of Jesus. And come to his word as Cornelius’s household did, expecting God to speak.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God breaks down the oldest wall in his people’s world: a Gentile household is welcomed into the church by faith in Christ, without first becoming Jewish. God prepares both men, a Roman centurion by an angel (vv. 1–8) and a Jewish apostle by a vision of clean and unclean animals, three times repeated (vv. 9–16), and the Spirit brings them together (vv. 17–23). In Caesarea Peter refuses worship, names the barrier and says God has removed it (vv. 24–33). He preaches Jesus, Lord of all, crucified, risen and appointed Judge, through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness (vv. 34–43). While he is still speaking the Spirit falls on the Gentiles as at Pentecost, and Peter commands that they be baptised (vv. 44–48).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals, but the lesson is about people, and Peter himself says so at verse 28. The food laws had never been about digestion. They kept Israel visibly distinct from the nations at every meal. The vision does not cancel anything God had said. The food laws were a shadow fulfilled in Christ (see the note on vv. 15–16). And Peter obeyed a command he found repellent and worked out the theology afterwards (see v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a word from the Spirit and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. Now: The instinct to take the gospel only to people like ourselves is seldom held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter had a lifetime of habit, and God was patient enough to take three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius is the most admirable Gentile Luke could have chosen, and the hardest case a Jewish church could have been asked to welcome. Every detail Luke gives of Cornelius makes both points.

At Caesarea. The Roman capital of Judea, built on the coast by Herod the Great with a harbour, a theatre and a temple to the emperor, and named after Caesar Augustus. Pilate governed from there; a stone bearing his name was found in its theatre in 1961. It was the most Roman city in the land.

A centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort. A centurion commanded about eighty men, the professional backbone of the Roman army: Cornelius is the occupation in person, the power behind the taxes and the crucifixions. Yet the centurions of the New Testament are almost always portrayed well, like the one whose faith astonished Jesus (Luke 7:2–10).

A devout man who feared God. He has brought his family and servants with him into the fear of God. His alms go to the people, which in Luke means the Jewish people, so a Roman officer was funding the poor of the nation he garrisoned; and he prays continually. But he is not a convert. A God-fearer attached himself to the synagogue, believed in Israel’s God and kept what he could of the moral law, but was uncircumcised and so remained formally outside: too Jewish for his Roman friends, never quite Jewish enough for the congregation.

The best Gentile in the empire. If moral seriousness and religious sincerity were enough, they would be enough for this man. Yet the angel does not tell him he is fine; he tells him to send thirty miles down the coast for a fisherman with something to say. Nothing Cornelius had done had earned him anything, and yet God had noticed every bit of it. Cornelius was groping in the half-light, and the Lord of all was coming to meet him.

The rank that stood at the cross. Luke’s readers have met this rank before: a centurion watched Jesus die and praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (Luke 23:47). Now, in the capital of the province that executed him, another centurion prays to the God of Israel without knowing the name of the man his fellow officer saw die. Before the chapter ends he will hear that the man hanged on a tree is Lord of all, Judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness (vv. 36–43). The best Gentile in the empire needed exactly what the worst needed: not more devotion, but Christ.

In everyday life. God sees those who seek him outside the church: the colleague who asks careful questions, the decent man who gives more to charity than you do. Do not assume they are fine, or that they are far away. Be ready to be the one God sends.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had heard a Gentile’s prayers and noticed his gifts, and he answered them by sending him the gospel.

About the ninth hour of the day. Three in the afternoon (see hours of the day), the hour of the evening sacrifice and of prayer (3:1): a Roman officer was keeping Jewish prayer times. His reaction to the angel is terror, as it usually is in Scripture.

As a memorial before God. The vocabulary is sacrificial. A memorial (mnēmosynon) was the portion of the grain offering that the priest burned on the altar, the token by which the whole offering came before God (Leviticus 2:2). So an uncircumcised soldier, who could not have carried a sacrifice past the outer court, is told that his prayers and his money have gone up like an offering God has noticed. The psalmist asked that his prayer be counted as incense before God (Psalm 141:2); Cornelius’s had been.

The hour Jesus died. A few years earlier, about the ninth hour, Jesus had cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last (Luke 23:44–46). So a Gentile was keeping the hour of the evening sacrifice without knowing that the true sacrifice had already been offered. His prayers rose like the memorial portion, but a memorial is only a token; it is the sacrifice that atones. The angel sends him to a man who will tell him of the Lamb whose once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:10) is the reason any sinner’s prayer can be welcome before God.
