God remembers. The God who heard Hagar in the wilderness and Hannah at the tabernacle kept every prayer of a Roman soldier, and his answers are better than the prayers that asked for them. Cornelius asked for light. God sent him Christ.

What it does not mean. His prayers and alms did not earn salvation (see the note on vv. 30–31). But neither is God indifferent to an honest man’s groping, which is a comfort to anyone praying for someone nowhere near the faith.

Does God hear the prayers of people who are not yet Christians? No one comes to the Father except through Christ (John 14:6), and the prayer of one who turns his ear from God’s law is an abomination (Proverbs 28:9). But God is not deaf to the cry of a person he is drawing to himself. Here he answers such a cry, not by saving the man without Christ, but by bringing him to Christ. So if you are not yet a believer and have been praying in the dark, keep seeking. The answer God gives to that prayer is himself, in his Son, through his word.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel does not preach the gospel; he sends for a man who will. God has appointed that the news of his Son should travel on human lips.

Send men to Joppa. A messenger from heaven, speaking to a man who wants God, gives a name, a town, a householder and a street. Angels in Scripture announce, warn, guide and rescue, but in Acts they never preach the gospel to anyone. The news of salvation travels on human breath, from someone who has it to someone who has not (Romans 10:14), so heaven goes to great trouble to get a fisherman onto a road. “We have this treasure in jars of clay” (2 Corinthians 4:7): a great dignity given to ordinary Christians, and a great responsibility.

Simon who is called Peter. The angel uses the name Jesus gave. Christ called Simon Cephas, Peter, the rock, at their first meeting (John 1:42), and after his confession promised him the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:16–19). The door of the kingdom is opened by the preaching of the gospel: Peter turned the keys for Jews at Pentecost (2:14–41), and he is about to turn them for Gentiles. So even the address points to Christ: Cornelius is to send for the man Jesus named and commissioned, who carries the confession on which Christ builds his church.

A tanner, whose house is by the sea. The angel distinguishes the two Simons and knows the second one’s trade, and that his house is by the sea, as tanneries often were. But Cornelius is not told why, or what Peter will say. Most obedience arrives like that: enough instruction to act on, and no explanation.

Why did God not just let the angel tell him the gospel? Because God has chosen to spread the news of his Son through people who have received it themselves. A forgiven preacher speaks of forgiveness as no angel can, for angels have never needed a Saviour. And the arrangement binds the church together: the Gentile is brought in by the Jew, the hearer by the speaker, so that no one can boast of finding the way alone. It also means the job is yours. If an angel would not do it in Caesarea, an angel will not do it in your street.

Textual note. The King James adds that Peter would tell him what he ought to do; those words are not in the earliest manuscripts, and the angel’s fuller message is given at 11:14.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius obeys at once, and shares what God has shown him with the men of his household.

He called two of his servants. Cornelius does not wait to see whether the impression fades by morning. The soldier he sends is devout (v. 2): a man under his command shared his faith.

Having related everything to them. Not an order but the whole story: a senior officer sat his subordinates down and told them what had happened while he prayed. It explains the room of relatives and friends already gathered and briefed when Peter arrives four days later. God prepares whole families for his grace, and he loves to save them together.

As the other centurion sent. At Capernaum a centurion with a dying servant sent elders to Jesus, saying he was not worthy to have him under his roof (Luke 7:3–7). Cornelius sends for the same reason: he needs what only Jesus can give. But Jesus is now risen and reigning, and he comes to a Gentile house in the word his servants preach.

In everyday life. When God speaks to you through his word, do not delay, and do not keep it to yourself. Tell those closest to you what he has been showing you; obedience that is spoken about tends to spread.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the messengers are on the road, God prepares Peter, timing his vision to their arrival.

The next day. Luke cuts between the two ends of the story: the messengers are perhaps an hour away when the vision comes. God’s timing is not approximate; he works on rooftops and on roads at once.

On the housetop to pray. The flat roof, reached by an outside stair, was the coolest and most private place in the house (see houses and flat roofs). The sixth hour is noon; the devout also prayed at midday (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10).

He became hungry. Luke keeps the unspiritual detail: noon, the meal cooking downstairs, and in the gap between the hunger and the food, God speaks to a hungry man in the language of food.

He fell into a trance. A state in which ordinary perception is suspended and God communicates directly (ekstasis; 22:17). The vision that opens the church to the whole Gentile world is given on the roof of a borrowed house that smelt of tanning, to a man who had simply gone up to pray.

What Jesus went on doing. Luke’s Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach (1:1); Acts is what he goes on doing from heaven. The Lord who said his witnesses would reach the end of the earth (1:8) is moving the last stage himself, setting a hungry apostle on a roof as the Gentiles reach the gate.

In everyday life. Peter was praying when God spoke. Keep your times of prayer, especially the unremarkable ones in the middle of a working day. You are not waiting for a vision; you are keeping company with the God who speaks through his word.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven opens and lets down a sign of what God is about to do: gather every nation.

The heavens opened. Luke uses the phrase sparingly, and always when something changes for good: at the Jordan (Luke 3:21), and when Stephen saw the Son of Man standing (7:56). The boundary between heaven and earth has been crossed from heaven’s side.

Something like a great sheet. Something like is Luke’s honesty when a witness describes an unfamiliar thing by the nearest familiar one: a large square of cloth, or a sail like those in the harbour below.

Let down by its four corners upon the earth. The prophets speak of God gathering Israel’s outcasts from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12). Held at the four points of the compass and full of every kind of living creature, the sheet announces its subject before a word is spoken: all nations. And it comes down; Peter does not go up. That is what the rest of the chapter is about: God moving toward people who could not have come to him, on their own roofs, at lunchtime.

Why heaven stands open. Every other opened heaven in Luke’s two books has Jesus at its centre. Jesus told Nathanael that he would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man (John 1:51): he is Jacob’s ladder, the one way between heaven and earth. So when heaven opens over a roof in Joppa, it is open because of him. The barrier between a holy God and the unclean nations was not lifted by a change of policy. It was removed by the Son who came down, died and ascended, and the sign that the nations are now to be gathered comes down by the way he opened.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands Peter to do what faithful Jews had died rather than do, because in Christ the line between clean and unclean is coming down. The sheet holds food, but the lesson, as Peter will see, is about people.

All kinds of animals and reptiles and birds. These are the categories Leviticus uses when it draws the lines (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), and the sheet is not a selection: clean and unclean together, the pig beside the sheep, the vulture beside the pigeon. Contact with unclean creatures defiled a Jew; eating them was unthinkable.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. Peter is to do the butchering himself, choosing from creatures he had been taught from infancy were an offence to God. This was no marginal scruple. Under the Greek king Antiochus two centuries earlier, a mother had watched her sons killed rather than eat pork, and the books of the Maccabees that told it were treasured. The voice Peter will call Lord commands the very thing faithful Israelites had died refusing to do, which is why the next verse holds one of the most understandable refusals in Scripture, and why God has to say it three times.

The one whom uncleanness could not touch. The command makes sense only because of who had come. Under the law uncleanness spread: touch a leper or a corpse and you were defiled. Then Jesus touched a leper, and the leprosy left him (Luke 5:13). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (Luke 8:54). A woman unclean for twelve years touched his garment, and she did not make him unclean; he made her whole (Luke 8:43–48). In him holiness ran the other way: the Holy One had come, and his cleanness was the stronger. The God who drew the lines in Leviticus erased them in Christ, faithful in both, and his purposes were always heading for a table with every nation at it.

The animals were the vehicle; the freight was people. This passage is often used for arguments it was not given for. It does bear on what Christians may eat: no food is unclean in itself, as Mark says in an aside (Mark 7:19). But Peter tells us what the vision was for, and it is not a menu: “God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean” (v. 28). It is used most faithfully against the habit the food laws had come to enforce, the sorting of human beings into those one can sit down with and those one cannot, a habit that long outlived the dietary code and has never needed a Bible verse to keep it going.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter refuses out of a lifetime of faithful obedience, and his refusal contradicts itself. A good man is defending a good thing at the very moment God is moving past it.

By no means, Lord. Two things that will not go together: “absolutely not”, and Lord. He stands where Ezekiel stood when he protested against eating defiled food (Ezekiel 4:14). And it is a recognisable habit: “Depart from me” (Luke 5:8); “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8); “Far be it from you, Lord!” (Matthew 16:22). He is the disciple who tells Jesus what will not be happening, and calls him Lord while doing it.

Common or unclean. Common means ritually unfit, for ordinary use rather than for God. Peter has never once eaten such food, to his credit. He is defending God’s own law, kept at cost, and defending it against God.

Jonah’s port. Joppa was where Jonah took ship the other way when God sent him to Gentile Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). Again a Jewish prophet in Joppa is sent toward the Gentiles, and again his first word is no. Between the two stands Christ, the greater Jonah who has been through the deep for the nations (Matthew 12:39–41), so this reluctant prophet needs no storm and no fish, only a word repeated three times.

Holding the scaffolding. What Peter cannot let go of is not a sin but a genuine obedience, kept for decades. The command had a purpose, what it pointed to has arrived, and Peter is holding on to the scaffolding after the building is up. Christians who are stuck are often stuck on something that was once right, was kept at cost, and has quietly become the thing they will not let God touch. A long record of obedience can also become what we stand on before God, until people without it begin to look unclean to us. Peter’s clean record could no more save him than Cornelius’s alms could save Cornelius; both needed the same Christ (v. 43).

The Lord answered the second word. Peter put “never” and “Lord” into one sentence, and the Lord answered the second word, not the first. He outlasts our protests, not by crushing the protester but by speaking again.

How do I tell a good conviction from a scaffold I should take down? Ask where it comes from and what it is for. If it rests on a plain command of Scripture that still applies to Christians, keep it, whatever it costs: no vision overturns the moral law. If it rests on a custom, a tradition, or an Old Testament ceremony the New Testament says is fulfilled in Christ, hold it loosely, and let it go when it starts to keep at a distance people Christ has welcomed. Peter changed because God himself spoke; we have God’s finished word for that, not new visions, and it is clear on which lines have been taken down (Colossians 2:16–17).
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has already made clean what Peter still calls common, and the cleansing has a name: Christ crucified.

What God has made clean, do not call common. God has acted already; Peter’s part is to stop describing things wrongly. The correction is aimed at his speech, do not call, and within thirteen verses he applies it to people himself: “I should not call any person common or unclean” (v. 28). Jesus had already declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18–19), and Peter had been standing there. He had heard it and not drawn the conclusion, a sobering thought for anyone who assumes that hearing good teaching is the same as being changed by it.

This happened three times. Three denials by a charcoal fire, three questions on a beach (John 21:15–17), and now three times the vision comes. God knows exactly how many repetitions this man requires.

Taken up at once. The vision ends without an application, leaving a man on a roof with a command he has refused and no idea what it is for. A great deal of Christian experience happens there: the instruction received, the meaning not yet arrived, and nothing to do but wait until somebody knocks at the gate.

Made clean at Golgotha. The tense is past because the work is finished. The food laws had separated Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24–26), and Christ abolished “the law of commandments expressed in ordinances”, to create in himself one new man in place of the two and reconcile both to God through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The line was not worn away by time or repealed by a council; it was fulfilled and taken down by a death. The food laws were a shadow, and the reality is Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). His blood cleanses from all sin, and no one it has washed can ever be called common again. The Father declared it three times over a tanner’s roof, and he declares it still over every sinner who comes to his Son: clean, accepted, mine.

In everyday life. Do not call unclean anyone God has made clean in Christ. Think of a Christian whose background or past makes you uneasy, and do one concrete thing about it: an invitation, a phone call, a seat beside him on Sunday.

Then why did God give the food laws at all? Not because pork was wicked or sheep were holy, but to teach and to protect. At every meal they taught Israel that she was set apart for a holy God, and that holiness means distinction (Leviticus 11:44–45; 20:25–26), and they kept her from being swallowed by the nations until the Messiah came. In Christ the holiness they pictured arrived, and God’s people were to be marked not by a diet but by faith in him, gathered from every nation. The laws were not a mistake that God corrected. They were a signpost, and Peter was standing at the place it pointed to.

Where Christians differ: are the food laws binding today? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews, still keep the Old Testament food laws, often out of an earnest wish to honour all of Scripture.

This commentary’s view: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); this vision confirms it; Paul teaches that food is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). The food laws were shadows fulfilled in Christ. Christians are free to eat anything with thanksgiving, though they should be considerate of the weaker conscience (Romans 14:15).

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter cannot work the vision out by thinking harder, and its answer is already standing at the gate. God often explains his word by his providence.

Inwardly perplexed. Thoroughly at a loss, and Luke mentions it twice (vv. 17, 19). The vision spoke of food but was about something more, and no amount of thinking could get Peter from the sheet to the Gentiles.

Stood at the gate. While the vision is still unresolved, its answer is standing in the street asking for Peter by name. He will understand the sheet by obeying the knock: some things are understood only when they are acted on. God’s word and his works fit together like a key and a lock, because the same Lord governs both.

Perplexed before. Luke’s Gospel shows the disciples failing again and again to understand what Jesus told them about his death (Luke 9:45; 18:34), until the risen Lord opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). The same Lord is at work on this roof. He does not leave his servants holding riddles, and his explanations always lead back to him: the sheet will make sense in a Gentile house, while Peter is telling them about Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit himself joins the two ends of the story and sends Peter with the Gentiles, telling him not to hold back.

The Spirit said to him. Three parties are being moved, and none can see the others: Cornelius has an angel and an address, the messengers a road, Peter a sheet of animals. The one connecting them is the Spirit himself, a person who directs, sends and commands. He hovered over the waters at creation, overshadowed the virgin, descended on the Son at the Jordan, and here sends Gentiles to fetch an apostle. He never sends his servants anywhere he has not gone ahead.

Accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them. The number is exact, two servants and a soldier (v. 7). As Peter later reports it, he was to go “making no distinction” (11:12): not only “do not dither”, but “do not sort these men” (see the note on the wording below). He is told neither who Cornelius is nor what the vision meant, only that the Spirit sent them, and that is what he produces when Jerusalem calls him to account: “the Spirit told me to go with them” (11:12).

The Spirit of Jesus. He is no free-floating influence. The exalted Jesus poured him out (2:33), and Luke will call him the Spirit of Jesus (16:7). He sends Peter to Gentiles because Christ has already claimed them, and his work is to bear witness about Christ (John 15:26).

How does the Spirit lead Christians today? Here the Spirit spoke directly to an apostle at a turning point in the founding of the church, and we should not expect such words as our normal guidance. Today he leads us chiefly through the Scriptures he inspired, complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), opening our understanding of them, working in us a desire to obey, and ordering our circumstances in his providence. And on this very point Scripture is unmistakable: we are to make no distinction among those Christ has received. You do not need a voice on the stairs to welcome the stranger at the gate.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “without hesitation” (diakrinomai) usually means to doubt or waver in the form used here, and the ESV takes it so. In its active form the same verb means to sort, to make a distinction, and that is how Peter reports the Spirit’s words at Jerusalem, “making no distinction” (11:12), and how he speaks at the council: God “made no distinction between us and them” (15:9). The main sense here is “do not hold back”; that Luke also hears the echo is likely, though not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter goes down and learns that a God-fearing Roman officer, sent by a holy angel, is waiting to hear what he has to say.

Upright and God-fearing. To Peter’s flat “I am the one you are looking for”, the messengers reply with a small masterpiece of diplomacy: the awkward fact first, a centurion; then what a Jewish hearer would most want to know, upright and God-fearing, well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation; and the clincher, directed by a holy angel. They had probably rehearsed it on the road, knowing how unlikely their errand sounded.

To hear what you have to say. That is the whole invitation: not to be healed or impressed, but to hear. Most preachers spend their lives trying to get people to listen; here a man sent servants a journey of days to secure a hearing for a message he could not yet describe. Peter was walking down those stairs toward the most willing audience of his life.

The voice of the Shepherd. What Peter has to say is a person. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17), and Peter’s message will be a man: anointed, crucified, raised, appointed Judge, offering forgiveness in his name (vv. 38–43). Jesus had said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, who would listen to his voice, so that there would be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). Some of them were waiting in Caesarea. The servants at the gate were fetching the voice of the Shepherd.

In everyday life. People around you are often readier to hear about Christ than you think, and what they need is not your opinions but his word. If someone asks about your faith this week, do not change the subject. Say what you have to say, simply and kindly.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s first act of obedience is to take Gentiles in as his guests, and his second is to bring witnesses.

So he invited them in to be his guests. Two Gentile servants and a Roman soldier stay the night: beds and a meal, and a meal means a table, precisely what a devout Jew did not share with Gentiles and precisely what the vision had been about. The man who said “By no means, Lord” before lunch had Gentiles eating in his lodgings by supper. He did not settle his theology first (that comes in v. 28); he obeyed one step at a time. And Joppa to Caesarea is about thirty miles, which the men had already walked: he gave them a night’s rest before setting out, a small kindness Luke did not have to record.

Some of the brothers. There were six, we learn at Jerusalem (11:12), where Peter had them beside him when the church demanded an explanation. A man does not take six witnesses on a pastoral visit. Peter made sure his account could be checked before anyone asked.

The table Jesus kept. Peter had watched Jesus go in to Zacchaeus while the crowd grumbled that he had gone to be the guest of a sinner (Luke 19:5–7), and recline at Levi’s feast saying, “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:29–32). Hospitality in the church is not good manners added to the gospel but the gospel acted out, because Christ welcomed us when we were strangers to God (Romans 15:7). Peter had sat at those tables as a guest; now he was laying one. Christ sends his servants into the roads and lanes to compel people to come in, until his house is filled (Luke 14:23), and two servants and a soldier asleep in a tanner’s house were among the first guests brought in from the lanes of the Gentile world.

In everyday life. Hospitality often comes before the gospel. Open your home this week to someone outside your usual circle: a meal, a coffee, a bed for the night. Christ welcomed you first.

Why does it matter that Peter brought witnesses? Because the gospel is public truth, not private experience, and God wanted the church to receive the Gentiles on evidence, not one man’s say-so. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Peter brought six. Here is wisdom for any Christian or leader involved in something sensitive: act in the open, bring others with you, keep your conduct checkable. Integrity that welcomes scrutiny protects both the leader and the people he serves.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius has gathered his relatives and friends to hear God’s messenger, and in mistaken reverence he falls at Peter’s feet.

Cornelius was expecting them. He has spent four days inviting people to hear a man he has never met. A serving officer has told his family and friends, probably brother officers too, that an angel told him to send for a Jewish fisherman; if nothing came of it, he would look ridiculous for years. That is faith expecting something, and love wanting the people he loved to hear. The Gentile mission begins in a room full of somebody’s relatives, because a Roman soldier could not think of a reason to hear this alone.

Fell down at his feet and worshiped him. The verb (prosekynēsen) means to prostrate oneself in reverence, the ordinary word for worship. Be fair to him. Four days ago an angel stood in his house and told him to send for this man, and in the world Cornelius grew up in, when something from heaven turns up, you get on the floor. It is the error of a man who does not yet know what he is dealing with, and it is corrected in the next verse, immediately and kindly.

A light for the Gentiles. Simeon, waiting in the temple, called the infant Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). Now, in the most Gentile house in Judea, a room full of people waits for that light. Cornelius goes to the floor because he mistakes the messenger for the one who sent him. But one who is worthy of worship has indeed come to his door: Christ, in the message Peter carries.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter refuses worship and lifts Cornelius to his feet: the messenger is only a man, and worship belongs to God alone.

Stand up; I too am a man. Not “You are embarrassing me”, but I too am a man: on the same level, made of the same material. And he takes hold of a Roman centurion and puts him back on his feet. The first thing Peter does in the first Gentile home to hear the gospel is pick a man up off the floor. The reverence was genuine, and refusing it risked chilling the room. There is a false humility that deflects with one hand and enjoys the compliment with the other. Ministries that last are built on Peter’s refusal, and many that collapse stopped making it somewhere along the way.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Two chapters later a king in this same city accepts the acclaim Peter refuses, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”, and Luke records his end in one unsparing verse (12:21–23; see Herod Agrippa I). Paul and Barnabas refuse worship at Lystra (14:14–15), and the angel refuses it from John (Revelation 19:10).

What Jesus did not refuse. Jesus accepted worship, from the disciples in the boat (Matthew 14:33) and from Thomas, who called him “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). He never once said, “Stand up; I too am a man.” Either he was the most dangerous blasphemer who ever lived, or he is God. And he too lifts the fallen: when John fell at his feet as though dead, the risen Christ laid his right hand on him and said, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one” (Revelation 1:17–18). Glory to the one at whose feet it is safe to fall.

Is it wrong to honour Christian leaders? No. Scripture tells us to esteem those who labour among us and are over us in the Lord very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). The line is crossed when honour becomes reverence: when a leader is treated as beyond question, his words as equal to Scripture, or his presence as bringing us nearer to God. Healthy honour says, thank God for this man; idolatry says, I cannot do without him. A good pastor will do what Peter did and lift you back on your feet.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images; Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians distinguish that honour from the worship due to God alone, and many are sincere in it.

This commentary’s view: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter names the wall between Jew and Gentile and announces that God has taken it down: he must call no person common or unclean. The vision was about animals; Peter has understood that it was about people.

How unlawful it is. Peter walks into a room full of Gentiles and opens by naming the barrier, to the people it applies to, rather than beginning with something warm and general and hoping nobody raises it. The word athemiton means taboo, not done, and the God-fearers there had felt it most: welcome at the synagogue door and not past it. The law of Moses nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile house, but a dense hedge of custom had grown around the purity laws, until strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12). It had once had a real purpose: a people surrounded by empires that swallowed nations whole survived by not eating with them. Peter’s honesty helped the room trust him. He had not come to tell them the division never existed, but who had ended it.

God has shown me. Nobody had told Peter that the vision was about persons. On the coast road with three Gentiles for company, he had worked it out: no human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation.

The doorway Jesus was led through. On the morning of the crucifixion the chief priests would not go into the Roman governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover (John 18:28). They stood outside; Jesus was taken in. The true Passover Lamb was led across the threshold they would not cross, condemned in a Gentile house by a Gentile judge and crucified by Gentile soldiers, for Jew and Gentile alike. What custom, history and fear had built, Christ demolished in a single afternoon outside Jerusalem. Peter steps through a Roman doorway now because his Lord went through one first, to die.

Our walls are no longer made of food. We like to think Peter’s barrier belongs to a tribal past; we will eat anything with anyone. But look at whom we let into our homes. The journalist Bill Bishop, in The Big Sort, traced how Americans over a generation increasingly chose neighbourhoods, congregations and friends who vote and think as they do, and how groups that talk only to themselves drift further apart. The old taboo said that a Gentile’s house would defile you; the new one says that a friendship with someone on the other side would, and the tolerant grow that hedge as high as the moralist, around those they have decided are intolerant. Peter’s hedge came down not because he became broad-minded but because God showed him a cleansing deeper than any custom, the same blood for everyone in the room. That is the only ground on which people who would never have chosen each other can sit down together, and stay.

In everyday life. Name your own barrier: a group you were raised to look down on, or simply to avoid. Say it honestly to God, and then cross the room. Christ broke the wall down at the cross; walk through the gap, beginning with the wall nearest you.

Does this mean every human being is already clean before God? No. Peter is speaking about race and nation, not sin. No one is unclean because he was born a Gentile, a Roman or anything else; but every one of us, Jew and Gentile alike, is unclean because of sin and needs to be washed (Romans 3:23), which is why Peter goes on to preach forgiveness through Christ (v. 43). The barrier of nationality is removed so that the gospel can reach everyone; the barrier of sin is removed only by the blood of Christ, received by faith. Hold both, or we end either with racism or with universalism.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The arguing is over: Peter has come without objection, and now he asks and listens.

I came without objection. Not quite the whole truth: he had said “By no means, Lord” until God repeated himself three times. But the arguing was finished on the roof. The God who turned Peter’s “By no means” into “without objection” works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely command; he changes the heart that hears the command.

I ask then why you sent for me. He has a vision, a word from the Spirit and an apostle’s authority, and the first thing he does in that house is ask, and wait. Cornelius’s answer, told to a room that has waited four days for it, establishes that the meeting was arranged from heaven at both ends. Peter could have asserted that; he let his host tell it.

The one who came without objection. Peter’s journey, made after three refusals, sits inside a far longer one made with none. The Son of God came from the Father’s side into a world not merely unclean but hostile, and the letter to the Hebrews gives his words on coming as, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). He came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10), and he went further than any centurion’s parlour: to a cross. Every servant who goes without objection follows, at a great distance, the Lord who came without one.

In everyday life. Ask before you tell. The next time you talk with someone about faith, begin by asking what has been happening in his life, and listen properly before you speak.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius tells how God heard his prayer and sent him to Peter, and the angel’s full message shows that, for all his piety, he still needed to be saved.

Four days ago. The angel’s message appears twice in this chapter and a third time in the next: Luke repeats what matters.

A man stood before me in bright clothing. Two men in dazzling apparel stood by the women at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4), and two in white robes at the ascension (1:10), each time with news about Jesus. This angel has only an address to give, but he belongs to the same story: the crucified man is alive, and he is Lord.

Your prayer has been heard. Both tellings in this chapter contain only that and the order to send for Peter. Reporting to Jerusalem, Peter adds what the angel said of him: “he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household” (11:14). That settles the question every thoughtful reader asks. Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, and his prayers went up before God like an offering. Was he already saved, with Peter merely bringing information? The angel says no: on the day he appeared, with all that piety behind him, Cornelius still needed a message by which he would be saved.

Hard and kind. Hard, because it will not allow the comfortable conclusion that sincerity is enough and the gospel an optional refinement. Kind, because God did not leave the honest seeker to his sincerity. He sent an angel and a vision, and moved an apostle down the coast against every instinct he had, to get the message to one Roman household. God is so far from indifferent to the man reaching after him in the dark that he will rearrange the church to reach him.

In everyday life. Tell what God has done for you. Your story, told simply and honestly, can open hearts that an argument would close: what you were, how Christ met you, what he has done since. It need not be dramatic to be his.

Textual note. The King James has Cornelius say he was fasting; the earliest manuscripts do not mention it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius’s household is a model congregation: all present, aware of God, and ready to hear everything the Lord has commanded.

You have been kind enough to come. A courtesy a Roman officer did not owe a Jewish fisherman: Cornelius recognises that Peter crossed a barrier to get here.

In the presence of God. Cornelius’s last sentence is worth learning by heart. We are all here: nobody is missing. In the presence of God: they know whose house this has become. To hear all: not the parts that suit them. That you have been commanded by the Lord: they do not expect Peter’s opinions; they assume he is under orders. And he was, under the risen Lord who sent the apostles to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19–20), as he will say (v. 42). The preacher stands under Christ, and the sermon is Christ’s own message about himself.

A model congregation. Few preachers have walked into a better room, and not by accident: behind it lie four days of telling a garrison town, and years of praying and giving (v. 2). Many of us hear preaching expecting some of it to be interesting, and assess it. Cornelius’s household came expecting to be commanded by God through a man, and the Holy Spirit fell on them before he had finished. Those two facts are probably connected.

What if the preaching at my church is poor? Pray for your preacher, and come anyway in the presence of God. Cornelius’s words rest not on the preacher’s eloquence but on the hearer’s expectation that God will speak through his word; where a sermon faithfully opens Scripture, God is speaking, however plain the delivery. Prepare: read the passage beforehand, pray for the preacher, arrive in time, and listen for what God is commanding rather than for what entertains. Preaching unfaithful to Scripture is a different and more serious matter, to be raised lovingly with the elders. But most of us need to bring more to church before we complain about what we take away.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not judge by nation or face: anyone, from any people, who fears him is welcome to him. Peter is only now grasping how far that reaches, and the rest of his sermon shows the one way through the door it opens (v. 43).

Peter opened his mouth. The formula for a weighty speech (8:35), and this is the first sermon ever preached to a Gentile household. Its first words are an admission: not “As I have always taught”, but “I am only now grasping this.”

God shows no partiality. Behind the phrase stands a vivid compound (prosōpolēmptēs), one who receives the face: courtroom language for a judge who decides by who the parties are. The compound first appears here, but the picture is from Moses, who says God is not partial, literally that he does not lift faces (Deuteronomy 10:17). Peter says it looking at a room of faces he had been raised to sort: he had known the principle all his life, and has finally seen how far it reaches. Paul builds on it: God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11), and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28).

Acceptable to him. Acceptable (dektos) means welcome: God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation. Peter only understood it that afternoon; the Father had purposed it from eternity. The sermon gives the reason: Jesus Christ is Lord of all (v. 36), and everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness (v. 43). It opens with the open door and closes with the only way through it.

Even his enemies said it. Peter had watched this impartiality walking about. Spies sent to trap Jesus opened with flattery that was nonetheless true: “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality” (Luke 20:21). He touched lepers and dined with Pharisees, healed a centurion’s servant and a synagogue ruler’s daughter. God’s glory shone in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and that face turned toward the poor, the foreign and the despised as readily as toward anyone.

In everyday life. God did not choose you by your face, and neither should you sort others by theirs. Notice this week whose company you seek out and whom you dismiss, and ask whether the face is deciding for you.

What about those who never hear? It is the question behind the question, asked with real anguish. Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (4:12; Romans 10:13–17), and that creation and conscience leave everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). It also tells us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and that infants dying in infancy who are among God’s elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, both 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on that good and merciful Judge. What Scripture never does is offer the unevangelised as a reason for the church to relax. Its answer is this chapter: God moved heaven and earth to get the gospel to one man. The right response is not speculation but mission.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists, Christians who believe that Christ’s death can save some who never hear of him, read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right, in whatever religion, may be saved through Christ without knowing his name. They hold it out of real compassion for those who never hear.

This commentary’s view: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, whatever his nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ, and Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message God sent first to Israel is good news of peace through Jesus Christ, and because he is Lord of all, no nation lies outside it.

The word that he sent to Israel. The gospel came to the Jews first, and Peter says so in a Gentile drawing room without embarrassment: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

Preaching good news of peace. The phrase comes from Isaiah’s runner coming over the hills with news that the war is over: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (Isaiah 52:7). Peter speaks to a professional soldier in the vocabulary of a herald announcing the end of hostilities. The peace is double: peace with God for sinners who were his enemies, his just anger turned aside because Christ bore it (Romans 5:1, 9–10), and peace between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–17).

He is Lord of all. Dropped into the sentence like a bracket comes the largest claim in the chapter, with all placed first in the Greek: of all, he is Lord (Romans 10:12). Peter says it in an aside, to an officer of an empire whose creed was that Caesar is lord, in a city named after Caesar. And here is the reason God shows no partiality: not that he has become broad-minded, but that the man at the centre of the gospel owns everything. A Lord of all has no outsiders, only subjects who have not yet been told. Peter was brought to a house he would never have entered, because the one who sent him already owned the address.

He paid for the peace himself. The Lord of all could have come to Caesarea as Rome had come, with standards and a garrison. He came preaching peace, and paid for it himself, “making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). Every other lord of the earth has made his peace by killing his enemies. This one made it by dying for them.

What does it mean in practice that Jesus is Lord of all? No part of the world, and no part of your life, lies outside his rule. He is Lord of the nations, so no people is beyond the gospel’s reach; of governments, so rulers answer to him, and Christians obey them under him, not instead of him (4:19); of your work, money, body, evenings and relationships. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian creed (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), dangerous because it left Caesar no room to be ultimate. It still leaves nothing else that room: not career, not comfort, not self.

Is it arrogant to call Jesus Lord of all? Only if Christians had invented him or earned their place under him. Peter has just admitted, in front of Gentiles, that God had to correct him. The claim is about Jesus, and it stands or falls with the resurrection (vv. 40–41): if he rose, he is Lord whether anyone likes it or not, and keeping quiet would be the unkind thing. And the respectable and the outcast come in exactly the same way, receiving forgiveness, not earning it (v. 43). A message that humbles everyone equally is the opposite of arrogance.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verses 36–38 is famously rough. “The word” stands at the head of the sentence without a verb of its own, and translations join it up differently: some take it with “you yourselves know” in verse 37, so that Peter says, in effect, you know the message God sent; the ESV sets it apart with “As for the word”. The meaning is not in doubt: the message God sent to Israel, peace through Jesus Christ, is a story Peter’s hearers already know in outline, and he is about to tell it.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter tells the public story of Jesus: anointed by God with the Spirit and with power, he went about doing good and freeing all whom the devil oppressed.

Beginning from Galilee. The story of a Galilean preacher had been talked of in the province for some three years and had ended in a public execution. So Peter starts where the public record starts, after the baptism John proclaimed: an account of what a particular man did, within living memory, for people who could check it. His outline is the shape of Mark’s Gospel, and early tradition says that Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching.

God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit. Anointed is the verb behind Christ, so Peter is explaining the title to a room that had not grown up with the vocabulary. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one with the Spirit, at his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18).

Oppressed by the devil. To be oppressed is to be tyrannised, held down under a cruel power, and Peter sums up Jesus’ ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue, prising people loose from the devil’s grip. The phrase reaches wider than open demon-possession, though not every illness is a direct demonic act: behind the reign of sickness, bondage and death in a fallen world stand “the works of the devil”, and “the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy” them (1 John 3:8). Jesus called a crippled woman one “whom Satan bound for eighteen years” (Luke 13:16).

For God was with him. Peter speaks of Jesus’ true humanity: a man anointed by the Spirit, in whom the Father was at work. In the same sermon he calls him Lord of all and Judge (vv. 36, 42). The eternal Son did not lay aside his deity; he lived his human life in dependence on the Spirit, which is why he can be our pattern as well as our Saviour.

The great Liberator. Every healing was a liberation and a preview of total victory. Jesus is the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27): “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). At the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15), and through death destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is mightier, and he rescues us “from the domain of darkness” into his own kingdom (Colossians 1:13). There has never been a life like his: the Son of God on the roads of Galilee with the Spirit upon him, touching lepers, opening blind eyes, freeing the oppressed.

In everyday life. The Spirit who anointed Jesus now lives in you, so go about doing good today, as he did: not grand deeds, but the next good thing, the visit, the repair, the meal, the word of comfort.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles saw it all: men hanged Jesus on a tree, under the law’s curse, and God reversed their verdict by raising him on the third day.

We are witnesses. Peter says it before he says anything about the cross, and again in the next verse. Everything rests on the claim that the men saying it were there (1:8; 2:32).

By hanging him on a tree. He does not say crucified, the ordinary word and the one a Roman like Cornelius would have expected. He reaches instead for a phrase out of Deuteronomy, “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23): a law every Jew knew, and the standing objection to the whole Christian claim. A crucified Messiah was a cursed Messiah, and that was the end of the argument.

The objection as the description. Peter does not avoid the scandalous word; he puts it in the sermon. Paul later shows what the verse is for: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). From very early on, the church understood that the worst thing about the crucifixion was the point of it. The holy Son of God was counted cursed so that cursed sinners might be counted sons, and the Father who laid the curse on him raised him in glory.

But God raised him on the third day. One conjunction carries the whole gospel: they put him to death; God raised him. In these early sermons the resurrection is consistently something God did to Jesus, which is the language of a verdict. A court had ruled; a higher court set the ruling aside. What men called a curse, God called his Son, and said so by emptying the grave. And he “made him to appear”, literally gave him to become visible: real appearances, to real people, which leads straight into the strangest sentence in the sermon.

In everyday life. When you are tempted to think that God is against you because of your sins, look at the tree and say slowly: he became a curse for me.

What does it mean that Jesus became a curse for us? The curse is God’s just sentence on sin, the opposite of his blessing (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10), and everyone who breaks his law is under it. On the cross Jesus, who had never sinned, took that sentence in our place: God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: the penalty was real, the substitute was Christ, and the debt was paid in full. So if you trust in him, there is no curse left for you. It fell on him at Golgotha, and the empty tomb is God’s announcement that it has been exhausted.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus showed himself not to everyone but to chosen witnesses, who ate and drank with him; the news was to spread by their testimony, not by spectacle.

Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses. An unlikely thing for the inventor of a story to include: a man fabricating a resurrection would hardly concede that the risen figure was not shown to the public. Peter raises the difficulty himself. Why not to everybody? Scripture does not fully say, and it is honest to admit it. But a public appearance in the temple courts would have compelled a belief forced on the unwilling, and God’s way is to give sufficient evidence to those who will testify rather than overwhelming evidence to those who will not. And there was to be a definite, countable body of witnesses who could be found and questioned, not a rumour everybody had heard from somebody (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). God spreads the news by witness, because faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29).

Who ate and drank with him. The proof Peter chooses is not “We saw him”, but meals. A hallucination shared by a dozen men does not take bread and hand it round. The risen Christ ate broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:41–43) and made breakfast on a beach (John 21:12–13). Ghosts do not eat, and no lash or sword could talk the apostles out of what they had seen.

A body at a table. The Lord of glory kept the habits of friendship on the far side of the grave. His resurrection is not a rumour of survival but a body at a table, and the table is not finished: he will drink the fruit of the vine new with his people in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29).

In everyday life. When doubts come, go back to the evidence the chosen witnesses gave: read Luke 24 or 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as testimony from men who had breakfast with the risen Lord.

Does it matter whether the resurrection was physical? Everything depends on it. If Christ was raised only as a spirit, death has not been defeated, only survived, and our bodies have no future. But the body laid in the tomb came out of it, transformed and glorified, with the marks of the nails still in its hands (John 20:27). That is why Christians bury their dead in hope, and why Paul could say that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). Because he rose bodily, we will too.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus is the appointed Judge of all people, and the same Jesus offers forgiveness now to everyone who believes in him. Peter’s last two sentences hold the whole of what the church has to say.

Judge of the living and the dead. The harder sentence comes first: this man will judge the human race (17:31; John 5:22), and the living and the dead closes every exit. Yet it belongs to the good news, when you consider the alternative: a universe in which nothing is ever finally called what it is, where the killer and the killed go into the same silence. What makes judgment terrifying is not that there is a judge but that we are in the dock. It is the holy God refusing to call evil good, and that same holiness is why the forgiveness in the next sentence could only be paid for by a cross.

To him all the prophets bear witness. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27). The God-fearers in that room had heard the prophets read in the synagogue, and Peter may have had in mind the Servant pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5) and the new covenant in which God says, “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). Forgiveness was what the prophets promised; Peter tells them where it is found.

Everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Look at the width of it. Everyone: not every Jew, not every circumcised person, everyone. Who believes in him: not achieves, qualifies or is born into; faith alone, not circumcision, law-keeping or good works. Receives forgiveness: a gift received, not a wage earned. Through his name: on his account, not ours. Paul’s word for it is justification: the Judge’s verdict that a guilty person stands forgiven and in the right with him, not because he has become good, but because Christ’s death has paid for his sin and Christ’s righteousness is counted to him (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Everyone is very nearly the last word Peter says before the Holy Spirit interrupts him, God’s way of saying that the word meant what it said.

The Judge is the Saviour. That is the only way anybody could survive that judgment: the bench before which we must stand is occupied by the one who bore our sentence, and he offers forgiveness now, in a front room in Caesarea, before the day comes. This is the answer to Cornelius’s prayers.

In everyday life. When you are careless about sin, remember that Jesus is the Judge. When you are crushed by guilt, remember that the Judge is the one who forgives, and that what he counts to you is his own perfect obedience, not your uneven record.

How do I know if I have really believed? Believing in Christ is not a feeling to measure but a trust to place. Ask: Do I rely on Jesus alone, and not on my goodness, to be accepted by God? Do I believe he died for my sins and rose again? Am I turning from sin to follow him, however falteringly? If so, the promise of this verse is yours. Assurance rests not on the strength of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust; weak faith in a strong Saviour saves as surely as strong faith. And the evidence that it is real will grow: love for Christ, a hatred of sin, and a desire to obey him (1 John 5:13).

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments or works, and many who hold this love Christ sincerely.

This commentary’s view: forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and here the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44): justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter is still speaking, God pours out his Spirit on the Gentiles who believe, before any baptism, circumcision or law-keeping, and the Jewish believers are amazed.

While Peter was still saying these things. A momentous sermon is cut off by the Holy Spirit. As soon as they heard that everyone who believes receives forgiveness, they believed, and God sealed it. No appeal, no prayer to repeat; nobody baptised first, circumcised, or pledged to keep the law. God simply does not wait (Galatians 3:2).

The believers from among the circumcised were amazed. The six Jewish Christians Peter brought had believed for some time that Jesus was the Messiah; they had not remotely believed this. It is a mercy that Luke recorded their amazement. Their Scriptures had foretold the inclusion of the Gentiles and their Lord had sent them to the end of the earth, yet when God did it in front of them they stood with their mouths open. That is a comfort to anyone whose first reaction to a work of God was bewilderment, not faith. It neither stopped God nor disqualified the six; they went back to Jerusalem and told what they had seen.

Even on the Gentiles. The Father had promised through Joel to pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and in a Roman parlour all flesh came to include soldiers, servants and a centurion’s relatives, uncircumcised, before anyone could earn the gift or argue about it. The Spirit came on Jewish believers at Pentecost (2:1–4), then on Samaritans (8:14–17), and now on Gentiles, with Peter present each time the gospel crossed a new boundary. That is why Peter rests his defence in Jerusalem on this moment (11:17).

Sealed in his name. The Spirit fell the moment the name of Jesus had been offered to everyone who believes in him. Jesus had sent his apostles to proclaim forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (Luke 24:47), and said the Spirit would glorify him (John 16:14). In Caesarea the two promises met: Christ’s Spirit, poured out from his throne (2:33), came down on Gentiles before the sentence was finished, the risen Lord setting his own seal on his own gospel. A seal is an owner’s mark: this is genuine, and this is mine. By giving the Spirit, God marked these Gentiles as his own and guaranteed their inheritance (Ephesians 1:13–14).

In everyday life. Expect God to be at work when his word is spoken, even before the speaker has finished. When you share the gospel, you are not the one who makes it effective; the Spirit is.

Is this a second experience after conversion? The Spirit fell the moment they believed; there was no second step. This was the Gentile Pentecost, God showing the church that Gentiles too received the Spirit on believing, and as an event it was unrepeatable. Pentecostal Christians read it as a pattern for a later baptism in the Spirit; but Peter himself says that God gave them the same gift “when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ” (11:17). They are our brothers, and their longing to be filled with the Spirit is right; the question between us is only whether Scripture makes it a separate, later step.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles speak in tongues and magnify God, the sign of Pentecost given again, so that the Jewish believers can see that God has received them just as he received the first disciples.

Speaking in tongues. How did anybody know the Spirit had fallen? The sign was the same as in Jerusalem (2:4, 11), recognisable at once by a man who had been there. Peter will tell the church that “the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning” (11:15), and the council that God made no distinction (15:8–9).

The demonstration was for Jerusalem. God could have converted that household quietly. Instead he gave a sign describable only in the words already used of Pentecost, in front of six Jewish witnesses. It settled the question before the argument began: there was no case left for treating Gentile believers as second-class members, accepted only if circumcised and kept at a separate table. God had decided publicly, and the church spent years catching up.

Extolling God. Extolling here means magnifying (megalynontōn), as at Pentecost. Moments earlier this household had heard that a man hanged on a tree had been raised and appointed Judge, and that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness. Their first praise, in languages nobody had taught them, was praise for that, as Mary had magnified the Lord for the same Christ (Luke 1:46): a foretaste of the multitude from every nation crying, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

In everyday life. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise. Take five minutes today simply to tell God what he has done, without asking for anything.

Were these tongues real languages, and is speaking in tongues the evidence of the Spirit? Since this was “just as on us at the beginning” (11:15), they were most likely real languages, as at Pentecost. They were a sign for the Jewish believers that God had accepted Gentiles, not the proof of the Spirit for every later Christian. Many Christians believe the gift continues today, and they are our brothers; the more likely reading is that it belonged to those foundational moments, because in Acts tongues accompany the gospel’s crossing of new boundaries, and the New Testament presents such signs as God’s confirming of the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4).

Then how do I know I have the Spirit if I have not spoken in tongues? By the signs Scripture gives every believer. The Spirit is present wherever a person confesses from the heart that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), cries out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), loves other Christians (1 John 4:13), and bears his fruit: love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). Paul asks whether all speak with tongues, and expects the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so the reverse is also true: if you trust Christ and belong to him, the Spirit is yours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God has given these Gentiles the Spirit, no one can refuse them baptism; Peter commands it at once and stays on as their guest. The sign follows the reality, and the wall is truly down.

Can anyone withhold water? Aimed less at the room than at the six men behind Peter, and through them at Jerusalem, the question is unanswerable. Withhold (kōlysai) means prevent, the word in the eunuch’s question by the roadside, “What prevents me from being baptized?” (8:36). These people have received the Holy Spirit just as we have: if God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign? Peter does not send to Jerusalem for a ruling, impose a probation, or require circumcision, which the church will argue about for years. He refuses to be more cautious than God.

He commanded them. The language of an order, which the head of that household would have recognised. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit.

In the name of Jesus Christ. This is no contradiction of Jesus’ command to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and no support for the teaching (sometimes called Jesus Only) that treats the phrase as a rival formula and denies the Trinity. Luke is describing the baptism’s character: Christian baptism, marking a person as now Jesus’ own, as distinct from John’s. To be baptised into his name is to be baptised into the whole triune God, and this very scene shows the Father anointing (v. 38), the Son saving and the Spirit falling (v. 44). So we baptise with the Lord’s own words, as the church has from the earliest days (the Didache, an early Christian manual from around AD 100, already prescribes them).

The Spirit before the water. These people received the Spirit before they were baptised, so the Spirit and forgiveness come by faith, and baptism follows as the sign and the Lord’s command, not as the means. Luke gives no one fixed order (compare 2:38; 8:16–17; 19:5–6), but here the Spirit did not wait for the water.

Then they asked him to remain for some days. The quiet triumph of the chapter: a Jewish apostle who days earlier would never have entered a Gentile house stays on as a guest, eating at that table. Jerusalem will complain of exactly this (11:3).

Under a new name. Roman soldiers swore their oath in the emperor’s name, and Cornelius had served for years under Caesar’s. Now he went down into the water under another, and came up owned by a better Master, who had bought him with his own blood (20:28). The promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, was kept that afternoon in one Gentile family, and in every family gathered in since. Every believer from every nation stands in a line that runs back through that house by the sea, and the God who swore an oath to Abraham kept it in Abraham’s greater Son.

In everyday life. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Refuse to create second-class Christians in your church by look, tone or seating plan.

If baptism does not save, why does it matter so much? Because Christ commanded it, and obedience to him is never optional (Matthew 28:19). Baptism is his appointed sign of union with him in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), a public confession that you belong to him, and the doorway into the visible fellowship of his church. It does not make you a Christian; it marks you as one. A believer who has never been baptised is not lost, but he is disobeying a plain command of his Lord and missing a means of grace by which Christ strengthens faith.

Does the baptism of a whole household support infant baptism? The household here were those who heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (vv. 44, 46), so all were believers. Christians who baptise infants see in household baptisms a covenant pattern including children, reasoning that as Israel’s sons received circumcision, the children of believers should receive the covenant sign; but this household, at least, was made up of believers. That is why the church baptises those who profess faith, while honouring the paedobaptist brothers who read the household texts differently.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). Acts 10 shows the means: the preaching of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him, and in Cornelius’s house that intention breaks into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home were brought together by two visions thirty miles apart.

Now: Every generation of the church is tempted to rebuild walls that God has torn down. The divisions that feel most natural (racial, cultural, economic) are the likeliest new versions of the old divide between Jew and Gentile. What God has made clean, do not call common.

keyVerse.quote: To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.
keyVerse.note: This is the sentence the whole chapter was arranged to deliver, and the Holy Spirit fell on the hearers as Peter spoke it. Its widest word is “everyone”: Jew or Gentile, devout or not, all come in the same way, by believing in Jesus and receiving forgiveness through his name. It answers both the wall Peter had to cross and the question of Cornelius’s piety: neither nation nor goodness brings anyone in, only Christ.

10.reflection:
Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, yet he was told to send for a man who would bring him a message by which he would be saved (vv. 1–6; 11:14). Why do good and sincere people still need Christ? How should that shape the way you pray for, and speak to, decent people around you who do not yet believe?

Peter’s “By no means, Lord” (v. 14) came from a lifetime of real obedience. Are there habits or convictions, once right, that now keep you at a distance from people Christ has welcomed? How can we tell a command of Scripture from a custom we should let go?

Peter told a Gentile household plainly that he had been raised to treat them as unclean, and that God had shown him otherwise (v. 28). Which people are you most inclined to avoid or look down on, and what one step could you take this month to cross that wall?

Cornelius’s household gathered “in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord” (v. 33), and the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking. How would it change your listening to sermons and your reading of the Bible to come with that expectation?

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
