Where we are. In chapter 10 Peter preached Christ to the centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit fell on a Gentile household as at Pentecost. Now the news reaches Jerusalem. Then Luke follows the believers scattered after Stephen’s death (8:1–4) to Antioch, the church that will send out Paul’s missions (chapter 13).

The message. Turning to God is God’s own gift, and he gives it to people of every nation on the same terms: faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Jew and Gentile receive the same Spirit, the same repentance and the same life, and so become one people, known by one name, Christ’s. Where God has given his gift, his people dare not stand in his way.

Why it was said. Many of Luke’s readers were Gentile believers or Jews in mixed churches (see the introduction). They needed to know that their welcome was no later compromise or idea of Paul’s, but God’s own doing, accepted with praise by the church in Jerusalem.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the verdict in Jerusalem. Criticised for eating with uncircumcised men (vv. 1–3), Peter tells what happened in order, his own refusal included, with six witnesses: God gave Gentiles the Spirit just as at the beginning (vv. 4–17). The critics fall silent and glorify God (v. 18). Then the same truth at work in Antioch. Believers scattered by persecution speak only to Jews (v. 19), but some begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and many believe (vv. 20–21). Barnabas rejoices at God’s grace and fetches Saul, and a year of teaching builds a church whose members the city calls Christians (vv. 22–26). When a famine is foretold, that Gentile church feeds the believers in Judea (vv. 27–30): the unity Peter defended becomes bread.

Where it leads. Every step is the work of the risen Christ. His word Peter remembers (v. 16); in him Jews and Gentiles believe (v. 17); exalted to God’s right hand, he gives repentance (5:31), now to Gentiles too (v. 18). He is the Lord preached in Antioch (v. 20), whose hand turns hearts (v. 21) and whose name the new church is given (v. 26). The table Peter was blamed for sharing is a picture of his own: the one who “receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2) welcomes people from every nation as his own.

For us. No one is saved by background or sincerity, and no one who believes is a second-class Christian. Invite the person you would hesitate to sit down with, rejoice at God’s grace in unlikely people, speak of the Lord Jesus to whoever is in front of you, and let your giving show that you belong to one family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself settled whether Gentiles could belong to his people without becoming Jews, and the church in Jerusalem bowed to his verdict with praise. Criticised for eating with uncircumcised men (vv. 1–3), Peter tells the story in order: the vision he refused, the voice that declared clean what God had cleansed, the messengers who arrived at that very moment and the Spirit’s command, with six witnesses beside him (vv. 4–12). Cornelius had been promised a message by which he would be saved, and as Peter began to speak the Spirit fell on the Gentiles just as at Pentecost (vv. 13–16). Who could stand in God’s way (v. 17)? The critics fall silent and glorify God for granting the Gentiles repentance that leads to life (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel’s Reach and the Church’s Lag

This passage shows not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken (see vv. 1–2). God settles the question not by a new decree but by doing the thing in public, before witnesses who could be questioned, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct, which is treated fully at v. 3.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter answered a hostile hearing by telling what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He pulled no rank. Now: In a disputed matter that is still the strongest thing available. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is hard to answer (on the claim with nothing checkable attached, see v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news that Gentiles had received the word of God reached Jerusalem before Peter did, and some Jewish believers met him with criticism instead of praise. The best news in the province became a dispute among sincere people.

Had received the word of God. The news travelled faster than the man: by the time Peter came up to the city, the whole province had heard a version. To receive the word is Luke’s language for welcoming the gospel in faith (8:14; 17:11).

The circumcision party. Literally “those of the circumcision”: here, it seems, Jewish believers in Jerusalem who held that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people (15:1, 5). Paul uses the same phrase of the men whose arrival at Antioch made Peter get up from a Gentile table (Galatians 2:12). (On the phrase, see the uncertain wording below.)

Criticized him. They took issue with him (diekrinonto). At root the verb means to separate or to sort one thing from another, and Peter will turn it back on them (see vv. 11–12).

Being fair to them. These men were not inventing a prejudice. They were defending a boundary God had drawn himself, in writing, which faithful Israelites had died rather than cross. These were serious men who had not yet been told what God had decided.

The circumcision made without hands. Their question is answered, in the end, by Christ himself. Circumcision marked a man as belonging to the covenant people. Paul would later tell Gentile believers that in Christ they had been “circumcised with a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11–12): the old sinful self put off, because they had been buried and raised with him. What the knife marked on the outside, Christ accomplishes within. The Gentiles in Caesarea lacked nothing the sign pointed to: they had been given Christ.

No faction could call it back. The word of the Lord is never bound (2 Timothy 2:9); it does not return to him empty but accomplishes what he purposes (Isaiah 55:11). He spoke Christ into a Gentile house, and the house believed. He is speaking him still into houses the church has argued about.

Is it wrong to question a Christian leader? No, and this passage shows it can be right. These believers did not gossip about Peter or split the church; they raised the matter with him directly, and he answered patiently. The Bereans were praised for checking even Paul’s teaching against the Scriptures (17:11). Question openly, not in whispers; by Scripture, not by preference. And be ready, as these men were in the end, to be persuaded and to praise God when you are shown to be wrong.

Uncertain wording. In 10:45 “those of the circumcision” simply meant the Jewish believers who had come with Peter, and at this stage almost every believer in Jerusalem was circumcised. So here it may mean Jewish believers in general, or already the stricter group of 15:1, 5. The ESV’s “circumcision party” takes the second view, which fits the complaint; either way, the objection came from inside the church.
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The complaint was about a meal, because in that world to eat with someone was to accept him as one of your own. They do not say, “You preached to Gentiles,” or “You baptised uncircumcised men,” the larger question that will dominate the council in chapter 15.

Eating as a verdict. In the ancient world a shared table was the plainest public statement two people could make about each other. A Jew could trade with a Gentile, serve under one and argue with one; sitting down to supper said, in front of everybody, that you belonged to one company. If Peter can sit at Cornelius’s table, the wall is down, and everything else follows.

The charge laid against his Master. Peter had heard the complaint before. The Pharisees and scribes grumbled at Jesus in almost the same words: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). Jesus answered with three parables of the lost being found and celebrated. The charge against Peter is the charge against his Lord, and the best thing that could be said of either; a church never accused of it has stopped doing what Jesus did. He ate with tax collectors, received a sinful woman’s tears at a Pharisee’s dinner, and on the night he was betrayed broke bread with the man who would deny him. Now he spreads a table for people from every nation and calls it his own supper. Who could ever be worthy to sit there? None of us. That is why it is grace.

The same man, later. Peter wins this argument completely. Some years later, at Antioch, he is eating with Gentile believers as a matter of course when men arrive from this same party, and he gets up from the table. The other Jewish believers follow, even Barnabas, until Paul confronts him in front of everybody because his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).

Where Christian failure lives. A conviction can be argued, defended in public and praised by the church, and still not have reached the part of a man that decides where he sits at dinner. Peter’s theology was right in chapter 11 and his feet were wrong in Galatians, and that gap is where most Christian failure lives. Paul names what moved Peter’s feet: he was afraid of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:12). The good opinion of the right people is one of the oldest idols of the religious heart, and the only cure is a heart more sure of Christ’s approval than of anyone else’s (Galatians 1:10): an approval won by his perfect obedience and counted as ours (Romans 5:19), which no failure at a table can undo.

In everyday life. Who would you be uncomfortable being seen eating with? Not in theory, but in your actual town, with your actual friends watching. That is the person to invite.

If Peter could fail like that, how can I hope to stand? By the same grace that restored Peter every time he fell. He denied Christ and was restored; he withdrew from the Gentiles and was corrected, and years later he calls Paul “our beloved brother” (2 Peter 3:15). Your standing rests not on never failing but on Christ, who keeps those the Father has given him (John 10:28–29). Meanwhile, close the gap on purpose: notice where your table, your friendships and your diary contradict what you say you believe, and let a faithful friend tell you when they do.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter answers his critics not with an argument but with an orderly account of what God did, beginning with a vision he had not sought.

In order. The word (kathexēs) is the one Luke used of his own orderly account (Luke 1:3). Peter tells it as he lived it, from the roof onwards, without quoting Scripture or appealing to his office. An argument meets a counter-argument and both sides go home unmoved; an orderly account with witnesses present must be accepted or called a lie.

Something like a great sheet. It began not with an idea of Peter’s, which the circumcision party would be entitled to object to, but on a roof at midday, when the whole thing came down on him from outside. He uses the same phrase Luke used in chapter 10 (10:11): even before a hostile room, Peter will not describe it more definitely than he saw it. And he adds: “it came down to me.”

Why Luke tells it again. Luke lets Peter retell a story just told in full because for his readers it was no side issue. Many were Gentile believers, or Jews in churches full of Gentiles, and the question was their own: did they belong to God’s people as they were, or only on sufferance? Luke answers that the welcome of the Gentiles was not Paul’s idea or a later compromise, but God’s doing, recognised first by Peter and then by the whole church in Jerusalem (v. 18). Ancient writers repeated what mattered most, as Luke tells Paul’s conversion three times (chapters 9, 22 and 26).

A witness, not an advocate. Peter is doing exactly what Jesus appointed him to do. “You will be my witnesses,” the Lord had told him (1:8), and a witness does not argue a case; he says what he saw. The apostles testify to what the risen Christ has done, so that their hearers must deal with him and not with them. Even this report, though it begins with a sheet, ends with the Lord’s remembered word (v. 16), faith in the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 17) and Gentiles given repentance that leads to life.

The Lord comes down. The vision came down unasked, as the Son once came down to a manger and a cross, unbidden and unearned; every work of grace has that direction. Sinners do not find him by searching the heavens. He finds them where they are, praying or not praying, and leaves them with nothing to say for themselves except to tell, in order, what he has done.

In everyday life. The best answer to criticism is often not a better argument but a patient, honest account, the parts against yourself included.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter does not soften the command that shocked him; he tells his critics exactly how offensive it was, because its offensiveness is part of the evidence that it came from God and not from him.

Beasts of prey. To law-observant Jews already angry with him, Peter names beasts of prey, wild carnivores, the creatures furthest from anything a Jew would eat: blunter than Luke’s own account (see the textual note below). And looking at it closely: he examined the sheet item by item, and knew exactly what he was being asked to do before he refused.

Making his own case worse. Every instinct would be to soften the account. But Peter’s case rests on the command having come from God, and a softened command is no longer the one that came.

The hardest fact in the apostles’ message. Peter had done this before, in a far greater matter. At Pentecost he did not soften the death of Jesus into a misfortune: they had crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men, and God had made him both Lord and Christ (2:23, 36). The apostles led with the most repellent fact in their message, a Messiah executed on a tree, because it was the fact that saves, and no one inventing a religion to please Jews or Greeks would have chosen it. God’s wisdom has always looked like foolishness, a sheet of unclean beasts, a crucified Messiah, Jews and Gentiles at one table, and has always proved wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).

Should we soften the hard parts of the gospel to make it easier to accept? No. The gospel has an offence that cannot be removed without destroying it: the cross is a stumbling block and folly to the world (1 Corinthians 1:23). We should remove every unnecessary offence, our rudeness, our jargon, our cultural baggage, so that the only stumbling block left is Christ himself. But we may not trim what God has said about sin, judgment, the uniqueness of Christ or the call to repent, because the very hardness of these truths shows they did not come from us. People are not won by a gospel made comfortable, but by a gospel made clear.

Textual note. In Luke’s own account of the vision (10:12) the earliest manuscripts list animals, reptiles and birds; some later ones, followed by the KJV, add wild beasts there too.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter admits that he refused God’s command at first, exactly as his critics would have; what overruled him was the voice from heaven, declaring clean what God had made clean.

By no means, Lord. The shrewdest thing in the speech is simple honesty. Peter puts his own objection on record in the words every man in that room would have used. They believed he had gone soft on the law; he testifies that he defended it to God’s face. He was the man who said no, so whatever changed his mind did not come from himself.

With the blood of a spotless lamb. Peter would later say how God makes people clean. At the council he said that God had cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (15:9), and in his first letter he told Gentile Christians that they had been ransomed from their futile ways not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). The voice on the roof announced not a relaxation of standards but a Lamb sacrificed, whose cleansing reached Gentiles too. Clean means fit to come near the holy God. The food laws were given with the words “be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44–45), and every meal taught Israel that the holy God is not approached on our terms. Christ did not lower that standard; he met it for us, so that a Gentile washed in his blood may draw near with a true heart (Hebrews 10:22).

It is God who justifies. The voice from heaven had the last word, and it always will. God does not need our permission to cleanse what he chooses to cleanse, and his declaration over a sinner washed in Christ cannot be overturned by any accuser. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Does the vision abolish the Old Testament food laws? Its first point is about people: Peter concludes that he should not call any person common or unclean (10:28). But it also reflects what Jesus had already declared (Mark 7:19, where the KJV’s purging all meats is generally read today as Mark’s comment that Jesus declared all foods clean): the food laws, which separated Jew from Gentile, are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and Christians are free to eat any food (Romans 14).

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision came three times, so that neither Peter nor his hearers could put it down to a passing impression. Peter produces the number as evidence, and in that room it was strong.

Drawn up again into heaven. Then it stopped, with no application attached. The application was already walking up the road and would be at the gate within the hour. Peter did not have to work it out. He had to answer the door.

The Lord who asks three times. Three is Peter’s number. Three denials by a charcoal fire; then, on a beach, the risen Jesus asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” and three times gave him his sheep to feed (John 21:15–17). The Lord did not restore him with one question and leave him wondering. Now he speaks three times on a roof, with the same kindness, not exasperation: he knew how many times this man would need to hear it. Christ’s patience is measured not by what we deserve but by what we need.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God timed the messengers to the minute, the Spirit told Peter to go without making distinctions, and Peter took witnesses who could confirm it all.

At that very moment. The sheet has just gone back up, and at that instant three strangers are at the door, sent the day before the vision was given. Nobody arranged that.

Making no distinction. The whole defence turns on that phrase, mēden diakrinanta, the verb Luke used in verse 2 of the men now questioning him. Peter quotes it back to a room doing the very thing it forbade, and does not point it out.

These six brothers. These: they are in the room. Leaving Joppa (10:23), Peter took men who could later say what they had seen. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); he has brought double. “Ask them,” he is saying. Being right is not the same as being believed, and the honest way to handle a claim nobody wants to hear is to make it checkable. And then, plainly: “we entered the man’s house.” The very thing he is accused of, he states as a fact.

All authority, down to the minute. The Lord who sent Peter had told his apostles on what ground he sent them: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:18–19). The Christ who upholds the universe (Hebrews 1:3) also governs the pace of travellers on a coast road, so that his word and his messengers meet at a door, and the Spirit’s “making no distinction” is that commission in its plainest form. Every step on the road to Caesarea was ordered, and so is every step of ours.

In everyday life. The Spirit makes no distinction among those who believe, and neither should the church. Look around your congregation and ask whether any group is quietly treated as second-class: the poor, the new, the foreign, the young, the old. Then do something to bring them in.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Peter was ever sent, God had promised Cornelius a message by which he and his household would be saved: it was the gospel, not his devotion, that saved him.

The angel in his house. Peter supplies Cornelius’s side of the story, and with it something Luke’s account twice held back (10:4–6, 30–32), where the angel’s message stopped at “send to Joppa”.

A message by which you will be saved. Now Peter finishes the sentence, and that clause is his whole defence. Before the vision and the knock at the gate, God had already told a Gentile that a saving message was coming. Peter did not go to Caesarea and then decide that Gentiles could be saved; he was sent to deliver a promise God had made without him.

It settles the question about Cornelius. He was devout, generous and prayerful, and God had noticed all of it; yet the angel said a message was coming by which he would be saved. Sincerity does not save; salvation comes through the gospel (Romans 1:16; 10:14–17).

You and all your household. The promise arrives with a family attached to it: the servants, the soldiers, the relatives Cornelius had gathered (compare 2:39). The whole household heard and believed (10:44).

What the message was. Peter had preached Jesus, hanged on a tree, raised, appointed Judge, through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness (10:38–43). Cornelius’s prayers could reach God’s notice; only Christ could reach his guilt. Peter had already told the council in Jerusalem that “there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (4:12). God did not leave the seeker to his seeking; he sent him the Saviour. God’s love is never content to admire our sincerity from a distance; it comes all the way to save.

Is it not unfair that a sincere man like Cornelius still needed the gospel? Only if salvation were a prize for the most sincere, and it never is. Peter, a lifelong keeper of the law, was saved exactly as Cornelius was, by a gift he had not earned (15:11). The gospel does not shut out the sincere; it shuts out boasting, for the devout and the careless alike. And God moved an angel, a vision and an apostle up the coast to bring him the one message that could save him. That is not a God looking for reasons to keep people out, but one going to great lengths to bring them in.

Can I trust God for my family’s salvation? Pray with great confidence, for God loves to work in families. But Scripture does not promise that every member of a believer’s family will be saved; each must come to Christ himself. Do what Cornelius did: bring your family under the word, gather them where the gospel is preached, live the faith in front of them, and pray for each of them every day. Then leave them with the God who is more willing to save than you are to ask.

Where Christians differ: does “you and all your household” mean that a family is saved together, or support infant baptism? Christians who baptise infants (paedobaptists) see a covenant pattern in the household baptisms of Acts, like circumcision given to Abraham’s sons. This commentary’s view: believer’s baptism, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2). Cornelius’s household heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (10:44–46): believing hearers. Faith does not pass to children automatically; each was saved by hearing and believing, as the households in Acts are described. We gladly honour the many faithful brothers and sisters, perhaps including you if you were baptised as a baby, who read these households the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit fell on the Gentiles as soon as Peter began, exactly as on the apostles at Pentecost, and Peter recognised in it the baptism with the Spirit that Jesus had promised.

As I began to speak. Peter is precise, and the precision is his argument. Luke said the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking (10:44); Peter says it was as he began. He had not finished or called for a response; God did not wait for the rest.

Just as on us at the beginning. Not a lesser or partial gift but the same, and the apostles in the room had been there for the first and could judge. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, the start of a new era, and says that in a Roman officer’s front room the beginning happened again to different people. God does not give Jews one Spirit and Gentiles another; he gives himself, wholly, to all who believe.

I remembered the word of the Lord. The theology arrived as a memory. Watching Gentiles speak in tongues, Peter did not reason his way to a conclusion; a sentence of Jesus from just before the ascension came back to him (1:5) and explained everything he was seeing. The words of Jesus interpret events, not the other way round. He could not look it up; he had what he had heard and kept, as Jesus had promised: the Spirit will “bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26).

In everyday life. A verse learned years ago can surface in a hospital corridor or a hard meeting, uninvited and exactly right. You do not know when you will need what you have stored, but the Spirit does.

What is the baptism with the Spirit? Christ’s act of pouring out his Spirit on his people, uniting them to himself and to one another. John the Baptist could only apply water to the outside; Jesus gives the Spirit, who cleanses and renews from within. Paul says that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). So every believer has been baptised with the Spirit, and the proof is not a particular experience but faith in Christ and a life being changed by him. If you trust in Jesus, the promise of Acts 1:5 has been kept in you (on whether this baptism is a second stage, see v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had given Gentile believers the very gift he gave the apostles, on the same ground of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, so to refuse them would have been to oppose God himself. The gift came with faith, not with circumcision or law-keeping.

When we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. Peter gives the full title. What the apostles and Cornelius’s household had in common was not a nation, a law or a history, but a Person believed in. Men who had walked with Jesus for three years and Gentiles who had first heard of him that afternoon received the identical gift, because it comes not from the believer’s past but from the Lord he trusts. To refuse those who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ would be to refuse the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who had given them his Spirit.

Who was I that I could stand in God’s way? The defence ends not with a claim to be right, to have authority or to have weighed the matter, but with a plea of incapacity. The leading apostle says in effect: “What was I supposed to do, stop him?” Stand in God’s way is kōlysai, hinder, prevent: the same word as in “Can anyone withhold water” (10:47). To refuse those whom God has accepted is to fight God (5:39).

What it does not mean. This verse is often quoted in church disputes to end discussion rather than resolve it. It is not a formula for winning arguments by claiming divine backing. It works here because of everything attached to it: a vision repeated three times, an independent vision given to a man thirty miles away, three messengers who arrived at the precise moment, an explicit word from the Spirit, six witnesses who can be questioned, and a public sign identical to the one the apostles had seen at the beginning. Only after thirteen verses of evidence does Peter draw the conclusion. A man who says God told him and produces none of that has said something quite different. And today, with the apostolic witness complete, the test of any claim is the written word of God.

Where Christians differ: is the baptism with the Spirit a second stage after conversion? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians look for a later baptism with the Spirit, usually shown by tongues, pointing to the Samaritans (8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (19:1–7), who received the Spirit after believing. This commentary’s view: Peter equates what Jesus promised (1:5) with what Cornelius received when he believed: the same gift. Samaria and Ephesus were moments when the gospel crossed new boundaries, and Paul teaches that every believer has been baptised in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). So the baptism with the Spirit is given to every believer at conversion. Many Pentecostal believers are earnest and fruitful Christians; the disagreement is about how to read these chapters, not whether the Spirit is real and powerful today.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The critics fell silent and then praised God, confessing that repentance that leads to life is his gift and that he has given it to Gentiles too. Luke then shows how slowly that agreed truth changed where believers actually took the gospel.

They fell silent. Silence first: the objection simply runs out. Then praise, from criticism to worship, the best possible response to correction.

God has granted repentance. Not “the Gentiles have repented”, but “God has granted”. Repentance is God’s gift (2 Timothy 2:25), and they praise him not because a barrier fell but because people were given life.

One part for the whole. Only repentance is named, yet these Gentiles had believed (vv. 17, 21). Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning to Christ, from sin and to the Saviour, and neither is real without the other. Scripture sometimes names both, “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15); sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19); sometimes only faith (“believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,” Acts 16:31). Never build a doctrine on the absence of a word, as if this verse made faith unnecessary, or Acts 16:31 repentance. And the turning itself is God’s gift, as faith is also called “the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8; compare Philippians 1:29).

The gift from the throne. Peter had told the Sanhedrin that God exalted Jesus at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins (5:31). Now the church hears that the exalted Christ gives the same thing to Gentiles. Repentance that leads to life is not a mood a sinner works up but a gift from the throne of the Saviour who died, and the life it leads to is his own risen life. The tears over sin, the first turn of the face toward Christ, the whole road from death to life: all of it is granted, in Jerusalem, in Caesarea, soon in Antioch, and still today. There is no heart so hard that he cannot give it repentance, and no nation he has not purposed to give it to.

If repentance is God’s gift, what am I supposed to do? Repent. God gives repentance not around you but in you, so that you yourself turn from sin, freely and genuinely. You are never told to wait until you feel repentant; you are commanded to repent and believe (17:30), and the very desire to obey that command is the first sign that God is granting it. And if you are praying for someone who shows no sign of repentance, this verse is your warrant. You cannot argue anyone into it, but you can ask the God who grants it to grant it to them.

Those who were scattered. Luke goes back several years to the persecution that killed Stephen and picks up the thread of 8:1–4. The scattered believers travelled as far as Phoenicia, the coast around Tyre and Sidon, and Cyprus, and Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire, with a large Jewish community.

No one except Jews. After verse 18 it lands like a cold draught: the church has just praised God for granting the Gentiles repentance, and Luke reports that believers had carried the gospel across three regions and told nobody but their own kind. The gap shows how long it takes for a truth the church has agreed on to change what believers actually do.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Jerusalem had agreed in principle, ordinary believers now did in practice, and the first great Gentile church was born. Most of those scattered by persecution spoke only to Jews (v. 19), but some men of Cyprus and Cyrene preached the Lord Jesus to Greeks in Antioch, and the Lord’s hand brought a great number to faith (vv. 20–21). Barnabas, sent from Jerusalem, saw God’s grace and rejoiced, then fetched Saul for a year of teaching, and there the disciples were first called Christians (vv. 22–26). When Agabus foretold a famine, the Gentile church sent relief to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul (vv. 27–30): the new unity in Christ shown in love.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the New Testament’s picture of a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with ordinary believers doing the obvious thing; Jerusalem did not plan it but recognised it afterwards; it was built up by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first act as a church was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Within two chapters it will give away its two finest teachers. A church is not measured only by what it gathers but by what it is prepared to give away.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The step that opened the gospel to the Gentile city was taken by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Now: Much of the work that matters most in any generation is done by people who will never appear in an account of it, who simply speak of Christ to whoever is in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene began telling Greeks in Antioch about the Lord Jesus, and the Lord’s own power brought a great number of them to faith. The whole future of the church is in this exception: “But there were some of them.”

Men of Cyprus and Cyrene. Luke tells us where they came from, not who they were: Greek-speaking Jews from Cyprus and from Cyrene in North Africa, used to living among Gentiles. Lucius of Cyrene (13:1) may have been among them, but Luke, who names dozens of minor figures, leaves these men unnamed. God delights to use the unknown, so that the glory is plainly his. Their names are not in Acts, but they are written in heaven.

Cyrene again. Men of Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem and were among those who argued with Stephen and could not withstand him (6:9–10). Luke does not say these are the same men. But the city that supplied some of Stephen’s opponents also supplied some of the first men to take the step his preaching had pointed toward.

No vision, no angel. Peter needed a sheet let down three times before he would enter a Gentile house. These men talked to Greeks because there were Greeks there. They already had their commission (1:8), and they obeyed it.

The hand of the Lord. An Old Testament phrase for God’s power actively at work (Isaiah 59:1). And they believed and turned, faith and repentance together, as in verse 18. Heaven’s verdict on the initiative of unnamed men was to bless it enormously.

Preaching the Lord Jesus. To Gentiles they did not start with “Jesus is the Messiah”, a Jewish title that meant little in a Greek city, but with “Jesus is Lord”, which every Greek understood and which claimed everything. Antioch was full of lords: Apollo at Daphne, the mystery cults, the emperor himself. Jesus went there in the mouths of his people, and was with them as he had promised (Matthew 28:20). Wise evangelism adapts its words, not its message.

Do I need a special call to tell people about Jesus? No; every Christian already has one. The command to make disciples (Matthew 28:19) and the promise of the Spirit for witness (1:8) belong to the whole church. Some are called and gifted to preach and lead, but speaking of Christ to your neighbour needs no ordination. These men had no title, no training we know of and no instructions, and they started the church that sent the first missionaries into the Gentile world.

Uncertain wording. The manuscripts divide between “Hellenists” and “Greeks”. Elsewhere in Acts “Hellenists” means Greek-speaking Jews (6:1; 9:29), but whichever word Luke wrote, the sense requires Gentiles, since this sentence is the contrast to verse 19.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem sent Barnabas to look at the new church, and he saw God’s grace in it, rejoiced, and urged them all to hold fast to the Lord.

They sent Barnabas. As with Samaria (8:14), unplanned advance brings a delegation, and the choice of delegate settles the outcome. Others would have come looking for a fault. They sent Barnabas, a Cypriot like some of the evangelists, and the son of encouragement (4:36).

He saw the grace of God. What did he see? A room of uncircumcised Greeks with pagan backgrounds and no synagogue training, worshipping the God of Israel, taught by nobody in particular. In that untidy crowd Barnabas saw what was really going on: God’s grace at work, plain enough to see shining.

He was glad. Not relieved, not cautiously satisfied: glad, a word from the same family as the grace he saw (chairō, charis). He had earned his name twice already, selling a field for the poor and vouching for Saul when nobody else would. He earns it a third time simply by being pleased: the Gentile mission survived its inspection because the inspector was capable of delight.

With steadfast purpose. Exhorted (parekalei) is the root of his nickname: he encouraged them. With steadfast purpose is literally “with purpose of heart”, a settled inward intention. He does not begin by correcting them, but tells a young church the one thing it will most need.

Holding fast to the Lord. The Lord they are to remain with is the Lord Jesus they had just turned to (v. 21), and the charge is the one Jesus gave his own disciples: abide in me, and I in you, for apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:4–5). Barnabas does not give a young church a programme. He points it to a Person and tells it to hold on.

How do I remain faithful to the Lord? Not “try harder” but remain: stay where grace has put you. And the one you are holding is holding you: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). Inside that safety, steadfast purpose looks like ordinary things done on purpose. Settle it again each morning. Tell him in a sentence that you are his today, before the day decides for you. Stay near his word. These new believers sat under teaching for a whole year (v. 26); a little Scripture read daily, with a prayer, keeps you near the voice that called you. Stay with his people. Faithfulness withers alone; Barnabas exhorted a church. Come back quickly. When you fall, do not keep your distance until you feel better; come back the same day, because the Lord Jesus has already paid for this sin too. Holding fast is not gripping by willpower but coming back, again and again, to a Lord who has never let go.

How do I see the grace of God in other Christians? Look for what only God could have done. A new believer’s doctrine may be muddled and his habits rough, but if he loves Christ, wants the word, is beginning to hate his sin and loves God’s people, you are looking at the grace of God. Name it to him and thank God for it aloud; then correction, when needed, comes from someone he knows is on his side. Barnabas did not skip the teaching (v. 26), but he started with gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barnabas could rejoice in another man’s harvest because he was a good man, full of the Spirit and of faith, and through such a man many more were added to the Lord.

A good man. Not brilliant or well connected, but good. The sentence sits between a man rejoicing over somebody else’s work and going to fetch somebody better at teaching than himself: a man with no jealousy in him.

Full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. Not a momentary filling for a single task (Acts has those too, 4:8, 31; 13:9) but a settled condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit governs his character, words and deeds, and the church can see the fruit. The same is said of Jesus (Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5): to be full of the Spirit is to be deeply like Christ. Nor is it a rare distinction. Every believer is commanded to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continuous filling sought by letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Colossians 3:16), praying, obeying, and walking by the Spirit rather than grieving or quenching him (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 5:19).

Borrowed from the Good Shepherd. Barnabas’s goodness is borrowed. Jesus is the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Barnabas’s goodness is that Shepherd’s in miniature: he gave away what he owned (4:36–37), went after a man everyone else avoided (9:27), and rejoiced over sheep he had not gathered himself. So his goodness added people to the Lord rather than to himself. Christ is the fountain, and every saint called good is a cup filled from it. He does not make sinners proud of their goodness, but glad over others, quick to fetch help and content to be forgotten, so that the people they serve look past them to him.

Is goodness enough to make a person a Christian? No. Barnabas was good because he was full of the Spirit and of faith, not the other way round. No one is good enough by nature to be accepted by God; “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18). This goodness is the fruit of grace, the Spirit forming Christ’s likeness in a forgiven sinner, and so it is open to every believer. You cannot make yourself good by effort, but if you belong to Christ, the Spirit who made Barnabas good is at work in you, and you can ask him daily to fill you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barnabas went and fetched Saul to share the work, a year of patient teaching built the church, and the city gave the believers a name that tied them to Christ.

To look for Saul. The verb means to search hard, to hunt up and down (anazētēsai). It had been years since Saul was sent to Tarsus (9:30). Barnabas travelled a hundred miles on the strength of remembering a man, knowing whom God had called to the Gentiles (9:15), and did not try to keep the work for himself.

The second time. The first was in Jerusalem, when every believer was afraid of Saul and Barnabas brought him to the apostles (9:27). Now years of obscurity end because one man would not leave him there. Humanly speaking, those two acts gave us Paul’s mission and letters.

Making room for a greater man. The leader of the most promising church in the world fetches a teacher who will eclipse him. Within two chapters Luke writes “Paul and his companions” (13:13). He went anyway, in the spirit of John the Baptist: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

For a whole year. Not a campaign but a year in one place, teaching. The launching point of the Gentile mission was built by twelve months of ordinary instruction from two men who stayed put.

First called Christians. The name (Christianos) is a Greek word with a Latin ending, the form used for the followers or partisans of somebody, as people spoke of Herod’s men as Herodians (Mark 3:6). It was very probably a nickname coined by outsiders (see the box below), and the believers came to wear it gladly (26:28; 1 Peter 4:16).

What the neighbours had concluded. That these people were somebody’s: outsiders could not describe them without his name. And Christ is not a surname but a title, the Greek for Messiah, the King God had promised (2:36), so the nickname meant, in effect, the King’s people. A church of Jews and Gentiles needed a new name: neither Jew nor Gentile, but Christ’s.

Called by his name. The Son of God has given his name to a people from every nation, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). To be a Christian is to be Christ’s, bought with his blood, sealed by his Spirit, named with his name: no higher title exists, and he gives it freely to sinners.

What makes someone a Christian? Not a family, a culture, a membership or a moral code, but belonging to Christ by faith: you are a Christian if you have trusted Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord, and he has made you his own. Many call themselves Christian because of where they were born; the neighbours in Antioch used the name because of how people lived and whom they talked about. The question to ask yourself is not whether you have the label, but whether you have the Lord.

Uncertain wording. Luke’s verb (chrēmatisai) means to bear a name, and does not say who first used it. Most think outsiders coined it: believers called themselves disciples, brothers or saints, and the other two New Testament uses come from an outsider’s lips (26:28) and a setting of persecution (1 Peter 4:16). Whether it began in mockery or simply as a label, we cannot tell.
verseByVerse.note: “Christians” means “Christ’s people” — probably a nickname given by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Agabus, a prophet from Jerusalem, the Spirit warned the church at Antioch of a great famine, and it came, as Luke notes, in the reign of Claudius. What Agabus supplied was not doctrine but a specific, checkable warning, given so that the church could act.

Prophets came down. Luke needs no explanation: prophets were a recognised ministry in the early church (13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11) in the years when its foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20). Agabus appears again in 21:10–11, foretelling Paul’s arrest. All the world means the Roman world.

In the days of Claudius. The emperor Claudius ruled from AD 41 to 54, and ancient historians record a series of severe grain shortages in his reign. A famine struck Judea around AD 45 to 48, severe enough that Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and had it shipped to Jerusalem, as Josephus tells. Luke ties his story to history that can be checked.

Jesus had said there would be famines. Jesus had told his disciples there would be famines in various places, and that such things were not to terrify them, for the end would not come at once (Luke 21:9–11). Now the ascended Lord who gives prophets to his church (Ephesians 4:11) gave notice through one of them of a trouble he had foretold, and his people answered it not with panic but with love.

What the warning was for. Not to fill their own storehouses: what follows is a collection, a chance to be generous early. Nothing takes the Lord of history by surprise. As through Joseph, the warning became a means of feeding the hungry. He is the provider, and his care reaches to tomorrow’s bread.

How should I respond if someone tells me he has a word from God for me? Kindly and carefully. Do not mock him; he may be a sincere brother with a different view of the gifts. But test it by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If it contradicts the Bible, reject it. If it repeats what the Bible says, receive it as a reminder, not new revelation. If it tells you something the Bible does not, a person to marry, a job to take, a date something will happen, you are not bound by it. Decide by Scripture, prayer, wise counsel and God’s providence.

Where Christians differ: do men like Agabus exist now? Continuationist Christians (those who hold that all the gifts continue today) believe that prophets like Agabus still speak in the church, pointing to 1 Corinthians 14 and to Christ’s giving of prophets in Ephesians 4:11–13. Others hold that gifts of this kind ceased with the apostolic foundation. This commentary’s view: the second is the better view. The signs and revelatory gifts of Acts accompanied the apostles as the credentials of their foundational witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20); what Agabus foretold came to pass, as true prophecy always did. What both sides agree on is the boundary. Agabus was not adding to Scripture, and nobody treated him as if he were; he gave practical information which the church acted on with its own judgment. Any claim that would correct, supplement or override what is written is a different thing altogether.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record severe famines in his reign, including in Judea.

parallels.desc: Agabus again

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young Gentile church answered the warning with a gift: each disciple gave as he was able, and Barnabas and Saul carried it to the elders in Judea. Watch which way the money goes: the church argued about in Jerusalem pays for the mother church’s food.

To send relief. Relief is diakonia, ministry, service: the new unity in Christ expressed in money. No request came from Jerusalem. The response to prophecy was not speculation but generosity.

Every one according to his ability. Each gave in proportion to what he had, the New Testament’s settled pattern (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:11–12): not equal amounts, but equal sacrifice. Money promises security, and a hand that opens for a hungry brother belongs to someone who has found his security somewhere else (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

To the elders. This is the first mention of elders in the Christian church. The Jerusalem church now had elders alongside the apostles (15:2), men entrusted with its care.

By the hand of Barnabas and Saul. The first joint mission of the partnership that will take the gospel across the empire is not a preaching tour but delivering money to hungry people, carried by trustworthy men, as Paul would later insist such gifts require (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

The collection never stopped. Paul spent years organising exactly this, a fund from Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and gives the reason in a sentence: “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings” (Romans 15:27). It began here.

Bread for the Lord he had persecuted. The money goes to some of the very believers Saul had dragged from their houses. On the Damascus road the risen Lord had asked, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, kindness included: “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). So when Saul walks into Judea with famine relief for the believers he once hunted, he is bringing bread to the Lord he once persecuted. Only the grace of Christ could write such a story.

How much should I give when a need like this famine comes? Scripture gives Christians no fixed percentage, but principles more searching than any. Give regularly (1 Corinthians 16:2), in proportion to what God has given you (2 Corinthians 8:12), cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7), and sacrificially, as the Macedonians gave beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:3). Many find a tenth a helpful starting point, and many who can give more should. Give first to your own church, which feeds you, then to believers in need and to gospel work. The measure is not the amount but the cost, and the motive is the grace of Christ, who though he was rich became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Where Christians differ: how does this visit fit with Paul’s account in Galatians 2? Many equate Galatians 2:1–10 with the council of Acts 15. Others read it as this famine visit, a private meeting with the leaders before the public council. This commentary’s view: the second fits better, since Paul, arguing about circumcision, never mentions the council’s decision. That is partly an argument from silence, and good scholars weigh it differently, but it is a weighty one.

parallels.desc: remember the poor

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. “God has granted repentance that leads to life” (11:18). Repentance is itself God’s gift, and the sinner who receives it really turns (see the note on vv. 18–19). This is the order of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory.
11.examples:
Then: Unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene crossed a boundary and began the church in Antioch.

Now: Antioch is a picture of a healthy sending church: mixed in its people, taught by gifted teachers, quick to meet need, and willing to send its best people out. A church may fairly ask whether it looks more like the anxious critics in Jerusalem or the glad, generous church at Antioch.

keyVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.”
keyVerse.note: This is the verdict the whole chapter turns on: critics become worshippers, and the church confesses that the turning of a sinner to God is God’s gift, given to Gentiles as freely as to Jews. Everything that follows in Antioch, from the preaching to Greeks to the new name and the famine relief, is this verse being lived out.

11.reflection:
The Jerusalem believers objected not to Peter’s preaching but to his eating with Gentiles (v. 3). Why was a shared meal so significant, and whom would you find it hardest to be seen at a table with?

Peter answered his critics by telling, in order and with witnesses, what God had done, including his own refusal (vv. 4–17). What can we learn from this about handling disagreements in the church, and about telling others what God has done for us?

The church praised God that he had “granted repentance that leads to life” (v. 18). How does it change your praying, and your witness, to know that repentance is God’s gift and not something we can produce in anyone?

Barnabas saw the grace of God in a crowd of new Gentile believers and was glad (v. 23), and the church at Antioch gave freely to believers who had once been suspicious of them (vv. 29–30). Where do you need to look for God’s grace in others more gladly, and how could your church show its unity in practical generosity?

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
Where we are. Acts 12 closes the part of the book (chapters 8–12) in which the word spreads from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and Antioch. Luke sets it between Barnabas and Saul taking famine relief from Antioch to Jerusalem (11:29–30) and their return (12:25); after it, Peter leaves the centre of the story and the mission to the nations begins.

The message. The church has no power but prayer, and its enemies have every power but God’s, and God’s is the only power that decides. Kings can kill one apostle, chain another and accept worship, but the King in heaven rescues his servants, brings down the proud and keeps his word growing, in his own wisdom: James dies and Peter goes free, and both are in his hands.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). A church that had just lost an apostle to a king’s sword, and would lose many more, needed to know who really rules, and how to go on praying when no reason is given.

How the chapter makes its case. Herod kills James and, because it pleases the crowd, arrests Peter (vv. 1–4). The church prays earnestly, and on the last night an angel wakes the sleeping Peter, the chains fall off and the iron gate opens of its own accord (vv. 5–11). The praying church tells Rhoda she is out of her mind, until they open the gate and are amazed (vv. 12–17). Herod has the guards executed (vv. 18–19), then at Caesarea lets a crowd hail him as a god and is struck down by an angel of the Lord (vv. 20–23). But the word of God increases and multiplies, and Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark (vv. 24–25).

Where it leads. The chapter is Psalm 2 acted out: the kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs. The family that hunted the child at Bethlehem and mocked him before the cross ends at Caesarea under God’s hand, and the risen Jesus has outlived it, not by escaping death but by dying as the true Passover lamb and rising. Every rescue in the chapter flows from the one prisoner who was not rescued, and the glory Herod stole belongs to the one in whom the voice of God and the voice of a man truly are one.

For us. Pray earnestly, and leave the answer with God, whether it is Peter’s or James’s. Do not fear the powerful or envy their applause; give God the glory. And when the answer comes knocking, open the gate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No king can stop the word of God: the Lord rescues his servants, brings down the proud and keeps his word growing, while his people pray. Herod Agrippa kills James and imprisons Peter to please the crowd (vv. 1–4). The church prays, and on the last night an angel leads Peter out past the guards and through the iron gate (vv. 5–11). The praying church can hardly believe it when he knocks (vv. 12–17). Herod has the guards killed (vv. 18–19), then accepts worship at Caesarea and is struck down by an angel of the Lord (vv. 20–23). But the word of God increases and multiplies, and Barnabas and Saul go back to Antioch with John Mark (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

Here what we teach about prayer is tested: it must be honest, or it will be cruel to the grieving. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; James was buried, and Luke gives no reason (see vv. 1–2). Prayer is not a machine that gives better results the harder we pray. Prayer is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God, who answers according to his own good purposes and does not always explain them. And God answered people who did not expect him to (see vv. 15–16): the power lies not in the praying but in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda’s news was met with you are out of your mind (see vv. 15–16), and the deliverance stood. Now: Many Christians pray without really expecting an answer, and feel like frauds. This chapter is kind to them.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod turns the power of the state against the church and kills James, one of the Twelve; Luke records it in a single sentence and gives no reason.

Herod the king. This is Herod Agrippa I. His grandfather, Herod the Great, tried to kill the child at Bethlehem; his uncle, Herod Antipas, beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus. Raised in Rome among emperors, he was made king of all Judea in AD 41 and worked hard to please the Jews. This is the first persecution of the church by the state rather than the religious leaders.

James the brother of John. Ten words, and one of the Twelve is dead, probably beheaded, around AD 44. Luke gave Stephen a chapter and a half; he gives James, one of the inner three, half a sentence, and wants the reader to feel it.

In the flow. Luke sets Herod’s attack between Barnabas and Saul setting out with famine relief (11:30) and their return (12:25): while a Gentile church was feeding Judea, Judea’s king was killing an apostle. Herod’s sword fell just as the mission to the world was about to begin, and it could not stop it.

No replacement. When Judas fell, a replacement was chosen (1:21–26); when James dies, nobody is. Judas had abandoned his office; James finished his. The Twelve were witnesses of the risen Lord, a foundation laid once and not laid again (Ephesians 2:20), not an office to be handed down.

The cup with the wrath drained. When James and John asked for the two best seats, Jesus asked whether they could drink his cup, and said they would (Mark 10:35–39). James drank it first; John drank it slowly and died old. Not that James would help to pay for sin: the cup Jesus dreaded in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) was the wrath of God against sinners, which he alone could drink, and drank to the bottom. What James drank under Herod’s sword was suffering for his Lord’s name, with every drop of judgment drained out of it. Herod could strike a body on earth; the Head sat at the right hand of God, beyond any king’s reach, receiving his servant home.

The sword was only the usher. James had stood on the mountain when the Lord’s face shone and his clothing became dazzling white (Luke 9:29), and in the garden when that same face was pressed to the ground (Mark 14:33–35). He had seen the glory and the agony. Herod meant the sword as an ending; in the hand of the Lord Jesus it was only the usher, bringing a friend home to the face he had seen shining on the mountain.

Was nobody praying for James? Four verses later the church prays for Peter, and Peter walks free. Luke does not say, but this was the same church, in the same city and weeks, and James an apostle they had known for over a decade. They very likely prayed for him as earnestly, and Luke offers not one syllable of explanation for the difference. That silence must be respected rather than filled. Nothing suggests that the prayers for James were less fervent, his faith weaker, or that God had a lesson for him that Peter did not need: every such explanation has been offered to grieving people, and all are inventions.

What can be said. It is smaller and truer. Jesus had told James this was coming (Mark 10:39). Peter’s deliverance is the exception Luke records, not the rule he teaches: by early and consistent tradition Peter was executed in the end, in Rome (compare John 21:18–19), and no angel came to that cell. A book that recorded only deliverances would be a lie, and useless to most of its readers.

Why does God rescue some of his people and not others? Scripture does not give the reasons in particular cases, and we must not invent them, but it tells us enough to trust him. James and Peter were equally loved, equally prayed for and equally safe in Christ. God’s purposes for each were different and both good: James taken home to glory, Peter given more years of work, and neither a failure of prayer or of love. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15), and not even the sword can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39). When you cannot see why, you can still see who: the Father who did not spare his own Son.
verseByVerse.note: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. James is the first of the Twelve to die for his faith.

parallels.desc: the cup that I drink you will drink

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod arrests Peter because killing James was popular, and surrounds him with every human precaution; but he has arranged everything except the Lord.

It pleased the Jews. Luke states the motive plainly. Herod killed an apostle not out of conviction but because it went down well, and moved on to a second for the same reason. Approval is a cruel god: it asked for one apostle, then another. By “the Jews” Luke means the leaders and people of Jerusalem, not every Jew; the church itself was still almost entirely Jewish.

The days of Unleavened Bread. Passover and the seven days of Unleavened Bread were kept as one feast (Luke 22:1). Waiting until it was over looked like respect for religion, and promised a larger crowd. And the irony: Passover celebrates the night God brought his people out of the house of bondage, while the king holds an apostle in prison until the celebrations are over.

Four squads of soldiers. Four squads of four, one for each watch of the night: two men chained to the prisoner, two at the door. Sixteen men for one fisherman, because the authorities in this city had once imprisoned the apostles and found in the morning the cell locked, the guards at their posts and the prisoners gone (5:19–23). Luke sets out precisely what was in place before the chains fell off.

To bring him out to the people. More than ten years earlier, in this same week, another prisoner was brought out to the people in Jerusalem, and the crowd asked for Barabbas and shouted for the cross (Luke 23:18–21). Jesus went out to that crowd as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose blood is why God passes over his people, and no angel came for him, because he had come to die. Every rescue in this chapter, and every mercy his people have received, comes through the one prisoner who was not rescued.

Everything except the Lord. Sixteen soldiers, two chains, an iron gate and a date: Herod had arranged everything except the Lord. He who sits in the heavens laughs at the plans of kings (Psalm 2:4); he holds the calendar on which they pencil them, and had already written in a different date for Herod. Herod needed sixteen men; the Lord needed one angel. Never measure your danger without measuring your God.

In everyday life. Herod’s sin starts very small in all of us: the joke told because the room will like it, the opinion softened because the boss holds another. Most days the question is quietly there: whom am I trying to please?

Should Christians expect hostility from governments? Sometimes. Scripture teaches us to honour and obey the governing authorities as God’s servants for our good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and many governments have been kind to the church. But rulers may rage against the Lord and his Anointed (Psalm 2:1–3; Acts 4:25–27), and Jesus said his followers would be brought before kings for his sake (Luke 21:12). So: respectful submission in everything lawful, prayer for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and quiet refusal when commanded to disobey God (5:29). We neither idolise the state nor fear it. We fear God.
verseByVerse.note: Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the night watches.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against all the power of the state the church sets earnest prayer, and the prisoner, in the Lord’s hands, sleeps.

But earnest prayer. Luke sets the whole apparatus of the state against a prayer meeting and joins them with but; by the end of the chapter it is the king who is dead. Earnest (ektenōs) means stretched out, at full reach; Luke uses a form of it of Jesus praying in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). And they prayed together, a church that had just buried James and knew what a Herod does with an apostle.

Sleeping between two soldiers. Chained by each wrist to a soldier on the night before his execution, Peter sleeps so soundly that an angel has to hit him. “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). The peace did not come from confidence about the outcome: Peter had no reason to expect an angel, and James had not got one. It came from the Lord, in whose hands both outcomes lay.

Another prayer for Peter. The church was not the first to pray for him. On the night of his arrest Jesus told Peter that Satan wanted to sift him like wheat, and then, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). That prayer carried Peter through his denial and back, and it was still in force. The Lord always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and the prayers rising from Mary’s house went up to a Father already listening to his Son.

In Gethsemane, he did not sleep. The keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), and so a chained fisherman can. The Lord who once slept on a cushion in the stern while the storm broke (Mark 4:38) shared his rest with Peter. And in Gethsemane the same Lord did not sleep: he prayed in agony while his friends slept around him. He kept that vigil so that his people may lie down.

What earnest prayer looks like. Not a special tone of voice, and not winning God over by effort. The church prayed like this because it knew how great the danger was, and how great the Lord was. Name the need plainly. They prayed for Peter, by name. Pray with others. Find one or two who will carry the same person with you. Keep going. The prayer was still going on when Peter knocked (v. 12). Leave the answer with him. This church had just buried James; earnest prayer asks boldly and still says, “your will be done” (Matthew 6:10). And take heart: your prayers need not be strong enough to get through on their own. They rise to the Father alongside the prayers of his Son, whom he always hears (John 11:42).

How can I have that kind of peace? Not by persuading yourself that everything will turn out as you want, but by entrusting yourself to the one who holds the outcome. Do not be anxious about anything, Paul says, but let your requests be made known to God, and his peace will guard your hearts (Philippians 4:6–7). Name the fear to God plainly. Remind yourself of his love, his power and his promises. Your life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), where the worst cannot touch what matters most. Then lie down. Peace is not the absence of danger; it is the presence of the Lord in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord sends his angel into the cell, and the chains fall off before Peter is awake enough to understand what is happening.

An angel of the Lord stood next to him. As with the shepherds (Luke 2:9), no approach is described. A light fills the cell, and none of the soldiers wakes.

He struck Peter on the side. Luke uses the verb (patassō) twice in this chapter: here an angel of the Lord strikes a man to wake him; at verse 23 an angel of the Lord strikes a man and he dies. One blow rouses a sleeping prisoner, the other ends a king who thought he was a god. And there is something almost comic here: the light has not worked, so the angel gives Peter a dig in the ribs.

Free before he knows it. The chains fall off, not unlocked or struck off, while Peter still thinks he is dreaming. This is how the gospel works. At Nazareth Jesus read that he had come to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1), and here the risen Lord does to one prisoner’s wrists what he does to every sinner’s heart: the chains come off by a power not his own, and understanding follows freedom. God makes us alive while we are still dead in our sins (Ephesians 2:4–5), and only then do we see what has been done. And the greater chains of sin, death and the devil fell at the word of the risen Christ, who holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

In everyday life. Pray for those in chains, literal and spiritual: persecuted Christians in prison today, and friends bound by addictions or despair. Name one of each before God this week.

Does God still send angels to rescue his people? Angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7), so God uses his angels for our protection, mostly unseen. But visible angelic rescues are rare even in the Bible, clustered at turning points in redemption, and we are never told to expect them, seek them, or pray to angels. Pray to God.
