How he answers, by angels, by people, by ordinary means or by none you can see, is his business, and every answer is from his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel gives Peter plain, practical orders and leads him out while Peter thinks he is dreaming: God’s rescue does not wait for Peter to understand it.

Dress yourself. A being from the presence of God has just dissolved Roman iron, and now tells a fisherman to put his shoes on. Somebody has thought about the cold. God does not find the practical beneath him (the risen Christ cooked breakfast on a beach, John 21:9); his greatness makes nothing too small for his care. And there is a division of labour: God does the impossible, the chains, and leaves Peter the possible, the sandals.

Follow me. Peter had heard those words from Jesus by the lake at the beginning and on the beach at the end (Mark 1:17; John 21:19). On the beach they came straight after Jesus told him that when he was old another would carry him where he did not want to go (John 21:18). Tonight Peter is in chains, and he is not old. Herod has fixed a date, but the Lord had fixed Peter’s days long before, and no king could bring the last of them forward by an hour.

He thought he was seeing a vision. Peter is not being obtuse: since the roof at Joppa (10:10) he knew what a vision felt like. He walks out not believing what God is doing while he does it, and soon the church will tell a servant girl she is raving. God did it anyway.

Does God only act when we have enough faith? No. Faith is the hand that receives God’s gifts, and we are to pray believing (James 1:6). But God answers out of his own goodness, not the size of our faith: the man who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” received what he asked (Mark 9:24). Do not despair because your faith is weak. Bring it to a strong Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every barrier Herod set up gives way in turn, down to the iron gate that opens by itself; then the angel leaves, and Peter walks on by ordinary means.

The first and the second guard. Luke dismantles Herod’s arrangements one at a time, and says nothing about how the guards were passed.

The iron gate. The last obstacle, the gate into the city. Of its own accord is automatē, from which we get automatic; the New Testament uses it only here and of the earth producing a crop by itself (Mark 4:28). No lock is picked and no guard overpowered; the gate behaves as though it had been asked.

The Lord of the doors. Prison doors open for the apostles (5:19) and for Paul and Silas (16:26); a door of faith opens to the Gentiles (14:27); the Lord opens Lydia’s heart (16:14). This is the risen Christ at work, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). His sovereignty reaches every barrier between his word and his people, the hard heart included.

To let his people look in. On the first Easter morning an angel of the Lord rolled back the stone from the tomb and sat on it (Matthew 28:2), not to let the Lord out but to let his people look in. Because the grave could not hold him, no prison, no iron gate and no grave will hold those who are his.

Immediately the angel left him. One street, and the angel is gone, leaving Peter alone in the dark in a city where a king wants him dead. He was sent to get Peter through a gate, and no further. God is not mean with his help; he gives exactly what is needed.

Why does God sometimes seem to leave us just when we need him? He does not leave us, though his extraordinary help may be withdrawn. The angel left Peter, but the Lord did not: Peter’s first thought is that the Lord had rescued him (v. 11), and his feet took him straight to the praying church. God often gives remarkable help through a crisis and then returns us to ordinary means: our own legs and judgment, the fellowship of other believers. That is not abandonment but the Father treating us as sons who can walk. He has promised, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter comes to himself and gives the Lord all the credit, then goes straight to the house where the church is praying.

When Peter came to himself. Luke used a similar phrase of the young man among the pigs who suddenly saw his situation for what it was (Luke 15:17): the moment the fog clears.

Now I am sure. Until now he was not. He does not mention his own part, because he had none; the Lord acts all through his sentence. Every Christian will one day say it with the fog cleared for ever and every prison behind him.

Whose angel. The Lord who “has sent his angel” is Jesus, whom God made both Lord and Christ, as Peter had told this city (2:36), and who spoke of the angels as his own (Matthew 24:31). The last time Peter stood in a Jerusalem courtyard at night, he said he did not know the man (Luke 22:57). Now he stands in a dark street and confesses that this same man has rescued him. The Lord who answered that denial with a look and a restoration has answered these chains with an angel.

The house of Mary. Mary has a house with a gateway and a servant, and is named in her own right, which suggests a widow of means who had put her property at the church’s disposal; that it was the house of the upper room cannot be proved. Her son John Mark, cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), has a long road ahead, and Peter will one day call him “my son” (1 Peter 5:13).

Many were gathered together. With Peter under sentence and James freshly buried, the church is gathered in numbers in a house in the dark, still praying. That took nerve, and it is why Peter knew which door to knock on.

In everyday life. If you have a room and a table, offer them to your church for a prayer meeting or a small group, and be the Mary of your street.
verseByVerse.note: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas. His mother’s house was large enough to hold a gathering.

parallels.desc: God sent his angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first to hear that the prayer has been answered is a slave girl, and she is so overjoyed that she leaves Peter standing in the street.

A servant girl named Rhoda. Luke does not name the soldiers or most of the church in that room, but he names a slave girl who answered a door. Rhoda means rose: a servant of no standing in a house she did not own, whose one recorded action was a mistake.

Recognizing Peter’s voice. She knew it through a closed door at night: she had been in the room often enough while the apostle taught. Evidently the church did not send the servants out when it met.

In her joy. One of the rare sentences in Scripture that is plainly funny. The most wanted man in Jerusalem is left in the street because the girl who found him was too happy to let him in. An angel opened the iron gate; a joyful girl kept the wooden one shut. Luke tells it with affection; those who come off badly in the next verse are the ones who were praying. She alone in that house at once believed it was Peter and was glad (the prayer meeting managed neither). If we must get something wrong on the night God answers, let it be Rhoda’s mistake: being too glad.

Like the women at the tomb. In Luke’s Gospel the first news that Jesus was alive came from women, and to the apostles their words seemed an idle tale (Luke 24:10–11). Peter was one of those apostles, though he ran to the tomb (24:12). Now he stands outside, and a servant girl carries news nobody will credit. The God who raised Jesus delights to put the news of his life-giving power first into the mouths of those the world does not count as witnesses, so that the power is plainly his (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

Does God notice people as ordinary as Rhoda? Every person in God’s story is ordinary until he notices them, and Scripture is full of servants, widows, children and slaves whom the world never named and God did. Rhoda was a slave in someone else’s house, and her name is in the Bible. If you feel invisible in your church or your life, the Lord who numbered the hairs on Peter’s head knew the name of the girl who answered his door. Your faithfulness in small places is seen, and your joy in his works delights him.
verseByVerse.note: Rhoda means “rose.”

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church that has prayed all night for Peter cannot believe its prayer has been answered, and God answers it anyway.

You are out of your mind. Said by people who have spent the night asking God for precisely what the girl has just announced. She stood her ground against a room of her betters, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!”: the prayer meeting produced, on the spot, a theological explanation for why the answer to their prayers could not be the answer to their prayers (on the belief, see the box below).

They thought they saw a spirit. On the first Easter evening the disciples thought the risen Jesus was a spirit, and even when he showed them his hands and feet they disbelieved for joy (Luke 24:36–41). Peter had been in that room; now he is outside, and the church reaches for the same explanation. The answer then and now was a real body: a Lord who ate broiled fish before their eyes, a fisherman knocking with real knuckles on a real gate.

They were amazed. Do not look down on them: they met at genuine risk to pray for a condemned man. Their problem is a common one: they prayed without expecting, and when the answer knocked they could think of every explanation but the true one. Meanwhile Peter kept knocking. The lesson is kinder than the rebuke this scene usually gets: God answered anyway. The deliverance did not wait on their expectation and was not withdrawn when they called the messenger mad. Their faith was real but weak, and God answered beyond it, as he is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). He is better than our faith, kinder than our expectations, and greater than our prayers.

Do believers have guardian angels? Angels serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and Jesus says of his little ones that in heaven their angels always see the face of his Father (Matthew 18:10). But no text clearly teaches that each person has one assigned angel, and Luke records this belief without endorsing it. God sends his angels for his people, and we are never to pray to them.

Is it wrong to pray when I do not really expect an answer? It is far better to pray weakly than not at all, and this church is proof that God hears such prayers. But ask him to grow your expectation, since he invites us to come boldly (Hebrews 4:16). Keep a record of what you ask and how he answers, and pray his promises back to him, so that your expectation rests on what he has said rather than on how you feel. Expectation is not presumption: it trusts that God hears and will answer in his way and time, even if not as you pictured.

Uncertain wording. What the household meant by “his angel” is not certain. Many Jews of the time believed that a person had a guardian angel, and the likeliest meaning is that they thought it had come to the gate looking and sounding like Peter. Some think instead that they supposed Peter already dead, and took the voice for his departed spirit. Either way, they reached for anything but the plain answer to their prayers.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter tells the church what the Lord has done, sends word to James and leaves Jerusalem; in the morning the soldiers find their prisoner gone.

Motioning to them to be silent. A fugitive in a courtyard at night has to quieten a houseful of astonished people before the street hears them. Then he tells them not how he got out but how the Lord brought him out, the only version he is in a position to give.

Tell these things to James. Not the James killed fifteen verses ago, but James the Lord’s brother, who did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), saw the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:7), and is generally held to have written the letter of James. It is a quiet change of leadership: from here on he presides at the council and receives Paul’s reports (15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9).

Another place. Luke does not say where, perhaps to protect him. Peter appears once more in Acts, at the council (15:7), then leaves the story without farewell. Acts is what Jesus went on doing and teaching from the throne (1:1), by his Spirit and his word; Peter can walk off the stage because he was never its centre. The Lord who brought him out of prison stays on it to the last page.

No little disturbance. Luke’s dry understatement: he means there was uproar.

Why tell the story to the church? What the Lord does for one of his people belongs to all of them. Peter could have slipped away; instead, at real risk, he stopped to tell the praying church what God had done. Testimony strengthens faith, answers prayer publicly and gives God the glory: “Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul” (Psalm 66:16). When God answers your prayers, tell those who prayed with you. It is part of the answer.

Where Christians differ: did Peter go to Rome? Some Roman Catholic tradition says Peter went to Rome at this point and was bishop there for twenty-five years. This commentary’s view: there is no evidence that Peter went to Rome now; he is in Jerusalem a few years later (15:7). Paul’s letter to the Romans, written around AD 57, greets many people in Rome but never mentions Peter. Peter probably did go to Rome late in his life and died there under Nero, as early tradition says. But the New Testament never presents him as bishop of Rome or head of the church.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cheated of his prisoner, Herod has the guards executed and leaves Jerusalem for good: Peter’s rescue came at a cost Luke does not hide.

Put to death. Under Roman practice a guard who lost his prisoner could expect the prisoner’s penalty (16:27; 27:42), so men die because an angel opened a gate. Luke reports it without comment, and it would be dishonest to supply the comfort he withholds. Deliverances happen inside a fallen world, and the Bible reports the price rather than hiding it, one reason it can be trusted about the rest.

Down to Caesarea. Herod leaves Jerusalem and never comes back. His final recorded act in the holy city, where he had been so careful to appear devout, was to have his own men executed for something none of them had done.

A keeper who loses none. Set beside Herod the keeper the gospel describes. Jesus told the Father that he had guarded those given him, and not one had been lost but the son of destruction (John 17:12); in the garden he told the soldiers, “if you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8). He was answerable for his people and paid with his life, not because he had lost them but so that he never would. Herod’s guards died for a prisoner they could not keep; the Good Shepherd died for sheep he will not lose, and rose to keep them for ever.

In everyday life. Pray for those who live under cruel rulers today, and for those who serve them in fear. And pray for rulers themselves, that they would come to fear God before it is too late.

Was God unjust to let the guards die? No. God did not kill the guards; Herod did, and Herod answered for it. God is not obliged to prevent every evil act of wicked men, and often lets them show what they are before he judges them. His ways in such things are often hidden, and Scripture does not invite us to explain them all. But the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25); no innocent blood is forgotten, and every tyrant will give account. The cross is the final proof: the most unjust act in history, done by wicked men, was the means by which God saved the world, and those men will answer to him.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod, who can starve two cities into submission, puts on his royal robes to receive them in splendour: the stage is set for a proud man’s fall.

Angry with Tyre and Sidon. We are not told why Herod was angry, but his hold over them is plain. The Phoenician ports had almost no farmland and had imported their grain from Galilee since Solomon’s day (1 Kings 5:11). Herod could not conquer them. He could starve them, and they knew it.

Blastus. The chamberlain controlled access to the king. Two ancient cities had to win over a courtier, very possibly with money, to get permission to eat.

On an appointed day. The Jewish historian Josephus, with no interest in defending Luke, describes the same occasion: Agrippa at Caesarea at games for the emperor, entering the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven of silver that blazed in the sun, and flatterers calling him a god. The king was seized almost at once with violent pain in his belly, carried out, and died after five days. Luke says an angel of the Lord struck him and Josephus does not, just the difference one would expect from independent witnesses: Josephus reports what the crowd saw, Luke was shown the cause behind it.

Access without a chamberlain. Compare the throne the gospel opens. Through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18), brought in not by a courtier to be bought but by the King’s own Son, who paid the cost of entry himself: we enter by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). Tyre and Sidon pleaded with a king who used hunger as a lever; the Father of Jesus gives his children their daily bread for the asking (Luke 11:3), and no Blastus stands at his door.

Borrowed light. The silver robe blazed in the morning sun, and within a week he was in the grave. The kingdoms of this world are lit by borrowed light; the Lamb is the lamp of the city of God (Revelation 21:23).

Why does it matter that Josephus confirms Luke? Because the Christian faith rests on things that really happened. Luke wrote so that Theophilus might have certainty (Luke 1:4), and he wrote as a historian, naming rulers, cities and dates that could be checked. Outside sources and archaeology have again and again confirmed his accuracy; a few details, such as the timing of Theudas (5:36), are still debated, but the pattern is strong. That does not prove every miracle, but it shows Luke a careful and truthful witness, and gives good reason to trust him about what only the eyewitnesses saw: an empty tomb, an angel in a cell, and a church that turned the world upside down.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod lets a crowd call him a god, and God strikes him down for taking the glory that belongs to God alone.

The voice of a god! Flattery from men who needed the grain to keep coming, and Herod knew what it was worth. Ancient rulers were often hailed as gods; the point is that he did not correct it.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Two chapters earlier, in this city, a Roman centurion fell at Peter’s feet in genuine reverence, and Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man” (10:26). Same town, same kind of moment, opposite responses, and only one of the two men is alive at the end of this chapter. Paul and Barnabas will do the same at Lystra (14:14–15).

Because he did not give God the glory. Not because he executed James, imprisoned Peter or killed his guards: none of that is cited. The charge is that he let himself be called divine and did not hand the honour back. “I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other” (Isaiah 42:8). To give God the glory is to acknowledge, in the heart and aloud, that he alone is God and that every good thing we have comes from him. The murders were real, but the theft of what belongs to God alone is the sin underneath all the others: a man willing to be worshipped will do anything to the people beneath him.

Eaten by worms. He died in AD 44, as Josephus also records (see vv. 20–21). Luke gives it a single sentence: the grandson of Herod the Great, in silver, on a platform, with a crowd calling him a god, and within the week a burial. “Pride goes before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18), as Nebuchadnezzar learned when he boasted on his palace roof and was driven out to eat grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (Daniel 4:30–37).

Two robes. On the day Jesus was condemned, Herod Antipas, this king’s uncle, mocked him, dressed him in splendid clothing and sent him back to Pilate (Luke 23:11). The uncle put a fine robe on the one man who truly was God, to laugh at him; the nephew put on silver and let a crowd call him what he was not. The cry was a lie about Herod; about Jesus the truth is greater still: in him the voice of God and the voice of a man are one voice. One day every tongue will give the honour to the right Man: “Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

Every one of us now has a platform. Herod needed a throne, a silver robe and cities dependent on his grain before a crowd would call him a god. We need only a phone. Our culture gives everyone a stage, counts the applause in public and urges us to build a personal brand, as if a self were a product. The hunger is very old. Augustine, surveying Rome’s history in The City of God, argued that the Romans did great and costly things for the love of praise, and God gave them exactly the reward they sought, a glorious name on earth, which is all such love can earn. And such glory must be won again every day, so every rival’s success feels like theft. Herod shows where the road ends. The gospel does not tell us to despise ourselves. It shows us the one who truly was God and said, “I do not receive glory from people” (John 5:41), who went down to a cross instead of up onto a platform and was given the name above every name. In him God speaks over the believer the one verdict that quiets the hunger, and it never has to be earned again tomorrow.

In everyday life. Watch the subtler forms of Herod’s sin: the secret pleasure in being thought indispensable, the irritation when someone else gets the credit. Bring them to God as soon as you notice them. None of us hands the glory back perfectly; the Son did, glorifying the Father on earth in our place (John 17:4), and for his sake even proud hearts are forgiven.

What it does not mean. This is not a template for reading illness or sudden death as divine judgment, and it has been misused that way with great cruelty. Luke tells us the reason here because it was disclosed to him. In almost every other case nobody has been told, and whoever claims to know why somebody is ill has made himself a judge when God has not appointed him one. Jesus warned against assuming that those who suffer disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5).

Is it not vain of God to insist on the glory? In us it would be, for a man who demands praise claims what he does not deserve. With God it is the reverse. He alone is worthy, and wanting us to see him as he is means wanting what is true and best for us, since we were made to find our fullest joy in him (Psalm 16:11). A God who let creatures be worshipped in his place would be leaving them to a lie. And he does not guard his glory from a distance: he gave his Son, who shared that glory before the world existed (John 17:5), to die for people who had stolen it.

How do I give God the glory when I am praised? Receive the kindness graciously, without false modesty, and turn it quickly toward God, in your heart and, where fitting, in your words: God has been very kind; I am grateful it helped. Inside, remind yourself that every gift you have was given (1 Corinthians 4:7), and refuse to feed on the praise in private afterwards. Herod’s danger was not that people admired him but that he kept what belonged to God. The test is whether, when praised, you feel larger, or more grateful.

Uncertain wording. “Eaten by worms” translates a single rare word, worm-eaten, which does not name a disease. Josephus speaks of violent pain in the belly and death after five days. Modern guesses at the illness differ, and none can be proved. A similar end is told of the persecuting king Antiochus Epiphanes (2 Maccabees 9:9), so Jewish readers knew it as the death of a tyrant who had set himself against God. Luke presents a real illness with a real cause: the Lord struck him.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king is dead, but the word of God goes on growing, and the men who will carry it to the nations head back to Antioch.

But the word of God increased. A king hailed as divine is dead, and the next thing Luke writes is a message spreading: the point of the whole chapter. “Increased and multiplied” is the language Genesis uses of creatures filling the earth (Genesis 1:22), and Luke’s progress reports (6:7; 9:31) each close a section of his book. Herod set out to destroy the church and ended as a warning in its records. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

The child Herod’s grandfather hunted. Herod the Great sent soldiers to Bethlehem to kill a child; his son Antipas mocked the man that child became and stood with Pilate against him (4:27); his grandson killed one of that man’s apostles and now lies dead at Caesarea. Jesus has outlived them all, not by escaping them but by dying and rising. The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and his Anointed (Psalm 2:2; Acts 4:26), and the Anointed has the last word. In Acts the word of God is the news of Jesus Christ, Lord of all (10:36), and its growth is his doing: the risen Lord adds to his church (2:47).

A message that gives life. The verbs of living things fit, because the message gives life. Herod’s body went to the worms, and the word of the risen Christ went on making dead hearts live in lands Luke never heard of. Nothing it has brought to life will ever die: not the church it gathers, and not one soul it has made alive.

When they had completed their service. The famine money from Antioch has been delivered (11:29–30), and Barnabas and Saul go back to Antioch (see the textual note below).

John, whose other name was Mark. Mary’s son, very likely in the house the night Rhoda left Peter at the gate. From Antioch he will go on the first missionary journey (13:5), turn back in Pamphylia (13:13), and so cause a sharp quarrel that splits Paul from Barnabas (15:37–39). Years later Paul will ask for him from prison, because he is useful for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11), and by the church’s earliest tradition he wrote down Peter’s recollections, which the church has read ever since as the Gospel of Mark. Here he is only a name, a young helper on other men’s journey.

In everyday life. When the news is full of powerful people doing terrible things, read Acts 12 again, and remember who has the last word. Then do something small for the word of God this week: give to a missionary, invite a friend to church, teach a child a verse.

If a Christian has failed badly, can God still use him? Mark is the answer. Barnabas did not write him off after the desertion and the split, and in the end neither did Paul; nor did the Lord write off Peter, who denied him and was restored to feed his sheep. If you have failed, confess it, receive Christ’s forgiveness, accept the consequences humbly, and get back to work. The Lord is not finished with you.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ between from Jerusalem and to Jerusalem. The ESV reads “from”, which fits the story; some manuscripts read “to”, which is harder to fit, since the two are leaving with Mark. Either way, they are going back to Antioch.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 shows a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies and Peter lives, both by God’s appointment. The church prays, and the answer still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour and is given worms. The fitting response is not to explain his ways but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no legal protection and no army, met in a house and prayed with everything they had. They were answered in a way they did not expect.

Now: Where power is set against the gospel, the church’s answer is neither despair nor political scheming but earnest, persistent prayer to the Lord who made heaven and earth. And when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

keyVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied.
keyVerse.note: After a murdered apostle, a prison opened by an angel and a king struck down, Luke gives his verdict in one sentence beginning with “But”. Kings rise and fall within the chapter, and the word of the risen Christ outlives them all. Its growth is God’s doing, not the church’s, and the earnest prayer of verse 5 shows how his people share in it.

12.reflection:
The church prayed earnestly for Peter, and he was set free; James, very likely prayed for too, was killed, and Luke gives no reason (vv. 1–5). How does this chapter keep us from treating prayer as a machine, and still encourage us to pray boldly? What would you say to a friend whose prayers seem to have gone unanswered?

Peter slept soundly on the night before he was to be executed (v. 6). Where do you find it hardest to rest in God’s hands, and what in this chapter speaks to that fear?

The church that had prayed all night told Rhoda she was out of her mind (vv. 13–16). Why do we so often pray without expecting God to answer, and what might help you, and your church, to pray with more expectation?

Herod was struck down “because he did not give God the glory” (v. 23). In a world that gives everyone a platform, where are you tempted to keep the praise that belongs to God, and how does Jesus free us from that hunger?

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
Where we are. The word has spread through Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria to a church of Jews and Gentiles at Antioch (chapter 11), and chapter 12 ended with “the word of God increased and multiplied” (12:24). Now the last stage of Jesus’ programme begins, “to the end of the earth” (1:8), and from here Paul is at the centre of the story.

The message. The risen Christ keeps God’s promises and sends his word to the nations himself. In Jesus, crucified and raised, God has kept his promise to David, and through him everyone who believes, Jew or Gentile, is forgiven and declared right with God, as the law of Moses could never do. Opposition cannot stop it, because those God has appointed to eternal life will hear and believe.

Why it was said. Many of Luke’s readers were Gentiles in mixed churches (see the introduction). They needed to know that the mission to the nations was the Spirit’s own initiative and the goal of Israel’s Scriptures, not a breakaway, and that rejection did not mean God’s word had failed.

How the chapter makes its case. The Spirit speaks to a worshipping church, which sends Barnabas and Saul (vv. 1–3). On Cyprus a sorcerer who opposes them is struck blind for a time, and the governor believes, astonished at the teaching (vv. 4–12). John Mark turns back; the others go up to Pisidian Antioch (vv. 13–15). There Paul preaches: God chose Israel and gave them judges and kings, and finally David (vv. 16–22); from David’s line he has brought Jesus, condemned by Jerusalem and raised by God, as the Scriptures foretold (vv. 23–37); through him forgiveness and justification are proclaimed to all who believe, with a warning to scoffers (vv. 38–41). A week later the whole city comes. Jealous leaders contradict, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe (vv. 42–49). The missionaries are driven out, but the disciples are filled with joy and the Spirit (vv. 50–52).

Where it leads. Christ is the subject from first to last: the Lord the church was worshipping when the Spirit spoke, the offspring of David God promised, the Holy One who did not see corruption, the one through whom pardon is proclaimed, and the Servant whose light reaches the nations through his messengers (v. 47). The whole of Israel’s history was moving toward him.

For us. Mission grows out of worship, and the message never changes: God has kept his word in Jesus, and everyone who believes is freed from everything. Ask whom your church will send, whether you rest on Christ’s verdict or your own record, and whether opposition has silenced you when it should only move you on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel’s move to the nations begins not with a strategy but with the Holy Spirit speaking to a worshipping church. While the leaders at Antioch worship and fast, the Spirit claims Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has called them, and the church fasts, prays, lays hands on them and lets them go (vv. 1–3). Sent out by the Spirit, they preach in the synagogues of Cyprus (vv. 4–5). At Paphos the Roman governor wants to hear the word of God, but his court magician tries to turn him away (vv. 6–8). Paul pronounces judgment, the magician is struck blind for a time, and the governor believes, astonished at the teaching of the Lord (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit speaks not privately to Barnabas and Saul but in the assembly, and the church fasts, prays and lays hands on them before letting them go. A person’s own sense of call is tested and confirmed by the congregation (see vv. 1–2), and the congregation acts on what the Spirit says. Neither the individual nor the church acts alone. On whom a church is willing to lose, see v. 3.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The leaders listed in verse 1 came from Cyprus, North Africa, Cilicia and a royal court, and most of them were in Antioch because persecution had scattered them there. Now: Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what its leadership looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From a worshipping church the Holy Spirit claims two of its leaders for the work he has already called them to, and the mission to the nations begins. The great turn toward “the end of the earth” (1:8) starts not in a planning meeting but in worship.

Prophets and teachers. The church’s leaders: prophets, who brought a word from God before the New Testament was written, and teachers, who explained the Scriptures.

The five names. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus (4:36). Simeon who was called Niger: Latin for black or dark, very likely a description, so Simeon may well have come from Africa; some suggest he was Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross (Mark 15:21), though no one can be sure. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa (compare 11:20). Manaen, a syntrophos of Herod the tetrarch, brought up with him at court: he had very likely shared a nursery with the Herod who beheaded John the Baptist. And Saul, last on the list, the former persecutor.

What a church looks like. Very likely an African, an aristocrat and a former persecutor, and not one of them one of the Twelve: this is a church that has stopped asking who is allowed in. Two boys grew up in the same palace; one became the murderer of the Baptist and the other a teacher of the church of Christ. Grace took one and passed the other by. Election is exactly this: God did not find something better in Manaen, but set his love on him freely, before he had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11; Ephesians 1:4).

Worshiping the Lord and fasting. The verb is the word for priestly service, ministering before God (leitourgountōn, from which comes our word liturgy).

Set apart for me. The pronouns matter. For me: they belong to him before they belong to Antioch. I have called: the call had already been given; the church only recognises it. The Holy Spirit speaks in the first person, claiming servants for himself: the voice of God, not of a force (compare Romans 1:1). And the church is asked for its two best leaders, not those it can spare.

Whose work it is. The risen Jesus had promised that the Spirit would make his followers witnesses to the end of the earth (1:8), so the voice in Antioch is Christ keeping his word from the throne. The man asked for is Saul, his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles (9:15). The Spirit who says for me owns every servant he sends, and has never called anyone to a work without going with him into it.

What is fasting? To fast is voluntarily to go without food, for part of a day or longer, to seek God. It is not dieting, nor a hunger strike to twist God’s arm, nor the self-punishment Scripture warns against (Colossians 2:23). The empty stomach says with the body: “Lord, I want you more than my daily bread.” In Scripture it goes with earnest prayer: for guidance and the sending of missionaries (here; v. 3; 14:23), in repentance (Joel 2:12; Jonah 3), grief (2 Samuel 1:12), crisis (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21–23), and steady devotion (Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasted forty days (Matthew 4:2).

Is fasting commanded of Christians? No: it is nowhere laid on believers as a law, and the letters barely mention it (2 Corinthians 6:5; 11:27 may even be involuntary hunger). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add fasting at 1 Corinthians 7:5 and in a few Gospel verses (such as Mark 9:29); the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it there. No one sins by not fasting or earns anything by it. Yet Jesus assumed his people would fast. He said “when you fast”, not “if”, warning only against doing it for show (Matthew 6:16–18), and said that when the bridegroom is taken away, then his disciples will fast (Matthew 9:15): this present age. Fasting is not a rule but a privilege and a means of grace the Lord expects his church to use.

So should you fast? Gently, yes: not from guilt, but because it is a help your Master meant you to have. In a season of weighty decision, heavy prayer or sorrow over sin, giving up even food to give that time and hunger to God humbles the heart and sharpens prayer; and the hunger itself preaches that “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Start small: skip a meal and spend the time in prayer and the word. Tie the fast to a purpose and to prayer, for fasting without praying is merely going hungry, and keep it secret (Matthew 6:17–18). Guard against pride: the Pharisee boasted that he fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and Isaiah 58 shows God despising a fast joined to hard-heartedness. And use ordinary wisdom about health: the unwell, the pregnant and those on medication should take care, and going without water is only ever brief. Out of one such fast at Antioch the Spirit launched the gospel to the nations.

How did the Spirit say this? Luke does not say; most likely through one of the prophets named in v. 1, speaking in the gathered church (compare 11:28). Today, with the Scriptures complete, the Spirit guides churches through his word, prayer, and the wisdom of the church and its elders, not by new revelations. Many faithful Christians believe the Spirit still speaks through prophecy, and they are brothers; this commentary holds that revelation of this kind belonged to the apostolic foundation, because the written word is now complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Does the Spirit still call particular people to particular work, and how would I know? Yes, though not usually by a voice in a meeting. He still gives gifts, lays burdens on hearts, opens doors and moves churches to recognise and send. The call here was heard by the church, not by Barnabas and Saul alone, and confirmed with fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands (v. 3). A call to missionary or pastoral work is not a private impression; it is tested by gifts, character, the desire to serve, and the recognition of the church and its leaders. So if you sense a pull toward some work for Christ, do not keep it private or wait for a voice: tell your elders, serve where you are, and let others test the gifts. The Spirit who called Barnabas and Saul called them in company, and he still does.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church confirms the Spirit’s call with fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands, and then lets its two best men go. Four verbs make a sending: they fasted, prayed, laid hands on them and released them.

After fasting and praying. Having heard the Spirit, they fast again: not doubt, but what serious people do before an irreversible step.

They laid their hands on them. This gives Barnabas and Saul nothing they did not have: the Spirit had already called them, and both had been in ministry for years. It is the congregation’s public act of identification and blessing, as with the seven (6:6): these are our men, this is our work, and we put our hands on it in front of everybody.

Sent them off. Literally, released them. The Spirit sent them (v. 4); the church let go of the two most valuable men it had, both at once.

The Sender behind the senders. This is the shape of the gospel. The Father did not send what he could spare; he sent his only Son, loved before the foundation of the world, into a world that would kill him (John 3:16; 17:24). And the Son, sent, now sends: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). A church that releases its best does, in a small way, what the Father did.

In everyday life. The test of a church’s heart for mission is whether it will give away the people it can least afford to lose, to work it will not see. A church can make an idol of its own stability, keeping its gifted people close in order to feel safe.

Does laying on of hands give the Spirit or special power? Not here. Sometimes in Acts the apostles laid on hands and the Spirit came in a special way (8:17; 19:6), marking key moments as the gospel crossed new boundaries. But this is done by the church, for men who already had the Spirit and the call: a solemn setting apart, much as a church today commissions missionaries or ordains elders. Nothing magical passes through the hands; what passes is the church’s blessing and its pledge to stand behind those it sends.

What does it mean to share in a missionary’s work? More than an occasional prayer. Antioch owned these men: praying, giving, welcoming them back and hearing their report (14:26–27). Paul calls such churches partners in the gospel (Philippians 1:5). Know the names of the missionaries your church supports, pray for one of them each week, find out what they actually need, and when they come home, give them a meal and an evening, not a five-minute slot.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent out by the Spirit, Barnabas and Saul begin in the synagogues of Cyprus, taking the word of God to the Jew first. The church sent them off; the Spirit sent them out: one act seen from two sides. The mission is his before it is ours.

To Cyprus. Seleucia was Antioch’s port, sixteen miles down the Orontes, and Cyprus a day or two’s sail away: the island where Barnabas grew up (4:36), where there were believers already (11:19).

In the synagogues of the Jews. In Salamis they set the pattern Paul will follow for fifteen years: “to the Jew first” (Romans 1:16). In every new city he goes to the synagogue first, however the last one treated him.

The word of God. On Saul’s lips that meant Jesus: in Damascus he proclaimed that he is the Son of God (9:20). Barnabas was a Levite, born into the tribe that served the sanctuary, and he came home to tell his own people that the sacrifice the sanctuary pointed to had been offered. Two men stood up to announce the one Moses wrote about (John 5:46).

John to assist them. An assistant (hypēretēs) does the practical work. John Mark is carrying things, and Luke mentions him so that we notice his absence eight verses later. If your part in the work is carrying the bags, there is honour in it: John Mark’s first job was luggage, and the Spirit wrote him into Scripture.

Why go to the synagogue first if they were sent to the Gentiles? Because God’s promises came through Israel, and it would have been strange to announce that Israel’s Messiah had come and skip Israel. The synagogue was also where people knew the Scriptures, and where God-fearing Gentiles gathered, so it was the natural first door. Paul never saw Jew and Gentile as rival audiences: one Christ, promised to the one and given to both.

Is it wrong to start where you have connections? No. Barnabas began on his own island, and Luke records it without reproach. God usually spreads the gospel along existing lines: families, friendships, workplaces, home towns. Andrew brought his brother; the Samaritan woman told her village. Start with the people God has put near you; just do not stop there. The journey that began in Cyprus went on over the mountains to towns where they knew no one.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the island’s capital a Roman governor wants to hear the word of God, but at his side stands a Jewish sorcerer whose place depends on his not hearing it. A hundred miles on foot are covered in a clause, and Paphos, the Roman capital, offers a study in contrasts.

A Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. A Jew, with the Scriptures, trading in the magical arts they forbid (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), attached to a Roman household. His name means son of Joshua, or son of Jesus.

A man of intelligence. The proconsul is shrewd, a man who understands things, and he sends for two travelling Jewish preachers because he wants to hear the word of God. Not all the powerful are closed to the gospel.

The proconsul. The title is one of the small marks of Luke’s accuracy. Cyprus became a senatorial province, governed by a proconsul, in 22 BC, and Luke uses the correct term; one or two inscriptions naming a Paulus who may be this proconsul have been found, though scholars debate the identification.

Kings shall see. Paul will close this chapter with Isaiah’s words about the Servant of the Lord, a light for the Gentiles (v. 47; Isaiah 49:6). The next verse says that kings shall see and arise, and princes shall prostrate themselves, because of the LORD who has chosen his Servant (Isaiah 49:7). The Servant is Jesus, and in Paphos the prophecy begins to come true in a Roman governor’s house.

In everyday life. Do not assume that the clever, successful or powerful person in your life is closed to Christ. Pray for one person in authority you know.

Is magic or the occult real, and should Christians be afraid of it? Scripture treats the occult as real enough to forbid and false enough to despise. Behind it stand real spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12), but they are creatures, and defeated ones: Christ disarmed them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). So a Christian should neither dabble nor dread. Keep away from horoscopes, mediums, spells, charms and anything that promises hidden power or knowledge apart from God. But if you belong to Christ, you are not at the mercy of any of it: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magician sets himself against the preachers and tries to turn the governor away from the faith, because the gospel threatens his place. But a stronger Lord stood behind the preachers.

Elymas the magician. Like Simon in Samaria (8:9–11), he sold access to power (on the name, see the uncertain wording below).

Opposed them. His motives were not purely theological. He is the resident authority on the invisible in the most powerful household on the island; if the proconsul believes the preachers, Elymas loses his post. Much opposition to the gospel has had self-interest behind it, and behind the self-interest the powers of darkness (Ephesians 6:12).

Seeking to turn the proconsul away. He does not attack the doctrine; he works sideways, through the relationship he already has. The gospel is rarely refuted in front of the person about to believe it. It is undermined afterwards, quietly, by somebody they trust. And the phrase shows how close the proconsul was: on the edge of believing, and Elymas could see it.

The stronger man. Jesus described this moment: the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved (Luke 8:12). But he also said that a strong man’s goods are safe only until one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him (Luke 11:21–22). The risen Christ is that stronger one, and Sergius Paulus is about to be carried out of the strong man’s house. No one, not even the most trusted adviser in the most powerful house, can snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28).

In everyday life. Is there anyone whose drift toward Christ, or toward deeper obedience, you are quietly discouraging because it would cost you something if they changed? A raised eyebrow, a joke at the right moment, a warning about getting too religious: that is Elymas’s method. If you find it in yourself, bring it to the Lord who forgave Saul for standing in the gospel’s way.

What if someone close to the person I am praying for is working against the gospel? Expect it, and do not be thrown by it. Pray for both, for Elymas too was within reach of mercy (v. 11). And remember that no adviser, spouse or friend can finally keep from Christ someone God is drawing. The proconsul believed with Elymas standing in the room.

Uncertain wording. Luke says that “Elymas the magician” is “the meaning of his name”, but how the name Elymas relates to Bar-Jesus and to the word magician is not certain. Elymas seems to be a second name or title meaning magician or wise man; scholars have suggested an Arabic word for a learned man or an Aramaic word for a dream-interpreter, but none is proved. The point is clear either way: the man was known by his trade, and his trade set him against the word of God.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled with the Spirit, Paul exposes the sorcerer as a son of the devil who is twisting the road by which the Lord was coming to a man’s soul. From this moment Luke calls him Paul, and from this moment he leads.

Saul, who was also called Paul. The name was not given at his conversion; like many Jews living outside the land he had two names, as John Mark did (12:12), a Hebrew one for the synagogue and a Roman one for everywhere else. What changes is his world: from now on his life is spent among Gentiles. From here on it is Paul and Barnabas, not Barnabas and Saul (v. 13). Luke first uses the name in the very scene where the proconsul is called Sergius Paulus, either a coincidence or a very dry joke. The Latin name means small, and the man who called himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) carried it well.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. The steady gaze is Spirit-given discernment. The words that follow are ferocious, and they echo what Jesus said to those who opposed him (John 8:44).

Making crooked the straight paths of the Lord. The prophet’s cry was to make straight in the desert a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and Luke’s Gospel tells us whose road that was: John the Baptist prepared the ways of the Lord (Luke 1:76; 3:4–6), and the Lord who came along them was Jesus. The straight paths of the Lord are the roads by which Christ comes to people, and Elymas has been putting bends in a road God was building toward a man’s soul. And he is named Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus, and the name Jesus means the LORD saves. He wears the Saviour’s name and fights the Saviour’s approach. Paul strips the name off him: not son of Jesus, but son of the devil.

When, if ever, should a Christian speak this sharply? Rarely, and almost never in our own cause. This is not temper but a prophetic sentence, spoken with apostolic authority to a man who had a governor’s ear and was using it to shut a door; Paul himself tells Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). The ordinary pattern is gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15–16), even with people who mock. Scripture keeps its severest words for those who deliberately twist God’s truth to keep others from it, and even then they are spoken to protect the vulnerable, not to win an argument. An ordinary believer’s duty, when someone is leading others astray, is usually to say clearly that it is false, warn those at risk, and leave the judgment to God. The Spirit knows when a word must be gentle and when it must be fire.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord strikes the false prophet blind for a time, and the governor, astonished at the teaching, believes. Judgment falls on the man who blocked the road, mercy reaches the man he was blocking, and even the judgment has an end date.

The hand of the Lord is upon you. The mighty hand that brought his people out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:8), and the Lord’s, not Paul’s. Remember who is pronouncing it. A dozen years earlier a light had struck him blind on the Damascus road, and he had gone into the city led by the hand (9:8). Paul is not enjoying this judgment. He recognises it, because it once fell on him.

For a time. A judgment with mercy in it. Paul had been blind for three days, and at the end of them a man laid hands on him and called him brother (9:17). The hand that struck Saul down was Christ’s, and so was the hand that lifted him. Nothing here puts Elymas beyond hope, and the one man in the room who knew that darkness is the one who set a limit on it. The man who had led a governor by the ear now needs a stranger to lead him by the hand. Luke never tells us what became of him.

Astonished at the teaching. Not at the miracle, but at the teaching. The sign opens the door and the word does the work; a man who believes only because he was impressed has not yet believed the gospel. Sergius Paulus is the first named Gentile ruler in Acts to believe.

The Judge of all became the one judged. The Light of the world went into the dark at Calvary, where the sun’s light failed at noon while he hung there (Luke 23:44–45). Elymas could not see the sun for a time. The Son of God went under the darkness of judgment itself, so that the blind could be led by the hand into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).

Did the proconsul really become a Christian? Luke says plainly that he believed, and in Acts that word means saving faith, not polite interest. Luke does not mention his baptism, but he often leaves such details out. The first convert of Paul’s Gentile mission was a Roman of the highest rank, and at Philippi the same gospel would reach a businesswoman and a jailer, and free a slave girl from the spirit that enslaved her (16:14–34): it came for the highest and the lowest alike.

Was it not cruel to strike a man blind? It was a judgment, and Scripture does not apologise for God’s judgments, because he is holy and Elymas was doing grave harm, trying to keep another man from eternal life. But look at its shape: it stopped the harm at once, and it was limited, as Paul’s own blindness had been. A God who never opposed evil would not be kind, only indifferent. This God judges, and even his judgment leaves a door open.

Why are such miracles not common today? Signs like this accompanied the apostles, marking them out as Christ’s authorised messengers while the new covenant word was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and Scripture complete, that ministry has ceased. Christians differ here, and many who expect such signs today love the Lord deeply; this commentary’s view rests on the link Scripture itself draws between the signs and the apostles. God still answers prayer, heals and judges as he wills. But the ordinary means he now uses to astonish people is the one that did the real work in Paphos: the teaching of the Lord, faithfully spoken.

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has kept his promise to David in Jesus, and through him forgiveness is offered to everyone who believes, Jew and Gentile alike. After John Mark turns back, Paul is invited to speak in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (vv. 13–15). He retells Israel’s history as God’s choosing and giving, up to David (vv. 16–22), then announces David’s promised offspring, Jesus, condemned in Jerusalem but raised by God, as the Scriptures foretold (vv. 23–37). Through him everyone who believes is freed from what the law could never free them from, and scoffers are warned (vv. 38–41). The next week divides the city: jealous leaders oppose, the appointed believe, and the expelled missionaries leave behind disciples full of joy and the Spirit (vv. 42–52).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul’s First Sermon

Verses 38–39 are the first explicit statement in Acts of justification by faith, a verdict the law cannot give and faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives (see the note there). And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends with Habakkuk’s warning to scoffers (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A city hungry for the word was met by jealous opposition from the synagogue’s leaders. Now: Those who have long been near the things of God are sometimes the slowest to welcome his work among newcomers, while outsiders receive it gladly; it is a warning for insiders in every church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now leads, John Mark goes home, and the two who remain climb into the interior and sit down in a synagogue, waiting to be asked to speak. Luke records a desertion without explaining it; Scripture later records its healing.

Paul and his companions. The man who fetched Paul from Tarsus and vouched for him in Jerusalem has become part of the phrase “and his companions”. There is no meeting, no vote. Barnabas, who had every reason to mind, appears not to have minded: overtaken by somebody else’s growth, he goes on walking beside him. His worth did not lie in his place in the phrase; his name was already written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

John left them. No reason is given. Homesickness, danger, malaria (compare Galatians 4:13), his cousin slipping to second place, a mission turning to Gentiles too fast: all are guesses. Luke does record the cost. Paul regarded it as desertion (15:38), and two chapters on it breaks up the partnership of the two men who walked out of Antioch together (15:36–41).

Antioch in Pisidia. A Roman colony a hundred miles inland and three and a half thousand feet up, over the Taurus mountains: danger from rivers, danger from robbers (2 Corinthians 11:26; see roads and travel).

They sat down. Going to the synagogue on the Sabbath was Paul’s usual practice (17:2). Two travel-stained strangers sat down like anybody else and waited to see whether they would be asked. Paul’s first recorded sermon begins with two men keeping quiet.

Another road to Jerusalem. Luke’s Gospel turns on a journey the other way: Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), knowing what waited there, and did not turn back when the road grew hard or his friends fell away. Mark went back to Jerusalem because the road ahead was too much. Jesus went up to Jerusalem because the road ahead was the cross. That is why the story of a deserter does not end at Perga. The young man who turned back lived to write a Gospel, by the church’s early testimony, and its great sentence is about the one who never turned back: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Mark could not finish one journey; he was given the honour of telling the world about the one who finished everything.

Failure need not be final. In what was probably his last letter, from a Roman prison with execution close, Paul asks for Mark by name: Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11; see also Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). The record of the desertion is in Scripture for ever. So is the request for him at the end.

I gave up on something God gave me to do. Can I come back? Yes, and Mark is your proof. His failure was real and public, and it hurt people he loved. But Scripture shows him restored, trusted and useful. Coming back usually means owning the failure without excuses, then taking up faithful work again, often smaller work, alongside people who will help you. You will not undo Perga, and you do not need to. The Lord who restored Peter after his denials restores deserters still.

How should I treat someone who let the team down? Paul and Barnabas both had a point. Paul saw that the work needed reliable men; Barnabas saw that a young man needed a second chance. In the end Paul himself came to value Mark. So take failure seriously, but do not write the person off. Give him a smaller task, an older friend, and time. Many of the most useful servants in the church were once somebody’s disappointment.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the Scriptures are read, the synagogue rulers invite the visitors to give a word of encouragement, and a polite formality opens the door on which the whole chapter turns. By the next Sabbath the whole city will be at the door; very often this is how God opens one.

After the reading from the Law and the Prophets. The service centred on two readings, one from the Law, the five books of Moses, and one from the Prophets, like the passage Jesus read from Isaiah at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–20). Then came a word of exhortation, which the rulers of the synagogue, lay leaders who organised the service, could invite a visitor to give. The practice has roots in Moses (Deuteronomy 31:10–13) and Ezra (Nehemiah 8:8); the synagogue itself probably grew up in the exile.

Any word of encouragement. A word that comes alongside and strengthens, the ancestor of the sermon: a logos paraklēseōs, the phrase the writer to the Hebrews uses of his own letter (Hebrews 13:22). Luke used the same noun of what old Simeon was waiting for, the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and Simeon found it in a baby in his arms. Paul is about to tell this synagogue that the comfort every Sabbath reading had promised has a name, and has risen from the dead.

The Word read and the Word made flesh. The Law and the Prophets had just been read, and Paul rises to show that every line pointed to Jesus (Luke 24:27, 44). For centuries the scrolls had been unrolled, Sabbath after Sabbath, across the world, carrying a name the readers did not yet know. The Word read and the Word made flesh were always meant to meet, and on that Sabbath in Pisidia they did.

Do Jews still do this? Yes. To this day the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and on Mondays, Thursdays and festivals), on an annual cycle that ends and begins again at Simchat Torah, “rejoicing in the Torah” (in ancient Israel the cycle probably took about three years), still paired with a reading from the Prophets and a teaching. It is the church’s inheritance too: Paul charged Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13), the shape of Christian worship ever since.

Is a sermon really encouragement, even when it is hard? Yes. Paul was invited to give a word of encouragement, and his sermon ended with a sharp warning (vv. 40–41). Biblical encouragement is not flattery but the word that puts strength into you, sometimes through rebuke, sometimes through comfort, always through Christ. A sermon that only made you feel good about yourself would not have encouraged you; one that brought you to Christ always does, even when it hurts on the way.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins where Israel’s story begins, with God choosing a people, multiplying them in slavery and bringing them out with power, because the gospel is where that story was always heading.

Paul stood up. In a synagogue the teacher normally sat to expound (Luke 4:20), but Paul stands, motioning with his hand, like a public speaker in the Greek world; Luke notices that hand twice more (21:40; 26:1). This is Luke’s fullest sample of Paul’s preaching in a synagogue, as the speech at Athens (17:22–31) is his sample of Paul’s preaching to pagans. It moves from Israel’s history (vv. 17–22), to the promise kept in Jesus (vv. 23–37), to the offer and the warning (vv. 38–41). Peter preached the same gospel at Pentecost (2:14–36): the apostle to the Gentiles has no different message from the apostle to the Jews.

You who fear God. His first sentence names two congregations. The God-fearers were Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel in the synagogue but had not been circumcised. Picture a man who has heard the promises to Abraham read aloud perhaps a thousand times, each time understanding that they were addressed to somebody else’s family. Cornelius was one (10:2), and Lydia (16:14). So the Gentile response in v. 48 is not a sudden lurch; the synagogue itself had been ploughing the ground for years.

Chose our fathers. The sermon opens on God’s choosing: Israel was chosen not for its greatness but because the LORD set his love on them (Deuteronomy 7:6–8). It will end on God’s choosing too: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (v. 48). Every man in that room would have said amen to the first. What split the congregation a week later was not whether God chooses, but whom.

Made the people great in Egypt. The promised family multiplied not in the promised land but in a foreign country, under a king trying to stop it: the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). God’s promise made its greatest progress in centuries that looked as if it had been forgotten.

With uplifted arm. Paul starts with the exodus (Exodus 6:6) because the gospel is a second one.
