On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and Luke’s word is exodos. Isaiah asked to whom the arm of the LORD had been revealed, and answered with the Servant pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities (Isaiah 53:1–5). The arm raised over Egypt was bared again at Golgotha, not to strike Israel’s enemies but to take the blow itself, and lead a people out of a worse slavery than Pharaoh’s. No Pharaoh, no sin and no grave can hold the people he has redeemed.

In everyday life. If you are in an Egypt of your own, a job, a family situation, an illness you would never have chosen, do not conclude that God’s purposes for you have stalled. His people grew most where it looked least likely.

Why does Paul start so far back? Because Jesus is not a new idea but the point of the whole story. Paul retells a history every hearer knew so that, when he reaches Jesus, they will see it landing where it was always heading. It is a lesson in reading the Old Testament: not a collection of moral examples but one long account of God choosing, rescuing, enduring and promising, all leading to his Son (Luke 24:27).
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God bore with an unbelieving people for forty years and then gave them a land they had not earned, judging nations whose wickedness he had long endured.

He put up with them. He bore with their ways (etropophorēsen; on the other reading, see the textual note below). Within weeks of Sinai they were dancing round a golden calf, and soon proposed choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt (Numbers 14:4); God’s own summary is that they put him to the test ten times (Numbers 14:22). The generation that saw the sea open died in the sand. Yet he did not leave, and he did not pretend. If you suspect God stays with you only because he has not looked closely, this is better news: he has looked, and he is still walking at the pace of the slowest man in the column.

As an inheritance. A gift, not an achievement. Nobody earns an inheritance; it comes because of who your father is. Moses made sure they understood: not because of your righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:5).

Struck so that they might drink. For forty years the Holy One walked through the sand with a complaining people. He fed them bread from heaven and gave them water from the rock, and Paul says that the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4): the Son of God was already among them, bearing with them, struck so that they might drink. The same Lord bears with us still, and will not set us down until he has brought us into an inheritance we never earned.

How could a good God order the destruction of the seven nations in Canaan? Paul passes over it in a phrase (Deuteronomy 7:1), but the loss of life is real and grievous. Several truths, held together, show it is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

First, it was judgment, not ethnic hatred. Israel had no general warrant to harm Gentiles; she was to offer peace to distant cities (Deuteronomy 20:10). This was a bounded act of justice on particular nations for appalling sin, held back four hundred years, for God told Abraham, “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). Among other things they burned their own children in sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Leviticus 18:21), until the land itself, defiled, vomited out its inhabitants (Leviticus 18:24–25).

Second, it was not favouritism toward Israel. It was not because of Israel’s righteousness but because of the wickedness of these nations (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), and if Israel did the same, the land would vomit them out too (Leviticus 18:28), as it did in the exile. And mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite was spared through faith and stands in the Messiah’s family line (Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5). The issue was never race but allegiance.

Third, the objection takes something for granted. We assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deuteronomy 32:39), and every one of us has forfeited life through sin (Romans 6:23). What needs explaining is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone is spared at all. On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives no glib answer; we rest in the One of whom Abraham asked, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones, as David did for his own child (2 Samuel 12:23), and refusing to pretend we see more than we do.

Finally, a unique event, never a model. Jesus refused the sword: my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). The church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:4); we love our enemies and leave vengeance to God (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19). No one may invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ’s name. The conquest is a sober preview of the final judgment, and at the cross that judgment fell on Jesus: the God who judged Canaan did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32), so that wrath and mercy met. The only refuge, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ.

Does God still put up with his people today? Yes, and every honest Christian depends on it: our grumbling, our forgetfulness, our small idolatries. But patience is not approval. It is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and Hebrews uses these very forty years as a warning not to harden our hearts (Hebrews 3:7–19). Take comfort that he bears with you, and take care not to treat his bearing as permission.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “he carried them” (etrophophorēsen, a difference of one letter), recalling what Moses said of these same years: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son (Deuteronomy 1:31). Both are true of that wilderness, and neither flatters Israel: God spent forty years either enduring them or carrying them, for the same reason, because they would not trust him.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s giving ran on through the long years of the judges, deliverer after flawed deliverer until Samuel, showing that the rescue never depended on the rescuer.

All this took about 450 years. In the ESV the number sums up what has just been said: about four hundred years in Egypt (Genesis 15:13; Acts 7:6), forty in the wilderness, and roughly seven to ten to take and divide the land. And Paul says about. (On the older reading, see the textual note below.)

He gave them judges. Consider what the book of Judges contains: a spiral of idolatry, oppression and rescue, until the book’s own closing verdict is that everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25). And God’s response, through three centuries of it, was to go on giving.

Look at what he gave. Not a roll of heroes. A left-handed assassin. A woman, with a general who would not go without her. A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it. The son of a prostitute, thrown out by his own family. A strong man who could not govern his appetites and ended blind, grinding grain in his enemies’ prison. God was not doing his best with poor material. He was showing that the deliverance never depended on the deliverer. The line ends with Samuel, prophet and last judge, who anointed the first two kings.

The Judge who did not die. Judges keeps raising up saviours (Judges 3:9, 15) and watching each rescue wear off, because whenever the judge died, they turned back (Judges 2:19). The cycle could only be broken by a deliverer who did not die, or who died and did not stay dead. That is where this sermon is going: God raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption (vv. 30–34). His rescue does not wear off.

In everyday life. Look at the imperfect people God has put over you, your pastor, your parents, your manager, and thank God for one specific good he has done you through one of them.

Does a chronological puzzle like this undermine the Bible’s reliability? No. A difficulty is not a demonstrated error. Here it disappears once you notice which clause the number belongs to, and that Paul says about. A few puzzles still lack a certain answer, and an honest reader can say so without alarm. Scripture is true in all it affirms; our understanding of ancient numbering and manuscripts is what needs patience. A book tidied up by later hands would have fewer such knots, not more.

Textual note. The older printed Greek text, followed by the King James Version, attaches the 450 years to what comes next, the judges. Then the sum will not come out, for 1 Kings 6:1 puts only 480 years between the exodus and the fourth year of Solomon. The better attested reading, which the ESV translates, attaches the number to what has just been said, and the difficulty disappears.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel demanded a king and was given Saul; God then removed him and raised up David, the man he had sought out, whose line points beyond him to the Son who did all God’s will.

They asked for a king. The asking was itself the sin: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). They wanted a king like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:5, 20), and God gave it. Not every answered prayer is approval: of the quails in the wilderness a psalm says he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Psalm 106:15). Sometimes God gives what we insist on, and it is a judgment.

For forty years. The forty is Paul’s, not the Old Testament’s. The text of 1 Samuel 13:1 is incomplete, as the ESV footnote there shows. Josephus, a generation after Paul, gives forty in one place (though twenty in another), so Paul is repeating a received figure of his day.

A man of the tribe of Benjamin. Standing in front of them is another Saul of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), stopped in his old course on the Damascus road. He does not point out the likeness.

He raised up David. The commendation joins Scriptures: a man after his own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), I have found David, my servant (Psalm 89:20), and words about doing all my will that echo what God says of Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28).

How can God call David a man after his own heart? This is the man who took another man’s wife and, when the husband proved too loyal to cover the pregnancy, had him posted where the fighting was heaviest and the line pulled back from him: adultery, then a murder arranged by letter. Three things matter.

First, the sentence describes God’s choice. It is not a character reference. God says it at the moment Saul is rejected, long before Bathsheba, and the stress falls on God’s seeking: the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart.

Second, what each did when he was caught. Saul, confronted over Amalek, argued: the people did it, the animals were meant for sacrifice, and he had obeyed anyway. When at last he said I have sinned, he asked in the same breath to be honoured before the elders (1 Samuel 15:24–30). David, confronted by Nathan with one sentence, you are the man, answered: I have sinned against the LORD (2 Samuel 12:13). No excuses, no blame shifted. Then he wrote it up, set it to music and handed it to the choirmaster, so that the nation could sing his worst hour back to him for ever (Psalm 51). He cared more about being right with God than about being thought well of.

Third, the direction of a life. “Who will do all my will” is measured against the man he replaced. Saul had one plain instruction at Amalek and kept the best of the livestock. David’s life, for all its wreckage, ran in the direction God pointed; he never went after other gods, the very measure the books of Kings apply to every later king.

The Son who did all his will. The commendation is bigger than the man. David did not do all God’s will; Bathsheba and Uriah are in the record. Only one son of David could say, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7, from Psalm 40), or that his food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34). His perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), which is why a sinner can afford to be as honest as David. David needed a Psalm 51; Jesus never did. And because the Son after God’s heart was crushed for the sins of a David, every broken sinner who comes to him is welcomed as a son. God raised up David, and Paul will use the same verb of raising Jesus from the dead (vv. 30, 37).

God’s man cannot stay down. If you fear your failures have disqualified you, remember that God’s chosen king has a murder in his file. If you are tempted to use that as cover, remember what it cost him: a dead child, a fractured house, a son in armed rebellion. God’s man is not the man who never falls, but the man who cannot stay down, because God will not leave him there.

In everyday life. The last time you were confronted with a fault, did you argue like Saul or confess like David? If it was Saul, go back to that person this week and say the plain words: I was wrong.

What does it actually mean to be after God’s heart? To want what God wants and love what he loves. In David it showed in his delight in God’s presence, his hunger for God’s honour, his refusal to touch the Lord’s anointed even when Saul hunted him, and his readiness to be broken over sin. It is not a temperament but a direction of the heart that only grace produces, seen most clearly not in success but in repentance. You can ask God for it today: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From David’s line God has brought the Saviour he promised, Jesus, and six hundred years of apparent silence could not cancel the promise. The last three words, “as he promised”, carry the weight.

The promise made. Settled at last in a house of cedar, David was struck that the ark of God was still in a tent, and proposed to build a temple. That night God answered through Nathan, declining the offer and returning it multiplied: you will not build me a house; I will build you one. I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

The promise buried. Four hundred years later Nebuchadnezzar’s army broke into Jerusalem. The last king of David’s line, Zedekiah, was caught fleeing; they killed his sons in front of him and put out his eyes, so that the last thing he saw was the end of the dynasty (2 Kings 25:7). No son of David sat on a throne in Jerusalem again. Some six hundred years went by, and the royal line came down to a carpenter’s shop in a village in Galilee.

God has brought. Not salvation made available in principle: a Saviour led in, in a body, to a particular people, at a particular date, under a named governor.

A Saviour. Rescuer (sōtēr), and the word had a rival in that town. In a Roman colony of old legionaries, Saviour was the empire’s word for its emperor, and Paul hands the title to a crucified Galilean.

Not as we still hope. Any observer would have called the promise dead. A travelling tentmaker stands up and says not “as we still hope” but “as he promised”, and here he is. Six hundred years of silence could not cancel one word God spoke to David in the night; the stump of Jesse put out a shoot (Isaiah 11:1) that will never be cut down. Every promise God has made finds its Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the King he brought sits on a throne no Babylon can break.

In everyday life. Every heart has its candidate for the title of saviour: a career, a marriage, a political cause, a bank balance. Each asks to be served and none can save; the Saviour God brought gives himself for those he saves. And name the promise of God you have quietly shelved because of how long it has been. Then look again at how late this one was, and how completely kept.

What exactly does Jesus save us from? From the guilt of our sin and the wrath of God it deserves, from the power of sin that enslaves us, and in the end from the very presence of sin and death: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). He is not first a helper for people who are mostly managing, but a rescuer for the lost. Jesus means the LORD saves, and the Saviour is the LORD himself come to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul calls John the Baptist as witness: the great prophet his hearers had heard of said plainly that he was not the Messiah, only the forerunner of one far greater.

John had proclaimed. Why John, five hundred miles from the Jordan? Because news of John had reached Jews far from Israel, though not always the news of what came after him (18:25; 19:1–7). Paul closes the gap: here is what John himself said he was for.

Finishing his course. A course is a runner’s track (dromos). Paul will use it of himself: if only I may finish my course (20:24), and at the end, I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:7). John’s course ended in a cell, cut short because a girl danced well at a birthday party (Mark 6:21–28): by every measure we normally use, a humiliating end. Scripture calls it finishing his course. God measures a life not by where it stopped, but by whether the ground assigned to it was covered.

I am not he. At the height of his influence, with delegations sent to ask who he was, John refused to be thought the Messiah (John 1:20). He used his influence to say who he was not.

Not worthy to untie. Untying sandals was a slave’s job (Luke 3:16). A later rabbinic saying excused a disciple from this one task; John says he is not fit even for it.

He knelt and washed their feet. The One whose sandals he was not worthy to untie took off his outer garment, knelt and washed his disciples’ feet, and then went to the cross to wash them entirely. He must increase. He has, and he will, until every knee bows.

In everyday life. This is the pattern for nearly everybody: the parent whose child will go further, the teacher whose pupil will preach better. “I am not he” is freeing, because the moment you stop being the point you stop having to be impressive. John’s whole value lay in making somebody else visible, and he called it his joy (John 3:29–30).

What was John’s baptism, and how is it different from Christian baptism? John’s baptism was a sign of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming Messiah. Christian baptism is into the name of the Lord Jesus, after he has died and risen, and signifies union with him and the gift of the Spirit. That is why the men at Ephesus who knew only John’s baptism were baptised in Jesus’ name once they believed (19:4–5). John pointed forward; Christian baptism looks back to a finished work. And repentance in both means more than feeling sorry: a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, which John spelled out for the crowds in their own jobs and homes (Luke 3:8–14).

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The history lesson becomes an address: the message of salvation has been sent to the very people in the room, Jews and God-fearing Gentiles alike. Every sermon has to make this turn, or it is only a lecture.

Brothers. Paul names the sons of the family of Abraham and the God-fearing Gentiles inside a single word.

To us. Not to them, back there, but to the people in this room, this morning. For years a God-fearer had been like a guest at the reading of another family’s will. Now a visiting rabbi says not “you may listen” but “to us has been sent”.

Has been sent. The message was not discovered by clever men but dispatched, deliberately, to a particular address; the Greek verb is the one our word apostle comes from.

This salvation. Not salvation in general, but what happened to a named man under a named governor. Christianity is not a theory about how people get saved but a report of something done.

The message and the Sent One. Hebrews calls Jesus the apostle of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), sent from the Father, and Jesus said that whoever receives the one he sends receives him (John 13:20). So this message is the way the sent Son himself arrives in a synagogue in Pisidia. God did not wait for us to find our way to him; he sent the good news across mountains and seas, carried by tired men on foot, until it reached the back row of that synagogue and, at length, your own door. The Father is the sender, the Son is the message, and the Spirit puts it into the hand of the one it was meant for.

How can I know the message is really for me? Because it is addressed to everyone who hears it, without a qualifying test. You need not first prove that you are chosen, good enough or sorry enough. The gospel comes to you as a sinner and says: this is for you; come. Election is discovered by believing, not before believing. If you have heard this message, it has been sent to you, and the right response is not to wonder whether you are allowed to take it but to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s rulers, deaf to the prophets they heard every Sabbath, fulfilled those very prophecies by condemning an innocent man, and they were guilty for it. God’s plan was carried out through their blindness, and the blindness was still their own.

Read every Sabbath. The prophets had been read in that synagogue not long before (v. 15). The men who missed the Messiah had heard them just as this congregation had. Paul later calls it a veil lying over the heart whenever Moses is read (2 Corinthians 3:14–15).

Fulfilled them by condemning him. Their blindness did not frustrate the Scriptures; it carried them out. They were not derailing God’s plan but were the instrument of it, and they did not know.

No guilt worthy of death. Were they then guilty? Paul answers in the same breath: yes. They found nothing in him that deserved death, and asked for the execution anyway; in Luke’s Gospel Pilate says three times that he finds no guilt in the man (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). They acted in ignorance, and they are answerable, as Peter had already told Jerusalem (3:15–17).

The Lamb led to the slaughter. The Lamb was led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) by men who did not know they were leading a Lamb. And the innocent one, condemned without a case, went willingly, because the guilt he died for was not his but ours.

Would we have known better? It is hard not to assume it; we have the end of the story and they did not. So be exact about who these people were: the most Scripture-soaked population on earth. Many could read it in the language it was written in. They heard it read publicly every week of their lives, in the city where it was kept. And they looked straight at the fulfilment and saw a blasphemer. Familiarity with the Bible is not recognition of Christ; you can read a chapter every morning for thirty years and be no nearer. That is not an argument for reading less, but a reason to pray before you read, because the difference between them and us was never that we are cleverer. And if you do read asking him to show you Christ, that very asking is a sign that he is opening your eyes (Luke 24:45).

In everyday life. The rulers had a reason to misread the prophets: recognising this man would have cost them their standing, their income and their control of the temple. Is there a passage whose plain meaning would cost you something, and is that the very passage you find unusually hard to be sure about? Ask the Lord who opened the disciples’ minds to open yours.

If God planned it, how can people be blamed for it? Because God’s plan does not force anyone to act against his own will. The rulers did exactly what they wanted, from motives of their own: envy, fear, the love of power. God in his wisdom ruled over their wickedness and turned it to the salvation of the world (2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture never lets God’s sovereignty excuse human sin, and never lets human sin escape God’s sovereignty. We are to believe both, and be glad that even the worst crime in history could not slip out of the hands of a good God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the Scriptures foretold of the Messiah’s suffering was carried out, down to his being taken down from the tree and laid in a tomb. The cross was not an accident God made the best of; it was the plan, written down beforehand.

All that was written of him. All of it (John 19:28, 30): thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12–13), silence before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7), hands and feet pierced and clothing divided by lot (Psalm 22:16–18), numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), not a bone broken (Psalm 34:20), a grave with a rich man (Isaiah 53:9). They were in the scrolls in that synagogue’s own cupboard, and Paul is preaching to men who could check him.

From the tree. Tree means simply wood (xylon): a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (5:30; 10:39; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24), to echo the Law: a hanged man’s body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). And they took him down and buried him at once, keeping that very command. Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). (Some also hear an echo of the curse that entered by a tree in Eden being undone on a tree at Calvary, a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy’s curse.)

Laid him in a tomb. In fact it was Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented, who laid him there (Luke 23:50–53). Paul is compressing, speaking of Jerusalem as a single actor.

Do not hurry past the burial. It is in Paul’s summary of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) and in the creed, because it proves he really died. Any theory that Jesus merely fainted and revived in the cool of the tomb has to explain how a man in that condition, sealed behind a stone he could not have moved from inside, presented himself three days later as the conqueror of death. The stone was moved from the outside.

Cursed, so that we might be blessed. To be cursed by God is to stand under his judgment, cut off from his blessing; Jesus took that place so that those who trust him might receive the blessing promised to Abraham (Galatians 3:14). He who laid the foundations of the earth was laid in a hole cut in its rock. The hands that formed Adam from the dust were wrapped in linen and folded still. He went all the way down, so that nothing in that darkness would be strange to him when he comes to raise his people out of it. A borrowed grave was enough. He needed it only until the third day.

Why does it matter so much that prophecy was fulfilled in detail? Because it shows that the cross was the plan, announced centuries ahead and carried out to the letter. That matters for your faith: Christianity rests on events God foretold and then did, which you can check. And it matters for your comfort: if God kept every word about his Son’s suffering, down to the dice and the vinegar, he will keep every word about your salvation and your future.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reversed the verdict of men by raising Jesus, and named witnesses who saw him alive over many days could still be questioned. The resurrection rests not on feelings but on public testimony.

But God raised him. In vv. 27–29 the subject is they, and what men do ends in a sealed tomb. Then the subject changes, and the whole history reverses, as in sermon after sermon in this book (2:24; 3:15; 4:10). Men did their worst, and the Father answered with life. Every “but God” in a believer’s life flows from this one, and the God who reversed the verdict of Calvary will reverse the grave for all who are his.

For many days he appeared. Not felt, but seen: forty days (1:3), not one moment at dawn that could be put down to grief and poor light, and to those who had come up with him from Galilee, the same men the whole way, there when it went wrong.

Now his witnesses. Present tense: some fifteen years on, they are alive and can be questioned, as he tells Corinth that most of the five hundred are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6), a strange thing to write unless you want readers to check. And Paul rests his case not on his own encounter, which Luke tells three times, but on the testimony of those he had once hunted. That is the right way round, and the opposite of how most of us argue for our faith.

In everyday life. Write down the two words “but God”, and put them where you will see them today, over the thing that seems finished: a marriage, a prodigal, a diagnosis, your own sin.

My own experience of God feels thin. Is my faith on weak ground? No. Your assurance stands not on the vividness of what happened to you, but on what happened to Jesus, in public, before people who could be named, in a city where the authorities had every motive to produce a body and never did. Feelings rise and fall; the empty tomb does not. The Spirit does give his people a living sense of God, but the foundation is history. On grey days, go back to the witnesses, read the resurrection chapters, and stand where they stood.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good news is that God has kept his promise to the fathers by raising Jesus, and the resurrection is God’s own public declaration: “You are my Son.” The fathers were given the promise; their children have been given the thing.

We bring you the good news. Not advice, or a technique for living better: a report that a promise has been kept.

To us their children. These all died in faith, not having received the things promised (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40). We are the generation that took delivery of what they signed for. The gospel is not a new religion but the completion of the old. Verses 32–37 rest on three texts: Psalm 2, who the risen Jesus is; Isaiah 55, what his rising brings; Psalm 16, why it lasts.

The second Psalm. A coronation psalm for the king of David’s line. Paul applies it to the resurrection, the day God installed Jesus as King, declaring him Son with power (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5; 5:5). (On whether “raising Jesus” means the resurrection, see the uncertain wording below.)

So what changed on the third day? Not who Jesus is, but who knows it. On the Friday the public verdict was that he was a blasphemer, justly executed, and heaven had said nothing. On the Sunday God spoke: this is my Son, here is the proof, and I am putting him on the throne. What God thinks of Jesus he said out loud, in an empty tomb: You are my Son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God’s Son at the resurrection. He is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; 17:5), and the idea that God adopted a man on Easter morning (adoptionism) is wrong, for four reasons. First, the psalm’s “today” is the day of enthronement, not of conception: Israel’s kings were called God’s son at their accession (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 89:27), so the language is throne language. Second, Paul says what the resurrection did: Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4); it published a fact, it did not manufacture one. Third, Hebrews calls him the Son through whom God created the world (Hebrews 1:2), and three verses later quotes this very psalm (Hebrews 1:5). Fourth, Peter’s “God has made him both Lord and Christ” (2:36) needs the same care: the eternal Son is installed in the office he came to fill, not turned into something he was not.

What does this mean for me if I am in Christ? You belong to a King who is already reigning, not to a cause that might one day win. Psalm 2 goes on to promise the Son the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession, which begins to happen in this very chapter. And united to the Son, you share the Father’s pleasure in him: you are adopted, a child of God (Galatians 4:5–7). The verdict of the empty tomb is the verdict over your life.

Uncertain wording. “Raising Jesus” could mean raising him up onto the stage of history, as God “raised up” David in v. 22, with v. 34 then adding the resurrection. Most take it as the resurrection, because v. 34 continues “as for the fact that he raised him from the dead”, and the New Testament elsewhere ties Psalm 2 to his rising and enthronement (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:3–5). This commentary takes that reading; either way the promise to the fathers is kept in Jesus.

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was raised never to die again, so the sure blessings promised to David’s line rest at last on a King who cannot lose them.

No more to return to corruption. This separates Easter from every other raising in the Bible: Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). The widow’s son at Nain sat up and spoke, and one day was buried again. Jairus’s daughter got up and ate, and in time she died. Lazarus came out, and somewhere there is dust that used to be Lazarus. Each was a reprieve, a body handed back on loan. Jesus was raised out the far side of death, into a body that will not wear out and cannot be reclaimed.

The holy and sure blessings of David. Isaiah 55:3, God’s everlasting covenant of steadfast love to David (see the uncertain wording below). The two texts share a word: Isaiah promises the holy blessings of David; Psalm 16:10 says you will not let your Holy One see corruption. In the Greek Bible these congregations used, the same root, hosios, stands behind holy in both. Linking passages by a shared term was a recognised Jewish method of argument.

Sure blessings need a living King. How sure can a covenant be if the man it was made with is in a tomb, and every heir ends in a tomb as well? A dynasty of corpses is not an everlasting kingdom. If the promises to David are to be sure, somebody in that line has to stop dying. So Paul reaches for Psalm 16:10, as Peter had at Pentecost (2:27). Death had one claim on the Holy One, and lost it for ever; and in losing it, it lost its claim on everyone who is his.

In everyday life. At a believer’s graveside, or awake at night thinking of your own death, this is what holds: not a longer loan, but a body given outright, because Christ lives for ever.

What are the blessings of David that come to us? Everything God promised to David’s house: a King who reigns for ever, steadfast love that will not be withdrawn, a people secure in his kingdom, and, in Isaiah 55, an invitation to everyone who thirsts to come and receive it without money. In Christ these become ours: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, an eternal inheritance. They are holy because God gives them, and sure because the King through whom they come can never die again and lose them.

Uncertain wording. The Greek is compressed, literally “the holy things of David, the faithful ones”, following the Greek translation of Isaiah 55:3, where the Hebrew speaks of God’s steadfast, sure love for David. Whether “the holy things” are the mercies promised to David or the blessings that come through his heir is debated; the ESV’s “blessings” is an interpretation. Paul’s point is clear: the promised covenant love is secure only if David’s heir lives for ever, and in the risen Jesus it is.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David served God in his own generation and then died and decayed, but the one God raised did not, so Psalm 16 points beyond David to Jesus. David’s grave proves the point, and Jesus’ empty one fulfils it.

David saw corruption. Psalm 16 cannot be finally about David, because David decayed, as Peter said at Pentecost (2:29).

In his own generation. Older versions turn the sentence the other way: David served his own generation by the will of God. Either way the boundary is the same: in his own generation, not in every generation, and not in ours. David did not fix Israel; he left a divided family and an unbuilt temple. He did what God gave him in the years he was given, and it is recorded as enough.

Fell asleep. The man after God’s own heart decayed in the ground; Jesus did not. Christians call death sleep, and the word is usable only because one body went into a tomb and did not decay. Without v. 37 “fell asleep” is a soft word for death; with it, the plain truth: those who sleep will wake. Because he lives, asleep on a Christian’s grave is not a kindness but a promise.

For every generation at once. David’s tomb was still pointed out a thousand years later. The Son of David served the purpose of God for every generation at once: in one afternoon outside Jerusalem he did the Father’s will for all his people in every age, and his tomb was empty by the third morning. He holds every small generation of his people, ours among them, inside his everlasting one.

In everyday life. If your work feels small and local, a congregation of forty, a family, a class of children, one difficult relative, keep this sentence. You are asked to serve the purpose of God in your own generation, the only one you have been given. Nobody in Scripture is commended for the size of his sphere.

What does serving my generation look like in practice? Taking the people, place and years God has given you as your actual assignment, rather than waiting for a bigger one. Ask whom God has put within your reach that no one else is placed to serve. Be faithful there, in the ordinary means: prayer, the word, hospitality, honest work, mercy. Then leave the next generation to the God who will raise up its servants too.

Does fell asleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes how death looks from this side and what it is for the believer: temporary, peaceful, with a waking to come. It does not mean the soul is switched off. Jesus promised the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43); Paul said that to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). The believer’s soul goes at once into the presence of the Lord, conscious and at rest, while the body sleeps awaiting the resurrection (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; the Westminster Confession 32.1).

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Jesus forgiveness is proclaimed, and everyone who believes is justified, declared in the right with God, from everything the law of Moses could never free them from. This is the sermon’s conclusion, and Galatians and Romans in embryo.

Forgiveness of sins is proclaimed. Not offered on terms you must first earn. Proclaimed is the word for a herald in a public square reading out what the king has decided. Paul is not explaining how to apply for a pardon but reading out an amnesty, through Jesus, offered to you.

Freed from everything. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified: dikaioutai, Paul’s great word, here for the first time in Acts. It is a courtroom word. To be justified is not to be improved or given a fresh start, but to have a judge declare, formally and on the record, that you are in the right. Everyone who believes: by faith alone. From everything: every sin, completely.

The courtroom. A man is in the dock. He did it. And the judge, who has read every page, says: not guilty. Not because the file was thin, or the judge easy-going, but because the sentence has already been served by somebody else, and the court holds the receipt. That is justification. And it is more than a blank slate: Christ’s own obedience is counted to the believer, like a gift paid into an empty bank account, so that God regards him as clothed in his Son’s perfect record (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Not by the law of Moses. The law showed sin but could not remove it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16), and its sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). But be specific. The ordinary offerings covered sins committed unwittingly; a few deliberate wrongs, such as theft confessed and repaid, had an offering too (Leviticus 6:1–7). But for sin done defiantly, with the eyes open and the hand raised, the law named no personal offering at all: the person who does anything with a high hand shall be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:30–31). A man could stand in the temple courts with his best lamb, and the law had no provision for accepting it.

David knew. He had committed adultery and arranged a killing with his eyes wide open, and he said so: you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it (Psalm 51:16). A king with unlimited access to the altar was saying that the altar had nothing for him. Now a thousand-year-old question is answered in a synagogue in Pisidia. The offer is aimed at the sin you did not drift into, the one you chose, the one nothing has ever touched: not resolutions, not service, not an unbroken run of Sundays, not a hundred confessions of the same thing.

Everyone who believes. Not everyone who improves or has the right ancestry. Believing is the whole entry requirement, deliberately the one thing a beggar can do as easily as a benefactor. No sin is so deliberate that his blood cannot cover it, and no beggar so poor that he cannot take it with an empty hand.

Two words of the decree. David stood at the altar with nothing to bring. A thousand years later his Son stood in Jerusalem as the offering the law had never contained, cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of his people (Isaiah 53:8), the deliberate sins among them included. God is just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26), and he sends a herald to read out two words of the decree: from everything.

In everyday life. Name the sin nothing has ever touched, and bring it, by name, to the One through whom forgiveness is proclaimed. When the memory of it accuses you this week, answer it with this verse rather than with a promise to do better.

Why can’t we admit we were wrong? Listen to any argument in a kitchen or a comment thread and you will hear people justifying themselves. The social psychologists Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson, in Mistakes Were Made (but Not by Me), showed how deep this runs: when our actions clash with our picture of ourselves as decent and sensible, the mind quietly rewrites the story, so that we keep the picture and lose the truth. We are all permanently in court, acting as our own counsel, and it is exhausting. Paul announces that the trial is over. If God has declared you in the right through Christ, you no longer need to win, and you can afford the most freeing sentence there is: I was wrong.

If I am justified by faith alone, does it matter how I live? Enormously, but not as the ground of your acceptance. The faith that receives Christ for pardon receives him as Lord, and the Spirit who gives it begins at once to change the believer (Ephesians 2:8–10). A justified person will fight sin and grow in good works, not to earn God’s verdict but because he already has it. Someone content to go on in deliberate sin should ask whether he has believed at all (James 2:17). A believer who hates his sin and keeps fighting it, even after many falls, is not that person: the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in him (Galatians 5:17).

What if I do not feel forgiven? Rest on what has been proclaimed rather than on what you feel. A herald’s announcement is true whether or not the prisoner believes it; the gates are open either way. Guilt often lingers after a sin has been forgiven, especially the high-handed sins. Take it back to the word: everyone who believes is freed from everything. Thank God for it in so many words, before the feelings follow. They usually do, but your pardon does not wait for them.

Where Christians differ: justification. Some teach that justification is a process in which faith and works, or faith and sacraments, together make us righteous. This commentary’s view: Paul says everyone who believes is justified, declared righteous, from everything, through Christ, not by the law. Justification is God’s legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to us (Romans 4:5; 5:1; Philippians 3:9). Good works follow as fruit, not as ground.

Uncertain wording. The last clause could be read as if the law freed people from some things and Christ frees them from the rest. Few take it so. The stress falls on “everything”: what the law could not do at all, since its sacrifices never took away sin (Hebrews 10:4), Christ does completely, including the deliberate sins for which the law named no offering. However the clause is weighed, nothing is left outside his pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends the offer with a warning from Habakkuk: God is doing a work in their day, and those who scoff at it will perish. He has just announced an amnesty; he ends by telling them what happens to those who laugh at one, as Peter did (3:23).

You scoffers. The quotation is Habakkuk 1:5, and its setting gives it teeth. Habakkuk had complained that God was doing nothing about Judah’s corruption, and God’s answer was this verse: the work was the Babylonian invasion, a judgment nobody would credit until the siege ramps were up against their walls. (Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament his hearers used, which reads you scoffers.)

Paul’s use of it. God has done another unbelievable thing in your days, this time a rescue, not a ruin: a crucified man raised and forgiveness proclaimed in his name. Your fathers refused to credit a work of God, and it arrived anyway and flattened the city. Do not assume that because this word is good news it can safely be laughed at. Blessed be the God whose works are too great for scoffers and exactly the right size for sinners who believe.

Perish. That is where Paul’s first recorded sermon lands. A gospel that has lost the ability to say that word is not the gospel Paul preached, and the kindness of a warning is proportional to the danger it names. Nobody shouts at a man about a fire that is not burning.

The one who wept over the city. Some fifteen years earlier Jesus had seen Jerusalem and wept over it, because it did not know the time of its visitation, and told it that its enemies would set up a barricade around it and tear it down (Luke 19:41–44). The Lord whose resurrection Paul proclaims is not a stranger issuing threats. He is the Saviour who weeps over scoffers and dies for them, among them a man from Tarsus who had once been a blasphemer and a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13). Paul’s warning carries Christ’s tears in it.

Who the warning is aimed at. It is a warning to scoffers: people who hear, understand, and treat the thing as beneath serious attention. The frightened Christian who reads it at midnight and wonders whether it describes him should notice that a scoffer is not troubled by warnings; the alarm you feel is itself evidence that it does not fit you. Its real question is whether you have been told and are declining to act.

Is it loving to end a gospel message with a warning? Yes. Jesus warned about judgment more than almost anyone in Scripture, and he was love made visible. A warning is what makes good news urgent. If perishing is real, a preacher who never mentions it is not being kind, only quiet. The aim is never to frighten people away but toward the only refuge. Paul’s warning comes straight after the widest offer imaginable, and that order is the pattern: the door first, then the reason to go through it now.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hearers beg to hear more, many follow Paul and Barnabas, and their first instruction to the new believers is simply to stay in the grace of God. The way in is the way on.

The people begged. For the same thing again next week. They could not take a copy home: they had heard the most important thing they would ever hear, once, and had seven days to hold it with nothing but memory and each other. We carry more sermons in our pockets than we will ever listen to; it is worth asking which of us is in the worse position.

One week apart. This is the congregation that will be filled with jealousy two verses on. Between the begging and the jealousy lies one week, and Luke does not say what happened in it. Enthusiasm for the word of God and hostility to it can live in the same building seven days apart, and sometimes in the same person.

Many Jews and devout converts. Born Jews, and proselytes, circumcised converts. The first fruit comes out of the synagogue, not around it.

Continue in the grace of God. The first pastoral instruction in that city was not do more, but stay. Grace is God’s free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ, salvation as a gift, never a wage. To continue in it is to go on living every day on the footing on which you first came in: not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6; compare Galatians 5:4).

Kept by the same hands. Grace is not a substance but a Person’s kindness, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 13:14), shown at the cross. To continue in it is to stay near him. Grace is not the porch of the Father’s house but every room in it. The Lord who welcomed you in with empty hands keeps you in with the same hands, holding you when you cannot hold on, and he will present you blameless at the end, not because you kept yourself, but because he kept you.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and the father ran to him, put the robe on him and welcomed him as a son. Now imagine him a week later, slinking off to the servants’ quarters to start earning his place after all. That is what drifting out of grace looks like. To continue in it is to stay at the Father’s table as a freely loved child, drawing on Christ’s daily mercy for strength, forgiveness and growth (2 Peter 3:18). The call to continue is real (Colossians 1:23), yet the God who began this grace keeps us in it. We persevere because he preserves us.

How can I tell if I have drifted onto the treadmill? You feel closer to God on days you performed well and distant on days you failed. You put off praying after a sin until you feel you have done enough penance. You resent Christians who seem to get away with less effort. You serve out of fear of disapproval rather than gratitude. The cure is not to try less but to go back to the gospel: confess the sin, receive the forgiveness Christ has already won, and serve from his acceptance rather than toward it.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When almost the whole city comes to hear, the synagogue’s leaders are filled with jealousy and move from contradicting Paul to reviling him. What set it off was not error in his teaching but the sight of the crowds.

Almost the whole city. Nobody organised this. Very likely, all week, God-fearers had gone home to Gentile neighbours and relatives saying: you will not believe what a man said in the synagogue on the Sabbath.

The Jews. Luke cannot mean the Jewish people as such: the preacher is a Jew, and so are most of the Christians in the story so far. He means the leaders of that synagogue and those under their influence, in that city, on that morning. The church’s long and shameful habit of reading such sentences as a verdict on a race is a misuse of Scripture that has cost innumerable lives, and the man speaking here wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3).

Filled with jealousy. The jealousy is not hard to understand. These men had kept a minority faith alive in a pagan colony, at real cost, for generations. Last Sabbath the synagogue was theirs; this Sabbath it is full of people who have come to hear two strangers. Luke records no answer to Paul’s argument. He says what set it off: they saw the crowds.

Reviling him. Watch the opposition degrade. First they contradict: an argument, which can be answered. Then they revile him (blasphēmountes, slandering): tearing down the man instead of answering what he said. When a case moves from the argument to the man, the argument has been lost. And when your own tone has made that move, it is worth asking what you are actually defending.

The jealousy Jesus met first. When the crowds followed Jesus, the Pharisees said, look, the world has gone after him (John 12:19), and Pilate could see that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over (Mark 15:10). A servant is not greater than his master (John 15:20). The Master’s answer to envy was not to shrink the crowd. He went on welcoming outsiders to the end, and the envy that sent him to the cross became the means by which the door was opened to every Gentile in that Pisidian street. The feast he is spreading has room for every outsider he calls.

In everyday life. Recall the last time God did something obviously good through somebody whose success made your work look small: the neighbouring church that grew while yours did not, the younger man who preaches better than you. What did you feel first, before you corrected it? Confess it to the Saviour who was handed over out of envy and died for the envious; then pray for that church or person, and ask God to bless them more.

Why would religious people oppose a work of God? Because religion can become a possession rather than a surrender. When people feel that God’s work belongs to them, his blessing on outsiders feels like a loss, as it did to the elder brother when the prodigal was welcomed (Luke 15:28–30). The danger is greatest for those who have served longest. The protection is to remember that we were outsiders too, brought in by grace, and that the work was never ours to own.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the synagogue’s leaders have refused the word, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, obeying the commission God gave his Servant to be a light to the nations.

Spoke out boldly. Boldness is the great virtue of Acts, prayed for and given (4:29–31). It does not mean loudly. It means without editing.

First to you. This order was not tact but owed: the promises were made to this people (see vv. 4–5).

You judge yourselves unworthy. Thrust aside is the word Stephen used of Israel rejecting Moses (7:27, 39). Nobody said, “I am unworthy of eternal life.” They said: not from him; not on those terms. Paul tells them it comes to the same thing. A refusal is a verdict, and the man who gives it passes it on himself.

We are turning to the Gentiles. These words have been read as though God finished with Israel that Sabbath in Pisidia. He had not, and Paul shows it with his feet: in the next city he goes to the synagogue again (14:1). He says the same in Corinth (18:6) and Rome (28:28), and goes first to the synagogue in each new city. Each time it was a local verdict on a local refusal, not a final verdict on a people. Has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Romans 11:1). Christians read God’s purpose for Israel’s future in more than one way, and Romans 11 is the place to weigh them; but no reading permits a Christian to treat the Jewish people as written off.

A light for the Gentiles. Isaiah 49:6 is spoken to the Servant, the Messiah, as Simeon understood (Luke 2:32). Paul takes a text about Christ and says “the Lord has commanded us”. He is not confusing himself with the Messiah. The church’s task is not a separate assignment alongside Christ’s, but a share in his: what the Servant was sent to do, his people now do in him, which is why Paul can say that God makes his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Too light a thing. The full sentence runs: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob; I will make you as a light for the nations. To some, Paul’s turning will look like abandoning his people’s hope. He answers with the one verse in which God calls that hope, taken by itself, not big enough.

The beam swung out across the nations. The Servant fulfilled that commission by being lifted up on a cross outside Jerusalem. From a shut synagogue in Pisidia the beam swung out across the nations, and it has not stopped moving. The prophet whose warning closed Paul’s sermon saw where it ends: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14).

Polite refusals. Most refusals of Christ are not defiant but polite, reasonable and postponed, and the politeness does not alter what has been decided. A man handed the only bread there is who says, thank you, not just now, has settled whether he will eat. If you have been saying not now to Christ, hear Paul: a polite postponement is still a verdict. Settle it today.

If God appoints people to life, how can people judge themselves unworthy? Both are true, and Luke sets them two verses apart on purpose. Those who reject the gospel do so freely and are fully responsible; no one is lost who wanted Christ and was refused. Those who receive it do so because God has worked in them (v. 48). Unbelief is ours; faith is God’s gift. We need not explain how the two fit in order to believe both, and we must not let either cancel the other.
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles rejoice and praise the word, and all who had been appointed by God to eternal life believe, while the word spreads through the region. God’s choice came first, and their faith followed as its fruit.

The Gentiles began rejoicing. The door stood open to them, from a Jewish prophet, on the very morning the leadership was shutting them out.

Glorifying the word. Not Paul, but the word of the Lord. Glorifying is normally kept for God himself, and Luke lets it fall on the message. The genuinely converted cannot stop praising what they heard, rather than the man they heard it from.

As many as were appointed. One of the clearest statements of election in Scripture. Appointed (tetagmenoi) means ordained, assigned. Luke does not say as many as believed were appointed, but as many as were appointed believed. The participle is perfect and passive, a completed action done to them by another, and the unnamed agent, as so often, is God. The order is decisive: faith is the fruit, God’s prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: two verses earlier the unbelieving judge themselves unworthy of eternal life (v. 46), while the believing Gentiles are those appointed to it: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. It fits a steady pattern: all that the Father gives me will come to me (John 6:37); you do not believe because you are not among my sheep (John 10:26); the Lord opened her heart (16:14); Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:29–30.

The word was spreading. Two verses later Paul and Barnabas are expelled, yet the gospel reached the upland villages, carried by people whose names nobody wrote down. The missionaries were removed. The word was not.

Names bought with his blood. Before the world was made, the Father set his love on a people and wrote their names in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8). The book is the Lamb’s because every name in it was bought with his blood. On one ordinary Sabbath in an upland colony some of those names heard the gospel for the first time, and believed, and rejoiced. Salvation from first to last belongs to our God: chosen by the Father, redeemed by the Son, called by the Spirit, and every one of them kept to the end.

What it does not mean. Not that God chose these Gentiles because he saw something good in them or foresaw their faith; the faith itself is the fruit of the appointing (Ephesians 2:8). Not that anyone who wants to come to Christ will be turned away for not being on a list: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Not that God is the author of anyone’s unbelief (v. 46 lays that on the rejecters). And not that we can know in advance who is appointed. The list is God’s, and it is read only in the believing.

In everyday life. If you believe, thank God today, in so many words, that your faith was his gift and not your achievement. Let it make you humble toward those who do not yet believe, since you were no better, and bold to speak to them, since God has his people still waiting to hear. Rightly held, election banishes boasting and turns assurance into worship.

How can I know if I am one of those appointed to eternal life? By looking where Luke looks: as many as were appointed believed. You do not discover your election by peering into God’s secret counsel but by trusting Christ. If you have come to him, resting on him alone for forgiveness, that faith is the evidence of your appointment, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you are not sure you have come, do not puzzle over decrees; come now. No one who comes is ever told he was not chosen.

Then why preach or pray, if God has already appointed? Because God appoints the means as well as the end: he brings his people to faith through the preaching of the word and the prayers of his church (Romans 10:14–17). The appointed believed when they heard. In Corinth Paul was told to keep speaking because the Lord had many people in that city (18:9–10). Election does not make evangelism pointless; it makes it hopeful.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Fairness would leave us all under judgment; election is God showing mercy to guilty people who deserved none.

Where Christians differ: election. Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Reformed in their view of election honour this verse and read it in other ways. Some take the participle as middle voice, as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life, describing the people’s own readiness rather than a prior decree (the form can be middle or passive). The classic Arminian reading (Arminians hold that God’s choice responds to faith he foresees) affirms a real appointing grounded in foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed them to eternal life (Romans 8:29). A few read it corporately: the destiny of the believing people as a body, entered by faith. What unites us comes first: every side believes that salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all. This is a disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and the same Bible, to be carried with humility, not point-scoring. This commentary’s view: given Luke’s usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive, with God as the one who appoints, is far more natural, and the word is used elsewhere of being appointed by authority (Romans 13:1, “instituted”). God’s sovereign choice is the cause of faith (Ephesians 1:4–5; John 6:37). It is a reason for joy and humility, not pride: they believed because grace chose them. And it fuels mission: God has his people in every city, waiting to hear (18:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opposition works through people of rank to have the missionaries expelled, and they shake the dust off their feet as Jesus commanded and move on to the next city. A closed city never closes the kingdom.

The devout women of high standing. The synagogue leaders could not expel the missionaries themselves, so they worked through women of rank, the synagogue’s own God-fearers, some very likely married to the men who ran the colony. A word in the right houses, and the missionaries were put out by due process. Much opposition to the gospel looks like this: not violence but influence, applied quietly by people who never have to raise their voices. And there is a hard irony in it: these devout women were the fruit of the synagogue’s patient work among the Gentiles, used to expel the men who had just told them the promises were theirs.

Drove them out. Perhaps this is when Paul was beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25). In his last letter he lists the town by name: my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11). He never forgot it, and never suggested it had been a mistake to go.

They shook off the dust. Not a gesture invented in temper, but an instruction Jesus gave his own men when he sent them out (Luke 9:5; 10:11), a sign that a town was being left to its own responsibility. And everybody would have caught its meaning: a devout Jew might shake off the dust of Gentile lands; to do it to a Jewish community was to say, in this matter you are the ones on the outside.

And went to Iconium. Eighty miles or so east, and they start again. Persecution moves the gospel on (8:4). When a door is shut in your face, you do not stop; you move on. No closed city has ever closed the kingdom. The Lord who was himself driven out of Nazareth and led outside Jerusalem’s gate turns every expulsion of his servants into a sending.

What the shaken dust does not license. It is not permission to write people off in a huff. It was done by apostles, under an explicit command from Christ, after a full and public hearing, when the answer had become a settled and organised refusal. They did not curse anybody, organise resistance, appeal to Rome, or stay to have the last word. The gesture is not revenge but a transfer of responsibility: you have been told, and it is now yours.

When should I stop sharing the gospel with someone who keeps refusing? Rarely, and usually never in the sense of giving up on them. Paul left a city, not a person, and only after an organised, public rejection. With family, friends and neighbours, keep loving them, keep praying and keep the door open, even if you stop raising the subject for a season because it has become an argument. Jesus told us not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but he also kept eating with sinners. Change your approach if you must; do not change your love.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment. Iconium lay about 80 miles to the east.

parallels.desc: persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young believers left behind, without their teachers, are filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. The preachers were expelled, but the Spirit stayed, and the joy came with him.

The disciples. Converts of a few weeks whose teachers have been expelled. There is no building, no elder and no New Testament. They have a few weeks of teaching, each other, and God.

Were filled. Not coping, not bearing up: filled, and the tense says they went on being filled. Antioch got rid of the preachers. It could not get the joy out of the town.

With joy and with the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is the source of the joy. If joy were a mood produced by circumstances, this verse could not exist; this joy arrives with a Person.

Whose joy it is. On his last evening Jesus told his friends that he had spoken so that his joy might be in them and their joy might be full (John 15:11), and that their sorrow would turn into a joy no one would take from them (John 16:20–22). He endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). The gladness of a handful of converts in a hostile colony is a share of that joy, poured out by the Spirit he sent: the joy of a Saviour who had looked past the cross and seen them.

What comes next. The pattern repeats at once in Iconium and Lystra (14:1–20), and Paul and Barnabas will come back to strengthen these very disciples (14:21–23). The joyful church in Pisidian Antioch is the sign that the risen Christ had not left with his preachers.

What it does not mean. Not a command to feel cheerful, nor a denial of grief. Paul and the Ephesian elders knelt, prayed and wept (20:36–38); Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). The Christian position is not joy instead of sorrow but sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10): two things at once, as anyone who has buried a believer knows.

What if I am a Christian and do not feel this joy? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and fruit grows; it is not switched on. Seasons of depression, grief, illness or spiritual dryness come to genuine believers, as the Psalms show again and again (Psalm 42; 88). Do not try to manufacture joy; go to its source. Keep near the means God uses: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the company of his people. Tell a mature Christian how you are. And if your low mood is deep or long, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is not a lack of faith.

parallels.desc: joy of the Holy Spirit in much affliction

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 states plainly that the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch rests on their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism: it undergirds preaching rather than stopping it (see the note on vv. 48–49). Election is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent from a worshipping, fasting church, arrive in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit; the appointed believe, and the disciples are filled with joy even when their teachers are expelled.

Now: The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; it was seeking God, and God spoke. A congregation’s mission grows out of its worship and prayer, and when the Spirit calls, it must be ready to send its best.

keyVerse.quote: Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.
keyVerse.note: Here Paul’s first recorded sermon reaches its point, and Acts states for the first time the truth that will fill his letters: a sinner is justified, declared right with God, through faith in Christ. Its two great words, “everyone” and “everything”, explain the rest of the chapter: why the gospel must go to the Gentiles, and why no sin puts a believer beyond its reach.

13.reflection:
The great missionary step of Acts began while a church was worshipping and fasting, and the Spirit asked for its two best leaders (vv. 1–3). What does this teach about where mission comes from? Whom might your church need to be willing to send, and what would it cost?

Paul retells Israel’s history as a story of God choosing, bearing with, giving and promising, all leading to Jesus (vv. 16–37). How does reading the Old Testament this way change the way you read it, and the way you see God’s dealings with your own life?

Verses 38–39 promise that everyone who believes is freed from everything the law could not free them from. Is there a sin you find hard to believe this covers? What difference does it make to rest on God’s verdict rather than on your own record?

In one city some begged to hear more, some were filled with jealousy, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (vv. 42–52). How should God’s choosing make us both humble and bold in sharing the gospel, and how should we respond when people shut the door?

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things?
