We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
Where we are. Acts 14 completes the first missionary journey (chapters 13–14), on which the church at Antioch sent Paul and Barnabas to the nations (13:1–3). Driven out of Pisidian Antioch after Paul announced the turn to the Gentiles (13:46–51), they come to Iconium; by the chapter’s end they are home, and the question the journey has raised, on what terms Gentiles belong, will fill chapter 15.

The message. The living God will not share his glory, with idols or with his own servants, and he keeps the churches his Son has gathered. Lystra would make gods of men; the apostles insist they are only men and point the crowd to the living God who has been good to the nations all along and now calls them to turn. And the road into his kingdom runs through many tribulations, because the King walked it first, and he holds all who follow him on it.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). A suffering church needed to see that hardship did not mean the gospel was failing, that pagans with no Bible could be reached and welcomed, and that young churches were safe in the Lord’s hands.

How the chapter makes its case. At Iconium the word wins Jews and Greeks, the Lord confirms it with signs, and the city divides until a plot drives the apostles on (vv. 1–7). At Lystra a man lame from birth leaps to his feet; the crowd hails Barnabas and Paul as Zeus and Hermes, and the two tear their clothes and preach the living God who gives rain, food and gladness (vv. 8–18). The same crowd, turned by opponents from Antioch and Iconium, stones Paul, and he gets up and walks back into the town (vv. 19–20). They retrace their steps to strengthen the disciples, warn of tribulation and appoint elders (vv. 21–23), then sail to Antioch to report that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles (vv. 24–28).

Where it leads. Lystra’s legend of gods walking the earth in disguise is a shadow of something true: God did come down in human likeness, not to inspect and punish but to be rejected and to save. The leaping lame man is Isaiah 35 fulfilled by the risen Messiah; the “must” of tribulation is the path of the Christ who had to suffer and so enter his glory (Luke 24:26); and the door of faith is opened by the one who holds the key. The apostles refuse worship. Jesus received it, because he is what Lystra mistook his servants for.

For us. Put no one on a pedestal, and step down from any you are offered: the glory belongs to God. Expect hardship on the road to the kingdom, and do not read it as a sign that God has gone. And commit those you cannot keep to the Lord in whom you have believed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word goes out to the nations, and neither flattery nor stones can stop it, because the risen Lord confirms it and keeps those who believe. At Iconium the preaching divides the city, and a plot moves the preachers on (vv. 1–7). At Lystra a healed cripple sets off a crowd that would worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, and the apostles turn them to the living God who made all things and has fed them all their lives (vv. 8–18). The same crowd stones Paul, who rises and goes on (vv. 19–20). The missionaries retrace their steps to strengthen the disciples, warn of tribulation and appoint elders (vv. 21–23), then report at Antioch that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles (vv. 24–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the path into the kingdom

The must of verse 22 is not gloom (see the note on vv. 21–22). It describes the way God brings his people home: the servant who shares his Lord’s cross will share his Lord’s resurrection, and the pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked back into the city where he had just been stoned. Now: Those whose life is secure in the risen Christ can go on witnessing after suffering for it, because their hope is his resurrection, not this world’s preservation of their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel wins both Jews and Greeks at Iconium, and its opponents answer it not with argument but with slander.

Now at Iconium. Iconium (modern Konya) was a substantial Greek-speaking city in the Roman province of Galatia, about ninety miles east of Pisidian Antioch. Paul’s letter to the Galatians was probably written to these churches.

They entered together into the Jewish synagogue. Just driven out of Pisidian Antioch, where Paul announced that he was turning to the Gentiles (13:46, 50), he walks first into the next city’s synagogue. The turn to the Gentiles did not mean giving up on his own people.

In such a way. Luke does not say they spoke faithfully, or at length, but in such a way: a comment on how the thing was put. There is such a thing as saying true things badly, and these two did not. The God who opens hearts is pleased to use human mouths.

Jews and Greeks believed together. In one synagogue, in the same weeks, Jews and Greeks believed the same message, and in the same breath Luke calls them simply the brothers. That is what Christ died to do: “he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). The slander that follows was aimed at a peace made at the cross, and it could not unmake it.

Poisoned their minds. The verb (ekakōsan) means embittered, made hostile: an audience worked on by people with access to it. Slander does not answer the preaching. It goes round it, to people who have not heard it yet, and gets there first. Spoken where you are not, it is discovered only in its effects: rooms that go quiet, an invitation that stops coming. You cannot answer a charge never put to you, and trying makes you look exactly like the man they were warned about.

Outliving it. So what did these two do about it? Nothing, so far as Luke records: no defence, no letter to the synagogue. They stayed (v. 3). Some slander can only be outlived, by going on doing the work in front of everybody until the account people were given stops matching the man they can see.

If faith is God’s gift, why does it matter how we speak? Because God gives faith through means, and our words are among them. Faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit is pleased to use speech that is clear, honest and warm, while careless, confusing or unkind speech can put real obstacles in a hearer’s way. Clever words cannot produce faith; only God opens hearts (16:14). But we should take care to understand the gospel, explain it plainly and speak with love. Paul asked for prayer that he might make it clear, “which is how I ought to speak” (Colossians 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia; Paul’s letter to the Galatians may be to these churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opposition only made them stay, and the risen Lord himself backed their preaching of his grace with signs and wonders.

So they remained for a long time. So means therefore: the poisoning of the city is given as the reason they stayed. When a place goes cold on us we start looking at the timetable. These men took the hostility as evidence that something worth opposing was happening, and dug in.

Who bore witness to the word of his grace. Their bold speech is the open, unguarded speech the church had prayed for in Jerusalem (4:29, 31). And the sentence runs the other way from what we expect: not the apostles bearing witness to the Lord, but the Lord bearing witness to their word. The gospel is “the word of his grace” (20:32): God giving what nobody has earned.

Signs and wonders. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4), and Paul reminds these same churches of the miracles worked among them (Galatians 3:5). They authenticate not the men but the word of his grace: a signature at the bottom of a particular document.

The Lord who works from heaven. In Acts the Lord is the risen Jesus, still doing what he began (1:1). From the right hand of God he takes the words of two hunted men in a provincial town and signs them as his own, and the grace they spoke of is the grace he showed when he gave himself for sinners. The preacher speaks of Christ, and Christ speaks for the preacher. He may not vindicate your witness when you would choose (Paul is stoned in the next town, and no sign prevents it), but the word of his grace has never yet gone out without him.

How does the Lord bear witness to his word now? By the Holy Spirit, who presses the preached word home to the conscience: convicting of sin, opening blind eyes, giving faith (1 Thessalonians 1:5). That is still a wonder, in some ways the greater one. Bitterness melting, a family beginning to pray, an addict walking free, a proud heart bowing to Christ: these are the Lord’s signature on his word today. When you speak the gospel, he stands behind it.

Should we expect signs and wonders in ministry today? Here the Lord granted them to confirm the word through the apostles. Continuationist Christians (who believe all the gifts of the early church continue today) expect such signs as the gospel goes to new places, and many of them are earnest, godly brothers. The more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic witness of the founding era: Paul calls them “the signs of a true apostle” (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews speaks of them as God’s confirmation of those who first heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4). God remains free to heal and to answer prayer in remarkable ways, but the ordinary pattern that continues is the Lord bearing witness to his word as it is preached.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel splits the city, and opponents who agree on nothing else unite to mistreat and stone the messengers.

But the people of the city were divided. Two good men preached with great effect, and the measurable outcome was a town split in half. Jesus said it would be so: “Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division” (Luke 12:51). Not because Christians are quarrelsome, but because a man can be neutral about most claims, and not about the claim that an executed Jew is the Lord of his life. Christ is a sure foundation for those who believe and a stone of stumbling for those who will not (1 Peter 2:6–8).

With the apostles. Luke calls Paul and Barnabas apostles here and at verse 14; everywhere else he keeps the word for the Twelve. Here they are men sent out on mission by the church in Antioch.

Both Gentiles and Jews. Two communities that agreed on almost nothing found something to agree on, as at the trial of Jesus, when Herod and Pilate “became friends with each other that very day” (Luke 23:12). Opposition to Christ unites people who would not otherwise sit in the same room, a strange backhanded testimony to who he is.

Two senses of apostle. In the strict sense an apostle had seen the risen Christ and been commissioned by him as an eyewitness and a layer of foundations: the Twelve, with Paul added later, “as to one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:8). That office cannot be repeated: the man had to have seen him (1:21–22), and a foundation is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). In the wider sense the word simply means one who is sent, as of Barnabas here and of the messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23); the church has always had these, and mostly calls them missionaries, the same word arriving through Latin instead of Greek. Behind both stands “the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1), the Son sent by the Father, who sends his people as the Father sent him (John 20:21).

When someone claims the title today. Ask which is being claimed. A sent one, yes, and thank God for them. A man whose word stands beside Scripture because he saw the risen Christ, no. That door closed when the last of them died, and mercifully: a church that can still be given new foundational revelation can be told anything.

What if following Christ divides my own family? Then you walk a road Jesus described in advance and walked first: even his brothers did not believe in him for a time (John 7:5). Do not provoke division needlessly; be the kindest, most honest and most dependable member of your family. Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ, keep loving those who disapprove, and keep praying. But do not buy peace by denying him. Many families split by the gospel have later been reunited in it, as Jesus’ own brothers were (1:14).
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Barnabas are both called apostles — men sent out on mission.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warned of the plot, the apostles flee over the border and go straight on preaching: running from persecution is no failure of faith when it serves the work.

They learned of it and fled. A plot involving the city’s rulers was known in advance to two travelling preachers, so someone on the inside probably got word out. Luke does not say who; this book is quietly full of such people. And they ran, as Jesus commanded: “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” (Matthew 10:23). Leaving is not always weakness, nor staying always faith. The mission is the point, not the missionary’s reputation for nerve.

To Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia. These were smaller towns to the south and south-east. Lystra is only about twenty miles from Iconium, but it lay over a boundary, outside the reach of the Iconian magistrates. It was a Roman colony, and probably Timothy’s home town (16:1).

They continued to preach. It is a step down in the world: a small colony in rough hill country whose people still shouted in Lycaonian when excited. They arrive as fugitives in a backwater whose language they do not speak, and start again. Luke does not say they recovered first. They fled, and they preached.

The hour that could not be fled. Jesus did it himself. At Nazareth he passed through the middle of a crowd that meant to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:29–30), and in the temple he hid himself when they picked up stones (John 8:59), because his hour had not yet come. Then the hour came; he set his face to go to Jerusalem, and in the garden he walked out to meet them. He fled until fleeing would have abandoned the work, and then he stayed, for us. That is why his servants are free to run from Iconium: the one death that had to be faced to save the world has been faced, by him.

What decides it. Hold verse 6 next to verse 20, where the same man, stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, walks straight back in. In both places the work decides: he leaves Iconium because staying would end the preaching; he re-enters Lystra because new disciples need to see him on his feet. So if you are weighing whether to leave something hard, ask not whether you would be braver to stay, but what happens to the work if you go and if you do not. Nobody grades his own courage accurately anyway.

Is it ever right for a Christian to flee persecution today? Yes. Believers in hostile countries sometimes face a real choice between staying and leaving, and Scripture gives freedom for both: Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt; the church scattered from Jerusalem (8:1–4); Paul was let down the wall at Damascus (9:25). What is never permitted is to deny Christ to stay safe. So pray, seek counsel, think of those who depend on you and of the work, and act in faith. And churches in safer places should pray for, welcome and support those who have had to flee.
verseByVerse.note: Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east, in the region of Lycaonia.

parallels.desc: Timothy of Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man lame from birth listens to the gospel, and Paul is given to see that he has faith to be made well: the faith is God’s gift, and the healing will be Christ’s.

Could not use his feet. Luke says it three ways where one would have done: he could not use his feet, he was crippled from birth, he had never walked. Not injured, not declining: a man who had never in his life taken a step. The healing closely resembles Peter’s at the temple gate (3:1–10), for Paul’s ministry bears the same marks. And this man had been listening in a town where Luke mentions no synagogue and few had ever heard the Scriptures.

Seeing that he had faith. Read carelessly, this says the healing happened because the man’s faith was sufficient, from which it follows, with awful logic, that where healing does not happen the faith was not. That is told at bedsides, and it has done great damage. But notice who is doing the seeing. Paul looks intently, as he fixed his eyes on Elymas (13:9), and most likely God showed him what he saw. This is not an apostle grading a candidate’s spiritual performance but an apostle given to know what God intended to do, and the faith he sees is itself something God has been producing through the preaching.

Faith to be made well. Made well (sōthēnai) is the ordinary word for being saved, and it points to what the man’s faith was faith in: Jesus, crucified and raised, through whom forgiveness is proclaimed (13:38). His faith was not a strength that qualified him. It was a lame man’s empty hands held out to the Christ he heard about, and the healing was Christ’s (9:34). If faith were a power, the weak would be lost. Because faith only receives, everything rests on the one received, and he is able for the weakest grip that ever reached for him.

Test it against the rest of the book. The man at the temple gate expected nothing but money, and was healed anyway (3:3–7). Dorcas was dead (9:40). The high priest’s servant was helping to arrest Jesus when his ear was healed (Luke 22:51). If healing ran on the sufferer’s faith, many of the healings in Scripture could not have happened. And Paul asked three times to be relieved of his thorn and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9), and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).

So if you are ill. If you, or someone you love, have been made to feel that the failure is yours, pick this verse up the other way round. It does not say that faith produces healing. It says that on one afternoon in one town, God let his apostle see what he was about to do. Your not being healed is not a report card on your faith. If it were, Paul failed his: the apostle through whom this man walked was never healed of his own thorn.

Should I still pray for healing? Yes, gladly and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them; using medicine is no failure of faith. Pray as a child asks a father, naming honestly what you want, and rest the answer in his wisdom, as Jesus did in Gethsemane: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). If healing comes, give thanks. If it does not, his grace is sufficient, and full healing is certain at the resurrection, when the lame will leap and the body will be raised imperishable.
verseByVerse.note: The healing closely resembles Peter’s healing of the lame man at the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Paul’s word the man who had never walked leaps up and walks: the risen Messiah is doing what Isaiah promised for the day God comes to save.

He sprang up. Walking is a learned skill, ten thousand small corrections a body makes without being told, and this man had never learned it. Yet sprang up (hēlato) means leapt, like the lame man of 3:8: not stood carefully, not helped upright between two men, but jumped, everything a person normally acquires over the first two years of life handed over complete. It is Isaiah 35:6: “then shall the lame man leap like a deer.” The prophet promised it for the days when God comes to save, when the promised King puts right everything sin has broken, and at last death itself (Isaiah 35:4–6; 25:8).

What is not in the sentence. Peter at the temple gate spoke “in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth” (3:6), and when the crowd stared at the apostles as though they had done it by their own power, he at once pointed them to the God of Abraham (3:12–13). Here Luke records no name at all, and a crowd that had never read the Scriptures is left to interpret what it has seen with the only religious vocabulary it has.

A miracle by itself teaches nobody anything. That is why what follows goes so badly wrong. A miracle compels attention, and then people explain it with whatever they already believe. Lystra had Zeus, and reached for him. Where nobody says what a sign meant, the crowd supplies its own meaning, and this crowd is already sending for oxen.

The sign Jesus pointed to. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with Isaiah’s list: “the lame walk” (Luke 7:22). The leaping lame were his credentials. So when a man in Lystra jumps to his feet, it is not Paul’s power on display but the Messiah of Isaiah 35, risen and reigning, still doing the work that identified him, in a town that had never heard his name until that week.

He gives whole what was never whole. The Christ who will raise his people imperishable gave one pagan town a glimpse of that morning: legs that had never borne weight, steady in a moment. He does not repair what is broken a little at a time, as we do. On the last day all who are his will rise like that man, at once and complete, and the first thing they do with their new feet will be to run to him.

Say who did it. When God does something good in your life, say plainly, to yourself and to others, who did it. Unexplained blessings drift into being called luck.

How should I respond to stories of miracles today? With openness and with care. God can do anything, and he does answer prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. But a remarkable event does not interpret itself, nor prove the teaching of whoever was standing nearby. Ask what is being taught, and whether Christ and his gospel are honoured, because Scripture warns that false teachers can come with signs (Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9). The test of any ministry is not whether wonders are reported but whether it agrees with the word of God.

Textual note. A few later manuscripts have Paul speak in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; the earliest do not.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd takes the miracle for a visit from their gods and hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes: a true longing for God to come down, fixed on the wrong gods.

Saying in Lycaonian. They cried out in the old country language, not the Greek Paul had been preaching in, and the apostles probably did not understand it; under strain people revert to the tongue they think in. That explains the delay: the two go on standing there while a sacrifice is organised around them, and find out when the animals appear.

The gods have come down. The reaction looks wild until you know the local story. The Roman poet Ovid, a generation or so before Paul, wrote up a legend set in neighbouring Phrygia. Zeus and Hermes came through the country disguised as travellers and were turned away from a thousand doors. One poor old couple, Philemon and Baucis, took them in; the gods turned their cottage into a temple and drowned the district that had refused them. When two strangers turn up and something impossible happens, you do not want to be the household that got it wrong. The shouting is fear with a long memory, and it explains why the priest comes at a run with cattle.

Zeus and Hermes. Zeus was the chief god; Hermes was his messenger, the god of speech, and inscriptions linking the two have been found near Lystra. So the man doing the talking is taken for the junior god, and the quiet one beside him, Barnabas, for the chief god. Luke, who has recorded Paul taking over the leadership of the mission, does not comment.

Sized up wrongly. Lystra took two preachers for gods, and before long would stone one of them as a criminal. Both verdicts were wrong, and it is the oldest mistake of all. When God himself came among us as a man, “he had no form or majesty that we should look at him” (Isaiah 53:2), and crowds looking for greatness looked straight past him to the cross.

How is the incarnation different from the Lystrans’ idea of gods coming down? Utterly, though there is an irony under the error: God did come down in human likeness, in Jesus (Philippians 2:7), and Paul is there to tell them. The crowd had the right longing and the wrong gods. In the myths the gods only looked human for a while, in disguise, to test people and then punish them. In Jesus the eternal Son truly became man, taking a real human body and soul, permanently, without ceasing to be God (John 1:14). Lystra pictured a chief god and his messenger; in Jesus the God who sends and the Word who is sent meet in one person, and neither is a disguise (Hebrews 1:2). He did not come to inspect our hospitality but to receive our rejection, and instead of drowning those who turned him away, he died for them. The Lystrans feared gods who came down to judge. The true God came down to save.
verseByVerse.note: A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting the region in human form unrecognised. Hermes was messenger of the gods, so the speaker, Paul, was taken for him.

parallels.desc: they said that he was a god

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town’s priest brings the costliest sacrifice Lystra can offer to honour two preachers: sincere, grateful, frightened worship given to the wrong ones.

The priest of Zeus. Literally Zeus-before-the-city: the town’s own guardian, whose shrine stood outside the walls, the local power over weather and harvest.

Brought oxen and garlands to the gates. Oxen were the most expensive offering a town could make, and the garlands were wound about the animals’ heads before they were killed. This is not under discussion. It is under way: the grandest religious act in the town’s calendar, arranged in honour of two preachers, with the whole population delighted.

The one man who may be worshipped. Every sacrifice belongs to one God, and only one sacrifice was ever enough: not oxen garlanded at a city gate, but the Lamb of God offered outside the gate of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12). When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up: “I too am a man” (10:26). When John fell before an angel, he was told not to (Revelation 19:10). Here two apostles tear their clothes rather than accept a garlanded ox. Yet when the disciples in the boat worshipped Jesus (Matthew 14:33), and Thomas called him “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), he did not stop them. Every true servant of God refuses worship, and Jesus received it. Either he was the worst of blasphemers, or he is what Thomas said; and within about twenty-five years of the cross Paul was already praying to him in Aramaic, Maranatha, Our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22).

Why this moment is dangerous. Because it is flattering, and because it is sincere. These people are grateful and frightened, and have brought the best they have. It is the easiest thing in the world to let run: not to endorse it, simply to be slow about correcting it, reflecting that the crowd is finally listening. Many a scandal of Christian celebrity has begun so: not with a man claiming to be more than a man, but with a man declining, for a while, to interrupt people who treated him as though he were.

Religion as a bargain. The oxen also show what religion at Lystra was: feed the god and he sends rain; refuse him and the district drowns. The same bargain survives among churchgoers: I pray, I give, I behave, so God owes me a good year. The living God had been sending rain to people who never thanked him (v. 17), and in Christ he gives himself to people who have nothing to offer. Grace is not a better deal with God. It is the end of dealing.

Is it wrong to admire or thank a pastor or Christian leader? No. Scripture tells us to esteem our leaders “very highly in love because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:13). The danger begins when admiration turns into dependence or exemption: when a leader is treated as beyond question, when his words carry more weight than Scripture, or when his failings are hidden to protect his image. Thank your leaders, pray for them, and hold them to account; and leaders should be quick, like Paul, to turn the glory to Christ.

Uncertain wording. Luke does not say which gates are meant. The word (pylōnas) can mean a city gateway, the entrance of a temple, or the gateway of a house. Most take it as the city gates, near the temple of Zeus at the entrance to the city; some think of the gateway of the house where the apostles were staying, which would explain why they only heard of it and had to rush out (v. 14). Either way, the sacrifice was ready to begin before the apostles could stop it.
verseByVerse.note: Garlands were wreaths placed on sacrificial animals.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Horrified, the apostles rush into the crowd to stop the sacrifice, insist that they are only men, and call the people to turn from empty idols to the living God who made everything.

They tore their garments. Tearing one’s clothes was a Jewish sign of grief and of horror at blasphemy, as when the high priest tore his at what he took to be blasphemy from Jesus (Mark 14:63). That is what they thought of the honour offered them. And they rushed into the crowd: not onto a platform, and not away, but into it, to get between the people and the altar.

We also are men, of like nature with you. Of like nature (homoiopatheis) means of the same feelings and sufferings, the word James uses of Elijah (James 5:17): the same aches, fears and capacity to be hurt. Before long Paul will be lying outside that same gate under a heap of stones, and the town will have its proof.

Harder than Caesarea. Herod at Caesarea accepted a crowd’s worship and was struck down because he did not give God the glory (12:22–23). But Herod’s flatterers wanted something from him (12:20); these people mean it. It is far harder to refuse worship from a man who simply wants to say thank you in the only currency he has, and will be hurt when you will not take it.

Preaching with no Bible to quote. This is the first sermon in Acts to people with no Bible at all: no Abraham, no Moses, no prophets, not even one God to start from. Set beside the synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch (13:16–41) and the later one at Athens (17:22–31), it shows the gospel unchanged while the starting point moves: Scripture for those who have it, creation for those who do not. It also raises the question chapter 15 must settle: when pagans like these turn to God, on what terms are they welcomed?

From vain things to a living God. Vain things (mataiōn) are empty, hollow, worthless, the Greek Old Testament’s word for idols (Jeremiah 2:5); compare turning “to God from idols” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). The gods of Lystra had to be fed by a priest; the God Paul preaches is alive. The closing words, “the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them”, come straight from Scripture (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6), but the apostles do not say so, because here it would have meant nothing.

Men like you, and the Man who is more. The apostles insist they are only men, so that the crowd will look past them. Their message is about one Man who is truly of like nature with us and also infinitely more: the Son who “had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest” (Hebrews 2:17), and through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Lystra tried to turn men into gods. The gospel announces that God has become a man without ceasing to be God: a man who wept and was weary, and who could say, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

Where they start, and what they demand. They took the one real point of contact a pagan farming town had, the sky, the fields, the food on the table, and used it. But they did not soften the demand by a syllable: turn, the same word Peter used in Jerusalem (3:19). The starting place moved. The call did not.

Carried from the womb to grey hairs. The god of Lystra waited in his temple for his priest to feed him. The living God needs nothing from our hands (17:25). Idols must be carried by their worshippers, as Isaiah mocked them, while the LORD carries his people from the womb to grey hairs (Isaiah 46:1–4), and at the cross he carried their sins, the guilt of having bowed to vain things included. So name the vain things you look to for security or joy, your bank balance, your reputation, a screen, and turn from one of them today.

How do I talk about Christ with someone who knows nothing of the Bible? Start where Paul started, with what they already know: creation, conscience, the goodness of ordinary life, the longing for meaning, the reality of death. Speak of the God who made all this and is not like the idols of our age, money, success, pleasure, image. Then move to the heart of it: he has come in Jesus, died and risen, and calls us to turn to him. Avoid church jargon, explain terms, ask questions, and be patient. The starting point can change; the message and the call to turn must not.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: turned to God from idols

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ came, God let the nations go their own way in patience, not approval; now that patience gives way to a call to turn.

In their own ways. Before Christ, God let the nations go their own way, as he gave his law to Israel alone (Psalm 147:19–20). Not that he approved, but that he was patient: “The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent” (17:30).

Patience paid for at the cross. How could a holy God let the nations go their own way for so long? God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood”, “because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin by bearing it in the sinner’s place. The centuries of patience were not God shrugging at idolatry: he could justly hold back judgment because he would deal with those sins at the cross. That is why the patience could end in a call to turn rather than in condemnation. The man who brought the summons was preaching the very death that made the waiting just.

What about those who never heard? The verse raises a question often put to a Christian by somebody he loves. Take what Scripture says, and refuse both comfortable answers.

First, nobody is judged against a light he was never given. Gentiles without the law are judged by what they did have: the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience accusing or excusing them (Romans 2:14–16). God does not weigh a man against a revelation he withheld from him, which is worth saying to anyone whose real fear is that God is unfair.

Second, they are not innocent. What can be known about God is plain from what has been made, so that people are without excuse; the charge is not ignorance but suppression, knowing something of God and not honouring him or giving thanks (Romans 1:19–21). Paul says it here in kinder language: God had been sending Lystra rain the whole time.

Third, the Judge is good. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25) answers itself. You are not asked to certify the eternal state of people you have never met, but whether the God who did not spare his own Son can be trusted with them. The Judge of all the earth is just, the Saviour of the world is kind, and they are one and the same God.

Refuse the false comfort in both directions. The nations are not safe in their ignorance: the era of overlooking has ended and a summons has arrived (17:30). Nor may we speak as though God owed them more than he gave, or pronounce on each individual. There is salvation in no one else (4:12), and it comes through conscious faith in Christ. Those who die in infancy are a separate case: we rest the elect among them in the mercy of the God who saves them in Christ, and parents who have lost a little one need not fear that God will judge a child by a gospel the child could never hear. David’s hope for his infant son, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23), has comforted many. For the rest, God has put a job in our hands: “how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14).

Then can someone be saved by following his conscience and the light he has? No. Conscience and creation show enough of God to condemn, never enough to save, because no one lives up to the light he has; all have sinned (Romans 3:23). That is precisely why Paul walked into Lystra, and why the church still sends missionaries (see “Where Christians differ” at vv. 17–18).

parallels.desc: the times of ignorance God overlooked

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has never left himself without witness: every shower, harvest and glad meal was his kindness to people who did not know him, calling them to the Giver. Even so, the apostles only just stop the sacrifice.

Yet he did not leave himself without witness. Even without Scripture, God left evidence of himself in creation and providence (Romans 1:19–20; Psalm 19:1). Speaking to farmers on the Anatolian uplands, Paul reaches not for the stars or the moral law within, but for rain, harvest, dinner and being glad. God sent rain on a town with a temple to Zeus at its gate, season after season: the people leading oxen to the wrong god had eaten every day of their lives at the table of the right one.

Food and gladness. The last item is the surprising one: the pleasure of a good meal, the ease of a year that has gone well. Paul tells idolaters that their happiness was evidence of God’s goodness to them.

Common grace. Common means not cheap but given to all in common: the goodness God shows believer and unbeliever alike. Here it is rain, food and gladness; beyond them are life and breath (17:25), the restraint of evil, the skill and beauty found even among those who do not know God, and the patience that delays judgment. God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). Two things must be kept clear. Common grace is not saving grace: it blesses this life without, by itself, reconciling anyone to God. And it is a witness, leaving people without excuse (Romans 1:20) and meant to lead them to repentance (Romans 2:4). The tragedy is to take the gifts and ignore the Giver (Romans 1:21).

Scarcely restrained. Verse 18 is deliberately anticlimactic. An apostle at the top of his powers, in an emergency, got the sacrifice stopped by the skin of his teeth; Luke does not even say the crowd was persuaded, only restrained.

Whose hand sent the rain. Paul does not name Christ in this short speech, but all things were created through the Son, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). The rain on Lystra’s fields fell at the word of the one Paul had come to preach. So common grace is not a separate religion of nature with its own road to God. It is the same Lord being kind to his enemies before they know his name, and the kindness on the farm points to a greater one: the one who had fed them all their lives would give himself for them.

When the true word barely lands. The best answer, given at the right moment by the right man, may only just hold. If you have said the true thing as well as you knew how and watched it barely land, you are in good company.

Is it right for Christians to enjoy food, harvests and ordinary pleasures? Yes, as from God, who “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17), for “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). The sin is not enjoyment but ingratitude, or making the gift into a god. So eat, laugh, delight in a good harvest or a good holiday, and thank the one who gave it. Gladness received from God and returned to him in praise is part of worship.

Where Christians differ: can creation save? Some Christians (often called inclusivists) argue that those who respond to God’s witness in nature may be saved without the gospel. This commentary’s view: God’s witness in creation is real and leaves everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20), but it cannot save. It shows God’s power and kindness, not his way of salvation through Christ, which is why Paul and Barnabas came to Lystra with the gospel. General revelation (what God shows of himself to everyone through creation and conscience) points to God; special revelation, the gospel, brings us to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turned by opponents from the cities behind, the crowd that wanted to worship Paul stones him and leaves him for dead; but he gets up, walks back into the town, and goes on to Derbe the next day.

But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium. Iconium is some twenty miles from Lystra; Pisidian Antioch more than a hundred. Somebody organised a journey of several days over hill roads to finish here what had been started at home. Hatred will make an effort that indifference never makes. They probably saw Paul not as a rival teacher but as a dangerous traitor: a Jew announcing that the law of Moses could not justify (13:39), and drawing off the God-fearers gathered round their synagogues (13:43, 50). Paul understood that zeal from the inside; he had once travelled to Damascus to do the same (9:1–2; Galatians 1:13–14).

They stoned Paul. The people who had to be physically restrained from worshipping this man now throw stones at him until he stops moving. Nothing had changed except who had been talking to them. A reputation handed to you by people who do not know you can be taken back by them, and the same afternoon’s excitement supplies both. Nor were these monsters by the standards of their town: they were ordinary, frightened, easily led people who had just been told a persuasive story, which is worth knowing about ourselves.

Supposing that he was dead. A stoning is an execution, and this one went far enough that the men doing it thought the job was finished. Paul later lists it: “Once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:25). Writing to these very churches he says, “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (Galatians 6:17). Some of them were made here.

He rose up. Luke says only that the crowd supposed Paul dead and that he got up; Luke, who readily reports a raising when one happened (9:40; 20:9–12), does not claim one here. And there were disciples in Lystra: a small ring of brand-new believers round the body of their teacher outside the wall, which took some nerve.

Timothy, perhaps. One of them may well have been Timothy. Lystra was probably his town (16:1–2), and writing to him for the last time Paul names the persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra as though Timothy needs no explanation (2 Timothy 3:10–11). The young man who had to be told more than once not to be afraid may have begun by watching his hero dragged out of town as a corpse, and followed Christ anyway. And the hero set out for Derbe the next day, some sixty miles on foot.

How much he must suffer for my name. None of this took the Lord Jesus by surprise: “I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (9:16). The man who had kept the coats while Stephen was stoned now lies under stones himself, and the same Lord stands in both scenes: he received Stephen home, and lifted Paul back onto his feet. Christ himself was hailed with “Hosanna!” and within days led out to a cross, and he did not stop loving the crowd that changed its mind.

There are scars in heaven. The risen Lord showed his hands and his side to his friends, and the wounds he took for us are the only wounds in the universe that heal. Paul carried away from Lystra the marks of Jesus, and got up off the ground because the Lord who was put to death outside a city wall had already risen. The stones could leave him for dead. They could not reach the life hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), and they cannot reach ours.

Pedestals and stones. Our culture runs the Lystra cycle at high speed. We lift someone gifted, a singer, an athlete, a preacher, a politician, far above ordinary life, and at the first flaw pull them down with the same energy. It looks like two moods; it is really one. We have asked a human being to carry what only God can carry: our hopes, our need for someone to look up to, our proof that goodness is possible. When they cannot carry it, disappointment turns to fury, because an idol that fails us is never simply set aside; it is punished. Paul had refused the pedestal (vv. 14–15), so the stones could not undo him. And the gospel offers the one person who can bear both our worship and our failures: the only man who deserves to be worshipped, who let himself be led out of the city and “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).

Why does God let his servants suffer like this? Scripture gives no single answer, but several true ones. Suffering conforms us to Christ, who suffered first (Philippians 3:10). It shows that the message is believed, not merely sold: nobody is stoned for a sales pitch. It strengthens other believers, who see that faith survives the worst (Philippians 1:12–14). And it is temporary and outweighed: “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). God does not waste a single stone thrown at his people.

What should I do if I am mistreated for my faith? Do not retaliate; bless (Romans 12:14). Do not be ashamed; rejoice to be counted worthy to suffer for his name (5:41). Use proper protection where you can, as Paul later used his citizenship, and where you are in danger, get to safety and report it. Let other believers gather round you, as the disciples did here. And keep going, even if, like Paul, it is the next day and you are still bruised. The Lord who stood by Paul stands by you.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch was about 100 miles from Lystra.

parallels.desc: once I was stoned

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After making many disciples at Derbe, the missionaries turn back through the cities that had persecuted them, to strengthen the new believers and tell them plainly that the road into God’s kingdom runs through many tribulations.

Had made many disciples. The phrase echoes the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19): not just converts, but disciples. The word (mathētēs) means a learner, an apprentice: not one who collects information but one who attaches his whole life to a master to become like him: “everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (Luke 6:40). Jesus made it costly and total (Luke 9:23), yet it was also the ordinary name for every believer before the name Christian existed (11:26). We can reduce the faith to a single decision and forget that the commission is to make disciples, “teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). Paul and Barnabas did not count converts and move on.

They returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch. Read verse 21 as a route. Derbe is the far end of the journey, and from there a road ran east through the Cilician Gates to Tarsus, Paul’s home town, and on to Syrian Antioch: the shorter way home, familiar and safe. Instead they turn round, back through Lystra, where Paul had been stoned; Iconium, where a plot to stone him had united the town; Antioch, where the leading men had had them driven out (13:50). They go back to make sure that what they started can stand without them, and the reason Paul walks back into the town where he was stoned is in what he told them.

Through many tribulations. Every convert in those cities faced the obvious question: is this what following Jesus will be like? And Paul’s answer, from a man recently stoned, was yes. Must (dei) means it is necessary: not optional, not a sign of failure (John 16:33; 1 Peter 4:12–13). That exposes a quiet hope many of us carry, that if we follow Jesus well enough life will run smoothly, and if it does not, God has failed us. Paul promises the kingdom, not comfort, and the kingdom is worth far more.

We, not you. He says we: he describes a road he is standing on, to people who had seen him on it. He does not tell them it will get easier. He tells them the difficulty is the road and not a diversion from it, the only comfort that survives real trouble, because it removes the second wound. Suffering hurts; suffering plus the suspicion that God has gone is unbearable, and it is that second half Paul takes away.

The same must. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). Necessary there is the same dei. The road Paul describes is the King’s own road. He entered his glory through the cross, and those joined to him enter the kingdom through tribulation behind him. Hardship does not mean the road has gone wrong; it is the sign that they are following the right Master.

In everyday life. Think of a newer Christian you know and strengthen them this week: a message, a coffee, a prayer, an honest word that following Jesus is hard and worth it.

Did we not already enter the kingdom? Paul says God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13), past tense, yet here entering is still future. Both are true: this is the already and not yet. God’s saving reign in King Jesus came at his first coming (Matthew 12:28), and every believer already lives under it and enjoys its blessings: forgiveness, the Spirit, adoption. But its full glory waits for his return, when he reigns openly and makes all things new, and in that sense we will yet enter or inherit it (Matthew 25:34; 1 Corinthians 15:50; 2 Timothy 4:18). It is one kingdom in two stages, as a decisive battle may be won while the victory parade still lies ahead. To assure us, Paul says we have been placed in it; to press us on in hope, as here, he points to the kingdom we have yet to enter, and the many tribulations are the appointed road into its fullness, “provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17).

Does this mean every Christian will be persecuted? Every Christian will face tribulations, though not all in the same form: for some prison or violence, for others mockery, lost opportunities, family pressure, illness, grief, or the long fight against sin. So do not seek suffering, and do not be ashamed if yours seems small beside others’. But when it comes, do not be surprised, “as though something strange were happening to you” (1 Peter 4:12). It is the road, and the King has walked it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before leaving, the apostles give every young church its own elders, and with prayer and fasting entrust churches and elders alike to the Lord who alone can keep them.

Appointed elders for them in every church. Paul and Barnabas did the appointing, in every church without exception. Elders led each church, as they led each synagogue.

The timing. These churches were probably only months old, every member a recent convert, with no training college and no New Testament. Paul did not conclude that it was too soon. He concluded that a church without elders was a church he could not leave, and raised leaders from the people in front of him. Keeping the churches dependent on himself would have felt safer and would have been fatal: a mission that only gathered converts would die with its missionaries; one that left shepherds could outlast them. Paul’s farewell to the elders of Ephesus (20:17–35) shows what such men were for: to care for “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (20:28).

They committed them to the Lord. The word is used of depositing something valuable with someone for safekeeping, and it is the word Jesus used from the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Paul and Barnabas hand over something never theirs to keep, to the only one who can keep it, and they do it fasting, as serious men did before a step that could not be taken back. Then they walked away, leaving new believers in hostile towns under brand-new elders, with no way of hearing for months how it was going. What made that bearable is the last clause: the Lord in whom they had believed.

No one will snatch them. That Lord had already said what he would do with such people: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18); “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The elders were real shepherds, but they were not the reason the flock would survive. The reason was a Shepherd who had laid down his life for these sheep and taken it up again. Paul and Barnabas were not leaving the churches alone; they were leaving them with their owner. What Paul could not hold, Christ holds; and he who committed his own spirit into his Father’s hands receives every church and every soul committed into his.

Resignation or entrusting. Anyone who has had to hand something over, a work, a child, a parent, knows the difference. Resignation lets go because it has run out of options. Entrusting lets go into hands it can name. So pray for your elders, and name the person or thing you are most anxious about, and hand it over today, in words, into the hands of the Lord in whom you believe.

Was this simply what these two men happened to do, or a pattern for every church? In every church shows fixed practice, and the rest of the New Testament confirms it. Paul left Titus in Crete to “appoint elders in every town” (Titus 1:5), a church without them being not yet in order, and every church we meet has them: Ephesus (20:17), Peter’s readers (1 Peter 5:1), James’s (James 5:14), Philippi (Philippians 1:1). Two things follow. First, three words name the same office from different angles: elder (presbyteros, maturity), overseer or bishop (episkopos, oversight), and pastor or shepherd (poimēn, care), all used of the same men (20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Peter 5:1–2). Second, it is always elders, plural: shared leadership, not a lone ruler.

What authority does that give them, and what does it not? Real, God-given authority: to lead (1 Timothy 5:17), to teach and guard sound doctrine (Titus 1:9), to shepherd and watch over souls (20:28); and the flock is told, “Obey your leaders and submit to them” (Hebrews 13:17). But it is strictly bounded. It is derived: they are under-shepherds of the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4), caring for the church of God, not their own. It is Word-bound: they may not bind consciences with rules God has not given (the error of Colossians 2); they declare God’s word, they do not legislate. And it is not the right to dominate: “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3); they lead as servants, not lords (Mark 10:42–45), and will give an account (Hebrews 13:17). Servant authority, then: derived from Christ, limited by Scripture, accountable, never tyrannical. The elders are no little popes.

And what qualifies a man for it? The two lists (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) stress character, not talent. Over them all stands “above reproach”: a life that gives no fair ground for accusation. Under it: faithful in marriage (a one-woman man), self-controlled, gentle, not violent or quarrelsome, not a lover of money, hospitable, not a recent convert, managing his own household well (1 Timothy 3:5), and well thought of by outsiders. Only one item is an ability: he must be able to teach, holding firm to sound doctrine so as to instruct and to rebuke those who contradict it (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:9), the chief thing that distinguishes an elder from a deacon. An elder is not the most gifted or successful man in the room, but a man of proven Christlike character who knows and can teach the truth: nearly everything on the list is simply the mature Christian life, on display in one fit to model it.

Then why does Paul say an elder must not be a recent convert, when these men were all new? Because circumstances differed. In a brand-new church there was no one else, and the apostles, with apostolic discernment, chose the most mature men available and kept close contact by return visits and letters; some may have been Jews or God-fearers who had known the Scriptures for years. In established churches like Ephesus, Paul could and did insist on it (1 Timothy 3:6). The principle is the same: appoint the most mature, tested men God has given, and do not leave a church without shepherds.

So how should churches choose elders today? Here the apostles appointed elders as they founded churches, with prayer and fasting; in Acts 6 the congregation chose and the apostles appointed. The more likely pattern for churches now is that the congregation recognises men who meet the qualifications Paul lays down (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and that existing elders confirm and set them apart.

Where Christians differ: church government. Episcopal churches have bishops over many churches; Presbyterians, elders gathered in courts; Congregationalists and Baptists, congregations governed by their own members and elders. This commentary’s view: the New Testament pattern is a plurality of qualified elders in each local church, recognised with the congregation’s involvement, with deacons serving alongside (1 Timothy 3). Elder and bishop (overseer) are the same office in the New Testament. Christ alone is head of the church.

Uncertain wording. The verb for appointed (cheirotoneō) originally meant to vote by a show of hands, but by the first century it had come to mean simply to appoint, with no vote implied. Here Paul and Barnabas are its subject. It may suggest that the congregations took part, but it cannot be pressed that far, and a single verb will not settle a system of church government.
verseByVerse.note: Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way home they stop to preach at Perga, the town they had passed through empty-handed on the way out, and then go down to the port: most faithful service is getting to the next place and speaking there.

Perga. Perga is where the journey went wrong: the town where John Mark left them and went home (13:13). On the way out they had passed straight through it, a man short, with nothing planted. Now, coming back, they stop and preach. Much of God’s work is done on the second pass. The place where you failed, or were failed, is often the place you are brought back to with something to give.

They went down to Attalia. Attalia, modern Antalya, was the port on the south coast, some twelve miles from Perga, where they waited for a ship east. Waiting for a ship is unglamorous, and much of the mission was made of such things.

To the other towns as well. When the crowds at Capernaum tried to keep Jesus, he said, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose” (Luke 4:43). The risen Lord still goes from town to town, now on the feet of his servants, and a town like Perga, passed over once, does not stay passed over.

Most of a life given to God. In two chapters: well over a thousand miles, probably the best part of two years, a string of cities evangelised, one man stoned. Most of a life given to God looks like these two verses: getting to the next place, speaking there, and going on.

My Christian life feels ordinary and repetitive. Is that a problem? Not in itself. Most faithfulness is ordinary: daily prayer, steady work, the same church on Sundays, kindness repeated. God values it and writes it down, as he did these two verses. The danger is not routine but drift, going through the motions with a cold heart. So keep the routine and warm it: ask God each morning for one person to serve and one word to speak. Plodding with Christ is still walking with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Attalia was the port on the south coast.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sail home to the church that sent them, and Luke marks the journey as a work begun, carried through and finished by the grace of God.

They sailed to Antioch. Home to Syrian Antioch, perhaps two years after setting out, and Luke identifies home by what had happened there: the place where they had been commended to the grace of God.

Commended to the grace of God. A congregation had fasted, prayed, laid hands on two of its leading teachers and let them go (13:1–3), and then there was nothing else it could do, with no way of knowing whether they were alive. To commend them to the grace of God was to put them somewhere it could not follow, and go on praying. It is what a parent does at a door, and what any of us does with somebody we love and cannot help, a child abroad, a friend in hospital; and this verse says it is not an empty gesture. The ship came in, and both men were on it.

The work that they had fulfilled. Not attempted, not begun: fulfilled. The commission of 13:2, “the work to which I have called them”, is completed here, and Luke uses the same word, work. Between those two sentences lie hundreds of miles of mountain road, a stoning, and churches in city after city. Grace sent them, kept them, and finished the work through them.

Because another work was finished. Before the cross Jesus said to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4), and on the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Paul and Barnabas added nothing to Christ’s saving work; they carried its news. A mission can be finished and laid down, because the work that saves is already complete.

How do I know when a piece of work for God is finished? Ask what you were actually given to do, not everything that could be done. When the task God assigned is done, it is right to lay it down with thanks, even if needs remain. Seek counsel from those who know you, pray, and see whether the door is closing. Finishing well is not doing everything; it is doing the given thing, and then handing over without guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Home again, they tell the church not what they had achieved but what God had done, above all that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles; then they stay and rest among their own people.

All that God had done with them. The wording of the report is the point: not what they had done for God, nor even what they had achieved with his help. God is the subject of the sentence, as he was when they set out, commended to his grace. That is not modesty; it is accuracy. A congregation that hears what its missionaries have accomplished will begin, quietly, to assess them. A congregation that hears what God has done will begin to pray.

A door of faith. The image stayed with Paul: “a wide door for effective work” at Ephesus, with many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9); a request from prison that God would “open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3). God opened it; they had walked through a door, not made one. And it is a door of faith: a Greek in Lystra did not have to become a Jew first, by circumcision and keeping the law of Moses, to belong to God’s people. He came in on the same terms as anyone else, by trusting Christ (Romans 10:12–13).

A door that would soon be challenged. Within a short time men would come down from Judea to say that the door had been opened too wide, and that these Gentiles must be circumcised (15:1). It is a pattern worth expecting rather than being wounded by: the clearest work of God tends to be followed, quite soon, by an argument about it inside the church.

What Christ has accomplished. Years later Paul summed up his whole ministry the same way: “I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience” (Romans 15:18). The one at work in Cyprus, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra was the risen Christ, gathering the nations promised to him (Psalm 2:8), and the missionaries came home as witnesses, not heroes. He holds the key to the door of faith, the one “who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). Through it have come Gentiles from every nation, at length us, all on the same terms, with empty hands and believing hearts, and he will not close it until the last of his people has come in.

No little time. Luke’s understatement: a good long while. The first great missionary journey ends with two tired men staying put for months with their own congregation. The Spirit who said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul” (13:2), is the same Spirit under whose hand they now sit still in Antioch and do nothing remarkable. There is a permission in that for anyone who believes faithfulness means never stopping. Rest, in this book, is not a lapse in obedience. It is part of obedience.

How can my church support missionaries when they come home? Do what Antioch did: gather to hear them, and listen for what God has done, not only for statistics. Give them time and real rest, not just a slot in a service. Ask about their struggles as well as their successes, and pray with them. Help with housing, transport, medical care and the children’s schooling. Returning missionaries are often exhausted and out of step with home. A church that welcomes them well is sharing in the work as truly as when it sent them.

parallels.desc: a wide door for effective work

14.theology: Suffering as the path into the kingdom. Acts 14:22 says plainly that tribulation is the road by which God’s people enter his kingdom. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way, and the church that follows a crucified Lord walks the same road. Paul speaks of filling up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24): not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, for nothing was lacking in it, but that his sufferings are reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes out into the world.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra (see vv. 19–20), later returned through the cities that had tried to kill him to strengthen the believers and appoint elders.

Now: Many Christians quietly expect the Christian life to be comfortable; Acts 14 says tribulation is the appointed road (see vv. 21–22). A suffering church is not a failing church.

keyVerse.quote: strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
keyVerse.note: This is the word the missionaries walked back through hostile cities to say, spoken by a man still bruised from the stones of Lystra. It holds the chapter together: the gospel does not promise an easy road, but it promises the kingdom, and its “must” is the same necessity by which Christ suffered and entered his glory. Hardship is not a sign that the road has gone wrong; it is the road, and the King has walked it first.

14.reflection:
Within days the crowd at Lystra moved from trying to worship Paul to stoning him (vv. 11–19). Where do you see that cycle of pedestal and stones in our culture, or in your own heart? Why can only Christ bear both our worship and our disappointments?

Speaking to people with no Bible, Paul and Barnabas began with rain, harvests and gladness (vv. 15–17). Who in your life knows nothing of the Bible, and what everyday gifts of God might be a starting point for speaking to them about him?

“Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (v. 22). How does this correct the hope that following Jesus well will make life smooth? How might knowing it in advance help a newer Christian you know?

The missionaries committed the young churches “to the Lord in whom they had believed” (v. 23) and came home to tell “all that God had done with them” (v. 27). What or whom do you find hardest to entrust to the Lord? How could your church better pray for, and welcome home, those it sends?

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
Where we are. Acts 15 stands at the centre of the book. Paul and Barnabas have just reported to Antioch that God “had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles” (14:27); now the church must decide on what terms Gentiles may come through it. Peter speaks here for the last time, and from here on the story follows Paul.

The message. Sinners are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus alone, and nothing may be added to it: not circumcision, not the law of Moses, not anything. Jew and Gentile come in by the same low door: “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” (v. 11).
