And people saved by the same grace must live as one family, giving up freedoms for one another’s sake, even when, like Paul and Barnabas, they cannot agree.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers lived in churches of Jews and Gentiles, where this question was live and painful (see the introduction). He shows how the church settled it: by what God had plainly done, tested by Scripture, decided together under the Holy Spirit.

How the chapter makes its case. Teachers from Judea tell Antioch’s Gentile believers they cannot be saved without circumcision, and the church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem (vv. 1–5). Peter argues from Cornelius: God gave the Spirit and cleansed hearts by faith, so why lay on the disciples a yoke no Jew has ever carried (vv. 6–11)? Barnabas and Paul report God’s signs among the Gentiles, and James shows from Amos that God always meant to rebuild David’s fallen house so that the nations might seek him (vv. 12–18). He rules that the Gentiles must not be troubled, asking only four abstentions for the sake of fellowship (vv. 19–21). A letter goes with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices (vv. 22–35). Then Paul and Barnabas quarrel over Mark and part, and two teams set out (vv. 36–41).

Where it leads. The whole chapter defends the sufficiency of Christ. The yoke no one could bear, he bore: born under the law, he kept it, and took its curse for those who broke it. David’s fallen tent is raised in him, the risen Son of David, whose name is now called over the nations. And the closing quarrel shows that his servants are not the heroes: only Christ holds both his work and the people he restores, as Mark’s later usefulness proves.

For us. Do not let anyone, your own anxious heart included, add a condition to Christ: rest on his grace alone. Then love your brothers and sisters enough to give up what you are free to keep. And when good Christians fall out, own your part and leave room for the Lord who reconciles.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one is saved by keeping the law: Jew and Gentile alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, and nothing may be added to it. Teachers from Judea unsettle Antioch by demanding circumcision, and the church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem (vv. 1–5). After long debate Peter appeals to what God did for Cornelius (vv. 6–11), Barnabas and Paul report God’s signs among the Gentiles (v. 12), and James shows from Amos that this was God’s plan from of old (vv. 13–18). The council lays no burden of the law on the Gentiles, asking only four abstentions for the sake of fellowship (vv. 19–21), and its letter, carried by Judas and Silas, brings Antioch joy and peace (vv. 22–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by faith alone: the council’s verdict

Peter’s speech (vv. 7–11) is the plainest statement in Acts that Gentiles are saved the same way Jews are: by grace through faith, not by keeping the law. The council confirms together what the Spirit had already shown in Cornelius’s house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The council produced a pastoral letter rather than a treatise: practical guidance that let Jew and Gentile live together in one church. Now: Churches still face questions about what may be required of believers. The council’s way of handling them (set out at vv. 12–13) remains a good pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teachers from Judea add one condition to the gospel, circumcision, and Paul and Barnabas fight it, because a single added condition turns grace into something else. The church at Antioch sends them up to Jerusalem to have the question settled.

But some men came down from Judea. They may be connected with the men of Galatians 2:12 who “came from James”, but Luke does not say so; the council’s letter says they went out with no instructions from Jerusalem (v. 24).

You cannot be saved. Almost everything in that sentence is right. It assumes Jesus is the Messiah, that he died and rose, and that these Gentiles must be saved. It is not the sentence of an unbeliever. What it does is add one condition. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17), and to receive it was to take on the whole law (Galatians 5:3): Christ plus circumcision. Paul called it a different gospel (Galatians 1:6–9). We tend to picture false teaching as a denial, but much of the most harmful error is an addition, made by sincere people, to a set of true statements. The most dangerous kind of sentence is not one that contradicts the gospel but one that agrees with it and then says “and”.

The background. The men from Judea were not inventing a rule. For centuries a Gentile who wanted to belong fully to Israel’s God had become a proselyte: circumcised, keeping the whole law, joined to the Jewish people. A God-fearer like Cornelius who stopped short of that remained outside (see the note on 10:1–2). So it seemed obvious that Gentiles turning to Israel’s Messiah must come in by the same door. What these teachers had not grasped is that the Messiah himself was now the door (John 10:9), and that God had already received uncircumcised Gentiles by giving them his Spirit (v. 8).

No small dissension and debate. Luke means a furious row. On this Paul would not give way: “to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment” (Galatians 2:5). The instinct that peace is the higher value is usually a good one, but on the gospel itself, refusing to fight is not gentleness; it is desertion.

Aimed precisely. Yet in the next chapter Paul circumcises Timothy himself (16:3), while he would not let Titus be circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5). Same rite, opposite decisions: one was a free choice made for the sake of the mission, the other was demanded as a condition of salvation. That is the whole of Christian wisdom about secondary things: what you may cheerfully do for love, you must refuse absolutely the moment somebody says you must do it to be saved.

Appointed to go up. The verb is passive; the church did the appointing. The man who insists his gospel came to him from no human being (Galatians 1:11–12) goes anyway, because being right on your own is not the same as the church being settled.

Nothing added to a finished work. Underneath the argument about a rite lies a question about the cross: “if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (Galatians 2:21). If something must be added, his death was not enough. But the Son of God did not lay the foundation of our salvation and leave us to build the last storey. He cried, “It is finished”, and the Father raised him: nothing can be added to a work God himself has declared complete. The whole chapter defends the sufficiency of Jesus, and blessed be the Lord who lets no one, Pharisee or apostle or our own anxious hearts, add a condition to his grace.

What does Jesus plus look like today? Rarely circumcision. It is any requirement added to faith in Christ as the ground of acceptance with God: you must be baptised in our church, speak in tongues, keep the Saturday Sabbath, perform certain rituals, reach a certain level of holiness, or belong to the right group, before God will really accept you. Many of these things may be good, or debatable, in their place. But made conditions of salvation, they change the gospel. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ’s finished work sufficient, received by faith alone, or does it add a step?

Why does one word matter so much? Suppose salvation is ninety-nine parts God’s grace and one part your compliance. That one part is now the part everything hangs on, the joint that can fail, and your standing before God rests, in the end, on you. So Paul told the Galatians: “if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. … You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law” (Galatians 5:2, 4). Not damaged. Severed. A gift with a condition attached is not a gift, and a rescue you have to help with is not a rescue.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved. This meeting in Jerusalem, about AD 49, is often called the Jerusalem Council.

parallels.desc: Paul’s account of a Jerusalem meeting

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to a hearing about whether the Gentile converts were really saved, Paul and Barnabas told the story of their conversions, and the churches rejoiced. Jerusalem welcomed them, and they reported what God had done.

Being sent on their way by the church. The New Testament’s phrase for helping travellers on with what they need (compare 3 John 6). They go as the congregation’s representatives, with the congregation behind them.

Describing the conversion. They do not spend the journey rehearsing arguments. Men on the way to a tribunal turn the trip into a preaching tour, which is worth copying on the way into any hard meeting.

Great joy. Those churches, Samaritans among them, had been outsiders not long before (8:4–14; 11:19). People who have just been let in are rarely the ones who want the door narrowed.

They were welcomed. Warmly, by the church and the apostles and the elders. The men of verse 1 were a faction, not Jerusalem’s voice (v. 24), which is worth remembering before writing off a whole church because of who turned up from it.

The map Jesus drew. Jesus had said, “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8). Now two men walk back to the centre of that map, through Samaria, carrying news from its far edges, not to ask permission for something new but to report that the plan Christ announced is being carried out, by him.

Part of his reward coming in. The gladness that ran from church to church began in the Son, who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2): “Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11). Every story told in Phoenicia and Samaria was part of his reward coming in.

Why should news of conversions bring such joy? Because heaven rejoices over it first: “there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10). A conversion is a dead person brought to life, an enemy made a child. If we hear such news coolly, we may have forgotten what it meant for us. Joy at others’ salvation is one of the surest marks of a heart that has tasted grace.

Is this the visit of Galatians 2? Many think so: the cast is much the same (Paul, Barnabas, Peter, James), and so are the issue and the outcome. Others place Galatians 2 at the earlier famine visit (11:30), because Paul is listing his Jerusalem visits precisely to prove his independence and would hardly skip one; Galatians would then come before this council. It is not certain, and little rests on it. On either reading the accounts agree on the decisive thing: Paul submitted his gospel to the Jerusalem leaders, and they added nothing to it. (Their later clash at Antioch, Galatians 2:11–14, was over Peter’s conduct, not a different gospel.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The challenge comes from inside the church: converted Pharisees insist that God requires Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the whole law of Moses.

Believers and Pharisees. Luke puts together two words most of us keep apart. These are not infiltrators. They are converted men who love the God of Israel and now trust his Messiah, and they are the crisis. The man who will argue hardest against them had been a Pharisee, son of a Pharisee (23:6; Philippians 3:5), which is why he refutes the position so exactly and with so little patience.

Feel the case from where they stood. They had been raised to believe that the boundary of God’s people was marked in the flesh, by God’s own command to Abraham, and had kept the law at real cost; now they are asked to receive as full members men who had lately been sacrificing to idols. Their objection is not malice but a lifetime of conviction meeting a new fact. And the Lord bore with Pharisees who believed, as he had borne with disciples who argued about who was greatest, and led them into the truth.

It is necessary. Necessary (dei) is Luke’s word for what God requires, the same “must” Jesus used of his own death (Luke 9:22). They are saying God requires Gentiles to become Jews to belong to his people. Nothing smaller would have needed a council.

Circumcised in him. The New Testament’s answer is not that circumcision never mattered, but that it has been fulfilled in a person. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), born under the law to redeem those under it (Galatians 4:4–5), and Gentile believers already bear the mark: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11). To ask the Gentiles for the knife now is to go back to the sign after the one it pointed to has come, for “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29).

A test, and a safeguard. Think of the thing you privately treat as the mark of a real Christian, and picture meeting, in heaven, somebody who trusted Christ and got that thing wrong all his life. If you hesitate, you have found the mark you have quietly added to Christ. Yet this does not mean nothing matters: the council will lay down four things (v. 29). The chapter turns on keeping two questions apart: what is required in order to be saved, and what is required in order to live together. Turn the rules for living together into conditions of salvation and you get a false gospel; decide that no rules are needed and you get a lawless church.

Why would sincere believers want to add a condition? Because a condition gives us something to hold. Grace leaves us nothing to point to but Christ, and that feels exposed; a rule we can keep feels safer, since we can check it and see at a glance who is in. Underneath lies an old desire to keep some control over our standing with God, and some credit for it. The religious moralist and the irreligious rebel are closer than they look: both want to be their own master, one by breaking the rules and the other by keeping them. The gospel takes control out of both their hands and gives them Christ.

Can a real Christian hold a seriously wrong view? Yes, as these men show. New birth does not make anyone instantly correct on everything, and believers can hold serious errors out of old habits of thought; hence the church’s need of teaching, patience and correction. But an error about the way of salvation is not small: hardened into a settled rejection of grace, it becomes another gospel. So treat brothers in error as brothers, reason with them from Scripture, and do not give way on the gospel itself.

parallels.desc: as to the law, a Pharisee

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After long, open debate, Peter reminds the council that God himself chose to bring the Gentiles in by the hearing of the gospel and faith. They had settled this once already, at Cornelius’ house.

Gathered together. The first church council: the apostles and the elders meet, and the whole church is involved (vv. 12, 22).

Much debate. Not a decree from above: a long argument, with apostles in the room and no voice from heaven to settle it. Yet this meeting produced the sentence, “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (see vv. 28–29).

Peter stood up. This is Peter’s last appearance in Acts. The man who has carried the first half of the book goes out not with a miracle but with an argument for somebody else’s freedom.

God made a choice among you. “In the early days”: Cornelius was perhaps ten years earlier (chapter 10), and Jerusalem had given its verdict then: “to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life” (11:18). Hearing and believing: that is how Gentiles came in, and nothing was said about circumcision. A church can formally agree something, mean it, and discover ten years later that the agreement never reached the place where convictions live. What is resisted here is not new information but the cost of what they already believed.

By my mouth. God chose; Peter’s mouth was the instrument. He has the strongest case in the room and takes no credit for it, which is why it carries weight. The God who chose Peter’s mouth to carry the word to Cornelius chose some mouth to carry it to you: behind every messenger is the Father’s sovereign choice to call his people by the gospel of his Son.

When you have turned again. On the night of his denial Jesus told this man, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). The man who denied by a fire that he knew Jesus now stands before the whole church to defend Gentiles who know Jesus and nothing of Moses. The best argument for grace in the room was the man making it.

Is it wrong for Christians to argue? Not if it is the right kind of argument about the right kind of thing. The apostles debated at length, openly, and the church was the better for it. Scripture forbids quarrelsomeness, harshness, pride and fighting over trivia (2 Timothy 2:23–25; Titus 3:9). Healthy debate keeps to the question, goes to Scripture, assumes good faith, and aims at agreement in the truth rather than victory. If you enjoy winning more than finding the truth, step back.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who sees the heart, gave the Gentiles the same Spirit he gave the Jewish believers and cleansed their hearts by faith, so he has already removed the distinction the council is being asked to restore.

God, who knows the heart. Heart-knower (kardiognōstēs) is found only here and at 1:24, when the eleven prayed, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen”. Both times the church must decide who is in, and reaches for the same name for God: men see the outside, and God sees the rest. In a debate about a mark in the flesh, Peter names God by the attribute that makes the flesh irrelevant.

Just as he did to us. Then the evidence, which is a fact. God gave them the Spirit before any circumcision: not a lesser measure, not a provisional instalment. The same. At Pentecost Peter had explained the outpouring: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this” (2:33). So the council is being asked whether it will refuse those whom the risen Lord himself has filled.

No distinction. The same verb as in 11:12, “making no distinction”, and here in the past tense: God has already done it. The question is whether to reimpose a distinction God has removed.

Cleansed their hearts. The clause that wins the argument. It echoes the voice Peter heard when the sheet was let down from heaven: “What God has made clean, do not call common” (10:15). The heart was always the problem, and the Old Testament always named it: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16); “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6); “I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26). The party of the Pharisees is asking for the sign; God has already given the thing the sign pointed to.

By faith. Not by ritual, descent, effort or a probationary period of good behaviour. The instrument by which a heart is made clean is empty-handed trust, which is why it is available to a Roman centurion, and to you tonight, and why no committee has ever been able to add a step to it.

He did not turn away. God knows the heart, and he does not stop at knowing it. He looked into the hearts of a Roman centurion and his household, saw everything there was to see, and did not turn away; he made them clean and came to live in them. The one from whom nothing is hidden loves without reserve, and no one is a second-class member of a family where the Father has made no distinction.

In everyday life. Look at the Christian you find hardest to accept: if God has given him the Spirit, what right have you to make a distinction?

How does faith cleanse the heart? Not by its own power, as if believing were a moral detergent. Faith joins us to Christ, and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7); through faith we also receive the Spirit, who makes the heart new. Faith is the empty hand; Christ is what fills it. So the cleansing is both a once-for-all washing of guilt and a continuing purification, as the Spirit works holiness in a heart that keeps trusting. If your heart still feels far from clean, keep looking to Christ: the cleansing is his work, and he does not leave it half done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To demand the law of Gentiles is to test God and lay on them a yoke no Jew has ever carried, for Jews and Gentiles alike will be saved only by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

Why are you putting God to the test? A serious charge, aimed at the men in the room most careful about right belief. The phrase belongs to the wilderness, to Israel at Massah demanding that God prove himself after he had shown them his power (Exodus 17:7; Psalm 95:8–9); of that generation God swore, “They shall not enter my rest” (Psalm 95:11). God has already acted: he gave the Spirit, cleansed the hearts, made no distinction. To require circumcision now is to tell him his way of saving them was not enough, while calling yourself a defender of his law.

A yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear. Teachers spoke of the law as a yoke to be taken up. Peter, an observant Jew, standing in Jerusalem in front of Pharisees, says: none of us has ever managed it. Not our fathers. Not us. Not me. He does not say the law is bad, but that no one has ever kept it perfectly (Galatians 3:10; James 2:10). The generation that received it broke it before Moses got down the mountain; the nation given the land was deported out of it for the same reason.

The inside. You can manage your outward behaviour. You cannot manage your heart, and the law asked for the heart, which is what makes it unbearable. A rule against murder can be kept; a rule against wanting what is not yours cannot. So the Pharisees would lay on these Gentiles a burden that has crushed everyone who tried to carry it, while Jesus offers a yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:29–30).

Just as they will. The sentence that turns the council over. Peter does not say the Gentiles will be saved the way we are, by becoming Jews. He says that we Jews will be saved the way they are, by grace. The Gentiles have become the standard. Every advantage of Israel still exists (Romans 9:4–5), and not one contributes anything at the point of being saved.

One low door. That cuts both ways, and the second is the comfort: if what makes you a better candidate counts for nothing here, so does what makes you a worse one. The Christian of forty years and the convert of last Tuesday are saved the identical way. There is one door, very low, and Jew and Gentile, the respectable and the ruined, stoop through it on the same terms into the same wide house; the grace that brings them in is the grace that brings them home.

The yoke he carried. The yoke that neither the fathers nor Peter could bear was borne by one. The Son of God was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4) and loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself every day of his life. Then he took the curse the law pronounced on its breakers (Galatians 3:13). Grace does not mean God quietly dropped his demands: Jesus met them and paid the penalty in full. His perfect obedience is counted as ours, so our imperfect obedience is accepted for his sake, and our failures do not undo our standing.

The tyranny of the should. Many people feel they left this kind of yoke behind with religion. Yet listen to an ordinary modern inner voice: I should be further on by now, I should look better, I should be a better parent, I should be over this. The psychoanalyst Karen Horney called it “the tyranny of the should”: the demand, built into an idealised picture of ourselves, that we be what we are not, kept in force by a self-hatred that is never satisfied. We did not get rid of the law when we got rid of God. We made ourselves its author and judge, and turned out harder masters than Moses, because our law has no sacrifice and no mercy seat. The gospel does not lower the standard. It tells you that someone has met it, that his record is offered to you, and that the last word spoken over you is not “you should” but “It is finished” (John 19:30).

In everyday life. If you are tired from carrying a yoke of trying to earn God’s favour, lay it down today. Say to God, in words: I will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and nothing else.

Then is God’s law useless for Christians? No. “The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). It cannot save, because no sinner can keep it, but it still shows us our sin and drives us to Christ, restrains evil in the world, and, in its moral commands summed up in love for God and neighbour, shows believers the shape of the life the Spirit is producing (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.6; the Westminster Confession 19.6). What is gone is the law as a yoke to earn acceptance, and the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ. The Christian obeys not to be saved but because he has been.

Will I be saved through grace, or am I already saved? Both. Peter speaks of the future, “we will be saved”, because salvation is completed at the last day. But believers have already been saved (Ephesians 2:8) and are being saved (1 Corinthians 1:18). From first to last it is the same grace: the grace that forgave you when you first believed will keep you and bring you safe to glory. You will never graduate from grace to something else.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly falls silent to hear what God has done among the Gentiles, and then James, the Lord’s brother, rises to sum up.

All the assembly fell silent. Five verses earlier there had been much debate. Now the argument has run out of road, and the men who were shouting are listening.

They listened to Barnabas and Paul. Since Paphos it has usually been Paul first. In Jerusalem the old order returns, because there Barnabas is the trusted man: the Levite who sold his field for the church (4:36–37), who vouched for Saul (9:27), Jerusalem’s own emissary to Antioch (11:22).

Signs and wonders among the Gentiles. The two do not argue theology; they report what God has done. That gives a method worth keeping. Testimony first: what has God actually done? Then Scripture: the prophets agree with it (v. 15). Then judgment (v. 19). Experience is admitted as evidence and never made the authority, which guards a church against deciding doctrine from stories, and against being so afraid of stories that it cannot see what God is plainly doing.

James replied. Not James the brother of John, executed at 12:2, but the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (12:17), remembered for strict law-keeping, whose judgment would carry weight with conservative Jewish believers. Peter speaks, but James, the leader of the local church, sums up, and the decision is taken by the apostles and elders with the whole church (v. 22). It is worth noticing, and not worth quarrelling over.

The brother who did not believe. He grew up in the same house, and “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5). Then Jesus was crucified, and then, Paul tells us in a bare line, “he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). The brother who did not believe now presides over the decision that his brother is the Saviour of the world. No one is too close, too familiar or too sceptical for Christ to reach.

For the family you pray for. If you are praying for someone in your family who knows the Christian at close quarters and is unimpressed, take heart from James. He lived in the same house as Jesus for years, and it still took a resurrection to convince him. But it happened.

How should a church weigh experience in a disagreement? Listen carefully, then test it by Scripture. Stories of what God is doing may show that your theory was too small, but experiences can be misread or counterfeited, and feelings are not revelation. Ask whether Scripture teaches it, whether it honours Christ and the gospel of grace, and whether the fruit and the doctrine agree. The council heard the reports with respect, and then let the prophets decide.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James interprets Peter’s story: God himself has come to the nations to take from them a people of his own, a title once used only of Israel.

Simeon has related. Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (compare 2 Peter 1:1). In a room debating whether Gentiles must become Jews, James refers to the man who argued for Gentile freedom by his most Jewish name, perhaps signalling that the case did not come from an outsider.

How God first visited the Gentiles. In Scripture this is what God does when he comes to rescue: he visited his people in their slavery (Exodus 4:31); “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68). It is the word for God coming to his own people, and James uses it of the nations: the God who visited Sarah in her barrenness and Israel in its slavery has visited the nations in their darkness.

The visit was a person. In Luke the verb has a face. At Nain the crowd cried, “God has visited his people!” (Luke 7:16), and Jesus wept over Jerusalem “because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:44). The visit Israel’s prophets longed for came in the Son, and has now reached Lystra and Antioch by his Spirit and his word.

To take from them a people for his name. The most provocative phrase of all. The Greek Old Testament keeps laos, the people, meaning Israel, apart from ethnē, the nations. James applies the word reserved for Israel to people taken out of the nations: a people for his name, God’s treasured possession, showing the world what he is like (Deuteronomy 14:2; 1 Peter 2:9–10). Nothing could have been more provoking to the men of verse 5, and he says it gently, in their own vocabulary, from their own Scriptures.

From them. Not all of them. God is taking a people out of the nations, which is remnant language (the part God keeps and calls for himself out of a larger whole), and it guards against two errors: that everyone is swept in regardless, and that the church has simply replaced Israel. The church is God’s one people, from Jews and Gentiles: very likely what Paul means by “the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16).

So are Gentile Christians now part of Israel? In this sense, yes: grafted into the one olive tree (Romans 11:17–24), heirs of Abraham through faith (Galatians 3:7, 29), fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:19), they belong to one people of God gathered around one Messiah. That does not erase the difference between Jew and Gentile as peoples, or settle every question about Israel’s future; Christians read Romans 11 in more than one way. But no believer is a guest in someone else’s family.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter).

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God has done among the Gentiles agrees with what he promised through the prophets: he would raise up David’s fallen house again, and he has done it in the risen Christ.

The words of the prophets agree. James does not say: the prophets predicted this, so we must accept it. The Scriptures are the fixed point, and what Peter, Barnabas and Paul have reported is measured against them. Had Amos not agreed, no number of signs and wonders would have settled the matter.

The tent of David. James quotes Amos 9:11 in its Greek form. The tent of David is David’s dynasty and kingdom, fallen into ruin, and Amos calls it not the house or the throne but the booth of David: a temporary shelter of branches in a vineyard at harvest, and a collapsed one.

I will restore it. God does not replace it with something grander. He goes back to the fallen shelter and puts that up again. James says this is being fulfilled now: in the resurrection and enthronement of Jesus, David’s son (2:30–36; 13:34), and in the gathering of the Gentiles into his kingdom.

The Hebrew and the Greek. Turn to Amos and you meet a difficulty: at the crucial point James’s Greek text does not read like the Hebrew. Amos 9:12 in our English Bibles, translated from the Hebrew, says “that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name”. James quotes it as “that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord”. Edom has become mankind, and possessing has become seeking.

Three things help. First, the differences are the kind that arise between two ancient copies, not the kind a translator invents: in Hebrew written without vowels, Edom and mankind differ by at most one easily missed letter, and possess and seek by a single letter. The Greek translators probably worked from a Hebrew manuscript that read the consonants one way; the text behind our Old Testament read them another. Second, the Greek Old Testament was the Bible most of the church actually read, Antioch included, and James quotes the form those readers knew, as Paul did at Pisidian Antioch (13:41), and as a preacher today quotes the translation his hearers use.

The argument stands on either text. Third, and most important: even in the Hebrew, the restored kingdom of David includes “all the nations who are called by my name”: Gentiles bearing God’s name inside David’s rebuilt house, the very point in dispute. The council did not smuggle the Gentiles in through a difference of wording. Both texts have them there; the Greek simply says it more warmly. Some details of how the texts came to differ remain uncertain, and believers can admit that honestly while holding that Scripture speaks truly.

A Son who will never fall. God does not abandon the ruins of his promises. David’s house fell to a garden hut, and then to nothing, and God raised it up again in a Son who will never fall. Every Gentile who seeks the Lord is a sign that the shelter is standing again, and the One who promised it is the One doing it.

Is it legitimate for the New Testament to use the Greek Old Testament? Yes. The apostles quoted Scripture in the form their hearers knew, and where the Greek differs from the Hebrew they never build a doctrine on a mistake; they use wording that faithfully carries the meaning, often drawing out what the Hebrew implies. And because they wrote under the Spirit’s inspiration, their use of the Old Testament is the authoritative guide to its meaning. When James says Amos is being fulfilled, that is how we should read Amos.

Where Christians differ: when is David’s tent rebuilt? Dispensational brothers (who see God as keeping distinct purposes for Israel and for the church) generally take the rebuilt tent to await a future millennial kingdom for national Israel, after the church age, and read James as showing only that the present Gentile ingathering is in harmony with the prophets. Both readings rejoice that Gentiles are saved by grace without becoming Jews, the very point of the council, and the difference should be carried with charity. This commentary’s view: James says the conversion of the Gentiles agrees with Amos now. David’s fallen tent is rebuilt in the risen Christ reigning on David’s throne, and in his church of Jews and Gentiles; the promise is fulfilled in the gospel age. This is the amillennial reading, which follows the apostles’ own use of the prophets.
verseByVerse.note: James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s fallen royal house.

parallels.desc: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s house is rebuilt so that the nations may seek the Lord and bear his name, not so that they must first become Israelites.

The remnant of mankind. Why is the tent of David rebuilt at all? Not so that Israel may have a king again for its own sake, but that the rest of humanity might seek the Lord. If the King was raised up for the sake of the nations, then requiring the nations to become Israelites first has the prophecy backwards.

Called by my name. Amos does not say the Gentiles will become Jews, but that God’s name has been called over them. So it is said of the temple: “this house that I have built is called by your name” (1 Kings 8:43). To bear his name is to be publicly marked as his, the way a name over a door tells you whose house it is.

The name called over you. James uses the same idiom in his letter, of the honourable name by which believers were called (James 2:7), and in Acts the name is always the name of Jesus (2:38; 4:12). The Gentiles do not need to be marked as Jews. They carry the name of the Son of David himself, and his rebuilt house is full of people who answer to it.

Says the Lord, who makes these things. James is about to hand down a ruling, but he does not finish on his own authority. The last voice in his quotation is God’s.

What if I do not feel that I belong? Here is a word for the Christian who suspects he is tolerated rather than wanted, who came in late, or from the wrong background, or with a history he would rather nobody knew. Belonging is not established by how you feel about the family, but by whose name has been called over you. That was done to you; you did not do it, and you cannot undo it by feeling unworthy of it. The Gentiles in Amos are not told to earn the name. They are told it is already on them.

Does seek the Lord mean people find God by their own searching? No: “no one seeks for God” on his own (Romans 3:11). When people truly seek the Lord, it is because he has first sought and drawn them. Here the seeking follows God’s rebuilding: the Lord does these things, and the nations seek him as a result. So if you find yourself seeking God, take it as a sign that he is already at work in you, and keep seeking, for he is found by those who seek him with all their heart.

parallels.desc: all the nations who are called by my name

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gathering of the Gentiles was no change of plan: God made it known long ago.

From of old. The inclusion of the Gentiles was God’s purpose all along, made known to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and announced through the prophets (Isaiah 45:21–22). Jerusalem had condemned Jesus because it did not understand the prophets it read every Sabbath (13:27); this time the men in the room see what had been written down.

The mystery hidden for ages. Paul calls it “the mystery hidden for ages in God”: that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (Ephesians 3:6, 9). The plan known from of old was never a plan about circumcision. It was a plan about a person: to gather a people from every nation into his Son, the offspring in whom all the families of the earth would be blessed.

In everyday life. The parts of your life that look like improvisation, the detour, the years that came to nothing, the door that shut, are being handled by someone who does not improvise. Name one of them to God today and thank him that he knew it from of old.

If God planned everything from of old, do my choices matter? Yes. God’s eternal plan includes our real choices and works through them, not around them. The council still had to debate, decide and write; the missionaries still had to walk. God’s purpose is the reason our obedience is not wasted, not a reason to sit still. We pray and choose as wisely as we can, and rest in a wise and good God who weaves even our mistakes into a plan that will not fail (Romans 8:28).

Textual note. In the King James, verse 18 is a whole sentence: “Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.” That longer sentence stands in the mass of later Greek manuscripts, the text the King James translators worked from; the shorter reading the ESV prints is in the oldest and best copies. On the shorter reading the words are still part of what God says through the prophet; on the longer, they become James’s own remark about God’s knowledge in general. Nothing is at stake: God’s eternal knowledge of all his works is taught plainly elsewhere (Isaiah 46:10; Ephesians 1:4). Most variants are like that, and the footnotes are there because translators are being honest with you. The shorter reading is in fact the stronger one for James’s argument. A general statement that God knows everything he does would be true but loose; the better text says that God makes these things known from of old, this particular thing. The ingathering of the nations was published centuries in advance, and the council is not deciding a new policy but catching up with an old announcement.

parallels.desc: who told this long ago?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James rules that the church must not burden Gentile converts with the law, asking only that they keep clear of four things that belonged to idol worship and would make shared tables with Jewish believers impossible.

My judgment. The word carries the weight of a ruling, and the first thing the ruling does is take something away: no circumcision, no burden of the law. Before one requirement is named, it says: stop making it hard for them. The verb (parenochlein) means to harass, to pile on difficulties, and the harassment must stop.

Those who turn to God. Turn is the conversion word, used as settled fact before anything is said about behaviour. The order is the gospel in miniature: they are in, and then we talk about how to live. The Lord receives those who turn to him as they are, old habits and new faith, and then, with infinite patience, teaches them to walk.

Four abstentions. James then names four things, probably echoing the law’s rules for foreigners living among Israel (Leviticus 17–18): food offered to idols; sexual immorality; meat from animals strangled rather than drained of blood; and eating blood, which Scripture had forbidden since Noah, long before Moses, out of reverence for the life in it (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17). These would deeply offend Jewish believers and make table fellowship impossible. All four also cluster around the pagan temple, whose feasts were full of idol-meat, blood, strangled animals and ritual immorality, so the decree keeps new converts clear of their old idolatry too.

Burdens hard to bear. James’s own brother had said it: “you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers” (Luke 11:46); “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Luke 18:16). The Christ who kept his sharpest words for those who made coming to God hard is the Christ whose brother now says: we should not trouble them. The church was not being lenient. It was being like Jesus.

Harassing people toward Jesus. A church can attach to the gospel a cloud of expectations, about dress, vocabulary, background, politics, a conversion story of the right shape, none stated as conditions and all functioning as conditions, and then wonder why people who genuinely turned to God do not stay. The first ruling the church ever issued about new believers begins: we should not trouble.

If the food laws are abolished, why forbid blood and strangled meat? The council had just decided that Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the law (v. 11), so these are neither kosher rules smuggled back in nor conditions of salvation. They are asked for love and unity: so that Jew and Gentile could sit at one table, the Gentiles, free in conscience, gave up a few things that would deeply wound their brothers. It is liberty limited by love (Romans 14), not a return to the law.

But does not Paul later allow food offered to idols? No contradiction (1 Corinthians 8–10), once two questions are distinguished. Eating as worship, at a temple feast, Paul forbids as flatly as the council: “flee from idolatry”; “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:14, 21). Meat that had merely passed through a temple and was sold in the market he treats as neutral (“Eat whatever is sold in the meat market”, 10:25), governed only by love for a weaker brother (8:9–13). Paul applies the decree’s two principles, flee idolatry and let love limit liberty, with more nuance. Its heart never changes, while the abstentions from blood and strangled meat are generally understood to belong to that moment: most Christians today do not observe them, seeing the reverence for blood fulfilled in the blood of Christ once shed. Keep clear of idols, and love your brother more than your dinner.

Why is sexual immorality in a list about food? Because in the pagan world it was bound up with idol worship and temple feasts, and treated as ordinary, much as many treat it today. But it is not a matter of custom; it is God’s moral law, forbidden again and again in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5), and its place on the list warned new converts that turning to God meant a break with the sexual habits of their old life. That part of the decree has never expired.

Where Christians differ: are these rules binding today? Some groups hold that Christians must still avoid blood, for example in black pudding, or even (Jehovah’s Witnesses) blood transfusions. This commentary’s view: these were not conditions of salvation (that was settled in v. 11), but practical rules for fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers at that time. Paul later teaches that food is a matter of conscience and love (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10). The rule against sexual immorality is permanent moral law; the food rules applied the principle of not offending a brother. Blood transfusions have nothing to do with eating blood.

Uncertain wording. Two of the four terms are less clear than they look. “Sexual immorality” (porneia) is the ordinary word for every sexual sin, but in a list that seems to echo Leviticus 17–18 some think it means particularly marriages within the forbidden degrees of kinship (Leviticus 18). “What has been strangled” most likely means meat from animals killed without draining the blood, though exactly which practices it covered is not known. Most likely porneia has its broad sense, which includes the Leviticus 18 cases.
verseByVerse.note: The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living in Israel (Lev 17–18), and would let Jewish and Gentile believers eat together.

parallels.desc: sacrifices, blood, and what dies of itself
sexual relations

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James explains the four requests: Moses is read in every synagogue, so in every city there are Jewish believers whose consciences the Gentile believers must respect.

Read every Sabbath. Wherever the gospel went, there was a synagogue where Moses was read aloud every Sabbath. James grounds the abstentions not in the Gentiles’ own holiness but in other people: believers, in towns these Gentiles will never visit, who could not sit at a table where blood was served. Not because those men are right; the council has just declared they are not right about circumcision. Because they are brothers.

The hardest form of love. Surrendering a liberty you are entitled to, for somebody whose scruple you privately think mistaken, is the hardest form of Christian love and much the commonest (Romans 14); it costs more than the grand sacrifices because nobody notices.

Christ did not please himself. The Gentiles of Antioch were asked to give up a dish for brothers they would never meet. “For Christ did not please himself” (Romans 15:3): he had every right to the glory of heaven and laid it aside, and to his own life and laid that down too, for the weak, the scrupulous and the wrong. Every small freedom surrendered at a shared table is a faint reflection of that Lord.

Moses wrote of me. And Moses, read every Sabbath, was writing about Christ: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46; compare Luke 24:27). The scrolls read every week in Iconium were witnesses for the Messiah the Gentile believers trusted, so nothing they did should put off a synagogue hearer whom Moses might yet lead to Christ.

How do I know when to give up a freedom and when to stand on it? Give it up when using it would genuinely harm a brother’s conscience or faith, cause him to stumble into sin, or block someone from hearing the gospel (1 Corinthians 8:13; 9:19–23). Stand on it when someone demands it as a condition of being right with God, because then the gospel itself is at stake (see Timothy and Titus at vv. 1–2). With a weaker brother who is hurt, love limits liberty. With a false teacher who imposes, liberty must be defended for the gospel’s sake.

Uncertain wording. James says “for” without spelling out the connection, and careful readers take the sentence three ways. Some read it as about the Jewish believers: Moses is preached in every city, so everywhere there are Christians of Jewish background with these scruples, and the four abstentions are the least a mixed congregation needs to eat together. Some read it as about the Gentiles: anyone who wants the law of Moses can hear it any Sabbath, so the church need not impose it. Others hear a reassurance to the Pharisees’ party that the ruling does no dishonour to Moses, who goes on being read every week. The first fits the ruling’s purpose best, is the one most take, and is followed above.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole church agrees, and sends the decision to the Gentile believers not only in a letter but with trusted men, addressing them from the first word as brothers.

With the whole church. Apostles, elders and the whole church are named together in the sending. Luke does not explain the mechanics, but the decision was not simply handed down from a room upstairs.

To choose men. Instead of simply posting the letter, they chose men to carry it. A ruling that arrives as a document leaves you alone with your questions and whatever tone you imagine in it; one carried by two respected men who will stay and answer anything you ask is a pastoral act. Antioch had been unsettled by men who came with words. Jerusalem answers with men who came with words, and the difference is that these were sent.

Leading men. Both Jerusalem men, and both, so far as we can tell, Jewish: the verdict for Gentile freedom is carried by the side that had most to lose by it, so nobody could say the Gentiles had voted themselves a privilege.

Remember the second name. Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters (2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1), who carried, and perhaps helped to write, Peter’s first letter (1 Peter 5:12). He has come to deliver a letter and go home. Within twenty verses he will be Paul’s partner, and before long singing in a Philippian cell at midnight (16:25). Men are forever setting out on errands that turn into their life’s work.

Brothers to brothers. The letter’s first word settles the question it was written to answer: brothers to brothers, on both ends of the address. Before a single clause of argument, the salutation has conceded everything the Judaizers (those insisting that Gentile believers must live as Jews) were contesting.

A fingerprint. The Greek word for “greetings” opens a letter in only three places in the New Testament: this letter, a Roman officer’s despatch (23:26), and the letter of James. So James, who proposed the ruling, may well have drafted the letter too.

Not only a letter. God himself did not only send words: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and stayed, and answered questions. Judas and Silas are a faint copy of that.

Does the council set a pattern for church government? Apostles, elders and the whole church took part, appealing to Scripture (vv. 15–18) and to what God had done, and the decision bound churches beyond Jerusalem because apostles were present and it agreed with Scripture. Churches today may meet together to settle questions, as Presbyterian synods do, and congregations take part in decisions; but no later council carries apostolic authority (see vv. 28–29).

Why does it matter that we call other believers brothers and sisters? Because it is true, and truth spoken shapes how we treat one another. In Christ we have one Father and one elder Brother: we are family, not a club or customers of a service, and families eat together, bear with one another, share burdens and stay together through quarrels. The word brother was a healing word to Gentiles who had been told they were outsiders. Say it, and mean it, to the believer who feels least at home.
verseByVerse.note: Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem disowns the men who unsettled Antioch, and sends its answer in one accord with the very men those teachers had undermined.

Gone out from us. The mother church puts it in writing that men who had used its name had no authority to do so, and honestly admits they came “from us” in the same breath as it disowns them. That is the right response from a misrepresented institution, and rarer than it ought to be: the temptations are to defend your own because they are your own, or to pretend they were never anything to do with you.

Unsettling your minds. The word (anaskeuazontes) is used of dismantling a building or plundering a house: they took your minds apart. People who had been sure they belonged to God were no longer sure, and that is the characteristic wound of adding anything to the gospel. An uncertain Christian cannot love, give or speak of Christ freely, because part of him is permanently occupied with checking whether he is in.

Having come to one accord. Luke’s word for the church’s Spirit-given unity (1:14; 4:24), placed eighteen verses after “much debate” (v. 7). They did not reach one accord by leaving the subject alone. The unity came after the argument, and that is the only kind that holds.

With our beloved Barnabas and Paul. The two men the circumcision party had been undermining are named in an official document with an adjective of affection, and Barnabas first: in a Jerusalem letter, the Jerusalem order.

The peace he left. Paul uses the same verb for “troubled” of the same kind of men: “there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ” (Galatians 1:7). The cure for a distorted Christ is Christ undistorted. In the upper room Jesus said, “Let not your hearts be troubled. … Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:1, 27). His peace rests not on our reaching some further standard but on what he did the next day, on the cross.

How can I have assurance if my mind has been unsettled? Go back to the gospel itself, not to your feelings or your record. “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36), and God cannot lie. Your assurance rests first on that promise, then on the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and then on the fruit of a changed life, imperfect but real (the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, both 18.2). If someone tells you that you need something more than Christ, test it by Scripture as Antioch did, and talk to a mature pastor or friend; unsettled minds are often settled in conversation.

parallels.desc: some who trouble you

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter commends Barnabas and Paul as men who have handed over their lives for Christ’s name, and sends two witnesses to confirm its message in person.

Risked their lives. Stronger than risked: they have handed over their lives (paradedōkosi), as at the stoning in Lystra (14:19). Jerusalem is not saying these are sound men whose theology we have checked, but: these men have already paid for this gospel with their bodies, and the people telling you they are wrong have paid nothing like it.

For the name. Not for a mission strategy, but for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The name runs through the chapter: a people for his name (v. 14), called by his name (v. 17), lives handed over for the name. The council exists to answer whether that name is enough by itself. It is worth a life, because he gave his life for his Father’s name and for the people he loved, and it is the only name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12).

By word of mouth. Two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), the written word and the living voice sent together. A letter can be read in a hostile tone, or explained away by whoever gets to it first, so they sent two men who could be asked follow-up questions.

In everyday life. Find out about a persecuted church or a believer imprisoned for their faith, and carry them to God in prayer this week.

Does suffering prove that someone’s teaching is true? Not on its own: people have died for false beliefs too. But suffering does show sincerity; it is hard to think a man is in it for gain when he keeps being stoned for it. And in Scripture faithful suffering marks true servants of Christ, unlike false teachers who look for comfort and profit (2 Corinthians 11:23–29; 2 Timothy 3:10–12). The test of teaching is always Scripture, but a teacher’s willingness to suffer for Christ rather than profit from him is a good reason to listen carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council’s decision is the Spirit’s and the church’s together: Gentile believers carry no burden beyond four abstentions, kept for the sake of fellowship and not as a condition of salvation.

To the Holy Spirit and to us. One of the boldest sentences any church body has written about its own decision, and it has been quoted ever since to justify a great deal that it cannot support. The Spirit led the council through Scripture, through what God had done, and through the agreement of the church. Three things stand under the sentence: the Spirit had already acted publicly before anyone voted (v. 8); Scripture agreed (v. 15); and apostles were in the room, holding a commission that cannot be repeated. A committee with none of those three has no business borrowing it.

The order of the words. The safeguard is in the order: “to the Holy Spirit and to us”. They do not write: we have decided, and we trust the Spirit approves. Nor: the Spirit has spoken and we merely wrote it down, which would have sounded more impressive and been a lie, because they had argued at length. Christians have wanted to delete one half or the other ever since: some claim a directness God did not give them, others reduce the church’s decisions to management with a prayer at the start. These men put their names next to the Spirit’s, a far more sobering thing than claiming a private impression.

No greater burden. They admit the four things are a burden, and promise that nothing further will be added, which was the whole anxiety of the Gentile churches, and remains the anxiety of anyone who suspects the requirements will keep coming.

Three versions of the decree. Luke gives the decree three times: James speaks it (v. 20), the letter writes it (v. 29), and years later James quotes it back to Paul (21:25). The letter tightens “the things polluted by idols”, broad enough to cover almost anything connected with a temple, into “what has been sacrificed to idols”, a specific and checkable thing, and moves sexual immorality to last, so that the three food matters stand together, the order James uses at 21:25. The decree did not quietly lapse once feelings cooled.

You will do well. Not “you will be saved”, but “you will do well”: advice for fellowship, not a condition of salvation (on whether the four still bind, see “Where Christians differ” at vv. 19–20). It ends gently, with no threat and no penalty. Farewell.

He will guide you into all the truth. Jesus promised that the Spirit of truth would “guide you into all the truth” and that “He will glorify me” (John 16:13–14). Here he does precisely that, guarding the sufficiency of Christ: nothing added to the grace of the Lord Jesus. Whenever the Spirit truly leads the church, Christ is made larger and the burdens on his people smaller, one sure way to tell his leading from a committee’s preferences.

How should I seek the Spirit’s guidance in my own decisions? Follow the council’s pattern on a small scale. Start with Scripture: what has God already said that bears on this? Look honestly at the circumstances God has arranged. Pray, and ask counsel of wise believers. Weigh the options by love for God and neighbour. Then decide, and own the decision humbly, without claiming that God spoke to you directly. The Spirit usually guides through his word, prayer, wisdom and the church, not private voices, and he is no less present for that.

Where Christians differ: the authority of church councils. Some see this council as the model for later councils whose decisions bind the church infallibly. This commentary’s view: this council included apostles, and its decision became Scripture. Later councils have no such authority. They are valuable and to be respected when they agree with Scripture, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err (Westminster Confession 31.4). Scripture alone is the final authority: sola Scriptura.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the letter is read aloud at Antioch, the unsettled Gentile believers rejoice: nothing more is required of them.

They delivered the letter. It was read to the whole church, at once, out loud. The people whose minds had been unsettled heard the answer with their own ears at the same moment as everyone else.

Stand in that room. Here a doctrine becomes a person’s own relief. You are a Gentile in Antioch. Not long ago you were sacrificing to the gods you grew up with; then you heard about Jesus, believed, and came alive. Then men arrived from Jerusalem, from the church of the apostles, and said you were not, in fact, saved: there was a further thing, and until it was done you were outside. For months you have not known whether you belong to God. And now a letter is read aloud, and its first word is brothers, and it says the men who unsettled you were never sent, and that nothing further is required of you.

They rejoiced. They were saved by grace, as they were. The gospel of grace brings joy; legalism brings fear. Nothing was added to produce that joy, no new experience, gift or vision. Something was taken away: a doubt. Most of the deepest joys of the Christian life are like that: the removal of something that had been standing between you and what you already had.

Nailed to the cross. What was removed had a destination. Antioch had been told it still owed a legal debt. Paul tells Colossae where every such demand has gone: “by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). The letter read in Antioch did not cancel anything. It announced a cancellation already made, on a hill outside Jerusalem. The joy of Antioch is the joy of every sinner who hears that nothing more is required, because Christ has done it all.

In everyday life. You may be carrying an unsettled mind of your own: some question about whether God has really accepted you that you have never put into words. Open the New Testament today at Romans 8 and read it aloud, as Antioch heard its letter.

Why does legalism produce fear? If acceptance with God depends even partly on your performance, you can never be sure you have done enough. Every failure becomes a threat, every rule a test, every other Christian a rival or a judge; so legalistic churches are often anxious, harsh and joyless, even when very busy. Grace produces a different kind of obedience: glad, grateful and secure, because it flows from acceptance rather than toward it. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas and Silas stay to strengthen the church with long, patient encouragement, and leave Antioch at peace.

Themselves prophets. Jerusalem sent not two couriers but two prophets, and they did not hand over the letter and catch the next ship. They stayed.

Encouraged and strengthened. One of the plainest pictures in the New Testament of what an early church prophet did with his time. There is prediction in Acts (11:28; 21:11), but here two named prophets in a local church talk to people for a long time and leave them stronger. Paul’s definition matches: “the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation” (1 Corinthians 14:3).

With many words. Luke cheerfully admits it took a while: hours of talking to frightened people, probably repeating themselves, a comfort to anybody who suspects his own ministry is unremarkable.

Sent off in peace. The chapter began with “no small dissension and debate” (v. 2), and now men are sent home in peace. It is not the peace of a subject nobody raised, but what is left when the thing has been fought out properly and settled.

A bruised reed he will not break. That patience has a source: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). Antioch was a reed bent by a false gospel. Its Lord did not answer its weakness with a sharp word and a deadline. He gave it two men and many words and as long as it took: the Servant still binding up the bruised through those he sends.

In everyday life. Christ has dealt gently with your bruises, so think of one shaken believer you know, and give them not a single sentence but an hour: listen, then speak the truths of the gospel to them, even the ones they have heard before.

Are there prophets like Judas and Silas today? Not in the sense of people receiving new revelation to stand alongside Scripture: that foundational gift belonged to the apostolic age, before the New Testament was complete (Ephesians 2:20), and the canon is now closed. But the work Judas and Silas do here, strengthening believers with many words drawn from the truth God has given, goes on in every faithful pastor, teacher and friend who opens the word to a troubled soul. Many Christians hold that the gift of prophecy continues in some form, and they are brothers; but none should claim for any word today the authority of Scripture.

Textual note. Your Bible goes straight from verse 33 to verse 35. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.” It stands in the King James but is absent from the oldest and best copies, and is probably a later addition. In verse 33 Judas and Silas are sent back to those who had sent them; in verse 40 Paul chooses Silas. A copyist reading the two in sequence saw a snag and supplied a line to keep Silas in Antioch. That is the shape of most textual variants, and it should steady rather than alarm you: the scribe was not inventing doctrine but tidying a wrinkle in the story, in good faith, and we can see him doing it because the copies without his tidying survived. Nothing is at stake: Silas may simply have gone back to Jerusalem and returned, or delayed his going.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the crisis, ordinary ministry resumes: Paul, Barnabas and many others go on teaching and preaching the word in Antioch.

Councils are rare; teaching is daily. One of the gravest crises in the church’s history has just been resolved, and the next sentence is that two men stayed in their own congregation and taught. This is the last time Paul and Barnabas appear together as partners; soon they will part over Mark.

With many others also. The ministry of the word was shared by many, and Luke names none of them. If you have measured your own service against the people whose names are known and concluded that yours does not count, Luke puts the many others in the same clause as Paul and Barnabas, with the same verbs. The distinction is ours, not his, and not God’s. The Lord knows the names Luke did not record, and on the last day he will read them out.

Gifts of the ascended Lord. Where did Antioch get so many teachers? When Christ ascended on high “he gave gifts to men”: the shepherds and teachers, “to equip the saints” (Ephesians 4:8, 11–12). The many others were presents from the throne, given by the risen Jesus to a church he had just defended at Jerusalem.

Does every Christian have a part in the ministry of the word? Yes, though not all in the same way. Some are called and gifted to preach and teach publicly, and the church should test and recognise them. But every believer is to “let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another” (Colossians 3:16): parents with children, friends over coffee, older women with younger, a word of Scripture in a hospital ward. The many others of Antioch were probably a mixture of all these. Ask where God has given you people to share his word with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even faithful servants of Christ can quarrel sharply, yet the Lord carries his work forward and restores those his servants give up on. Paul proposes going back to visit the churches of the first journey (v. 36). Barnabas wants to take John Mark, who had deserted them in Pamphylia, and Paul refuses (vv. 37–38). The disagreement grows so sharp that they part: Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus, and Paul, commended to the grace of the Lord, takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches (vv. 39–41). Luke gives no verdict between them, and Paul’s later letters show him at peace with both Barnabas and Mark.
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s rule over his servants’ conflicts

Luke does not approve the quarrel, and something real was lost when these two partners parted (see vv. 39–40). Yet God worked through it: two teams went out instead of one, and John Mark, the cause of the dispute, later proved his worth (see vv. 36–37 and 39–40). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark back to Cyprus to restore him (see vv. 39–40). Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both bore fruit. Now: When Christians disagree on something that does not touch the gospel, they can still each go on with the work, speak well of one another, and leave room for God to heal the break in time.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wants to go back and see how the young churches are doing, and Barnabas wants to give John Mark a second chance. Both desires are good, and they are about to collide.

See how they are. The last clause shows what kind of man Paul is: “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28). He has been driven out of most of those towns, and what is on his mind is whether the people he left behind are all right. Keep that in view, because the quarrel is about to make both men look small. The plan becomes the second journey, which carries the council’s decisions to the churches whose freedom it defended (16:4), and then into Europe; and it begins with a quarrel, so we learn that the gospel goes forward through forgiven and imperfect servants.

John called Mark. The John Mark who had turned back (13:13). Barnabas wanted to give him a second chance, and any attentive reader knows what is coming. Barnabas first appears selling a field, nicknamed son of encouragement (4:36–37); when the church was afraid of a newly converted persecutor, he brought him to the apostles (9:27), and later fetched him from Tarsus (11:25–26). His whole biography is taking a chance on somebody others had written off.

The irony. The man refusing to take a chance on Mark is a man whose ministry exists because Barnabas took a chance on him (9:27). That is not said to convict Paul, whose case was serious: Mark had abandoned the mission. It is said because it is one of the most human things in the New Testament: to have been rescued by a kindness, to be grateful for it all your life, and to be unable to see the same situation when it turns up with somebody else’s name on it.

An honest complication. Mark was Barnabas’s cousin (Colossians 4:10). It does not make Barnabas wrong (a man may be right about somebody and partial to him at the same time), but it is part of the picture.

Tell his disciples and Peter. Paul would come round: “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). It is the pattern of the Lord Jesus with deserters. On the morning of the resurrection the message at the empty tomb, as Mark’s own Gospel records it, singled out the worst of them by name: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). The Christ Paul and Barnabas preached takes runaways back into his service, and the young man at the centre of this quarrel would live to prove it.

In everyday life. Look for the person in your church whom others have quietly written off, and take a chance on them, as Barnabas did for Saul and Christ did for you.

How do I care for people I helped bring to faith? Keep in touch, as Paul wanted to, and ask how they are, in life as well as faith. Pray for them specifically. Read the Bible with them, or find someone who will, and help them settle in a church. Be honest about your own struggles, so they do not think the Christian life should be easy. And do not take it personally if they need others more than you: your aim is their growth in Christ, not their attachment to you.

parallels.desc: Mark the cousin of Barnabas

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul refuses to take Mark because Mark had deserted the work the Holy Spirit had given them, and he takes that commission with deadly seriousness.

Withdrawn from them. Paul’s case is stronger than usually allowed. Luke’s verb is not “left”, as at 13:13, but a heavier word (apostanta): to stand off from, to desert, the root of our word apostasy. Paul saw it as abandoning the work, and he needed reliable companions for dangerous journeys.

To the work. Paul states the charge precisely. Mark had not gone with them “to the work”, the word the Holy Spirit used when it all began: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (13:2).
