Paul’s objection is not that a young man let him down personally. It is that a man walked out on a commission the Holy Spirit had named, and that the same commission is now being proposed again.

Two men looking at two things. So the two are not looking at the same thing at all. Barnabas is looking at a person, and asking what will become of him; Paul at a commission, and what will become of it. Both concerns are real, each man is right about what he is looking at, and neither can see why the other will not be reasonable. Anyone who has sat on a church committee or in a family where two people of unquestioned goodwill could not be reconciled has watched this. Our instinct is that one party must be the problem; Luke gives no such verdict.

Each right about something. What we do get, later, is that each turned out to be right about something. Barnabas was right about Mark, as Paul himself later said (2 Timothy 4:11). And Paul was right that the second journey would need men who would not go home: within a chapter Silas is in the inner cell of a Philippian prison with his feet in the stocks.

No one who looks back. Paul’s seriousness came from his Lord: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). The Christ who welcomed sinners also spoke with great severity about the cost of following him, and set his own face toward Jerusalem to finish his work. Paul could not treat the commission lightly, because his Master never had.

Commission and person in one hand. Barnabas held on to the person and Paul held on to the work, and neither could hold both. In Christ the two meet perfectly: he guards his work with a holy jealousy, and he restores deserters with a tender patience. He did not drop Peter after the denials, and he did not let the work of the gospel fail either. Only he holds the commission and the person in one hand without losing either.

When two good Christians disagree, must one of them be sinning? Not necessarily. Two believers, both seeking God’s glory, can weigh different goods differently, as Paul and Barnabas did. There is often sin in how they disagree, in harsh words, pride or refusal to listen; but the disagreement itself may simply reflect the limits of our wisdom. So when you are in one, examine your heart before your opponent’s, assume the other person may see something you do not, and ask God to show you what each of you is rightly guarding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disagreement becomes so sharp that Paul and Barnabas part, yet both go on in the Lord’s work, and the break is not the end of the story.

A sharp disagreement. Luke’s word is paroxysmos, a violent flaring, from which we get paroxysm. He does not soften it: Christians, even apostles, can disagree strongly. The noun appears once more in the New Testament: “let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24), where it lies behind “stir up”. The same heat that tears two missionaries apart is the thing Christians are commanded to provoke in each other. Passion is not the problem in either verse; what it is aimed at is.

They separated. The common comfort is that God used the quarrel to double the mission, and both men did go on to fruitful work. But that must not become approval. Two men who had faced mobs together never work side by side again in this book. Something real was lost. A reader estranged from a Christian brother is helped by seeing that the Bible records a break that hurt, and does not tidy it away.

Barnabas took Mark. Cyprus is Barnabas’s own home (4:36), and the first leg of the very journey Mark abandoned. Barnabas takes him back over the ground where it went wrong and walks it again with him, at cost to himself. That is what restoring somebody looks like. It worked: Mark became Paul’s fellow worker (Philemon 24), and by early tradition he wrote the Gospel that bears his name.

Commended to the grace of the Lord. Antioch did not treat the quarrel as disqualifying. It sent Paul with the same words as when he first went out (14:26), putting him where it could not follow, into the keeping of God’s grace: not his own judgment, just out of a furious argument, nor his record, but to the grace the council had just said saves Jew and Gentile alike: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The grace that saved us is the grace that sends us, and it is the only thing that covers the faults we bring with us onto the road.

The camera angle. This is Barnabas’s last appearance in Acts. Luke follows Paul from now on because his story is travelling toward Rome, not as a verdict on the man. Do not mistake the camera angle for the assessment of God: a great deal of the best work in the church is done by people the story stops following.

Not permanent. And then the hope, which rests on evidence. Years afterwards Paul writes, “Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?” (1 Corinthians 9:6): a throwaway line that puts their two names in one clause and treats Barnabas as a fellow worker in good standing. And he introduces Mark to the Colossians, warmly, as “the cousin of Barnabas” (Colossians 4:10). A real break, and not a permanent one. The Lord Jesus is the great Reconciler, who made peace between God and sinners by his blood and who will one day bring every estranged believer to one table, where there will be no more quarrels.

What should I do if I have fallen out with a fellow Christian? Own your part honestly before God, without waiting for the other person to own theirs. Do what you can to seek peace (Romans 12:18): a humble message, an apology, an offer to meet. If you cannot agree on the issue, you may still part without bitterness and speak well of each other, as Paul later spoke of Barnabas. Do not gossip about the quarrel; pray for the other person’s blessing. And leave room for God to heal over years what cannot be healed in a week.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Mark were later reconciled.

parallels.desc: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sets out on his second journey by quietly strengthening the small churches of his home region, carrying the council’s gospel on foot.

Syria and Cilicia. Cilicia, whose chief city was Tarsus, was Paul’s home province, where he had worked during his hidden years (Galatians 1:21). This verse and the council’s letter (v. 23) are the only places in Acts that mention churches there.

The hidden years. Acts never records their founding. Sent off to Tarsus (9:30), Saul disappears until Barnabas fetches him (11:25), perhaps for the best part of a decade, and this verse is the only trace of that work: no account of the preaching, only churches on the ground. That is worth having if the most obscure stretch of your own life is the one you cannot see any fruit from. Paul’s years in Tarsus were not a holding pattern before the real ministry started.

Strengthening. Luke’s third use of the word in quick succession (14:22; 15:32): plainly something the church needs more of than it gets. Part of it was the council’s letter, delivered as he went (16:4): the theology of chapter 15 arrives in the churches on foot. The journey that will plant the churches to which many New Testament letters were written begins not with a vision but with a man who has just parted from his oldest partner, walking through his home province, propping up small churches nobody has heard of.

The hidden years at Nazareth. Of Jesus between his boyhood and his baptism Luke gives one sentence: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52). Yet before he had preached a sermon, the Father said: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22). The unrecorded years of his servants are lived in the footsteps of a Lord whose own were precious to his Father. And “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25): he will present her to himself in splendour, every one of those small churches in Cilicia among her number.

What does it mean to strengthen a church? Helping believers stand firmer in Christ: teaching them the truth so they are not tossed about by every new idea (Ephesians 4:14), encouraging them in trials, reminding them of the gospel of grace, correcting error gently, building up love. Every member can do some of it. A word of Scripture to a struggling friend, faithful attendance that encourages others, prayer for the leaders, a meal for a family under strain, patience with a difficult member: all of these strengthen a church.

15.theology: Saved by grace alone, through faith alone. Peter’s summary, “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will”, is the heart of what the Reformers later contended for. The men who demanded circumcision were sincere believers, but sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The law cannot save and never could; it shows our need of grace rather than offering another way. The cross of Christ is sufficient (see the note on vv. 1–2).
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over what a person must do to be saved was settled not by compromise but by clarity: Scripture (James’s use of Amos), tested alongside what God had plainly done.

Now: The same error keeps coming back in new clothes: grace plus something as the ground of salvation (see “What does Jesus plus look like today?” at vv. 1–2). The church’s task in every generation is to say the council’s answer clearly, defend it firmly, and live it gladly.

keyVerse.quote: But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.
keyVerse.note: This is the sentence that settles the council. Peter, a law-keeping Jew in Jerusalem, does not say the Gentiles will be saved as Jews are, but that Jews will be saved as Gentiles are: by grace, with nothing added. It holds the gospel of the whole chapter, and of the Reformation after it: the grace of the Lord Jesus is enough, from first to last, for everyone who believes.

15.reflection:
The teachers from Judea believed almost everything true about Jesus, and then added one condition (v. 1). What are the “Jesus plus” conditions people are tempted to add today, in churches or in their own hearts? Why does even one addition change the whole gospel?

Peter says that Jews will be saved “through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” (v. 11). How is it humbling, and how is it comforting, that the most respectable believer and the newest convert are saved in exactly the same way?

The council lifted the burden of the law but asked Gentile believers to give up a few freedoms so that Jewish believers could share their table (vv. 19–21, 28–29). What freedoms might you need to lay aside for the sake of other Christians, and where must a freedom be defended rather than given up?

Paul and Barnabas, both good men, parted after a sharp disagreement, and were later reconciled (vv. 36–41). What helps Christians disagree without bitterness? Is there a broken relationship you need to bring to the Lord who reconciles?

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview:
Where we are. Acts 16 sets the second missionary journey on its way. The Jerusalem council has just ruled that Gentiles are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus without being circumcised (15:11, 19), and Paul, now with Silas after parting from Barnabas (15:36–41), goes back to strengthen the churches; before the chapter ends, the gospel has crossed into Europe.

The message. The risen Lord Jesus steers his own mission and saves every kind of person by the same free grace. He closes doors and opens one, opens a devout woman’s heart, breaks a demon’s hold on a slave girl, and shakes a prison until a hardened jailer asks how to be saved; and the answer for all of them is one: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved.”

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). Believers needed to see that the gospel’s advance into new lands was the Lord’s doing and not Paul’s scheme, that closed doors and beatings did not mean it was failing, and that Christians were no threat to Roman order: in Philippi it is the Roman magistrates who break the law.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul takes Timothy with him and delivers the council’s decisions, and the churches grow (vv. 1–5). The Spirit closes Asia and Bithynia, and at Troas a vision calls the team, Luke now among them, over to Macedonia (vv. 6–10). In Philippi, a proud Roman colony, the Lord opens Lydia’s heart by the river, and her house becomes the church’s home (vv. 11–15). Freeing a slave girl from a spirit of divination costs Paul and Silas a flogging and the stocks (vv. 16–24); at midnight they sing, an earthquake opens the prison, and the jailer and his household believe (vv. 25–34). In the morning Paul makes the magistrates come in person, encourages the church at Lydia’s house, and leaves (vv. 35–40).

Where it leads. The Spirit who directs the road is “the Spirit of Jesus” (v. 7), and the heart that opens is opened by “the Lord” (v. 14): Acts is still the story of what Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), now continued from heaven. The girl is freed by his name; the prisoners sing in the dark as he sang on the night of his arrest; the jailer is turned from the “lords” on his floor to the Lord Jesus; and two servants beaten publicly, uncondemned, walk where their Master walked before Pilate. The chapter’s great question is answered not with a task but with a person.

For us. Expect the Lord to guide you by closed doors as well as open ones, and keep walking. Pray for hearts to be opened, because only he can open them, and speak, because he opens them through words. And let your church be the one room in town where the businesswoman, the rescued and the jailer sit at the same table.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Lord directs his mission, and his ways of directing it are not ours. Paul takes Timothy, a young disciple of mixed Jewish and Greek family, and carries the Jerusalem council’s decisions through the churches, which are strengthened and grow (vv. 1–5). Then the Spirit of Jesus closes Asia and Bithynia, and at Troas a night vision of a man of Macedonia calls the team, Luke now among them, across the sea (vv. 6–10). In Philippi, a proud Roman colony with no synagogue, they find women praying by a river, and the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a dealer in purple; she and her household are baptised, and her house becomes the church’s home (vv. 11–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit directs the mission

The Holy Spirit kept the team from preaching in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them into Bithynia; the door to Europe opened only after those two had closed (see vv. 6–7 and 9–10). The church’s part is to obey both the open doors and the closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia’s household became the first church in Europe that Luke records, gathered in a businesswoman’s home around the word of God. Now: The church is still built wherever the Lord opens hearts, in homes as often as in church buildings, and through work and friendship as often as through programmes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back in Lystra, where he was once stoned, Paul finds Timothy, a young disciple from a divided home whom God had been preparing for years.

Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A crowd here had tried to sacrifice oxen to Paul and, days later, stoned him and dragged him out for dead (14:19). He walks back into it on purpose.

A disciple was there, named Timothy. Timothy is already a disciple, probably converted on the first journey, and he knew at first hand what Paul had suffered at Lystra (2 Timothy 3:10–11). Paul later names his believing mother and grandmother, Eunice and Lois, in whom his faith dwelt first (2 Timothy 1:5), and from childhood he had known the sacred writings (2 Timothy 3:15). He became Paul’s closest co-worker, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2).

His father was a Greek. A Gentile, perhaps dead by now, never called a believer, who had probably not allowed his son to be circumcised. So Timothy grew up in a home divided down the middle, belonging fully to neither community.

He was well spoken of by the brothers. Two churches, eighteen miles or so apart, gave the same verdict, and a good reputation is a qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:7). It is still the soundest test for ministry: not what a man says about himself, but what those who have known him for years say when asked.

One new man in a divided house. Jew and Greek had met in Timothy’s home and stayed apart there. They met again in Christ, who came “that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). What a marriage could not reconcile, the cross did. And the God who shepherds the generations was at work in that house long before Paul came back down the road, in a grandmother’s faith and a mother’s teaching. He wastes nothing: not the stones of Lystra, not the awkwardness of a mixed home, not the quiet years of Bible reading at a kitchen table.

If you have grown up between things. A divided home, two cultures, a family where the faith came down one side only: Timothy is in Scripture partly for you. The thing that made him awkward is the thing Christ made useful.

I am the only believer in my home. Is there hope for my children? Yes, and Timothy is one of the Bible’s answers. His father did not believe, yet a mother and grandmother quietly taught him the Scriptures, and God made him a pastor. Paul tells a believer married to an unbeliever that the children are not shut out but set in a place of blessing (1 Corinthians 7:14). Read the Bible with your children, pray with them and for them, take them to church, and live the faith gladly in front of them. You cannot convert them, but you can put the word in front of them, and God is pleased to use exactly that.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul circumcises Timothy not to help him be saved but to help him be heard: what can never be a condition of salvation may be freely done as a kindness for the gospel’s sake.

He took him and circumcised him. With chapter 15 still open, it looks impossible: Paul has just won a public fight against men who said Gentiles must be circumcised, and is carrying the letter that settles it. The contradiction dissolves once you see two things.

First, the principle. Because Jerusalem has ruled that circumcision saves nobody, Paul is free to circumcise a man without the act meaning anything about salvation. Once the doctrine is settled, the practice is free.

Second, Timothy was not a Gentile. This is the point usually missed. By the Jewish reckoning that later became the rule, and may already have been common, a child’s standing followed the mother. In Jewish eyes Timothy was a Jew, and an uncircumcised Jew, whose state his own town knew all about, would look to the synagogue like an apostate. Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5): Titus was a Gentile, and the gospel was at stake. For Timothy, circumcision removed an obstacle.

Because of the Jews who were in those places. The reason is the mission. Paul starts in the synagogue in every town, and an uncircumcised companion would have ended that conversation in five minutes over a distraction. “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20).

What it cost Timothy. An operation on an adult: no anaesthetic, days of pain, some risk, and then a long walk. His first recorded act as a missionary is to accept that, to gain a hearing among people who had looked down on him all his life.

Born under the law. Timothy’s wound has a pattern older than Paul’s strategy. “God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5), and on the eighth day the child was circumcised (Luke 2:21). He who owed the law nothing kept every word of it, and became a servant to the circumcised so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (Romans 15:8–9). That is the mind Timothy is learning: the free man who makes himself a servant for others’ sake (1 Corinthians 9:19), because his Master did it first at far greater cost. The Lord who bore that small wound in infancy bore the great wounds at Calvary, and every cost his servants accept for the gospel is a share in his self-giving.

In everyday life. Look for the small, unremarked cost that would remove an obstacle between somebody else and the gospel. Most such costs are noticed by no one but God, and that is enough.

How do I know when to adapt for the sake of the gospel and when to refuse? Ask two questions. Would doing this compromise the gospel or require me to sin? If someone says you must do it to be right with God, or Scripture forbids it, refuse. Would it remove an unnecessary obstacle for the people I want to reach? Then you are free to do it, even at cost. So a missionary may learn a language, change his diet, dress modestly by local standards or give up a legitimate habit; but he may not join in idolatry, hide the cross or add conditions to grace. Freedom in practice; firmness in the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council’s ruling, carried from town to town, told Gentile believers that nothing need be added to Christ, and churches sure of their footing grew.

They delivered to them for observance the decisions. The Jerusalem ruling went into a bag, was carried round Galatia on foot, and was read out in one small congregation after another. Decisions (dogmata) are the council’s decrees: Gentile believers need not be circumcised or take on the law of Moses, and were asked only to keep from what had been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what had been strangled and from sexual immorality (15:28–29), so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share one table. Addressed to Antioch, Syria and Cilicia (15:23), it is carried on to Galatia because the same question touched these churches.

When doctrine is settled. We think of doctrine as settled when the argument is won. It was settled in Iconium when a handful of frightened Gentile believers watched Paul unfold a document from the apostles telling them they were already in. If Galatians was written to these very churches, as many think, men like those of 15:24 had already unsettled them (Galatians 1:6–7).

So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased. One of Luke’s progress reports (6:7; 9:31), and the order is an argument: strengthened first, then grown, and the opening “So” ties both to the decrees. A church that does not know where it stands cannot grow, because its members are too busy checking their own footing to look outward.

Through the grace of the Lord Jesus. The letter told those Gentiles that nothing could be added to Christ (15:11). Jesus had not done most of their salvation and left circumcision to finish it; he had done all of it. And the growth has the same author: “the Lord added to their number day by day” (2:47). Christ guarded the truth about himself, and then filled the churches that held it.

Is careful doctrine the enemy of warm evangelism? Luke answers in one sentence, with the causal word in the middle. Churches that know clearly that they are saved by grace alone are freed to love, to welcome and to witness. Churches that are vague about it either harden into legalism or drift into having nothing to say. Good doctrine is not the opposite of warm evangelism; it is its fuel.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus, by his Spirit, closes two doors in a row on faithful men, because he is steering his mission somewhere they cannot yet see.

Forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, populous and full of great cities, with Ephesus its chief city. There is no suggestion of sin or rebuke: two good men with a right aim are stopped. We are not told how; prophecy, inner conviction and circumstances are all guesses. Luke’s silence stops us turning the episode into a method and grading one another on our ability to detect the same signal.

The Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Bithynia was a rich province in the north, on the Black Sea. Luke has called him the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord, and simply the Spirit; only here in Acts is he the Spirit of Jesus: sent by the risen Jesus and acting for him, as Paul speaks of the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), the Spirit of his Son (Galatians 4:6) and the Spirit of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:19).

He is doing the steering personally. The phrase appears exactly where the direction of the mission is taken out of the missionaries’ hands. The one steering is the Jesus who said, “you will be my witnesses … to the end of the earth” (1:8). These men are not executing a strategy of their own and asking God to bless it; they are being moved. The risen Jesus is no absent founder, and his refusals are as loving as his permissions: the Lord who stopped Paul at the border of Bithynia was already preparing a riverbank in Macedonia and a woman’s heart to hear.

Closed doors. They did not sit and wait; they kept moving, and the Spirit closed doors. God guides moving feet, and a good plan that fails is not evidence that he has stopped paying attention. On that road they had two refusals and no explanation, and found out later. Almost everybody finds out later, and many never find out at all: not every closed door has a Macedonia behind it. What Scripture shows is that the Lord of the mission can steer by refusal.

Was the ban on preaching in Asia permanent? No. Within a few years Paul spent more than two years in Ephesus, so that “all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord” (19:10). God was ordering the mission; it was not yet the time.

How can I tell whether a closed door is God’s guidance or an obstacle I should push through? Often you cannot tell at once, and that is all right. Some obstacles are meant to be overcome by perseverance; others are God’s no. Pray, look honestly at your motives, ask counsel of mature believers, and check that you are not running from duty or toward mere comfort. If the way stays shut after reasonable effort, accept it without bitterness and look for the open path. God holds both the doors and you, and he is not offended by sincere mistakes made in obedience.

Textual note. The KJV reads simply “the Spirit”, following later manuscripts; the earliest read “the Spirit of Jesus”, as most modern Bibles do.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refusals bring the missionaries, apparently at a dead end, to the one port from which Europe was two days away.

So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. A few words cover a long, dispiriting walk, through country Luke does not say they preached in, until they run out of land. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy, and three men with no commission for anywhere they can reach on foot are standing on a beach.

What Troas actually was. They could not see it, but Troas was the crossing point between two continents, where any ship for Macedonia would sail. And it is where Luke appears to join them: soon the narrative changes from “they” to “we”, and the man who wrote more than a quarter of the New Testament walks into the story at the town they reached because everywhere else was forbidden. The refusals put an apostle and a historian in the same room, and neither of them chose it.

The Lord who walked the road of defeat. The Spirit who stopped them is the Spirit of Jesus, and Jesus knows from the inside what it is to walk a road that looks like the end. To every eye at the time his journey to Jerusalem finished in failure: friends scattered, the Teacher dead, two disciples walking home saying, “we had hoped” (Luke 24:21). Yet he was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (2:23), and the greatest dead end in history was the hinge of the world’s salvation. A Lord who turned a cross into a crown can turn a beach at Troas into a door. He once made a way through the sea for his people, and he makes one still.

What should I do when I have reached the end of my road and can see nothing ahead? Keep doing the next faithful thing where you are, and wait for God to show the next step. Troas was not wasted time; it was where Luke joined and the call came. Keep up prayer, Scripture and the company of believers. Be honest with God about your confusion, as the psalmists were, and do not force a door just to end the uncertainty. The God who brought you to the shoreline knows exactly where the boat is.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the team across the sea to Macedonia through a vision they must think through together, and Luke, joining them, quietly writes himself into the story as “we”.

Come over to Macedonia and help us. After two refusals, a vision in the night, and it is a request: not an order, not a rebuke, but a man asking for help. Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, and here, for the first time that Luke records, the gospel enters Europe. Acts changes direction (1:8), not because Paul planned it but because the Lord shut two doors and opened a third: Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and Corinth (16:11–18:17) all flow from this night at Troas.

Concluding. The word (symbibazontes) means putting things together, reasoning to a conclusion. Even after such a vision Paul did not simply know what to do. The team interpreted it together (note the plural), and reached a judgment, not a certainty handed down: the man had said “help us”, and working out that the help meant the gospel was their own conclusion. Closed doors, vision and discernment together showed God’s will. If Paul had to conclude, you are not failing when you have to conclude.

Immediately. Having reasoned it out, they moved the same day. Deliberation and prompt obedience are not enemies; here they are consecutive.

We. The first of the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), where Luke joins the story as an eyewitness, perhaps as Paul’s doctor (Colossians 4:14), and says so by changing a pronoun and nothing else. He never names himself in either of his books, which is part of why he is believed, and he stayed with Paul to the end: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). In his own account he is only the word “we”, a gentle rebuke to the way most of us tell the story of what God has done with us.

The help was Christ. Paul knew whose help he carried: he would speak only of “what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience” (Romans 15:18), and he said the risen Christ himself “would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles” (26:23). What came to Philippi was the Helper of the helpless, the Lord Jesus, speaking through his servants and opening hearts by his Spirit: still doing “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (1:1), crossing into Europe in the persons of four men in a boat. Behind every such crossing stands the first. A lost world stood before the Father with no voice to plead for itself, and the Son came over, from heaven to earth: he helps “the offspring of Abraham”, and was “made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:16–17).

Who is crying out for help today? Everyone who does not know Christ, whether or not they put it that way. The cry rarely sounds like a request for the gospel. It sounds like loneliness, anxiety, addiction, a marriage falling apart, a question about death at a funeral, a refugee’s need for a friend. Meet real needs with real kindness, and do not stop there: the greatest help you can give anyone is Christ.

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit still guide like this, through visions and direct prohibitions? Many faithful Christians, especially in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, believe God still gives such dreams, and some missionaries report them; they too insist that every impression be tested by Scripture. This commentary’s view: such revelation belonged to the founding of the church, and the New Testament ties it to the apostles’ foundational work (Ephesians 2:20). With Scripture complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel, the needs before us and the doors he opens and closes in his providence. He may still close a way by circumstances, as here, but we do not wait for visions to know what to do. We hold this while gladly owning those who differ as brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel’s first home in Europe is Philippi, a proud little Rome in Macedonia, and that setting shapes the whole story.

We made a direct voyage. Two days straight across, probably with a following wind; the same crossing the other way later takes five (20:6), the kind of detail that fits a writer who was there. Neapolis was Philippi’s port.

A Roman colony. Philippi was named after Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. A colony was a piece of Rome transplanted: settled with discharged legionaries, governed under Roman law, its citizens holding Roman citizenship and immensely proud of it. The story turns twice on that pride: in the charge, “customs that are not lawful for us as Romans” (v. 21), and when beating two Roman citizens costs the magistrates their dignity in the street (vv. 37–39).

We remained in this city some days. There is no synagogue to preach in, and for several days the mission to Europe consists of a few men walking round a strange town waiting for the Sabbath.

A colony of heaven. A Philippian lived in Macedonia but belonged to Rome, and took his identity from a city he might never have seen. So when Paul later told this church that “our citizenship is in heaven”, from which they awaited a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20), they understood: they were a colony of heaven on earth. In a town that hailed Caesar as lord and saviour, those were not neutral words. He set before them the one who emptied himself to the death of the cross, “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). The colony that boasted of Rome was about to receive a church that boasted of Christ, before whom the emperor himself will one day kneel.

What does it mean in practice to be a citizen of heaven? Your deepest loyalty, identity and hope belong to Christ’s kingdom, while you live as a good resident where God has placed you: obeying the laws of the land unless they command sin, working honestly, seeking the good of your town (Jeremiah 29:7) and praying for those in authority. But you do not take your values from the culture around you, nor set your hope on its approval. Like a Philippian veteran, you live by the customs of home, and you wait for your King to come from there.

Uncertain wording. “A leading city of the district of Macedonia” is an awkward phrase in Greek, and its wording differs slightly between copies. Philippi was neither the provincial capital (Thessalonica) nor the chief city of its district (Amphipolis, 17:1), so “leading” may reflect local pride or mean a city of the first rank. Because the Romans had divided Macedonia into four districts, some modern editions adopt a small correction that reads “a city of the first district of Macedonia”.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel enters Europe not in the forum but on a riverbank, where a few travellers sit down and talk with women gathered to pray.

Outside the gate to the riverside. Each detail is humbler than the last. Foreign cults were often kept beyond the walls of a Roman colony. “Where we supposed”: they were guessing where a handful of Jews might gather. The river was probably the Gangites, west of the city. By the rule in later Jewish writings it took ten Jewish men to form a synagogue, and the leading city of the district apparently could not produce ten.

We sat down and spoke to the women. So Christianity arrived in Europe: a few travellers walked out of a side gate on the Sabbath, found women praying by a river, sat down on the bank and started talking. Paul the trained Pharisee took the ordinary posture of a Jewish teacher and taught women, where at Pisidian Antioch he had stood like a public speaker (13:16). Out of that conversation came the church that alone supported Paul when no other church did (Philippians 4:15–16), his joy and crown (Philippians 4:1). Perhaps the warmest letter Paul ever wrote went to people who started as the women at the river.

The Teacher who sat by a well. Paul learned that posture from his Lord, who, “wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well” in Samaria, and spoke of eternal life to a woman nobody else would have stopped for (John 4:6–7). When his gospel reached Europe it came, as he had so often come, to the people the world overlooked, sitting down beside them. Those women were praying to the God of Israel without yet knowing the name of his Son, and the Son had already sent his answer across the sea. He hears prayers that have not yet learned his name.

In everyday life. The apostles did not decide that a handful of women was too small a return on a sea crossing. If your own service feels absurdly small for the effort it took, this verse is the shape of most of what God actually does. Go to your small meeting this week as though it mattered, because it does.

Where Christians differ: does Paul’s practice here mean women may preach in church? Paul taught these women the gospel, which shows how highly it values women as hearers, disciples and partners in the work; women such as Euodia and Syntyche laboured beside him (Philippians 4:2–3). Many faithful Christians read Paul’s other instructions differently and welcome women as pastors. This commentary’s view: that is a different question from who should preach and exercise authority in the gathered church. Paul reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the congregation to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), and grounds this not in local custom but in the order of creation (1 Timothy 2:13). Both truths stand: women are equal heirs of grace and indispensable in gospel work, and the church’s oversight is entrusted to men who serve with self-giving love. We honour the brothers and sisters who disagree.

Uncertain wording. “Place of prayer” (proseuchē) can mean simply a spot where people met to pray, or, as often in Jewish writings and inscriptions of the time, a synagogue building. Here, outside the gate, found by guesswork and with only women mentioned, an open-air meeting place is more likely.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul spoke, but the Lord opened Lydia’s heart, and the first fruit of her new faith was an open house.

A woman named Lydia. Luke tells us four things about Lydia, the first person in Europe whose conversion he records. She is a woman, in a world where her name would not normally appear in a history. She is from Thyatira, in Asia, the province the Spirit had just closed: they were stopped from going to her country, and she had already come to theirs. She sells purple goods, the luxury trade that clothed magistrates and emperors, so she has means, and a house big enough for a household and soon a church (v. 40). And she is a worshiper of God: a Gentile who had attached herself to the God of Israel without becoming a Jew (see God-fearers). No strategist would have picked her: the vision showed a man of Macedonia, and the first person helped is a foreign businesswoman.

The Lord opened her heart. Paul could reach her ears; only the Lord could open her heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). She did pay attention, really and freely, but because the Lord opened her heart. And she was already religious: a worshipper of God, at a prayer meeting, on the Sabbath. Religion can bring a person to the riverbank; only Christ can bring her to life, which is good news for the devout and the careless alike.

Effectual calling. Here is one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of what Reformed Christians call effectual calling: God’s call that does not only invite but brings the hearer to faith. Grace is the cause, faith the fruit (compare 13:48). Other Christians hold that grace enables every hearer but can be refused. For the believer it is pure comfort and humility: if you believe, it is because God opened your heart, so no boasting, all thanks.

Her household. A first-century household was far larger than our nuclear family: servants and slaves, employees, dependants, sometimes extended kin. Lydia seems to head her own house (no husband is mentioned), so her household probably means her servants and dependants, perhaps children, though Luke gives no list. He records Lydia’s faith and the household’s baptism, but nothing explicit about the household’s faith, which is why this is one of the texts in the friendly disagreement over baptism (see the box at the end of this note).

If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house. The first recorded act of any Christian in Europe. She rests the invitation on her new standing: if she truly belongs to the Lord, they cannot refuse her house. Within hours she has understood that being received by Christ means being received by his people.

And she prevailed upon us. She pressed until they gave way, which suggests they hesitated: Paul was careful about being kept at anybody’s expense (compare Philippians 4:15). It is one of the very few places in Acts where somebody argues Paul down and wins, and it is a convert of a few hours. Anyone who thinks they have no ministry because they cannot teach or lead should notice that Lydia’s contribution to the New Testament is a room: the church at Philippi first gathered in her house.

The risen Lord who opens. The verb is a deliberate echo. At Emmaus hearts burned “while he opened to us the Scriptures” (Luke 24:32); then “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures”, that repentance and forgiveness should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (Luke 24:45–47). By a river in Macedonia the same risen Lord does for a Gentile woman what he did for his disciples on the evening of his resurrection: his own commission fulfilled, one opened heart at a time. He opens hearts by his Spirit, gently and unfailingly, so that a sinner who could not attend begins to listen and to love. He knocked, then opened the door from the inside, and came in to stay.

A comfort for households. What is beyond dispute is that God loves to save whole households: the conversion of one is so often the open door of grace to a home (compare v. 31). Pray, then, for your whole household. And with Lydia the house followed the heart: whom could you invite to your table this week for Christ’s sake, a missionary, a new Christian, a lonely church member, a neighbour who has never been in a Christian home?

If God must open the heart, is there any point in my praying and speaking? Every point. Lydia’s heart was opened while Paul was speaking, not instead of his speaking. God uses the means he commands: the word spoken, and prayer for those who hear. So pray before you talk to someone about Christ, asking the Lord to open their heart, then speak as clearly and kindly as you can. If they do not respond, you have not failed, and they are not beyond hope. Leave the opening to the only one who can do it, and keep praying.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists (who baptise the infants of believers) note that only Lydia’s faith is mentioned, yet the whole household is baptised on the faith of its head, as in the old covenant pattern (Genesis 17); they see the household baptisms as including any little ones, and so as supporting infant baptism. Many of the most godly and learned Christians in history, Calvin among them, have held this from a sincere conviction that God’s covenant embraces the children of his people, as in Abraham’s day; they do not think baptism saves the child. This commentary’s view: no infants are mentioned in any household baptism in Acts, and where Luke tells us more, the households baptised heard and believed. In the jailer’s house the word was spoken to all (v. 32), and the whole household rejoiced that he had believed (v. 34); in Cornelius’s, all heard and received the Spirit (10:44); Crispus believed “together with his entire household” (18:8). So Lydia’s household most likely believed and were baptised as believers, Luke compressing the story. We hold this charitably: we differ on who should receive the sign, but share the same gospel, the same Saviour and the same hope for our children.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel sets people free, and freedom costs. Paul’s word in the name of Jesus Christ frees a slave girl from a spirit of divination, and her owners, robbed of their income, have Paul and Silas beaten and put in the stocks on a charge of un-Roman customs (vv. 16–24). At midnight the prisoners pray and sing, an earthquake opens every door, and Paul stops the jailer from killing himself; asked what he must do to be saved, they answer, believe in the Lord Jesus, and the jailer and his household believe, are baptised and rejoice (vv. 25–34). In the morning Paul makes the magistrates who flogged two Roman citizens release them in person, protecting the young church, and leaves it encouraged (vv. 35–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
Praise at midnight

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight, after being stripped and beaten with rods, and the other prisoners listen. Paul later wrote that we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance (Romans 5:3). Where that joy was anchored, and why not every believer can sing on such a night, is treated at vv. 25–26.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked what he must do to be saved, and the answer had no doing in it: believe in the Lord Jesus (see vv. 29–30 and v. 31). Now: The answer is still the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but trust in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A possessed slave girl advertises the missionaries with words that are true but serve a lie, and the Lord will not be commended by such a voice.

A slave girl who had a spirit of divination. Luke gives her no name and three kinds of ownership: she is a slave, she is possessed, and she is an income. Few people in Acts are more thoroughly owned. Lydia’s heart was opened quietly; this girl will be freed by a word of command; a Roman jailer will follow: every kind of person and every kind of bondage.

The python spirit. Literally “a spirit, a python” (pneuma pythōna), as the ESV notes. The Python was the serpent that guarded Delphi before Apollo killed it; Delphi’s priestess, the Pythia, then spoke Apollo’s oracles, the most prestigious in the ancient world, and by Paul’s day a python meant a soothsayer thought to be inspired by Apollo. Such a slave was a commercial oracle of the highest value. In truth she was possessed by a demon.

These men are servants of the Most High God. True words from a demonic source, as demons spoke true words about Jesus (Mark 1:24; 5:7). And to a Greek ear the Most High God was a title used of Zeus, while the Greek has no word for “the” before “way”, so it could be heard as “a way of salvation”, exactly what every cult in a Roman town claimed to offer. A pagan could agree with every word without changing a thing he believed, and an oracle’s endorsement would tie the gospel to the very system it was displacing.

Neutralised by agreement. That is still the commonest way the gospel is neutralised: not by contradiction but by warm agreement on slightly different terms. Christ is affirmed as one of the great spiritual teachers. Nothing is denied, and nothing is left.

No other name. Paul is doing what his Lord did. A demoniac cried out, “Jesus, Son of the Most High God” (Luke 8:28), and Jesus “would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (Luke 4:41). Nor is he one way among many: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (4:12). The powers of darkness can borrow true words, but they cannot borrow him. Delphi’s oracle sold the future by the hour; the Lord Jesus holds the future and gives it freely, and the girl made to speak for darkness was about to be set free by the Light.

Is it wrong to consult horoscopes, tarot or mediums just for fun? Yes. Scripture forbids every attempt to gain hidden knowledge or guidance from sources other than God (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they always work, but because they turn us from him to rival powers, some of them real and dark. Treating them as harmless fun trains the heart to look elsewhere for direction. A Christian has something far better: a Father who knows the future and holds it, a Saviour who guides, and a word that is a lamp to his feet.

Why would a modern person read the stars? We like to think the slave girl’s world has gone, and then we check the horoscope on our phones, half as a joke. Augustine did it in earnest. In his Confessions he tells how, as a young man, he kept going back to the astrologers, and he is honest about the attraction: they offered not only a glimpse of the future but an excuse. If the stars had fixed his conduct, his sins were not quite his. That is still the double pull, whether through a zodiac app or the scientific-sounding claim that my genes, upbringing or personality type made me do it. We want enough knowledge to feel in control and enough fate to feel excused. The gospel gives us neither. It hands us not the future but the One who holds it; and instead of an excuse it brings better news: Christ took the blame on himself, so that we can own our sins at last without being crushed by them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python”, linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After many days Paul commands the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ, and the power that had owned the girl for years leaves within the hour.

This she kept doing for many days. Paul did not act at once. Day after day she trailed them through the streets shouting, and day after day he let it run.

Having become greatly annoyed. The word (diaponētheis) means troubled, worn out, exasperated: perhaps at the confusion she caused, perhaps in distress for the girl herself. Not a serene apostle choosing his moment, but a tired man who has had enough; God used it, and Luke recorded it untidied. We imagine God works through us only when our composure is intact, yet the best-known exorcism in Acts is done by a man at the end of his patience.

I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. Paul speaks to the spirit, not the girl, and by Christ’s authority. He does not bargain or require anything of her. He names a name, and what had held her for years leaves that very hour.

The stronger man. When the seventy-two reported that even the demons were subject to them in his name, Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Paul speaks the name of the stronger man who overpowers the strong man and carries off what he held (Luke 11:21–22), and the New Testament is never uncertain about the outcome of that collision. The girl was owned three times over, and one Name broke the strongest of the three in an hour. Every chain that falls at his word is a preview of the day when no one will be owned by anything but him.

What became of her? She is not said to have believed. So far as the text goes, she is still a slave the next morning, now one who has stopped earning, owned by furious men. Perhaps she joined the church at Lydia’s; we do not hear. Scripture is not embarrassed when deliverance leaves someone with a harder life, the addiction broken and the debts still there. If you have helped someone out of a bondage, do not walk away when the dramatic part is over.

For you, then. You need not fear demons, nor go hunting for a deliverance minister. If you are in Christ, the strongest Being in the universe lives in you, and at the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). Fight your sins as your own, by the Spirit, resting in your Lord’s finished victory. Where missionaries meet open occult darkness, the remedy is the same: the gospel and the name of Christ, humbly.

How should we think about exorcism today? Demons are real, personal and evil, the name of Jesus has all authority over them, and the Christian’s ordinary weapons are the gospel, prayer and the armour of God. The Reformed position is cautious, for scriptural reasons. (1) The dramatic commanding of demons clusters in Christ’s ministry and the apostolic founding. (2) The letters, which teach the church to fight the devil, never establish an office of exorcist or a ritual of deliverance; they say, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7), and put on the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:10–18). (3) A true believer, indwelt by the Spirit, cannot be possessed, for “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4): harassed from without, but not inhabited. (4) Blaming sins on demons evades repentance, when Scripture lays sin at our own heart (James 1:14; Mark 7:21–23). So deliverance comes through the gospel (Colossians 1:13), prayer, and Christ’s authority humbly invoked when needed: never a technique, a specialist or a spectacle. Do not deny the demonic, and do not see a demon behind every sin and sickness. Where someone seems tormented in mind, pray, and also involve a biblical counsellor and a doctor; medicine is no failure of faith.

Where Christians differ: exorcism and deliverance. Some churches keep a formal rite of exorcism, and much of the charismatic world practises deliverance ministry, often for Christians; we honour the seriousness and the zeal to help. Others reduce possession to ancient descriptions of mental illness. This commentary’s view: Scripture gives no office of exorcist, and a believer cannot be possessed (see above); and Scripture distinguishes the sick from the demonised (Mark 1:32–34), so possession cannot be reduced to illness.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The owners’ real grievance is lost income, but they dress it as civic concern and reach for the nearest prejudice.

When her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone. The motive, stated before any charge is laid. Gone (exēlthen) is the verb of v. 18: their hope of gain went out of her when the spirit did. Much opposition to Christianity has this shape. It comes less from argument than from money: when the gospel changes what people do with their money, bodies or time, somebody’s revenue falls, and the objection is dressed in principle and never mentions the accounts. At Ephesus the silversmith says, before he mentions the goddess, “from this business we have our wealth” (19:25).

They seized Paul and Silas. The leaders, and both Jews. Silas, a leading man of the Jerusalem church and a prophet, had carried the council’s letter and then joined Paul in place of Barnabas (15:22, 32, 40); like Paul, he was a Roman citizen (v. 37). Timothy, whose father was Greek, and Luke, almost certainly a Gentile, are left alone, and Luke’s “we” drops out of the narrative here.

These men are Jews. Not a word about the girl or the money. The charge appealed to live prejudice: Claudius had recently expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2), and a town full of veterans was in the mood to hear it.

They are disturbing our city. A charge used against Christians for centuries: not that the message is false, but that things were quieter before. It never has to prove anything, and the gospel really does disturb a city where a girl can be owned and worked.

Treated as their Master was. When Jesus freed the man at Gerasa and the pigs were lost, the people “asked him to depart from them” (Luke 8:37): a man restored was worth less to them than a herd. At his trial the charge was that he was misleading the nation and stirring up the people (Luke 23:2, 5). “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). The men dragged into the market walk in their Lord’s footprints, causing the trouble he caused, by setting a captive free. Her owners counted her in coins, and when the coins stopped they had no further use for her. The Lord Jesus counts his people in blood: ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Men sell what they own; he bought what he loves, and nothing he has paid for will ever be put up for sale again.

Should Christians challenge industries that profit from evil? Yes, wisely and lawfully. Freedom often costs someone their profit: traffickers, pornographers, exploitative lenders, gambling and drug trades. Christians should refuse to profit from such things, help their victims, speak for them and support just laws, and expect resistance disguised as concern for jobs, tradition or freedom. But remember Paul’s order: he did not set out to reform Philippi’s economy; he preached Christ and set one girl free. The deepest change in any city begins with the gospel changing people.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge of un-Roman customs was meant to inflame, yet in its way it was true: Christ claims the whole of life, not a corner of it.

Not lawful for us as Romans. In Philippi it was the one sentence sure to land. Rome generally tolerated Judaism as an ancient national religion, but not a foreign cult recruiting Roman citizens out of their own religion: you could be a Jew; you could not make a Roman into one. Tell veterans in their own square that two foreigners are undermining Roman custom and you will not need evidence. And nobody could see the irony: the two men in the dock were Roman citizens themselves.

The charge was, in its way, accurate. A man who confessed “Jesus is Lord” in a colony where the loyal formula was “Caesar is lord” had changed allegiance, and everything from his household gods to his guild dinners would feel it. The gospel is welcome as long as it is one more thing a person has. It becomes intolerable when it starts reorganising what he already had.

A King whose kingdom is not of this world. Pilate had heard the same fear: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar” (John 19:12). Jesus did not deny being a king: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). He does not ask to be added to our lives as one more interest; he claims the whole, and the claim is our freedom, for his yoke is easy and his rule is love.

In everyday life. Christ’s Spirit is at work reorganising what you already had: ask which arrangement in your life you have not yet let him touch.

Does following Christ make me a bad citizen? No; it makes you a better one, but never a worshipper of the state. Christians are to pray for rulers, pay taxes, obey the law and seek the good of their nation (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). But when any authority demands what belongs to God alone, “We must obey God rather than men” (5:29), respectfully and without violence. Many of the best citizens in history have been Christians precisely because their conscience was bound to a higher King.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without a hearing, Paul and Silas are stripped, flogged and jailed: a real injustice, and a share in the sufferings of their Lord.

The crowd joined in attacking them. Mob justice, and fast. Nobody calls a witness; the prisoners are not asked to answer. Between the accusation and the flogging there is nothing at all.

Gave orders to beat them with rods. The clothes are ripped away in the market square. Then the rods, wielded by the lictors, the magistrates’ officers who carried bundles of rods as the sign of their power to punish. A Roman beating with rods opened the back, and men died of it.

Many blows. Paul remembers this day: “Three times I was beaten with rods” (2 Corinthians 11:25); and “though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict” (1 Thessalonians 2:2). Shamefully treated means publicly humiliated, not merely hurt. He walked on to Thessalonica and preached there with the marks still on him.

They threw them into prison. No charge recorded, no sentence, no term: two bleeding men put away with an instruction about security. Paul will protest that they were beaten publicly and uncondemned (v. 37). God used this night magnificently, but the earthquake does not make the flogging right.

Granted to suffer for his sake. Jesus too was stripped and scourged on the order of an official who had found no guilt in him (Luke 23:14–16; John 19:1), and Paul regarded this day as fellowship with Christ. Years later he told this church, “it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had” (Philippians 1:29–30); some of them may have watched these rods fall. The stripes on Paul’s back were the marks of belonging to a crucified Lord.

In everyday life. Pray today for Christians who are beaten, imprisoned or shamed for their faith: find one name or country, and pray for them as you would want to be prayed for in the inner prison.

If God brings good out of injustice, does that make the injustice less wrong? No. God’s sovereignty over evil never turns evil into good. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20): both are true, and the brothers were still guilty. When you have been wronged, you may grieve it, name it and seek lawful justice, while trusting that God will not waste it. Do not let anyone hurry you past the wrong in the name of his providence. Scripture never does.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer goes beyond his orders, and Luke darkens the scene on purpose, so that what the prisoners do next will astonish us.

He put them into the inner prison. Told to keep them safely, the jailer exceeds his orders: the innermost cell, and the stocks as well. The inner prison was the windowless interior room: no light, no air moving, the floor filthy.

And fastened their feet in the stocks. A heavy timber with holes in which the legs were fixed, sometimes forced wide apart: hours in it brought cramp that became agony, with no way to lie down or reach your own torn back. Luke builds the picture deliberately, backs untreated, legs clamped, the dark, no charge, to make what these two men did next almost unbelievable.

I was in prison. There is someone else in that cell. On the Damascus road the risen Lord had asked, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4): what was done to his people he counted as done to himself. So the jailer who clamped those feet was, without knowing it, doing it to the Lord. “I was in prison and you came to me” (Matthew 25:36): before morning he will wash the wounds he left untended, and so become the first in Philippi to visit Christ in prison. The Lord who knows the way into every dark cell holds the keys of death and Hades, and he has never yet lost a prisoner who belongs to him.

What if I am in my own inner prison right now? Then you are in a place God knows well: Joseph in the prison, Jeremiah in the cistern, Paul and Silas in the stocks, the Lord Jesus in the darkness of Gethsemane and the cross. Your prison may be illness, depression, grief, or a trapped situation at home or work. Do not pretend it is not dark. Tell God plainly how it is, as the psalmists did, and ask a friend to come and sit with you. If darkness of mind will not lift, talk to a biblical counsellor and see your doctor for a check-up: medicine is no failure of faith. If you are not safe at home, tell someone and get help today. No cell is so deep that Christ is not there, and none so locked that he cannot open it in his time.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beaten and in the stocks, Paul and Silas pray and sing at midnight, and God answers with an earthquake that frees not only them but every prisoner.

Praying and singing hymns to God. Joy in suffering, as when the apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (5:41). Both verbs are continuous: not one defiant snatch of a psalm, but long enough to be heard down the corridor. They probably sang psalms: men in the dark asking how long, and then turning to praise before anything has changed. They had a hymnbook written for nights like this one.

And the prisoners were listening to them. The tense suggests they went on listening. Consider what those men were used to hearing at midnight in that room, and then consider hearing this. Nothing had improved, and the singers did not know an earthquake was coming; their gladness came from somewhere the magistrates could not reach.

A great earthquake. God answered, as he had once shaken the place where the church prayed (4:31), and the surprise is in the last clause: every door, and every prisoner’s bonds. God’s reply to the two who prayed was wider than the two who prayed.

The Lord who sang on the way to Gethsemane. Their gladness came from a Person: “Rejoice in the Lord always”, Paul later wrote to this church from another prison (Philippians 4:4). On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26), probably the closing Passover psalms (Psalms 113–118). He sang on the way to his arrest, “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). Paul and Silas followed a Lord who had sung first and gone further into the dark than they ever would, and who came “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). Praise in the dark is not wasted; it rises to a throne that is never dark, and the One who sits on it hears.

A caution. This verse is regularly used as a stick to beat struggling Christians. It is not a command to feel like singing, nor a measure you have failed. Paul himself writes, “we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself” (2 Corinthians 1:8). Scripture gives you Philippi at midnight, and it also gives you Gethsemane, and the psalm that ends with darkness as the only companion (Psalm 88:18). If tonight you can only manage the praying half of verse 25, you are still inside the verse.

In everyday life. Learn one psalm of lament and trust by heart this week, Psalm 42, 46 or 130, so that you have something to sing, or at least to pray, when the night comes.

Does God always deliver his people from prison like this? No. Sometimes he does, as here and with Peter (12:6–11). Sometimes he does not: James was killed (12:2), Paul spent years in custody and, as the early church remembered, was eventually executed, and many believers today remain in prison for Christ. The earthquake shows that God can deliver, not that he always will in this life. What he always does is stand by his people (2 Timothy 4:17), give them grace to endure, and bring them through death itself into his presence. Final deliverance is certain even when earthly release is not.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer, sure his prisoners have fled, is about to kill himself, and the men he chained save his life by staying where they are.

He drew his sword and was about to kill himself. He reaches for his sword before he reaches for a light. It looks like panic, but it was calculation: a guard who lost his prisoners could face their penalty (compare 12:19), and falling on his own sword was the respectable Roman way out. For such a man honour was worth more than life, and that is what an idol looks like: something so precious that losing it feels like a reason to die. The gospel was about to give him a worth no magistrate could take away.
