Do not harm yourself. Both halves of Paul’s cry are astonishing. First, he knew: from the innermost room he grasped what was happening in the doorway and shouted before the sword went in, attending to somebody else at the one moment nobody would have blamed him for thinking of himself.

For we are all here. Second, and far harder: every door open, every chain off, every legal grievance a man could have, and nobody moved. Not Paul, not Silas, and not one of the other prisoners, men with no faith at all and every reason to run. Luke does not explain it; it is the quietest miracle in the chapter. The first thing Christianity did for the jailer was stop him killing himself.

He saved others. At the cross the rulers scoffed, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God” (Luke 23:35). He could have come down. He stayed, and because he stayed, those who mocked him could be forgiven. Paul’s refusal to walk out of an open prison is a small, true likeness: the man who could have saved himself stayed, and so the man who had chained him lived. And a bleeding prisoner shouting through the dark to spare his jailer had learned that love from the Lord who prayed from the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts of Luke lack the prayer, but many scholars judge it genuine, and Stephen’s prayer echoes it, 7:60). The sword never fell in Philippi because grace reached the jailer first, and the sword of God’s justice never falls on Christ’s people because it fell on him.

What should I do if I, or someone I love, is thinking of suicide? Treat it as urgent, as Paul did: speak up at once, and do not leave the person alone. Tell them plainly that their life matters to God and to you. Get help the same day: call emergency services or a crisis line, involve a doctor, tell a trusted pastor or friend. If it is you, tell someone today. Despair lies; it says there is no way out, but the jailer’s worst night became the night of his salvation. Christ came to give life, and there is no shame, sin or loss so great that he cannot meet you in it.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shaken to the core, the jailer falls before his prisoners and asks the greatest question anyone can ask: what must I do to be saved?

Trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. A few hours ago this man locked two prisoners in the dark; now he is on the floor in front of them. He did not tremble at death a moment earlier. Sinners who sense the nearness of the holy God have always shaken (Isaiah 6:5), and the wonder of this night is that the God who shook the prison sends the jailer a word of mercy.

Sirs, what must I do to be saved? The answer he gets is bigger than the question he asked, so it is worth asking what he meant. Saved was an ordinary word: from drowning, from illness, from a sentence. Seconds from suicide in a prison fallen round him, he may simply have meant how he gets out of this alive. But his prisoners were all present, so that danger had passed. And these were the men a slave girl had followed through the streets announcing that they proclaimed the way of salvation (v. 17), whose singing had filled his prison at midnight while their backs were in ribbons. The earthquake had shaken more than the prison. He knew he needed saving from more than Roman punishment, and a man who had never asked anything of the sort found the words in his mouth in the middle of the night.

What must I do? The instinct of every religious person who has ever lived, and of every irreligious one the moment he is frightened: give me the requirement and I will meet it. The crowd asked it at Pentecost (2:37), the rich young ruler asked it of Jesus, and the Jerusalem council had just fought over it. He is a practical man in a uniform, and he wants the procedure. What he is about to be handed has no procedure in it at all.

Not these lords but the Lord. He calls them “Sirs”, kyrioi, lords, on his face before them. The answer moves the word to where it belongs: believe in the Lord Jesus. As at Lystra (14:14–15), the servants will not stand in the place of the one they preach; every knee that bends in fear before his servants is meant to rise and bow before him. And God had answered the jailer’s question before he was born, on a hill outside Jerusalem, where his Son did everything that must be done for sinners to be saved.

What did the jailer need saving from? From the wrath of God against sin, the deepest danger anyone faces, deeper than any prison or sentence. All have sinned, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; 6:23); those who die without Christ face a just and conscious judgment that does not end (Matthew 25:46). To be saved is to be rescued from that: forgiven, reconciled to God, given his Spirit, and brought at last into his presence. The jailer may not have grasped all of that at midnight. He grasped enough to know that he needed it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to the jailer’s question asks him to do nothing but trust a person: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. This is the summit of the chapter: the council’s ruling that Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus (15:11), spoken to a pagan Roman in one sentence. The slave girl had shouted a way of salvation (v. 17); now the way is named, and it is a person.

Believe in the Lord Jesus. He asked what he must do, and the answer contains no doing at all. One verb: believe. Not believe and be circumcised; not believe and make amends to the men you flogged; not believe and reform your life first, which is what most people privately assume. Salvation is by faith alone, in Christ alone. Paul’s word for it is justification: God, the holy Judge, declares the sinner righteous, not because he has become good, but because Christ’s obedience and death are counted to him, received by faith (Romans 4:5; 5:1).

The Lord Jesus. Jesus is the man from Nazareth executed some twenty years before. Lord is a word this man had heard used of Caesar all his working life, and the confession would cost Christians in this colony their standing and sometimes their lives. He is being told to transfer his allegiance, by a man with the magistrates’ rod marks on his back.

And you will be saved. Future and certain: not you may be, but you will be.

You and your household. His first coherent thought after his own rescue was his house, and the offer reaches the whole household in the same sentence. The household’s baptism (v. 33) is another of the texts in the friendly baptism discussion (see the box at the end of the note on vv. 14–15): the promise reaches as wide as faith reaches, and those baptised in this house heard the word and believed.

Is that not too easy? It is easy to receive because it was costly to give. Believing is not a small effort God kindly accepts in place of a large one; it is giving up every effort to save yourself and putting your whole weight on Christ, which proud hearts find hardest of all. The religious man wants to contribute something, the irreligious man wants to stay his own master, and “believe in the Lord Jesus” refuses both. Nor does it leave a life unchanged: that same night the jailer washed the wounds he had caused (v. 33). Salvation is free to us because it cost Christ everything: he “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

In everyday life. When you are tempted to measure your standing with God by what you have done, come back to this verse: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19). And pray by name for each member of your household who does not yet believe.

Does “you and your household” promise that if I believe, my family will be saved? No. Salvation is not passed from one person to another; Luke shows the word spoken to all in the house (v. 32) and the whole household rejoicing (v. 34). The promise is that the same way of salvation is open to all of them. A parent whose grown child does not believe has not been failed by this verse. He may pray for his child, speak and live the gospel, and trust the God who saves.

What does it actually mean to believe in the Lord Jesus? To trust him: to rely on him alone for forgiveness and acceptance with God, and to receive him as your Lord. It includes knowing who he is and what he has done (the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again), agreeing that it is true, and resting your whole weight on him: the difference between knowing a bridge will hold and standing on it. It is not a feeling, though feelings may come with it, nor a work that earns anything; it is the empty hand that receives a gift. If you are unsure whether you have ever believed, you can do it now: tell him that you have no hope but him, and that you trust him to save you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That night the whole household hears the gospel, and the jailer washes the wounds he caused and is himself washed in baptism: faith shows itself at once in a changed heart.

They spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. In the middle of the night, with earthquake damage on the floor and two men who ought to be lying down, everybody under that roof is woken to hear the gospel explained more fully. Nobody is told they can hear about it in the morning. The word of the Lord is the good news about the Lord Jesus (who he is, his death and resurrection, the call to believe, v. 31), and it comes with his authority: the jailer was hearing not two men’s opinions but “the word of God, which you heard from us” (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

He took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds. Consider whose wounds those were. This man had put them in the inner cell with their backs already opened and fixed their feet in the stocks without a thought, because they were only prisoners. The blood had been drying on them for hours while he slept. Now he kneels with water, cleaning the injuries he had been content to ignore. That is repentance, and nobody asked him for it. Conversion does this before it does anything else: it changes who a person is able to walk past.

He was baptized at once. Luke’s word order is surely deliberate: he washed their stripes; they washed him in baptism. Two cleansings in one sentence, and the man doing the first receives the second. The faith was already working before the sign was given to it.

Washed in the name of the Lord Jesus. The jailer could wash blood off a back; he could not wash a single sin off his own soul, and the water did not pretend to. In Acts believers are baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (2:38; 10:48; 19:5), and the sign directs every eye to him: “Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name” (22:16). All who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). So the jailer’s baptism tells the night’s story in water: the old man who drew a sword on himself died with Christ, and a new man rose with him before dawn. The water did not change him; by faith he had been joined to Christ.

Grace stoops lower than we ever can. Hours before his arrest the Lord of glory tied a towel round his waist, poured water into a basin and knelt to wash the feet of men who would desert him (John 13:4–5). That same Lord, risen and reigning, reached into a Philippian prison and taught a jailer’s hands to kneel with water. He washed the man inwardly before the man washed anyone, and he does not leave hard hands as he finds them. Grace stoops lower than we ever can, and then teaches us to stoop.

How can an ordinary reader be confident of what the word of the Lord means? Three things give solid confidence. First, God made the saving word clear (what theologians call the perspicuity of Scripture): a rough jailer and his household heard it at midnight and were rejoicing in God before dawn. “The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple” (Psalm 119:130). Second, he does not leave you to puzzle it out alone: the Spirit who gave the word opens hearts and minds to receive it (16:14; John 16:13; 1 Corinthians 2:12). Third, the word proves itself by converting and transforming, and we test what we hear against the rest of Scripture, as the Bereans tested even Paul (17:11). One honest limit: not every passage is equally easy (Peter says some things in Paul’s letters are hard to understand, 2 Peter 3:16), and the clarity is chiefly of what is needful for salvation and life. So hold the heart of it with real confidence, and read the harder edges humbly, in the church, under faithful teaching. Your assurance rests not on your own cleverness but on God’s clarity and the Spirit’s witness.

Does this household baptism support infant baptism? Luke says the word was spoken to all who were in his house (v. 32) and that the whole household rejoiced with him (v. 34); the question is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: household baptisms” at the end of the note on vv. 14–15.

Should new converts be baptised as quickly as this? In Acts baptism normally followed conversion closely, often the same day (2:41; 8:38; 9:18; 10:48), as the public confession of faith in Christ and the sign of entry into his people. Many churches today rightly take a little time to make sure a profession is credible and baptism understood, especially where people have little Christian background. But the aim should be to baptise believers without needless delay, not to make baptism a reward for maturity.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer brings his prisoners to his own table and rejoices with his whole household: nothing in his circumstances has changed, and everything in him has.

He set food before them. From the innermost cell to the jailer’s own table in one night. It is probably their first food since before the flogging, and the man serving it is the man who locked them up: hospitality like Lydia’s, a Roman jailer and two Jewish prisoners at one table. One of the first Christian meals recorded in Europe was eaten in the small hours, in a prison official’s kitchen, with the plaster down off the walls.

He rejoiced along with his entire household. A strong word: exulted, was overjoyed. Nothing in his circumstances has improved since the sword at midnight; he still has to explain a wrecked prison to the magistrates in the morning. Yet everything in him has changed. He had been God’s enemy and was now forgiven and welcomed as a son; he had been ready to throw his life away and now had eternal life (John 5:24).

Today salvation has come to this house. In Luke’s Gospel Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector who had made his living off other people, received Jesus joyfully into his house and promised to put right his wrongs, and Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). Now an official who had made his living holding people down has washed the wounds he caused, opened his house and rejoiced. The same Saviour is doing the same thing: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10), and he found this man in the dark. And the Lord who brought two prisoners up out of the pit to a jailer’s table will bring all his people up out of the grave to the marriage supper of the Lamb, where every nation and rank will sit together, and the joy that began in a prison kitchen will be full for ever.

Can I really be joyful when my circumstances are still hard? Yes, though not with a joy that ignores the hardship. Christian joy is gladness in God himself, in what he has done for you in Christ and promised you, and none of that is touched by your circumstances. It sits alongside sorrow rather than replacing it: “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). It grows as you dwell on the gospel, pray, sing and spend time with God’s people. Do not wait for your situation to change; the jailer did not. Begin by thanking God for one thing that is true of you in Christ today.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magistrates try to make the problem disappear quietly, and the new believer, meaning only kindness, urges Paul to go along with it.

Let those men go. Luke does not say why. Perhaps the flogging looked worse in daylight, or the earthquake had unsettled a superstitious town, or they thought a night in prison enough. What is certain is the shape of it: no summons, no hearing, no finding, no record, just a message, early, by a subordinate. That is how an institution behaves when it knows it has done wrong: nothing admitted, the problem removed from the premises before anybody important asks. And police (rhabdouchous) means rod-bearers, very likely the same officers whose rods had been used the day before.

Therefore come out now and go in peace. The messenger is a Christian of a few hours’ standing, and he is delighted: a warm send-off, spoken as a brother. He has no idea that Paul is about to refuse. Out of sheer goodwill, he urges a course that would leave an injustice standing and a young church unprotected.

A peace the magistrates could not give. “Go in peace” is Jesus’ word to the forgiven woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). The jailer has that peace now, and it did not come from the magistrates: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). That is why Paul can refuse the magistrates’ quiet without losing anything. Their peace, a problem removed, is the peace the world gives; Christ’s was already settled in that house (John 14:27). And the officers who carried the rods at dusk carried the release at dawn, with no idea whose errand they were running: “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1). The risen Christ, head over all things for the church, sent the earthquake at midnight and the messengers in the morning with the same hand.

A kind person who wants it to stop. Sometimes the pressure to let a thing drop comes not from enemies but from a kind person who wants the unpleasantness over. If you are newer in the faith, be slow to urge an older Christian to let something go until you understand why he is standing firm; if you are older, explain gently what you are protecting.

How do I know when to let something drop and when to pursue it? Ask who is affected and what is at stake. If only your own comfort or pride is involved, letting it go is usually the way of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:7; 1 Peter 2:23). If others, especially the vulnerable, will be harmed by silence, or the honour of the gospel is at stake, love may require you to pursue it, lawfully and without vindictiveness. Seek wise counsel, especially if you are hurt or angry. Wanting peace is good; the question is whether the peace offered is real or only quiet.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, who took the beating without a word for himself, now insists on his rights as a Roman citizen, not for his own sake but to protect the young church he is leaving behind.

They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens. Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial (see Roman citizenship), and the claim would normally have stopped the rods; in Jerusalem Paul speaks up before the whipping (22:25). Why not here, yesterday? Luke does not say, and honest answers are limited. In the uproar of verse 22 perhaps nobody was listening, or he said it and was not heard; Luke is careful to record that the magistrates never asked them anything. Or he may have chosen to suffer for Christ first. What we can say is that he did not use his rights to protect his own back, and he did use them the next morning. The difference between those two moments is the key to the verse.

Do they now throw us out secretly? No! He demands not compensation, nor an apology for himself, but that the thing be undone publicly. The offence was committed in the market square, and a private release would leave the town’s last memory of these men as the morning they were flogged as criminals. Paul will not be in Philippi to correct that. Lydia will, and her household, and the jailer, who must go on working for these magistrates. A church of a few weeks’ standing will live or die partly on whether the authorities think they can treat its founders as vermin without consequence. This is not a man standing on his dignity or taking revenge, but one securing, on his way out of town, the only legal protection his converts will ever have. Christians may use their legal rights for the sake of the gospel and the church (22:25; 25:11).

The gospel is not a crime. Paul’s protest also serves one of Luke’s steady purposes. Again and again Roman officials who look at the facts find that the Christians have broken no Roman law (18:14–16; 19:37; 26:31–32). Here the pattern begins, and it is the magistrates who turn out to be the lawbreakers.

Why do you strike me? Paul’s Master had walked this line before him. Pilate three times found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and still handed him over to be scourged: beaten publicly, uncondemned, in the fullest sense, so that we who were truly condemned might go free. Jesus went to the cross willingly and opened not his mouth to save himself. Yet when an officer struck him before the high priest, he answered, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). The Lamb who would not resist his death still named injustice as injustice. So Paul bore the rods without a word for himself, and will not let a lie about Christ’s servants stand in the square where Christ’s little church must live.

When should a believer insist on his rights, and when should he absorb the wrong? Paul does both in this chapter, and the line between them is not comfort but other people. He took the beating without invoking the law when the only person who would have benefited was himself; he invoked it the moment the beneficiaries were the church he was leaving behind. It is the principle he presses on the Corinthians, who were suing one another: “Why not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Corinthians 6:7), because there only their own advantage was at stake. So the test is not whether you are entitled; you may well be. It is whether the person protected by your insisting is you.

Is it unspiritual for a Christian to go to the police or the courts? No. The governing authorities are God’s servants for our good, to restrain wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and Paul used Roman law repeatedly. Crimes such as assault, fraud or abuse should be reported to the authorities; abuse in particular must never be hidden or tolerated, in the church or anywhere else, and victims should be protected first. What Paul discourages is believers suing one another over private disputes before unbelievers, when the church could help them settle it (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Using the law to protect others and see justice done is a proper Christian act.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magistrates, frightened at what they have done to Roman citizens, come in person and apologise: God publicly vindicates his servants, though fear, not repentance, moves the men who do it.

They were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. The magistrates are as afraid in the morning as the jailer was at midnight, and rationally: ordering a Roman citizen flogged without trial could end a career, and a colony that allowed it could lose its privileges. The irony is complete. The only people in the story who broke Roman law were the Romans, in the act of defending it, against two men who held the citizenship their accusers were so proud of.

So they came and apologized to them. They came, as Paul had required: the men who ordered the public stripping walked down to the prison in daylight, where everyone would see them go. They asked them to leave; they were in no position to order anything.

Two things, pulling opposite ways. God vindicated his servants publicly, and it is right to be glad. But Luke chooses his words: they were afraid. Nothing suggests these men were sorry or thought better of the gospel; they wanted the problem gone politely, and an apology extracted by fear is not repentance. The vindication was real, and it changed nobody’s heart, and a Christian who has finally been proved right about something will need both halves of that sentence.

The verdict reversed. The rulers of Jerusalem condemned Jesus, and God overturned their verdict on the third day: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (2:36). The magistrates at the prison gate are a small picture of that. But this reversal changed no one, whereas when God vindicated his Son, three thousand were cut to the heart (2:37, 41): the vindication of Christ is also the salvation of sinners. And one day every magistrate and emperor who ever held a rod will stand before the one the rulers of this age crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), coming as Judge. On that day the servants stripped and shamed for his name will need no one to escort them out. He will bring them in himself, and show before all the world that they are his.

What if I am never vindicated in this life? Many faithful believers are not. Stephen was not vindicated before the Sanhedrin; countless martyrs died with their names blackened. God will vindicate his people, but often on the last day rather than this one (Romans 12:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Commit your cause to him who judges justly, as Jesus did (1 Peter 2:23). Do what is right, speak the truth where it helps, and leave your reputation in his hands. The verdict that matters most has already been given: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before leaving, the battered missionaries go to Lydia’s house to encourage the church, an unlikely family that only Christ could have made one.

So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. Vindicated and asked to leave, they could have gone straight to the gate. Instead the last thing they do in Philippi is walk across town to the church in Lydia’s house. The Philippian story closes where the church began, and sets the pattern for the journey: a church born, persecution driving the missionaries on, every expulsion carrying the gospel further (17:1–10).

They encouraged them. Two men whose backs were opened by rods the day before encourage the church, rather than the other way round.

When they had seen the brothers. Count the church they leave behind. A foreign businesswoman in the luxury trade, with her household. A jailer, with his. A slave girl, if she came; Luke does not say. And “the brothers”, a word appearing here without introduction, which suggests others Luke has not named. At the top of the town, a woman of means; at the bottom, a girl who had been owned and worked; in between, a man employed to hold people down. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank, the one place where those three could sit in the same room was a house church.

The mind of Christ in Lydia’s house. What held such a room together? Not class, race or taste. Paul later set Christ before this church: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:5–7). The businesswoman and the jailer had nothing in common except a Lord who had come down further than either of them and made himself the servant of both.

What it cost, and what it gained. Two provinces closed, weeks of walking toward nothing, a sea crossing, days in a strange city with no way in, a public flogging, a night in the stocks and an expulsion. What was gained was a room in a woman’s house, a jailer’s household, and a letter we still read. Philippi became one of Paul’s most loving and generous churches (Philippians 1:3–5; 4:15–16), and he wrote to it in chains, to the church born in a jail. Luke seems to have stayed behind: the “we” stopped after verse 17 and resumes at Philippi in 20:5.

In everyday life. The Christ who made himself the servant of both the businesswoman and the jailer still gathers that kind of room. Look round your church for the people who would never meet anywhere else, the wealthy and the poor, the respectable and the rescued, and make sure they are sitting at the same table.

How can I encourage others when I am the one who is hurting? Often your hurt is what makes your encouragement believable: people listen to someone who has suffered and still trusts God. You need not pretend you are fine; Paul’s back was visibly torn. Tell honestly what God has been to you in the trouble, point others to the same Lord, and keep it simple. Comfort received from God becomes comfort you can give (2 Corinthians 1:4). And let others encourage you too: a church is a place where the wounded take turns.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual calling and the opened heart. At Philippi Paul preached and the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14). Both are real and both are needed: without the preaching she has nothing to believe, and without the Lord’s work the words stay outside her. The Reformed call this effectual calling: God’s call through the gospel that brings a person to faith. On why prayer goes with every act of evangelism, see the note on vv. 14–15.
16.examples:
Then: A dealer in purple cloth, a slave girl and a Roman jailer, as different in rank, race and circumstance as three people could be, were met by one gospel in one city, and the church at Philippi was born from them.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts, and still steers his church by closed doors as well as open ones. The answer to the jailer’s question has not changed: believe in the Lord Jesus.

keyVerse.quote: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.
keyVerse.note: The jailer asked what he must do, and the answer contains nothing to do but trust a person. It is the Jerusalem council’s ruling (15:11) spoken to a pagan Roman in one sentence, the same free grace that reached Lydia and freed the slave girl, and it is as true at a kitchen table today as it was on a prison floor at midnight.

16.reflection:
The Spirit closed two doors before he opened one (vv. 6–10). Can you look back on a closed door that God used for good? How can we keep moving and trusting when we cannot yet see why a way has been shut?

Paul spoke, but “the Lord opened her heart” (v. 14). How should that truth shape the way you pray for, and speak to, the people you long to see come to Christ?

At midnight, beaten and in the stocks, Paul and Silas prayed and sang (v. 25). What helps you to pray, or even to praise, in your own dark nights? How can a church bear patiently with those who can only manage the praying?

A businesswoman, a slave girl and a jailer: the church at Philippi began with people who would never otherwise have shared a room (v. 40). Who would be missing from your church’s table, and what could you do to welcome them?

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Where we are. Beaten and released at Philippi (chapter 16), Paul and his companions carry the gospel’s first steps in Europe west across Macedonia, through three very different cities. By the end of the chapter Paul is alone in Athens, the old intellectual capital of the Greek world.

The message. The risen Jesus is the Christ the Scriptures promised and the Lord and Judge of every people, so no one may keep him at a distance as a curiosity. To Jews Paul shows from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise; to Greeks with only creation and conscience he begins with the God who made them; both roads end at the same man, raised from the dead. God now commands all people everywhere to repent, and the right response is neither to shout him down nor to sample him, but to examine the evidence and believe.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). Here the gospel meets the two great worlds of his day, the synagogue and the philosophers.

How the chapter makes its case. In Thessalonica (vv. 1–9) Paul reasons from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise and that Jesus is he; a church is born, and jealous opponents hire a mob and charge the believers with treason. In Berea (vv. 10–15) hearers receive the word eagerly and test it daily against the Scriptures, until the trouble follows. In Athens (vv. 16–34), grieved by a city full of idols, Paul reasons in synagogue and marketplace and is brought before the Areopagus. From their altar to an unknown god he moves to the Creator who needs nothing, the one human race made to seek him, the command to repent, and judgment by the man God raised (vv. 22–31). Some mock, some put it off, and a few believe (vv. 32–34).

Where it leads. Every road in the chapter ends at Jesus: the suffering and rising Christ of the Scriptures, the King whose claim unsettles Caesar’s, the true Image of the God no craftsman can carve, the one Man appointed to judge the world. The empty tomb is God’s public guarantee that the one Athens laughed at will sit on the throne, with hands pierced for sinners.

For us. We live among both Berea and Athens: people with Bibles they no longer open, and people open to every idea except the gospel. Paul shows us how to speak: with reasons, patience and courage, starting where people are and not stopping short of the risen Christ. And the chapter asks us the Berean question: will we examine and believe, or only listen for something new?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Jesus is the Christ of the Scriptures, and those who search the Scriptures eagerly find him there. In Thessalonica Paul reasons for three Sabbaths that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is he (vv. 1–3). A church is born, largely from Gentiles, and jealous opponents hire a mob and charge the believers with proclaiming another king (vv. 4–9), a charge false as treason and true as a claim. Sent away by night, Paul finds in Berea hearers who receive the word with eagerness and test it daily against the Scriptures, and many believe (vv. 10–12). When the trouble follows, he goes on to Athens, leaving Silas and Timothy to strengthen the young church (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean pattern

The Bereans received the word eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily (17:11): eager hearing joined to careful testing by Scripture (both halves, and sola Scriptura, are treated at vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Thessalonian accusers said these men had turned the world upside down, and they were right that the gospel had rearranged households, loyalties and a synagogue. Now: The gospel still unsettles whatever opposes Christ’s kingdom. The question for a church is whether it is unsettling the right things, sin, death and injustice, or only offering comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fresh from a beating at Philippi, Paul walks a hundred miles to the next city and goes straight back to the synagogue to reason from the Scriptures, as his Lord had done before him.

To Thessalonica. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road from the Adriatic to Byzantium. From Philippi to Thessalonica is about a hundred miles, and Paul walked it with a back opened by rods a few days earlier. Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia and a busy port, was a city from which a message could travel in every direction; within months Paul could tell the church there that the word of the Lord had sounded forth from them everywhere (1 Thessalonians 1:8).

As was his custom. The last time he entered a public place in this province he came out stripped and flogged. His custom did not change. In each new city he went first to the synagogue, to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), to show those who already held the Scriptures that the Christ they hoped for is Jesus.

As his Lord had done. Luke has used this phrase once before. When Jesus came to Nazareth, as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, read Isaiah’s promise of the Spirit-anointed one who would proclaim good news to the poor, and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). His hearers were amazed, then furious, and drove him out of the town. Paul’s custom is his Master’s, and so will be the result. The risen Christ is still going to the synagogue on the Sabbath, in the person of his apostle.

He reasoned with them. The word is dialegomai, from which we get dialogue: for three Sabbaths men who knew the Scriptures put their objections, and he answered from the Old Testament, which both sides owned. Christian preaching appeals to the mind as well as the heart, and it is not afraid of a question.

Three Sabbath days. This is often taken to mean Paul was in Thessalonica only three weeks, which is very unlikely. He worked night and day with his hands so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9); the Philippians, a hundred miles away, sent him help there more than once (Philippians 4:16); and the congregation had turned to God from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), which does not describe synagogue Jews. Luke is counting the synagogue phase, not the whole mission. After it closed to him Paul worked on among Gentiles, who make up most of the church he writes to. Luke summarises; the letters fill in the rest, and the two fit.

Is it right to argue about the faith? Yes, if by arguing you mean what Paul did: giving reasons from Scripture, with patience, and listening to the objection before answering it. Peter tells every believer to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). What Scripture forbids is quarrelling: the point-scoring, the raised voice, the need to win (2 Timothy 2:24–25). If you are still listening, still gentle and still praying for the person, you are reasoning. If you are enjoying his defeat, you have stopped.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s case has two steps: the Scriptures show that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and Jesus is the one who did. The cross was not a disappointment to be explained away but the very thing the prophets foretold.

Explaining and proving. Explaining is opening up, prising apart (dianoigō), a word Luke keeps for remarkable company: Jesus on the Emmaus road, when he opened to them the Scriptures and their hearts burned (Luke 24:32), and that evening, when he opened their minds to understand them (Luke 24:45); and the Lord opening Lydia’s heart to pay attention (16:14). Paul opens the Scriptures; only God opens the person. Proving is setting food before somebody (paratithemenos, the ordinary word for it), as the jailer at Philippi did (16:34). Paul lays the evidence out where people can reach it, serving rather than performing.

Necessary for the Christ to suffer. Here is the whole quarrel between church and synagogue in one sentence. Most Jews expected a conquering Messiah, the son of David who would break the oppressor and reign; a crucified Messiah was not a disappointing version of the hope but a contradiction of it. Paul knew how it sounded: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Where did he prove it from? Luke does not say here, but the trail is easy to follow, because the risen Christ had walked two disciples through the same argument, asking almost the same question: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26) The texts are the ones the apostles use everywhere: the servant pierced for our transgressions and numbered with the transgressors, who afterwards shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53); the sufferer of Psalm 22, whose hands and feet are pierced and his garments divided (the Hebrew of the word pierced is uncertain, but the ancient Greek translation and most English Bibles read it so), and whose psalm ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD; the Holy One whose body will not see corruption (Psalm 16); the Anointed One who is cut off (Daniel 9:26); the pierced one they will look upon and mourn (Zechariah 12:10). The suffering was in the book the whole time, read aloud in that synagogue for generations.

This Jesus is the Christ. First, from the Scriptures: this is what the Christ must be, one who suffers and rises. Second, from history: here is the man who matches. Paul does not begin with Jesus and hunt for texts to fit him; he establishes the pattern and then produces the person. It is a model of preaching for every age: from Scripture to Christ.

Written before a nail was forged. The cross was not God’s rescue of a plan gone wrong. It was necessary because the Father had determined to save sinners through the suffering of his Son, and the Son had agreed to it gladly. Every lamb on every altar pointed to him, and the empty tomb was promised before Bethlehem was a village. He suffered because it was written, and it was written because he loved us before the world began.

How can I read the Old Testament and see Christ without forcing it? Read a passage first for what it meant to its first hearers. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward, which pattern it sets up (the lamb, the priest, the king, the temple), which longing it leaves open that only Christ answers. You are not hunting for secret codes in every tent peg but following roads the New Testament has already walked. Start with Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 16, read slowly beside the Gospel accounts of the cross and the empty tomb, and you will be doing in your own chair what the Bereans did in theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel wins some Jews and many Gentiles, and jealous opponents answer it not with argument but with a hired mob. The cost falls hardest on Jason, the local man who had opened his home.

Some were persuaded. God uses argument: the Spirit does not bypass the mind; he opens it, and then the reasons do their work. The numbers tell the story. Of the Jews, some; of the devout Greeks, the God-fearers attached to the synagogue, a great many; of the leading women, not a few. Paul’s letters show that many more were Gentiles converted straight from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

But the Jews were jealous. That imbalance lights the fuse. These God-fearers were the synagogue’s own fruit, Gentiles it had taught at cost over years, and they were walking out behind two visitors after three weeks. It had happened at Pisidian Antioch too (13:45). What is new here is the method.

Wicked men of the rabble. Marketplace men, Luke calls them (agoraioi): the idlers of the public square, loafers and thugs who could be hired cheaply by anyone wanting a crowd in a hurry. Respectable people who would not have thrown a stone themselves used men who neither knew nor cared what the argument was about. It was done to the Lord himself: Pilate knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered Jesus up, and they stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas instead (Mark 15:10–11). The crowd got its way, and God raised him from the dead. A crowd is not always what it seems, and it never has the last word.

The house of Jason. Jason was probably Paul’s host, a local who had done nothing except offer a spare room. When the missionaries move on, as they will tonight, he stays, with his door broken, his name on a charge sheet and his money posted as a bond. Luke tells us nothing more of him, unless he is the Jason Paul later greets as a kinsman (Romans 16:21), which would mean he came through it and was still standing years later.

The cost nobody writes down. This part of the cost of the gospel gets least attention, because those who bear it do not write the letters. The visiting preacher is beaten and moves on; the local believer who housed him goes on living among the neighbours who watched. If you have quietly paid for somebody else’s ministry, in your family, workplace or street, Jason is in Scripture for you. Christ sees the broken door. He who said that whoever receives one of his servants receives him (Matthew 10:40) counts every spare room opened for his sake as a room opened to himself.

Why would religious people be so jealous of the gospel? Because the gospel takes away the one thing religious pride lives on: being the ones who are in, by the right birth, the right effort, the right observance. When outsiders come in freely by grace, without the long apprenticeship, those who trusted in their apprenticeship feel robbed. It is the elder brother’s complaint (Luke 15:28–30). The cure is not less religion but remembering that we too came in by grace alone. If you catch yourself resenting how easily someone else was welcomed, take that jealousy to the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The believers are charged with treason for proclaiming “another king, Jesus”: false as a charge of revolt, but true in a deeper sense, because Jesus is Lord over Caesar too.

The city authorities. They were called politarchs, a title almost unknown in surviving literature but found in more than a dozen inscriptions from Thessalonica alone. Luke uses exactly the right local title, the kind of small detail that fits a careful historian.

Turned the world upside down. A famous compliment paid to the church by its enemies, usually quoted more cheerfully than Luke meant it. The verb anastatoō is not gentle: to unsettle, throw into disorder, drive out of house and home. Luke uses it once more, of an Egyptian who stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins into the wilderness (21:38). The charge is that these men are insurgents. And yet it is also a compliment, for the gospel turns the world the right way up.

Another king, Jesus. This accusation could kill: treason. Thessalonica was a free city, self-governing, without a Roman garrison. That freedom was Rome’s gift and could be taken back, and a city that harboured men proclaiming a rival king would not stay free long. So the charge is aimed with skill, and in the sense intended it is false: Paul had spent three weeks in a synagogue arguing about Isaiah, not organising a revolt.

Not simply untrue either. Jesus is King of kings: not a political rival to Caesar in the world’s way (John 18:36), but Lord over Caesar too. Paul really was announcing round the empire that a man had been raised from the dead and made Lord, and that a day of judgment had been fixed with him as judge; within months he wrote to this church about the Lord descending with a cry of command (1 Thessalonians 4:16), in words also used when an emperor visited a city. The early Christians would not say “Caesar is Lord”; they said “Jesus is Lord”. The mob was wrong that Paul was plotting revolt, and right that the claim of Jesus collides with Caesar’s; no political arrangement is finally neutral about him. The emperors worshipped as lords are names in a textbook, and the carpenter Rome crucified sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high; his throne was reached by a cross, and his subjects are not conscripts but sinners he died to free.

Why does politics now feel like a religion? Because something has to carry the hopes that used to rest on God. When a culture stops believing there is another king, it does not stop longing for a kingdom; it hands the longing to the state, the party or the cause, and then politics has to save us. So public argument takes on the heat of a heresy trial: if my side is salvation, yours is not mistaken but wicked. Because Jesus is King, Caesar is not god, and neither is any movement that wants his throne. That frees a Christian to care about politics without worshipping it: to vote, argue and work for justice, and still sleep the night after a lost election, because the King said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). And it frees him to love the people on the other side, since his King died for his enemies.

Does “another king” make Christians political revolutionaries? No. Christ’s kingdom advances not by the sword or the ballot box but by the word and the Spirit, and his subjects are commanded to pray for rulers, pay their taxes and do good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But no ruler is ultimate. When a government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, a Christian must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully and accepting the cost. Because Caesar is not his god, he can serve him honestly and still refuse to worship him.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd and the magistrates are alarmed, not by the question whether Jesus is King, but by what a riot might cost them with Rome. Authorities manage disturbances; they rarely weigh the truth, and the church does not depend on their verdict.

A rumour and a calculation. The crowd has a rumour of sedition; the politarchs are frightened of Rome. A city that could not keep order would have order imposed on it, as the town clerk at Ephesus says aloud: “we really are in danger of being charged with rioting” (19:40). They are not weighing a theological claim but calculating the cost of a report to the governor.

The pattern of the authorities. It repeats through the book and most of history: the authorities never actually rule on the truth of the matter. Gallio will refuse to hear it (18:15); Felix will keep Paul two years and decide nothing (24:27); Festus will find nothing deserving death and send him to Rome only because he has appealed to Caesar (25:25). Here the magistrates take a bond and make the problem go away. Institutions are rarely in the business of deciding whether something is true, only of keeping things quiet, and a church that pins its hopes on being officially found innocent will wait a long time.

What is truth? The pattern began at the trial of Jesus. Truth itself stood before a Roman governor and said, “Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice,” and Pilate asked, “What is truth?” and went out without waiting for a reply (John 18:37–38). He found no guilt in him, then gave the crowd what it wanted to keep the peace. The magistrates of Thessalonica, taking a bond and closing the file, do on a small scale what Pilate did on the largest: managing a disturbance instead of weighing a King. The verdict Pilate would not give, God gave on the third day, and every court that has since declined to ask whether Jesus is Lord has been ruling, without knowing it, in a case already decided.

The throne is occupied. The rulers took counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens was not disturbed (Psalm 2:2–4). Cities rage, magistrates calculate, and the Son reigns on, unthreatened. Our peace is not that the world is quiet; it is that the throne is occupied.

Should we not want the gospel to have a fair hearing in public? Yes, and Paul used every legal right he had (16:37; 25:11). It is good to seek and pray for justice and freedom of worship (1 Timothy 2:2), but the church does not depend on them; in this book the gospel spread fastest where the authorities were indifferent or hostile. So work for fairness, and do not be crushed when it does not come. The verdict that matters has been given, in the resurrection, and no magistrate can overturn it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jason buys peace with a bond, the believers send Paul and Silas away by night, and Paul goes straight into the next synagogue. A defeat settled in an office is overruled by Christ, and the word goes on.

Money as security. Jason and the others paid a sum they would lose if the trouble returned. In practice Paul had to leave and stay away: he could not come back without putting Jason’s property, and probably Jason, at risk.

Satan hindered us. A few months later Paul writes that he wanted to come to them again and again, but Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18). We are not told what the hindrance was and should not pretend to certainty, but this bond is a likely explanation, and many have suggested it. If so, what Paul calls Satan’s work was a piece of municipal paperwork nobody could appeal: not every obstacle to God’s work is dramatic. Paul does not pretend it did not hurt, yet he did not sit still: he wrote letters, he sent Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2), and the church he could not visit became one of the great joys of his life. Satan hinders; Christ overrules. No bond lodged in Thessalonica could bind the word of God.

Away by night. By night, as at Damascus when Paul was let down the wall in a basket (9:25), then about fifty miles south-west, off the main highway, to a quieter town. And straight into the synagogue: after two cities in a row had ended in violence, they changed towns and kept the same method.

Imitators of the Lord. Paul himself tells us how he read this flight. To the church he had just been torn from he writes: “you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 1:6). They had suffered from their own countrymen, as the churches in Judea had, where the Lord Jesus himself was killed (1 Thessalonians 2:14–15). Paul, a Jew writing of his own people with grief, is not blaming a race but tracing one road: the Lord rejected and killed, his apostles driven out, his young church suffering, all following him toward the same resurrection.

Is it cowardly for a Christian to run from persecution? No. Jesus told his disciples that when persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul did so repeatedly, though never by denying Christ. Fleeing is wrong when it means abandoning the faith or deserting people who depend on you; it is wise when staying would only waste a life the Lord can still use elsewhere. Here the local believers made the decision, and Paul accepted it. He did not run from the work. He ran to the next synagogue.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bereans show what noble hearing looks like: they welcomed the word eagerly and tested it daily against the Scriptures, and the testing led them to faith.

More noble. Better born, of finer stock (eugenesteroi): a word about social class, which Luke gives to a country-town synagogue over the one in the provincial capital. He is quietly redefining nobility as character: what a man does when handed something new he did not ask for.

With all eagerness. Luke describes what they did in two halves that must be kept together. This is the first, and it is not the cautious half. They were not braced against the word; they wanted it, and received it gladly, before they had checked it.

Examining the Scriptures daily. The second half, and the verb is a legal one: to sift evidence, as in a court (anakrinontes). And daily, well past the Sabbath. Men with a living to earn went home, opened the scrolls, and worked through Isaiah and the Psalms to see whether a visitor had told them the truth.

Neither credulous nor cynical. Either half alone is something the Bible does not commend. Eagerness without examination sweeps people into every enthusiasm that has ever damaged a church. Examination without eagerness is the more respectable disease: the hearer who arrives armed, Bible open to catch the preacher out, unmoved by anything in twenty years. Luke praises men who did both at once, which is much harder than either.

Many of them therefore believed. “Therefore”: the daily examination did not produce sceptics who could never be satisfied; it produced faith, more of it than the city up the road had managed, for these are the Scriptures that bear witness about him (John 5:39). The Bereans did not believe in spite of their Bibles. They believed because their Bibles were about him.

How do I actually examine the Scriptures when I hear a sermon? Keep it simple. Open the passage and read the verses around it: does the point come from the text, or is the text just a launching pad? Ask whether it fits the rest of the Bible’s teaching. If something puzzles you, ask, kindly. And make the daily part real: a regular, unhurried reading of the Bible for yourself gives you the ear to notice when something is off, and the joy to notice when something is gloriously right.

Does sola Scriptura make every Christian his own pope? No. The Bereans examined Scripture together, in a synagogue, under teaching, not alone against everybody. Sola Scriptura means Scripture is the only infallible rule, not the only help. God gives the church pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11–12), the wisdom of the centuries and confessions that summarise Scripture’s teaching, all valuable and all under the Bible, to be corrected by it. A believer who thinks he has found something no Christian has ever seen should be humble and slow. One who hears from the pulpit something the text plainly does not say should open his Bible, and then go and talk to his pastor.

Where Christians differ: the final authority. Some say the church or tradition must interpret Scripture for the believer, and that individuals should not test teachers; Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, who love the Scriptures, hold that the church’s tradition and teaching office share Scripture’s authority. This commentary’s view: the Bereans tested an apostle by Scripture, and Luke calls it noble. Scripture is the final authority by which every teaching is tested (Isaiah 8:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1). This is sola Scriptura (Latin for Scripture alone): not that teachers and tradition are useless, but that Scripture judges them all. We answer those who differ gently, from this very verse.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opponents travel fifty miles to stir up trouble again, so Paul is sent on; but Silas and Timothy stay, because the young church needs teachers more than it needs Paul.

They came there too. Fifty miles, on foot, to break up a meeting in a town they did not live in. Men had followed Paul to Lystra before and got him stoned (14:19): hatred will spend an effort that indifference never will.

Stirring up the crowds. They did not preach against him; they agitated, the same trade as at Thessalonica. And they went not to the synagogue, where the Bereans were examining the Scriptures daily and would not be hurried, but to the crowds. When a case cannot be won in the room where the evidence is, it gets taken outside to people who have not seen any.

Silas and Timothy remained. This is easy to miss and is the more important detail. Silas and Timothy stay, in a town just stirred up against them, to strengthen a young church. The work at Berea did not require Paul; it required somebody. Paul had learned that from his Master, who spent three years making men who could carry the work, then told them it was to their advantage that he go away, because he would send the Helper (John 16:7). A Paul who thought the mission stood or fell on his own presence would have misunderstood the Lord he served.

How do I know when to stay and when to step back? Ask whose presence is the problem and whose is needed. Paul’s was drawing fire onto the believers; Silas’s and Timothy’s was building them up. Sometimes love means staying when it would be easier to leave; sometimes it means stepping out of the way so that others can do the work. Take counsel, as Paul accepted the brothers’ decision. And be willing not to be the centre of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s escort leaves him in Athens, and the apostle, alone and feeling it, sends for his friends; the Lord who stood by him there stands by his lonely servants still.

As far as Athens. The escort, Bereans who were converts of a few weeks, had travelled several hundred miles to see Paul safely there, and went home; nobody records their names, and without them the next scene does not happen. Athens, home of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, was past its political glory but still a famous university city, full of philosophers and temples. Here the chapter changes ground: Thessalonica and Berea were synagogue cities, but in Athens the gospel walks into the heart of Greek learning and religion, where most hearers had no Bible at all, one more step towards the end of the earth (1:8).

Alone in Athens. Paul almost never worked alone; his letters are full of names. This is the one extended stretch in Acts where he is by himself, and we know how he felt about it: when he could bear it no longer, he told the Thessalonians, he was willing to be left behind at Athens alone (1 Thessalonians 3:1). Scripture will not support a picture of Paul as indestructible. The man who sang at midnight in a Philippian cell sends an urgent message from Athens asking his friends to hurry. The loneliness was not a failure of faith; the Areopagus address was preached out of it.

The Lord stood by me. Paul was alone, but not left alone. At the very next stop, Corinth, the Lord spoke to him in a vision by night: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (18:9–10). And at the end of his life, from another prison, Paul would write that at his first defence no one came to stand by him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). The Lord who stood by him had himself been forsaken by all his friends, so that none of his people would ever be finally forsaken. That is the pattern of Athens: the friends far away, the city indifferent, and the risen Christ beside his servant, so that the sermon preached out of loneliness becomes one of the most famous ever given.

Is it wrong for a Christian to feel lonely? No. Being alone and finding it hard is not a sign that something has gone wrong in your Christian life. It happened to Paul, and he did not apologise for minding. God himself said it was not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and our Lord in Gethsemane asked his friends to watch with him. Loneliness is not sin; it is a need. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and do what Paul did: ask for company. Tell a friend or your pastor you are struggling. The body of Christ exists partly so that no member has to carry that alone.

In everyday life. Look round your church for someone who is in their Athens at the moment, new to the area, recently bereaved, or carrying a ministry by themselves, and be the answer to their message before they have to send it.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God whom Athens worshipped as unknown has made himself known in a man he raised from the dead, and he now calls everyone to repent. Alone and grieved by a city full of idols, Paul reasons in synagogue and marketplace until the philosophers bring him before the Areopagus (vv. 16–21). Starting from their altar to an unknown god, he proclaims the Creator who needs nothing (vv. 22–25), who made every nation from one man to seek him and is not far from any of us (vv. 26–28). Idols are therefore folly, and the times of ignorance are over: God commands repentance, because he will judge the world by the man he raised (vv. 29–31). Some mock, some postpone, and a few believe, among them Dionysius and Damaris (vv. 32–34).
verseByVerse.theology:
What creation can and cannot tell

At the Areopagus Paul uses what can be known of God through creation, often called natural theology: God has not left himself without witness (14:17), and every nation lives within boundaries he has set (17:26). But creation cannot tell anyone the gospel. To move from the God who made everything to the man he has appointed takes the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection, some said they would hear Paul again, and some believed: dismissal, deferral and faith. Now: The gospel still divides its hearers along much the same lines. The church cannot prevent the first two responses; its task is to preach so plainly that the third is open to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is provoked by a city full of idols, and his grief for God’s glory and for its people sends him not away from Athens but into its synagogue and marketplace, to reason with anyone he meets.

His spirit was provoked. Stirred, distressed, angered (parōxyneto). Luke used its noun for the sharp disagreement that parted Paul and Barnabas (15:39). The fierceness that cost him something at Antioch now drives him into the marketplace at Athens. Grace does not hand us a new temperament; it makes the one we have holy.

Full of idols. Luke’s word is found in no earlier surviving Greek writing and may be his own coinage: something like idol-infested, as you would describe a house overrun. A Roman satirist joked of one region that it was easier to meet a god there than a man; Athens would have qualified at least as well. Many were masterpieces, in one of the great collections of sculpture in the ancient world. Paul walked through some of the finest art the human race had yet produced and felt grief and anger, because he was looking not at the workmanship but at what it was for: the glory belonging to God was being handed to objects, beautifully (Romans 1:23).

Zeal and tears. Paul felt two things at once, for God’s honour and for the people, and he learned both from his Lord. When Jesus found the temple turned into a market, his disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17). And when he drew near and saw Jerusalem, he wept over it, because it did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41–42). The Son of God was jealous for his Father’s glory and broken-hearted for the people robbing it. The cold zealot who does not weep and the soft sympathiser who is never provoked have both lost half of Christ. God did not burn Athens; he sent an apostle to reason with it. His zeal for his name and his love for idolaters meet in the gospel, where the Son bore the wrath that idolatry deserves, so that those who had bowed to stone could bow to him and live.

In the synagogue and in the marketplace. He did not withdraw from the city or stand in the street shouting at it. He talked to people: first, as usual, those who had the Scriptures, then in the agora, the centre of public life where Socrates had taught, among shoppers, loafers, philosophers and slaves on errands. That is what to do with whatever grieves you about the place you live: not a post, not a private lament, but a conversation with somebody who is in it.

How can I be grieved by idolatry without becoming self-righteous? Remember that the idols of Athens are in your own heart too. Calvin called the human heart a factory of idols, and every Christian was rescued from some version of that city. Paul’s grief was for God’s glory and for the people, not against them, which is why it sent him into the marketplace to reason, not out of it to sneer. Today’s idols are rarely statues: money, success, the body, romance, a cause, comfort. When you see them ruling the people around you, let it move you to pray and to speak, gently and with reasons, as one beggar telling another where the bread is.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The philosophers sneer at Paul as a scavenger of ideas and suspect him of bringing in foreign gods, because he preaches Jesus and the resurrection; so they take him to the Areopagus to explain himself.

Epicureans and Stoics. These were the two live schools in Athens. The Epicureans held that the gods exist but are remote and uninterested in us; the world is atoms falling, there is no providence, and death is simply the end, which was the good news of the system, because it meant no judgment. The aim of life is pleasure, understood as tranquillity, the absence of pain and fear. The Stoics held nearly the opposite: the divine is the rational principle running through all things, so everything is ordered, and in some sense God is the universe; the aim of life is to live in harmony with nature, accept fate calmly and endure without complaint. Paul’s sermon will agree with each school about something and disagree with both about God.

What does this babbler wish to say? The word is spermologos, a seed-picker: first a bird pecking up scraps, then slang for men who scavenged the market floor for what fell off the carts, and finally an insult for someone who picks up bits of ideas and passes them off as learning. It is the sneer of the professional at the amateur, and the first thing the philosophers of Athens said about the apostle to the Gentiles.

Foreign divinities. Any educated Athenian would have felt the shadow over the phrase: introducing new divinities was the charge on which Athens had tried and executed Socrates, four and a half centuries earlier. Luke does not need to say so.

Jesus and the resurrection. It is quite possible they misheard him. Jesus and Anastasis, the Greek word for resurrection, a feminine noun, could sound to a pagan ear like a god and his consort, which would explain the plural divinities exactly. If so, the cleverest men in Athens heard the gospel and concluded that Paul was recommending two new gods, one of them called Resurrection.

I am the resurrection. The mistake was nearer the truth than they knew. Jesus and the Resurrection are not two deities but one person. At the tomb of Lazarus Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25).
