The resurrection is his own deed and his own life, laid down and taken up again by his own authority (John 10:18). Paul was not offering Athens two new gods for its collection, but the one Lord who has death in his hands.

The Areopagus. The Mars Hill of older English Bibles, a rocky outcrop north-west of the Acropolis, gave its name to the venerable council that was Athens’s supreme authority in religion, morals and education. This was less a formal trial than an examination by the gatekeepers of which ideas and gods Athens would entertain.

Do I need to understand philosophy to share the gospel? No, but it helps to understand the person in front of you. Paul knew what Epicureans and Stoics believed because he had listened in the marketplace. Your neighbours have working beliefs too: that this life is all there is, that God is distant, that everything happens for a reason, that you should just be true to yourself. Hearing those beliefs, and kindly showing where Christ answers what they reach for, takes curiosity and love more than a degree.

Uncertain wording. “Areopagus” can mean the hill or the council that took its name, and Luke’s wording does not settle which he means, here or in verse 22. By Paul’s day the council may often have met down in the marketplace, and standing “in the midst of the Areopagus” (v. 22) suits a body of people at least as well as a hilltop. Most likely Paul was brought before the council, wherever it sat; nothing in his message depends on the place.
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Athenians call Paul’s message strange and ask what it means: an open door, which he gladly walks through, though curiosity is not yet faith.

Strange things. A courteous sentence and also a summons. Strange (xenizonta) means foreign, belonging somewhere else. They are not calling the message offensive; it simply fits none of the shelves they own. No Athenian would have invented a God who becomes a man, dies for his enemies and rises to judge the world. It is foreign because it is from heaven.

We wish to know. Curiosity, at least, and an open door. Paul takes it at face value, without complaining about their motives or demanding a better attitude before he will speak. But Luke’s next remark is about the Athenian appetite for something new (v. 21): he knows the difference between an appetite for the interesting and a willingness to be changed.

Herod was glad to see him. Luke has shown this curiosity before, aimed at Jesus himself: Herod was very glad, for he had long desired to see him and was hoping to see some sign done by him (Luke 23:8). Jesus made him no answer. Now the risen Christ, through his apostle, answers another audience that wants to know, fully and plainly, down to the day of judgment and the empty tomb. That is grace. But the answer is no curiosity to be enjoyed; it ends with a command to repent.

Interest is not yet obedience. A person can consume a great deal about God, sermons, books, podcasts, with genuine interest, and let the interest stand in for obedience. If you fear that this describes you, bring your interest to Christ as it is: he does not turn away those who come wanting to want him (John 6:37).

What should I do when a friend is curious about Christianity? Treat the curiosity as an open door, as Paul did. Answer the question actually asked, honestly; if you do not know, say so and find out. Offer to read a Gospel together; Mark can be read in an evening. But do not confuse interest with faith, theirs or yours. At the right moment, gently make it personal: what would it mean for you if this were true?

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athens treated ideas as entertainment, always hungry for the next new thing, and it was that appetite, not a love of truth, that the gospel was about to meet.

Something newer. Luke steps aside to describe the city, because everything on the Areopagus depends on it. His Greek says literally “something newer”: an appetite always for the next new thing, which can never be satisfied, only fed. And Luke includes the foreigners: a culture forms its residents more quietly than they realise.

Investigation or entertainment. This is a description, not a denunciation; Luke has just praised Berea for examining the Scriptures daily. The difference between Berea and Athens is not how much they liked ideas but what they thought ideas were for. Berea tested a claim to find out whether it was true, because if it was, something would have to happen. Athens sampled a claim to see whether it was interesting: entertainment with a serious face on. It is a danger for every generation: always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth, gathering teachers to suit itching ears (2 Timothy 3:7; 4:3).

The one thing that cannot be sampled. When Paul reaches the resurrection, the city that would listen to anything finds its limit. An audience open to every idea is usually open only to ideas that ask nothing of it, and Athens is about to be handed something that cannot be tasted and put down, because it is not an idea at all. It is a man, raised from the dead and appointed to judge the world, and he will not stay on the shelf. Athens wanted something newer. It was offered someone eternal.

Is it wrong to enjoy new ideas and learning? Not at all. Every true discovery is a glimpse of God’s world and wisdom, and Christians have been among the most curious people in history. The problem is curiosity that never commits, that treats God as a topic rather than as the Lord. So enjoy learning, and let it end in worship. When you meet something new about God, ask not only whether it is interesting but whether it is true, and if so, what it requires of you. Old truths, rightly heard, are often the newest thing a person can learn.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins from the Athenians’ own altar to an unknown god: their religion confesses in stone that it has not found the God it reaches for, and he offers to make that God known.

Very religious. The opening word is double-edged (see the box below): a compliment they could accept and an accurate diagnosis at the same time. The ambiguity is the truth about them. They genuinely are reaching for God, and they are getting it comprehensively wrong.

The shape of the speech. One of the most carefully built speeches in Acts moves from their altar (v. 23) to God the Creator who needs nothing (vv. 24–25), humanity made from one man to seek him (vv. 26–28), idolatry and the command to repent (vv. 29–30), and judgment by the man God raised (v. 31): from what they half knew to what they could not know without being told. Nor was it brought in his luggage: “as I passed along”, he says, so it was gathered in the streets by a man paying attention to what the people in front of him actually did.

An altar to the unknown god. Ancient writers mention altars to unknown gods in Athens, set up so that no god was offended or left out. Diogenes Laertius tells how, centuries earlier, during a plague no sacrifice would lift, the Athenians sent for Epimenides of Crete, the poet many think Paul quotes in a moment; on his advice they turned sheep loose on the Areopagus and built an altar wherever one lay down, to whatever god was responsible and had not yet been named. The altar was not humility. It was insurance.

What you worship as unknown. A great deal is built on this sentence that it will not carry. It is sometimes read as though the Athenians were worshipping the true God all along under another name, and all sincere religion arrives at the same place. Paul does not say that. He says they worship in ignorance, and within seven verses he tells them that the times of that ignorance are over and God commands them to repent. You do not summon people to repentance for worshipping the right God correctly. What he says is subtler and better. Their altar is an admission, carved in stone in the middle of their own city, that their religion is incomplete: there is a God they have not named. Paul takes their confession of ignorance and offers to fill it.

What could the Athenians know of God? God’s eternal power and divine nature have been clearly perceived in creation (Romans 1:20), and the work of the law is written on every heart (Romans 2:14–15). The altar shows a people who knew there was more than their idols. But that knowledge left them without excuse, not without need; it could not tell them who God is or how a sinner may be reconciled to him.

He has made him known. Paul will make the unknown God known not by a better argument about altars but by a man. The sermon that opens at this altar closes with the man God raised from the dead, and the whole distance between them is the distance the Son came. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18). Jesus told Philip, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The Athenians built an altar at the edge of their knowledge and left it blank. God has written on that blank space a name, Jesus, and a face that can be known.

Every person’s unknown altar. Paul does not open with their sin, though he will reach it, but with the thing in their own life that does not add up, which they have already half admitted. Everyone has an altar to an unknown god somewhere: a longing they cannot account for, a standard they hold others to and cannot meet, a fear of death they do not discuss. The question is whether you have been paying attention as you passed along.

Do people of other religions worship the true God without knowing it? No; as shown above, this verse says the opposite. Many religions contain true and beautiful insights, but no one is reconciled to God by sincere worship of a god they do not know. Salvation comes through conscious faith in Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and men (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). That is not narrowness; it is why Paul crossed the sea to tell them.

Uncertain wording. Deisidaimonesterous was used both for careful piety towards the gods and for superstitious fear of them, and nothing in the sentence decides between the two; Paul’s hearers could have heard both. The KJV’s “too superstitious” takes the harsher sense; most modern translations take the kinder one, “very religious”, which suits an opening meant to win a hearing. The likely meaning is a fair observation with an edge: you take your gods very seriously indeed.

Textual note. The KJV’s “whom” follows later manuscripts; the earliest read “what”, which fits Paul’s point that they did not know the one they reached for.
verseByVerse.note: “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious.” Ancient writers mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made everything is Lord of it all, needs nothing from us and gives everything to us, so no temple can house him and no sacrifice can put him in our debt.

The God who made the world. With no Bible to appeal to, Paul begins with what every human being has in front of him: the world exists, and it did not make itself.

Being Lord of heaven and earth. In one clause he parts company with both schools in the room. God made the world, so he is not the indifferent absentee of the Epicureans; he is Lord of it, over it and distinct from it, so he is not the Stoics’ divine reason diffused through everything. He is personal, and other than what he made: against pantheism, which says everything is God, and materialism, which says there is nothing but matter.

Does not live in temples made by man. If the council met near the Areopagus, Paul had the Parthenon over his shoulder, one of the most beautiful buildings in the world, holding a statue of Athena some forty feet high in gold and ivory, the pride and treasury of the city. And he tells the men responsible for it all that the God who matters lives in none of it. Stephen had said much the same of the temple in Jerusalem shortly before he was stoned (7:48), and it holds for Jerusalem and Athens alike: a God who can be housed is a God who can be managed.

A temple not made with hands. Yet God has chosen to dwell with men in a way no architect could have designed. Jesus’ accusers quoted him: “I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands” (Mark 14:58), and he spoke of the temple of his body (John 2:21). The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9): not a part or a likeness of God, but God himself living in a human body. Athens built the most beautiful house on earth for a goddess who was not there. God built his own temple, in the person of his Son, the only one ever truly filled.

Not served by human hands. Athens ran on the assumption that the gods required feeding: sacrifices, festivals, a priesthood, and the meat trade that went with it. Religion was a transaction: the gods got what they needed and the city got protection. Paul says God needs nothing, not our sacrifices, our worship or anything else (Psalm 50:9–12), so the whole arrangement is upside down. Many keep the same bargain in Christian clothes: if I pray, give and behave, God owes me a quiet life. Paul’s God cannot be put in anyone’s debt (Romans 11:35–36), and that ends the bargain.

He himself gives. Then a clause of enormous kindness: the traffic runs the other way. They have been carrying things up the hill to a God who has been supplying them all along. He needs nothing, and has been happy from all eternity in the love of Father, Son and Spirit. And this self-sufficient God gives: breath to the councillors who are about to laugh, rain on the fields of idolaters, and at last his own Son to those who had nothing to give him back.

A comfort for the useless. If God needed nothing from Athens, he needs nothing from you either. Your service, giving and usefulness are not contributions to a God running short; he asks for them for your sake. So the day you can do none of them, through illness, age or exhaustion, you have not become a worse investment. You were never an investment. You were always a child being given things.

If God needs nothing, why should I worship, pray or serve? Because he is worthy, and because it is good for us. A father does not need his child’s drawing, yet he delights in it and puts it on the wall. God does not need our worship, but he is glorified and delights in it, and we were made for it: in his presence there is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11). Prayer does not inform him; it is how he has chosen to give what he has promised. Service does not add to his wealth; it shares in his work. Nothing we do makes him more. Everything we do for him makes us more fully what we were made to be.

In everyday life. Try counting the gifts of one ordinary day, from breath on waking to sleep at night, and thank him for each by name.

parallels.desc: who gives breath to the people

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every nation comes from one man, and God has set the times and places of them all so that people would seek him, the God who is never far from any of us.

From one man. The Athenians held that they were autochthonous, sprung from the soil of Attica itself, not migrants like everybody else. Their orators repeated it at public funerals: Greeks above barbarians, and Athenians the truest Greeks, because they alone had grown where they stood. Before the council of that city Paul says every nation on earth came out of one man.

Every race of one blood. All humanity comes from one man, Adam (Genesis 1–2; Romans 5:12). Then the Athenian in the front row, the slave carrying his shopping and the Scythian on the edge of the world are relatives. Every scheme that has ever ranked human beings by descent contradicts this verse, and Paul preached it to the people most invested in the opposite.

Periods and boundaries. God has fixed for every nation its times, the rise, fall and duration of every people, and its places, the borders of its lands. Determined (horisas) means marked out, decreed: not blind chance, the Epicurean view, nor impersonal Fate, the Stoic one, but the appointment of the living, personal God, who removes kings and sets up kings (Daniel 2:21). It humbled proud Athens, and it steadies us when the headlines look out of control.

Feel their way toward him. Feel their way (psēlaphēseian) means to grope, as a blind man in the dark. And it applies to you: your century, country, town and family were set on purpose, that you would seek him and find him (Psalm 139:16). Where and when you live is not an accident but an appointment, a kindness designed to bring you home.

Not far from each one of us. The problem is not his distance but our blindness. There is no place where God is absent and no one he is far from (Psalm 139:7–10; Jeremiah 23:23–24), and Paul preaches it to a city full of shrines built on the opposite assumption.

One man and the Man. Paul’s sermon is bracketed by two men: the one man from whom God made every nation, and the man God has appointed to judge the world and raised from the dead (v. 31). Paul explains the pairing elsewhere: “as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). From the first man every nation inherited its life, its scattering and its death. In the second, a new humanity is being gathered from all those nations, one by one, through faith, and in him the walls between Jew and Greek, slave and free, come down (Galatians 3:28). The God who set the boundaries of the nations sent his Son across every boundary to gather a people out of all of them.

Isn’t human equality simply obvious? To us it feels obvious, and that is the surprising thing. It did not to the most brilliant city in the ancient world. Aristotle, who taught in Athens, argued that some people are slaves by nature, made to be ruled as a tool is used. The historian Tom Holland, in Dominion, has argued that the West’s conviction of equal human dignity came not from Greece or Rome but from the Christian story, and that a secular culture still lives on that inheritance while doubting its source. Paul gives the reason: we all come from one man and were all made by one God. Equality is not obvious. It is a gift, and it has a source.

Does one human race mean ethnic and cultural differences do not matter? No. They are God’s good gift: he made the nations and set their places, and in the end people from every tribe and language will stand before the throne, recognisably themselves (Revelation 7:9). What this verse forbids is ranking them. No nation is nearer to God by birth, and no race is lesser. In a church that means the stranger is welcomed as family, prejudice is repented of rather than excused, and the fellowship around the Lord’s Table is the clearest picture on earth of the one blood and the one Saviour.

Does this mean that unbelievers really seek God? Paul says “no one seeks for God” (Romans 3:11). Here he states God’s purpose, that people should seek him, and “feel their way toward him” pictures the groping of the blind, who may not find. Left to themselves, people turn away from the God they half know. Those who truly find him do so because he first seeks them (18:10; Luke 19:10).

How do I seek him? If you are not sure you have ever found God, this verse is an invitation with a surprise in it: the seeking began on his side. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10), and the God who is not far from each one of us has come as near as a manger and a cross. Go where he has spoken. Read one of the Gospels, Luke or John, slowly, and ask of each page who this Jesus is. Speak to him honestly. Pray even if you are unsure anyone is listening: tell him what you doubt, and ask him to show you. Go where his people gather. Sit under the preaching of his word, and put your real questions to a Christian you trust. Do what you already see. Light obeyed is followed by more light. The promise stands: “You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). And Jesus adds his own: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: one man. Some today regard Adam as a symbol rather than a historical person, often from a sincere wish to honour both Scripture and science, and they deserve a patient hearing. This commentary’s view: Paul here, and in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, treats Adam as a real man from whom all nations descend, and whose sin and death spread to all. The unity of the human race and the gospel of the second Adam rest on it: Paul’s parallel between Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–19) needs both to be real men, and Adam and Eve to be real people, specially created by God (Genesis 2:7, 22).

Textual note. The KJV and NKJV read “of one blood”, following later manuscripts; the earliest read simply “from one”, and most modern Bibles say “from one man”.

parallels.desc: he fixed the borders of the peoples

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul borrows two lines from Greek poets to say something true, that every human life comes from God and depends on him, and he claims those words for the true God whose name the poets had wrong.

Some of your own poets. Paul quotes pagan poets to a pagan audience, and both lines probably come from poems about Zeus; the second is from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a Stoic poet of about 270 BC from Cilicia, Paul’s own home region (on the first, see the box below). What is he doing, and how far does it license us to go?

A true sentence in a false frame. He does not say the poets were right about Zeus, or treat their religion as another road to the same place; he is two verses from telling them to repent. He takes a true sentence out of a false frame and puts it in the true one. Pagans said something accurate about the dependence of every living thing on God and got the name of the God wrong, and Paul keeps the accurate part and corrects the address. Writing to Titus, he quotes Epimenides on the Cretans and says flatly that this testimony is true (Titus 1:12–13): he is quite willing to say that an unbeliever has told the truth.

Two errors avoided. One error treats everything outside the church as poison; Paul could not have preached this sermon if he had thought so. The other quotes whatever is popular to seem approachable; Paul uses two lines and then turns them against the whole religious system the poets belonged to. He is not leaning on the poets for approval but claiming their true words for the true God.

Total dependence. This is not pantheism; Paul has just insisted that God is distinct from what he made. It is total creaturely dependence: your life and breath at this moment are on loan. The New Testament names the one who holds us so. All things were created through the Son and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17); he upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). And the Lord who sustains every life entered one, became dependent as a child is dependent, and laid his own life down. The poets glimpsed a God in whom we live. They never imagined a God who would die for those who live in him.

The turn of the argument. “For we are indeed his offspring” is the hinge of the speech. Paul lets it stand, in the sense that every human being is God’s creature and bears his image, and then turns it on them: if we are his offspring, then whatever God is like, he is at least as alive as we are. And that is exactly what a statue is not.

If we are all God’s offspring, are we all God’s children? In one sense yes, in another no. Every human being is God’s offspring by creation: made by him, in his image, and dependent on him. But Scripture keeps the name children of God, in the saving sense, for those who receive Christ and are born of God (John 1:12–13; Galatians 3:26). So we can say to anyone, you were made by God and for God; and we must also say, you need to be adopted into his family through his Son. The gospel needs both.

Can I use films, songs and books in sharing the gospel? Yes, as Paul did, with care. Look for the true thing a story or song has glimpsed: a longing for home, a hunger for justice, a sense of guilt, a hope that death is not the end. Name it honestly, then show where it is fulfilled in Christ. But, as above, do not endorse the frame along with the line, and do not stop at the common ground.

Uncertain wording. Paul names no poet, and only the second line can be traced with confidence: “For we are indeed his offspring” matches a line of Aratus, and a hymn to Zeus by the Stoic Cleanthes says much the same. The source of “In him we live and move and have our being” is less certain. It is traditionally credited to Epimenides, the Cretan sage of about 600 BC, but that attribution comes from Christian writers centuries later, and some think Paul is simply using a familiar philosophical way of speaking.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides.

parallels.desc: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are God’s living offspring, God cannot be a lifeless image of our own making; and the long patience in which God passed over that ignorance has ended, for he now commands all people everywhere to repent.

Not like gold or silver or stone. The argument is powerful because it is simple. If we are God’s offspring, living, thinking, choosing, then God is at least that, and a thing of metal or rock is not. A living creature manufactures a dead object and then bows to it. Whatever is true of God, he cannot be less alive than the man holding the chisel.

Art and imagination. The idol is not merely stone but stone plus a human idea: somebody decided what the god should look like, and made it look like that. So the worshipper is finally kneeling to his own conception, and the god will never require anything of him that he did not first think of himself. That is why idolatry is so durable, and why its modern form is not statues. We still assemble a God out of the qualities we approve of, offended by the sins we do not commit and relaxed about the ones we do, and it has exactly the defect Paul names: it cannot say anything to you that you did not put in it. The living God will not be imagined into our shape. Yet the God who will not be made into an image has given us his own Image: the Son, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), not formed by human art but born of a virgin by the Holy Spirit.

The times of ignorance God overlooked. Overlooked does not mean excused, or that God did not care. It means passed over, let go by without pressing the matter, holding back judgment in patience: the patience Paul described to the farmers at Lystra, where God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways and yet sent them rain and harvests (14:16–17). This is the other end of that patience. It had an expiry date, and the date has passed.

Why the overlooking could end. It ends now because of what has happened meanwhile. God put forward Christ Jesus as a propitiation by his blood (an offering that satisfies God’s holy wrath, so that the judgment sinners deserved is spent on the substitute), to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins (Romans 3:25–26). The overlooking was never indifference; God held back the full judgment of the nations’ sins because he had determined to deal with sin justly at the cross. The times of ignorance were the long night before the Son came; the “but now” of this verse is the daylight of Good Friday and Easter, and that is why the command can go out to everyone.

But now he commands. Commands: not a recommendation to those who find it congenial, but an order. And all people everywhere, said to a council that divided the human race into Greeks and barbarians, philosophers included. The “one man” and “every nation” of verse 26 return as a summons: if we all came from one, we are all answerable to one.

What repentance is. A change of mind about God that turns the whole person round: turning from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Not merely feeling sorry, nor first giving up bad habits, it is a new verdict on God, that he is real, holy and good, and on ourselves, that we have been worshipping what is not God, followed by a turn of the whole life towards him, trusting his mercy in Christ. It is the first word of demand in the whole sermon: only now, having taken the ground from under the idols, does Paul tell them to turn round.

In everyday life. Ask honestly: when did the God I believe in last contradict me? Then open your Bible at a passage you have tended to avoid, and let God say something you would not have said yourself. Where he contradicts you, repentance begins, and the God who commands it is faithful to forgive all that you find there (1 John 1:9).

Were those who lived before the gospel saved by their ignorance? No. Their ignorance was not innocence; they had the light of creation and suppressed it (Romans 1:18–21). God held back the judgment their sins deserved, as explained above; he did not cancel it. Now that Christ has come, he commands all people everywhere to repent, because judgment is coming by the risen man (v. 31).

If repentance is commanded, is it something I do or something God gives? Both, and Scripture says both without embarrassment. God commands everyone to repent, so no one may excuse himself by waiting for a feeling. Yet repentance is also God’s gift: he granted repentance that leads to life even to the Gentiles (11:18), and he opens hearts as he opened Lydia’s (16:14). The two do not compete. When you hear the command and turn to Christ, you are doing what you were told, and you will discover afterwards that it was God working in you to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). So do not wait. Obey the command, and thank him for the gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has fixed a day when he will judge the world justly through the man he has appointed, and he has proved it to everyone by raising that man from the dead. The judge is Jesus, which makes the day both a warning and, for those who trust him, a hope.

He has fixed a day. To an Athenian every clause here is an impossibility. A fixed day: not a cycle, not the endless recurrence of ages the Stoics taught, but an end, a date already set in a diary that is not ours, whether or not the Areopagus finds it believable.

In righteousness. The Epicureans believed that death ends the matter and there is nothing to fear; that was the comfort their whole system was built to give. Paul removes it in a single clause: God will judge the whole world, justly. Yet judgment is not only a threat. For anyone genuinely wronged, a fixed day when the world is finally assessed in righteousness is the only hope there is. Nothing done in the dark to a person nobody defended will go unaddressed, which is why the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth (Psalm 96:12–13).

By a man whom he has appointed. Here the sermon stops being philosophy. God will judge the world not through fate or a principle but by a man, with a name, who lived at a particular address. It is Jesus, not yet named, and there is mercy in that. The one who will assess a human life has lived one; he knows from the inside what it is to be tired, poor, betrayed and afraid. The Father has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27). The man who stood silent before Pilate will sit on the throne of the world, and the judge of all the earth has hands that were pierced.

He has given assurance to all. Assurance (pistis, usually faith) meant in the courts and the market a guarantee, the security that makes a claim credible: God has posted a bond. The resurrection is offered not as a comforting doctrine but as the evidence for the appointment, the public demonstration that this man is the one: good news, and also a warning that the risen man will judge you. And it is offered to all, a public event open to anyone willing to look into it. Like all the great sermons in Acts (2:24, 32; 10:40–42; 13:30–37), whether the hearers have the Scriptures or not, the speech ends at the empty tomb. The sermon that began with an altar to a god nobody could name ends with a man everybody can.

In everyday life. The only way to be ready for the fixed day is to be found in the Judge himself, trusting him now as Saviour: not with a record of your own, for even your best obedience is flawed, but with his perfect obedience counted as yours (Philippians 3:9). If you have been wronged and see no justice coming, hand the case to the one who will judge in righteousness. You do not have to settle every account yourself; a day has been fixed.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God. That was settled at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Believers will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), where their lives are opened and what was done for him is acknowledged, but the verdict on their persons has already been given. That verdict is justification: the Judge’s own acquittal of the guilty, pronounced in advance, resting on Christ’s record instead of theirs and received by faith (Romans 5:1). The man appointed to judge is the man who bore our judgment, which is why a Christian can call the last day a hope.

Why did Paul not mention the cross in this sermon? Very probably he did, or meant to. Luke gives a summary, and the speech was interrupted (v. 32). The resurrection presupposes a death, and Paul everywhere preached Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). With hearers who had no Bible he had to lay the foundation first: who God is, who we are, and why we need a Saviour, because judgment is coming. That is a wise order for anyone speaking to people with no Christian background: do not begin with the answer before they know the question, but do not stop before you reach the cross.

parallels.desc: he will judge the world in righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the mention of the resurrection the council divides: some mock, others put off deciding, and Paul leaves, having said what he came to say without softening it.

Some mocked. Creation, providence, the unity of the human race, even the summons to repent had been strange but discussable. The resurrection is where an audience that would listen to anything stopped listening. It was not stupidity. Most educated Greeks did not want the body back. Many thought it the soul’s prison, so a bodily resurrection sounded like returning a prisoner to his cell. The resurrection was the stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23; 15:12).

On their own hill. In the Eumenides of Aeschylus, a play set at the founding of this very council and known to every educated Athenian, Apollo declares that when the dust has drunk up a man’s blood, once he is dead there is no resurrection, and the word he uses is anastasis, Paul’s word. That was the Athenian creed on the subject, spoken on the Areopagus in their own literature, and Paul stands on the same ground and contradicts it.

Flesh and bones. Athens was not the first audience to find the news unbelievable: the women’s words seemed to the apostles an idle tale (Luke 24:11). What changed their minds was the risen Lord himself: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). The Areopagus was laughing not at a soul escaping but at a body raised: the mockers on Mars Hill were laughing at a man who had eaten broiled fish in front of his friends.

We will hear you again. The second response is the most common in any century: not refutation but postponement. Some may have meant it, and at least one councillor came to believe (v. 34). But a subject can be kept permanently open, as Felix will do at greater length, sending for Paul often and deciding nothing (24:25–27).

Paul went out. The speech was interrupted, as speeches often are in Acts. He had reached the resurrection, the thing he came to say, and when it was refused he did not stay to soften it.

What should I do when people laugh at what I believe? Expect it, and do not take it as the last word. The resurrection was laughed at the day it was first preached to the clever, and it has outlived every one of the men who laughed. Do not answer mockery with mockery, or water down the claim to stop the laughing. Say the true thing clearly and kindly, and leave it. Then notice the others in the room: the ones who want to hear again, and the quiet one who believes.

Isn’t keeping an open mind the humble thing to do? Many thoughtful people today would stand with those who said, “We will hear you again about this.” But G. K. Chesterton remarked that the point of opening the mind, as of opening the mouth, is to shut it again on something solid. An open mind is a door, not a house to live in. And Pascal saw that on this question the middle ground is not really there: if a day has been fixed and a judge has risen, not deciding is itself a decision, because life goes on being lived one way or the other; in his phrase, we are already embarked. Paul gave the council an event to look into, not a demand to believe without evidence. But he would not let them shelve it, because the Judge who rose is also the Saviour who offers mercy now, and Scripture’s word for the time to answer him is always today (Hebrews 3:15).

Is it reasonable to believe in a bodily resurrection today? Yes, and not because people now know less than the Athenians did. Everyone on that hill knew that dead men stay dead. The Christian claim has never been that dead men usually rise, but that this one did. The tomb was empty, and nobody could produce the body. More than five hundred people saw him alive, most of them still living when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Frightened men became witnesses who would die rather than deny it. Sceptics propose other explanations, from a stolen body to visions born of grief; Christians answer that none accounts for all these facts together. Read the accounts for yourself. Timothy Keller often pointed out that everything hangs on this one event: if Jesus rose, you must take seriously all that he said; if he did not, you need not worry about any of it.

Was Athens a failure that Paul learned from? It is often suggested that he over-reached with philosophy and poetry, got a poor return, and so resolved in Corinth, the very next city, to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). There are reasons to doubt this tidy theory. Paul did preach Christ risen at Athens; that is precisely what they mocked. Luke gives this speech more space than almost any other and presents it as a model of preaching to people with no Bible. And the contrast Paul draws in 1 Corinthians is not with wise engagement but with polished oratory and human cleverness as a means of persuasion, a warning written to a church addicted to celebrity speakers. Athens was hard ground, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. Some places take a long time. That is not the same as having done it wrong.
verseByVerse.note: Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A few believe, among them a member of the council and a woman named Damaris: a small harvest, honestly recorded, and the fruit of God’s own drawing.

Dionysius the Areopagite. Luke names two people. Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council itself, a man of high standing, one of those who had summoned Paul to explain himself. The court examined the gospel, and one of the judges came over. Tradition, recorded by Eusebius, made him the first bishop of Athens.

Damaris and others. We know nothing more of her, and should not invent it. But Luke keeps her name in one of the most male settings in the book, and the two converts he names are an aristocrat and a woman. And others with them, unnumbered and unnamed: that is the whole recorded harvest of one of the most celebrated sermons in Acts.

The honest figure. At Thessalonica, a great many. At Berea, many. At Corinth, where he goes next, so many that the Lord tells him he has many in that city who are his people (18:10). At Athens, two names and some others. And Luke writes it down, without padding it or explaining it away.

The judge who met the Judge. That morning Dionysius had sat in judgment on a strange teacher, and heard that God will judge the world by the man he raised. He believed, bowed to the Judge of the world, and found him a Saviour. In the very hour his resurrection was mocked, the risen Christ was drawing his own to himself, as he had said: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).

The apostolic standard. If your own work, like Paul’s at Athens, has produced a handful, you are not below the apostolic standard. You are on it. Nobody remembers who mocked. We know who believed.

Why do some believe and others mock at the same sermon? Because faith is God’s gift, not the preacher’s achievement. The same words fell on the whole council; the difference was not in Paul but in what God did in the hearts of Dionysius and Damaris. As Luke said at Pisidian Antioch, “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (13:48). Behind that sentence stands election: God’s choice, before the foundation of the world, of those he would save, made out of his own love and not on the basis of their merit (Ephesians 1:4–5). This is no reason for careless preaching, for God uses means, and Paul prepared carefully. But it is a great comfort. You are responsible for faithfulness, not for results, and you never know which quiet listener’s heart the Lord has already chosen to open.
verseByVerse.note: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council.

17.theology: General revelation and the need for the gospel. Acts 17 shows what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God open to everyone through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20; see the notes on vv. 22–23 and 26–27). Creation raises the question, and only the gospel answers it: the God who made the nations and is not far from any of us has now spoken in a man he raised from the dead, and calls all people everywhere to repent.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, his spirit provoked, stood before the city’s learned men with the news of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mocked, some believed, and he moved on, leaving Dionysius, Damaris and a few others behind him.

Now: Many people around us are, like Athens, educated, restless and wary of exclusive claims to truth. The Areopagus speech shows a way to speak to them: begin where they are, own what is true in their searching, and then speak of the risen Christ without apology. The resurrection is still the stumbling block, and still the answer to the altar to an unknown god.

keyVerse.quote: because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter arrives here. Whether Paul starts from the Scriptures in a synagogue or from an altar in Athens, every argument ends at the man God raised from the dead and appointed to judge the world. That is why repentance cannot be postponed, and why the Judge’s pierced hands are also the sinner’s hope.

17.reflection:
Paul reasoned from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise (vv. 2–3). Which Old Testament passages help you see Jesus, and how would you explain to a friend why the cross was not an accident but the plan?

The Bereans received the word “with all eagerness” and examined the Scriptures daily (v. 11). Which comes more naturally to you, eagerness or examination? What would it look like to practise both when you hear a sermon this week?

Paul was provoked by the idols of Athens, yet went into the marketplace to talk with people (vv. 16–17). What are the idols of the place where you live, and how can grief over them lead us into conversation rather than complaint or contempt?

At the Areopagus some mocked, some put off deciding, and a few believed (vv. 32–34). Which response do you meet most among people you know, and how does the resurrection, God’s “assurance to all” (v. 31), shape the way you speak to them?

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
Where we are. Acts 18 closes Paul’s second missionary journey and opens his third. Driven out of Thessalonica and Berea and given a cool hearing in Athens (17:32–34), Paul arrives in Corinth alone; by the end of the chapter he has stayed there eighteen months, reported home to Antioch and set out again.

The message. The risen Lord Jesus gathers his people in the hardest places through the plain preaching of his word, and he keeps his servants while they preach it. He tells his frightened apostle, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking”, because he is with him and already has “many in this city who are my people”; and through an emperor’s edict, a tentmaker’s bench, a governor’s indifference and a teachable preacher, he brings them in.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught, and shows along the way that the gospel is no threat to Roman order (see the introduction): here a Roman proconsul himself refuses to treat the Christians as criminals. Believers facing hostility in proud and immoral cities needed to know that fear is not failure and that the Lord has his people there; and young churches needed to see how to help a gifted teacher who had not yet seen everything.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul arrives in Corinth, works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, exiles from Rome, and reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath (vv. 1–4). When Silas and Timothy come he gives himself wholly to the word; reviled, he moves next door, and the synagogue’s own ruler believes, with many Corinthians (vv. 5–8). The Lord’s word in the night keeps him there eighteen months (vv. 9–11). A united attack before the proconsul Gallio collapses, exactly as promised (vv. 12–17). Paul sails with his friends, leaves them at Ephesus, and reports to Jerusalem and Antioch (vv. 18–22), then sets out again to strengthen the disciples (v. 23). In Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila take the eloquent Apollos aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and he goes on to help the believers in Corinth (vv. 24–28).

Where it leads. The voice in the night is Christ’s own, and the people in Corinth are his before they have heard his name, given to him by the Father (John 6:39). Gallio’s tribunal recalls Pilate’s: Christ was condemned at one so that his servants can stand at others unharmed, and Paul would later remind this city that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). And the chapter’s message comes down to one sentence, preached by Paul at its start and by Apollos at its end: “the Christ was Jesus” (vv. 5, 28).

For us. Fear need not silence us, for Christ is with us and has people where we live. He builds his church through ordinary work, patient teaching week after week, gentle private correction and servants glad to be outshone; so keep speaking, keep learning, and leave the walls to him. And if your past seems to disqualify you, remember what Corinth was, and what Christ made of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord who has people in Corinth keeps his frightened servant there until they are gathered. Paul arrives alone, finds work and friends in Aquila and Priscilla, and reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath (vv. 1–4). When Silas and Timothy bring help he gives himself wholly to the word; reviled, he moves next door, and the synagogue’s ruler believes, with many Corinthians (vv. 5–8). A vision in the night tells him not to be afraid, and he stays eighteen months (vv. 9–11). The attack before Gallio collapses as the Lord promised, and the proconsul’s refusal to hear the case shelters the church (vv. 12–17). Paul then sails for home, leaving his friends at Ephesus and reporting to Jerusalem and Antioch (vv. 18–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Tentmaking and the support of ministry

Here for the first time Acts mentions Paul’s manual work as a means of supporting his mission (see v. 3). Paul’s letters show it was an adaptation, not the only pattern (see the box “Where Christians differ: should ministers be paid?” at the end of the note on v. 3), and in Corinth itself the gifts brought by Silas and Timothy from Macedonia freed him to preach full time (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Gallio’s dismissal of the charge against Paul protected his preaching at Corinth by treating it as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God still uses civil authorities and courts to shelter the preaching of the gospel, even when those in power have no understanding of it or sympathy with it.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul comes alone and afraid to the most notorious city in Greece, and the Lord has already sent ahead of him, by an emperor’s decree, two friends who will become his closest co-workers.

To Corinth. About fifty miles west, and a different world. Athens was a university town living on its past; Corinth was money. Destroyed by Rome and refounded a century later as a colony for freedmen and veterans, it had the brashness of new money: the capital of Achaia and one of the richest ports in the empire, on the isthmus between two seas, with a harbour on each.

To Corinthianise. Its reputation had been appalling for centuries; the Greeks had a verb, to Corinthianise, meaning to live immorally. So Paul walks from the Greek world’s most famous seat of learning, where he had won only a handful, into one of its most notorious cities, alone and with no contacts, and he was with them “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3).

Aquila and Priscilla. A married couple who became Paul’s close friends and co-workers (Romans 16:3–5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). Priscilla (Prisca) is often named first, perhaps because she was more prominent or of higher social standing. Luke never records their conversion or calls them Paul’s converts; they simply appear as believers, so they may already have been Christians in the church at Rome.

Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. Here the New Testament and Roman history touch. The Roman biographer Suetonius records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, probably a garbled form of Christ; the expulsion is usually dated about AD 49. If the gospel had reached Rome’s Jewish quarter, a Roman official would have seen what Acts shows in city after city: a synagogue in uproar over a man called Christ.

A forced removal. If so, the edict that drove Aquila and Priscilla from their home concerned a quarrel the emperor did not understand, about the very gospel about to be preached in Corinth; and it delivered to a lonely, frightened apostle two of the most useful colleagues he would ever have. They would house him, work beside him, teach Apollos, risk their necks for him (Romans 16:4) and host churches in more than one city. One of the most fruitful partnerships in the New Testament began with an expulsion.

Another emperor, another decree. Luke has shown us this before. “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered” (Luke 2:1), and it sent a carpenter and his pregnant wife to Bethlehem, where the ruler of Israel was to be born (Micah 5:2). Now Claudius signs an order about a riot over Christ, and it sends a tentmaker and his wife to Corinth, where Christ means to build his church. The emperors issue their decrees, and the Son of God moves through them unhindered.

What if my move, job loss or upheaval was forced on me? Then you are in good company, and in good hands. Aquila and Priscilla lost home, business and city by an emperor’s signature, and the Lord used it to put them exactly where his apostle needed them. The loss was real, and you need not pretend yours was painless. But the decision taken over your head was not the last word on your life: the God who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28) does not wait for better rulers before he can use you. Ask him, in the new place, whom he has set beside you, and whom he has set you beside.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy trading city with a reputation for immorality. The Roman historian Suetonius mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome over disturbances, around AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostle earns his living at a workbench, and his ordinary trade is part of his ministry, not an interruption of it.

Tentmakers. They worked with leather and with the coarse goats’-hair cloth for which Cilicia, Paul’s home province, was known: a trade of the awl and the knife, hard on the hands. Jewish teachers were encouraged to learn a trade rather than make money from teaching the law, so Paul the Pharisee, trained under Gamaliel, had also learned to cut leather, and in Corinth it kept him alive.

Six days at the bench. The working day ran from first light until the light went, and Paul was at the bench for it. He reminds this very church that the apostles labour, working with their own hands (1 Corinthians 4:12), and the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to burden them (1 Thessalonians 2:9). He supported himself to remove any suspicion that he preached for money, a charge he had to answer more than once at Corinth. And a workshop in that world opened onto the street: customers came, apprentices worked, neighbours stopped. Much of the conversation that founded this church probably happened over the bench, with both men’s hands busy.

The carpenter’s apostle. At the bench Paul is following his Master more closely than it might seem. Nazareth knew Jesus simply as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3): the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3) probably made doors, yokes and roof beams for the village. So the apostle cutting leather in Corinth has not stepped down from his calling. He walks where his Lord walked first, and in the Lord, he later wrote to this city, your labour is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

How can my ordinary job serve the gospel? In three ways, all visible here. The work itself is service to God when it is done honestly and well, as for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23); a good tent is not spiritually neutral. It puts you among people a pastor may never meet, on their ground and on equal terms, where conversations happen naturally. And it gives you a life that commends the gospel: paying your way, keeping your word, not being a burden. You do not need to preach at the photocopier. Be the colleague whose faith people ask about, and be ready when they do.

Where Christians differ: should ministers be paid? Some say ministers should always work a trade like Paul; others that the church must always support them. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that those who preach the gospel have a right to live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18), and he accepted gifts (Philippians 4:15–16; 2 Corinthians 11:8–9), but he sometimes gave up that right for the gospel’s sake. Both patterns are biblical. Churches should support their ministers generously; ministers may work when the work requires it.

Uncertain wording. The word for tentmakers (skēnopoioi) is rare, and its exact sense is uncertain: makers of tents and awnings, in leather, cloth or both, or, as some early Christian writers took it, leatherworkers more generally. Either way it was skilled manual work.
verseByVerse.note: Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth. Jewish teachers commonly had a trade; Paul supported himself so as not to burden the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reasons patiently week after week, and when gifts from Macedonia free him from the bench, he gives himself wholly to one message: the Christ is Jesus.

Every Sabbath. Not a campaign but a routine, Sabbath after Sabbath in the synagogue, by a man who spent the other six days cutting leather. The second verb is honest: he tried to persuade. Luke does not say he persuaded them, and the wording leaves room for weeks when nothing seemed to happen.

Occupied with the word. Something changes when Silas and Timothy arrive. Occupied (syneicheto) means wholly absorbed, held fast: he is no longer fitting the gospel round the working day. Why? Paul tells us: “the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need” (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15). Silas and Timothy probably brought gifts from the churches there, Philippi above all, and good news from Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:6), and the apostle put down his tools and preached full time.

What a gift buys. The Macedonians were not wealthy: they gave out of extreme poverty, beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:2–3). What their gift bought was hours, the hours Paul would have spent at a bench, turned straight into hours in front of people. The church at Corinth exists partly because Christians in Philippi went without something. Behind their giving stood the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), and every gift given for his name is only grace flowing back toward its source.

That the Christ was Jesus. Not that Jesus was a Christ, or a good man, or a way, but that the Christ they had waited and prayed for every Sabbath in that building was this particular man. In Corinth Paul “decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2): not a Messiah who had driven out Rome but one Rome had nailed up, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, yet the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). Everything else Paul preached hangs on that one claim.

If nothing seems to happen. If you teach, whether children, a home group or a Sunday school, take heart that Paul tried to persuade week after week when nothing seemed to happen. Turning up again is part of the work.

How much should I give, and to what? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for Christians, but gives principles: give regularly, in proportion to what you have, cheerfully and generously (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). Your first responsibility is to your own church, so that those who teach you can give themselves to the word (Galatians 6:6); beyond that, the Macedonians show the joy of supporting gospel work far away. Many Christians find a tenth a good starting point and grow from there. The question is not how little is required but what the grace of Christ moves you to give.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the synagogue turns to open abuse, Paul declares himself clear of their blood, like a watchman who has blown the trumpet, and sets up the church next door.

When they opposed and reviled him. Reviled (blasphēmountōn) can mean slandering a man or blaspheming God, and here probably both: insults against Paul and against the Christ he preached. The argument has stopped being an argument, and to insult the Son is to insult the God who sent him (Luke 10:16).

He shook out his garments. A gesture of breaking off responsibility, like shaking the dust from the feet (13:51; Nehemiah 5:13). It says: I have nothing of yours on me, and I carry nothing away.

Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. The language of the watchman in Ezekiel 33. If he sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, God will require the blood at his hand; if he blows it and the people take no warning, their blood is on their own heads, and he is free of blame (Ezekiel 33:1–9; compare 20:26). The watchman answers for the trumpet, not for whether anybody comes inside the walls. Paul has reasoned in that synagogue for weeks and been reviled for it; his conscience is clear, not because he succeeded, but because he spoke.

The house of a man named Titius Justus. A bold choice. He sets up the Christian meeting on the other side of the wall, in the house of a worshiper of God, a Gentile who had presumably been sitting in that synagogue listening to him; some identify him with Gaius, Paul’s host in Corinth (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14). There is steel in that, but not spite. The congregation that threw him out will have the believers meeting next door, including, in the very next verse, their own ruler: a door of mercy open beside a door of judgment.

The watchman who wept. Paul learned this from his Lord, who also warned a city that would not listen: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). Ezekiel’s chapter gives the heart behind every warning: God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Christ is that heart in flesh. He did not only sound the alarm; he suffered outside the gate of the city that rejected him (Hebrews 13:12), so that people who had reviled him could be brought home. Paul shakes out his cloak; his Master wept over the city that refused him.

For the one who grieves. That distinction matters to anyone grieving over somebody unconverted: a father, a brother, a child who has heard it all and wants none of it. There is a burden that belongs to you and one that does not, and mixed together they wear a person out, praying under the weight of an outcome he was never given charge of. You answer for the trumpet, not for the walls; only Christ can open an ear, and salvation belongs to the Lord. So lay the weight down in prayer, and keep speaking when you can, loving always.

What it does not mean. Not a licence to give up. Paul says this to a synagogue that had turned hostile after long patience, not to someone who had said no once, and his resolve to go to the Gentiles holds for Corinth only: in the next city he goes to the synagogue first again (v. 19).

When is it right to stop speaking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never in the heart. Paul stopped arguing in this synagogue after months of open blasphemy, but he did not stop loving its people or praying for them; he could wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). With family or friends the lesson is usually to change the approach, not to walk away: when words only provoke scorn, keep praying, keep loving, keep living next door, and be ready when the door opens again. Jesus warned against throwing pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but that is wisdom in speaking, not permission to stop caring.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility.

parallels.desc: his blood shall be on his own head

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after Paul leaves the synagogue, its ruler believes, with his household and many Corinthians: no one is too respectable to need grace, and no one too ruined to receive it.

Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord. Luke has put this immediately after verse 6 on purpose. Paul has just shaken out his garments at that synagogue, and the first convert Luke names afterwards is the man who ran it. A synagogue ruler was not a rabbi but the official responsible for the building and the services, the man who had been giving Paul the platform and quite possibly had to withdraw it: a person of standing, with everything to lose. Years later Paul was thankful he had baptised almost none of the Corinthians, except Crispus and Gaius (1 Corinthians 1:14). The ruler was not saved by his religion any more than the drunkards of Corinth were saved by turning over a new leaf; he came by the same door they did, with empty hands.

Many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed. Hearing, believing, baptism: the order again. Many, in the town whose name was a byword for vice. Paul later lists what some of them had been: idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, swindlers, the sins that city was famous for. Then he writes a sentence that has carried countless people out of their past: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Were. If you have a history you assume disqualifies you, that verb was written to the church founded in this verse: not “are”, but “were”. It changed not because the Corinthians reformed themselves but because of the name in which they were washed: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). Washed of guilt, set apart as God’s own, declared righteous by the Judge, not because they had become sinless overnight but because Christ’s righteousness was counted as theirs (Romans 4:5): the past is real, and it is past, because he has dealt with it.

Pray for the unlikely one. Name to yourself the person you have quietly decided will never come to Christ, and pray for him: the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth was converted.

If I was baptised as an infant, should I be baptised now? Take the question seriously and kindly. On the view this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, baptism is for those who have repented and believed, so a believer baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, not as a rejection of his parents’ love but as obedience to Christ’s pattern. Talk it through with your pastor. If your church baptises infants, be honest with its elders about your conscience, and seek peace. Many godly Christians differ here; none of them is saved by water, and all who trust Christ are washed by his blood.

Where Christians differ: does this household baptism support infant baptism? Christians who baptise infants read the household baptisms of Acts as a covenant pattern, in which a believer’s household is included with him. This commentary’s view: Luke says the household believed, so this describes believers, as with Cornelius (10:44–48) and the jailer (16:34).

parallels.desc: I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord comes to his frightened apostle in the night and tells him to keep speaking, for three reasons: Christ is with him, no attack will defeat his work, and Christ already has many people in this city.

Do not be afraid. You do not tell a man not to be afraid unless he is. He had been beaten in Philippi, chased out of Thessalonica and Berea, mocked in Athens, and now the synagogue had turned on him. The man who wrote more of the New Testament’s letters than anyone knew what fear was.

But go on speaking and do not be silent. Not rest, and not go somewhere safer: the same instruction twice, positively and negatively, as you might speak to someone on the edge of stopping. The cure for the fear is to keep doing the thing that caused it, with the Lord beside you.

For I am with you. Not a promise to protect his reputation or his comfort, but presence: the promise of God to Joshua, to Jeremiah and to the apostles at the end of Matthew (Joshua 1:9; Jeremiah 1:8; Matthew 28:20). The risen Jesus who promised to be with his church always now comes into one frightened man’s room in Corinth and says it to him alone. The voice Paul first heard on the Damascus road is the voice beside him in the dark.

No one will attack you to harm you. It does not say nobody will attack him; in two verses’ time he is dragged before the tribunal. It promises that no attack will land as harm, which is not a lesser promise but a truer one: for eighteen months what happened to Paul could not stop what God was doing through him. He was later arrested and, by early tradition, executed elsewhere, which is no failure of this word, because it was given about Corinth and about that time.

I have many in this city who are my people. The third reason is the strangest and best. Corinth, wicked as it was, held many whom God had chosen: not yet converted, but already his. And it is Jesus who says “my people”. They were the Son’s before they had heard his name, given to him by the Father, and of all that the Father gives him he will lose nothing (John 6:39). This is election: before the world was made, God set his love on particular people to be his own, freely, with nothing in them to prompt it (Ephesians 1:4–5). Paul preached not knowing who they were; Christ knew, and the gospel would find them. No city is too dark for the Good Shepherd who says, I have other sheep, and I must bring them also (John 10:16).

In the flow. The vision stands at the centre of the Corinth story, between the break with the synagogue (vv. 6–7) and eighteen months of teaching (v. 11) and an attack that fails exactly as promised (vv. 12–17).

When a promise seems to fail. God’s particular assurances of protection in Scripture are almost always attached to a work and a season: they promise that the work will not be defeated, not that you will not be touched. The promises that cover every believer at every hour go deeper: nothing will separate us from the love of God in Christ (Romans 8:35–39), and not a hair of our head will finally perish (Luke 21:18).

Hear it as spoken to you. Name the fear that has made you quiet, of being mocked, of losing a friendship, of saying it badly, and hear the three reasons as said to you. The Spirit who made Paul bold lives in you (1:8), so have one conversation this week you would otherwise have avoided. And where you have kept silent, as all of us have, remember that Christ never once withheld his Father’s word, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19).

Does this verse teach election? Arminian Christians, who hold that God’s choice rests on his foreknowledge of who will believe, read “my people” as those he foresaw would believe, and many of them are faithful and fruitful evangelists. But the Lord calls them his people before they believe, and gives that as the reason Paul should stay and preach; the more natural reading is that God has chosen his people and calls them through the preaching of the gospel (13:48).

How do I know if the person I am speaking to is one of the elect? You do not, and you need not. Paul knew only that there were many. Election is God’s secret until it shows itself in faith (Deuteronomy 29:29); our instruction is to offer Christ freely and sincerely to everyone, pleading with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). Treat every person as someone the Lord may be about to call, and you will speak with hope. And if you are worried whether you yourself are chosen, do not search the hidden decree but come to Christ: all who come to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: does election discourage evangelism? Some think that if God has chosen his people, there is no need to preach. This commentary’s view: here election is the reason to keep preaching. God has his people; the gospel is the means by which they are called (Romans 10:14–17; 2 Timothy 2:10). Election guarantees that preaching will not be in vain.

parallels.desc: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s promise lets Paul put down roots: he stays eighteen months and lays in Corinth the only foundation there is, Jesus Christ.

A year and six months. His longest stay so far, and against the rest of the book an extraordinary number: weeks or months at Thessalonica, weeks at Berea, days at Athens. In the first two journeys Paul plants and is moved on, usually by force. Here he stops, and Luke puts the verse straight after the vision because the vision explains it.
