A man hunted from town to town does not build; a man told that there are many in this city who belong to God can unpack.

Teaching the word of God among them. Sustained instruction, taking a mixed congregation of Jews, God-fearers and converted pagans through the Scriptures. Paul later told this church what those months had been: “like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation”, and “no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:10–11). The church was not built on Paul’s personality, though some talked as if it were, and when his letters came to correct them he laid no new foundation but took them back down to the one already there. The Lord Jesus is a patient builder: he lays his church stone by stone, sermon by sermon, over months and years and centuries, and never tires of the work.

Letters written from Corinth. Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this time (1 Thessalonians 3:6), among the earliest of his letters we possess: written by a tentmaker to a church he had been driven from and could not get back to, and now in every Bible on earth.

Put down roots. If you are tempted to leave a church because it is not exciting, ask first whether it is feeding you on Scripture week by week. If it is, stay and put down roots, and thank God for the pastors and teachers who give years, not weeks, to the same people.

Why does solid teaching matter so much if the gospel is simple? Because the gospel is simple enough for a child to receive and deep enough to occupy us for eternity, and Christians who are not taught are easily confused, discouraged or led astray (Ephesians 4:14). The Corinthians had eighteen months of Paul and still went wrong on factions, sex, lawsuits, worship and the resurrection; imagine them without it. Good teaching does not replace faith; it feeds it. So sit under the preaching of the Bible gladly and regularly, join a group that studies it, and be patient. Growth in grace is slow, like a tree, and most of it happens out of sight.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opposition finally unites and brings Paul before the new Roman governor, with a charge framed to make Rome do what it cannot do itself.

When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia. With one name Luke hands historians one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for fixing dates. An inscription at Delphi carries a letter from the emperor Claudius which mentions Gallio as proconsul of Achaia and dates his term to about AD 51–52. Proconsuls usually served for a year, so Paul was in Corinth in the early fifties, and most other dates in his life, his conversion, the Jerusalem council, the letters, are reckoned outward from this verse.

What a proconsul was. A senior senator sent out, usually for a year, to govern a settled province for the Senate, with supreme civil and judicial authority: a governor who was also the province’s chief judge. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was such a province at this time; its status shifted over the years, and Luke names it correctly for this moment.

The man on the bench. Gallio was the elder brother of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and tutor to the young Nero, who dedicated books to him and spoke of his charm as something nobody could resist. That is the temperament on the bench: cultivated, easy-going, and entirely uninterested in the matter in front of him.

The Jews made a united attack. After months in which the synagogue had lost its ruler and many members, the opposition coordinates and chooses its moment: a new governor, freshly arrived, who might want a quiet province. The tribunal (bēma) was the judgment platform in the forum (see v. 16).

Contrary to the law. The charge is carefully built, and its ambiguity is the whole strategy. Which law? If Gallio hears Roman law, which permitted Judaism as a lawful religion, Paul is promoting an unlicensed religion and can be shut down across the province by a single ruling; they probably wanted Rome to rule that Christianity was not Judaism and so had no legal standing. If he hears Jewish law, it is a synagogue quarrel and none of his business. Everything depends on a busy proconsul hearing the word law and reaching for the wrong one.

A charge Luke’s readers have heard before. The leaders once brought Jesus to a Roman governor and said, “We found this man misleading our nation” (Luke 23:2), hoping Rome would do what they could not. Pilate found no crime in him and handed him over anyway. Here the same move fails at once, and not because Gallio is a better man than Pilate. Pilate’s tribunal stood on the road God had appointed for his Son, the road to the cross (4:27–28), and Christ went there alone, condemned in the place of his people. Paul, who preaches him, comes to Gallio’s tribunal under a word given for Corinth: “no one will attack you to harm you” (v. 10).

Why does it matter that the Bible gets names and dates right? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas but a report of things that happened: a man was crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day. If Luke were careless about proconsuls, we might wonder whether he was careless about the resurrection. Instead, again and again, inscriptions and histories confirm his titles, places and dates. That does not prove the gospel by itself, but it shows the witness is trustworthy; Luke wrote “that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4). Not every question is settled (the census of Luke 2:2, for instance, is still debated), and believers hold Scripture true while admitting honestly that some such puzzles remain unresolved.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52 — one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. The tribunal (bema) still stands in the Corinthian marketplace.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Paul can say a word, Gallio throws the case out as a Jewish quarrel about words and names, and his careless ruling shelters the church for years.

When Paul was about to open his mouth. He draws breath to make his defence, and the governor cuts across him and decides the case. It is one of the few hearings in Acts where Paul says nothing at all, and it goes better for him than almost any other.

Wrongdoing or vicious crime. Gallio has seen through the ambiguity. A Roman court would hear a case of real wrongdoing or serious villainy, and this, he observes, is neither.

Questions about words and names and your own law. Gallio has filed the whole business as a dispute over terms within a foreign religion: whether a particular Jewish title belongs to a particular dead Jew. He is not entirely wrong about the subject and completely wrong about its weight. The name he waved away is the one name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12). One day the judge of Achaia will give account to the one he would not hear, and the name he could not be bothered to weigh will be the name by which he is judged.

A crucial ruling. The consequence was enormous and entirely unintended. Treated as an internal Jewish matter, Christianity was sheltered for now under the legal standing Judaism enjoyed as an ancient, permitted faith, probably for years, until Nero; and Luke likely records the ruling partly to show that Christianity was no threat to Rome (see the introduction). God gave his church that cover through a man who could not have been less interested in it. Gallio was not kind or secretly sympathetic; he was declining to waste an afternoon. Yet Christ had said that no one would harm his servant, and he kept his word through a man who did not care. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1).

Classification. This is the commonest reaction the gospel meets in a comfortable society: not persecution, not conversion, but classification. It is filed as a private religious preference and set aside without hostility by somebody with other things to do. Athens laughed; Gallio simply did not think it was about anything.

Pray, then rest. Think of the authority over your circumstances who seems most indifferent: the employer, the council, the court, the government. Pray for them, as you are told to (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and then rest. Your safety does not depend on their goodwill. The Lord who used Gallio’s boredom can use their busyness.

Isn’t faith a private matter? It sounds tolerant, and Gallio would have agreed with every word. Lesslie Newbigin, who spent decades as a missionary in India and came home to find Britain a mission field in its own right, argued that the modern West has divided life into two rooms: public facts, which everyone must accept, and private values, which each of us may choose. Religion is given a place in the second room and called respected, which mostly means ignored. But the arrangement is not neutral; it is itself a belief about the world, that nothing God has done could ever count as a fact. The gospel will not stay in the private room, because it is news before it is advice: a man was crucified under a Roman governor and raised on the third day, in a world with courts and calendars and named officials like Gallio. That is why it is for everyone, not only the religiously inclined. A private faith could at best comfort me; a true one can save my neighbour too.

How should I respond when people treat my faith as just words and names? Without anger, and without accepting the label. Show that it is about something: a real man who really rose, a real God to whom all must give account, a real forgiveness that changes lives. Gallio could dismiss a vocabulary; it is much harder to dismiss a neighbour whose marriage, honesty and hope have been visibly changed by Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a Roman crime.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers are swept from the judgment seat before the whole city, and Paul would later point his readers from that platform to a greater one, the judgment seat of Christ.

He drove them from the tribunal. The verb is not polite. He had them driven off, perhaps by his lictors, the attendants who enforced a magistrate’s orders: the case not merely dismissed but swept out. The delegation that came with a coordinated complaint, timed for a new governor and framed to make Rome act, is pushed away from the bench in front of the city, told that their religion is not worth a magistrate’s time.

The judgment seat. The tribunal was the bēma, the raised platform in the Corinthian marketplace from which a magistrate gave judgment; a platform identified as this one still stands. Paul did not forget it. He wrote to these Christians that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10), and to Rome that “we will all stand before the judgment seat of God” (Romans 14:10). The Corinthians had seen their apostle dragged in front of one.

Two judgment seats. Set them side by side, as Paul may well have meant his readers to. At the first, the judge would not hear the case, the accused was never allowed to speak, and the verdict came from a man who thought the matter beneath him. At the second, every case is heard, nothing is dismissed as a quarrel about words and names, and the Judge has taken the trouble to become one of the accused. That should sober us before it comforts us: the holy God hears every case and sees every motive. Yet the Judge was himself condemned in a court that would not hear the truth, so that those who trust him will be acquitted in the court where truth is all. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Can God really use people who do not know him? Yes, constantly: Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, and Caesar Augustus, whose census brought Mary to Bethlehem. God’s providence governs all his creatures and all their actions (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1; the Westminster Confession 5.1), without making him the author of their sin or excusing them for it. So a Christian can pray for unbelieving rulers, employers and relatives with real hope: God can use them for good whether they intend it or not. But do not mistake being used for being saved. Gallio rendered real service to the purposes of God and remained entirely outside them. The only safe place is not on the right side of history, but in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The indifference that protected Paul now lets the synagogue’s ruler be beaten in front of the bench; and Paul, left in peace, stays on, then sails for home with Priscilla and Aquila, keeping a Jewish vow in Christian freedom.

They all seized Sosthenes. A crowd has watched the delegation thrown out of court, and does what crowds do with people publicly stripped of protection: it beats their leader where the proconsul can see. Sosthenes had probably led the failed case. Who beat him? Perhaps Greeks venting anti-Jewish feeling, perhaps Jews angry at his failure (see the textual note below). Either way, nobody here is defending Paul; the mob simply turns on whoever has just lost.

Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue. Most likely the successor of Crispus, who had believed (v. 8), or else a fellow ruler, since a synagogue could have more than one (13:15). Now read the first line of Paul’s later letter to this city: “Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes” (1 Corinthians 1:1). It is not certain they are the same man, and it should not be asserted. But it is a striking coincidence, and if it is the same man, this beating is the last thing the New Testament records of him before he turns up as a Christian beside the apostle he had prosecuted.

Gallio paid no attention to any of this. The indifference that had just protected the church now watches a man beaten in front of the bench and declines to intervene. Luke sets the two effects of one man’s temperament side by side without comment. Detachment is not a virtue: it served the gospel in one verse and left a man bleeding in the next.

The Judge who pays attention. Luke’s Gospel has another beaten man in it. On the night of his trial the men holding Jesus mocked him as they beat him, blindfolded him and struck him (Luke 22:63–64), and no one in authority lifted a hand. So the battered ruler of the synagogue, whom Rome would not even look at, is not beyond Christ’s sympathy: we have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). The Lord is the opposite of Gallio in everything that matters. He sees the blow the bench ignores and hears the case the court will not hear.

Paul stayed many days longer. He does not leave in a hurry, a mark of how completely Gallio’s ruling had changed things. And when he goes, the couple who took him in go with him, leaving the city and the business they had rebuilt after being expelled from Rome.

At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port, and a church grew there too, served by our sister Phoebe (Romans 16:1), who probably carried Paul’s letter to Rome. There the apostle of justification by faith, the teaching that God declares sinners right with himself through faith in Christ and not by keeping the law, had his head shaved because of a vow. It has the shape of the Nazirite vow, in which a man separated himself to the LORD for a period, drank no wine, let his hair grow, and cut it off at the end (Numbers 6:1–21); perhaps it was a vow of thanksgiving, ended as he left Corinth (see the box at the end of this note).

May a believer still keep the law? Paul’s vow raises the question. The Reformed answer distinguishes three strands in the law of Moses. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God’s unchanging character and abides; we are not saved by it, but believers gladly obey it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, food laws, circumcision as rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (Colossians 2:16–17); no Christian is bound to keep it. The civil law of Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5; the Westminster Confession 19.3–5).

The careful line Paul walks. Here a Jewish vow, later a temple purification (21:23–26) and Timothy’s circumcision (16:3); yet a flat refusal to circumcise Titus (Galatians 2:3–5), and thunder against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Galatians 5:2–4). The difference is always the reason. Made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, a practice denies the gospel; kept freely, as heritage, devotion, conscience or love that wins a hearing (to the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews, 1 Corinthians 9:20), it is Christian liberty. And the freedom is real because the substance has come: every vow and feast pointed to Christ, and all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The two cases. So a Jewish believer may in liberty keep ancestral customs, feasts or a vow, as heritage, devotion and witness among his people, provided he never makes them the ground of his standing nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation to the ceremonial law (the verdict of Acts 15), and must never put himself under the law as a system, which is to fall from grace (Galatians 5:1–4). The test in every case: am I doing this to be accepted, or because I am accepted in Christ? Whether the fourth commandment continues as a Christian Sabbath is one place believers differ; many, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that it does, kept on the Lord’s Day. This commentary takes the view that the Sabbath is a shadow whose substance is Christ (Colossians 2:16–17): Christ is our rest, and the Lord’s Day is a gift gladly kept, not a law.

Should Christians today make vows to God? Scripture permits them but does not require them, and warns against rash ones: it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). Jesus forbade oath-making that treats some promises as binding and others as not, and told us to let our yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37). A lawful vow is a voluntary promise to God of something good and within your power, made thoughtfully, never as a bargain to get something from him or to earn his favour (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 23; the Westminster Confession 22.6–7). Marriage vows and church membership vows are the most common today, and should be kept with the seriousness of a promise made before God.

Uncertain wording. Whose vow was it, and what kind? The grammar could refer to Aquila, named just before, but Paul is the natural subject of the sentence. The vow has the shape of a Nazirite vow, but the law had a Nazirite’s hair shaved at the sanctuary when the vow was completed (Numbers 6:18), not in a port, so it may have been a private vow of a similar kind, with the hair perhaps offered later in Jerusalem. Luke does not say. What is clear is that a Jewish believer kept a vow freely, as Paul would again (21:23–26).

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, say that all the Greeks seized Sosthenes; the earliest say only that they all did.
verseByVerse.note: A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port. Cutting the hair marked the end of a vow of special devotion.

parallels.desc: the Nazirite vow
Phoebe of Cenchreae

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul leaves two tentmakers in the greatest city of Asia and, when an eager synagogue begs him to stay, declines: an open door is not always a summons.

They came to Ephesus, and he left them there. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, where the Spirit had forbidden him to preach at the start of this journey (16:6), and where he would later spend three years. Now the door opens, and what he leaves behind is a married couple with a trade. Within a few verses they will finish the education of one of the most gifted preachers in the eastern Mediterranean, and later a church meets in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19). Paul’s strategy for the greatest city in Asia was to leave two tentmakers in it.

He himself went into the synagogue. Days off the boat, in a city he is only passing through, and he is in the synagogue arguing. There is no version of Paul that takes a week to look round a town.

He declined. After Pisidian Antioch, Lystra, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and the tribunal at Corinth, here at last is a receptive synagogue in the most strategic city in the province, asking for more, and he leaves. He wanted to reach Jerusalem, perhaps for a feast, and there was a sending church to report to.

The one who holds the key. Behind every door on this journey stands one person. The Spirit forbade Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus would not allow Bithynia (16:6–7). So in declining an open door Paul is not losing his nerve but waiting on the one who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7). A few years later, writing from this city, Paul would say that a wide door for effective work had opened to him (1 Corinthians 16:9). The door was the same; the hand on it was Christ’s, and he chose the hour.

An open door is not a summons. On the road to Troas every door was shut, and the shutting turned out to be direction; here every door is open, and it is still not the instruction. Paul had a genuine opportunity, urged on him by people who wanted the gospel, and he said no and went home to his church. Not every good thing you could do is a thing you are being asked to do; some belong to somebody else, or to a later year.

How do I know whether an opportunity is from God? Ask more than whether it is open and good. Ask whether it fits what God has already given you to do: your existing responsibilities, your church, your family, the work in hand. Ask those who know you well and whose wisdom you trust, as Paul went back to his sending church. Ask whether you can say yes to it without saying no to something God has clearly called you to. Pray, and be willing to wait. Scripture gives no promise of private signals for every choice, but it gives wisdom (James 1:5), and wisdom often sounds like “not yet”.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul promises to return if God wills, and means it; then he greets the church in Jerusalem and reports to the church that sent him, and the second journey is over.

I will return to you if God wills. Paul meant the words literally. He writes the same to Corinth, that he will come soon, if the Lord wills (1 Corinthians 4:19), and James turns it into a settled Christian habit: instead of boasting about tomorrow, we ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:13–15).

A phrase with teeth. In our mouths it is often a pious formula; in Paul’s it had teeth. On this journey he had been forbidden to speak in Asia, forbidden to enter Bithynia, sent to Macedonia by a vision, and driven out of three cities in succession. And God did will it (19:1): he returned, and stayed. The phrase was not pessimism but accuracy about who was arranging the itinerary.

He went up and greeted the church. You always go up to Jerusalem, set among the hills, and down from it; so “went up and greeted the church”, with no city named, means the mother church in Jerusalem, a visit Luke covers in a handful of words.

And then went down to Antioch. Home to the sending church that had fasted, prayed and laid hands on Barnabas and Saul (13:1–3), presumably to report as after the first journey (14:27). So ends the second missionary journey, roughly three years and perhaps 2,800 miles: churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth, Priscilla and Aquila left in Ephesus, and probably the letters to the Thessalonians written. The journey that began with a quarrel about John Mark ends in the same city, with the mission enormously enlarged.

Learned from the Son. Paul learned this from his Lord. Jesus came down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of him who sent him (John 6:38), and on the night of his arrest he prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The Son of God lived every day as one long “if God wills”, and for him the Father’s will meant a cross. So the phrase is not fatalism in a Christian’s mouth: the will we bow to is the will of a Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and whatever he wills for our tomorrow cannot be against us.

Accountable to a local church. Paul had seen the risen Christ and been given the gospel by revelation, and he still travelled hundreds of miles to come back to the ordinary local church that had sent him. If you serve in any way beyond your local church, report back to it as he did: tell them what God has done, and let them pray and rejoice with you.

Does saying if God wills mean I should not make plans? No. Paul made detailed plans, and Scripture commends the forethought of the ant and of the builder who counts the cost (Proverbs 6:6–8; Luke 14:28). What James forbids is planning as if we owned tomorrow, a quiet rival to God that tells us we are safe only when tomorrow belongs to us. So plan carefully, work hard, and hold every plan with an open hand. Say “if the Lord wills” and mean it: when a plan is overturned you will be disappointed, but not shaken, because you never thought the itinerary was yours.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that Paul said he must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem; the earliest manuscripts do not have the words.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s church grows by going back as well as going on, and by believers helping one another to see him more clearly. Paul begins his third journey by revisiting the churches of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (v. 23). In Ephesus a learned and fervent Alexandrian, Apollos, teaches accurately about Jesus, though he knows only the baptism of John (vv. 24–25). Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and he accepts it (v. 26). The church sends him to Corinth with a letter, and there he greatly helps those who through grace had believed, showing from the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Complete teaching

Apollos’s knowledge was accurate as far as it went but stopped short of the full apostolic message (see vv. 24–25). Priscilla and Aquila show how to help (see v. 26), and that is the work of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went on to Achaia and strengthened the believers there by showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. Now: The church is still built by ministers whose gifts complement each other: one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins his third journey by going back over old ground, strengthening every disciple in the churches he had already planted.

He departed. Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey, probably around AD 53, centred on Ephesus. No commissioning service, no vision, no laying on of hands: Paul simply leaves and starts walking.

From one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia. Back over the same ground. These regions take in the towns of the first journey, Derbe, Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch, where he was stoned and expelled, and which he had already revisited twice. The phrase suggests an unhurried, methodical circuit rather than a dash through.

Strengthening all the disciples. Nothing here is new territory or new converts. It is maintenance, and Luke’s verb, making firm what is already standing, is the one he used of Paul’s earlier return visits (14:22; 15:41). And it is “all” the disciples: not only the promising or the strategic ones.

In the flow. Two journeys meet in this verse: the second has just ended at Antioch (v. 22), and the third begins with Paul going the long way to Ephesus (v. 21), while Luke pauses for Apollos (vv. 24–28).

The chief Shepherd’s rounds. Behind Paul’s long walk stands his Lord’s own care. Jesus told Peter that he had prayed for him, that his faith would not fail, and that when he had turned again he must strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Christ does not only plant churches; he keeps them, praying for them and sending his servants back to make them firm. Every return visit to Lystra or Iconium was the risen Christ looking in on his own sheep by the feet of a servant, and no disciple in those small towns was too small for his rounds.

Going back. It is tempting to believe that the real work is the founding and everything afterwards is administration. Paul spent much of his life going back, and his letters are the same work conducted by post. If your service to God consists largely of turning up again for the same people, you are doing what the apostle to the Gentiles did with his time.

What does strengthening other Christians actually look like? Mostly ordinary things. Turning up. Remembering what someone told you last week and asking how it went. Opening the Bible with them at a promise that fits their trouble. Praying with them, not only for them. Warning them gently when they drift, and reminding them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22). A message on the anniversary of a bereavement. None of it is dramatic, and almost all of it matters.
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos is learned, powerful in the Scriptures, on fire and accurate about Jesus, and yet incomplete, for he knows only the baptism of John. Luke will not let us file him as either sound or unsound.

A native of Alexandria. Alexandria explains the man. It was the second city of the empire, the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library and of the largest and most cultured Jewish community outside Judea, where by tradition the Old Testament had first been translated into Greek. A Jew educated there, like Apollos, could be as well educated as anyone in the empire.

An eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. Luke piles up commendations before he raises any difficulty. Eloquent: learned, articulate. Competent: mighty in the Scriptures. Some in Corinth later preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6), and some, from Luther on, have guessed he wrote Hebrews. And he had been instructed in the way of the Lord.

Fervent in spirit. Fervent (zeōn) is a word used of boiling water: glowing with zeal (on “spirit”, see the box below). And he taught “accurately”: Luke is not damning him with faint praise; what Apollos said about Jesus was true, as far as it went.

Though he knew only the baptism of John. Then this clause. There is nothing wrong with Apollos: he is not a false teacher, a self-promoter, lukewarm or careless. He is excellent, and he is incomplete, and the two are not in tension; the news had simply not all reached him.

What does knowing only the baptism of John mean? John’s baptism was a preparatory baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Luke 3:3), getting people ready for the Messiah who was coming, and John pointed beyond himself to the one who would baptise with the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11). So Apollos’s grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that point. He knew John’s call to repentance and Jesus as the coming one, perhaps even his life and death, and proclaimed him truly as far as it went, but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message: Pentecost, the gift of the Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus.

Apollos and the twelve at Ephesus. His case is close kin to that of the Ephesian disciples of 19:1–7, with a difference: Apollos is simply taught more accurately (v. 26) and is never said to be rebaptised, whereas those men, who had not even heard that the Spirit was given, are baptised into Jesus and receive the Spirit.

In the flow. Luke breaks off Paul’s travels here because Apollos will go on to water what Paul planted in Corinth (vv. 27–28; 1 Corinthians 3:6).

The things concerning Jesus. Luke has used that phrase before. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to two disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). That is what made Apollos formidable: he read the Scriptures as the risen Christ taught his church to read them, with Jesus as their subject, and the Greek Bible of Alexandria, Moses, the Psalms and Isaiah, opened in his hands onto one face. Whatever he still lacked, he had the main thing.

Let the fire give light. Keep learning; the Spirit of truth delights to lead Christ’s people into all the truth. Choose one area of Christian teaching you are hazy on, such as the Holy Spirit, baptism or the last things, and read one good, clear book or passage of Scripture on it this month. Be on fire, by all means, but let the fire give light.

How should I think of a Christian whose understanding is incomplete? As most of us are, in one area or another. Many real believers love Christ and teach truly but have not yet seen everything clearly, because no one has taught them; they need help, not suspicion. Be quick to recognise what is right in them, as Luke was, and slow to assume bad motives. And turn it on yourself: there are things you have not yet understood, and the Lord may send a Priscilla to you. Be ready to be taught.

Uncertain wording. “Fervent in spirit” could mean fervent in his own spirit, full of zeal, or aglow with the Holy Spirit; the Greek allows both, as in Romans 12:11, where Paul uses the same phrase of every Christian. Since Luke adds that Apollos knew only John’s baptism, many take it of his own zeal; others think Luke means the Spirit was already at work in him. Either way he was on fire for the truth he knew.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Priscilla and Aquila hear a gifted preacher fall short and, instead of correcting him in public, take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately; and the great preacher lets himself be taught.

They took him aside. Not up, not out, but aside: privately, away from the congregation, perhaps in their home. They could have corrected him from the floor, which would have humiliated and probably hardened him; warned people about him afterwards, which takes no courage at all; or said nothing, since he was gifted and they were only tentmakers. Instead, tentmakers taught a scholar, gently and in private.

Explained to him the way of God more accurately. Luke’s word is not rebuked or refuted but explained: set it out for him. And not “accurately”, as though he had been wrong, but “more accurately”, because he had been right as far as he went. That is the whole art of helping someone whose understanding is incomplete: privately, personally, over a meal, beginning with what is right.

Priscilla named first. A husband and wife teach together, and Luke names Priscilla first, as the New Testament does in most places the couple appear. In the ancient world that order is unusual enough to be deliberate; a natural explanation is that she took a leading part, or was the more prominent of the two.

More of the same Christ. What did “more accurately” add? Most likely what John’s baptism lacks. John had pointed to one who would baptise with the Holy Spirit; Priscilla and Aquila could tell Apollos the rest as the apostles preached it: that this Jesus, crucified and raised, had been exalted at the right hand of God and, having received the promised Spirit from the Father, had poured him out (2:33), and that his people are now baptised in his name. Not a new subject, but the same Christ seen whole: not only the coming one John announced, but the reigning Lord now giving his Spirit to his church.

And Apollos was taught. Consider what it cost him. He was the most gifted speaker in the room, and he sat down with two tentmakers and let them teach him. His greatest asset here is not his eloquence but that he could be taught. And the Lord who used a tentmaking couple’s table to finish the training of one of his finest preachers is the Teacher who never humiliates, of whom it was written, a bruised reed he will not break (Matthew 12:20). He leads his people from accurate to more accurate, from glory to glory, until we know as we are known.

How do I receive correction well? Like Apollos: assume the person might be right, and listen before defending yourself. Correction given privately and gently is a gift of love; faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). Thank the person, even if you are not yet sure they are right, and take what they said to Scripture, as the Bereans did. If they were right, change, openly if your error was public. A teachable spirit is not weakness; it is the mark of someone God can go on using.

So what may a woman do? A great deal, and churches holding the complementarian view this commentary takes (see the box below) should be quick to say so and make room for it. Like Priscilla, a woman may explain the faith to others in many settings, including to men, as she did here with her husband. She may teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), lead Bible studies, share the gospel with anyone, pray and serve visibly in the church’s life, counsel, write, and use every gift God has given her. What this view reserves to qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. The aim is never to silence women’s gifts but to honour God’s order while putting those gifts to full and joyful use.

Where Christians differ: Priscilla and women teaching. Egalitarian Christians point to Priscilla, named first, together with Phoebe, Junia and the prophesying daughters of Philip (21:9), as evidence that women taught men in the early church, and some use this verse to argue that women may serve as pastors or preachers in the church. This commentary’s view: Priscilla, with her husband, instructed Apollos privately, probably in their home; this was not preaching in the gathered church or exercising authority as an elder. Scripture reserves the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the church’s gathering to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women like Priscilla rightly teach, explain and serve in many ways. This is the complementarian view, held with deep respect for women’s gifts and ministry. And any position on the wider question has to be able to hold this verse comfortably and gladly, because Luke plainly regarded what Priscilla did as one of the most useful things anybody did in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church that helped Apollos now commends him, and in Corinth he waters what Paul planted, helping those whom grace had brought to faith and showing from the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.

The brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. Apollos went with a letter of recommendation, the ordinary means by which the early church moved people around a world where nobody could check anybody’s credentials (2 Corinthians 3:1). So the Ephesian church put its name behind a man who not long before had been preaching an incomplete gospel in their synagogue: not a warning sent ahead of him, but an endorsement.

Those who through grace had believed. In a passing clause about travel arrangements Luke has slipped in a whole doctrine of how anybody comes to faith. Grace means God’s free kindness to people who have deserved the opposite, and faith itself is its gift (Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 1:29). The same is said of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened (16:14), and of the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch (13:48). Before Apollos opened his mouth in Corinth, grace had gone ahead of him.

Showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. The work Paul had done in Corinth (v. 5), now done by somebody else in the same words. Apollos may well have been the more polished speaker; some Corinthians thought so, and said so unkindly about Paul’s own delivery (2 Corinthians 10:10).

Paul pushed him back. Apollos went to Corinth, Paul’s own church, and was such a success that a faction formed round his name: “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul refuses the rivalry: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). And he strongly urged Apollos to go back there (1 Corinthians 16:12), pushing him toward the congregation that preferred him.

One name passed from hand to hand. Priscilla and Aquila taught Apollos; Apollos strengthened the Corinthians; Paul urged him back to them. No link in the chain was jealous of the next, because what was passed along was not a reputation but a name: the Christ was Jesus (v. 5). When Christ is the message, his servants can afford to be small. “He must increase,” John the Baptist said of him, “but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

A letter of your own. Write a short letter of commendation this week: a note telling someone how God has used them, or an encouraging word to a church about a believer moving their way.

What if someone else is more gifted than me in the same ministry? Then thank God for him and pray for his success, as Paul did for Apollos. Jealousy in ministry is common and deadly, because it makes the work about us. The cure is to remember whose field it is: one plants, another waters, God gives the growth, and sower and reaper rejoice together (John 4:36–37). Would you be glad if the church you love grew faster under someone else? If not, take that to Christ, who washed feet and was content to be overlooked.

If faith is a gift, why am I commanded to believe? Because God gives faith through the very command and promise of the gospel. When Christ is offered, you are truly called to trust him, and you truly do the believing; yet when you do, you discover that he opened your heart to do it, so that you cannot boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). The doctrine is a reason not for waiting passively but for humility and assurance. If you have believed, thank God: what he has begun he will finish. If you have not, do not wait to feel chosen. Come to Christ now, and you will find that grace brought you.

Uncertain wording. “Through grace” could go with “he greatly helped”, meaning that Apollos helped them by the grace given to him, or with “had believed”, meaning that they had come to faith through grace. The Greek allows both. Most translations rightly take the second, and that is the reading followed above.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the ground of courage in mission. The Lord’s word to Paul in the night (v. 10) is the doctrine of election given as a promise to a frightened missionary. God’s answer is not that people will respond, but that he already has his people in the city and calls them through the preaching of the gospel. So election is a reason to keep speaking (see vv. 9–10, and the box at the end of that note).
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, kept there by a vision and a promise for eighteen months. The church that came out of those months would cause him more trouble than any other, and would receive his letters on the cross, the resurrection and love.

Now: Every city has people God means to save. The church’s task is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay where the Lord has put it, and to trust that the harvest is his. The believer who speaks of Christ in a hard place is not alone.

keyVerse.quote: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.
keyVerse.note: The Lord’s word in the night is the hinge of the chapter: it keeps Paul in Corinth for eighteen months, and it is kept to the letter when the attack before Gallio fails. It joins Christ’s presence with his servant to Christ’s ownership of his people, and so turns election into a reason to keep speaking, because Christ already has people wherever his word is preached.

18.reflection:
Paul came to Corinth “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3), and the Lord told him not to be afraid but to go on speaking (vv. 9–10). What fears keep you quiet about Christ, and how do the three reasons the Lord gives answer them?

Paul made tents six days a week until gifts from Macedonia freed him to preach full time (vv. 3–5). How can your daily work serve the gospel, and how might your giving buy hours for gospel work somewhere else?

Gallio dismissed the gospel as “questions about words and names” (v. 15). Where do you meet that kind of polite indifference today, and how can a Christian show that the faith is about something real?

Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more accurately, and he listened (v. 26). What helps you give correction gently and receive it humbly? Is there someone you need to encourage, or to learn from?

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Where we are. Paul’s second journey ended with a brief stop in Ephesus and a promise to return (18:19–21); his third keeps it. He settles in the capital of the province of Asia, a great port famous for the temple of Artemis and for magic, and stays nearly three years (20:31), longer than anywhere else.

The message. The risen Christ, by his word and Spirit, prevails over every rival power. Nothing incomplete, borrowed or rival can stand beside him: not an out-of-date religion, not his name used as a spell, not a library of magic, not a goddess backed by a city’s pride and money. The word of the Lord grows and wins, not by force but by truth, and those it conquers give up their idols gladly.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught, and shows along the way that the gospel is no threat to Roman order (see the introduction). Here the faith meets the religion of Asia at its strongest, and a city official finds its preachers innocent.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul finds twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism; baptised in Jesus’ name, they receive the Spirit, the last of the frontier outpourings in Acts (vv. 1–7). Three months in the synagogue and two years of daily teaching in the hall of Tyrannus carry the word through all Asia (vv. 8–10). Extraordinary miracles, and exorcists routed for borrowing Jesus’ name, bring fear on the city; believers confess their secret magic and burn their books, and the word prevails (vv. 11–20). Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then Rome, setting the course of the book (vv. 21–22). Then Demetrius, whose trade in silver shrines is suffering, drives the city into the theatre to chant for Artemis, until the town clerk declares the Christians innocent and dismisses the assembly (vv. 23–41).

Where it leads. Every scene points to Jesus. He is the one who baptises with the Spirit, as John promised; his name is so much his own that hell knows it and no one can borrow it; he is worth more than fifty thousand pieces of silver; and he has walked the road to Jerusalem ahead of his servant. Artemis needed craftsmen and a shouting crowd. The Lord of the church needs no one, gave himself for her, and still walks among the lampstands of Asia (Revelation 2:1).

For us. The word that won Ephesus has lost none of its power, and it still works through patient teaching more than spectacle. Ask what you are keeping just in case, a hidden practice, an idol, an income that bends the truth, and bring it into the light. Christ is worth the bonfire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Ephesus the word of the Lord meets every rival power and prevails. Paul brings a dozen of John’s disciples the rest of the way to Jesus, and the Spirit comes on them (vv. 1–7). Three months in the synagogue and two years of daily teaching in a hired hall carry the word through the whole province (vv. 8–10). Extraordinary miracles and a failed exorcism show that Jesus’ name is not a spell, and magicians burn their books (vv. 11–20). Paul sets his course for Jerusalem and Rome (vv. 21–22), and when a silversmith stirs the city to riot in defence of Artemis and his trade, the town clerk finds the Christians innocent and sends the crowd home (vv. 23–41).
verseByVerse.theology:
The word of the Lord prevailing over magic and idolatry

The magicians who burned their books did not cut back their practice gradually; they made a clean, costly, public break (see vv. 19–20). Luke’s summary in verse 20 is his verdict on the whole Ephesian story: the word wins, over magic, over money and over the riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius’s complaint, that his trade would fall into disrepute and the temple of Artemis be counted as nothing, is an honest statement of why many oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel still threatens arrangements that profit from idolatry (on how such opposition dresses itself, see v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul finds a dozen sincere disciples in Ephesus whose knowledge stopped short of Pentecost, and one question uncovers the gap: they have never heard that the Spirit has been given.

To Ephesus. While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul kept his promise to return if God willed (18:21). The inland country was probably the high road across the Anatolian plateau, several hundred miles on foot. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis, with perhaps 250,000 people.

Some disciples. Luke’s ordinary word for Christians, so at first it looks as if Paul has met part of the Ephesian church. But verse 3 shows that, like Apollos (18:25), they knew only the baptism of John the Baptist: followers of his message rather than ordinary Christians.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? Paul was evidently watching, and sensed that something was missing. His question assumes that receiving the Spirit is what happens to a person who believes, and that you would know about it. Paul is not asking whether they have had a further experience, but whether the ordinary thing has happened.

Not even heard. They cannot mean they had never heard of the Spirit, for John spoke of him plainly (Luke 3:16), but that they had not heard he had been given, that Pentecost had happened. They were not converts waiting for something more, but men whose information had run out before the story reached its end.

Like Acts 8, but not the same. Like the Samaritans (8:14–17), these men receive the Spirit some time after a baptism. But theirs was only John’s, so they were not Christians awaiting a second blessing; what they lacked was the rest of the gospel, not a second stage of the Christian life (see the note on vv. 6–7).

Because Jesus was glorified. Their news stopped short of the thing that sent the Spirit. He had not yet been given, John’s Gospel explains, because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:39); at Pentecost Peter said that the exalted Jesus had received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33). The Spirit is not a reward we work up to but the gift of an enthroned Christ, the sign that his death was enough and that the Father has accepted it. These men knew John’s promise of one who would baptise with the Spirit; they did not know that he had died, risen, ascended and kept his word. Underneath, Paul’s question was about Jesus: have you heard what he has done?

One question. These twelve were sincere and out of date, and the gap was found because one man asked one question. Of the people in your congregation whom everybody assumes are fine, has anybody ever asked them anything? Behind the one man stood his Lord, who sent Paul across a plateau to find twelve men who had not heard the end of the story. He does not leave his people half-told.

How do I know whether I have received the Holy Spirit? Not first by a feeling or a particular gift, but by the fruit of his presence. The Spirit makes you confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3) and cry “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15–16); he makes you hate the sin you once loved and fight it (Romans 8:13), and slowly grows love, joy and peace in you (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have truly trusted Christ, the Spirit is in you, for anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). The question for most believers is not whether to receive him, but whether to keep in step with him.

What does keeping in step with the Spirit look like? “If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25): a soldier marching in line, matching a pace he did not set. The Spirit is a Person, sent by the risen Christ to make Christ real to you, and he sets the pace by the word he inspired. Keeping in step is mostly ordinary. Read Scripture expecting him to show you Jesus, and do the next thing it shows you. When your conscience is pricked over a sharp word or a hidden habit, turn at once; do not grieve him (Ephesians 4:30). When you do not know what to pray, lean on him, for he helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26). Stay among his people: he gives his gifts in a body, not to loners. And when you fall out of step, as every believer does, do not march off alone in shame. The Spirit was given because Christ’s death was enough, so come back to the cross, confess it, and fall in again.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces the gap to its source: these men had John’s baptism of repentance, which pointed to Jesus, but they had stopped at the signpost.

Into what then were you baptized? Paul does something wise with a wrong answer. He neither corrects nor dismisses them, but asks a second question that finds the fault, since receiving the Spirit goes with baptism in Jesus’ name. He is not deciding whether they are in or out, but finding where the gap is: what were you told, by whom, and how far did it go? Much unhelpful conversation between Christians would be avoided if the second question came before the verdict.

Into John’s baptism. A baptism of preparation. These men were neither pagans nor half-hearted: they had repented and were waiting for the one John had promised. They were simply living some twenty years behind the news.

That is, Jesus. John’s baptism was never a destination; it pointed past itself to a person. Paul closes a twenty-year gap in a few words: the one you were told to wait for has come, and here is his name. Every hope John stirred in them, of sins forgiven and a Spirit poured out, now stands before them in a person, crucified, risen and reigning.

Real and unfinished. Paul does not tell these men that their repentance was worthless or their waiting wasted, but that what they had was real and unfinished: a rare and difficult thing to hold about anybody’s spiritual history, including your own.

What if I was religious for years before I really understood the gospel? Then this passage is for you. Those years may have taught you real things: that God is holy, that sin matters, that you needed someone to come. Many believers look back on a churchgoing childhood or a sincere but confused search and see God preparing them, as John prepared the way. But preparation is not arrival. If you now trust Christ crucified and risen, you have reached what the signposts pointed to. Do not despise the road, do not mistake it for home, and thank God for both.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing of Jesus, the twelve are baptised in his name: not a second Christian baptism, but their first. John’s baptism looked forward to a hope; this one joins them to a person.

On hearing this. At once: no interval, no long course of instruction, no probation. All through Acts baptism follows promptly on believing: three thousand at Pentecost, the eunuch at the roadside, Lydia apparently the same day, the jailer in the middle of the night. No believer in Acts is made to wait for years, and the order is always hearing, believing, then baptism.

Their first Christian baptism. Men already baptised are baptised again, the only such case in the New Testament, yet it is not a repeat: they had never received Christian baptism. John’s rite belonged to the era before the cross, valid in its time but preparatory. There is no record that the apostles, some of whom came from John’s circle (John 1:35–40), were baptised again; they received the Spirit at Pentecost.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. That phrase is the whole difference. John’s baptism was into a hope; this one is into a person and everything that belongs to him. To be baptised into someone’s name was to be transferred into his ownership and protection, so men who had waited on John’s promise are now publicly attached to a named Lord. He is not ashamed to put his name on twelve forgotten men in Ephesus, or on us. The water is the sign; the reality is that he has washed us in his own blood and joined us to himself for ever.

Does this conflict with Matthew 28:19? No. Jesus commanded baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Luke describes whose name and authority the person comes under, not the words spoken at the water. Oneness Pentecostal teaching, which denies that God is three persons and insists that only Jesus’ name may be used, reads a formula into a description. Christian baptism is into the one name of the triune God, revealed in Jesus Christ.

Why does Luke record such a small episode? Because the gospel had reached Ephesus in an incomplete form and God did not leave it there. Somebody had preached a half-message and moved on, as Apollos had (18:25–26), and in both cases the correction came privately, patiently, and without anybody being humiliated.

What if I was baptised before I truly believed? Talk honestly to your pastor. If you were baptised as a believer, however young and however little you understood, and have trusted Christ ever since, your baptism stands; faith grows, and baptism does not need repeating every time it does. If you are clear that you had no faith in Christ at all at the time, and were baptised for other reasons, many credobaptist churches would see a baptism now as your first true baptism, as with these twelve. The aim is to obey Christ with a clear conscience.

Where Christians differ: rebaptism. Some use this passage to justify rebaptising anyone baptised as an infant or in another church. Paedobaptists (who baptise the infants of believers) regard any baptism with water in the triune name as valid and not to be repeated, from a sincere reading of God’s covenant promises. This commentary’s view: this case was unique, as John’s baptism was not Christian baptism. Holding with the 1689 London Baptist Confession that baptism belongs to believers, this commentary sees the baptism of someone baptised only as an infant, or before he truly believed, as his first true baptism, not a repetition. But those baptised as believers in the name of the Trinity should not be baptised again; there is one baptism (Ephesians 4:5). We honour our paedobaptist brothers, while differing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Paul lays his hands on them, the Spirit comes with visible signs, marking these last followers of John as full members of the one church of Jesus. It is the fourth and last such outpouring in Acts, each at a new frontier of the gospel.

When Paul had laid his hands on them. As with the Samaritans (8:17), the Spirit came through an apostle’s hands, perhaps to bring John’s followers fully into the one church, and to show that Paul’s apostleship equalled Peter’s.

Tongues and prophesying. The four public outpourings in Acts repay being seen together: Jerusalem at Pentecost, Jews (chapter 2); Samaria, a people Jews kept at arm’s length (chapter 8, where Luke says only that the Spirit’s coming could be seen); Caesarea, Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10); and now Ephesus, men still belonging to John’s time of preparation. Each time the Spirit falls visibly at a frontier, where the gospel reaches a new group, with an apostle present. Luke is documenting not the normal Christian life but the joining up of a divided world, all publicly given the same Spirit, with apostolic witnesses to certify it. It does not happen again in Acts, and the letters, even where they regulate tongues at Corinth (1 Corinthians 14), never tell believers to seek such an outpouring.

About twelve. Perhaps a hint of a renewed Israel, but “about twelve” sounds like reporting, not symbol-building. In a city of perhaps a quarter of a million, the work begins with a dozen men who had been following an out-of-date sermon; within three years all Asia will have heard the word of the Lord (v. 10).

In the flow. Verses 1–7 finish a story that began at 18:24, gathering the last followers of John the Baptist into the church of Jesus, as John wanted (John 3:30). They set the chapter’s theme: nothing incomplete, borrowed or rival can stand beside the risen Lord, whether an out-of-date religion, a stolen name, a library of spells or a goddess.

The map the risen Lord drew. The four frontiers are not random. Jesus told the apostles they would be his witnesses “in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8). Jerusalem, Samaria, Caesarea, Ephesus: the outpourings trace that map outward, the ascended Christ keeping his word at each new border. John had said that the one coming after him would baptise with the Holy Spirit. Here the last of John’s own disciples meet that baptiser. The Spirit falls, and the one pouring him out is Jesus.

Are tongues and prophecy for today? Many godly Christians believe such gifts continue, and we honour their love for Christ and desire for his power. The more likely reading is that tongues and prophecy, as sign gifts through which God gave new revelation, belonged to the foundational age of the apostles and ceased with it, the church being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Scripture now complete (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). This cessationist view is held charitably. Nothing here makes tongues the evidence of the Spirit for every believer, and God remains free to answer prayer in wonderful ways.

If I have never spoken in tongues, am I missing something? No. Paul asks, expecting the answer no, whether all speak with tongues (1 Corinthians 12:30). What no believer lacks is the Spirit himself, with everything that matters most: union with Christ, adoption, assurance, the power to pray, and the slow growth of love, the greatest gift of all (1 Corinthians 13:13). If you love Christ and are learning to love his people, you are not a second-class Christian. You have the same Spirit who came at Ephesus.

In everyday life. Treat the believer from a different tradition, charismatic or not, as one who has the same Spirit you have. There is one body and one Spirit (Ephesians 4:4).

Where Christians differ: a pattern for today? Pentecostals see here a second blessing, a distinct experience of the Spirit after conversion, usually shown by tongues; Roman Catholic teaching finds in the laying on of hands a basis for confirmation. It is a family disagreement: all agree that a Christian without the Spirit is a contradiction (Romans 8:9), and many who seek such an experience do so out of real hunger for God. This commentary’s view: these men were not yet Christians in the full sense; they had not believed in Jesus as having come. When they believed and were baptised, they received the Spirit at once. This is not a two-stage experience for Christians but conversion, and Paul’s question ties receiving the Spirit to believing, as the letters do (Ephesians 1:13). The tongues were a sign for a transitional moment in the history of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reasons in the synagogue for three months, and when opponents begin running the faith down in public, he moves the disciples down the street to a lecture hall.

Three months. Set beside three Sabbaths at Thessalonica (17:2), the longest synagogue ministry Luke measures anywhere.

Reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. Paul is making the case for King Jesus. The kingdom of God is his kingly rule, and the news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, reigns now and will return to reign in full. To persuade about the kingdom is to show from the Scriptures who Jesus is and urge people to bow to him, entering his kingdom the moment they repent and trust the King. You need not be a clever debater to do the same.

Stubborn. The ending came in three stages. They became stubborn, the word used of Israel in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8); they continued in unbelief; then they began speaking evil of the Way, an early name for the Christian faith (9:2), before the congregation, running it down in public to put off those still listening. Paul bore the first two for three months. What he will not do is go on providing a platform where the message is being poisoned for everybody else in the room.

He withdrew. But not from Ephesus. In Pisidian Antioch he was driven out of the district; in Thessalonica he was smuggled out at night. Here he simply moves down the street, taking the converts with him: one of the clearest pictures in Acts of a congregation separating from a synagogue. The Lord bears long with hardened hearts, and when one door shuts he opens another down the street.

The hall of Tyrannus. Probably a lecture hall, a scholē (our word school), a public room with no religious associations; Tyrannus was its owner or the lecturer who normally taught there. Shut out of the sacred space, Paul taught daily for two years in the ancient equivalent of a rented conference room, alongside his trade (20:34). The gospel needs no grand temple.

Is it pushy to try to change other people’s beliefs? Only if Paul were selling his own opinions. Reasoning treats people as minds to be persuaded, not targets to be pressured, and he did it in the open, where anyone could answer back. If Jesus really rose from the dead, keeping quiet about him is not humility but a lack of love. And the Christian persuades not as one who is better, but as one forgiven who wants the same mercy for the person in front of him.

When should a Christian leave a church? Not lightly, and not over preferences, personalities or a dull season; Paul stayed three months in a synagogue that argued with him. But leaving is right when the gospel itself is denied or ridiculed, when Christ is publicly spoken against and the leaders will not be corrected, or when you are prevented from obeying Scripture. Even then, go as Paul went: without bitterness, after patient effort, caring for others who need help, and joining a faithful church promptly. Never leave the Way because you left a building.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, not the earliest, add that Paul taught from the fifth hour to the tenth, roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, when the hall stood empty and most people rested. Most modern Bibles leave it out.
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For two years Paul teaches daily in one room, and through the people who pass through it the word of the Lord reaches the whole province.

All the residents of Asia. With the three months in the synagogue, the two years make nearly three in Ephesus (20:31). Asia was a Roman province of many cities, running down the western seaboard of what is now Turkey and inland for a hundred miles and more. Luke’s “all” is a historian’s broad language for a whole region reached, not a head count, but the claim is large, and Demetrius will confirm it (v. 26).

Paul did not travel to them. So far as Acts records, he stayed in Ephesus. He seems never to have gone to Colossae, many of whose believers had not seen his face (Colossians 2:1), and probably never to Laodicea or Hierapolis; of the seven churches of Revelation he is recorded as visiting only one. But Ephesus was the greatest port on that coast and the end of the roads from the interior: traders, pilgrims, officials and students came through it, some wandered into a lecture hall in the afternoon, and went home with the gospel. Churches at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis were probably founded in these years through co-workers like Epaphras (Colossians 1:7; 4:13), a man of Colossae who carried the gospel a hundred miles inland to a town Paul never saw. Paul trained others, who went out.

The Lord who walks among the lampstands. Luke calls it the word of the Lord, and decades later the Lord himself spoke to the churches it planted. In Revelation the risen Christ addresses seven churches of this very province, beginning with Ephesus, as the one “who walks among the seven golden lampstands” (Revelation 2:1). That is the deeper story of these two years. Paul taught in a hired room; Christ was lighting lamps across Asia, and he never stopped walking among them, knowing, correcting and comforting them. The word that spread from the hall of Tyrannus was his own voice, and the churches it made were his.

The strategy of staying still. The most travelled man in the New Testament reached a whole province by staying still, a comfort for anybody whose service is fixed in one place. You do not know who is in the room, or where they are going afterwards.
