Is my work wasted if I serve in one small place where nothing seems to spread? No. You cannot see where the people you teach will go, any more than Paul could see Epaphras walking home to Colossae. Any class, Bible study or conversation may hold someone who carries the gospel where you will never go. Your task is to teach faithfully what you have been given, and to entrust it to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). The spreading is the Lord’s work, and he has never been short of roads.
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a city famous for magic, God does unusual miracles through Paul, even through cloths from his workbench, showing that his power is greater than any spell. The power is God’s, not Paul’s and not the cloth’s.

Extraordinary miracles. God was doing them, not Paul. Luke’s phrase is literally miracles not of the ordinary kind, unusual even by apostolic standards; from the man who has recorded the lame walking, the dead raised and prison doors opened, that says a great deal.

Handkerchiefs or aprons. Probably a workman’s cloths: the sweatband a labourer tied round his head and the apron a craftsman wore at the bench. The working clothes of a tentmaker, not relics. It is like Peter’s shadow (5:15).

What Luke does not say. This passage has been put to uses it will not bear. Luke does not say that Paul handed out the cloths, blessed them, charged for them or recommended the practice, or how it worked. He mentions no one’s faith, only that the sick were healed; if superstition was mixed in, God was merciful beyond it. God acts; the cloths do nothing. Somebody took Paul’s sweatband to a sick relative, and God, who was not obliged to, healed them.

Why God stooped to it. Ephesus was a famous centre of magic; written charms from the city, called Ephesian letters, were known across the Mediterranean, and its people believed absolutely in power conveyed through objects. God met the city where its convictions were, then spent the next eight verses showing the difference between his power and magic.

Power that went out from him. Luke has told a story like this before. A woman who had bled for twelve years touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment and was healed, and he said that power had gone out from him (Luke 8:44–46). He would not let her go home thinking the cloth had done it: her faith had made her well (Luke 8:48). At Ephesus the risen Lord goes on, through his apostle, with what he “began to do and teach” (1:1). Cloth is only cloth; the healing came from the person of the Lord.

Should we expect miracles like these today? Luke calls them extraordinary, and they confirmed Paul as an apostle: the signs of a true apostle were performed among them, he told the Corinthians, with signs and wonders and mighty works (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). God is still free to heal in answer to prayer, and often does, but Scripture does not promise that such miracles will accompany ministry today, and the cloths are not a technique (see the box below).

So should I pray for healing when I am ill? Yes, without hesitation. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15); the Lord often answers by healing, through medicine or without it. What this passage warns against is not prayer but technique: the idea that healing comes through objects, formulas or special people with a gift for sale. God is a Father to be trusted, not a power to be accessed. If he heals, thank him. If he does not yet, his grace is sufficient for you, and the final healing is certain (2 Corinthians 12:9; Revelation 21:4).

Where Christians differ: prayer cloths. Some ministries today sell or send anointed cloths, promising healing or prosperity. This commentary’s view: Luke calls these miracles extraordinary, done by God through an apostle at a unique time, to confirm the gospel in a city of magic. Nothing in Scripture tells believers to use objects for healing, and Paul never sold anything. Seeking power through objects is close to the magic Ephesus was about to renounce (v. 19).
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Travelling Jewish exorcists try to use Jesus’ name as one more spell, borrowing it from Paul’s preaching without any faith of their own.

Itinerant Jewish exorcists. Exorcism was a common, often paid, trade worked by technique, above all reciting powerful names believed to compel the spirits. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, because they could invoke the name of the one true God (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). These men added Jesus to the list as a magic word.

The Jesus whom Paul proclaims. The whole disaster is in their wording: not “by Jesus” but by the Jesus somebody else preaches. That is second-hand faith. They route the name through another man’s relationship with him, like quoting an authority they have never met, and admit it in the act of trying.

An honest confession. That is the position of many religious people, then and now. They have watched Christianity work in a parent, a spouse or a friend whose faith is obviously real, and would like the results: not Christ, but the effect he has on other people. Yet what they reached for second-hand was on offer first-hand, not a power borrowed from another man’s life but a Lord who says to anyone, “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28). You cannot borrow his authority while keeping him at arm’s length; but he never refuses himself to someone who comes.

Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva. A family firm with the best credential the trade could offer. If the title was a claim rather than a fact (see below), the fraud runs all the way down: a bogus priest’s sons using a borrowed name.

Is it wrong to end a prayer in Jesus’ name? Not at all; Jesus told us to ask in his name (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). But it is not a password attached to a request; it is coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, trusting him as mediator, and asking what fits his character and purposes. A child who says “please, father” is not using a formula; he is speaking to someone he knows. Pray as one who belongs to him, and you will never be using his name as Sceva’s sons did.

Uncertain wording. No Sceva appears in the lists of Jewish high priests that we have, and the name is Latin. The word (archiereus) was also used of members of the leading priestly families, so Sceva may have belonged to such a family, or simply claimed the title to impress customers. Which is meant cannot now be known.
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil spirit knows Jesus and recognises Paul, but not these men, and it drives them out beaten and naked: the authority of Jesus cannot be borrowed by people who do not belong to him.

Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you? A chilling sentence, with two different verbs. The first, ginōskō, is the word for knowing a person; the second, epistamai, for recognising, being acquainted with, having someone on file. The change may be partly for variety, but it fits the scene, and the third part has no word for knowing at all. The demons believe that God is one, and shudder (James 2:19); they know his true servants; they do not fear people who use his name without knowing him.

Three tiers. There is the Lord, whom hell knows exactly as the Holy One of God (Luke 4:34), who went into the darkness and came out with the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). There is his servant, known in that world because he has been doing it damage for two years: the powers of darkness take note of people who are actually doing something. And there are these seven men, who are nobody. The Lord whom the demons know with terror, his people know with love.

Leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them. Luke piles up the verbs: one possessed man puts a family of professional exorcists into the street, naked and wounded, the only exorcism in Acts that fails.

Not a technology. The lesson is not only that the demonic is dangerous to meddle with. Christianity is not a technology: no formula, no words that work, no transferable method. That is a mercy, for a faith that worked by technique would be available to the manipulative and the cruel. The authority of Jesus is inseparable from Jesus, and cannot be used by somebody who has not submitted to him. So let the question land: if the powers of darkness were asked about you, would the answer be “I recognise him”, or “Who are you?” If that unsettles a believer who feels small and unfruitful, take heart: the answer rests not on your usefulness but on whose you are, for “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

But did Jesus not say not to stop a man casting out demons in his name? He did (Mark 9:38–40), and he also warned of some who would cast out demons in his name and yet whom he never knew (Matthew 7:22–23). The man in Mark was apparently a genuine follower outside the twelve; the sons of Sceva used Jesus’ name as a borrowed spell, with no faith of their own, and the demon knew it.

Should a Christian be afraid of demons? No. A believer belongs to Christ, who disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Do not be curious about the occult, do not dabble, and do not give the devil a foothold through unconfessed sin (Ephesians 4:27). Resist him, firm in the faith, and he will flee (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9). God’s armour is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18), not rituals. If someone seems to be in serious spiritual trouble, go to your pastor and pray together. The name of Jesus on the lips of his own is enough.

Uncertain wording. “All of them” translates a Greek word (amphoteroi) that normally means both. Since there were seven sons, either Luke uses it loosely to mean all, as some writings of the period seem to do, or only two of the seven were there that day. The ESV takes the first view, which is likely; the point is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The failed exorcism makes the whole city fear and honour the name of Jesus, and believers who had secretly kept up their magic bring it into the open.

This became known to all. Not the miracles: Ephesus was full of wonder-workers. What went round the city was a story about the name of Jesus refusing to work for people with no right to it. A humiliating public failure became some of the most effective evangelism in the chapter, because it told a city of magicians what no success could: this name cannot be bought or borrowed.

Fear fell upon them all. Not admiration, but the recognition that they were dealing with something real and unmanageable. Ephesus had spent centuries handling the invisible world by technique, and had met a power that could not be handled. That is what holiness feels like from outside: when Isaiah saw the Lord he cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5). The holy God is never anybody’s instrument.

The name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Made great, magnified. In Acts the name of Jesus is never a label but Jesus himself in his saving power, the name by which a lame man walked (3:16). The exorcists treated it as a tool small enough to carry about; the city found it was larger than they were. That is how his name has always grown great, through humiliation: he was mocked and crucified, and therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9).

Confessing and divulging their practices. Now the sting, aimed at the church. These are believers who had kept up their magic secretly. Divulging means disclosing what was hidden, and since spells were thought to draw their power from secrecy, revealing them broke them. Real repentance brings sins into the light (1 John 1:9; James 5:16).

Keeping one door open. Most likely not rebellion, but the ordinary instinct to trust Christ and keep the amulet too, in case. The modern version is rarely amulets. It is the habit you have never mentioned to anybody, the arrangement you have not brought into the light, the thing you would not want read out. These people were genuinely converted yet holding something back; then they said it out loud, to somebody, and found Christ’s forgiveness already waiting in the light.

Do I need to confess my sins to another person, or only to God? To God always, and to others sometimes. Every sin is against God, and he forgives all who confess it to him through Christ (1 John 1:9); no priest is needed between you and him. But James tells us also to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be healed (James 5:16). Secret sins grow in the dark, and naming one to a trusted, mature believer often breaks its hold. If you have wronged someone, confess to them. If a hidden sin has its grip on you, tell one wise Christian friend or your pastor: not for absolution, but to bring it into the light where Christ’s forgiveness already shines.

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Former magicians burn their books of spells in public at enormous cost, and Luke sums up the whole Ephesian story: the word of the Lord grew and overpowered everything set against it.

Their books. Scrolls of incantations, charms and spells, copied laboriously by hand (see letters and scrolls): a magician’s livelihood, reputation and protection. Nobody raided the houses; the owners went home and came back carrying them.

In the sight of all. The one method that leaves no way back. A man who quietly disposes of something can quietly replace it; a man who burns it in the square before his neighbours has ended a career.

Fifty thousand pieces of silver. Somebody added it up while it burned. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, roughly a day’s wage: well over a century of a working man’s income, gone up in smoke in an afternoon.

Why not sell them? Every scroll had a buyer somewhere in Asia, and the proceeds could have gone to the poor, the church or Paul’s support. It would have looked responsible. They burned them, because selling would have put back into circulation the very thing they had been delivered from. Repentance that is careful to get its money back is not yet complete. Some obedience costs us nothing, because we found a way to profit from giving the thing up; the obedience in this verse cost a fortune.

Is burning books not what fanatics do? Not this kind. Nobody seized or banned these scrolls; their owners carried them to the fire, at their own loss, because they had been set free from what was written in them. The gospel advanced in Ephesus by reasoning and persuasion (v. 8), and Luke never shows Christians destroying other people’s property or silencing opponents. What burned was a confession: we were wrong, and we will not pass this on. A church that tried to win by burning other people’s books would have forgotten this chapter.

The word of the Lord continued to increase. Why does Luke make the word the thing that grows, rather than saying more people believed? It is a favourite way of speaking (6:7; 12:24; 13:49), and this is the last of his short progress reports before the story turns towards Jerusalem and Rome, closing the battle that began at verse 11. Increase (auxanō, grow) is the language of living things, the word of Jesus’ parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29), and “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11). By making the word the actor, Luke also takes the credit off the preachers: not Paul’s cleverness or the church’s strategy conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God’s power (Romans 1:16; Isaiah 55:11). Watch the word, not the men, and take heart: it is still growing.

And prevail mightily. Prevail means grew strong, overpowered: the word overpowered the magic of Ephesus at the point where Christians destroyed their own property in public. That is the kind of victory Christ wins, not by force but by love, until his enemies become his worshippers.

Counted as loss. Paul, in Ephesus in these years, later wrote that arithmetic from the inside: whatever gain he had, he counted as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:7–8). So the bonfire was no tragedy. The magicians had found something worth more than their trade, not a better technique but a person. Christ had given himself for them, and a library of spells was a small thing to give back. The smoke over the square was a confession that Jesus was worth more.

Should Christians do the same today? Things that are themselves tools of the occult, divination or idolatry should be destroyed, not sold or passed on. The principle reaches further: whatever feeds your particular sin, a subscription, an app, a bottle, a contact in your phone, should be cut off decisively rather than kept within reach. Jesus spoke of tearing out an eye rather than keeping it to sin with (Matthew 5:29–30). Christian freedom is real, but what has become a snare should go in the fire, not in the attic.

In everyday life. What do you need to burn? Christ gave himself for you and his Spirit lives in you, so get rid of whatever ties you to sin, whatever it costs, and leave no way back. No break of ours is ever as clean as it should be, but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); so each time you find a scroll you kept, bring it to him and burn that too.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the work in Ephesus done, Paul sets his course, under God’s necessity, for Jerusalem and then Rome: the plan the rest of Acts works out.

Now after these events Paul resolved. Many see this as the hinge of the book. Paul was collecting money from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26), and meant to deliver it himself.

I must also see Rome. He goes through Macedonia and Achaia (chapter 20), is arrested in the temple at Jerusalem (chapter 21), and reaches Rome years later, after governors, a king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a snakebite, in chains at the empire’s expense (chapter 28). The plan was right, God kept it, and keeping it cost Paul his liberty. Must (dei) is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the word Jesus used of his own cross: not fate but God’s settled purpose, for he works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). Paul had long wanted to see Rome (Romans 1:11–13), but this is obligation, and the Lord confirms it: as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify also in Rome (23:11).

Timothy and Erastus. He sends helpers ahead, as he now always does: Timothy, and an Erastus who may be the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23), whose name may appear on a paving stone found there, recording an Erastus who laid the pavement at his own expense. The identification is debated, but if it holds, a senior city official is serving as a messenger.

He himself stayed in Asia for a while. Having decided to go, he stayed and finished, writing 1 Corinthians from Ephesus at this time (1 Corinthians 16:8). The riot happens to a man who had made up his mind to leave and had not yet left, the moment when most of us are most inclined to coast.

The Master’s road. In Luke’s Gospel Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), under the same must: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be raised (Luke 9:22). Now the servant resolves to go to Jerusalem, and what waits for him there is the Master’s road walked again: a mob shouting “Away with him!”, a Roman officer, trials before governors and a king. Paul is not copying Jesus to earn anything. He follows the one who went first and went further, to a cross where he bore what no servant ever could. Because he went up and suffered and rose, his servants go up to their own Jerusalems unafraid.

In everyday life. If you have decided to move on from something, a job, a ministry, a town, finish well where you are. Do not coast in Ephesus.

How may a believer know his decisions are Spirit-guided today? Do not be anxious about it. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering for their unique founding role; God’s ordinary way is quieter, and he has not promised you a voice in your head for every choice. He leads chiefly through the Bible he inspired, a lamp to our feet (Psalm 119:105; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Most of God’s will is already plainly revealed: be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, serve. So the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life.

A renewed mind. For what Scripture does not settle, which job, where to live, the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but by maturing it: be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God (Romans 12:2); if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously (James 1:5). Add prayer (Proverbs 3:5–6), godly counsel (Proverbs 15:22) and the providence of opened and closed doors. Inner promptings and a sense of peace may play a part (Philippians 2:13), but never alone; they must be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jeremiah 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

The shape of a life. Most freeing of all, the clearest mark of being led by the Spirit is not a feeling about one decision but the shape of a life. All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14): led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God’s children, bearing the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). A choice made in love, humility, holiness and faith is Spirit-led even if no special feeling attends it; one driven by pride, greed or self-will is not, however peaceful it feels. Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed and sought counsel? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome: “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). He redeems even our wrong turns (Romans 8:28); the Guide is faithful.

What if I made a decision in good faith and it went badly? Then you are in Paul’s company: his right plan took him through arrest, storm and shipwreck. A hard outcome does not prove a wrong decision; obedience often leads through suffering, as it led our Lord. If you acted in pride or haste, confess it; if in faith, do not torment yourself with what might have been. The Lord who establishes our steps also works through the steps we wish we had not taken, and nothing in your path is outside his care.

Uncertain wording. “Resolved in the Spirit” is literally he set it in the spirit, and the Greek does not show whether Paul’s own spirit (he made up his mind) or the Holy Spirit is meant. Since the Spirit steers Paul throughout Acts, and soon binds him to go to Jerusalem (20:22), the Spirit-guided sense fits well; in practice the two meet, in a resolve formed in Paul’s spirit under the Spirit’s leading.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis stirs up a great disturbance against the Way, because the gospel is hurting the trade that lives on the goddess.

No little disturbance. Understatement for a riot that filled the city’s great theatre. A line later Demetrius brought no little business to the craftsmen, and the repeated “no little” is probably deliberate: the size of the disturbance is measured against the size of the profits, and Luke expects you to notice which caused which.

The Way. One of the earliest names of the Christian movement (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Jesus said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6); the Old Testament pictures the life of faith as a road, the Way of Holiness (Isaiah 35:8); and Christianity is a road travelled after Jesus: “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (Colossians 2:6).

Demetrius, a silversmith. Ephesus lived on its temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, said to be four times the size of the Parthenon. Pilgrims came from across the empire, and miniature silver shrines of the goddess were the premium souvenir. Demetrius made them.

Artemis. The Romans’ Diana, but not the classical huntress: a local mother goddess of fertility, shown with many breasts or eggs, protectress of the city. So the gospel collides with a formidable alliance: a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess’s temple keeper, v. 35), and big money. Having burned the magic books (v. 19), it now threatens the idol trade.

Religion was big business. The man who starts the riot is not a priest or a philosopher but a manufacturer, and what has gone wrong is his order book (on the order of his reasons, see v. 25). Luke writes not a clash of religions but a trade dispute dressed in religious words. In verses 11–20 the word overcame demons and magic; in verses 23–41 it meets money and civic religion, and again wins without a blow struck, while an official of the empire finds no crime in it.

A goddess who could not walk. The silversmiths made shrines for a goddess who could not walk with anyone; the living God came down to walk with us, and laid down his life to open the road home. Artemis needed craftsmen to keep her in business. Christ needs no one, and gives everything.

What if my own job is connected to something I now see is wrong? Then you face the craftsmen’s choice. Some work is plainly incompatible with following Christ: making idols, selling occult services, producing pornography, defrauding people. If your livelihood depends on such things, you must leave it, trusting God to provide, as the magicians did with their scrolls. Much work is a mixture, an honest job in a company that also does wrong things: there, refuse to do wrong yourself, pray about whether to stay, and talk it through with your pastor. Christ asks for costly obedience, and no one who gave up something for his sake has been the loser in the end (Mark 10:29–30).
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Demetrius rallies the trades with the real issue first, their income, before he ever mentions the goddess. Luke lets us hear the private motive before the public principle.

These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades. Not priests, but a guild meeting: his own silversmiths, plus perhaps the men who supplied the silver and the shops that sold the shrines. Demetrius understood that his grievance was an industry’s, and organised accordingly.

From this business we have our wealth. One of the most candid speeches about opposition to the gospel in Scripture. No theology: the first thing out of his mouth is the money. As in Philippi (16:19), the gospel threatens those who profit from falsehood.

The engine and the paintwork. Watch the order, for it is the anatomy of much resistance to Christ. First, in private, the interest: our wealth. Then, in public, the principle: the honour of the goddess and the city. The interest is the engine and the principle the paintwork, and Luke lets us hear the private version first. Demetrius is not lying; the falling sales and the threat to the temple’s standing are real. He is choosing which true thing to say to which audience.

Lovers of money who ridiculed him. Luke’s Gospel showed this in miniature: “You cannot serve God and money,” Jesus said, and the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, ridiculed him (Luke 16:13–14). Demetrius is the same pattern on a civic scale. But the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58); he is the one Master who gives to his servants rather than taking from them, and so those who belong to him can loosen their grip.

Not only in Ephesus. This is not only about first-century idol makers. When the gospel threatens something we are getting, an income, a position, a habit, the objection that forms in us almost never presents itself as a cost. It presents itself as a reasonable difficulty with the faith. So ask of your own objections: what would I have to give up if this were true? Arguments must still be answered on their merits, but Demetrius is in Scripture to tell us that the stated reason and the real reason are often different, and that the man himself may not have noticed.

Is it wrong for a Christian to want to be wealthy? Wealth itself is not sin: Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and honest work that prospers is God’s gift. But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and many senseless and harmful desires, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:9–10). The test is Demetrius’s: when money and truth collide, which gives way? A Christian holds wealth with an open hand, gives generously, refuses to gain it dishonestly, and is content with what God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; Hebrews 13:5). If truth is bending to protect your income, money has become your master.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Demetrius, a hostile witness, confirms how far the gospel has spread, and fears what it does to idols: it shows them to be nothing.

Not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia. Among the best evidence in the chapter. Demetrius has every interest in exaggerating, but he is speaking to men who can check him, about a market they all trade in, and he reports an effect measurable across the province. Luke’s claim in verse 10 might be read as an evangelist’s enthusiasm; here is the same claim from the accounts department of the idol trade.

Gods made with hands are not gods. Paul’s preaching summarised by an opponent, and accurately (17:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4). It is the argument of the prophets: Isaiah’s mockery of the man who burns half a tree to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half (Isaiah 44:14–20), and Jeremiah’s idols, like scarecrows in a cucumber field, which cannot speak and have to be carried (Jeremiah 10:5). And Demetrius is the one man in Ephesus who cannot honestly disagree, because he makes them.

The escalation. The trade, which is what he actually cares about, gets one clause. Then the temple, then the goddess, then her standing before Asia and the world, until a fall in souvenir sales has become a threat to the order of the world, which nobody can be accused of self-interest for defending.

Counted as nothing. He has accidentally said something truer than he knows. That is exactly what the gospel does to an idol: not vandalise it, but reduce it to what it always was. An idol has power over a person only while he believes it holds something up: his safety, his luck, his city’s greatness. Once he sees that an idol has no real existence and that there is one God (1 Corinthians 8:4), the silver shrine may still be on the shelf, but it has lost its grip. Paul’s letter to this city says the same: for all their gods, the Ephesians had been “having no hope and without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12).

Deposed from her magnificence. Within a few centuries she was. Her temple, sacked by the Goths and later quarried for stone, had to be dug out of a marsh in the nineteenth century; today a single reconstructed column stands. Artemis whom all Asia worshipped is a heap of stones in a marsh, and Jesus whom Demetrius despised is worshipped in every nation under heaven.

The temple not made with hands. Ephesus was proud of one building; Paul later wrote to the Christians there about another: in Christ “the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord”, a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:21–22). That is the final answer to the silversmiths. The temple of Artemis was a wonder of the world; the church in Ephesus was living stones in a temple the Lord himself was building.

What are the idols made with hands today? Most of ours are not carved, but we still make them: money, status, a career, a body shaped and photographed, a home, a political cause, a relationship, a reputation, even a ministry. Anything we look to for the security, meaning or approval only God can give has become an idol. Ask what would devastate you to lose, and where your money and time go when no one is watching. Idols are removed not only by smashing them, but by finding something better. Show your heart the beauty of Christ, and the shrines lose their shine.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Self-interest turns into religious fury, and the whole city pours into the theatre, dragging two of Paul’s companions with it.

Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! A cry of civic and religious pride used in Ephesian worship; inscriptions confirm the title. A guild meeting about profits ends in religious chanting, and the change takes no time at all: the two things fuse completely. That fusion is one of the most dangerous things in the chapter. A man can defend an interest with real religious passion and be quite sincere in it; these men were genuinely enraged. But the passion had been aroused by a threat to something else, and its sincerity is what makes it so hard to see. And they shouted greatness over a goddess who needed their shouting. “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised” (Psalm 145:3), but he is not great because we say so; he is great, and so we say so.

Into the theatre. The theatre at Ephesus is still there, cut into the side of Mount Pion and looking down the marble street to the old harbour. It seated about twenty-five thousand, and you can sit where the crowd sat. That is where a mob went when it wanted to be a public meeting.

Gaius and Aristarchus. They could not find Paul, so they took two of his colleagues, seized simply for being near him: the ordinary lot of everyone close to a person in the front line, the family, the colleagues, the host who lent the house, as Jason had found in Thessalonica (17:5–9). Aristarchus turns up again and again: on the journey to Jerusalem (20:4), on the ship to Rome (27:2), and in prison with Paul, his fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10). Dragged into a theatre by a mob, he stayed with the apostle to the chains.

Let these men go. One arrest in the Gospels went the other way. When the soldiers came for Jesus in the garden, he said, “if you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8), and his friends walked free while he was bound. Paul could do nothing to protect Gaius and Aristarchus. Christ is the one leader whose nearness, in the end, buys his people’s safety. They may suffer for being near him, as Aristarchus did; but the sentence that mattered, God’s judgment on sin, fell on him alone, and they go free.

How do I tell whether my zeal is for God or for something of mine? Ask what makes you angry, and why. Righteous zeal is grieved most by what dishonours God and harms others; self-interested zeal flares when our comfort, status, group or pride is threatened, and then borrows God’s name. Does your passion make you more like Christ, patient, truthful, willing to suffer, or more like the theatre, loud, vague and ready to drag someone off? Ask a wise friend. Zeal is good when it is according to knowledge (Romans 10:2), and when it would be just as fierce if nothing of yours were at stake.

In everyday life. Think of the Aristarchuses in your church, who suffer because they stand near the front line: the pastor’s family, the missionary’s children. Bring them before God one by one.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wants to face the crowd, but the disciples and even some of the province’s leading men, his friends, hold him back, and he lets them.

The disciples would not let him. Of course he wished to go in: the largest audience he would ever have, and his two friends on the theatre floor. He was the apostle, they were converts of two or three years, and they overruled him; Luke records it without a hint that they were wrong. A man who cannot be restrained by the people around him is not brave but unaccountable. Paul submitted.

Some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his. The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province, associated with the provincial council, the imperial cult and the public games: part of the official religious establishment. Luke does not say they were converted, yet men whose duties included promoting a religion Paul preached against sent urgent messages when his life was in danger: another sign for Theophilus that respectable men did not see Paul as a criminal (see the introduction).

Both at once. Paul had preached against idols in the city of Artemis hard enough to dent an industry, and the officers of the rival religion liked him enough to try to save his life. Those two things are meant to be held together, and most of us manage only one.

Not before the hour. Paul’s Lord had walked this line first. At Nazareth a furious crowd drove Jesus to the brow of a hill, and passing through their midst he went away (Luke 4:29–30); no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). When the hour came he gave himself up. Paul’s friends were asking him to keep his life for the hour God appointed, not to spend it on a theatre.

Can I be friends with people whose beliefs I think are false? Yes, and you should be. Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul’s friendship with the Asiarchs did not soften his message. Friendship is not endorsement but the love of neighbour, and often the road the gospel travels. Be honest about what you believe, never mock what they hold dear, and let your convictions make you kinder, not harder. The danger is not in having unbelieving friends but in letting them shape your loves more than Christ does (1 Corinthians 15:33). Keep your heart anchored in him, and open your door.

In everyday life. Who in your life has permission to tell you no? If no one does, give it to someone this week.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The so-called assembly is a mob that does not know why it has gathered, and Alexander, pushed forward by the Jews, never gets a hearing.

The assembly was in confusion. Luke uses the ordinary Greek term for a citizens’ assembly (ekklēsia, as in v. 39), also the New Testament’s word for the church. So this chapter has an ekklesia that is a mob, gathered by a grievance and unable to say why it is there. Christ’s ekklesia is called out by his voice and gathered around him (Matthew 18:20); it always knows why it has come.

Most of them did not know why they had come together. “You shall not fall in with the many to do evil” (Exodus 23:2). This is what idolatry does to a mind: claiming to be wise, people become fools (Romans 1:21–22). Worshippers grow like what they worship, and a god that cannot think makes a crowd that cannot think. The Word gives a man back his mind, as the man Jesus freed from demons sat “clothed and in his right mind” (Mark 5:15).

Alexander. The Jewish community pushes a spokesman forward, perhaps to show that they had nothing to do with Paul, since Jews also refused idols and were in real danger of suffering for somebody else’s preaching. The synagogue Paul had left two years earlier finds that the city cannot tell Jews from Christians.

How do I avoid being swept along by the crowd? Know what you believe and why, before the noise starts. Let daily Scripture, not the latest outrage, shape your mind. Be slow to share, quick to check, and wary of anything that makes you feel certain without giving you reasons. Keep company with wise people, not only loud ones, and pray for a calm mind (Philippians 4:6–7). The majority has often been wrong: the crowd once chose Barabbas. A Christian is free to stand alone, because he never stands alone; he stands with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For two hours the crowd shouts one slogan, sure of itself and unable to give a reason, and Alexander is never heard.

When they recognized that he was a Jew. To the crowd, Jews and Christians were the same, since both rejected Artemis. Alexander never said a word; they shouted him down before he began.

For about two hours. Thousands chanting five words in a stone bowl built to carry sound, like the prophets of Baal crying from morning until noon, with no voice and no one answering (1 Kings 18:26). Repetition is not truth, and their goddess could not hear them.

With one voice. The one unanimous thing in the day. Most of them did not know why they had come (v. 32), and did not need to: a slogan requires not a reason but a side, and supplies the feeling of certainty at no cost. Two hours of “Great is Artemis” settled nothing; Paul’s argument was not refuted and Alexander was not heard, but the theatre was full of people who felt entirely sure. The slogan asserts not that Artemis is true but that she is ours: civic pride wearing a goddess. People seldom need two hours of chanting about something nobody doubts; the volume is the sound of a religion that has begun to feel the ground move.

Another crowd, another cry. Scripture shows one other vast crowd crying out with one voice. John saw myriads of myriads around the throne, saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:11–12). They too repeat and are unanimous, but their song gives its reason: “for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Ephesus shouted that Artemis was theirs; heaven sings that the Lamb has made them his. One chant needed two hours of noise to keep itself sure; the other will never run out of reasons.

The crowd is a place to hide. Much modern life is lived in the theatre at Ephesus: a feed, a hashtag, a pile-on. Søren Kierkegaard, lampooned for months by a Copenhagen satirical paper while the town laughed along, wrote that the crowd is untruth. He meant not that most people are always wrong, but that in a crowd nobody has to answer for anything, so it can do what no single person in it would dare. The gospel calls us out of the crowd, though not into proud isolation. The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and on the last day there will be no crowd to stand behind. But there is one man who stood alone for us, when the crowd cried “Crucify him” and every friend had fled. He bore alone what the crowd did together, so that we could step out of it and be forgiven by name.

Is repetition in Christian worship wrong too? Not in itself. Psalm 136 repeats “for his steadfast love endures forever” twenty-six times, and heaven repeats “holy, holy, holy” (Revelation 4:8). What Jesus forbade was heaping up empty phrases, as if God would hear us for our many words (Matthew 6:7). What matters is whether the words are true, understood and meant. A chorus sung with the mind engaged to a God who hears is worship; five words shouted for two hours to a goddess who cannot hear is noise. Sing gladly, and sing with understanding (1 Corinthians 14:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk quiets the crowd by agreeing with it: the city’s honour is beyond question, so there is no need to riot.

The town clerk. He was the city’s senior executive officer, who drafted decrees, ran the assembly and answered to Rome for order: the strongest personal reason in the theatre to end this.

Who is there who does not know. He begins by agreeing with them, the shrewdest thing in the speech. He does not tell an inflamed crowd it is wrong, but that it is so obviously right that the shouting is unnecessary. Temple keeper (neōkoros) was an official title of honour Ephesus held, confirmed by inscriptions and put on its coins: your status is not in question.

You ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. And there is the turn. Artemis is secure; why riot? A city certain of its goddess does not need to roar for two hours in a theatre.

The sacred stone that fell from the sky. The clerk waves it as his clinching argument (on what it was, see below). They worshipped the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), revering an object that fell from the sky and missing the God who made the sky. The church worships the Son who came down from heaven, not by accident but of his own will, out of love.

What cannot be denied. The clerk’s undeniable things were a title, a temple and a rock, and history has denied all three. Luke’s book has a different list. The council that wanted the apostles silenced had to admit that a notable sign had been done through them and they could not deny it (4:16), done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and whom God raised from the dead (4:10). The faith rests not on a stone that fell from the sky but on a man who came out of a tomb, seen alive by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:6).

Why does Luke include a pagan speech without correcting it? Scripture records the words of Satan and of Job’s comforters too; inspiration guarantees that the record is true, not that every speaker was right. Luke reports this speech at length and with evident approval, not of its theology but of an ordinary official doing his job properly, and expects us to see the irony: a man defending what cannot be denied, in a city whose temple is long gone. The clerk was wrong about Artemis and right about the riot, and God used the second for his people’s good.

Uncertain wording. “The sacred stone that fell from the sky” translates one Greek word (diopetēs), literally fallen from Zeus, that is, from heaven; the ESV supplies “stone”. The word was used of sacred images believed to have come down from the sky, so the clerk may mean a meteorite revered at the temple, or the ancient image of Artemis herself. What object he meant is not known; his point is that the goddess had heaven’s own credentials.
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clerk declares Paul’s companions innocent of any crime against the goddess, and sends Demetrius to the courts if he has a real case. After two years of preaching against idols, no one could charge the Christians with vandalism or mockery.

Neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. A formal public finding by the city’s senior officer, dismissing two charges: sacrilegious means temple robbers, a serious crime everywhere in the ancient world; blasphemers of our goddess means public abuse of Artemis.

Without vandalism and without mockery. Paul had dented the magic trade, damaged the souvenir industry across the province and persuaded a great many people to abandon the city’s religion, yet nobody in the theatre could name a shrine he had touched. He argued that the idols were nothing; he did not throw anything at them. The church has often failed that standard since, calling the failure boldness; ridicule is quicker than argument, and flatters the heart, letting us win the room without loving the person in front of us. Paul’s two years produced a bonfire lit by the magicians themselves, and not one prosecutable act. The truth undermines idols without our ridicule.

The courts are open. Now the clerk turns it back on Demetrius: if he has a case, there are courts sitting and proconsuls to hear it. He had no case at law, which is why he went to the guild and the theatre instead. A grievance that will not go to the proper place for a hearing usually would not survive one.

Innocent, like his Master. Luke has recorded verdicts like this before. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and the centurion at the cross said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (Luke 23:47). Now a pagan official pronounces Paul’s companions blameless. But one difference matters more than any likeness. Paul’s companions were declared innocent and let go. Jesus was declared innocent and crucified anyway, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).

But are Christians not supposed to call false religion false? Yes, and Paul did, plainly: gods made with hands are not gods. The question is how. You can say that something is untrue without sneering at those who believe it or ridiculing what they hold sacred. Speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15) means being clear about what is false and gentle with those deceived, remembering that we were once deceived too (Titus 3:3). Mockery hardens people; patient truth, by God’s grace, sets them free.

In everyday life. Read back over the last thing you posted or said about another religion or worldview, and ask whether a thoughtful adherent would find it fair. If not, put it right.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clerk keeps his real fear for last: Rome may punish the city for a riot it cannot justify. Disputes belong in lawful process, not in a shouting crowd.

The regular assembly. The constitutional assembly, meeting on fixed days with an agenda and a procedure: ekklēsia again, in its precise civic meaning. The difference between that and the crowd before him is not numbers or strength of feeling, but whether there is a process by which anybody could be shown to be wrong.

In danger of being charged with rioting. The real argument, kept until last. Rome could punish a city for rioting by removing its privileges as a free city. The clerk was worried about Rome, not Artemis: they had spent the afternoon handing the proconsul a reason to take their liberties away.

No cause that we can give. Nothing they could put in writing, and the man who would have to draft the report is him. So the riot called to defend the greatness of Artemis ends with the city’s chief officer explaining that it cannot be explained.

The charge of rioting. Luke knows the irony. At Jesus’ trial his accusers said he stirred up the people (Luke 23:5), and Pilate released instead a man thrown into prison for an insurrection (Luke 23:19, 25). The innocent was condemned as a troublemaker and the rioter went free. At Ephesus it falls the right way round: the innocent go free and the rioters are warned. Yet every believer is a kind of Barabbas: the guilty one let go because the innocent took the sentence. The peace we enjoy, with God first and in the city after, was bought by his condemnation.

Why should Christians value law and order? Because God ordained governing authorities for our good, to restrain evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), and the gospel spreads more freely in peace. Paul urged prayer for rulers so that believers might lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way, and so that all may hear the truth (1 Timothy 2:1–4). The state is not our saviour, nor every law just, but a Christian should be a good citizen, thankful for open courts and officials who do their jobs, and should pray for them, as God used this clerk.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great riot ends quietly, with an official sending everyone home: God has protected his church through ordinary means.

He dismissed the assembly. Not an earthquake or a sermon, but a municipal officer sending everybody home. Luke closes the whole Ephesian ministry with a man closing a meeting. That is how God most often works, and not how we most often tell the story. Nothing happened that anybody would call supernatural. The church was preserved that afternoon by an official’s professional instincts, the friendship of some provincial aristocrats, and a few disciples who would not let Paul go in.

Ordinary means. Every one of them was the hand of God, and none of the people involved knew it. A habit of mind that counts God present only when something inexplicable happens leaves most of a life looking empty. The God who threw open the prison at Philippi with an earthquake protected his people at Ephesus with a competent civil servant, and Luke gives both the same weight.

Two assemblies. One last contrast. The assembly of Ephesus is dismissed by a clerk; the assembly of Christ answers to another Lord. Jesus said, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), and in this chapter he has done it in the city of Artemis. The clerk’s ekklesia went home. Christ’s ekklesia in Ephesus would receive an apostle’s letter, and later a word from the risen Lord himself (Revelation 2:1–7). He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he has never once dismissed her.

The letter that followed. To this congregation would be written the letter that begins with God choosing his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4); since some of the earliest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” at Ephesians 1:1, it may have been meant for several churches of the province, Ephesus among them. Luke’s own summary stands at verse 20: “So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.”

How can I see God’s hand in ordinary things? By remembering that providence is God’s most holy, wise and powerful preserving and governing of all his creatures and all their actions (Westminster Shorter Catechism, answer 11; compare the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1 and the Westminster Confession 5.1), and that he works through means far more often than without them. The doctor’s skill, the friend’s warning, the delayed train, the job that fell through: these are not God’s absence but his usual way of working. At the end of a day, ask where he kept you, fed you, warned you or guided you. You will grow more thankful and less anxious, for the God of the ordinary is the God of every hour.

19.theology: The word of God as the power of mission. Ephesus shows what the word of God, taught day after day, can do (see v. 10). The word creates the church. That is why Paul later charges Timothy to preach the word, in season and out of season (2 Timothy 4:2).
19.examples:
Then: All Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus, a bonfire worth more than a century’s wages is lit in public, and the word of the Lord prevails, not by weapons or political power, but by the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: Churches are always tempted to replace patient teaching of the word with something more immediately impressive: spectacle, experience, technique, programmes. Ephesus was won by a man who reasoned from the Scriptures daily for two years. The word has lost none of its power; the question is whether we will give it the time and the central place it needs.

keyVerse.quote: So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
keyVerse.note: Luke’s summary is his verdict on the whole Ephesian story. Over incomplete religion, demons, magic, money and a rioting city, the word of the Lord grows like living seed and overpowers everything set against it. The credit goes not to Paul but to the word, alive with the power of the risen Christ, and it is still growing.

19.reflection:
The twelve disciples Paul met were sincere but had not heard the whole story (vv. 1–7). How can we notice, kindly, where someone’s grasp of the gospel has stopped short, and what question might help, as Paul’s did?

Paul taught daily for two years in one hired room, and the word reached all Asia (vv. 9–10). What does this suggest about the value of patient, ordinary teaching, and of faithful service in one place?

The sons of Sceva tried to use “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims” (v. 13), and believers in Ephesus kept their magic secretly until they confessed it and burned their books (vv. 18–19). Where are we tempted to treat Jesus as borrowed power, or to keep one door open, and what would a clean, costly break look like?

Demetrius spoke to his guild about wealth and to the city about the goddess (vv. 25–27). How can self-interest disguise itself as principle in our own objections or zeal, and how does Christ free us to loosen our grip?

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
Where we are. Acts 20 follows the riot at Ephesus (19:23–41). Paul’s three years there are over; he sets out, by way of Macedonia and Greece, for Jerusalem, on the journey that will end in chains.

The message. The church belongs to God, who bought it with his own blood, and he keeps it when its best servants are taken away. At Troas the risen Lord gives life back in the middle of his people’s worship; at Miletus his apostle hands the church over, not to a successor, but to God and the word of his grace, charging its shepherds to watch over themselves and the flock. A servant who knows whose the church is can hold his own life cheap and finish his course.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may be sure of what he has been taught (see the introduction). As the apostles died, churches had to learn to live without them, and this chapter shows how: gathered on the Lord’s Day, led by elders who guard the flock, fed by the word, and kept by God.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul strengthens the churches, escapes a plot, and travels with men from the Gentile churches carrying their gift (vv. 1–6). At Troas, as the church gathers on the first day of the week, Eutychus falls to his death and is given back alive (vv. 7–12). Paul hurries on for Pentecost (vv. 13–16). At Miletus he reminds the elders how he served among them (vv. 17–21), faces the chains ahead (vv. 22–27), charges them to guard the flock against wolves from outside and within (vv. 28–31), and commends them to God and his word, with his own working hands as their example (vv. 32–35). They kneel, weep and see him to the ship (vv. 36–38).

Where it leads. Paul’s road, warned of suffering and walked anyway, follows his Master’s road to Jerusalem. Yet the centre of the chapter is not Paul but “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (v. 28): Christ, God the Son in our flesh, is the Shepherd who bought the flock, the risen Lord whose life returns to a dead boy, and the Giver whose words “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (v. 35) describe his own cross. Paul leaves; Christ stays.

For us. The church you belong to cost the blood of God the Son, so love it, gather with it, and, if you lead it, watch over yourself first. Hold your life loosely, give rather than grasp, and when the people you lean on are taken from you, trust God and the word of his grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord keeps his church and his servant on the road, and nothing on it is wasted. Paul leaves Ephesus encouraging the disciples and spends months strengthening the churches of Macedonia and Greece (vv. 1–2). A plot forces a long detour by land, with men from the Gentile churches carrying their gift to Jerusalem’s poor, and Luke rejoins the party at Philippi (vv. 3–6). At Troas the church gathers on the first day of the week to break bread; when Eutychus falls from a window and is picked up dead, Paul takes him in his arms and he is given back alive, and the meeting goes on until dawn (vv. 7–12). Then the party hurries down the coast, past Ephesus, to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Table on the Lord’s Day

The gathering at Troas on the first day of the week to break bread (v. 7) is the clearest picture in Acts of the church’s Sunday worship (see vv. 7–8). Reformed churches see here the pattern of Christian worship: the word taught and the Supper shared, together, when the church meets on the Lord’s Day.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked the twenty miles from Troas to Assos alone while the others sailed (see vv. 13–14). Now: Time alone with God still prepares Christ’s servants for costly obedience, and it usually has to be made on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not slip away from Ephesus after the riot: he gathers the believers and puts heart into them, and then spends months doing the same for the churches of Macedonia and Greece. The chapter opens as it will close, with an apostle strengthening churches he is about to leave.

Not driven out. The riot did not drive Paul away; he had resolved to leave for Macedonia before Demetrius ever called his guild together (19:21). The Christians of Ephesus would still be living in that city after his ship sailed, so he gathered them and encouraged them before he went. Strengthening people you are leaving behind is a different discipline from inspiring people you are about to lead, and it has almost no reward in it.

And departed for Macedonia. Luke compresses some of the most turbulent months of Paul’s life into this sentence. Paul went to Troas expecting Titus with news from Corinth, and Titus was not there; his spirit was not at rest, so he left an open door for the gospel unused and went on to Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:12–13). There he was afflicted at every turn, with fighting without and fear within (2 Corinthians 7:5). Then Titus arrived with good news, and out of that relief Paul wrote 2 Corinthians, the most personal of his letters. Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth. Luke gives us the route; Paul’s letters give us what the route cost.

Comfort that comes through Christ. In that letter Paul names the source of his encouragement: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (2 Corinthians 1:5). It was not a gift of temperament but the comfort of a crucified and risen Lord, passed on by a man who had been afflicted himself.

What if I feel anxious even while serving God? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. The apostle who wrote “do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:6) once could not use an open door because his spirit was not at rest. Anxiety is not the same as unbelief; it is a burden to be carried to God, and God comforted Paul by the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6). So tell God plainly what you fear, ask others to pray, and look for the Titus he sends. And do not judge other believers by their outward record: the calmest face in your church may be fighting fears within.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A winter’s wait and a murder plot become, in God’s hands, the setting for the letter to the Romans and the cause of everything else in this chapter.

There he spent three months. Very probably at Corinth, and probably in winter, when the sea lanes closed and few ships sailed.

The letter written in the wait. This is very probably when Paul wrote Romans, around AD 57. Luke does not mention it, but the evidence inside the letter is clear. Paul commends Phoebe of Cenchreae, Corinth’s eastern port (Romans 16:1). He sends greetings from Gaius, host to him and to the whole church (Romans 16:23), one of the two men he baptised at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14), and from Erastus, the city treasurer; a paving stone at Corinth still records an Erastus, possibly the same man. And he is on his way to Jerusalem with the collection from Macedonia and Achaia (Romans 15:25–26), exactly where Acts finds him.

Enforced inactivity. So the letter that had a part in Augustine’s conversion, set Luther free and has shaped Christian thought for twenty centuries was composed during a three-month wait by a man who could not travel, and Luke covers those months in five words. The most productive quarter of Paul’s life looked from outside like a delay. God is often doing the most in us when we can do the least.

A plot. Luke gives no details. Perhaps the plan was to kill him on a pilgrim ship bound for Passover, crowded with Jews going up to the feast, while he carried a large sum of money.

Back through Macedonia. A longer route by land, with weeks of delay. Yet the detour produced the week at Troas, the raising of Eutychus and the farewell at Miletus. None of it happens if the ship sails. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10), and no detour in the life of his people is wasted.

Romans 8 under a death threat. On Paul’s desk in those weeks were the words that God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8), and that nothing in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:31–39). Within weeks those sentences were tested by a plot against his life, and they held.

Is it lack of faith to take precautions against danger? No. Faith trusts God; it does not ignore what God lets us see. Jesus withdrew when his enemies sought to kill him before his hour (John 8:59; 10:39), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and changed his route here. To refuse sensible precautions in the name of faith is testing God, which Jesus refused to do (Matthew 4:7). So lock your door, take your medicine, avoid the dangerous road, and pray. Then, when danger cannot be avoided in the path of obedience, as it could not at Jerusalem, go forward without fear.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s companions are the Gentile churches’ messengers, carrying their gift to Jerusalem’s poor believers and keeping the money above suspicion.

Seven men. Luke rarely gives a list like this, and when he does the list itself is the point: seven men, named with their home towns, from three Roman provinces, Macedonia, Galatia and Asia, with Timothy among them, walking together in one party.

The collection. For years Paul had been gathering a relief fund from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–26). These men probably represented the giving churches (1 Corinthians 16:3–4; 2 Corinthians 8:19–21): Gentile believers carrying their own gift, a living picture of the Gentile church’s love for the Jewish church.

An audit committee of seven. Paul aimed at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Corinthians 8:21). He would not carry other people’s money alone, not because he might steal it, but because somebody might one day say he had, and the gospel would be blamed with him. An apostle who had seen the risen Christ travelled with what was in effect an audit committee of seven.

Two names to keep. Tychicus will carry the letters to Ephesus and Colossae for Paul from prison (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). And Trophimus, an Ephesian, is the man some Jews will claim to have seen with Paul in the temple: the false accusation that sparks Paul’s arrest and eventually sends him to Rome in chains (21:29).

Is this Gaius the same as the others? Probably not. Gaius was a very common name, and Luke gives this Gaius of Derbe a different homeland from the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29; nor is he likely to be the Corinthian Gaius of Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14.

The grace these men carried. When Paul pleaded with Corinth to finish this collection, his final argument was not need or duty but the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was rich and became poor for their sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). Seven men walking to Jerusalem with a purse were acting out in miniature the journey of the Son of God from glory to the poor.

Why should a church care about financial accountability if its leaders are godly? Because godly leaders are still sinners, and because the reputation of Christ is at stake, not only theirs. Paul was as trustworthy as any man who ever lived, and he still insisted on witnesses. Good practice protects the innocent from suspicion as much as it guards against the guilty: more than one person counting the offering, clear records, independent checking, open reporting to the members, and no leader with sole control of funds. If you are a treasurer or deacon, welcome scrutiny gladly; if you are a member, ask kindly how it is done.
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi, and the party, though in a hurry, waits a whole week at Troas to meet with the church on the Lord’s Day.

We again. The pronoun has changed: Luke is back. His “we” last appeared at Philippi in chapter 16 (16:17); then the narrative went back to “they” for four chapters and some years, and now, at Philippi, it becomes “we” again. Many conclude that Luke had stayed there all along, in the city where Lydia was converted and the jailer’s household baptised, while Paul was in Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth and Ephesus.
