Nobody wrote a chapter on what he did. Yet Philippi is the church Paul singles out as the only one that supported him when he left Macedonia (Philippians 4:15–16), and the one he writes to with most warmth. Perhaps that warmth is the fruit of Luke’s quiet years there.

After the days of Unleavened Bread. Passover week, spring of AD 57. They waited for the feast to finish before sailing, and Luke notes it without comment. A Jewish believer was free to keep such days as custom, provided no one made them a condition of acceptance with God.

Five days. The crossing had taken two days the other way (16:11), probably because of contrary winds; Luke does not say.

Seven days. A long stop for a man in a hurry, and the Sunday gathering is the only thing Luke mentions that could account for it. Paul would refuse to enter Ephesus because he could not spare the days (v. 16), yet he sat in Troas for seven of them, waiting for the day the believers already met. The apostle worked round the congregation’s diary rather than the other way about.

The Lamb already slain. Paul spent that Passover week knowing what the feast had always pointed to: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Every Jewish household that week was sweeping out leaven and remembering a lamb; the little church at Philippi could keep the same days with open eyes, for the Lamb had come, and the whole Christian life had become the feast that follows the sacrifice.

The host is already in the room. Paul kept one appointment with the church; its Lord keeps every one. He has not missed a gathering of his people since the evening of the first Easter Day, when he stood among his frightened disciples and said, “Peace be with you.” When his church gathers, in a city hall or an upper room or a kitchen, the host is already in the room.

Is it so important to gather with the church every week? Yes. It is not the only place we meet God, but it is where he has promised to meet his people together, in the word, the Supper and prayer, and we are told not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25). Illness, necessary work, caring for others or travel may sometimes keep us away, and there is no guilt in that. But a Christian who regularly lets lesser things crowd out the Lord’s Day gathering is starving himself and depriving others of his gifts. Plan your week around it.
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within about twenty-five years of the resurrection, a church far from Jerusalem already meets on the first day of the week to break bread and hear the word: the New Testament’s plainest picture of Christian worship.

The first day. Sunday was an ordinary working day in a world where the seventh day was the recognised Jewish holy day, and it was not a public holiday in the empire for another two and a half centuries. So believers met very early or, as here, in the evening, after work. They met on the first day because that was the day the tomb was found empty (Luke 24:1), and it became the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10; 1 Corinthians 16:2). Nobody in the New Testament argues for this; it has simply already happened.

To break bread. Luke’s phrase covers both a shared meal and the Lord’s Supper, which the early church did not separate (2:42, 46; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26), and this was most likely the Supper eaten within a meal. The New Testament does not fix how often the Supper should be observed; this passage suggests it was a reason for the weekly gathering, and many churches celebrate it weekly for that reason, while others hold it monthly or less often.

Which evening? If Luke counts the day from sunset, as Jews did, the gathering may have been on Saturday evening; if from midnight, as Romans did, on Sunday evening. Paul planned to leave on the next day, which fits either.

Until midnight. To discuss, to reason back and forth: the verb is dialegomai, used of him in the synagogue and the hall of Tyrannus. There were questions, and he was leaving in the morning and might not be back, so he kept going. Anyone who has sat up too late with somebody they will not see again understands that clause.

Many lamps. Very likely an eyewitness detail. Many oil lamps in a crowded upper room on a spring night throw out heat and fumes: the reason a young man was sitting in an open window at midnight, and the reason he could not keep his eyes open. Luke gives the cause of the accident one verse before it happens.

A meal whose host had risen. Luke used the phrase on the evening of the very first Lord’s Day, when the two from Emmaus told how Jesus had been known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35). At Troas they were not remembering an absent founder; they were keeping a meal whose host had risen. And every Lord’s Day is a foretaste of the eternal day when the whole church will be gathered at his table and the lamps will never need lighting, for its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).

Fulfilled in Christ. The Sabbath was God’s weekly picture of rest, remembering a finished creation and a rescue from Egypt (Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 5:15). In Christ the thing pictured has come: he has finished the work of our salvation, and whoever trusts him rests from trying to earn God’s favour (Hebrews 4:10). The believer’s deepest rest is not a day but a person, and the first day is the day we gather gladly to celebrate him.

So what does a faithful Lord’s Day look like? At its heart, what Troas shows: gathering with God’s people, hearing the word explained, sharing the Lord’s Supper, prayer and fellowship. Around that, rest from the week’s grind, time with family, works of mercy and necessity, visiting the sick and lonely, reading and conversation that feed the soul. Whatever your view of the Sabbath (many Reformed Christians hold that Sunday is the Christian Sabbath; both views are set out below), avoid two errors: treating the day as just another day for shopping and chores, and turning it into a grim list of prohibitions. It is the day of resurrection. Let it feel like one.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and Sunday. Seventh-day Adventists and others hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath; some Christians see no special day at all. Between these, two views are held by many Reformed and evangelical Christians. One, the historic position of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds that the fourth commandment is moral and abiding, and that from the resurrection the Sabbath was changed to the first day, the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy in worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). The other holds that the Sabbath, as a sign of the old covenant, is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is the church’s day of gathering without Sabbath law. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), and the church from the beginning gathered on the first day, the day of resurrection. The Lord’s Day is not a burdensome law but a gift: a day Christians gladly set apart to gather, worship, break bread, hear the word, rest and do good, out of joy and wisdom rather than under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the church’s meeting a tired young man falls from a third-storey window and is picked up dead: the worst thing that can happen to a family happens in the room where the resurrection is being proclaimed.

Eutychus. The name means fortunate and was often given to slaves; given what is about to happen it is either painfully ironic or, in the end, exactly right. Perhaps he was a slave who had worked all day. Luke calls him “the youth” in verse 12, very possibly still a boy, sitting on the ledge of a hot room full of lamp smoke. He went under gradually and then completely; anybody who has fought sleep in a warm room knows that the second stage is not a decision.

Taken up dead. Not “as though dead”. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14), who was in that room, says he was picked up dead. He could have softened it and made the story less exposed to challenge; instead he says the young man was dead, in a house full of witnesses, in a document addressed to a named reader who could have asked them.

Told against nobody. The story is often told as a joke against the boy or against long sermons, and Luke tells it against nobody. Paul does not scold, and Luke does not moralise. It is a comfort to preachers whose hearers doze, and a gentle warning to long-winded ones: even Paul put someone to sleep.

He is already on the stairs. Death came on the first day of the week, among people who had met because Jesus had been dead and was alive. Either the Lord they had gathered to remember holds the keys of death, as he said he does (Revelation 1:18), or they had nothing left to celebrate. And he knows the weight of tired eyes. In Gethsemane he found his friends asleep and said, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:38); he did not cast them off, but died for them before the next sunset. He sees the youth at the window as surely as the apostle in the centre of the room, and when the worst falls on his people, he is already on the stairs.

What if I struggle to stay awake or concentrate in church? Most Christians do sometimes, and God knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Tiredness after a hard week is not a sin. But there are helps: enough sleep on Saturday, a seat where you can see and hear, the passage open in your Bible, notes, and prayer beforehand that God will open your ears. If you are a preacher, love your hearers by being clear and not needlessly long. And if you see someone nodding, be gentle. The Lord did not scold Eutychus; he gave him back his life.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul goes down, takes the dead young man in his arms as the prophets of old did, and announces that his life is in him; then the church goes back upstairs to break bread and talk until dawn.

Down the stairs. Paul goes down, gets on the ground, and picks the boy up and holds him. Any Jew in the courtyard would have recognised that posture. Elijah stretched himself upon the widow’s dead son three times and cried to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21–22); Elisha lay upon the Shunammite’s dead boy, and the child’s flesh grew warm (2 Kings 4:34). Paul is doing what the prophets did.

His life is in him. Paul speaks to the crowd standing round in the dark, and in the present tense: not that the boy was never dead, but that his life had returned.

Until daybreak. Very probably the Lord’s Supper, at last, after midnight. A young man has just been raised from the dead in the courtyard, and they go back upstairs, break bread, and talk until the sun comes up; Luke gives the raising one verse and the talking much the same. The extraordinary thing was not treated as the important thing: the church had one night with the apostle, and spent it at the Lord’s Table, asking him questions until it was light.

A greater than Elijah in the room. Elijah cried out, asking; Paul announces that the boy’s life is in him. Jesus took a dead girl by the hand and her spirit returned (Luke 8:52–55); Peter told a paralysed man that Jesus Christ heals him (9:34), and knelt beside Tabitha and she rose (9:40). The apostle bends over Eutychus in the prophet’s posture, but the life that comes back into him is the risen Lord’s to give. The Lord of life was himself laid in a tomb, so that death might lose its sting for everyone who is his; every broken loaf at his Table proclaims his death until he comes, and his coming will empty every grave of his saints. And before Paul tells the elders that he does not count his life precious (v. 24), Luke lets us see that his Lord has power over death: a man who has seen a dead boy given back can walk toward prison without fear.

Why does God raise some and not others? We do not know, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. He raised Eutychus and Tabitha, and he let James be killed by the sword and Stephen be stoned. These raisings were signs, pointing to the resurrection of Jesus and to the final resurrection of all his people, not promises that every death will be reversed now. What Scripture does promise is better: for those who are in Christ, death is not the end, and on the last day every believer will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:52). If you have buried someone you love who trusted Christ, their life is in them still, hidden with Christ in God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young man is taken home alive, and the church is comforted beyond words.

Alive. They took him away, presumably home, to whoever had been waiting up, and Luke does not tell us that scene: somebody had to be told what had happened and then how it ended. “Not a little comforted” is an understatement that makes the reader supply the feeling, which is how people who have been through it usually describe the deepest relief.

The same word. To comfort, to come alongside and hold a person up (parakaleō): the verb of verses 1 and 2, for what Paul had been doing in town after town. On this night God did it.

A small Easter at Troas. Eutychus was given back for a few more years, and he would die again. The comfort that outlasts him rests on another death and rising: since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). That is the hope for every family whose dead are not given back on the stairs.

Not a rule about outcomes. The church has been carrying its own dead ever since, and this is not a promise that the young man in your house will be given back (see the note on vv. 10–11). What this night shows is what the apostle did when the worst had happened: he went down the stairs, got on the floor and put his arms round the young man.

How can I comfort someone whose loved one has died? Do what Paul did first: go down the stairs. Be there. You do not need the right words; your presence, your arms, your tears and your practical help say more than explanations. Do not offer quick answers or promise what God has not promised. Listen, and pray with them if they want it. Bring meals, remember the anniversaries, keep calling after the funeral when everyone else has stopped. And when the time is right, gently hold out the hope of the resurrection for those who are in Christ, for we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a sleepless night Paul sends his companions round by sea and walks some twenty miles alone to Assos: a deliberate choice of hours by himself, on the harder road.

Paul’s own arrangement. Luke tells us this was arranged in advance and was Paul’s own decision, and does not tell us the reason. The ship had to round Cape Lectum; the road across the neck of land was about twenty miles on foot. Paul had been awake all night, time was short, and he was almost never alone; this whole chapter is a crowd. When he wanted hours to himself he did not cancel anything; he took the harder route to the same place.

Why walk alone? We are not told, and the honest thing is to say so. Perhaps he wanted the day for solitude and prayer, entirely plausible for a man heading toward imprisonment; perhaps he wanted to visit believers on the way, or simply could not face company after the night at Troas. Luke may well have known, and he did not write it down.

A ship’s log. Assos, Mitylene on Lesbos, then Chios, Samos, Miletus: Luke writes down the ports of call day by day, as a man keeping a log does, and many think he kept just such a record.

The road one man walked ahead. That road to Jerusalem had been walked before. When Jesus went up for the last time he was walking ahead of the Twelve, and those who followed were afraid (Mark 10:32). In the end he went alone: his friends slept, fled and denied him. That is why no servant of his walks that road as alone as he did. Paul could take the harder way without companions because the Lord who had gone ahead had promised to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20).

How do I find time alone with God in a busy life? Paul walked twenty miles rather than lose the hours. Most of us need something less dramatic but just as deliberate. Choose a regular time, often early before the house wakes, and guard it; use the walk to the station, the drive, the lunch break. Take a Bible and a simple plan: read a passage, think about it, pray it back to God. Our Lord himself rose very early and went out to a desolate place to pray (Mark 1:35). If he needed it, so do you.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sails straight past Ephesus, the city of nearly three years of his life, because he is hurrying to bring the Gentile churches’ gift to Jerusalem by Pentecost.

Three days. Three anchorages, each recorded: coastal ships often sailed by daylight and put in at night. Miletus lay about thirty miles south of Ephesus.

Past Ephesus. His ship goes past and does not turn in, and the reason Luke gives is not danger but time. If he set foot in that city the whole congregation would come, with meals and questions and people needing to be seen, and a day would become a fortnight. Love has a way of detaining people, and he had a deadline. So he sends for the elders and meets them in a port where nobody can keep him.

By Pentecost. Fifty days after Passover. He was carrying the collection, and Pentecost was a pilgrim feast, so the city would be full of Jews from every province: the largest possible gathering to see a gift from Gentile churches to Jewish believers. And Pentecost was the feast of firstfruits, and the day the Spirit fell.

If possible. Absolute clarity about the destination, and no pretence of certainty about the timetable.

The harvest of that first Pentecost. On that day the exalted Christ received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33). Paul is hastening back to the same feast with its fruit from far beyond Israel, calling his work a priestly service, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:16). The Lord had promised his witnesses would reach the end of the earth (1:8), and here is a party of Gentile believers on its way to show that he kept his word.

Christ never needed those words. The Lord Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him aside, because he was going there to die for us. His servant hastening to the same city with a gift for the poor is a faint picture of the Saviour hastening to the cross with the gift of himself. Paul hoped to arrive in time, if possible. Christ never needed those words: his hour arrived exactly when the Father had appointed it, and nothing in our salvation was ever left to chance.

How do I say no to people I love without being unloving? By remembering that love has a direction, not only a warmth. Paul loved the Ephesians as much as any church, and he still sailed past, because the work God had given him lay in Jerusalem. Saying no to a good thing in order to do what God has given you is not coldness but faithfulness. Explain honestly, as Paul did by sending for the elders; make what time you can without derailing the calling; and trust God with the people you cannot stay with. They are his before they are yours.

Is this a proof that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part. Paul, a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast, though his haste was very likely as much for mission as for ceremony (24:17; Romans 15:25–26). He honours the festival; he does not keep it as a law required for righteousness. Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.

How does that square with dying to the law? In Romans 7 Paul says we have died to the law (7:4–6), yet calls the law holy and righteous and good (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master, so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost is no contradiction: his justification is in Christ alone, so he is free to keep the feast as heritage, devotion and a bridge to his people. Reformed teaching distinguishes the moral law (God’s lasting commands, summed up in the Ten) from the ceremonial law (the rituals that pointed to Christ) and the civil law (Israel’s national statutes), and the test for any custom is this: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a stop at Trogyllium; the earliest do not.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church belongs to God, who bought it with his own blood, so its shepherds must guard it and can leave it in his hands. At Miletus Paul gives the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders. He reminds them how he served among them, humbly, with tears, holding nothing back (vv. 17–21). He goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit, expecting chains and caring only to finish his course (vv. 22–27). He charges them to guard themselves and the flock against wolves from outside and twisted teachers from within (vv. 28–31), and commends them to God and the word of his grace, pointing to his working hands and Jesus’ words about giving (vv. 32–35). They kneel, weep and walk him to the ship (vv. 36–38).
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder, Overseer, Shepherd

Elder (v. 17), overseer and shepherd (v. 28) name one office (see the notes on v. 17 and vv. 28–29). Reformed churches have long seen here the clearest description of the pastoral office: men placed by the Holy Spirit to guard, feed and care for the people in their charge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned of wolves from outside and of men from within who would twist the truth. Both came (Revelation 2:1–7; see vv. 30–31 and v. 38). Now: Every congregation faces both dangers, and the safeguard is the same: the word of God’s grace, held by leaders whose lives match what they teach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul spends days he can hardly spare waiting for the Ephesian elders, because what he must say about the church after he is gone is for its leaders.

What the summons cost. A messenger travels a day or more, and the elders have to drop everything and travel back, so Paul probably waited several days at Miletus: a considerable sacrifice from a man who has just refused to enter Ephesus for lack of time. He would not spare a fortnight for the city; he spent days on the men who would have to act on what he said.

The elders of the church. Elders, plural: a group of leaders in one church (14:23). There were by now believers all over the city and probably several house congregations, yet Luke calls them the church in the singular and their leaders elders in the plural.

The only speech to Christians. Paul’s other recorded addresses in Acts are to synagogues, philosophers, governors and mobs. This one is to the church, and it is the closest thing in Acts to Paul talking the way he talks in his letters, recorded by a man who was sitting there.

Three words for one group. He sent for the elders, and in verse 28 he tells the same men that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to shepherd the flock. Whatever distinctions later centuries drew between elder, bishop and pastor, Paul calls the same men by all three names inside eleven verses.

Titles borrowed from Christ. Before these words belonged to the men at Miletus, they belonged to Christ. Peter, a fellow elder, calls the Lord Jesus the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (1 Peter 2:25), and promises elders the unfading crown of glory when the chief Shepherd appears (1 Peter 5:1–4). The flock has one Shepherd who owns it and many under-shepherds who keep it for him, doing on a small scale, under orders, what the risen Christ does for his whole church. And he is never too hurried for her: he spent his whole life and death on her, and he waits for her still, at the harbour of glory, until every one of his sheep has come home.

Does this settle how a church should be governed? It settles less than some think and more than others admit. Episcopal churches hold that bishops as a distinct order developed rightly from the apostles’ own oversight; Presbyterians see the elders of local churches joined in wider courts; Congregationalists and most Baptists see each local church, under its elders, as self-governing. What this passage plainly shows is that in Ephesus a plurality of elders shepherded one church, and that elder, overseer and shepherd named the same men. Whatever your church’s structure, look for these marks: more than one leader, men qualified by character (1 Timothy 3:1–7), feeding and guarding the flock, and accountable to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins by calling the elders as witnesses to how he lived among them: as the Lord’s slave, lowly, often in tears, and through plots against his life. In this speech an apostle hands his work over to ordinary local leaders, the pattern for the church after the apostles.

You yourselves know. He puts himself on trial and calls them as witnesses (again in v. 34). He is not telling them what his ministry was like but asking them to confirm it, and some had watched him at the bench, in the lecture hall and in their own houses. Ministry is first a life lived openly before people (1 Thessalonians 2:10), and a man can only speak like this if the record will bear it. It is the opposite of a testimonial, which is what you produce when the people who actually know you are not in the room.

With all humility. He names four things in his life’s work: serving, humility, tears and trials, and not one is what a man would choose for himself. Serving (douleuōn) is the word for a slave’s work: Paul begins the summary of his apostolic career by describing himself as somebody else’s property. Then humility. In the Greek world lowliness was the attitude of slaves, and moralists commonly counted it a fault. Christianity took a quality the world despised and made it the first thing an apostle says about his ministry.

And with tears. Paul wept (v. 31; 2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18), repeatedly, over years, and counted it a defining feature of his work. He had planted churches across a continent, written letters that would outlast the empire, and raised the dead; asked to characterise the three years, he says: I was a servant, I was lowly, and I wept a great deal.

And with trials. The only one of the four that came from outside, and he names it without heat. The man who could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3) describes what some of them had done to him without a word of bitterness.

Why humility changed sides. Paul gave the answer himself: Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). The word for servant there means a slave, and Paul’s verb here comes from it. Humility changed sides in the ancient world because the Lord of glory took a slave’s form, and when Paul calls himself the Lord’s slave, he is wearing his Master’s clothes. Jesus served with all humility, washing feet and touching lepers; with tears, weeping over Jerusalem and at the tomb of his friend; through trials, plotted against by his own people until the plotting ended in a cross. Paul’s ministry was only an echo of his.

In everyday life. Could the people who know you best stand up and confirm the way you have lived among them? If not, the remedy is not a better testimonial but a changed life, and it begins at the cross, where Christ freely forgives what those people have seen.

What does humility look like in a church leader, or in me? Not thinking little of yourself so much as thinking of yourself less: doing jobs no one sees, admitting mistakes quickly, listening more than speaking, being glad when others are praised, accepting correction, and refusing titles and privileges that set you above the flock. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and said, “I have given you an example” (John 13:15). Humility is not a technique for leadership; it is what grows in someone who has seen the cross and knows what he has been forgiven. Ask God for it, and ask the people closest to you where you most lack it.

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul held back nothing that would do them good, in public or in their homes, and the heart of all he taught, to Jew and Greek alike, was repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus.

I did not shrink. The verb means to hold back out of fear; it could also be used of drawing in a sail. It is what a man does when he sees where a conversation is going and decides not to go there. Paul chooses the negative deliberately, here and at verse 27: “I did not shrink” admits there was something to shrink from. He knew which subjects would cost him a hearing, a friendship or a household’s welcome, and he went ahead anyway. Everyone who has had to say a hard thing to somebody they love knows that moment, and the reason we shrink is nearly always the same: we want to be liked more than we want the other person to be well. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

In public and from house to house. Both matter, and the second is the expensive one. Public teaching is efficient: one preparation, many hearers. House to house means the same truth delivered again and again to small groups in their own rooms, where they can interrupt, and where you have to know their names.

Repentance and faith. Three years of teaching in two words, which go together but are not the same thing (Mark 1:15; Hebrews 6:1). “Repentance toward God” is a turning round, and the turn is toward God, not merely toward better behaviour: less a regret about what we did than a change of master. “Faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” is trust, placed in a person, not merely in a doctrine.

Our Lord Jesus Christ. Imagine saying the full title in a synagogue. Jesus: the man from Nazareth crucified within living memory. Christ: the Messiah Israel had waited for. Lord: the word Greek-speaking Jews read aloud for the name of the God of Israel. To call for faith in our Lord Jesus Christ was to say that a crucified man is Israel’s King and shares the name of God. That claim cost Paul synagogue after synagogue, and it is the only thing that makes repentance safe: a sinner can turn to God without terror because the Lord he trusts has already borne his sin.

Today salvation has come to this house. The Lord Jesus taught in public and from house to house before his servant did. At one door in Jericho he said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9), and a lifetime of grasping turned round in an afternoon. He grants the repentance he calls for (11:18) and gives the faith that rests on him (Ephesians 2:8), and there is joy before the angels of God over each sinner who turns.

Which comes first, repentance or faith? They are two sides of one turning, and in real life they arrive together: you cannot truly turn from sin to God without trusting his mercy in Christ, nor truly trust Christ while clinging to the sin he came to save you from. Sometimes Scripture names one first (Mark 1:15), sometimes the other (Acts 11:21). Repentance without faith is remorse, which has destroyed people; faith without repentance is mere agreement, which has comforted many who never changed direction. So do not wait to feel sorry enough before you trust Christ, and do not imagine you can trust him while refusing to turn. Both are gifts of grace, and both go on for the whole Christian life: we keep repenting and keep believing until we see him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit, knowing only that chains and suffering wait for him there, and he goes anyway.

Constrained by the Spirit. The word means bound: bound by the Spirit before being bound by chains (21:33). The binding was not a voice overriding his will, but a settled conviction, formed in prayer and confirmed over months, that God wanted him in Jerusalem.

Not knowing. He has the direction and the general shape of the outcome, and no details at all. That is almost always the arrangement in Scripture, though we tend to imagine that guidance means being shown the plan. Abraham was told to go to a land that God would show him, which is not the same as being shown it.

In every city. Through prophets (21:4, 11). The Spirit who constrains him to go has been telling him, city after city, what is waiting at the other end. He is being sent, and being told what it will cost, and both are the work of the same Person.

The Spirit who foretells sufferings. The Spirit of Christ in the prophets was predicting the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:11). Jesus told his disciples three times that rejection and death waited for him in Jerusalem, and then went, willingly, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Now the Spirit does for the servant what he did for the Master: he names the suffering beforehand and leads into it. Because he walked the road to Jerusalem with his eyes open, every one of his people can walk their own road without fear, held by the Spirit who binds them not to chains but to Christ.

If God is leading me, should I expect things to go smoothly? No. Following the Spirit led Paul into chains, the apostles into prison, and our Lord to the cross. Hardship is not proof that you have missed God’s will, and ease is not proof that you are in it. In the world you will have tribulation, Jesus said, but take heart: he has overcome the world (John 16:33). So do not measure guidance by comfort; measure it by Scripture, by wisdom, and by whether you are walking in faith and love. Sometimes the right road runs straight through the hard place, and the Lord walks it with you.

Was Paul disobeying the Spirit by going on? The question arrives shortly. Disciples at Tyre tell Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem (21:4), and when Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and prophesies his arrest, everyone present begs him not to go (21:11–12). This verse points to the best answer, and may be one reason Luke recorded it. What the Spirit revealed, in every city, was the suffering. What the disciples added was the conclusion, “therefore do not go”, and that was love talking, the inference any of us would draw about somebody we loved. Agabus, notably, does not tell him not to go; it is the bystanders who beg. Luke’s wording at 21:4 is strong, and honest readers still find it hard; but this reading fits everything Luke tells us.

Uncertain wording. The Greek says simply that Paul is bound “in (or by) the spirit”, and it is not certain whose spirit is meant. Some take it of Paul’s own spirit (KJV, “bound in the spirit”), an inner compulsion; most modern versions read it as the Holy Spirit, which fits 19:21 and the mention of the Holy Spirit in the next breath. Either way the sense is close: a settled conviction that God was sending him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has stopped treating his own survival as the thing to be protected: what matters is to finish the course the Lord Jesus gave him, bearing witness to the grace of God. This is the sentence the whole speech turns on, and it is not bravado. Paul is not saying his life is worthless; he is ranking, not despising (Philippians 1:21). Finishing matters more to him than surviving.

My course. The word means a race, the distance a runner is set to cover, used of John the Baptist at 13:25. Paul will use the picture once more, from a Roman prison with his execution close: “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). A course is a fixed distance. The question is never how far you have got compared with anybody else, but whether the ground assigned to you has been covered.

The ministry that I received. It was handed to him, not chosen (9:15; Galatians 1:1), on a road to Damascus, to a man travelling the opposite way. That is why he can hold his life so lightly. A man who chose his own work has to defend it, and himself with it; a man who was handed his work has only to finish it.

The gospel of the grace of God. The whole of it, in a single phrase: not to build a movement or win arguments, but to bear witness that God gives what nobody has earned. Grace in Paul’s mouth is never a vague kindness: the grace of God has appeared, he would write, in our Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us (Titus 2:11–14), and he knew it at first hand: though formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent, he had found the grace of our Lord overflowing for him (1 Timothy 1:13–14).

The only race run without a stumble. The Son of God did not count his life precious to himself. He laid it down for us, and on the cross he cried, “It is finished.” His was the only race ever run without a stumble. Paul could spend his life like a runner spending the last of his strength because his Lord had already reached the line for him, and he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion.

The safest generation, and one of the most anxious. By most measures people in the modern West are safer than almost anyone who has ever lived, and many of us are more anxious than our grandparents were. Part of the reason is in this verse. If there is nothing beyond this life, this life has to be protected at all costs, and I become its full-time guard: of my health, my options, my reputation, my time. A life guarded like that slowly becomes a small one. Paul is not careless with his life; he is free with it, which is something else. He can spend it because it is not the only life he has, and because someone else has already done the guarding. The Lord Jesus laid down his life of his own accord and took it up again (John 10:18), and now the life of everyone who trusts him is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). A life held as safely as that can be given away.

Does this mean I should not care about my health or safety? No. Your life is a gift from God and your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and the sixth commandment requires us to preserve our own life as well as others’ (Westminster Larger Catechism 135). Paul took precautions, changing his route to escape a murder plot (20:3); what he refused was to make safety his highest value. When staying safe and staying faithful collide, faithfulness wins. Few of us will face that choice in its starkest form, but we face smaller versions daily, comfort against obedience, and this verse tells us which to choose.

What is my course, if I am not an apostle? Every believer has one: the life, callings and relationships God has assigned you, and the good works he prepared beforehand for you to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). For most of us that means faithfulness in ordinary things: loving a husband or wife, raising children in the Lord, working honestly, serving in a local church, bearing witness to neighbours, enduring illness or loss with faith. You finish your course by keeping the faith in the place God put you, until he calls you home. So ask what your own version of Paul’s sentence would be: what you would have to finish for the rest to be worth spending. Most of us have never written it down, which is why so much of our lives is spent protecting things we would not, on reflection, have chosen to protect.

Textual note. The KJV’s “finish my course with joy” follows a fuller text; “with joy” is missing from the earliest manuscripts, and the sense is unchanged.

parallels.desc: I have finished the race

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expecting never to see them again, Paul formally hands over his charge: as God’s watchman he has warned them faithfully, so from this day the responsibility is theirs. It is this word, that they “would not see his face again”, that will break the elders’ hearts (v. 38).

Proclaiming the kingdom. Paul sums up his three years in a Gentile city as proclaiming the kingdom. Acts is framed by it: the risen Jesus spoke about the kingdom for forty days (1:3); Philip preached it to Samaritans (8:12); Paul reasoned about it at Ephesus (19:8); and the book closes with him in Rome proclaiming the kingdom of God (28:31).

Innocent of the blood of all. Legal language, and Ezekiel’s (Ezekiel 33:1–9). The watchman who blows the trumpet has delivered his soul; the one who stays silent has the blood of the fallen required at his hand. The watchman answers for sounding the warning, not for whether the city heeds it. Judgment is coming because sin is real and the Judge of all the earth is just, so silence about it is never kindness.

A handover. Paul used the same formula at Corinth (18:6), to people who had rejected him. Here he says it to men who have believed him, and it is his formal release from the charge, dated like a legal handover: from “this day” the responsibility is theirs.

The King is the gospel. The King whose kingdom Paul proclaimed reigns now at the right hand of God. Every herald of his kingdom is only a voice, and when the herald goes, the King remains; the King himself is the gospel.

Am I responsible for the blood of people I never warned? The watchman’s words are first for those with a public charge, like Paul and these elders, and they are solemn. But every Christian has neighbours who will one day face God, and love will not leave them unwarned. The point is not to load you with guilt for everyone you have not evangelised; Christ’s blood covers that failure too, for those who confess it. The point is to make you faithful from today. Pray for the people around you, live so that your faith is visible, and when the door opens, speak of Christ plainly and kindly. Blow the trumpet you have been given. The walls belong to God.

Did it turn out to be true? Honestly, we do not know. The letters written after Paul’s first Roman imprisonment appear to have him back in this region: he had urged Timothy to remain at Ephesus while he went into Macedonia (1 Timothy 1:3), which is hard to fit anywhere except a later journey. If so, his expectation was not fulfilled as he thought, and there is no need to be uncomfortable about saying so. What he knew was that imprisonment awaited him (v. 23), and he drew the natural conclusion. An apostle writing Scripture is protected from error in what he teaches; he is not thereby given a timetable of his own future, and Luke faithfully records what Paul expected. It is also possible that Paul passed through the region later without seeing these particular men again.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom. Many of our dispensational brothers (who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, with God’s purposes for Israel kept distinct from his purposes for the church) reserve the kingdom, especially the Davidic kingdom of the Old Testament promises, for a future, literal reign of Christ over restored national Israel in the thousand years of Revelation 20; on the classic scheme the kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected and postponed. Their concern is worthy: they want God’s promises to Israel taken seriously, not quietly absorbed into the church. And many of them now grant that the kingdom was genuinely inaugurated at Christ’s exaltation (Acts 2:30–36), while still holding a future fulfilment for Israel. This commentary’s view: Scripture, nowhere more than in Acts, treats the kingdom as a present reality preached and entered: Christ already reigns on David’s throne at the Father’s right hand. Believers have already been transferred to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13); “the kingdom of God has come upon you,” said Jesus (Matthew 12:28). The church is not simply identical with the kingdom, for God’s reign is wider, but it is the kingdom’s present people, awaiting the day it comes in full over all the earth. If you belong to Christ, you already live under the reign of the King, even as you pray “Your kingdom come”.

parallels.desc: the watchman

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s innocence rests on one word, “whole”: he declared everything God had revealed, not only the parts that went down well.

The whole counsel of God. Not the important parts, not the parts that pleased Ephesus, but all of it: sin and grace, judgment and mercy, election and evangelism, doctrine and duty. And the shrinking verb returns (v. 20). Nobody omits doctrine by deciding to be unfaithful. It happens by small, reasonable decisions: this congregation is not ready; this is not the moment; I will come back to it.

What tends to go missing. In a comfortable generation it is judgment, hell and the wrath of God. In an anxious one it is assurance, election and the sheer freeness of grace. In a moralistic church it is justification; in a lax one it is holiness. Every age leaves out what its own people dislike, so the omission is almost never visible from inside. The test is not only whether your preaching is true but whether it is whole. A ministry can say nothing false for thirty years and still leave a congregation with a God smaller than the one in Scripture.

The counsel has a centre. Paul would soon write to this church that God has made known the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him (Ephesians 1:9–10). What Paul declared was not a syllabus of topics laid side by side but one plan with one centre, the Son, and every doctrine he taught in Ephesus was a road leading to him. The whole counsel of God is not a burden to be endured but a treasure to be explored, and it will take eternity to see it all.

How can I make sure I am getting the whole counsel of God? Read the whole Bible, not just your favourite parts, with a plan that takes you through every book over a year or two. Sit under preaching that works through books of the Bible, so that the text sets the agenda. Notice the subjects you instinctively avoid, judgment, suffering, giving, sexual holiness, election, and go and read them. Use a good confession or catechism, which summarises the whole of Scripture’s teaching. And let every part lead you back to the centre: Christ crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders must watch over their own souls first and then the whole flock, for the Holy Spirit put them there and the church is God’s, bought with his own blood; and wolves are coming. Here the speech turns from “I” to “you”: the watch he kept, they must keep (v. 31).

Yourselves first. That order is not politeness; everything that follows depends on it. A man who neglects his own walk with God does not stop working; he goes on preaching, visiting and organising, and the machinery runs for years on nothing. What he is then feeding people is his own emptiness, competently disguised.

All the flock. Not just favourites: not the promising members, not the ones who contribute, not the ones who are easy to be with.

Made by the Holy Spirit. Not Paul, though he had appointed elders elsewhere (14:23), and not the congregation alone: the Holy Spirit put them there. That is steadying, because a man placed by the Spirit does not have to keep earning the position, and the Spirit will supply what the work demands; and frightening, because he cannot lay it down lightly, and the accounting will be with the one who appointed him.

To care for the church of God. Overseers (the word that gives us bishop) are the same men as the elders of verse 17 (Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–2), and to care for is to shepherd: to feed the flock with sound teaching, guard it from wolves and error (vv. 29–30), lead it, and care for souls (Hebrews 13:17). It is the care of souls by the Word, not the managing of people’s private lives.

With his own blood. Before he tells them what to do, he tells them what the flock is worth. Obtained is a purchase word: bought for oneself. The church belongs to God, and the price is named. Pastors care for people Christ died for; that is why they matter so much.

How can God bleed? God is spirit and has no blood. The blood of the cross can be called God’s own blood only because the One who shed it is God: the man who hung there is the eternal Son in our flesh, who took flesh so that he could bleed, and bled so that he could buy a people for himself (so too they “crucified the Lord of glory”, 1 Corinthians 2:8). Theologians call this the communication of attributes: what is true of either of Christ’s two natures may be said of the one person. It is one of Scripture’s strongest affirmations of Christ’s deity, and two things shine in it: the height of the One who died for you, and the worth of a flock so precious that God bought it with his own blood.

Fierce wolves. False teachers from outside, false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). Paul expects the attack as soon as the apostle is gone.

How do I pay careful attention to myself? Paul gives Timothy the same charge: “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16). It is meant first for elders, but every Christian who cares for anyone, a child, a friend, a home group, needs it: not navel-gazing, but keeping your own soul near the Shepherd who bought it. Be fed before you feed. Read Scripture and pray over it for your own heart, not only to prepare something for others. Watch the small drifts. Notice where prayer has grown thin, or where resentment, lust or the love of praise is quietly growing, and bring it into the light early. Let someone watch you. Give one or two people permission to ask you hard questions. Rest. A worn-out shepherd is the easiest prey a wolf could ask for. And do it without despair, for you are yourself one of the sheep bought with his own blood. Your standing does not hang on how well you keep watch, because the Chief Shepherd keeps watch over you, and he never sleeps (Psalm 121:4).

Lording it and leaving it. There are two ways to fail the flock. Overreach: elders are not to domineer over those in their charge, but to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3); “it shall not be so among you,” said Jesus (Matthew 20:25–26). An elder’s authority is ministerial: he applies God’s Word; he does not make new laws. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2), so an elder may not bind believers with man-made rules where Scripture is silent (Colossians 2:20–23), or police what God has left to Christian liberty (Romans 14:1–4). Negligence is the opposite ditch and just as grave: Ezekiel’s woe falls on shepherds who fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak or seek the straying (Ezekiel 34). An elder who will not teach hard truth, watch for wolves, or address serious, unrepentant sin (1 Corinthians 5) has abandoned his post.

Where is the line? The Word of God. Elders are firm where God is firm: the gospel, sound doctrine, clear moral commands, the church’s worship and order, grave unrepentant sin; and free where God leaves free. The flock is not theirs but God’s: they are under-shepherds, accountable to the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:2–4), serving gladly, never for power, money or ego, and the elder who watches his own soul shepherds with the right blend of courage and gentleness. Abuse of that trust, spiritual, emotional or any other kind, is never to be tolerated or covered: it is the wolf in the shepherd’s coat, and the flock must be protected from it.

In everyday life. Think of the member of your church you find hardest to love, and remember the price paid for them.

What should I do if I think my church leaders are overstepping, or neglecting the flock? Pray first, and examine your own heart; it is easy to mistake faithful firmness for overreach, or patience for neglect. Then go to the leader privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15), with specifics rather than complaints. Leaders are to be respected and obeyed in the Lord (Hebrews 13:17), but they are not above Scripture, and an accusation against an elder, properly attested, is to be taken seriously (1 Timothy 5:19). If there is abuse of any kind, do not stay silent: protect the vulnerable first, go to other elders or outside authorities, and report crimes to the police. Christ owns his flock, and he hates the shepherd who harms it.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die only for the church? Reformed teaching holds that he died to secure the salvation of his people (John 10:11; Ephesians 5:25), often called definite or particular atonement. Many faithful Christians, Arminians among them (those who hold that Christ died equally for every person and that each one’s free response decides), read verses such as 1 John 2:2 as teaching that he died for all in the same way, and they love the cross no less. This commentary’s view: the verse does not by itself say “only”, but it shows that Christ’s death had a definite object: his church. He did not die to make salvation merely possible for everyone and certain for no one; he died to buy a people, and he will have every one of them. All agree that Christ is to be freely offered to everyone.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “the church of the Lord”; but “the church of God” has strong early support and is followed by most modern Bibles.

Uncertain wording. “With his own blood” can also be translated “with the blood of his Own”, meaning his own Son (an alternative the ESV gives in its notes). Either rendering expresses what the church has always confessed: the one who died is God the Son.
verseByVerse.note: Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers — two names for one office. “With his own blood” — the blood of God’s own Son. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”; “his own blood” may also be rendered “the blood of his Own” (ESV notes).

parallels.desc: shepherds who feed themselves

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gravest danger will come from inside, from trusted men twisting the truth to gather followers, so the elders must stay awake, as Paul did, warning everyone with tears.

From among your own selves. The wolves were coming from outside. This is worse: some of the men in that room, or men very like them, currently sound and trusted. That is a hard thing to say to friends on your last afternoon together. And it happened: Paul later wrote to Timothy in Ephesus about false teachers there (1 Timothy 1:3–7, 19–20), and Jesus commended Ephesus for testing false apostles (Revelation 2:2).

Twisted things. Bent out of shape. Heresy is rarely a flat denial; it is truth bent just enough to mislead (Colossians 2:4), and almost every distortion adds to Christ, subtracts from him, or perverts his grace. In the apostles’ day: the legalism that added circumcision and the law of Moses to Christ for salvation (Galatians; Acts 15); the Colossian error of secret knowledge, angel-worship and asceticism (Colossians 2); the denials of Christ’s true humanity (1 John 4:2–3) or of the resurrection (2 Timothy 2:17–18); and grace perverted into sensuality (Jude 4). And much was teaching for shameful gain (Titus 1:11).

After them. The goal is not first a new doctrine but a personal following gathered round a man. The false teaching is the means; the following is the aim. A teacher whose followers are known chiefly by their attachment to him has already shown you what Paul is warning about, whatever the content turns out to be. False teachers draw disciples after themselves; Christ draws all his people to himself, by the cross, and holds them fast.

Therefore be alert. One imperative, and it is not “be learned” or “be organised”. It means stay awake, the word of a watchman on a night shift. The danger it assumes is not that the elders will lose the argument but that they will not notice in time.

To admonish every one with tears. Admonishing means to warn and earnestly counsel (noutheteō). Chiefly Paul was guarding them from exactly these twisted teachers, pleading with each to hold fast to Christ; more widely, he was declaring the whole counsel of God (v. 27), including the suffering on the road into the kingdom (14:22). Three years, night and day, every one, with tears: a record and a standard, what it took to build what they now must keep. Souls were at stake, and Paul loved these people. Real pastoral love is never bland; it warns, and warns weeping (Philippians 3:18). The tears answer both failures named at verse 28: no negligent shepherd, for he warned relentlessly; yet no domineering one, for he warned with tears, not contempt. It is the model for every parent, friend and elder who must say a hard word.

Three years? Chapter 19 gives three months and two years (19:8, 10), and a further while (19:22). Ancient reckoning often counted any part of a year as a year, and the total comes close to three.

The Shepherd who never lapsed. No elder meets Paul’s standard without fault, and Paul himself had not yet arrived (Philippians 3:12). The Chief Shepherd kept his watch without a lapse, and his faithfulness, not theirs, is their standing before God; that frees them to keep the watch gladly, and to begin again when they fail.

The same three twists today. Adding: the prosperity gospel, promising health and wealth to enough faith or giving, and the perennial legalism that makes rules the measure of acceptance (Colossians 2:16). Subtracting: the denial of Christ’s deity, the bodily resurrection, the atonement or Scripture’s authority, leaving a tame God who exists to make you comfortable; and the universalism that twists “God is love” into “all paths lead home”. Perverting grace: a cheap grace that drops repentance and holiness. So apply the Berean test (17:11): does this teaching exalt Christ and humble me, or exalt the teacher and serve his crowd and his wallet? A heart full of the real Christ (Colossians 3:16) is not easily sold a counterfeit.

How can an ordinary Christian tell a true teacher from a false one? Look at three things. His message: does it agree with the plain teaching of Scripture and put Christ crucified and risen at the centre, or does it add to him, take from him, or make grace an excuse for sin? His life: is he humble, honest with money, faithful in marriage, accountable to others (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? His fruit in his followers: do they become more like Christ and more attached to the whole church, or more attached to him and suspicious of everyone else (Matthew 7:15–20)? You do not need to be a scholar. Read your Bible, belong to a faithful church, and ask whether the teacher is pointing you to Jesus or to himself.

Who are we to call anyone’s teaching false? We would have no right, if the standard were our own opinion. But Paul measures teachers by the gospel God revealed, and applies the same test to himself: if even he or an angel from heaven preached a different gospel, he would be under God’s curse (Galatians 1:8). Humility does not mean pretending every claim about Jesus is equally true. It means submitting your own views to Scripture first, and then loving people enough to warn them when a message will cost them their souls. A shepherd who sees the wolf and says nothing is not humble; he is negligent.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul leaves the church not with a successor or a structure but with God and the word of his grace, which can build it up and bring it to its inheritance; and he leaves with nothing of theirs.

God and the word of his grace. Having sobered them thoroughly, he tells them what they actually have: God, and the word of his grace, the gospel now preserved in Scripture. That is the protection against wolves. He does not appoint a replacement, set up a chain of command back to Jerusalem, or tell them whom to consult; he leaves the church he had worked hardest for with God and a message. That is either reckless or the most confident thing in the chapter, and the next clause tells you which.

Commend. To entrust, to hand over for safekeeping. Paul deposits the elders with two keepers who never leave: God himself, and the word of his grace. The under-shepherd departs, but the Chief Shepherd remains; the Father who chose us, the Son who bought us and the Spirit who sealed us are not going anywhere, and the word that reveals them abides for ever.

Able to build you up. “Able” carries the whole weight, whether it refers to God or, as most take it, to the word of his grace: not a hope that they will manage but a capacity that belongs to the word itself. Build up is the construction word (Ephesians 4:12). The gospel is a living means by which God grows his people strong (1 Peter 2:2), as in this very city the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (19:20). So even after a great leader is gone, a church grows by the word of grace, fed on and held fast.

The inheritance. The future hope of all God’s holy people (26:18; Ephesians 1:14, 18; 1 Peter 1:4), secured by the same word that builds them up now. It is an inheritance, not a wage: given to children by grace, not earned.

Those who are sanctified. A settled standing, not an achievement: all true believers, everyone God has set apart for himself in Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11; Hebrews 10:10), not an elite who have made themselves holy enough.

Silver or gold or apparel. The turn from the inheritance of the saints to other people’s clothes is not odd in the ancient world. Wandering teachers living off admirers were a recognised trade and nuisance, and good clothing was portable wealth, the sort of gift a grateful household gave a visiting teacher. So Paul establishes that he is leaving with nothing (1 Thessalonians 2:5): there will be no suggestion, after the ship sails, that the apostle did well out of Ephesus.

Heirs because of the Heir. God has appointed his Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and those who belong to him are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The word of grace is the message about him, the holiness is his gift, and the inheritance is his estate, opened to his brothers.

If the word is enough, why do we need pastors and teachers? Because the word is God’s chosen instrument, and pastors are his chosen servants of the word. Paul did not commend them to God and the word instead of elders; he commended the elders themselves to God and the word. Teachers do not add to Scripture’s power; they open it, apply it and guard it. The danger is when people trust the teacher more than the text, or think a church cannot survive without a particular man. It can. Every faithful pastor’s goal is to point his people so firmly to God and his word that they would stand if he were gone.

parallels.desc: whose ox have I taken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s working hands show the elders how to labour so as to help the weak, as Jesus taught: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

These hands. He very likely held them up, and everyone there knew what was on them: the calluses of a man who had cut leather and cloth for a living, for years, in their city, and paid for his companions too.

To help the weak. We would expect him to say he worked so as not to be a burden, and he says that elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Here the reason is better: he worked so that there would be something to give away (Ephesians 4:28). Work is not what prevents ministry, nor merely what permits it; it is the source of the surplus that makes generosity possible.

The words of the Lord Jesus. Jesus never says this sentence in Matthew, Mark, Luke or John; it was passed down by those who heard him, the only saying from Jesus’ earthly ministry that Paul quotes in Acts, one line of the enormous remainder the world itself could not contain (John 21:25), preserved by the providence of God. And Paul says “remember”, not “as it is written”: these men may never have read a Gospel, and he expects them to have it by heart.

The hands behind these hands. Paul held up his own calloused hands and then pointed past them to the Lord Jesus, who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The tentmaker’s hands had given years of evenings to the weak of Ephesus; the hands of Jesus were nailed open for the weak of every nation. “It is more blessed to give than to receive” is not a proverb from a wise man. It is the self-portrait of the Giver.

A life of glad giving. The blessedness of giving is God’s own before it is ever ours. The Father gave the Son, the Son gave himself, and the Spirit is given and distributes his gifts to every member of the church. From all eternity the life of God has been a life of glad giving, and the Lord Jesus put it into one sentence his friends could not forget. Every time one of his people gives in his name, a little of that eternal joy spills over into a tired world.

What it means to be blessed. Nearly everyone alive believes, in practice, that receiving is the better arrangement. Jesus says it is the other way round, and the man quoting him had built a life on it and was standing there with the calluses to prove it. Today “blessed” usually means having more: the new house, the photo captioned “so blessed”. Jesus uses the word the other way round. To be blessed (makarios) is to be in the condition God approves and fills with his own gladness, the well-being of a life going the way life was made to go. Why then does receiving feel safer? Because what we hold is often what we lean on: the savings, the evening that is ours, the thanks we need. Giving it away feels like losing a piece of ourselves. Timothy Keller often pointed out that when Paul wanted the Corinthians to give, he did not shame them or set them a figure; he pointed them to Jesus, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). If you are already rich in him, giving is not a loss but an overflow. This week, give something you will actually feel, quietly, to someone who cannot pay you back, and find out what he meant.

Does this mean pastors should work and not be paid? No. Paul insists that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). He gave up that right for the sake of the gospel in some places. Both are honourable: a paid minister, and one who works to support himself.

Is it wrong to receive help when I need it? No. The saying does not make receiving shameful; it makes giving blessed. Paul gladly received the Philippians’ gifts and called them a fragrant offering (Philippians 4:18). In seasons of illness, poverty, old age or grief God calls us to receive, and pride that refuses help can rob others of the blessing of giving. Receive with gratitude and without embarrassment, and when the season turns, give with the same joy. The church is a circle of grace, in which every member both gives and receives, and Christ is the first giver of all.
verseByVerse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was remembered and passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The farewell ends on the ground in prayer and tears: a family that only Christ could have made.

He knelt down. Very likely near the harbour, in front of a ship’s crew, a group of grown men got down on the ground. Standing was the ordinary Jewish posture for prayer; people knelt when something weighed too much for standing: Solomon at the temple, Daniel, Stephen as the stones came down, Jesus in Gethsemane. And “with them all”: not over them, but down among them. Paul’s ministry in Ephesus ended, as it had been carried on, in prayer.

Much weeping. Grown men, church leaders, weeping, and Luke does not tidy it up. There is a strain of Christian teaching in which composure is next to godliness; here is the apostle who wrote that we do not grieve as those who have no hope, on the ground, in tears, in public, with his arms round men he did not expect to see again.

They embraced Paul. Literally, they fell on his neck: the phrase used of the father running to the prodigal (Luke 15:20) and of Joseph with Benjamin. Luke reaches for the language of family reunion to describe a parting, because that is what these men are and what they are losing.

A family made by Christ. A few years earlier most of these men had not heard of Jesus Christ, and several had probably bought silver shrines of Artemis. Now they are weeping by the water over a Jewish tentmaker. Only one thing turns strangers into family like that. The Son of God shared our flesh and blood and is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11, 14), and whoever is joined to him is joined to everyone else who is. And because he knelt in Gethsemane and prayed with loud cries and tears, his people may kneel anywhere and be heard.

Is it unspiritual to cry? No. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he was about to raise him (John 11:35), and wept over Jerusalem; Paul wept, these elders wept, and the psalms are full of tears. Tears are not a failure of faith but often an expression of love, for those we lose, for sin, for the suffering of others. Christian hope changes not whether we weep but how. So do not be ashamed of tears, your own or anyone else’s. God keeps count of them, and one day he will wipe every one away (Psalm 56:8; Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What broke the elders’ hearts was not the warnings but the loss of Paul’s face, and Luke lets that grief stand as a true measure of Christian love.

His face. Luke tells us which sentence did it, and it was not the one about chains, or wolves, or traitors. What these men could not bear was that they would not see his face. Not his letters, not his teaching. His face.

A human sorrow, uncorrected. Scripture does not correct that sorrow. Paul longs to see the Romans (Romans 1:11), and to see the Thessalonians face to face (1 Thessalonians 2:17). The New Testament, largely a collection of letters, is oddly insistent that letters are not enough. These men were not being sentimental; they were being accurate about what a relationship is.

To the ship. They walk him down to the water, very likely as a formal escort, and stand there until he is aboard; Luke’s next verse says they had to tear themselves away (21:1). What Paul left them were the two things he named in verse 32, God and the word of his grace, and on the evidence of the following decades it was enough, though even then Christ had to call that church back to the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4–5).

God did not send only a letter. That insistence on the face goes back to God himself. Long ago God spoke to the fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). He did not save the world by correspondence. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), with a face that could be seen and a hand that touched lepers, and the light of the knowledge of the glory of God now shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Gone ahead to prepare the far shore. The elders watched one ship go and could not follow it. The Lord Jesus has also gone from his people’s sight, but he has gone ahead to prepare the far shore, and he is coming back for every one of them. The parting at Miletus was real, the reunion will be more real still, and at the centre of it will be the face that was marred more than any man’s for our sake, now shining like the sun.

Will we really know one another in heaven? Yes. The hope of Scripture is not that we dissolve into a crowd but that we are raised as ourselves and gathered together with the Lord; Paul comforts the Thessalonians precisely with a reunion (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah were recognisable. And the face we will see above all others is his: “they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4). Every other face will be dearer for that.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God. Paul could tell the elders he was innocent of their blood because he had not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God (v. 27). That is the standard for every ministry of the word: not only true but whole (see v. 27).
20.examples:
Then: On the shore at Miletus, a man going to chains spent his last hours not arranging his escape but commending the elders to God. Their tears at parting were the fruit of three years of his tears among them.

Now: The questions for any ministry are Paul’s: did we hold anything back, or give people a comfortable Christ without his commands, grace without repentance, the promise without the warning? A church that has been taught the whole counsel is the one best able to recognise a twisted message when the wolves come.

keyVerse.quote: Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the farewell and of the chapter. Paul’s charge to the elders rests on what the church is worth: God bought it with his own blood, so it is his, and those who lead it are under-shepherds answerable to him. Every warning, tear and gift in the chapter is measured by that price.

20.reflection:
At Troas the church met on the first day of the week to break bread and hear the word, and Paul, in a hurry, waited seven days to be with them (vv. 6–7). What does your week show about the place the Lord’s Day gathering has in your life, and what helps you come to it gladly?

Paul says, “I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course” (v. 24). What would you need to finish for your life to be well spent, and what are you tempted to protect instead?

The church is “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (v. 28). How should that price change the way we treat the people in our church we find hardest to love, and the way we pray for, support or (if we lead) carry out its leadership?

Paul left the elders with God and the word of his grace (v. 32), and with Jesus’ words, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (v. 35). Where do you most need the word to build you up, and what could you give this week to someone who cannot repay you?

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
