21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed <sup>6</sup>and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>9</sup>He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>16</sup>And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law, <sup>21</sup>And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. <sup>22</sup>What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. <sup>23</sup>Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; <sup>24</sup>take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. <sup>25</sup>But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>29</sup>For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>34</sup>Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. <sup>35</sup>And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, <sup>36</sup>for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” <sup>37</sup>As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? <sup>38</sup>Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” <sup>39</sup>Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” <sup>40</sup>And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
21.overview:
Where we are. Paul has said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, warned by the Spirit that chains await him in Jerusalem (20:22–23). This chapter brings him there and turns the missionary into a prisoner; the rest of Acts follows him in chains to Rome.

The message. When the Lord’s will leads into suffering, his servant goes, and his people learn to say, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” God rules over loving pleas, wise plans, false rumours and a riot, and turns even chains into a road for the gospel. And because Paul is free in Christ, he can bend as far as love asks on customs while never bending on grace.

Why it was said. Readers like Theophilus needed to know why the great apostle ended up a Roman prisoner, and whether he was the lawbreaker his enemies said (see the introduction). Luke shows the rumour false, the charge invented, and the arrest no accident but foretold by the Spirit and accepted in advance.

How the chapter makes its case. At Tyre disciples who see the danger by the Spirit beg Paul not to go, then kneel with him on the beach (vv. 1–6). At Caesarea, in Philip’s house, Agabus binds himself with Paul’s belt; everyone pleads, Paul is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they hand him to God (vv. 7–16). James and the elders welcome him gladly, and to answer a false rumour Paul joins four men completing a vow, while the Gentiles’ freedom stands (vv. 17–26). Falsely accused of bringing Greeks into the temple, he is nearly lynched, then rescued by Roman soldiers and put in two chains (vv. 27–36). On the barracks steps he asks to speak, and the crowd falls silent (vv. 37–40).

Where it leads. Luke tells Paul’s road in the shape of Jesus’ road: set toward Jerusalem, handed over to the Gentiles, met with the cry “Away with him!” The likeness shows the difference. Paul is pulled out at the top of the stairs; Christ went all the way, bound so that we could go free, and by his torn body broke down the very wall the mob was defending (Ephesians 2:14). That a man would gladly die “for the name of the Lord Jesus” shows what that name is worth.

For us. When following Christ will cost us and those who love us beg us to stop, receive their love, weigh their counsel by Scripture, and pray, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” Bend for love wherever the gospel is not at stake, never on grace, and trust that in Christ’s hands no chain is wasted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul goes up to Jerusalem knowing that chains wait for him there, and the church learns to let him go. The voyage to Tyre runs smoothly toward his arrest (vv. 1–3). At Tyre disciples, shown the danger by the Spirit, beg him not to go, then kneel with him on the beach and pray (vv. 4–6). At Caesarea he stays with Philip, whom he once drove out of Jerusalem (vv. 7–9), and Agabus binds himself with Paul’s belt to show what is coming (vv. 10–11). Everyone pleads; Paul is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they say, “Let the will of the Lord be done” (vv. 12–14). They go up and lodge with Mnason, an early disciple (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Guidance: a Revelation and an Inference

Nobody in this passage is a villain. The Spirit revealed what was waiting in Jerusalem; the “do not go” was added by people who loved Paul (see the note on vv. 4–5), and Agabus announces the outcome without instruction (see vv. 10–11). God’s providence, his rule over all that happens, makes sense of this: because God plans both the goal and the road to it, a warning of suffering is often not a sign telling us to turn aside but a description of the road he means us to take. Paul is told the cost in advance so that he can pay it with his eyes open.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A whole congregation at Tyre, children too, kneeling on the shore of a working harbour to pray for a man they had known for seven days, and then going home to supper while he sailed toward chains. Now: When someone we love walks toward a costly obedience we cannot talk them out of, we need what that church found on the beach: the grace to lose the argument and keep the love, and to pray with them that the Lord’s will be done.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tears himself away from the Ephesian elders and sails fast for Jerusalem, hurrying toward the city where he has been told chains are waiting. The voyage runs smoothly, and the smoothness is carrying him to prison.

Parted. The word is too gentle. Luke’s verb means to pull away (many translations have “tore ourselves away”); it is the word for drawing a sword from its sheath (Matthew 26:51). Nobody walks away from an embrace like the one at Miletus (20:36–38). You have to be pulled out of it.

By a straight course. Then the ship’s log: short daylight hops down the island chain off the south-west corner of Asia Minor, the shore always in view. Luke used the same word when the gospel first crossed into Europe (16:11). The winds are behind them; nothing in the voyage resists.

A ship crossing to Phoenicia. Patara was the great harbour of Lycia, where coastal traffic met the deep-sea freighters running east (see roads and travel). A ship crossing over would strike out across open sea: some four hundred miles to Tyre, perhaps five days with a following wind.

Why change ships? Because Paul is racing the clock: “he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost” (20:16), and hopping from port to port would be too slow. So a man told in city after city that chains await him books a faster passage, in order to arrive sooner. We hurry toward what we want; Paul hurries toward what he has been warned about, with a traveller’s care for the right harbour, ship and sailing date. Obedience here is not a leap off a cliff. It is logistics.

A baptism he longed to have done. One other traveller in Luke’s writings hurried toward suffering. On his way to Jerusalem Jesus said, “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50), meaning his suffering and death. He did not drift toward the cross; he pressed toward it. Paul on a fast freighter is not repeating that finished work, but showing the same kind of obedience, learned from the Lord who first set out for that city.

Does a smooth journey mean God approves of my plans? Not necessarily, and this voyage is the proof: every circumstance is quietly cooperating to deliver Paul to the city where he will be seized, beaten and chained. Easy circumstances are a mercy and hard ones are no sign of God’s displeasure, but neither tells you by itself whether you are walking in his will; that is learned from his word, a good conscience and wise counsel. Give thanks when doors open, and when they slam shut, do not assume you have taken a wrong turning. Paul’s smoothest crossing took him to his chains, and his chains took him to Rome.
verseByVerse.note: Cos, Rhodes and Patara were ports along the south-west coast of Asia Minor; from Patara they crossed the open sea east toward Phoenicia.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cyprus slides past and the ship puts in at Tyre to unload, and a cargo schedule sets Paul down for a week among a church his own persecution once helped to plant.

Leaving it on the left. A sailor’s sentence: running south-east, Cyprus slides past on the left, and Luke, on board, writes down which side it went by. Details like this are why many historians think these “we” passages come from an eyewitness (see the introduction).

Cyprus on the horizon. Cyprus is Barnabas’s home (4:36), where the first missionary journey began (13:4–6), and where Barnabas sailed with Mark when he and Paul parted (15:39). Now it passes and the ship does not stop. The longer you serve the Lord, the more of your life sits on the horizon like that: real, visible, unreachable, going by on the left while the wind takes you somewhere else.

Tyre. The great port of Phoenicia, whose pride the prophets had denounced (Ezekiel 26–28). In that region a Gentile mother had begged Jesus for crumbs from the children’s table and gone home with her daughter healed (Mark 7:24–30). The crumbs have become a church.

To unload its cargo. Unloading a freighter by hand could take the better part of a week, and that is how long they stay (v. 4). God uses a dockworker’s timetable to put Paul in front of a church he would otherwise have sailed past.

Where did the church at Tyre come from? Nobody in Acts was sent to plant it. Those scattered by the persecution over Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia (11:19), so there are very probably disciples in this port because a young Pharisee once ravaged the church and dragged men and women off to prison (8:3). Paul is about to be fed and housed by a church his own violence helped to plant, and to kneel on their beach with their children. The gospel does not merely forgive the persecutor; it seats him at the table of the people he scattered.

Did Paul and Barnabas ever make it up? Scripture suggests they did, though Acts does not tell the story. Years later Paul mentions Barnabas warmly as a fellow worker who, like himself, earned his own living (1 Corinthians 9:6). Mark, the young man they quarrelled over, is with Paul in his imprisonment (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24), and at the very end Paul asks for him as useful for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). The disagreement was real, and so was the healing. Christians can disagree badly and still be reconciled, and God can use even their parting to send out two missions instead of one.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a major port of Phoenicia, north of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The believers at Tyre, shown by the Spirit what awaits Paul, keep begging him not to go; but “do not go” is love’s conclusion, not the Spirit’s command, and when they lose the argument they kneel with him on the beach and pray.

Having sought out the disciples. The verb means to find by searching. There was no building and no address; the church at Tyre was invisible from the street, and it was there.

Through the Spirit. Then the hard sentence. The tense suggests they said it again and again through the seven days, and Luke does not say they were mistaken about the source. Was Paul then defying the Spirit? He had answered that a chapter earlier: the Spirit revealed the suffering (20:22–23), and the Spirit himself was leading him to Jerusalem (19:21). These disciples had a genuine revelation and added a conclusion of their own, “therefore do not go”: love talking, not prophecy. That is the most widely held explanation and fits Luke’s words, but this is one of the hard verses of Acts, and Christians who puzzle over it are not being faithless.

Right about the revelation, wrong about the inference. The Gospels have a moment shaped exactly like this. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, revealed by the Father in heaven; soon after, when Jesus says he must suffer in Jerusalem, Peter rebukes him, “This shall never happen to you,” and hears, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:16–23). Right about the revelation, badly wrong about the inference, and the motive for the error was affection.

With wives and children. This is a church that lost the argument and did not sulk. The whole congregation, small children included, walked a man they had known for seven days out through the gate and down to the water.

Kneeling on the beach. They knelt in the wet sand of a working harbour, in front of dockers and sailors. Luke keeps kneeling in Acts for moments that cost something: Stephen under the stones (7:60), Peter beside a dead woman (9:40), Paul with the Ephesian elders (20:36). If a church cannot do in years what Tyre did in a week, the difference is not time. On that sand strangers became family, because the Son of God made one people out of the scattered.

What do I do when a Christian friend says God has told them I should not do something? Separate what is claimed as revealed from what has been concluded from it, and test both by Scripture: no private impression can add a command to God’s finished word or cancel one in it. A true word about coming trouble is not an instruction to avoid it; often it is God telling you the price in advance, so that you cannot say afterwards you were tricked into paying it. Receive your friend’s concern gratefully, weigh it with your elders and wise believers, and if it is love speaking rather than the word of God, thank them for the love and do what God has plainly called you to do.

Where Christians differ: can prophecy be mistaken? Some cite this verse to argue that New Testament prophecy was fallible, mixing God’s revelation with human interpretation; they hold this out of care to take Luke’s words at face value, and the question is a fair one. This commentary’s view: what the Spirit revealed was true: chains awaited Paul. What the disciples drew from it, that he should avoid them, was their own conclusion. Revelation must be distinguished from our application of it. The Spirit’s word is never mistaken; our inferences can be.
verseByVerse.note: The Spirit revealed the danger ahead; the disciples concluded that he should not go.

verseByVerse.quote: "and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two parties leave the same beach, one for chains in Jerusalem and one for home, and Luke records both: the hidden faithfulness of those who went home is written into Scripture too.

They returned home. Luke could have made a scene of the farewell and refuses: farewells are exchanged and the gangplank is crossed. One party boards a ship for Jerusalem, chains and a Roman barracks. The other shakes the sand off and goes home, to the nets and the warehouses and the children who now want their dinner. We are trained to think the ship is the real story. Luke wrote both halves of the verse down.

The ones who went home. This church took in strangers, fed them, prayed with them about a decision it could not change, and walked them to the water. No sermon of theirs survives, and perhaps none of them ever saw Paul again, yet the Holy Spirit had it recorded in Scripture. Most of us are Tyre. The great work of God in our generation will pass through our town for about a week, and our part in it will be a spare bed, a meal, and a prayer on the way out. That is not the small version of the Christian life. That is the Christian life, and it is written down.

The hidden years in Nazareth. The Lord himself lived most of his life in the same hidden way. Luke records one episode from those years, and then that “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (Luke 2:51). Before he had preached a sermon or worked a miracle, the Father declared himself well pleased with his beloved Son (Luke 3:22). Those years were part of the perfect obedience by which he saved us, and they make the kitchen, the workbench and the nursery holy ground when the work is done for him (Colossians 3:23).

Is my ordinary life really service to God if I never do anything dramatic? Yes, and this verse says so. The believers who returned home did not stop serving God when the ship left; they went back to the place he had put them. Hospitality, prayer, faithful work, raising children who have knelt beside a missionary: these are not the waiting room of the Christian life. Whoever receives one of Christ’s servants receives him, and even a cup of cold water given to one of his disciples will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40–42). God sees the spare bed, and he wrote it in his book.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, who once drove Philip out of Jerusalem, now stays many days as a guest in Philip’s house: the gospel has made the persecutor and the persecuted one family.

Ptolemais. The old port of Acco, modern Acre, just north of Carmel. No mission to it appears in Acts, yet there are brothers to greet, the second church in this chapter that no one in Acts founded: refugees from Jerusalem had walked up this coast preaching as they went (11:19). Much of the map of Christianity was drawn not by strategy but by people running for their lives and talking as they went.

Philip the evangelist. Philip was one of the Seven appointed to wait on tables (6:5). He preached Christ in Samaria, baptised an Ethiopian official on the Gaza road, and was last seen preaching his way up the coast to Caesarea (8:40). That was some twenty years ago, and he is still there, still serving, the only man in Scripture to wear the word evangelist as a title (compare Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 4:5). It is often suggested that Luke gathered much of his early history in these weeks, from the man who had lived it.

Why was Philip in Caesarea at all? Because Saul of Tarsus drove him out of Jerusalem. Saul approved of Stephen’s execution and ravaged the church, dragging off men and women to prison; those who were scattered went about preaching the word, and Philip went down to Samaria (8:1–5). He was a colleague of Stephen, chosen on the same day, and Stephen had died at the hands of a mob whose coats were minded by the man now on his doorstep asking for a bed.

The first wound was Christ’s. On the Damascus road the risen Lord did not ask Saul why he was persecuting Stephen or Philip. He said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (9:5). Christ counted every house Saul broke into as an attack on himself, and Christ was the first to forgive it. So when Philip opens his door, he is not deciding whether Saul’s past can be overlooked. The one most wronged has already settled it.

And he says come in. Not for an hour: they “stayed with him”, and by verse 10 it has been “many days”. Reconciliation is not a warm feeling about someone at a distance; it is an address you are willing to sleep at and a table you are willing to eat at. Philip opened his door, but first Paul had to knock, which for a proud man is the harder half. And behind that doorway stands a greater one: God opened his house to us while we were his enemies and gave us a place among his children for ever, like the Father running down the road to the son who wasted everything.

In everyday life. If there is someone you have wronged, or who has wronged you, and Christ has been at work in you both, take one step toward that table this month: a letter, a call, a meal.

Does forgiving someone mean I have to have them in my home? Not always, and wisdom matters here. Forgiveness means giving up the right to repay, wishing the other person good and praying for them, and it is never optional for a Christian (Matthew 6:14–15; Ephesians 4:32). Full fellowship of the kind Philip offered rests on repentance: Saul had been changed by Christ, and everyone knew it. Where a person has not repented, or where there has been abuse, keeping a safe distance is not unforgiveness, and no one should be pressed to share a roof with someone who may harm them. But where Christ has truly changed both people, the gospel aims at more than a truce. It aims at a table.
verseByVerse.note: Ptolemais is modern Acre. Philip was one of the seven chosen in Acts 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip’s four unmarried daughters prophesied: in an ordinary home in Caesarea, God was keeping his promise through Joel that daughters as well as sons would prophesy.

Four unmarried daughters. Luke drops the words in as if noting the number of rooms in the house, and the casualness is the point. More than twenty years earlier Peter had read out Joel at Pentecost: “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (2:17). Here the promised age of the Spirit is seen in four young women at the family table. Women received and exercised the gift of prophecy in the apostolic church (1 Corinthians 11:5), and nobody makes a fuss about it.

Whose daughters they are. Philip preached to Samaritans and to an African official when nobody else would. Households take the shape of what the head of the house believes God is like.

Luke’s silence. Luke records that they prophesied and not one word they said, though the next paragraph gives Agabus’s prophecy in full. His interest is the fact of the gift, so we should build neither a doctrine nor a grievance on the silence. The historian Eusebius records that the daughters later lived at Hierapolis in Asia and were remembered as living sources for the earliest days (though ancient writers sometimes confuse this Philip with the apostle). Not one syllable of theirs is in our Bible, and the church’s memory ran through them anyway.

What the gift was for. Peter gave the reason the day it began: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out (2:33). The daughters prophesied because the crucified Nazarene was reigning, and “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” (Revelation 19:10). The Spirit never speaks to make his servants famous; he speaks to make the Son known. And the Lord keeps his promises down to the details of an ordinary home: what he spoke through Joel he fulfilled in four young women whose names we do not know, and he will keep every promise to his church until the last is kept on the day his Son appears.

Holding both together. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the church (1 Corinthians 11:5) in the same letter in which he orders that gathering (1 Corinthians 14). Luke is describing a household, not installing anyone in a pulpit (see the box at the end of this note); what he plainly says is that God pours out his Spirit on daughters.

Do women prophesy like this today? The church still needs the voices of its daughters, but the particular gift Luke describes belonged to the founding years (whether it continues is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: do prophets like Agabus still speak today?” in the note on vv. 10–11). What remains for every woman, as for every man, is the Spirit’s gift of speaking God’s finished word to others: teaching children and younger women (Titus 2:3–5), explaining the way of God more accurately as Priscilla did with Apollos (18:26), encouraging, comforting and warning one another (Hebrews 3:13). A woman who brings Scripture to bear on a friend’s grief is doing in her generation what these four did in theirs.

Where Christians differ: prophesying women and church leadership. Some argue that because women prophesied, they may also hold the office of elder or pastor. This commentary’s view: prophecy and the office of elder are different things. Women prophesied, prayed and served in the apostolic church, and are honoured for it; the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the gathered church Scripture gives to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:6). The complementarian view (that men and women are equal in worth and gifting, with different callings in the home and the church) honours both truths: the full dignity and gifts of women, and the order God has given for the church.

parallels.desc: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

verseByVerse.quote: "While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul's belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit, "This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agabus, a proven prophet, acts out Paul’s arrest with Paul’s own belt: the Holy Spirit announces that Paul will be bound in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles, as his Lord was. He says what will happen, not that Paul must turn back.

Agabus. We have met him. He foretold a great famine years before, and Luke adds drily that it took place in the days of Claudius (11:28). He has a verified track record.

Paul’s belt. He takes the long cloth belt from Paul’s waist and ties his own feet and hands with it in front of the whole household. This is prophecy in the old manner: Isaiah walked barefoot for three years as a sign (Isaiah 20:2–4); Jeremiah wore a yoke through the streets (Jeremiah 27:2); Ezekiel laid siege to a brick (Ezekiel 4). Everyone in that room would forget the sentence. Nobody would forget the belt.

Thus says the Holy Spirit. “Thus says the LORD” is the prophets’ regular opening, marking the speech of the covenant God. Agabus, a Jewish prophet in a Jewish house, puts the Holy Spirit’s name in it as naturally as breathing. The doctrine of the Trinity was not invented by a later council; it is built into the church’s earliest speech, because these men saw no difference between the Spirit speaking and God speaking. There is none: the Spirit is God.

Into the hands of the Gentiles. Agabus does not say “do not go”. He says only what will happen, and that is the difference between him and the disciples at Tyre, which is why Luke places them side by side. And the wording is the wording of the passion: Jesus said he would be “delivered over to the Gentiles” (Luke 18:32).

He let himself be tied. The road the Spirit described for Paul was the road the Son of God had already walked: bound by his own people, handed over to the Gentiles, and led out to die. But Paul’s binding would carry the gospel to Rome; Christ’s binding carried our sins away. He let himself be tied so that we could go free.

Did the prophecy come true, when it was the Romans who bound him? Yes, in the way Scripture ordinarily speaks. The Jews try to lynch Paul and the Romans put on the chains (vv. 30–33), but Scripture routinely credits an act to those who caused it: Peter tells Jerusalem that they crucified and killed Jesus by the hands of lawless men (2:23), though no Jew drove a nail. And the man in the chains settles it: years later Paul tells the Jewish leaders in Rome that he was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans (28:17), Agabus’s prophecy quoted back almost word for word. The fit is not exact in every detail, and some readers press the difference.

Where Christians differ: do prophets like Agabus still speak today? Many Christians believe the gift continues, and they love the Lord and his word. They often point to 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 and 14:1, reading prophecy as lasting until Christ returns, and it is a serious argument. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20) and ceased with the completion of Scripture. Agabus’s words came true in substance: Paul was bound and handed over to the Gentiles. We hold this charitably toward brothers who see it differently, and we expect the Spirit to speak to his church today through the Scripture he has given, which is sufficient for everything we need for life and godliness.
verseByVerse.note: Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone in the house, Luke included, begs Paul not to go: the strongest pull away from obedience here comes not from enemies but from the tears of friends.

We urged him. Read the pronoun. Luke is in the room, and on the wrong side. Writing years later, knowing Paul was right, he could have left himself out; instead he puts himself among those who tried to talk the apostle out of obeying God. A writer polishing his own part would hardly do that. A man who knows he has been forgiven might.

The pressure of love. Tyre for seven days, and now the whole household, the travelling companions, and Luke himself, who will be with him to the last (2 Timothy 4:11). Every Christian in the building is telling him not to go, like Peter trying to stop Jesus going to the cross (Matthew 16:22): natural, loving, and wrong. We prepare for opposition from enemies, but often the strongest force against obedience is the affection of people who cannot bear what it will cost you. They are not wicked. They are weeping, and their tears can do what threats never could. There was one man whom no tears could turn aside, and we are saved because Jesus would not be persuaded.

Love received but not obeyed. Their love is precious and should be received warmly, but it is not an argument: it settles nothing about what God has said. Nor is it an enemy: Paul does not rebuke them or accuse them of unbelief. Yet the approval of people we love, one of the sweetest things God gives, can for that very reason become the thing we most fear to lose, taking the place that belongs to God alone (Galatians 1:10).

In everyday life. Be careful your love does not hold others back from God’s call: the missionary son, the friend taking a stand that will cost him his job. Tell them you will miss them, and then help them pack.

How do I know when to listen to people who love me, and when to disappoint them? Ask what their counsel rests on. If they point you to Scripture, to a clear duty you are neglecting, or to wisdom you have not weighed, listen hard; there is safety in many counsellors (Proverbs 11:14), and most of the time the people who love you are right. If they ask you to step back from something God has plainly called you to because the cost frightens them, thank them and stay the course. And if you are the one urging, as Luke was, ask honestly whether you want someone to be careful because God has spoken, or because you cannot face losing them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "Let the will of the Lord be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heartbroken by their tears but ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, Paul will not be moved, and his friends, out of arguments, hand him over to God: “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? He is not made of stone. The word translated breaking (synthryptō) means to break in pieces, and so to crush someone’s resolve; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Paul is under two pressures, and only one of them is chains. A Roman prison he can face; what is crushing him is the sound of people who love him, sobbing.

Ready to die. Not braced or resigned but prepared, as a soldier is; not reckless but resolved, like his Lord, who set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). “Not only to be imprisoned but even to die”: he has already counted the cost of the worst outcome, which is why the weeping cannot move him. You cannot threaten a man with something he has already agreed to (Philippians 1:21). And he is ready to die not for a cause or for the collection in his luggage, but for the name of the Lord Jesus. Persons are worth dying for in a way that projects never are.

Let the will of the Lord be done. It may be the quietest great moment in Acts. They were not convinced; they ran out of arguments in front of a man who would not move, and they stopped. The sentence they said is the one from the garden: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). This is Gethsemane in a front room in Caesarea, prayed by ordinary Christians over a friend they expect to lose. It is not resignation, which gives up on the outcome; they are handing it to a Person. There comes a moment in most Christian lives when the praying stops being about changing the verdict and starts being about trusting the Judge, and this is the sentence to have ready.

He drank every drop. The prayer the church at Caesarea managed through its tears had already been prayed perfectly, in the dark, by a man with nobody awake to hear him. The cup was not taken away, and he drank every drop. The will of the Lord was done, in his body, on a hill outside the walls, and that is the only reason there was a church in Caesarea to pray it at all.

Is it right to want to die for Christ? Paul is not seeking death, and Scripture never praises those who throw their lives away. He had escaped over the Damascus wall in a basket (9:25) and would shortly use his Roman citizenship to avoid a flogging (22:25). He has settled in advance that his life is not his own, so that if obedience costs him his life, he will not hold it back. That is what every Christian is called to: not a death wish, but a heart that has already handed everything over. Most believers will never be asked to die for Christ. All of us are asked to live as people who would.

Is this not just religious fanaticism, the kind that makes people dangerous? Paul is ready to be bound and to die, not to bind or kill anyone. The Assassins of these very years carried daggers into festival crowds (v. 38); Paul carries a message, and when the mob beats him he asks to speak to it. The fanatic will sacrifice others for his cause. The Christian has a Lord who gave himself for his enemies (Romans 5:8), and so will lay down his own life for that Lord’s name, and never take another’s.

Is saying “Let the will of the Lord be done” giving up on prayer? No. These believers had pleaded, and rightly; the Lord Jesus himself asked that the cup might pass. Asking boldly and submitting belong in the same prayer. What changes at the end is not that we stop caring but that we stop insisting, and hand the outcome to a Father who is wiser than we are and loves the person we are praying for more than we do. That is not defeat. It is the deepest kind of trust.

parallels.desc: not my will, but yours

verseByVerse.quote: After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the argument is over, obedience looks like packing: the party walks up to Jerusalem, where an early disciple from Cyprus, at home with Gentiles, has beds ready for them.

We got ready. The ordinary word for packing baggage and loading animals. After days of tears and prophecy, a group of men strap on their bags for a walk of some sixty-five miles up to the ridge, for Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet above the plain. Obedience, once the argument is over, mostly looks like luggage.

In the flow. The long journey reaches its goal, told as Luke told the last journey of Jesus (Luke 9:51): warnings, friends who would hold him back, and a final going up to the city. From here the missionary becomes a prisoner, and the rest of Acts shows the gospel reaching Rome through his chains.

What is in those bags? Luke does not say, and it is one of the most striking silences in Acts. For years Paul had organised a relief fund among the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem: he gave Corinth detailed instructions (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), spent two chapters of a letter urging them to finish it (2 Corinthians 8–9), and asked the Romans to pray that it would be acceptable (Romans 15:25–31). It was the great labour of his later ministry, a tangible proof that the Gentile churches and the mother church were one body. Luke mentions it once in the whole book, and not until Paul is on trial (24:17). The thing Paul travelled for years to deliver gets no paragraph; the evangelist who had stayed in Caesarea for twenty years gets a verse and a title. There is a lesson there for anyone who handles money in the church, or quietly funds it: Luke is not measuring by what a thing cost to arrange, and neither, in the end, is God.

Mnason of Cyprus. The lodging was arranged in advance, and look who was chosen: a Cypriot with a Greek name, like Barnabas (4:36), and an early disciple, perhaps from Pentecost itself. Paul arrives with uncircumcised Gentiles in a city of law-zealous believers (v. 20), and his host is a disciple of long standing, at home with Gentiles: a man who can put Trophimus the Ephesian in his spare room without the neighbours calling it a scandal.

Receiving the Lord at the door. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), and he said that a welcome given to the least of his brothers is given to him: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). When an old disciple from Cyprus made up beds for a Jewish apostle and his uncircumcised friends, he was opening his door to Christ, and Christ will remember it. And the Lord goes ahead of his servants: the one who arranged lodging for an apostle in a hostile city has arranged ours for eternity, and the door is already open.

What does Christian hospitality look like when my home is small or my life is busy? It looks like Mnason: an open door to the person who needs one, when they need it. It needs no large house, polished meal or tidy kitchen, only a willingness to make room and some thought about who would be uncomfortable elsewhere: the newcomer, the overseas student, the believer from a different background, the person others hesitate to have. Scripture makes hospitality a duty for every Christian, not a gift for a few (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), and older believers are often its best practitioners. A bed, a bowl of soup and a welcome can be the most strategic thing in the whole mission.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church welcomes Paul and the Gentile mission gladly, but a false rumour and a false charge put him in chains, and even that will serve the gospel. James and the elders praise God for Paul’s report, then warn him of a rumour among Jewish believers that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses (vv. 17–22). To answer it Paul joins four men completing a vow, while the letter that freed the Gentile believers stands (vv. 23–26). Near the end of the week Jews from Asia accuse him of bringing Greeks into the temple, and the city tries to kill him (vv. 27–30). The Roman tribune rescues him, binds him with two chains, takes him for an Egyptian rebel, and lets him speak to the crowd (vv. 31–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
Liberty, Accommodation, and the Line That Does Not Move

Paul in the temple paying for offerings does not contradict Galatians; he applies it: the freedom the gospel gave him is what let him keep the customs without trusting them (see the note on vv. 25–26). To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The line is drawn not at the act but at what the act is made to mean (see vv. 23–24), and here nothing is required of any Gentile (vv. 25–26). So bend as far as love can on matters of culture and conscience, and not at all on what makes us acceptable to God. And this wise and humble course failed; the outcome belonged to God, who made it the road to Rome (see vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An apostle with Roman citizenship in his pocket, chained at the door of a fortress, spending his one request not on rescue but on permission to preach to the mob that had just beaten him. Now: God’s help does not always come from where we expect it (see vv. 31–32), and the platform we are given is rarely the one we asked for (see vv. 39–40). What has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem church receives Paul and his Gentile companions gladly, and the next day he reports to James and all the elders: the mother church and the Gentile mission embrace.

Received us gladly. Relief as much as pleasure. Months earlier Paul had asked the Romans to pray “that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints” (Romans 15:31). He was not sure the mother church would take what he was bringing. The first half of that prayer would be answered in an unexpected way; the second is answered here.

James and all the elders. The formal meeting comes the next day, with the full leadership assembled. James, the Lord’s brother, presides (15:13; Galatians 2:9) with a body of elders; Luke mentions no apostles, for Peter had left Jerusalem years before (12:17). The apostle to the Gentiles does not summon them. He goes in to them, with his delegation, and reports.

A delegation with a bag. “Went in with us”: Luke is there, and presumably the delegates of 20:4, men from several provinces, many of them uncircumcised Gentiles, carrying a large sum for Jewish believers they have never met (24:17). Paul had worked for years so that the unity of the church would be more than a doctrine. Here it is: a delegation standing in a room with a gift. Whatever happens in the next twenty verses, this happened first, and it happened gladly.

In the flow. Acts began in Jerusalem with the promise of witness to the end of the earth (1:8), and now the man who carried it furthest comes back with its fruit in his hands. This is the last time Acts shows the Jerusalem church, and Luke lets us watch the embrace before he shows what the city will do with the man who brought it.

Two men the risen Christ appeared to. James, presiding, is the brother of Jesus, and during the Lord’s ministry not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Paul, reporting, tried to destroy his church. Paul tells what changed them both: “Then he appeared to James … Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me” (1 Corinthians 15:7–8). The sceptical brother and the persecuting Pharisee sit in one room as leaders of one church because Jesus came out of the tomb and showed himself to each.

The only gift he wants. Gentiles once far off came carrying gifts to Zion, as the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 60:5). But the true fulfilment is greater than any purse: the nations lay before Christ the only gift he wants, themselves, made one body by the blood that has brought near those who were far off (Ephesians 2:13).

Why does it matter how a church is governed? Because Christ is the head of his church and has given it an order. In the New Testament, local churches are led by a plurality of elders, also called overseers and shepherds (20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7), with deacons serving alongside them (Philippians 1:1). Christians differ fairly over whether congregations are bound together under wider assemblies or govern themselves, but every faithful view agrees on what this verse shows: leadership is shared, accountable and humble, and even an apostle submits his work to the brothers.
verseByVerse.note: James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells what God has done among the Gentiles and the elders praise God; then, calling him brother, they name the problem: tens of thousands of Jewish believers who are zealous for the law.

One by one. Item by item, and not brief: Cyprus, Lystra, Philippi, Corinth, Ephesus; the jailer at midnight, Lydia, Eutychus alive on the floor at Troas. Years of work, told to men who had not seen any of it.

The grammar of a servant. In every sentence God is the one who acts; Paul is only the one he acts through. God opened Lydia’s heart, shook the jail at Philippi, and had a people in Corinth before Paul arrived (18:10). That way of seeing let Paul survive both the applause at Lystra and the stoning that followed. He wrote it to the Romans: “I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me” (Romans 15:18).

They glorified God. They did not congratulate Paul; they worshipped (compare 11:18). A church that can hear of work it did not do, in places it will never see, and praise God rather than measure itself, is in good health.

How many thousands. Then, in the same breath, the problem. The word is myriads, tens of thousands, though it can be used loosely of a vast number, and the elders say it with joy. And they call Paul brother: they are not interrogating an opponent but briefing a member of the family about a fire in the house.

Zealous for the law. The word is the one that gave the Zealot party its name. These are Jewish believers who keep the law of Moses as their way of life, not their way of salvation: the Sabbath, the circumcision of their sons, the feasts, the food laws. It is their culture and identity, and with Jewish nationalism building toward the war with Rome within a decade, such zeal could easily turn into suspicion of anyone who seemed to loosen it. Neither James nor Luke rebukes them: the Jerusalem Council had freed Gentiles from the law, but never said that Jews who believe must abandon it, and Paul never taught that either. One gospel has produced two cultures, a triumph, and a danger one spark could set alight.

In everyday life. Give an account of your last year of Christian service, out loud, the way Paul did: not what you managed or built, but the things God did, through you.

Should Jewish believers keep the law today? Paul himself kept Jewish customs where they did not compromise the gospel (“To the Jews I became as a Jew”, 1 Corinthians 9:20), and a Jewish Christian is free to keep them as a matter of heritage and witness. What no one may do is make them necessary for salvation or impose them on Gentile believers (15:19–20; Galatians 2:14–16). The sacrifices and the temple are another matter: they were shadows fulfilled in Christ, and when the temple fell in AD 70 God himself brought that part of the old order to its end (Hebrews 8:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rumour says Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses: false as it stands, though it grew from his true teaching that no custom makes anyone right with God, and the elders know that words alone will not undo it.

They have been told. The verb is the word for instruction, from which we get catechism (Luke 1:4): the report had been passed on, perhaps even taught, to a great many people, and Luke does not say by whom.

An accusation nobody could check. The offence is said to have happened among the Jews who are among the Gentiles, in synagogues hundreds of miles away. Nobody present can disprove it, and that is what gives it its grip.

Children and customs. The cradle and the calendar. Say that a man is dissolving Jewish family life, in a city of law-zealous believers, and you have made him dangerous.

Was the rumour true? As stated, no, though it grew from a seed of truth. Paul never taught Jews to forsake Moses or to stop circumcising their children. He kept the customs himself, freely and gladly: he took a vow (18:18), circumcised Timothy (16:3), hurried to keep Pentecost (20:16), and worshipped in the temple. He told the Corinthians that a man called when circumcised should not try to undo it (1 Corinthians 7:18). The word in the charge is apostasia, rebellion or abandonment, and of that Paul was simply innocent; he called the law holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12).

The seed of truth. What made the rumour believable is that Paul really did teach something radical: that nothing, not circumcision, not law-keeping, makes anyone right with God; that justification, God’s verdict declaring a sinner righteous in his sight, is by faith in Christ alone (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28); that Gentile believers need not keep the law at all (15:19; he refused to circumcise Titus, Galatians 2:3–5); that the ceremonial law is a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17); and that the believer has died to the law as a way of standing before God (Romans 7:4–6). In hostile retelling, “you are free from the law” was twisted into “you must abandon the law”, and the difference between the two is the whole point. Paul preached freedom, not abandonment (on what that freedom meant for Jewish believers, see vv. 19–20).

What then is to be done? A real pastoral problem. “They will certainly hear that you have come”: Jerusalem is filling for Pentecost, and Paul has walked in with a band of Gentiles and a purse. There is no possibility of a quiet visit.

Living your way back. The elders do not offer to explain, draft a statement or call an assembly so Paul can clear his name. Experienced pastors, they know something we are slow to learn: a reputation is rarely repaired by explanation. Once a man is widely believed to be a certain kind of man, even true words about him are heard as a defence and discounted. So they look for something he can do: not a denial that can be disputed, but a week of conduct in public view. Whether the plan was wise is the question of the next verses. That the instinct was right is hardly in doubt.

Condemned as a lawbreaker. Paul was not the first to be falsely accused of destroying Moses. The Lord Jesus came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them (Matthew 5:17), and he was condemned as a lawbreaker. He kept the law perfectly and then bore its curse for those who had broken it (Galatians 3:13). That is why Paul could be free from the law and still honour it.

What should I do if false things are being said about me? First, ask honestly whether any of it is true; as Paul’s case shows, there is often a seed. Repent of what is yours and put it right. Then, where the charge is false, say so plainly once, to those who need to hear it, without bitterness. After that, let your life answer. Peter told believers slandered by their neighbours to keep their conduct honourable, so that those who speak against them would see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). And commit your name to God, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled (1 Peter 2:23).
verseByVerse.note: The rumour was false; Paul opposed circumcision only when it was treated as necessary for salvation, especially for Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders ask Paul to show Jerusalem that he still honours the law, by joining four men at the end of a vow and paying for their offerings; he can do it freely, because no custom is his way to God.

The plan. Specific and public: Paul is to join four men near the end of a vow, be purified with them, settle their bill at the temple, and be seen doing it for a week, in the busiest place in the Jewish world at the busiest season of the year.

Four men under a vow. These men were ending a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6): a voluntary dedication to the LORD for a set period, with no wine or anything from the vine, no razor on the head, the uncut hair being the visible sign of consecration, and no contact with a dead body, even of a parent. At the end the Nazirite brought a male lamb as a burnt offering, a ewe lamb as a sin offering and a ram as a peace offering, with grain and drink offerings (Numbers 6:13–21); his head was shaved and the hair burned in the fire under the peace offering. Sponsoring these costly offerings was a recognised form of piety: Josephus records that King Agrippa I paid for many Nazirites to be shaved when he came to Jerusalem.

Purify yourself along with them. Paul himself goes through a rite of purification, very likely the seven days of verse 27 (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Pay their expenses. Four times over: a wealthy patron’s gesture, from the man who had held up his calloused hands at Miletus (20:34).

Not an act. James is not asking Paul to put on an act. The week is meant to show Jerusalem something true: Paul had taken a vow himself at Cenchreae (18:18), and his respect for the law was real, but it had been lived out far away, where Jerusalem could not see it.

The line he will not cross. When men demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield to them even for a moment (Galatians 2:3–5). The same knife, razor or offering can be a denial of the gospel or a free act of love; the difference is what the act is made to mean. A ceremony required for salvation or imposed on Gentiles Paul will fight to the death; a free man’s courtesy to his own people he will pay for out of his own pocket. “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20): this is what it looked like in practice.

Freedom bought with blood. Paul could walk into the temple without fear because he already stood before God in Christ, clothed in a righteousness no ceremony could add to or take away. His freedom to pay for mere shadows was bought by Christ, the reality they pointed to, with his own blood.

But how could a sin offering mean anything after the cross? Even in Moses’ day it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); the sacrifices were shadows pointing to the one sacrifice that would, and a godly Israelite trusted the God who promised it, not the animal. A shadow kept after the substance has come adds nothing to Christ’s work and takes nothing from it, as long as no one trusts it. So while the temple stood Paul could keep its customs for his brothers’ sake, as a man might keep an old family custom whose meaning has been fulfilled, but never rely on it.

Where Christians differ: was this a compromise? Some think Paul compromised the gospel here, since temple offerings point to a sacrifice already fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: Paul taught that the law was not the means of salvation; he did not forbid Jewish believers to keep customs as an expression of devotion, and he became a Jew to the Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). The closing offerings did include a sin offering (Numbers 6:14), and that is the hard part. But Paul did not offer them as the ground of his acceptance with God, which rested on Christ alone (Hebrews 10:14); this was Jewish custom kept while the temple still stood, as he had circumcised Timothy for the sake of Jews who knew his family (16:3), an act of love for weaker brothers, not a denial of grace. That it ended in his arrest does not prove it was wrong; God used it to send him to Rome.

Uncertain wording. Luke does not say exactly what Paul’s own purification was. “Purify yourself along with them” could mean that Paul joined the men’s vow for its closing days, but a Nazirite vow usually ran longer than a week, so most think he underwent a separate cleansing: a man back from the lands of the nations was probably reckoned unclean, and the remedy took seven days, with sprinkling on the third and the seventh (Numbers 19:11–13), which fits verse 27. Nor does Luke name the vow, though shaved heads and offerings fit Numbers 6 so closely that it is almost certainly a Nazirite vow. The likely meaning: Paul was purified alongside the four men while they completed their vow, and paid for their closing offerings.
verseByVerse.note: These men were ending a Nazirite vow, which required costly offerings; paying for them was a recognised act of piety.

parallels.desc: the offerings when the days of separation are complete

verseByVerse.quote: "But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality." Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James makes plain that nothing asked of Paul binds the Gentile believers, whose freedom the Jerusalem letter settled; and Paul, free in Christ, goes into the temple the next day on a wise and humble course that will end in his arrest.

But as for the Gentiles. In the middle of asking a Jewish apostle to keep a Jewish vow, James says, unprompted, that none of this touches the Gentiles.

A document still on file. This is the third statement of the Jerusalem decree. In the council James listed idols, sexual immorality, what has been strangled, and blood (15:20); the letter used a different order (15:29); and here, years later, James quotes the letter in exactly that order. Settled business, still binding: the Gentiles’ freedom was not a temporary concession that quietly expired.

Saying what an action does not mean. Seeing Paul pay for sacrifices, someone will conclude that the Gentile churches must be next, and James closes off that inference in the same breath. Wise leadership says out loud, in advance, what an action does not mean, while it can still be heard.

The next day. No argument, no conditions. The man who wrote that “if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you” (Galatians 5:2) submits to the purification, and he can do it precisely because he believes what he wrote. A ceremony that cannot save him cannot endanger him either; because he is free, he can use it to serve his brothers (1 Corinthians 9:19).

Giving notice. The plan failed completely. The vow put Paul in the temple, in public, just when Jews from Asia who knew him by sight were in the city, and the advice of the wisest men in the Jerusalem church, offered in love and accepted in humility, became the immediate cause of his arrest. Yet the Lord rules over our wisest plans and our failed ones alike, and he has never yet wasted a chain.

Ashes and blood. The rite was very probably the purification of Numbers 19, with the ashes of a red heifer. Hebrews names that very rite and sets it beside the cross: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:13–14). The ashes, a mere shadow, touched only Paul’s skin. The blood of Christ, the reality, had washed his heart.

Is bending to other people a betrayal of yourself? Our culture prizes authenticity: be true to yourself, never trim your sails to fit in. The literary critic Lionel Trilling, in Sincerity and Authenticity, traced how an older ideal, being honest with others, gave way to a more demanding one, being true to one’s own inner self. By that measure Paul in the temple can look like a man playing a part. But a self that must constantly express itself is fragile: every accommodation feels like a small death. Paul’s self had been given to him and was kept by Christ, so he could keep the customs among Jews and set them aside among Gentiles (1 Corinthians 9:20–21) without losing himself, and still refuse to move an inch when the gospel was at stake. That is not the chameleon’s flexibility, which has no centre, but the freedom of a man whose centre is safe. The gospel does not tell you to find yourself and guard it. It gives you a self, in Christ, secure enough to give away.

Was the plan a mistake, then? Some think so. More likely Paul acted in good conscience to remove a false charge and keep peace with Jewish believers. Yet most of us carry a private theology that says if we take the humble course, seek counsel and pay the cost ourselves, it ought to come out right. Here it does not: James was not foolish and Paul was not weak, and the plan blew up in their faces. Yet two nights later, in a Roman barracks, the Lord stood by Paul and told him to take courage, for as he had testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome (23:11). The failed plan was the road. Wisdom is not a guarantee of outcomes; it is faithfulness in the choosing, and God takes responsibility for the rest.

Does that decree still bind us? Its permanent parts, avoiding idolatry and sexual immorality, are moral commands repeated throughout the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14). Its food rules, about blood and strangled meat, were for love’s sake in that setting, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share a table, and Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love rather than law (1 Corinthians 8; 10:25–33).

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Days before the rite is complete, Jews from Asia seize Paul and shout the charge that nearly kills him, that he has brought Gentiles into the holy place; it is false, and the wall they defend is the one Christ has already broken down.

Almost completed. Another day or two and Paul would have walked out with his name cleared. It is not the Jerusalem believers who end it but Jews from Asia, pilgrims from Ephesus, where “some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way” (19:9). They know his face and his companions’ faces, and they are standing in the temple court when he walks past.

Stirred up the whole crowd. They do not lodge a complaint with the temple authorities standing right there. They work the crowd.

Against the people and the law and this place. False witnesses said of Stephen that he never ceased to speak words against this holy place and the law (6:13–14), and behind both lies the charge against Jesus, that he would destroy the temple (Mark 14:58). The young man minding the coats at Stephen’s death was Saul of Tarsus (7:58), and before the next chapter is over he will tell this crowd so (22:20). The charge he once helped to prosecute is now the charge against him: not God settling a score, but something better, the persecutor so joined to the people he hunted that he now stands where they stood.

He even brought Greeks into the temple. This clause turns a shouting match into a death sentence. Inside the outer court of the temple, which anyone could enter, a low stone barrier ran around the sacred courts, with notices at its openings warning foreigners away. Two of those stones have been found, in Greek: a complete one discovered in 1871, now in Istanbul, and a fragment found in 1935. The wording is preserved: no foreigner may enter within the barrier and enclosure around the sanctuary, and whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows. Josephus records that Rome, which jealously kept the power of execution to itself, allowed the Jews this one exception, even against a Roman citizen. This is a capital charge, shouted in a crowded court, which is why the chapter goes from accusation to attempted murder inside two verses.

The wall that was already down. Out of the imprisonment that begins here comes a letter to Ephesus, the accusers’ city, saying that Christ “has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), so that Gentiles are “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (2:19). The wall the mob was defending had already been demolished by the cross: the hostility was taken into Christ’s own body and put to death there, and every Gentile who has drawn near to God has come in through a torn body. The mob was right that God is holy and the unclean cannot stroll into his presence, but wrong about where the uncleanness lay. What keeps any of us out is sin, not birth, and the blood of Jesus alone gives us confidence to enter the holy places (Hebrews 10:19). The stone with its warning sits in a museum under glass, out of work for nearly two thousand years.

In everyday life. Ask whether you still keep any walls in your heart that Christ has torn down: a kind of Christian you would rather not sit beside. And if you feel like the outsider, hear Ephesians 2 as addressed to you. You are not a guest in God’s house. You are family.

Why did God put up the wall in the first place? The stone barrier of Herod’s temple was a later Jewish arrangement, but it expressed something God had built into the old covenant: courts and curtains taught that sinners cannot simply walk into the presence of a holy God. They were never meant to be permanent. From the beginning God promised that all nations would be blessed through Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 12:3), and that his house would be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). The wall kept the distance visible until the one came who could close it.
verseByVerse.note: Inscriptions have been found from the temple’s barrier, warning Gentiles not to go beyond it on pain of death.

parallels.desc: the dividing wall of hostility

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The capital charge rested on a guess: they had seen a Gentile friend with Paul in the city and supposed the rest, and the whole city ran with the supposition.

They supposed. Luke shows step by step how the charge was manufactured. First, a true observation: they had seen Trophimus, an Ephesian delegate (20:4), with Paul in the city. Second, an inference: they supposed Paul had taken him inside. Nobody saw it, and no witness is ever produced. Third, certainty: by verse 28 the supposition is a shouted fact, and one man has become “Greeks”. Fourth, a crowd, and after that nothing can be undone, because a crowd cannot be shown evidence.

Sincerity is not a safeguard. These men very likely believe it, defending the holiest place on earth from a defilement that never happened, and they will nearly kill an innocent man out of what they think is reverence. That is what religion becomes when it is a way of guarding ourselves rather than knowing God: zeal for his house without love for his ways. Jesus warned that “whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). The cure is not less reverence but the gospel, which humbles the temple zealot and the Gentile sinner at the same cross.

All the city was stirred up. Festival crowds, people running toward the noise with no idea what has happened, as the tribune will find them at verse 34.

The gates were shut. Partly crowd control, but very probably also because a killing inside the sacred courts would defile them: the man must be got outside before he is beaten to death. It is the reflex of the men who would not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, on the morning they arranged a crucifixion (John 18:28): meticulous about the floor, indifferent about the murder.

The last door. This is the last time Paul is recorded inside the temple, and its final act toward the apostle to the Gentiles is a door closing behind him. Within little more than a decade there would be no temple. Luke had written in his first volume that as Jesus died the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Luke 23:45). While the priests were bolting the gates against one man, the way into the true holy place stood open, and no one could shut Paul out of the presence of God, because the door is a Person: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

How do I avoid becoming one of those who supposed? When you find yourself repeating something about somebody, say out loud which part you saw and which part you supposed; much of what we are certain about will not survive being spoken in that form. Then follow the rule Scripture gives the church: a charge is established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and love believes the best until the facts say otherwise (1 Corinthians 13:7). Before you share, forward or post, ask whether you know it, or only assume it. Most mobs today begin with a screenshot.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the mob tries to beat Paul to death, Roman soldiers come running and stop it: God rescues his servant through a pagan garrison, the very kind of authority Paul had called God’s servant.

As they were seeking to kill him. Not threatening to: seeking to. A lynching is in progress on the pavement of the outer court, and the only reason it does not finish is a piece of Roman administration.

The tribune. He commanded the cohort in the Antonia Fortress, at the north-west corner of the temple platform, with stairs running down into the outer court; his title means commander of a thousand. Josephus records that at the great feasts soldiers were posted on the colonnade roofs, because festivals and riots came as a pair. He is Claudius Lysias (23:26), who had bought his citizenship for a large sum (22:28), and God uses him to preserve the apostle to the nations.

Centurions. Plural: at least two centurions with their men, well over a hundred soldiers, and they ran, down the stairs and into the court, in armour.

They stopped beating Paul. Not when a conscience woke up, but when armed men appeared. That is often the way with human beings in a mass: restraint arrives from outside, or it does not arrive.

The doctrine comes down the steps. Only months before, Paul had written that the ruler “is God’s servant for your good” and “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). Now the doctrine came down the fortress steps in hobnailed boots and saved the man who wrote it.

In the flow. Again a Roman official stands between Paul and a hostile crowd, as Gallio did at Corinth (18:12–17) and the town clerk at Ephesus (19:35–41). Luke is building a case that runs to the end of the book: the authorities find in Paul nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29; 26:31).

The same sword, given from above. These soldiers served the power that had stood guard at another trial in this city some twenty-five years before. When Pilate told Jesus that he had authority to release him or to crucify him, Jesus answered that he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). The Roman sword never belonged to Rome. On that Friday God allowed it to fall on his innocent Son, who had come to bear the sentence his people deserved; on this afternoon he sent it running down the stairs to keep his servant alive. Both times the sword moved only as far as heaven allowed.

Where was the church? Jerusalem held tens of thousands of believers (v. 20), and not one appears in this paragraph; perhaps they could have done nothing against a mob, and Luke does not say. Here the church is absent and the pagan garrison is everything. Sometimes the help God sends does not come from the people we would have expected, and is still from God.

Should Christians thank God for the police and the courts? Yes. Paul tells us to pray for kings and all in authority, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Government is a gift of God’s common grace, his kindness to all people, given to restrain evil even when those who hold office do not know him. That does not make every ruler just or every act of government right: the same Rome that rescued Paul would one day execute him, and Christians must obey God rather than men when the two conflict (5:29). But where the law protects the weak and stops the mob, we should give thanks, pray for those who enforce it, and support them in doing it justly.
verseByVerse.note: The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune puts Paul in two chains and Agabus’s word comes true; but Paul has been bound to Christ’s will for months, and the iron only confirms a captivity he had already accepted from God.
