Two chains. Agabus’s prophecy is fulfilled (v. 11). Two chains probably means a wrist shackled to a soldier on either side, as when Peter slept between two soldiers, bound with two chains (12:6). That night an angel came, the chains fell off Peter’s hands and he walked out into the street. Nothing of the kind happens here. Paul’s chains stay on, and to the end of Acts he is a prisoner.

One loosed, one left. Two men, the same chains, the same God, opposite outcomes, and Luke reports both without a syllable of explanation. Scripture refuses to teach that faith always produces release, and equally refuses to teach that suffering is the mark of the truly spiritual. The Lord loosed one man’s chains and left the other man’s on, and both men were his.

A bound man already. Follow one word backwards, because Luke has been laying a track: the verb for binding appears five times in two chapters. At Miletus Paul said he was going to Jerusalem “constrained by the Spirit” (20:22), literally “bound”. At Caesarea Agabus bound his own feet and hands and said the Jews would bind the owner of the belt (21:11). In the front room Paul said he was ready “to be imprisoned” (21:13), literally “to be bound”. Now the tribune orders him bound with two chains. The Spirit’s chain came first. By the time Rome puts iron on him, Paul has been a bound man for months, and willingly; the tribune only confirms in metal a captivity Paul had already accepted from God. That is why there is no panic in him, and no sense anywhere in the rest of the book that something has gone wrong.

Who he was and what he had done. Arrest first, investigate second: poor justice, and here it saves a life. Those two questions open a process that runs through the Sanhedrin, two governors, a king, an appeal to Caesar and a shipwreck. A quarter of Acts is the answer to a soldier’s routine enquiry at the top of a staircase.

A prisoner of Christ Jesus. Writing from custody he calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1, 9) and a prisoner for the Lord (Ephesians 4:1), never once Caesar’s prisoner. The chain changed owner the moment it was fastened: his imprisonment was an assignment from his Lord, and would last exactly as long, and achieve exactly as much, as Christ intended (Philippians 1:12–13). Every prisoner of Christ wears iron that his Master has already worn, and wears it for a little while, on the way to a glory that will make it look like nothing.

In everyday life. Name the chain you are wearing: the illness, the caring duty, the job you cannot leave, the limitation you did not choose. Then ask whose prisoner you are. If you belong to Christ, the answer is not the illness or the boss or the circumstance. It is him, and he does not waste his prisoners.

Why does God rescue some believers and not others? Scripture does not give his reasons in each case, but it gives his character and purpose. James was killed by the sword in the same chapter in which Peter was set free (12:2, 7). Hebrews 11 lists those who escaped the edge of the sword and, in the same breath, those who were sawn in two. Neither group had more faith; both are commended. His purpose in each life is his glory and our good, served sometimes by rescue and sometimes by endurance. So if your chains have not fallen off, do not conclude that your faith is too small or that God has forgotten you. Paul’s stayed on, and through them the gospel reached Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd cannot even agree on the charge, and Paul, beaten and chained, has to be carried up the steps by soldiers; yet even helpless he is being carried toward his chance to preach.

One thing, some another. Luke wrote this sentence of the theatre at Ephesus too (19:32): a crowd united in fury and unable to say what the charge is. Mobs have not gone out of fashion; they have moved indoors and online. The test is not how many are angry or how certain they sound, but whether any two of them, asked separately, would give the same account of what the accused actually did.

He could not learn the facts. The tribune asks for a charge, and thousands cannot produce a coherent answer. The first casualty of an outraged crowd is the truth it believes itself to be defending.

Carried by the soldiers. The press is so violent that the soldiers haul their beaten, chained prisoner up the steps above the crowd like baggage. The apostle to the Gentiles goes up the last flight with his feet off the ground, unable to help himself in any way.

Another beaten man on the road. On the road out of this same city, after the scourging, the soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene and laid the cross on him, to carry it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26). The Son of God accepted the help of a stranger. He let soldiers handle him, strip him and nail him down, and he went to the bottom of human helplessness first, so that no believer would ever be carried anywhere he had not already been. The arms that held Paul on the stairs were Roman. The love that held him was Christ’s.

When you are carried. Some Christians will recognise this at once, because they are living in it: seasons in which you do not walk but are carried, by other people’s arms, where you did not choose, with no dignity left to protect. Luke does not treat that as a failure of faith. And the soldiers who thought they were suppressing a disturbance were carrying the word of God up a staircase; in a moment their prisoner will ask to preach.

What if I feel helpless and humiliated, unable to do anything for myself? Then you are in good company, and not outside God’s care. Illness, old age, disability, a breakdown, a long hospital stay can all leave a believer carried by others and stripped of dignity. Scripture never measures your worth by your independence. The Lord says to his people that even to their old age and grey hairs he will carry them; he has made, and he will bear (Isaiah 46:4). Let others help you without shame, and pray even from the stretcher. Paul’s most helpless moment was a minute from his greatest sermon in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mob’s cry, “Away with him!”, is the cry once raised against Jesus in the same city: Paul shares his Lord’s rejection, though never his saving work.

Away with him. Two words in Greek. At the trial before Pilate “they all cried out together, ‘Away with this man’” (Luke 23:18; compare John 19:15). Luke sets it down without comment: Paul shares his Lord’s rejection, in the same city, perhaps a few hundred yards from where Jesus was condemned.

The passion beneath the arrest. It is the fourth echo of Christ’s passion, his suffering and death, in this chapter: “deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles” (v. 11; Luke 18:32); “Let the will of the Lord be done” (v. 14; Luke 22:42); “against the people and the law and this place” (v. 28); and now the crowd’s cry.

Nobody else could go the whole way. When that cry was raised against the Lord Jesus, twelve legions of angels were within call (Matthew 26:53), and he let the sentence stand. He went out of the city he had wept over, carrying the beam of his own execution, and did not open his mouth. Paul walked a road his Master had already walked to the end, with one difference: Paul was pulled out at the top of the stairs, and Christ was not, because there was nobody else who could go the whole way.

What it does not mean. Paul is not a second saviour. Nothing he suffers atones for anybody; he is carrying not sin but a message. The likeness is family resemblance: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). And the Lord had said it of this man at his conversion: “I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (9:16). That promise is being kept on this staircase.

Being answered. Paul had asked for this: “that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death” (Philippians 3:10). We ask to be made like Jesus and are surprised at the shape the answer takes, but there is only one Jesus to be made like, and his road to glory went through a crowd exactly like this one. If we are given even a little of it, we are not being punished. We are being answered.

Does every hardship I face count as suffering for Christ? Not every hardship, but more than we think. Peter makes the distinction: suffering as a murderer or a thief or a meddler is no honour, but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:15–16). Mockery because you will not join in, the promotion lost because you would not lie, family coldness because you follow Christ: these share in his rejection. Other troubles, sickness and loss and grief, are not persecution, but Christ is with you in them too, and he uses them to make you like himself (Romans 8:28–29). What matters is not to bring suffering on yourself by foolishness, and not to be ashamed of it when it comes for his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beaten and chained at the barracks door, Paul asks courteously, in good Greek, for leave to speak, and the tribune, who took him for a notorious Egyptian rebel, finds he has misjudged his prisoner.

May I say something to you? Beaten by a mob, chained between two soldiers, carried up the last flight, seconds from being swallowed by a Roman fortress, Paul turns to the officer and asks, in courteous, educated Greek, for permission to speak. Remarkable composure.

Do you know Greek? The tribune’s astonishment is the comedy of the scene. He had assumed he was dragging an illiterate agitator out of a temple brawl, and one well-formed sentence collapses his whole assessment.

Are you not the Egyptian? A real man and a recent manhunt. The historian Josephus tells the story twice: a false prophet from Egypt gathered a following in the wilderness, led them round to the Mount of Olives, and promised that at his command the walls of Jerusalem would fall so they could take the city. The governor Felix sent troops; the movement was cut to pieces; and the Egyptian himself escaped and was never caught. It had happened within the last few years, and the file was still open. So when an unidentified man is pulled out of a temple riot, the tribune reaches for the obvious explanation, which explains the two chains: he believed he was holding a rebel leader with followers somewhere in the hills.

The four thousand men of the Assassins. Josephus gives two different figures for the Egyptian’s following: thirty thousand in one work, a number many think inflated, and in the other an affair in which four hundred were killed and two hundred captured. Luke reports the tribune as saying four thousand, a sober figure, and gives them a name current at the time: the Assassins, sikarioi, the dagger-men, who carried short curved blades under their cloaks and mingled with festival crowds to stab a man and disappear before he fell. Josephus describes them in these very years, though he treats them as a group distinct from the Egyptian’s followers; a Roman officer lumping rebels together is just what we might expect. That is the vocabulary of someone who knew Judea at the time.

A careful writer. This is Luke’s habit everywhere: he gets the titles right, a proconsul on Cyprus, politarchs at Thessalonica, Asiarchs at Ephesus, a town clerk, and here a tribune. Accuracy in small things does not by itself prove a resurrection, but the man who is this careful about the size of a rebel band is the same man who tells you that a tomb outside Jerusalem was empty on the third day, and he expects to be read the same way in both places.

The guilty rebel walked free. The Lord rules over misunderstandings as surely as over storms: because the tribune had him wrong, he asked, and the conversation began that ended with permission to preach. And the true Messiah was mistaken for a rebel too. The crowd chose Barabbas, “a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city” (Luke 23:19), and sent the Prince of Peace to the cross in his place. The guilty rebel walked free while the innocent one died, and that exchange is the gospel Paul is about to preach.

Why should historical details like this matter to my faith? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas; it rests on events: a man who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and appeared to witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Luke investigated everything carefully so that his reader might have certainty (Luke 1:3–4), and reliability in small things we can check gives good reason to trust him in the great things we cannot. Your faith rests finally on God’s word, which the Spirit confirms in your heart, but God has given his word in history, and where historians can check it, it stands up well.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led followers to the Mount of Olives a few years earlier and escaped when the Romans attacked. The “Assassins” were extremists who stabbed opponents with hidden daggers in crowds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of standing who could claim his rights, Paul spends his one request on permission to speak to the mob that has just beaten him, and when he lifts his hand they fall silent to hear him in their own tongue.

No obscure city. A deliberate understatement, which an educated Greek would hear as good manners, and it was true: Strabo said the people of Tarsus surpassed even Athens and Alexandria in devotion to learning. In one clause Paul tells the tribune: I am not your Egyptian; I am a Jew, and a man of standing.

What he does not say. He does not mention that he is a Roman citizen, the most powerful fact about him in that fortress; he will produce it in one quiet question when they stretch him out for a flogging (22:25–29). He is not asking to be rescued.

Permit me to speak to the people. They are still howling at the foot of the stairs, and a man with a legal trump card in his pocket, at the door of safety, uses his one request to go back out and talk to them. He had written of “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his fellow Jews, and that he could wish himself “accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Romans 9:2–3). He meant it, and this staircase is the proof.

Motioned with his hand. The speaker’s gesture (13:16; 26:1), except that this hand is bruised and chained to a soldier.

A great hush. Thousands who were screaming for a lynching fall silent. The same mercy that silenced Saul’s rage on the Damascus road now silences a crowd on the temple steps, so that it can hear the name it hated. He could have used Greek. He chooses their mother tongue, and “they became even more quiet” (22:2). The last thing he does before he tells them about Jesus is honour them.

What Paul could only wish. No man’s curse can save another, and Paul knew it. But one did what Paul could only wish. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and he was cut off, outside the walls of this very city, for the sake of people who had rejected him. The love that made Paul ask to face the mob was first the love that sent his Lord to the cross for people like them, and for people like him.

Stand back and look. James’s plan has failed and everything Paul arranged has come apart, and he is standing above perhaps the largest Jewish crowd he has addressed in years, in total silence, with Roman permission, about to tell them how he met Jesus of Nazareth. He did not get the platform he might have asked for; he got the barracks steps. Years later he wrote the sentence that explains this chapter: “what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12).

In everyday life. Think of the person who has most recently hurt you, and ask what your instinct toward them is: to shut them out, or to speak to them. Then look for a chance to speak of Christ in a language they can hear.

How can I love people who have hurt me badly? Not by pretending the hurt did not happen, and not in your own strength. Paul had once been the one shouting, and Christ had loved him anyway. The more clearly you see how much you have been forgiven, the more room there is in you for those who wrong you (Luke 7:47; Ephesians 4:32). Begin by praying for them, honestly, even if the first prayers are short. Then look for one concrete good you can do or say to them, as the Lord commands (Luke 6:27–28). Love for enemies does not mean trusting the untrustworthy or staying where you are in danger. It means wanting their salvation more than your vindication.

Uncertain wording. “The Hebrew language” translates a phrase that in the New Testament can mean either Hebrew itself or Aramaic, the related language most Jews in Judea spoke every day. Hebrew was still used, especially in worship and learning, so certainty is not possible; most think Paul spoke Aramaic, the language of the street and the kitchen; either way, he chose his hearers’ own tongue over Greek.
verseByVerse.note: Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning. The “Hebrew language” was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 shows that knowing the will of God does not mean being spared the suffering it includes. Paul knows chains await him and goes anyway; his friends, who cannot change his mind, submit. Their words are not fatalism but the willing trust of people who know whose will it is. God works his purposes through suffering, not only around it: Paul’s chains will take the gospel to Rome.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, with weeping friends who have said all they can and now can only pray.

Now: Every Christian has to learn to pray “Let the will of the Lord be done” when his will leads into what we would not choose: illness, loss, rejection, persecution. We pray it as followers of a Lord who first prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done”, and went to the cross for us.

keyVerse.quote: For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.
keyVerse.note: Every warning in the chapter presses on this one answer. Paul has counted the worst cost in advance, so neither chains nor his friends’ tears can turn him, and he will die not for a cause but for a Person. It is the answer of a man following the Lord who set his face toward the same city, and it moves his friends to pray, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

21.reflection:
At Tyre and Caesarea believers who loved Paul begged him not to go, and he went anyway (vv. 4, 12–14). How can we tell when the counsel of people who love us is God’s wisdom and when it is love afraid of the cost? Have you ever been on either side of that?

Philip opened his home for many days to the man who had once driven him out of Jerusalem (vv. 8–10). What does that show about what the gospel does to past wrongs, and where might Christ be calling you toward a table rather than a truce?

Paul kept a Jewish custom for love’s sake but would never let a ceremony be made necessary for salvation (vv. 23–26). Where in our church life do we need to bend for others, and where must we refuse to bend?

A rumour and a supposition nearly got Paul killed (vv. 21, 29). How do rumours spread among Christians today, and what would it look like for us to stop them?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul answers the charge that he has turned against Israel by telling how Israel’s God turned him. Speaking in the crowd’s own language, he presents himself as one of them: a Jew raised in Jerusalem, trained by Gamaliel, zealous enough to hunt the Way to the death with the council’s letters (vv. 1–5). Then come three scenes. On the Damascus road at noon the risen Jesus of Nazareth stopped him and received his surrender (vv. 6–11). In Damascus a devout, law-keeping Ananias restored his sight, called him brother, spoke of the commission of “the God of our fathers” and urged him to be baptised (vv. 12–16). In the temple itself the Lord sent him away from Jerusalem, far off to the Gentiles (vv. 17–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias’s word for what God did to Saul is appointed (22:14), and Paul wrote later that God had set me apart before I was born (Galatians 1:15). Nothing in the account belongs to the convert (see the note on vv. 9–10).

Two cautions belong here. Scripture does not tell us the moment of Saul’s new birth, and we should not claim to know it: the new birth is the Spirit’s secret work, known by its fruits (see the note at vv. 9–10). And in wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign, baptism, is spoken of in words that belong to what it stands for (see the note on vv. 16–17).

The chapter’s summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen’s stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen’s message. The blood of the Righteous One proved stronger than the guilt of the blood Saul helped to shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He walked into that house and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb: someone with a history, and a history with you. Suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long before anyone says “brother”, and means it? (See the note on v. 13.)

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul opens his defence with Stephen’s opening words and speaks to the crowd in their own language, and the mob that had been beating him falls silent.

Brothers and fathers. This is how Stephen began his defence before the council (7:2), and the young man holding the coats that day was Saul of Tarsus. He opens his own trial with the dead man’s opening line, and before he finishes he will say Stephen’s name aloud (v. 20). He has seen what Stephen saw, the Son of Man at the right hand of God (7:55–56), met since on a road at noon, and he stands on the steps to say what Stephen said: the one you crucified is alive and reigning.

A defence that is a story. A defence (apologia) is a formal answer to a charge, the word that gives us apologetics (1 Peter 3:15). Paul has a good legal argument, but given one chance to speak to people who have just tried to kill him, one of the best trained minds in the early church tells them what happened to him.

Even more quiet. A Jew from Tarsus was easily suspected of having gone half Greek. Then out comes the language of the street and the kitchen, fluent and native (see “Uncertain wording” below), and their theory about the man dies in three syllables. That courtesy cost Paul nothing and bought him twenty verses of silence from a crowd that had been beating him ten minutes earlier. The gospel does not need softening, but its messenger can make it as easy as possible to hear, or as hard.

God in a human voice. The God who stilled this crowd stills the tumult of the peoples (Psalm 65:7), and he speaks to sinners where they are. He did it supremely in his Son: the eternal Word took flesh and spoke Aramaic in Galilee, so that we could hear God in a human voice, calling us by name.

Do I need a dramatic story to give my testimony? No. What made Paul’s story a testimony was not the drama but that it was true and pointed to Christ. A testimony is an honest account of what Jesus has done for you: what you were like, how he showed you your need, how you came to trust him, and what has changed. For many raised in Christian homes the honest story is quiet: I cannot remember not knowing about Jesus, but I remember when he became mine, and I can tell you what he has been to me since. God uses that. Keep it short, keep Christ at the centre, and keep yourself out of the spotlight.

Uncertain wording. Luke says Paul spoke “in the Hebrew language”. The phrase can mean Hebrew itself, but the everyday language of Jews in Judea at the time was Aramaic, a close relative, and Greek writers often called it “Hebrew”. Most scholars think Paul spoke Aramaic here. Either way the point stands: not the Greek of the empire, but the mother tongue of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd.

parallels.desc: Stephen’s same opening

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul presents himself as one of the crowd: a Jew raised in Jerusalem, trained by the greatest teacher of the day, and once as zealous for God as they are, zealous enough to hunt down the followers of Jesus.

I am a Jew. Some twenty years after the Damascus road, before a crowd that has just accused him of apostasy, Paul says “I am a Jew”, not “I was”. Then the usual outline of a Jewish upbringing in three verbs: born, brought up, educated. The weight falls in the middle: raised from youth in Jerusalem (26:4), the city they are standing in. He is no outsider legislating for it from a distance.

At the feet of Gamaliel. Literally: pupils sat on the floor before the rabbi’s seat, and Gamaliel the Elder was the most respected teacher of the age. When the council wanted the apostles dead, Gamaliel told them to leave these men alone, in case they were found opposing God (5:34–39). His own student went out with warrants. You can sit at a wise man’s feet for years and miss the one sentence he said that mattered.

Zealous for God. He credits them. To a mob that has just tried to lynch him he says, in effect: your zeal is real, and it is for God, and I know because it was mine. He would write that “they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10:2), kind and devastating at once, because he had been the clearest example.

To the death. And men and women (8:3). A man making a real confession does not round the number down. His audience hears qualifications; he means charges, and the whole speech turns on that difference.

Every credential counted loss. He would tell the Philippians that his training, his zeal and his blamelessness under the law (Philippians 3:5–6) were all counted as loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Whatever went wrong in Saul of Tarsus, it was not slackness. He had every advantage religion can give, and none of it could find the Messiah. The Messiah found him, and made the most devout persecutor in Israel the apostle of grace, so that no one could ever say that God saves the worthy.

Is sincerity enough before God? No, and Paul is the proof: utterly sincere, disciplined and devout, and fighting God. Sincerity shows how earnestly a belief is held, not whether it is true. Jesus warned that whoever killed his disciples would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2). What saves is not the strength of our zeal but its object, Christ himself. The safeguard for earnest Christians is not less zeal but zeal kept open to Scripture and ready to be corrected by it.

In everyday life. Before your next conversation with someone who opposes the faith, find one thing about them you can honestly credit, and say it.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day; students sat at their teacher’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s persecution was official and planned, backed by letters from the high priest and the council, until at noon on the Damascus road a light from heaven stopped him.

The whole council of elders. Paul names witnesses who could contradict him. The high priest had since been replaced, but the council could confirm that such letters had been issued, by men with no reason to protect him.

Letters to the brothers. Paul still calls the Jews of Damascus brothers. And letters makes Saul something worse than a hothead. Damascus lay outside Judea, so he applied for warrants; somebody drafted and sealed them, and a journey of about a hundred and forty miles was funded and planned. This was not a riot but a filing system. Some of the worst things done to the church are done on paper, in office hours, by men who believe they are serving God.

In bonds. He tells the story from inside a Roman chain: the man who set out to bind is bound.

About noon. Chapter 9 does not mention the hour; before Agrippa Paul adds that the light was brighter than the sun (26:13). At midday this was not dawn, heat-shimmer or a dream. Jesus had called himself the light of the world (John 8:12), and the man who believed he was defending the light of Israel met that Light on a public highway at the brightest hour of the day, and it struck him blind. Christ did not wait for his enemy to come looking for him. He came down into the noon of a Syrian road and blazed around a persecutor with warrants in his bag.

What if I cannot point to a moment like this in my own life? Then you are like most Christians. Paul’s conversion was unique because his calling was unique: he was made an apostle, a witness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:8). The absence of a light from heaven is no sign that God has not called you. Lydia’s heart was opened quietly while she listened by a river (16:14); Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). The question is not how vividly you remember the beginning, but whether you trust Christ now. The same God who blazed around Saul has shone in every believer’s heart “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus called Saul by name and asked why he was persecuting him, so closely is he joined to his people; and he named himself by the despised title “Jesus of Nazareth”.

Saul, Saul. When God says a name twice in Scripture it is never filler: “Abraham, Abraham”, with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11); “Moses, Moses”, at the bush (Exodus 3:4); “Simon, Simon” (Luke 22:31). It is the address of someone who knows the person and means to stop them where they stand. And it is the Hebrew form of the name, spoken “in the Hebrew language” (26:14): the risen Lord, out of a light brighter than the sun, addressed a man in his mother tongue, as Paul now addresses this crowd. He learned it from the Lord.

Why are you persecuting me? Not “my people” or “my church”, but “me”. Jesus had ascended to the Father’s right hand, and Saul had never been one of his followers. Yet every door Saul kicked in, every woman he dragged out, every prison sentence he arranged, the Lord of glory counted as done to himself, as personally as the nails. Here is the seed of much of Paul’s theology: the church is the body of Christ, and no one ever hated his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ does the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 5:29–30). He did not construct that doctrine in a study. It was handed to him in one question on a road, and it cost him his sight.

Who are you, Lord? The word can mean no more than “sir”, and on Saul’s lips at that instant it may have meant little more. But you cannot ask that question of that light and keep the word small.

Jesus of Nazareth. In chapter 9 the answer is simply “I am Jesus” (9:5), and before Agrippa the same (26:15). Only here, to a Jerusalem crowd, does Paul add “of Nazareth”, the name with the sneer in it: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). The believers’ opponents called them “the sect of the Nazarenes” (24:5).

Heaven’s glory has a carpenter’s address. He had every right to announce himself by his titles. Out of that light he gave instead the name that had been a joke: the despised man whom Jerusalem crucified is the Lord of glory. He carries the marks of the nails still, and will answer to the name of the town they sneered at for ever. The Lamb who was slain is not ashamed of the village, or of a single scar.

Does Jesus really feel what happens to his people? Yes. He is glorified, beyond suffering in his own body, but joined to his people by the Spirit and by faith, as the head to the body (Ephesians 1:22–23; 1 Corinthians 6:17), so that what touches them touches him. He said the same of the last day: “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). So if a believer in your church is mistreated, overlooked, gossiped about or frozen out, Christ takes it personally, and he does not grade the offence by how important the person is. And if you are the one suffering, you are not suffering alone or unnoticed. Long before Saul was stopped on that road, heaven had registered every name.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s companions saw the light but did not make out the words; only Saul heard Christ speak, and his first question as a disciple was a surrender: “What shall I do, Lord?”

Saw the light but did not understand. People bring this verse as a contradiction, and it deserves a straight answer. In chapter 9 the men were “hearing the voice but seeing no one” (9:7). They saw the light, but not the Person in it; they heard a sound, but not the words (see “Uncertain wording” below). Stand next to someone on a phone call: you hear a voice, and not a word of what it says. Everyone on the road heard something. One man heard words.

Inside the light and hearing only weather. Several men stood in that light, close enough to lead Saul by the hand, and not one is heard of again. Nearness to revelation is not revelation. You can sit in the same pew, close enough to touch someone whom God is at that moment laying hold of, and hear only a noise.

What shall I do, Lord? The question of a new disciple, and total surrender: “Lord”, a new master. For years he had known exactly what to do: a mandate, letters in his bag, a route, a list of names, the backing of the highest religious court in Israel. In one question all of it is handed over. He does not ask whether the letters are still valid. He asks for orders.

All that is appointed. The answer tells him very little: go into the city and wait. Not the journeys, the letters, or Rome. God gives the next step and withholds the itinerary. Handed his whole assignment on that road, shipwrecks and cells included, Saul would have received it as information. Instead he received it as obedience, one instruction at a time, from a Lord he was learning to trust, who has already walked every step of the road ahead of his servants.

Was Paul born again at this moment? We are not told, and should not pretend to know. Luke tells Paul’s conversion as a connected whole: the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16). The new birth is the Spirit’s secret work; we see its fruits, not its moment. What we can see is that by verse 10 Paul calls Jesus Lord, surrenders his whole programme, asks for orders and obeys, and soon is found praying: marks of a heart already being turned by grace, since the new birth produces faith and repentance. What Scripture leaves unclear, the when, it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear, the who. Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, and summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul.

Could Paul’s experience have been a hallucination or a seizure? The details tell against it. A hallucination is private, but his companions saw the light and heard a sound. A seizure does not overturn a man’s deepest convictions and send him for thirty years through beatings and prisons to preach the faith he had tried to destroy. And Saul met not a vague presence but a person who named himself: Jesus of Nazareth, whom Saul had every reason to think cursed by God, since he had been hanged on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Nothing in Saul’s mind was waiting to invent that. No argument compels a sceptic, but the best explanation of the changed man is the one he gave himself: the crucified Jesus was alive, and appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:8).

Uncertain wording. “Did not understand” translates the ordinary Greek verb for hearing (akouō), which can mean to hear a sound or to hear with understanding; in 9:7 the same verb is rendered “hearing”. Luke uses a slightly different construction in each place, and scholars weigh the difference variously, but the verb’s double sense is not in doubt. Most likely the companions heard a voice without making out its words.
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The persecutor entered Damascus blind and led by the hand, and the man God sent to him was a devout, law-keeping Jew respected by all his Jewish neighbours.

Led by the hand. The verb for guiding a small child or a blind beggar. He set out to bring believers back in bonds, and arrives helpless, unable to find a door. Three days without sight, food or drink (9:9, 11): his learning, his warrants, his certainty, all taken off him in an afternoon, and what was left sat in the dark and prayed.

A devout man according to the law. Luke introduced Ananias simply as a disciple at Damascus (9:10). Paul, before a crowd that believes he abandoned Moses, stresses his Jewish piety and his good name not with the church but with the synagogue, among neighbours who did not share his faith. Before a king in chapter 26 he leaves Ananias out altogether, because a provincial holy man means nothing to Agrippa; to this crowd he means everything.

A guide to the blind, led by the hand. Paul later described the man he had been: sure that he was “a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness” (Romans 2:19). Jesus came so “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39), and on the Damascus road both happened to one man. Christ would send him to open the nations’ eyes (26:18), and he began that mission by closing Saul’s.

A good name outside the church. Paul cites not Ananias’s gifts or visions but his reputation among outsiders. An overseer “must be well thought of by outsiders” (1 Timothy 3:7), Paul would write; perhaps he learned it here, from the first Christian to lay hands on him. Ask what your own neighbours would say about you. Ananias’s good name opened a door for the gospel; so can yours, in paying bills, keeping promises and treating people kindly.

Is it dishonest to tell my story differently to different people? No, as long as everything you say is true. Paul never changed the facts; he chose, from among true things, the ones that would help a particular audience, as you explain your work one way to a child and another to a colleague. Dishonesty would be inventing details, hiding what you believe in order to be accepted, or telling one group what you would deny to another. Paul became “all things to all people” (1 Corinthians 9:22), but he never became a liar. Ask of every version of your testimony: is it true, and does it point to Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias greeted the man who had come to arrest believers with the word “brother”, and at that very hour Saul saw again. The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

Brother Saul. These (9:17) are the first words a Christian is recorded as speaking to Saul the believer. Ananias had protested that he knew how much evil this man had done to the saints (9:13–14). His own name may well have been on the letters; to knock on that door was to walk into the one house in Damascus a Christian had most reason to fear. He came anyway, and his first word was not a caution or a probation but “brother”, with no conditions and no waiting period, because the risen Christ had claimed him.

At that very hour. The first thing Saul’s restored eyes rest on is the face of a man he had come to put in chains, calling him family. He had been blind for three days, and in a deeper sense far longer: a learned man who could not see the one at the centre of his own Scriptures. Both blindnesses ended in the same room, through an ordinary, obedient disciple.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. Brother is the word Christ is not ashamed to say to us (Hebrews 2:11). He said it on the morning of his resurrection, of men who had just deserted him: “go to my brothers” (John 20:17). Every welcome the church gives a forgiven enemy echoes his welcome to us, when we were the ones with warrants against him.

How quickly should a church trust a notorious sinner who professes faith? Welcome and trust are not the same, and Scripture gives us both. Ananias welcomed Saul at once, because the Lord had told him plainly that Saul was his chosen instrument (9:15). The Jerusalem church, without that word, was afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (9:26–27). We have no vision to tell us, so the church receives a professing believer warmly, as a brother, while positions of trust, leadership or access to the vulnerable wait for the fruit of a changed life (1 Timothy 3:6, 10). Where someone has abused others, wise safeguards are an act of love for everyone, including him. But the greeting should not wait. Say brother, and mean it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of Israel’s fathers chose Saul to know his saving purpose, to see the risen Messiah and hear his voice, and to bear witness of it to everyone.

The God of our fathers appointed you. Paul’s whole defence hangs on this phrase, used by Peter (3:13; 5:30) and Stephen (7:32): not a new God, but the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The charge is apostasy; his answer is that the God who commissioned him is the God of his accusers’ own fathers. Appointed means chosen for a task: God had set him apart before he was born (Galatians 1:15). The light at noon was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed, which is worth knowing if your own conversion looked, from the inside, like an accident.

To know his will. Most of us hear “God’s will” and think of a hidden plan we must somehow find: the right job, the right city, the right person. Ananias means God’s saving purpose, and it has a face. Paul came to know it in the same breath as he saw the Righteous One, because Christ is that will made visible: God has made known to us “the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ” (Ephesians 1:9). To know God’s will is first to know what he is doing in Jesus: reconciling sinners to himself, gathering a people from every nation, and making all things new. Paul was shown it on the road; we are shown it in the pages he and the other apostles wrote. And it reaches into ordinary lives: “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). So before you agonise over what God has not told you, give yourself to what he has: trust his Son, grow like him, and speak of him. Much of the rest becomes clear as you walk in that.

The Righteous One. A title for the Messiah. Peter used it in the temple (3:14), and Stephen in the sentence that got him killed: “the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered” (7:52). Saul was very likely there. The title may have gone into his ears from a dying man he was helping to execute; the next time he heard it, it belonged to the one who had just spoken to him from heaven. Jesus is the only righteous man who ever lived, betrayed and murdered by the unrighteous, and raised to make the unrighteous righteous.

Seeing and hearing. These verbs are the foundation of Paul’s apostleship: “Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” (1 Corinthians 9:1). His authority rests not on intellect or results but on having seen the risen Christ and heard him speak.

A witness to everyone. A witness in court is asked only what he saw and heard, which is why the least articulate Christian can be one. And “to everyone”: not a syllable about Gentiles yet. The words already take in every nation, but so gently that the crowd lets them go by.

Are there apostles like Paul today? Not in the sense Paul was one. An apostle in this full sense had seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the church’s foundation once, and we build on it through their writings (Ephesians 2:20). Missionaries are sometimes loosely called apostles, meaning sent ones, but no one today carries the authority of Peter or Paul. That is no loss: the voice of the apostles still speaks, unchanged, every time we open the Bible.
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias urged Saul not to delay but to be baptised, calling on Christ’s name: baptism is the outward sign of the washing away of sins that faith in Christ receives.

And now why do you wait? You have sat in this dark room for three days, Ananias is saying. That is long enough. Stop being a secret.

Wash away your sins. This sentence is often used to argue that the water itself saves. It does not say the water washes. It holds four things together (rising, being baptised, the washing away of sins, and calling on his name), and the last clause carries the weight: faith, calling on Christ, receives forgiveness (Romans 10:13); baptism is its outward sign.

Calling on the name he came to bind. Saul had come with authority to bind all who call on the Lord’s name (9:14). Now he is to call on that name himself, the name of Joel’s promise that “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved”, which Peter applied to Jesus at Pentecost (2:21, 36). He goes down into the water trusting not the water but the Christ he calls on.

Let Paul interpret Paul. If anybody had reason to believe his sins went down a Damascus drain, it was Saul of Tarsus. Yet he wrote that Abraham received circumcision as a sign and seal of the righteousness he had by faith (Romans 4:11): the sign certifies a righteousness already given. He wrote that “Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17), and could barely remember whom he had baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14–16), which is not how anyone speaks about the thing that saves. In Cornelius’s house the Spirit fell before anyone brought water (10:44–48), and the dying thief, never baptised, was promised paradise that day (Luke 23:43).

The sign and the thing signified. Scripture often speaks of a sign in words that belong to what it stands for, because God does not mean the two to be pulled apart. A sign points beyond itself, as a wedding ring points to a marriage it did not create. Baptism pictures the washing that only the blood of Christ performs, assures the believer that it is real, and joins him publicly to the one who did the washing. Ananias is not telling Saul how to get clean, but telling a man who has been made clean to go and say so, in water, before witnesses. And Saul believed, then was baptised: the pattern throughout Acts, and why this commentary holds to believer’s baptism. Many faithful Christians, christened as infants, see baptism as the sign given to believers and their children as circumcision was; we gladly honour them as brothers who love the same Saviour.

Not managed, but washed. Saul’s sins were not vague. He had faces in his memory, and Stephen’s blood, and he was told that the whole account could be washed: not managed, not offset by a life of service, but washed. The man who guarded the coats at a murder was made as clean as if he had never touched them, by the blood of the Righteous One. That blood has never met a stain it could not lift.

Praying in the temple. Then Paul moves the story somewhere his accusers will not expect. On trial for defiling the temple, he tells them his commission was given inside it, while he was praying: the God they think he has abandoned met him in their own house. This was probably the visit of Galatians 1:18, some three years after Damascus, so the commission came to a man who had already been preaching Christ (9:20–22), not to a new convert.

I believe in Christ but have never been baptised, so does it matter? Yes, though not because your salvation hangs on the water. Christ commanded his disciples to be baptised (Matthew 28:19), and every believer in Acts was baptised promptly, often the same day. Baptism is the Lord’s appointed way to confess him publicly, to be marked as belonging to his people, and to receive the strengthening of faith he gives through it. Staying unbaptised is like keeping a wedding ring in the drawer: the marriage is real, but you are hiding it. Speak to your pastor or elders this week. For a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, baptism was the point of no return; it is meant to be that for us, too.

In everyday life. If you have been baptised, ask whether anything else in your following of Christ is still unannounced: a faith your colleagues have never had to notice, an obedience pending because going public would cost something. You need not wait until you can obey perfectly: the water points not to your record but to Christ, who obeyed in your place. Why do you wait?

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sins? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians take this verse to teach that baptism itself removes sin, pointing also to Peter’s words at Pentecost (2:38) and to the statement that baptism now saves you (1 Peter 3:21). This commentary’s view: Saul had already met the risen Lord, called him Lord, and been addressed as brother before his baptism. Sins are washed away by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), received by faith; baptism is the God-given picture and sign of that washing (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal to God for a good conscience). Baptism should not be delayed, but it is not the cause of forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the temple the Lord told Paul to leave Jerusalem, because the city would not accept his testimony; Paul argued that his past made him the ideal witness there, and the Lord said no.

Get out of Jerusalem quickly. A new detail: in Acts 9 the believers sent him away because of a plot (9:29–30). Luke gives the human side there; Paul gives the divine side here. This is the scene he has been building toward. He is charged with teaching everyone everywhere against this place (21:28); his mission to everyone everywhere was commanded by the Lord in this place, at prayer.

Testimony about me. The testimony is about Jesus, so to reject it is to reject him: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). Paul has not failed as a preacher; the city that would not have the Lord will not have his witness either.

Lord, they themselves know. And Paul argues, with a good case: in Jerusalem, the man saying that Jesus rose is the man they commissioned to stop it. They have the paperwork. If that change will not persuade them, what could? Nor is it selfish, for Jerusalem is the most dangerous city on earth for him. He offers the Lord the most strategic use of his own conversion, and the answer is: get out, quickly.

A good plan refused. God’s refusal is not always a verdict on the quality of the plan. He has a larger map you are not being shown. This no took Paul to Tarsus, Antioch, Galatia, Macedonia, Asia and, in the end, Rome: the whole Gentile mission flows from a refusal he argued against. And on the barracks steps, some twenty years later, he is running the same experiment before the very audience the Lord said would not accept it, and the riot that ends the speech shows who was right.

He knows the way. The Lord who said no to Paul in the temple was sending him to the nations, to us. Behind it stands the Father who once said no to his own Son’s prayer that the cup might pass, because a greater salvation was coming through the cross. He refuses us because he is bringing many sons to glory, and he knows the way.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? Not if it is the honest pleading of a child who will still obey. Abraham pleaded for Sodom (Genesis 18:22–33), Moses argued for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), and the psalms are full of complaint and reasoning. What makes Paul’s prayer godly is what he does next: when the Lord answers, he goes. It becomes sin when it turns into refusal, or into the sulking assumption that God owes us an explanation. Pour out your case; then say, as Paul in effect did, “your will be done”, and pack your bags.

In everyday life. Name before the Lord the good thing you were not permitted to do: the ministry you were suited for and not given. Then look at where his no has taken you instead, and thank him for the larger map you cannot yet see.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul confessed his part in Stephen’s death without softening it, and the Lord’s answer was not a rebuke but a commission to the nations.

Stephen your witness. The evidence Paul offers is not his training or his zeal but the worst thing he ever did. Witness (martys) is the courtroom word used of Paul’s own calling (v. 15); because of days like this one the church came to use it of someone killed for his testimony, which is how we get the word martyr (see Stephen).

Standing by and approving. Three verbs, none softened. Standing by: close enough to see it. Approving: agreeing. Watching over the garments: the smallest job at the scene, and the one he names. A man managing his guilt reaches for the version in which his part was marginal; Paul knows that the man who holds the coats is part of the stoning, making it easier, wanting the outcome. He never forgot it (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13).

Far away to the Gentiles. At Pentecost Peter told a Jewish crowd the promise was “for all who are far off” (2:39), and nobody rioted, because a Jerusalem crowd hears “far off” and thinks of Jews in Babylon. Paul names the far-off ones in the one word they cannot bear. “I will send you” comes from the root that gives us “apostle”: the mission to the Gentiles was Christ’s command, given in the temple, to a man on his knees in the middle of an argument he was losing.

The mountain top. Not a lesser assignment, either: Paul is sent to the ends of the earth with the message he tried to strangle. Stephen died praying, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (7:60), as his Lord had prayed for the men driving the nails (Luke 23:34). The most famous answer to that dying prayer was standing at the edge of the crowd with his arms full of coats. The blood Saul helped to spill is answered by the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than any martyr’s (Hebrews 12:24), and which had already covered Saul’s guilt when the Lord said, “Go.”

If God has forgiven me, why do I still remember what I did? Because forgiveness is not amnesia. God promises to remember our sins no more (Hebrews 8:12), meaning he will never hold them against us; he does not promise that we will forget. Paul remembered Stephen all his life, but the debt had been cancelled at the cross (Colossians 2:13–14), and the memory humbled him without crushing him: he called himself the least of the apostles, and in the same breath said, “by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). When the memory comes back, neither argue with it nor wallow in it. Take it straight to the cross, and let it become a reason for praise.

Is it fair that the man who helped kill Stephen was forgiven? Not if fairness means everyone getting what he deserves, for grace is by definition what nobody deserves. But it is not unjust, because Saul’s guilt was not ignored. It was laid on Christ and punished there in full (Isaiah 53:5–6), so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The religious person who resents mercy to the worst of sinners has forgotten that he needs exactly the same mercy. The person who thinks himself too far gone has just been answered: if Saul, then anyone.

In everyday life. If something in your past seems to disqualify you from serving Christ, bring it to him unsoftened, as Paul did, and hear what he says to forgiven sinners: “Go.” And pray by name for the church’s persecutors today, as Stephen did. You may be praying for the next Paul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — The Roman Custody and Paul's Citizenship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace to the Gentiles is the real offence, and God protects the messenger who carries it. At the word “Gentiles” the crowd that had listened in silence erupts, crying for Paul’s death and flinging dust and cloaks (vv. 22–23). The tribune, still not understanding, orders him to be examined under the scourge, until Paul quietly asks whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen (vv. 24–25). The centurion and the tribune hurry to undo their mistake, and Paul’s citizenship by birth outranks the tribune’s purchased one (vv. 26–29). Next day the tribune summons the council to learn the real charge, and Paul stands before the court that condemned his Lord (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology:
Rights as Tools, Not Shields

Paul neither renounces his citizenship nor hides behind it (on why he kept it back at Philippi and on the steps but uses it here, see the note on vv. 24–25). The deciding question is not what will hurt least but what will serve most, and it has to be asked fresh each time.

God gave the sword to the state (Romans 13:4), and he uses it, often through officials with no interest in him (see vv. 26–27). God’s providence does not need the cooperation of the people it employs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four officials in turn, Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, examined the case against Paul, and not one could name a crime (23:29; 25:18, 27).

Now: Where the church is opposed, it is worth being clear about which thing is happening. Sometimes Christians are rebuked for genuine wrongdoing, and the right response is repentance, not a persecution story. But when one inquiry after another finds no wrongdoing and the offence is the message itself, the answer is not outrage but to carry on quietly with the good you were doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.' And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the one word “Gentiles” the crowd that had listened quietly erupted, because they could not bear that God would show mercy to outsiders without first making them Jews.

Up to this word they listened to him. They gave him a real hearing: the light, the voice, Ananias, the trance. Then one word, and the crowd went off like a match in a gas leak. They could accept a vision, even a converted persecutor, but not mercy to Gentiles on equal terms. It was the same at Nazareth: when Jesus spoke of God’s mercy to a widow of Sidon and a Syrian leper, the synagogue tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:25–29).

Away with such a fellow from the earth! It is the cry they raised at the bottom of these same steps minutes earlier (21:36), and the one Luke recorded when a Jerusalem crowd stood before Pilate and shouted, “Away with this man” (Luke 23:18). The servant is getting his master’s reception, in his master’s city, in his master’s words.

Cloaks and dust. Dust in the air is an old gesture of grief and rejection (Job 2:12; 2 Samuel 16:13; see mourning customs); throwing off cloaks a gesture of horror, or a preparation for stoning (7:58). Paul has just told them he minded the garments at Stephen’s execution, and now a mob that wants him dead is throwing off its garments. Luke does not need to comment.

Grace as a possession. It is not simply racial hatred but a sincere conviction that God’s grace is a possession rather than a gift; once you believe you hold something by right, everyone who receives it freely looks like a thief. Their own Scriptures had said it: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). In this very temple Simeon had called the infant Jesus “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). This crowd is not defending the Bible against Paul; it is shouting down the book it holds. The grace that offended Jerusalem is the grace that reached us, far off, strangers to the covenants, and made us fellow heirs.

Could I be like this crowd? Yes. It is easy to read them as monsters and move on. But every one of us has a sentence about God we would find hard to say amen to: that he could save the person who wronged you, or loves people of a nation or party you despise, or that your own good record earns you nothing. Find yours. The sentence that makes something in you go quiet and resistant marks the place where you have decided that God belongs to you, rather than you to him. Bring it to him and ask him to change your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of outrage.

verseByVerse.quote: "the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, 'Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune ordered Paul to be examined under the Roman scourge, and as they stretched him out for the whips Paul calmly asked whether the law allowed them to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. From here to the end of Acts Paul speaks as a prisoner, with Roman law setting the pace.

Examined by flogging. The tribune has understood nothing, so he reaches for the standard tool and seeks the truth by torture. Not the synagogue’s thirty-nine lashes, which Paul had taken five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), but the Roman scourge: leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, the punishment that went before crucifixion, which could cripple or kill. And not even as a sentence, only as a way of getting information. There is no malice in it, which is what makes it chilling: the tribune has just saved Paul’s life twice. Great cruelty is often committed by ordinary people following procedure.

Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned? A calm, legal question at the last moment, put to the centurion standing by. Two words carry it: Roman, and uncondemned (akatakritos), untried, with no verdict entered. Under the old Roman laws a citizen could not be scourged without trial, and the principle was so deeply felt that Cicero built a famous prosecution on it, declaring that to bind a Roman citizen is a crime and to flog him an outrage. Paul is not asking a favour. He is telling a Roman officer that he is about to break Roman law. And the citizenship he is about to claim is the thread by which God will draw him to Rome (23:11; 25:11).

The back that was not spared. One prisoner in this city had already felt the scourge. Pilate had Jesus flogged though he found no guilt in him (John 19:1–4), and Jesus said nothing to stop it: “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6). Paul holds a right and uses it. His Lord held every right in heaven and on earth and laid his back down for the whip, because he had come not to escape our punishment but to bear it.

Why did he not say this at Philippi? He did, but only afterwards. He and Silas were beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison, and only the next morning, when the magistrates wanted them quietly gone, did Paul mention that they had beaten uncondemned Roman citizens publicly (16:37). He took that beating with the card in his pocket, and out of it came a midnight hymn, an earthquake, and a jailer and his household saved. The difference is what the suffering would accomplish. At Philippi a beating served the gospel, so he took it. Here a scourging might well have killed him, and he was meant to testify in Rome. A chapter ago, on these same steps, he held the same card and did not play it, because what he wanted then was a pulpit, not a rescue (21:39).

So when should a Christian stand on his rights, and when should he suffer wrong? Paul’s rule seems to be: what will serve the gospel and the good of others? Jesus taught us to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), and Paul told the Corinthians it was better to be wronged than to drag a brother to court (1 Corinthians 6:7). Yet he also appealed to Caesar and claimed his citizenship. Personal insults and losses we are usually called to bear quietly. But where injustice threatens our life, our ability to serve Christ, or people who depend on us, using lawful protection is not unspiritual. Victims of abuse, for example, should never be told that Christian meekness means staying silent; the law is God’s gift for their protection. Ask God for wisdom, and ask what will honour Christ most.
verseByVerse.note: Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; flogging an uncondemned Roman citizen was illegal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, 'What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.' So the tribune came and said to him, 'Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?' And he said, 'Yes.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion warned his commander, the tribune came himself to ask, and Paul’s one word, “Yes”, stopped a Roman cohort.

What are you about to do? The centurion knew the law. He does not argue with Paul or check his story; he goes straight to his commander. The junior officer at the whipping post knows something his commander has forgotten on a bad afternoon: that a career, and possibly a neck, is about ten seconds from ending.

Tell me, are you a Roman citizen? The tribune comes himself. There were no papers to produce on a staircase: a citizen’s status was registered in his home city, and checking would take weeks or months. But falsely claiming citizenship was punishable by death, so the claim was usually believed. The law threatened both men, the officer who flogged a citizen and the prisoner who falsely claimed to be one. A man in Paul’s position either was a citizen or was signing his own death warrant, and the tribune could see he was no fool.

And he said, “Yes.” Count what Paul had already endured without saying it: the mob’s beating, the chains, being carried up the stairs like freight, being tied to the post. Until now saying it would have bought him comfort and cost him a hearing.

Rights held as Christ held his. Self-denial is neither pretending you have no rights nor noisily renouncing them. It is holding them loosely enough that the question is never “what may I claim?” but “what will serve?” Paul had learned that from Christ, “who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6). Every lesser right a Christian has is to be held in the same way.

God’s quiet instruments. None of these men cares about the gospel; they are protecting themselves, and God uses a frightened officer’s self-preservation to keep his servant alive. The God who prepared Paul’s yes is preparing, in hidden ways, every provision his children will need, all the way home.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune answered, 'I bought this citizenship for a large sum.' Paul said, 'But I am a citizen by birth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune had bought his citizenship at great cost, but Paul was born a citizen, an older and more honourable claim that God had prepared long before.

A large sum. There is a jab in that sentence, and some wounded pride: he had paid a fortune for his status, and he is looking at a battered provincial just untied from a post. Under Claudius citizenship could be bought through bribes; Dio Cassius says it became cheap as the market grew crowded. His name probably records the transaction: Claudius Lysias (23:26), the emperor’s name taken with the citizenship.

But I am a citizen by birth. Literally, he was even born one. He does not gloat. The prisoner has the older claim, the commander bought his way in, and it is the commander who is now in legal danger.

How did people become Roman citizens? It was a prized and fairly rare status, carrying real protection: no flogging without trial, the right to a proper hearing, and the right of appeal to Caesar, which Paul will later use (25:11). It came by birth from citizen parents, as with Paul; by purchase, often through bribery, as with the tribune; by being freed from slavery by a Roman master; or by grant of the emperor, for service to Rome, for long service in the auxiliary army, or to a family or a whole city. A man could hold it as a Jew and a citizen of Tarsus at once, as Paul did.

The freest man in the room. Paul in chains keeps turning out to be the freest man in every room he is dragged into, calmer than the officers holding him. He learned it from his Lord, who stood bound before Pilate and told him he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

Bought not by us but for us. Paul prized far more a citizenship neither bought nor inherited: “our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). The tribune paid a large sum for his. Ours was bought not by us but for us, with Christ’s blood, by the one who became an outcast so that outcasts could be “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).
verseByVerse.note: Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. Paul was born a citizen, probably because his father or grandfather had been granted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afraid of what he had done, the tribune next day set Paul before the council to learn the real charge, and no court could find one.

The tribune also was afraid. Even chaining a citizen without trial was illegal. Yet he still leaves Paul in custody overnight. Fear of consequences is not repentance, and it does not produce prompt justice; it produces a sleepless night and a decision in the morning.

The real reason. A thread Luke has pulled for two chapters. At the riot the tribune could not learn the facts (21:34); later he will write that Paul was charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29), and Festus will find no charge of the evils he expected (25:18). Official after official examines this case and finds no crime. That is Luke’s quiet defence of the faith: Christianity is not being convicted; it is being disliked. And before God no charge against Paul could stand either, because every charge had already been answered at the cross: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

All the council. The Sanhedrin, which condemned Jesus and Stephen. A pagan officer with no authority over their religious business orders them to convene, and they come, at the convenience of a Roman soldier trying to fill in a form correctly. The one this council condemned in the night now stands at the right hand of God interceding for us, and no court on earth can reverse his verdict.

The whole way round the room. The chapter opened with Paul telling the crowd that the council could bear witness that he had walked out of their chamber with warrants (v. 5). It closes with him standing before that same body, in Roman custody, as one of the people those letters were written against. The Lord had said so when he claimed him: “I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (9:16). The young man who left the council with warrants returns as the accused, and would not trade places with his younger self for anything.

What does Luke want me to learn from all these trials? That the faith you hold is innocent of the charges brought against it (see “The real reason” above). That should give you courage. When Christianity is mocked as harmful or hateful, you need not be ashamed: examine the charge, admit any real faults in Christians, and stand calmly, as Paul did, knowing that the truth will bear examination. And it should give you patience: God often vindicates his people slowly, through ordinary courts and procedures, rather than by lightning.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

22.title: Paul's Defence Before the Crowd
22.text: <sup>1</sup>“Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.” <sup>2</sup>And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said: <sup>3</sup>“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. <sup>4</sup>I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, <sup>5</sup>as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. <sup>6</sup>“As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. <sup>7</sup>And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ <sup>8</sup>And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’ <sup>9</sup>Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. <sup>10</sup>And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’ <sup>11</sup>And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. <sup>12</sup>“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, <sup>13</sup>came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. <sup>14</sup>And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; <sup>15</sup>for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. <sup>16</sup>And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ <sup>17</sup>“When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance <sup>18</sup>and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ <sup>19</sup>And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. <sup>20</sup>And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ <sup>21</sup>And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’” <sup>22</sup>Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth!
