For he should not be allowed to live.” <sup>23</sup>And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air, <sup>24</sup>the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. <sup>25</sup>But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” <sup>26</sup>When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” <sup>27</sup>So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” <sup>28</sup>The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” <sup>29</sup>So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. <sup>30</sup>But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
22.overview:
Where we are. Paul has been seized in the temple on the false charge of bringing Greeks into it, rescued by Roman soldiers, and given leave to speak from the barracks steps (21:27–40). This is his first defence, the second of three tellings of his conversion in Acts (9:1–19; 26:9–18), and the turn from missionary journeys to the courtrooms that will carry him to Rome.

The message. The mission to the Gentiles was not Paul’s invention or his betrayal of Israel. The God of Israel’s fathers, in the risen Jesus of Nazareth, stopped Israel’s fiercest persecutor, washed him, and sent him with mercy to the nations. The real offence of the gospel is grace that no one owns, and God guards the messenger who carries it, even through Roman law.

Why it was said. Paul stood accused of teaching everyone everywhere against the people, the law and the temple (21:28). Luke’s readers, like Theophilus, needed to know whether the man at the heart of the Gentile mission was a renegade Jew and a disturber of Roman order (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Speaking in the crowd’s own language, Paul presents himself as one of them: a Jew trained by Gamaliel, zealous enough to persecute the Way to the death (vv. 1–5). Then three scenes. The risen Jesus met him at noon on the Damascus road (vv. 6–11); a devout, law-keeping Ananias restored his sight, told him of the commission of “the God of our fathers”, and urged him to be baptised (vv. 12–16); and in the temple itself the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles (vv. 17–21). At that word the crowd erupts (vv. 22–23). About to be scourged, Paul asks whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen, and the alarmed tribune brings him before the council to learn the real charge (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. To the risen Christ, who calls himself by the despised name “Jesus of Nazareth”, counts every blow struck at his people as struck at himself, and turns the man who held the coats at Stephen’s death into the bearer of Stephen’s message. Paul is spared the scourge; his Lord was not. Jesus was flogged though no guilt was found in him, so that the guilty, Saul first among them, could be washed and sent.

For us. No one is too far gone for this grace, and no one owns it. Tell what Christ has done for you truthfully, in words your hearers can follow, with him at the centre. And when the gospel’s welcome to outsiders gives offence, hold it fast, using lawful means to serve it, not to escape the cost.

keyVerse.quote: Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter and the word the crowd could not bear. The mission to the nations was not Paul’s idea but the risen Lord’s command, given in the temple to a man who had just confessed his part in Stephen’s death. The grace that sent a persecutor far away is the grace that reached us, who were far off.

22.reflection:
Paul answered a hostile crowd not with an argument but with his story, told in their language and full of things they valued (vv. 1–16). What would it look like for you to tell someone in your life what Christ has done for you, truthfully and in words they can follow?

Ananias’s first word to the man who had come to arrest believers was “Brother” (v. 13). Who would be hardest for our church to welcome like that, and what is the difference between welcoming someone at once and trusting him with responsibility?

The crowd listened until one word, “Gentiles” (vv. 21–22). Is there a truth about whom God saves, or how freely he gives, that you find hard to say amen to? Why?

Paul took a beating at Philippi without mentioning his citizenship, but claimed it here (vv. 25–29; 16:37). How do you decide when to stand on your rights and when to bear a wrong for Christ’s sake?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Before the Sanhedrin and the Plot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The court that condemned Jesus cannot condemn his apostle, and the plot sworn against him only shows that the Lord keeps his word. Paul claims a clear conscience, is struck on the high priest’s order, rebukes him, and yields at once to a verse of the law (vv. 1–5). Naming the resurrection as the issue, he splits the council, and soldiers carry him off before he is torn apart (vv. 6–10). That night the risen Lord stands by him and promises Rome (v. 11). At dawn more than forty men swear to kill him, with the chief priests’ approval (vv. 12–15), but Paul’s nephew overhears, and the warning reaches the tribune, who takes the young man aside and believes him (vv. 16–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise That Does Not Remove the Danger

Acts 23:11 is the hinge of the second half of the book. The Lord does not promise release or comfort; he gives an assignment and guarantees its completion: you must testify also in Rome (on that “must”, see the note on vv. 11–12).

God ordains the end, and he ordains the means, and the means are startlingly ordinary: a boy who overhears something, an officer protecting his career, a duty roster (on Paul’s calling the centurion, see vv. 17–18). And the instruments need not be godly or even willing (see vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conspiracy of more than forty men, sworn under a self-curse and endorsed by the chief priests and elders, was defeated by an unnamed young man who heard something and had the nerve to walk across a city and say it.

Now: Few of us are given a Paul-sized life; many of us are at some point given the nephew’s. You know something, or you are near enough to act, and you have about a minute to decide whether it is your business. The act looks too small to matter, and you may never be told how it turned out. Do it anyway, and ask for the courage the Spirit gives (2 Timothy 1:7). The size of the outcome has never been the measure of the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: "And looking intently at the council, Paul said, 'Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.' And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul faces the court he once served and claims, before God, a life with nothing hidden; the high priest answers with a fist.

And looking intently at the council. Luke’s verb, to fix the eyes and not look away, is what the council did to Stephen when they saw his face like the face of an angel (6:15), and what Stephen did when he gazed into heaven and saw the Son of Man standing (7:55). Now the man who held the coats that day stands where Stephen stood, before the same body, and he does the gazing, because he has seen the same Jesus. He once left this chamber with letters to arrest Christians in Damascus (9:1–2; 22:5); some of the older men facing him may remember signing them.

In all good conscience. The verb means to conduct oneself as a citizen, as a member of God’s people; Paul uses its root when he tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). It is a public word: not a warm inner feeling but a claim that his conduct will stand inspection. And he calls them “Brothers”, not rulers, speaking as an equal.

To strike him on the mouth. No charge, no witness, no verdict, and the presiding judge orders the defendant hit in the face. Striking an accused man before trial was illegal, as it was when Jesus was struck before an earlier high priest (John 18:22). Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest from about AD 47 to 58. Josephus, no friend of Christians, records that his servants seized at the threshing floors the tithes that belonged to the ordinary priests, so that some of the poorer priests starved. When the revolt against Rome began in AD 66, rebels found him hiding in an aqueduct and killed him.

The blow that fell on him. No one but Christ has lived a single day of perfect obedience, and because his obedience is counted as ours, we can look at our own record without dread. He too was struck before a high priest, and every blow that fell on him fell for us, for all the guilty consciences we could never clear. His blood now speaks peace, so that a man who once persecuted the church can stand before Israel’s highest court and say, without pride and without fear, that he lives before God with a good conscience.

Is Paul claiming to be sinless? No. He wrote that he was not aware of anything against himself, but that did not acquit him, for it is the Lord who judges (1 Corinthians 4:4): a clear conscience is evidence in your favour, not the Judge’s verdict. He called himself the foremost of sinners for persecuting the church (1 Timothy 1:15), though he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13). He was sincere then and is forgiven now. His claim is that he has played no double game: before his conversion he opposed Jesus because he thought it was obedience, and after it he served Jesus for the same reason. No stretch of his life is hidden.

How do I know whether my conscience is really clear? Feeling fine about yourself is not the same thing; anyone can manage that with a low enough standard or a short enough memory. A conscience is only as good as what has taught it, so it must be trained by Scripture, not by feelings or culture (Hebrews 5:14). Paul’s test is practical: is there anything in your life you would need to edit before it could be read aloud to the people you live and work with? Take five minutes tonight to ask the Lord to show you; confess it to him, put right what you can, and receive his cleansing (1 John 1:9). And where your conscience still accuses you of what Christ has forgiven, remember that his blood purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).
verseByVerse.note: Ananias was high priest from about AD 47 to 58; Josephus describes him as greedy and violent.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Paul said to him, 'God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?' Those who stood by said, 'Would you revile God's high priest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s rebuke is true: a judge who breaks the law he sits to uphold is a whitewashed wall, and God will bring him down. But it is spoken in heat, and the next verse shows what governs him.

You whitewashed wall! The image is Ezekiel’s: builders coat a flimsy partition with whitewash so that it looks like masonry, and God says the rain will come and the wall will fall, whitewash and all (Ezekiel 13:10–15). Jesus called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within (Matthew 23:27). The whitewash is the dignity of Ananias’ office; behind it there is no justice to hold anything up.

God is going to strike you. Best read as a prediction, not a curse: Paul asks God to do nothing; he states what is coming. And God did strike Ananias, murdered some eight years later (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Are you sitting to judge me according to the law? The charge is precise rather than merely rude: it concerns how the court is run. The law forbade punishing without trial and required judges to judge righteously (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 25:1–2). Israel’s judges sat in God’s name, “for the judgment is God’s” (Deuteronomy 1:17), so a judge who breaks the law from the bench does not only wrong a prisoner; he profanes the seat of the Judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25).

Would you revile God’s high priest? Insulting the high priest was serious, and a bystander says so.

A true High Priest. The God who strikes whitewashed walls has given us a High Priest who is “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26): all the way through what he appears to be, and merciful to those whose walls have fallen. When an officer struck him before the high priest, he said, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). That challenges injustice without a raised voice; Paul’s answer is hotter. Only one man has ever been reviled and answered with perfect meekness and perfect truth at once.

How long did the correction take? Everyone has flares of temper. The measure of a man is rarely whether something rises in him when he is struck in the face, but what governs him immediately afterwards: whether a word of Scripture can stop him mid-sentence, or whether he must be right for another twenty minutes first. Paul was stopped by one line of Exodus (v. 5).

Is it ever right for a Christian to speak sharply against injustice? Yes. The prophets did, Jesus did (Matthew 23), and Paul’s protest was just. Silence before wrongdoing, especially when the weak are being harmed, is not meekness but cowardice (Proverbs 31:8–9). But sharp words must be true, aimed at the wrong rather than at humiliating the person, and governed by love for God’s honour rather than our own. Ask: is this true, is it necessary, and am I angry for God’s sake or for mine? When you get the tone wrong, as Paul acknowledged he had, say so quickly, without retracting the truth.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong to speak this way? Some contrast his words with Jesus, who did not revile when reviled (1 Peter 2:23). This commentary’s view: Paul’s words were true and prophetic, and his protest against injustice was right. Yet he at once acknowledged that speaking evil of a ruler was forbidden (v. 5), showing a humble, teachable spirit. Even apostles could speak in heat; what marks Paul is not perfection but his quick submission to Scripture when reminded.
verseByVerse.note: A whitewashed wall looks solid but hides the crumbling beneath.

parallels.desc: you shall do no injustice in court

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Struck without a charge and right in substance, Paul still stops the moment he is reminded of God’s word about rulers, and puts himself under it.

I did not know, brothers. On trial for his life, Paul has just delivered a stinging and accurate rebuke; a bystander says one sentence, and he stops. He neither flatters nor retracts the substance; he puts himself under a verse.

For it is written. Exodus 22:28 reads, “You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.” The two halves sit in one line: contempt for the office was close to contempt for the God who allowed it to exist, even when the officeholder was a disgrace. Paul had written, under Nero, that the authorities that exist “have been instituted by God” (Romans 13:1). He was right about Ananias, and angry, and provoked, and still a text of Scripture brought him to a full stop.

The Ruler they reviled. The verse has an edge no one in the room would have wanted to hear. Micah had promised a ruler from Bethlehem to shepherd God’s people Israel (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6), and this is the court that condemned him. The men guarding Jesus that night mocked him, beat him, blindfolded him and heaped insults on him (Luke 22:63–65), and the council took him to Pilate. Paul bows to that verse for one hot word against a corrupt priest; the same verse had condemned this council on the night it handed Israel’s true Ruler to the Gentiles, and the council never noticed.

Did Paul really not know? We cannot be certain. The plain reading is a genuine apology, and there are possible reasons. Paul had been away from Jerusalem for years, and high priests were then appointed and deposed often by the Herodian kings and the Roman governors. This was an informal session called by a Roman (22:30), so the high priest may not have been robed or in his usual seat. And Paul may have had poor eyesight, which some infer from Galatians 4:15 and 6:11. A few read the sentence as irony: I did not recognise a man acting like that as God’s high priest. Either way there is no reason to doubt Paul’s honesty, and what matters most is clear: the moment he learns it is the high priest, he yields to Scripture.

How can I respect leaders who do not deserve it? By separating the office from the person, as Paul does. Rulers, employers, church officers and parents hold their position by God’s ordering, and Scripture tells us to honour the position even when the person is unworthy (1 Peter 2:17–18). Honour does not mean pretending they are good, flattering them, or obeying them when they command sin (5:29). It means speaking of them without contempt, praying for them, challenging wrongdoing through proper channels, and refusing to mock them, even online. You can tell the truth about a leader’s failings and still guard your tongue; Paul did both in the same breath.

parallels.desc: nor curse a ruler of your people

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, 'Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.' And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the real issue, the resurrection of the dead, and one true sentence splits the court sitting in judgment on it. It was not a trick to save his skin but the heart of his case.

One part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees. Paul knew where the council was divided, because he had been trained on one side of it. The Pharisees, probably “the separated ones”, were a renewal movement of laymen, popular with ordinary people, devoted to the Scriptures and to the tradition of the elders, the oral law Jesus rebuked them for exalting (Mark 7:8–13). They affirmed the resurrection, angels and spirits, and God’s providence; their besetting danger was legalism and pride, yet Nicodemus, Gamaliel and Paul himself were Pharisees. The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and cooperated with Rome; they rejected the oral tradition and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits. After Jerusalem fell in AD 70 they faded, and later rabbinic Judaism descends from the Pharisees.

I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. True, and in the present tense (22:3). The tradition ran in his family: he is no recent recruit borrowing a label. Years after his conversion he still wrote, “as to the law, a Pharisee” (Philippians 3:5; compare 26:5), for he saw the gospel not as the abandonment of Israel’s hope but as its fulfilment. The Pharisees were waiting for the resurrection of the dead; Paul’s news was that it had begun.

The hope and the resurrection of the dead. Was this a shabby trick, setting his enemies against each other? Two things say no. First, it is true. He is on trial because he preaches that a crucified man is alive; take the resurrection out and there is no case: no riot, no council, no chains. He said the same to Felix (24:21), to Agrippa (26:6–8), and to the Jewish leaders in Rome: “it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain” (28:20). A man does not repeat a courtroom trick before four audiences; he repeats a conviction.

The assembly was divided. Second, it exposes the court. Paul did not create the division; he revealed that the body sitting in judgment on the resurrection of Jesus could not agree whether there is any resurrection at all. The supreme court of Israel takes up the case of Jesus Christ for the last time in Acts, and it cannot reach a verdict.

A short walk from the empty tomb. The council that could not agree about resurrection sat a short walk from where it had already happened. The risen one, the firstfruits of the harvest Israel was waiting for (1 Corinthians 15:20), would stand by his servant that very night.

Why does the resurrection matter so much? Because everything hangs on it. If Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection declares Jesus the Son of God (Romans 1:4), shows that his death paid for sin in full, for he “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25), and beats death itself. Justification means God declaring a sinner righteous, not for anything in him, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to him through faith (Romans 4:5). And the risen Christ is the pattern of our future: the body that is buried will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42). So the believer’s hope is not merely that the soul goes to heaven at death, though it does, but that on the last day Christ will raise our bodies and make all things new. That is the hope of Israel, and Paul was willing to wear a chain for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and contended sharply, 'We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees allowed nothing beyond the grave; the Pharisees, to score against them, will grant that a spirit or an angel spoke to Paul, but no one in the room will say the name of Jesus.

No resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit. Luke pauses to explain the parties to his Gentile reader. The Sadducees seem to have held the five books of Moses as binding and rejected doctrines they could not find clearly there. A man who believes there is no resurrection and no judgment has every reason to run the temple as a family business, which, by the accounts we have, is much what they did.

What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him? Party loyalty overcame the Pharisees’ hostility. Some of their scribes allow that what Paul met on the Damascus road might be genuine, an echo of Gamaliel’s caution (5:39). What nobody says is the name Paul actually said. An angel is a safe explanation: the Pharisees were still right about everything, and nothing need change on Monday. But if it was Jesus of Nazareth, risen and speaking, the men who arranged his execution have a problem no correct doctrine about resurrection in general can solve.

Jesus answered them from Moses. When Sadducees tried to make the resurrection look ridiculous, Jesus pointed to the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, centuries after all three were buried: “Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him” (Luke 20:38; Matthew 22:31–32). They are alive to him tonight, and so is every believer who has died in Christ. On this the Pharisees were right.

An inch away. The most dangerous position in the chapter is not the Sadducees’. The Pharisees are an inch from the truth and perfectly comfortable: orthodox, defending the apostle, reasonable, and unconverted. It is possible to hold the resurrection as a doctrine, defend it, be annoyed by those who deny it, and never once deal with the risen Christ himself.

If I believe all the right things, how do I know I have actually dealt with Christ? Ask whether your beliefs have brought you to him or only to agreement about him. Saving faith is not mere assent; it is trusting Jesus himself, coming to him as a sinner and resting on him for salvation (John 1:12; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2; the Westminster Confession 14.2). The signs are personal: you pray to him and not only about him; you are sorry for sin because it grieves him; his word governs your choices; you love his people. If you are unsure, do not settle it by examining your doctrine again. Go to him now and ask him to receive you: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). A heart troubled by this question is usually a heart he is already drawing.

Uncertain wording. Luke literally says the Pharisees “acknowledge both”, though three things are listed, and a denial of angels is puzzling in men who accepted the books of Moses, where angels appear. So some take Luke to mean that the Sadducees denied any life after death, whether as an angel or as a spirit, while the Pharisees affirmed both resurrection and that existence before it. Others take “both” loosely, as Greek could, to mean all three, as the ESV does. Either way, the Sadducees allowed nothing beyond the grave.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s supreme council dissolves into violence, and pagan soldiers have to snatch the prisoner from his own judges.

Torn to pieces. Luke’s word means to tear in two, used of the man who wrenched apart his chains (Mark 5:4): the tribune fears the two parties will pull Paul apart between them. This is the supreme council of Israel, traditionally seventy-one men, convened to weigh a question of God’s law, and soldiers must break it up before somebody is killed.

Take him away from among them by force. The verb is for snatching out of danger (8:39; 1 Thessalonians 4:17). Count the rescues: in two days the tribune has saved Paul from the temple mob (21:32), from his own flogging order (22:29), and now from the court that was meant to try him. Every institution in Jerusalem that exists to do justice has failed in turn, and the only working authority left in the holy city is a Roman garrison under a nervous officer who does not worship Israel’s God.

What institutions become. Paul is safer this week in the custody of the empire that, by early tradition, will one day behead him than in the hands of those who taught him the Scriptures. That is no argument against the Scriptures, but a warning about religious institutions that stop believing what they exist to guard, “having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5).

Torn for us. When this council condemned God’s Son, no soldiers snatched him away, because he had come to be torn for us. He was given into the hands of sinners so that no one could ever snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). And none of this takes him by surprise. He had warned that his disciples would be brought before synagogues, prisons, kings and governors for his name’s sake, that this would be their opportunity to bear witness, that some would be put to death, and yet that not a hair of their head would perish (Luke 21:12–18). Paul is living that sentence line by line; the Lord who foretold the hearing also set its limits.

What should I do if my church or denomination seems to be losing its way? First, ask whether it really has: is the gospel at stake, or only preferences and style? If the gospel is truly at stake, speak up through proper channels, pray for your leaders, and stand with others who hold to Scripture. Churches can be reformed; the Reformation began as a call to return to the word. If, after patient effort, a church has abandoned the gospel or will not discipline serious error, it may be right to leave quietly and join a faithful church, without bitterness. But be slow to give up on God’s people. Christ is still head of his church, and he purifies it in his own time.

verseByVerse.quote: "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.' When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On Paul’s lowest night the risen Lord himself stands beside him, calls his battered week testimony, and binds his future to a divine “must”: he will testify in Rome. By dawn forty men have sworn to kill him, but their oath is doomed before it is sworn.

The following night. Paul had come to Jerusalem with a relief fund from the Gentile churches, meant to show that the two halves of the church were one. Instead: a rumour campaign, a temple vow ending in a riot, a near lynching, chains, a whipping post escaped by seconds, and a supreme court dissolved into a brawl. And another voice was available that night. At Tyre the disciples had told him not to go up (21:4); at Caesarea Agabus had bound himself with Paul’s belt while the company wept and begged (21:10–13). Each warning could now become an accusation: you were told; this is your own doing.

The Lord stood by him. That is the night the Lord came. Not an angel; when it is an angel later in the voyage, Luke says so (27:23). Here it is Jesus himself (compare 2 Timothy 4:17), and the verb can mean he stood over him, as someone stands at the bedside of a man who cannot get up.

Take courage. It is what Jesus said to the terrified disciples on the water, “Take heart; it is I” (Matthew 14:27), and to the eleven on the last night, “take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). It is never a general encouragement to be positive, but what the Lord says to frightened people, at close range, about himself.

As you have testified… so you must testify also in Rome. The sentence first looks back over that week, with its riot, its interrupted speech and its brawl, and calls it testimony. That quietly settles the question hanging since chapter 21, whether Paul was wrong to come: the risen Christ’s own summary is that his servant bore witness in Jerusalem. Then the promise. Luke uses “must” for the fixed purposes of God: “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (Luke 9:22). Paul’s arrival in Rome, his long desire (19:21; Romans 1:10–11), is placed in the same category as the cross and the empty tomb, and this promise will hold him through two years in prison, a storm, a shipwreck and a snakebite.

What the Lord does not promise. He does not say, I will get you out of this. The cell, the storm and the wreck are still coming. Paul is given not an exemption from trouble but a task he is certain to complete.

When it was day. Luke sets the two sentences side by side: the promise comes at night, the conspiracy is sworn at dawn. A hunger strike for murder, sworn the morning after the Lord has said this man will preach in Rome, is doomed before it begins.

He came himself. Consider the Lord in that room. He did not send word. He came, into a garrison cell in an occupied city, stood over one bruised man in chains, and spoke about the future as one who owns it, as he came to Elijah under the broom tree with food and sleep before any word of correction. He had been tried by this same council and struck in the face in this same city. He stands by his servants still, when every human support has gone, and says what only he has the right to say: take courage.

Does God make promises like this to me? Not this exact one; you have not been told you will preach in Rome. But every believer has promises from the same Lord that are just as fixed: that he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), that nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39), and that he will raise you up on the last day (John 6:40). They do not tell you how next month will go. They tell you how the story ends, and that the work God has given you will not be cancelled by anything this week can do.

How do I take courage when I am afraid? Not by talking yourself into a better mood; courage in the Bible comes from outside you. Tell him the fear. Name it plainly in prayer, as the disciples cried out in the boat; he is not offended by frightened people. Remember who is standing by. The risen Christ still stands by his servants, so “we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear’” (Hebrews 13:6). Look back before you look ahead. The Lord called Paul’s wretched week testimony. Ask him to show you what he has already done in yours, and above all at the cross, where he faced the worst for you. Do the next thing. Paul’s courage was not a feeling in the cell but faithfulness in the next room he was taken to. Do not stay alone. Tell a Christian friend and let them pray with you. The Lord often speaks his “take courage” through his people: when the brothers came out to meet Paul on the road to Rome, “Paul thanked God and took courage” (28:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, 'We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than forty men stake their standing before God on a murder, and the chief priests, guardians of God’s law, take up the plan without a word of protest.

More than forty. Not a mob but an organisation: someone recruited them and chose the ambush point, all between dawn and the time the nephew overheard it.

We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath. They put themselves under an anathema, a self-curse: may God do so to me and more also if I eat before this man is dead.

They went to the chief priests and elders. The assassins lay it out to the men Paul stood before the previous afternoon, as men who expect a welcome, and Luke records no objection. Not one priest says this is murder. The custodians of the law that says “You shall not murder” respond with silence and then cooperation.

Not the blow but the memo. The council is asked to contribute not the weapon but a letter (v. 15): an ordinary official request that Paul be brought down for further questioning, accurate in form, innocent on paper, and fatal. That is how respectable people take part in evil: not the blow, but the memo; not the lie, but the phrasing that lets the lie work.

They had welcomed such an offer before. When Judas came to the chief priests to betray Jesus, “they were glad, and agreed to give him money” (Luke 22:5). That plot put the Son of God on a cross, and even that was God’s chosen way to save the world. The men who now agree to an ambush for the servant bought the betrayal of his Master, and they are no more in control this time than then. Our God is not outnumbered by forty, or by four thousand. One word from his mouth outweighs every oath sworn against his people.

Did forty men really starve to death? Almost certainly not. The rabbis allowed vows to be released if they became impossible to keep; the Mishnah’s tractate on vows discusses exactly this. Religion of that kind can produce the zeal to swear before God that you will commit a murder, and also the legal machinery to let you off when the murder does not come off: enormously serious about outward form, with nothing underneath.

How might I be complicit in wrong without realising it? By the small things that make someone else’s wrong possible: signing off a report you know is misleading, wording a reference to hide what you know, staying silent while someone is treated unjustly, forwarding a rumour, looking away from abuse because raising it would be awkward for the organisation. Scripture holds us responsible for the evil we enable or excuse (Proverbs 24:11–12; Ephesians 5:11). Ask the Lord to show you any paper you have signed, sentence you have worded, or silence you have kept that made possible what you would never have done with your own hands. Then put it right if you can.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plotters make a court hearing the bait for a murder, and God answers forty sworn men with one unnamed young man who overhears and speaks.

As though you were going to determine his case more exactly. A hearing is the bait, and the ambush is set in the narrow streets between the fortress and the council chamber.

The son of Paul’s sister. Out of nowhere, Paul has family: the only mention of his immediate family in the New Testament, lasting seven verses. After verse 22 the young man walks out of Scripture; we do not know whether he was a believer, or how he heard. Paul wrote that for Christ’s sake he had “suffered the loss of all things” (Philippians 3:8), and we are not told what that cost him at home. Here at least one of his family was willing to cross the city for him.

He went and entered the barracks and told Paul. Brave and entirely ordinary: he heard something, walked to the barracks, and said it to the right person. On one side, forty sworn men, the chief priests and elders, the machinery of the Sanhedrin; on the other, one unnamed young man. He wins completely, not because of who he is but because of the sentence the Lord spoke the night before: “you must testify also in Rome.” That word needed nothing more than a young man’s ears and feet.

Small acts, great purposes. God hides great purposes in small faithful acts, so that the glory is his: a manger in Bethlehem, a boy’s five loaves, an unnamed nephew in Jerusalem.

Is God really involved in small coincidences like this? Yes. God governs all his creatures and all their actions, down to the fall of a sparrow and the hairs on our heads (Matthew 10:29–30; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1; the Westminster Confession 5.1). Usually he works not by miracles but through ordinary means: someone in a particular room at a particular hour, with the nerve to speak. That is what providence looks like from the inside. So when you happen to hear or notice something, or find yourself near enough to help, do not dismiss it as coincidence. Ask whether this is the moment God has placed you for, and act.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Certain of the Lord’s promise, Paul acts at once and sensibly to protect his life: faith in God’s ends uses God’s means.

Paul called one of the centurions. Hours earlier the risen Lord had told him he would testify in Rome. He could have done nothing and called it faith. Instead he calls a centurion with a short, calm request.

God ordains the means as well as the end. On a sinking ship, told by an angel that every soul aboard would survive, the same Paul saw sailors lowering the boat and said, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved” (27:31). He believed the promise absolutely, and he spoke up. A man sure that God’s promise cannot fail is free to be thoroughly practical, because he is no longer trying to save himself by his competence.

Paul the prisoner. The centurion says more than he knows: a Roman officer has just run an errand for a man in chains. Paul later called himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1), not Rome’s. He is the calmest man in the barracks, because his Lord has spoken; that peace comes not from knowing everything will be easy, but from knowing whose prisoner you are.

If God is sovereign, why should I bother taking precautions or making plans? Because the God who decides the end also decides the means, and our actions are among them. He promised Hezekiah fifteen more years and also told him to put a cake of figs on his boil (Isaiah 38:5, 21). He feeds the hungry through work, heals the sick through doctors and medicine, and saves sinners through preaching. Trusting God means doing the wise thing and leaving the outcome to him, without panic or presumption. Lock your door, see your doctor, plan your budget, and pray: faith and prudence are not rivals but friends.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A pagan commander treats a frightened young informant with kindness and good sense, and God uses him, mixed motives and all, to keep his promise.

The tribune took him by the hand. Claudius Lysias commands a thousand men and has spent two days on riots, yet he takes a frightened young man by the hand and walks him aside: an almost fatherly touch. Luke’s word allows a wide range of ages; he may have been a boy. Asking “privately” is good sense, not sentiment: if it became known who had informed, the boy’s life would be in danger, so the tribune manages the disclosure so that no one in the barracks sees who told what.

As though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely. The report is brief, specific and honest. He claims to have seen no knives; he gives the shape of the coming request and why it is a lie, and lets the officer draw the conclusion.

God uses him as he is. Luke quietly sets this pagan’s conduct beside that of the chief priests, who heard of a murder and said nothing. The tribune has no interest in Israel’s God, and his motives are mixed: he is protecting a Roman citizen he has already wrongly chained, and he knows what happens to officers who lose prisoners to lynch mobs. God uses him anyway, without improving him first. Our God is never at the mercy of the people around us; they are always, though they do not know it, at his service.

In everyday life. When someone younger, weaker or frightened comes to you with something hard to say, do what the tribune did: take them aside, make it safe to speak, and protect them afterwards. Above all, when a child or vulnerable person tells you about abuse, believe them enough to act, report it to the proper authorities, and never hush it up to protect a church or a family’s name.

Does God use unbelievers to help his people? Constantly. He used Pharaoh’s daughter to save Moses, Cyrus the Persian to send Israel home (Isaiah 45:1–4), and Roman soldiers to rescue Paul three times in two days. The kindness of unbelieving doctors, teachers, neighbours and officials is part of God’s common grace, his goodness to all people and through all people. That should make us grateful rather than suspicious, and it should make us pray that the God who is using them would also save them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole machinery of murder stands ready, waiting on one permission, and the one man who could give it now knows everything.

Waiting for your consent. Everything waits on one signature from one Roman officer who is about to refuse: enormous preparation, total commitment, and one small permission that never comes. That is the plot against Paul, and in a sense every plot against the purposes of God.

Tell no one that you have informed me. It is the last thing anyone says to Paul’s nephew in the Bible. The plotters think they are hunting; they will wait hungry for a prisoner who left under armed guard at nine in the evening, in the opposite direction. Luke never tells us what became of them.

Against the Lord and against his Anointed. The Jerusalem church had prayed over plots like this. When the council threatened Peter and John, the believers quoted the second psalm, where the rulers gather together against the Lord and against his Anointed, and named its fulfilment: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against the holy servant Jesus (4:25–27). The rage that fell on the Anointed now falls on his witness, and the same psalm says what heaven does about it: “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4).

What if I never see what came of my faithfulness? Then you are in the company of most of God’s servants. The nephew may never have known that his walk across Jerusalem helped carry the gospel to Rome. The faithful died not having received the things promised, but having greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). God does not owe us a report on our obedience; much of it will be shown to us only at the last day, when the Lord brings to light the things now hidden and each one receives his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5). Do the one thing you can do, and leave the report with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his promise of Rome through entirely ordinary means: soldiers, a letter and a governor’s routine. The tribune sends Paul out at nine in the evening under an escort of 470 men (vv. 23–24). His letter to Felix tells the story in a way that flatters its writer, yet declares Paul charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment and hands the case to a Roman court (vv. 25–30). The infantry turn back at Antipatris and the cavalry take Paul on to Caesarea (vv. 31–33). Felix confirms that the case is his, promises a hearing when the accusers arrive, and has Paul kept in Herod’s praetorium, where two years of waiting begin (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses an officer’s fear, a troop deployment and a self-serving letter.

Two cautions keep this from turning into fatalism, the idea that nothing we do matters. Providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and when Luke lets Lysias’s self-flattering letter pass without comment, that is not approval. And providence does not promise comfort: this chapter’s happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor hoping for a bribe. The pattern is Joseph’s: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune’s letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He moved one clause and let his superior draw a generous conclusion.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode: why the job ended, why the friendship cooled. Every detail probably happened. Lay it beside a transcript, as Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask whether the sequence is right and whether the motive you imply is the one you had (see the note on v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To keep one prisoner alive the tribune sends nearly half his garrison into the night, and the Lord who promised Rome keeps his word through a Roman officer’s caution.

Two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. Do the arithmetic, as Luke expects: 470 men to protect one prisoner from forty assassins on a night journey of some sixty miles, nearly half the Jerusalem garrison, in a city that has rioted twice in three days. Luke lets both of the tribune’s reasons stand. The threat is real: forty men sworn to die trying. And his own neck is at risk: he has already wrongly chained a Roman citizen, and a dead one in his custody would finish him.

At the third hour of the night. About 9 p.m. More than one mount was provided for Paul, perhaps for changes of horse so the pace never dropped, or for his companions.

Bring him safely to Felix the governor. The verb means to bring through danger to safety, and Luke will use it again of every soul reaching land from the wreck (27:44; 28:1). The tribune wants his prisoner delivered alive to a governor; the Lord wants his witness delivered alive to Caesar. For one night the two intentions run on the same road.

Seventy horsemen and twelve legions. In Gethsemane Jesus said he could appeal to his Father and at once be sent more than twelve legions of angels, and he would not, because the Scriptures had to be fulfilled (Matthew 26:53–54). The Master refused an escort from heaven so that he could be handed over; the servant is given an escort from Rome so that he can be kept for his work. Both nights were ordered by the same Father, and the servant is kept only because the Master went unguarded to the cross.

Why does God protect some Christians so dramatically and not others? We are not always told, and should not pretend to know. This same Lord let James be killed by the sword (12:2) and Stephen be stoned, and, as the early church remembered, would one day let Paul be executed in Rome. What we know is that no believer dies one moment before his work is done, or lives one moment after God calls him home: “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). God’s protection in this world is real and often wonderful, but it is not the whole of his care. His deepest protection is that nothing, not even death, can separate us from his love in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “spearmen” occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere. It seems literally to mean those who take with the right hand, and suggestions include spearmen, slingers or archers, light infantry, or even spare horses led by the hand. Spearmen or light-armed troops is the commonest view; whatever they were, the escort was large and the tribune was taking no chances.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune commits Paul’s case to writing and sends it to Felix, a corrupt governor, and the Lord is sending his apostle into that man’s court on purpose.

Claudius Lysias. The commander finally gets a name, very likely taken from the emperor Claudius when he bought his citizenship (22:28). “His Excellency” is the title Luke uses for Theophilus (Luke 1:3).

The governor Felix. Felix will hold Paul for two years, so it is worth knowing who he was. Antonius Felix was a freed slave whose brother Pallas was the powerful freedman secretary of Claudius; that connection, not merit, raised him to govern Judea, an almost unheard-of post for a former slave. Tacitus said he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave. He was cruel and corrupt. He had persuaded Drusilla, a Jewish princess, daughter of the Herod Agrippa who killed James (12:1–2), to leave her husband for him; she will sit beside him while Paul reasons about the judgment to come (24:24–25). He would keep an innocent man in custody two years hoping for a bribe (24:26). Into that man’s jurisdiction the Lord Jesus Christ is sending his apostle, on purpose, under armed guard.

Why would God send Paul to a man like Felix? For the same reason he sent Moses to Pharaoh, and Jesus ate with tax collectors: wicked rulers need the gospel too. Felix heard Paul speak about faith in Christ Jesus and was alarmed (24:25). As far as we know he did not repent, but he was given the chance: a corrupt governor heard the truth from the one man in his province who could not be bribed. God often puts his people before the hardest hearts by appointment. If you work for, live with, or answer to someone like Felix, you may be the only clear witness to Christ they will ever meet.
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every fact in the tribune’s letter is true, and the way he arranges them still deceives, casting him as the hero of a rescue he nearly botched.

Having learned that he was a Roman citizen. This last clause changes what the whole sentence means. Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen, and implies he rescued Paul because he was one. Lay the letter beside the record: he intervened because a riot was in progress (21:31–32), chained Paul, ordered him examined under the scourge, and learned of the citizenship at the last moment, from Paul himself, tied to the post (22:25–29). He invents nothing; he moves one clause and lets the reader assume a motive.

An honest historian. Luke includes the letter and says nothing, trusting the reader of chapter 22 to notice. That is a quiet reason to trust him: a man inventing a case for Paul would hardly leave discrepancies lying about in his own evidence.

The mirror. We are fluent in this too: the technically correct sentence about a colleague, the account of why a relationship ended or why you left a job, in which nothing is invented and the shape is still wrong. Underneath is usually a heart that wants people’s approval more than it fears God. The gospel loosens that grip, because in Christ we already have the one approval that finally counts, and there is nothing left to win by editing (Galatians 1:10). Christ has read the transcript, every clause, and loved us anyway, and died to make liars into truthful children of God.

Is it lying if everything I say is true? It can be. Truthfulness is not only avoiding false statements but not deceiving. The ninth commandment forbids anything that prejudices the truth, including the misleading arrangement of facts and leaving out what would change the picture (Westminster Larger Catechism 145). If you intend someone to believe something false, the accuracy of each sentence does not make you honest. Ask: what will my hearer conclude, and is that true? Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and his people are to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), not merely avoid technical falsehood.
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rome finds Paul guilty of nothing, and files the resurrection of the dead under “questions of their law”.

Accused about questions of their law. Religious disputes, as Gallio said (18:15): that is what the empire saw. A Roman officer heard a man say his whole case turned on the resurrection of the dead and filed it as a dispute about Jewish regulations. He was looking straight at the most important claim ever made and could not see it.

Charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Luke records such Roman verdicts repeatedly: Festus will find none of the evils he expected (25:18, 25), and Agrippa will say this man could have been set free (26:31–32). Paul, like Jesus, was innocent under Roman law; in Luke’s Gospel Pilate three times finds no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). Luke is building a legal case in the pages of a history, and never once tells the reader what to conclude.

Is Christianity just a private religious matter, as the tribune thought? No. The resurrection of Jesus is either the hinge on which everything turns or it is nothing; the one thing it cannot be is a question of religious law. If a crucified man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, death has been beaten on its own ground, every grave is provisional, and the risen one holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). That makes Christ Lord of public life as well as private devotion: of work, politics, money, family and the future of the world. The world often treats the gospel as a harmless local matter. It is the news that the King has come.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one administrative sentence the tribune lifts Paul’s case out of the council’s reach, and the plot meant to keep him from Rome becomes his road to Rome.

Ordering his accusers also to state before you. The tribune passes the problem upwards and puts the plot on the record, and these words move the trial to another court, out of Jerusalem and the Sanhedrin’s reach. There, before Festus, Paul will do what no man could do before the Sanhedrin: appeal to Caesar (25:11), compelling the state to carry him, at its own expense and under guard, to Rome.

The plot that carried him to Rome. The forty men achieved exactly one thing: they frightened a Roman officer into moving Paul to a court from which he could appeal to the emperor. The plot to keep Paul from Rome is the means by which he reaches it. Luke has shown this before: the scattering meant to destroy the church spread it (8:1–4). Joseph said it first: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). And Luke’s Gospel closed with the deepest case of all, the risen Jesus asking two bewildered disciples whether it was not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26). Paul is walking his Master’s road.

Does this mean the evil done to me does not hurt, or does not matter? No. Paul spent two years in custody as a direct result of this letter, and it hurt. God never calls evil good, and he will judge those who do it. The comfort is not that opposition will fail to wound, but that it cannot get outside God’s use of it: no hostile act is available to your enemies that God has not already given a purpose. So you can grieve honestly, seek justice where it is right, and still trust that your Father is weaving even this into good for you and glory for himself (Romans 8:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tired soldiers on a dark road, with no prayer and no miracle in sight, are God’s promise being kept.

By night to Antipatris. The logistics are the point. From Jerusalem the road drops out of the hill country through narrow passes, perfect ambush country where cavalry is nearly useless, and comes out on to the plain at Antipatris, a town Herod the Great built and named after his father, some 35 to 40 miles from Jerusalem. Beyond it lay open, mostly Gentile country.

Letting the horsemen go on with him. The foot soldiers went back to a city short of troops; the cavalry took him the last 25 miles or so to Caesarea at speed.

The fulfilment, unfelt. The sentence spoken in a cell is being carried out by 470 men on a road in the dark, most of them tired, few if any praying, all simply doing their job. The Lord is not named in these verses, and he is doing everything in them. The night march is not the gap between the promise and its fulfilment; it is the fulfilment, in progress, unfelt. He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Psalm 121:4), and by morning his servant is where he meant him to be.

Why does God feel absent when I most need him? Feelings are not a reliable gauge of his presence. Here he was keeping his promise through every mile, and nothing in the scene felt holy. The psalmists knew nights when God seemed far away (Psalm 13:1; 88:14), and they kept praying into the silence. He has promised to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20), whether or not we sense it. When you feel nothing, hold on to what he has said, keep to the ordinary means he gives, his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people, and expect one day to look back and see that he was carrying you the whole way.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reaches Caesarea a prisoner, out of the council’s hands for good, handed over to the Gentiles as his Lord was.

When they had come to Caesarea. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. Paul would be held here two years (24:27), and from here he would sail for Rome. Here, in the house of Philip, Agabus had bound his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt (21:8–11); his words have come true in substance, though Roman soldiers put on the chains (21:33). Jesus had told the Twelve that the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32); it has happened to the servant as it happened to his Lord.

They presented Paul also before him. Paul is now, formally and finally, out of the council’s jurisdiction. The high priest who had him struck on the mouth will next appear as a plaintiff, coming down in person with a hired advocate (24:1), and he will lose.

A real loss and a door. About twelve days earlier (24:11) Paul had walked into Jerusalem hoping to be welcomed by the church and heard by his own people. He leaves under armed guard at night, rejected by his nation, and Luke does not dress up the loss. But when the temple gates shut behind him (21:30), they shut him out on to the road God meant him to take. He came back to Caesarea in chains, and the chains were carrying the gospel to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Felix takes the case and lodges Paul in the governor’s palace, where two quiet years will pass before the road to Rome opens.

He asked what province he was from. Felix’s first question is not about God or the resurrection or even the riot, but jurisdiction: is this case legally mine? Cilicia was then attached to Syria, whose governor would hardly want a minor case from Judea, so Felix kept it, and that small procedural moment decided where Paul would spend the next two years.

I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive. Roman law required the accused to face his accusers (25:16). Felix will hold the hearing, find nothing, and leave Paul in custody anyway, partly to please the Jewish leaders, partly in hope of a bribe (24:26–27).

Herod’s praetorium. The palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, by the sea, was now the governor’s residence. Paul was probably not in a common cell, and Felix would later allow him some liberty and let his friends care for him (24:23).

The governor’s house, again. From this residence Pontius Pilate had governed Judea a generation earlier, so Paul is lodged in the house of the office that sentenced his Lord. He would later remind Timothy of “Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession” (1 Timothy 6:13). Now the servant is kept under a governor’s roof to make his own confession before governors and kings.

The chapter from end to end. It opened with a man struck on the mouth; it ends with him alive in a palace by the sea, on record as charged with nothing. Yet nothing is resolved. He is still a prisoner, well over a thousand miles from Rome, and two years are about to disappear here: no journeys, no new churches, no visible fruit. Paul did not know that the voyage was coming, or that he would preach without hindrance in the capital of the world at the end of it. He knew one sentence, spoken in the dark by someone who stood beside him: take courage. On some days that is the whole visible foundation of a Christian life, and it holds, because of who said it: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

What do I do with long seasons of waiting? Hold both halves together, because this is where most Christian lives are lived: the promise is certain, and the waiting is long. Paul did not waste his two years. He spoke with Felix and Drusilla about faith in Christ, received his friends, and was being prepared for Rome. Keep the means of grace, serve whoever is in front of you, pray for the work you cannot yet do, and refuse to call the time wasted. “They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31). Waiting is not God’s absence from your life; it is often where he does his deepest work in you.
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Where we are. Paul, seized in the temple and rescued by the Roman tribune, has told the crowd how he met Jesus and escaped a flogging by naming his Roman citizenship (22:25–29). Now the tribune brings him before the Sanhedrin to learn the charge. By the chapter’s end Paul has left Jerusalem for good, and the trials before governors and a king (chapters 24–26) are about to begin.

The message. The risen Lord keeps his word to his servants, and no court, conspiracy or oath can stop him. He stands beside Paul in the dark and promises Rome, then keeps it without a single miracle, through a nephew’s ears, an officer’s caution and a Roman escort on the road at night. Those who oppose him end up serving him.

Why it was said. Readers like Theophilus needed to know why the apostle was a prisoner and whether the charges were true (see the introduction). Luke shows the highest Jewish court unable to agree on a charge, its leaders party to a murder plot, and a Roman officer finding Paul accused of “nothing deserving death or imprisonment” (v. 29).

How the chapter makes its case. Before the council Paul claims a clear conscience, is struck, rebukes the high priest, and yields at once to a verse of Scripture (vv. 1–5). Naming the resurrection as the real issue, he divides Pharisees from Sadducees, and soldiers rescue him from his own judges (vv. 6–10). That night the Lord stands by him: “Take courage… you must testify also in Rome” (v. 11). At dawn more than forty men swear to kill him, with the chief priests’ consent, but his nephew hears of it and the tribune believes him (vv. 12–22). Paul is sent by night under heavy guard to Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that finds no crime in him (vv. 23–35).

Where it leads. Paul walks his Master’s road: struck before a high priest, tried by the same council, declared innocent by Rome. The likeness shows the difference. Paul is snatched from the council and guarded by 470 soldiers; Jesus refused the legions of angels and was handed over, so that no one could snatch his people out of his hand. The Lord who stands by Paul in the cell once stood alone before this council, and rose: the very hope Paul is on trial for.

For us. Christ promises not an easy road but his presence, and that the work he gives will be finished. When plots form and nights are long, take courage from his word, do the ordinary faithful thing in front of you, and trust that he rules even through people who do not know him.

keyVerse.quote: Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.
keyVerse.note: This word in the night is the hinge of the chapter and of the rest of Acts: the foiled plot, the night march, the trials, the storm and the shipwreck are all this promise being kept. It gives Paul no exemption from trouble, only a task he is certain to finish and the presence of the Lord who sets it.

23.reflection:
Paul could say he had lived before God “in all good conscience” (v. 1), yet one verse of Scripture stopped him mid-sentence when he was angry and in the right (vv. 3–5). What helps you hear correction quickly in a moment like that, and what makes it hard?

The Pharisees were right about the resurrection and still kept Jesus at arm’s length, preferring “a spirit or an angel” (vv. 8–9). How can someone hold true doctrine and never deal with Christ himself, and how would you know the difference in your own life?

On Paul’s worst night the Lord stood by him and spoke of what he must still do (v. 11). Which of Christ’s promises has carried you through a dark season, and who might need to hear it from you now?

A nephew’s report and a soldier’s caution kept Paul alive (vv. 16–24), and neither may ever have known what came of it. Where might God be placing you to protect or help someone in a small way, and what keeps you from acting?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s first trial before a Roman governor shows the gospel to be innocent and the man who judges it to be the one in danger. Tertullus flatters Felix and brings four charges, and the delegation adds only agreement (vv. 1–9). Paul answers each charge with facts anyone could check, confesses his faith in the God of his fathers and the resurrection of the just and the unjust, and reduces the case to that one hope (vv. 10–21). Felix, who knows the Way, adjourns without a verdict (vv. 22–23). In private Paul reasons with him about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and the governor, alarmed, puts him off (vv. 24–25). Hoping for a bribe, Felix keeps Paul two years and leaves him in prison (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is one of the most sobering figures in Acts because nothing about him is dramatic. He understands the gospel accurately (v. 22), sends for the preacher often (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him. Yet, as far as Scripture records, nothing stands between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground (Hebrews 3:15; 2 Corinthians 6:2; see the note on vv. 24–25), and hearing the gospel again and again without obeying it hardens the heart (see vv. 26–27).

So conviction is not conversion: a frightened conscience saves nobody (on what to do with conviction, see the note on vv. 24–25). Grace is sovereign and free: no one comes unless the Father draws him, and whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44).

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast between them is the point of the chapter. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and cheerful (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asked by the man who could have freed him to speak about faith in Christ Jesus, Paul chose righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, each aimed at the governor’s own life (see vv. 24–25). He did not soften any of the three.

Now: Most of us will have something true to say to someone who holds an advantage over us. The pressure is not usually to lie but to select: to say the two things that will land well, leave out the third, and call it tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and why it is always the same one. Love tells the truth about sin and judgment, and then tells of the Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest’s hired advocate opens the case by thanking the governor for a peace Felix never gave.

After five days. Caesarea, sixty miles from Jerusalem, was a Gentile city with a temple to Augustus on the hill. The high priest goes anyway, with elders and a hired professional. The man who a week ago ordered Paul struck (23:2) now stands in a Roman hall as a plaintiff, where his office counts for nothing. Tertullus may have been a Greek-speaking Jew, or a Roman.

Much peace. Tertullus begins, as every trained speaker did, with flattery to win the judge’s goodwill before a single fact is mentioned, and it is mostly false. Felix had governed Judea for about five years, and the province had rarely been less peaceful. He crucified rebels in numbers, and his rule provoked more unrest than it ended. Josephus records that he arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, who had been urging him to govern better. So the high priest of Israel listens while his paid advocate thanks a murderer for the peace. But God searches the heart and tries the mind (Jeremiah 17:10), and no smooth word has ever bought his favour.

The things that make for peace. Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41–42), and he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20).
