Now the high priest of that city pays a man to praise Felix for a tranquillity that never existed, while the prisoner in the dock carries the only peace Jerusalem was ever offered. That God cannot be flattered terrifies the flatterer and is the best news in the world to the sinner, because the God who cannot be bought has given freely what no one could pay for. We come with nothing, and he receives us for the sake of his Son, in whose mouth was no deceit.

Why is flattery so dangerous? Because it is not a compliment but a transaction: the flatterer wants something and judges that you will pay for it in goodwill. Felix took the payment, letting a delegation from a nation he had bled thank him for their tranquillity. Scripture warns that a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28) and that a man who flatters his neighbour spreads a net for his feet (Proverbs 29:5). The deeper danger is to the one who swallows it: every time we accept praise we know is false, we lose a little of our ability to hear the truth from anybody, including God. So give honest encouragement freely, but be suspicious of praise that is useful to the giver, and most suspicious of the praise you most enjoy.
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flattery ends with a promise to be brief: this second attack on Paul, unlike the first, is entirely respectable.

To detain you no further. The standard promise of brevity. Kindness here means clemency, the quality of a judge who does not press the law to its harshest edge.

Respectable persecution. The forty men under an oath failed. This attempt has a lawful summons, a professional advocate, correct procedure and courteous language. The assassins could not lay a finger on him; the lawyers very nearly did. Persecution rarely arrives dressed as persecution; it comes as a correctly worded complaint, with everyone behaving well. And Luke lets the other side’s best speaker go first, uninterrupted. A book nervous about its case seldom does that.

We and I. Tertullus says “we” throughout: “we accept this”, “hear us briefly”, “we have found this man”, the professional pretence of a speaker who has known the case for days. Paul will say “I”: “I went up to worship”, “I always take pains”, “this I confess”. He has no delegation behind him and no advocate beside him. Faithfulness usually has to be done in the first person singular, by someone standing up alone.

He stood alone for us. The Lord Jesus stood alone, with no advocate, while his friends fled. And because he stood alone for us, we never stand alone again. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who pleads for his people in the highest court of all and has never lost a case.

What should I do when I have to stand alone for Christ? Remember that you are not as alone as it feels. Paul had no advocate in that hall, but he had the Lord’s word from the barracks (23:11), and he would later write that at his first defence no one stood by him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). When you are the only one at work, at home or in class who will speak for Christ or refuse to join in wrong, speak calmly, speak for yourself, and do not pretend to a crowd you do not have. Then tell your church, ask for prayer, and let others stand with you next time.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four charges, each built to alarm a Roman judge: Paul is a public menace, an agitator across the empire, the leader of an unlicensed sect, and a would-be desecrator of the temple.

A plague. First, the man himself: not troublesome but a disease, something to be stamped out rather than answered. Before you can do something terrible to a man, you have to stop describing him as one. Luke’s reader has heard this opening before. At the trial of Jesus the council told Pilate, “We found this man misleading our nation” (Luke 23:2), and the servant is now charged in the words once used against his Master.

Stirs up riots. Second, sedition, the most serious accusation before a Roman governor. It attaches a false cause to a true fact. Riots really did follow Paul, from Pisidian Antioch to the temple days ago, so Tertullus concludes that Paul makes them. Did the preacher start the fire, or only switch on a light that showed what was there? That is exactly the question the charge is built to skip.

A ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Third, the sect. Ringleader means the man in the front rank of soldiers. Sect means a party, like the Pharisees (15:5); here it suggests an unlicensed splinter group. Nazarenes, a Jewish name for Christians still used in Hebrew and Arabic, appears only here in the New Testament, and it is meant as a sneer (compare 22:8).

He even tried to profane the temple. Fourth, the religious charge, and false (21:28–29). It was the one charge that could bring death under both Jewish and Roman law, since Rome allowed the Jews to execute even a Roman citizen for defiling the temple. It has quietly shrunk: in the temple they said he had defiled it (21:28); here he only “tried”. And “we seized him” is a polite description of trying to kill him.

The name heaven answers to. The sneer tells the truth, and no one in that hall knew it. The risen Lord called himself “Jesus of Nazareth” from a light that outshone the noon sun (22:8), and Pilate fixed the name above his cross as a taunt (John 19:19). Men use it as an insult; he wears it as a name. The Lord of glory chose the despised village, manger and cross, so that no one could boast before him (1 Corinthians 1:28–29). Every insult thrown at his name only shows how low he stooped to save us.

What should I do when Christians are called a danger to society? First check whether there is any truth in it, and repent where there is: Christians have sometimes deserved criticism. Then answer calmly, with facts, as Paul does, and keep your conduct honourable, so that accusers may see your good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). The gospel does disturb things: a quiet town gets loud when the light is turned on, because sin does not like to be seen. That is not the same as causing a riot. Do not be ashamed of disturbing darkness; be ashamed only of disturbing it unlovingly.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add, at the end of verse 6 and in verses 7–8, that they would have judged him by their own law, but Lysias took him away with violence. It is probably a later addition: the earliest and best Greek manuscripts lack it, and it looks like a scribe’s attempt to explain how Paul came to be in Roman custody, shifting the blame onto Lysias. It has Tertullus complain that Lysias snatched Paul out of their hands with great violence, when those hands were at that moment beating him and seeking to kill him (21:31–32). A scribe’s tidying accidentally records the prosecution’s view of a rescue: how dare the Romans stop us.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having charges but no witnesses, Tertullus invites the judge to find the evidence himself by questioning the prisoner.

By examining him yourself. The shrewdest sentence in the speech. Roman law required evidence, and when the evidence is thin an advocate hands the work to the judge. It sounds like confidence and is the opposite. His advice was taken: Felix examined Paul often, over two years (v. 26). What he found was not sedition but a sermon on righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and it frightened him into ending the interview.

A verse with no number. In an ESV the text runs from verse 6 to verse 8. Verse numbers are not part of Scripture; they were added in 1551 by the printer Robert Estienne, working from a Greek text based on late manuscripts. Far older copies found since lack the words of verse 7, and translators follow them but keep the old numbering; the KJV and NKJV still print the words. You meet the same thing at 8:37 and 15:34, and will again at 28:29.

The Judge who examines his people. The one who examines all hearts is not like Felix. When he examines his people, he finds them clothed in the righteousness of his Son, and nothing is left on the charge sheet.

Words that will not pass away. Behind the patient work of copyists stands the Lord’s promise that his words will not pass away (Luke 21:33). They reach us through thousands of hands, some careless and a few meddling, and the word still comes through. The church’s care does not keep it; the Lord keeps it, and the church’s care is one of the means he uses.

Does this mean the Bible is unreliable? No, it shows the opposite. We can see where a line entered the text precisely because we have thousands of manuscripts, from many centuries and countries, more than for any other ancient book, and scholars can lay them side by side. Nothing in the Christian faith depends on any of these few disputed lines. And the translators print them in a footnote in your own Bible. A book with something to hide does not publish its own variants for the ordinary reader to check.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delegation adds nothing but agreement: none of them saw anything, and consensus is offered in place of evidence.

The Jews also joined in the charge. Luke’s word means piling on: a crowd rather than a witness list.

Consensus is not evidence. A courtroom insists on the difference; ordinary life rarely does. As far as we know, none of these men was in the temple court when Paul was seized. The Jews from Asia who started the riot are not in the room, and Paul is about to say so (v. 19). Agreement feels like confirmation, when often it only means everyone heard it from the same place. Nor is sincerity innocence. Most of these men probably believe every word, taken from a source they never checked. A man can be entirely honest and entirely wrong, and do great damage while behaving well throughout. Paul knew that better than anyone in the room.

A chorus he once faced. When Jesus stood before the council, many bore false witness against him, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56); in the end he was condemned on his own confession that he was the Christ. He stood silent before the chorus and was condemned, so that Satan, the true accuser of our souls, whose charges against us were not false, would have nothing left to say. His servant now meets the same chorus, and the same Lord stands with him.

How do I avoid joining in when everyone around me agrees about someone? Ask the courtroom question: who actually saw it, and where are they? If the answer is nobody, or someone who is not here, you do not know it, however many people are nodding. Refuse to add your voice to a charge you cannot verify. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and it refuses to multiply rumours. Where there is a real concern, go to the person, or to those with proper responsibility, not to the crowd (Matthew 18:15–17). And if you find you have joined in unfairly, put it right with the person you wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers cheerfully, with one true courtesy and no flattery, and begins with a fact the court can check: he came to Jerusalem only twelve days ago, and he came to worship.

For many years you have been a judge. Felix had been in office five or six years. Paul’s one sentence of courtesy is true and relevant: he is glad to answer to someone who knows Jewish affairs and can weigh a Jewish religious dispute. There is a way to address a powerful and corrupt man that neither grovels nor postures, and it consists mostly of refusing to say anything untrue.

Not more than twelve days. Paul starts with arithmetic, because arithmetic can be verified. Against a charge of worldwide sedition, he has been in the country a week and a half, and the governor’s own staff can confirm every day of it. And he came “to worship”: not to organise or agitate, but to keep a feast and bring gifts to the poor.

In the flow. This is the first of three defences before Roman rulers (25:8; 26:1–29). It answers each charge in turn, sedition (vv. 11–13), the sect (vv. 14–16) and the temple (vv. 17–19), and then brings the whole case down to the resurrection (vv. 20–21).

Cheerfully. In good spirits, with a settled heart. He has been beaten, chained, nearly flogged and targeted by a murder plot, and has just been called a plague. That cheerfulness is not temperament. The Lord had stood by him in the dark and said “Take courage” (23:11), and a man who knows his Lord’s promise stands can be cheerful in a courtroom, because the courtroom does not decide what becomes of him. The judges of the earth sit by the Lord’s permission. He does not need his servants to win their cases, only to be faithful, and he will see to the rest.

How should I answer someone who attacks my faith? Like Paul: calmly and factually, with gentleness and respect, keeping a good conscience (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not flatter your opponent and do not sneer at him. Begin, where you can, with something true you can honestly acknowledge. Then answer the actual charge, not a different one, with facts that can be checked. If you cannot answer everything, say you will think about it. The outcome does not rest on your performance; your Lord has his own purposes for the conversation, and you are free to be cheerful in it.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul denies stirring up trouble anywhere, and points out that his accusers cannot prove a word of it.

In the temple and in the synagogues. Paul answers the sedition charge with a list of places, every place where an agitator would have had to be seen agitating: let them produce one person who saw it. The list has an echo. Questioned by the high priest on the night of his arrest, Jesus said he had spoken openly to the world, had always taught in synagogues and in the temple, had said nothing in secret, and that his hearers could be asked (John 18:20–21). An officer struck him for it. The faith that follows Jesus has nothing to whisper in a corner, because its Lord never did.

Neither can they prove. Everything rests on this. Under Roman law the burden of proof lay on the accusers, and an accuser who could not sustain his charge might himself be liable. Paul is not asking for mercy; he is pointing at an empty table and asking the court to notice that nothing has been put on it. His Lord had stood where nothing could be proved against him either, and yet he was condemned, because he had come to bear charges that were true, ours, and to answer for them in full.

A faith that asks to be examined. Christianity has never asked to be exempted from the question of evidence. It is a set of claims about things that happened in public: a man executed under a named governor, a tomb found empty, witnesses who could be questioned and were. Paul wrote, within about twenty-five years of the events, that most of the five hundred who saw the risen Lord were still alive and could be asked (1 Corinthians 15:6).

Can a Christian always demand proof when accused? Only if he is innocent. Paul can say prove it because there is nothing to find. A Christian accused of something he has actually done may not hide behind procedure, and a church may not hide wrongdoing, especially abuse, behind lawyers, silence or a concern for reputation. The church has sometimes done exactly that and brought the name of Christ into disgrace. The right to say prove it belongs only to the one who could survive the investigation. If you are guilty, the Christian path is confession, repentance and making things right (Proverbs 28:13), not a clever defence.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul confesses what he is: a worshipper of Israel’s God who believes all the Law and the Prophets and hopes, with Israel, that God will raise the dead, both the just and the unjust.

This I confess. Here the defence becomes testimony. Confess is the word the New Testament uses for openly acknowledging Christ before men. The Way is Luke’s name for the Christian faith (9:2; 19:9, 23): not a club or a theory but a road to walk, because Jesus himself is the way to the Father (John 14:6). It is not a new religion but the fulfilment of the old. In front of Israel’s high priest, Paul tells a Roman court that the man in chains is the one worshipping Israel’s God rightly.

Believing everything. This answers the rumour that started the trouble in chapter 21, that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. He believes more of the book than his accusers, not less; the difference is that he has seen its promises come true in Jesus. He reads it as the risen Jesus taught his disciples to, finding in Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The Law and the Prophets have not been discarded; their promises have been kept.

Which these men themselves accept. The Pharisees among them did, at least. Paul grants that his accusers believe rightly here, when he could have scored a point against them.

Both the just and the unjust. Then the phrase nobody asked for, the only place in Acts where Paul spells out that the resurrection is not only for the righteous. It is Daniel’s vision (Daniel 12:2) and the Lord’s own teaching: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). Why say it to a governor who has asked nothing about the last things? Perhaps because Felix is listening. A few verses later Paul will reason with him in private about the coming judgment, and Felix will be afraid. Words spoken in open court do their work later, in the conscience.

The God of the empty tomb. The God of the fathers had not grown tired of his promise in two thousand years. He spoke to Abraham about a family and to Daniel about the dust waking, and he kept every word at a grave outside Jerusalem that could not hold the one laid in it. The hope of Israel and the risen Christ are not two things, and no court in the world has jurisdiction over either.

What will the resurrection body be like? For believers, Scripture says it will be our own body, raised and transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, and fitted for the life of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), like Christ’s glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The risen Jesus could be touched, ate fish and still bore his wounds, so our future is not a ghostly existence but real, bodily life in a renewed creation. Until then, believers who die are with the Lord, conscious and at rest (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The unjust will also be raised bodily, to stand before God. So the question is never whether you will rise, but what you will rise to.

Where Christians differ. On the resurrection of the unjust, some teach that the wicked will simply cease to exist (annihilationism), or will never be raised. Some sincere evangelicals hold annihilationism, reading Scripture’s language of destruction as a final ending.

This commentary’s view. Paul says both the just and the unjust will rise, and Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life (Matthew 25:46; John 5:29). The wicked are raised to stand before God and face conscious, eternal judgment. This is the historic Christian teaching, sobering and true. Eternal punishment, set beside eternal life in the same sentence, tells against annihilationism, but we differ from those who hold it as brothers.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the dead will rise to judgment, Paul keeps his conscience clear before God and people, and he came to Jerusalem with gifts for the poor and offerings for God, not trouble.

So I always take pains. So: because of the coming resurrection and judgment, and Paul knew whose judgment it is: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). Take pains is the athlete’s word: a clear conscience is not a temperament but a practice, built daily by keeping the accounts short. He says “toward both God and man” because people try to put things right with God while leaving a wrong against a person unsettled. It is the claim that got him struck on the mouth (23:1), and the quiet foundation of his defence: he can invite investigation because he has spent more than twenty years making sure there would be nothing to find.

A clear conscience. Not sinlessness: he called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). It means nothing is left buried: every sin brought to God is washed in the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14), and every wrong done to a person is put right as far as it can be.

Alms to my nation. The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28), money carried across the empire by Gentile Christians to show that the church was one body and not two. This is the only time Acts mentions it. He came with gifts, not trouble, and was arrested in the act of worship, not of agitation, which is the point of the next verse (on “offerings”, see “Uncertain wording” below).

Half a line. For Paul the collection was years of letters and personal risk (2 Corinthians 8–9); for Luke it is half a sentence. Much of the work that costs a Christian most is recorded nowhere, and known in full only to God, who keeps the record of cups of cold water and widows’ mites. There is a bitter irony too: the mention of alms in open court may have planted a thought in Felix’s head, for near the end of the chapter we learn that he hoped money would be given him by Paul (v. 26).

He gave more than alms. The Lord is not unjust so as to overlook our work and the love we have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). And he gave more than alms: he gave himself. The Lord Jesus, rich beyond all counting, made himself poor for our sake so that his poverty might make us rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and Paul set that truth at the heart of his appeal for this very collection.

How do I keep short accounts with God and others? At the end of each day, ask the Lord to show you where you have sinned, and confess it specifically, not vaguely (1 John 1:9). Then ask whether anyone needs an apology or a repair from you, and do it soon, before it hardens; Jesus said to be reconciled to your brother first, then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24). Pay what you owe. Return what you borrowed. Correct what you said that was untrue. None of this earns God’s forgiveness, which is free in Christ. It is how a forgiven person lives, and it keeps the conscience tender instead of calloused.

Uncertain wording. It is not quite clear what Paul means by “to present offerings”. The word can mean sacrifices or gifts in general. Most take it as the temple offerings he was presenting when he was seized, including those that closed the four men’s vows (21:24–26), and the next words, “While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple”, support that. Some read it as the alms again, described a second way. Either way Paul’s point stands: he came to give and to worship.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was found quietly worshipping, ceremonially clean and with no crowd, and the only people who claim to have seen him do wrong have not come to court.

Purified in the temple. Accused of profaning the temple, he was in fact ceremonially clean, in the middle of the rites of purification. Accused of stirring up riots, he had no crowd and no tumult until his accusers created one. He had completed a purification and paid the expenses of four other men’s vows (21:23–24) when men from Asia pointed at him and started shouting.

Some Jews from Asia. The sentence breaks off into the sharpest legal point of the speech. The men who actually saw the alleged offence, who assumed he had brought Trophimus past the barrier and raised the shout (21:27–29), are not in the room. Roman law expected accusers to appear in person, and abandoning a charge you had raised was itself an offence. Paul does not call them liars; if they have a case, let them make it. That is the confidence of a man who would rather be examined than excused.

Let them come and make it. Paul had already put this challenge to a higher court, writing to Rome: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies, and Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). A man who has heard every charge against his soul answered by the death and intercession of Christ can say calmly to a human court: if they have anything against me, let them come.

What if someone has a complaint about me but will not say it to my face? You cannot force them, and you are not bound to answer charges no one will own. But you can make it easy to be honest with you. Let it be known that you welcome direct correction, and when you hear second-hand that someone is unhappy, go to them gently and ask whether you have wronged them (Matthew 5:23–24). If they will not speak, commit the matter to God and keep your conscience clear. And refuse to treat anonymous accusations against others as established, especially in church. Scripture requires charges to be brought openly, on the evidence of witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and a church that acts on whispers will soon be ruled by them.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul dares his accusers to name any crime the council found, and reduces the case to the one thing he is really on trial for: the resurrection of the dead.

What wrongdoing they found. You were at the council a week ago, Paul says; tell the governor what crime you established. It is a safe dare: the council collapsed into a brawl and never reached a finding.

This one thing. This settles the question raised by his cry in the council (23:6): was it only a manoeuvre? A week later, before a single judge who cannot be divided, with nothing to gain by it, he repeats it as the one accurate summary of the case. A trick is used once and dropped; Paul says it again and again (26:6–8; 28:20). So the charge sheet is reduced to one question, theological, not criminal: are the dead raised? Felix knows Paul is right, which is exactly why he gives no verdict. The only crime Paul could be charged with was believing that God raises the dead, and of that he was gloriously guilty. The tomb outside Jerusalem is empty; no court can try that fact, and no power can reverse it.

Why is the resurrection, and not something else, the heart of the matter? Because it is God’s verdict on Jesus. The cross by itself might have been the death of one more good man. The resurrection declares that the man who died was the Son of God (Romans 1:4), that the sacrifice was accepted and our justification secured (Romans 4:25), and that he now reigns as Lord and Judge, for God has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). Justification is God’s verdict that a guilty sinner is right with him, not because of anything in the sinner but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts him. Every other Christian truth rests on the resurrection. That is why the defence of the faith in Acts keeps coming back to the empty tomb, and why yours can too. When you are unsure what to say, say this: Jesus rose from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Felix knows Paul is innocent, but instead of releasing him he adjourns the case indefinitely and avoids a decision.

A rather accurate knowledge of the Way. Felix understood the Christian movement better than the people arguing before him. Perhaps from his Jewish wife, or from Christians in Caesarea, he seems to have known that the Nazarenes were not insurrectionists and that Paul was innocent. And he did nothing.

Put them off. He cannot convict Paul, and releasing him would cost him with the Jewish leaders. So he takes one of the most recognisable ways out in human affairs: he asks for more information. It sounds like diligence. But Lysias never came, as far as we know, and there is no sign that anyone sent for him. The adjournment was not a step toward a verdict but a substitute for one.

Some liberty. A loosening of the conditions. Prisoners relied on friends for food and care, and Luke and others probably visited. The two years were not blank: the God who gave a prisoner his friends, and perhaps Luke the doctor for company, was at work while the governor did nothing.

Another governor who knew. Luke’s reader has met this judge before. Pilate examined Jesus, found no guilt in him and said so, yet when the crowd pressed him he released the man they asked for and delivered Jesus over to their will (Luke 23:22–25). Felix too knows the charges are empty, and leaves Paul in chains to please the same leaders. The servant is treated as his Lord was, by the same kind of man, for the same reason.

The sin that does not look like sin. This is the sin of the chapter. Felix is scrupulously reasonable; he simply declines to act on what he already knows and dresses the refusal in procedure, and because the procedure is real, nobody can accuse him of anything. We are more likely to fail this way than any other: not by deciding against the truth, but by finding a legitimate reason to postpone deciding for it. Felix just never got round to it, on purpose, for two years. Our God has never once put off what he knows to be right: he spoke, and it came to be; he promised, and he performed.

Is it wrong to want more information before making a big decision? No; wisdom often requires it, and Scripture commends hearing before answering (Proverbs 18:13). The question is whether you are gathering information in order to decide, or in order not to. When the facts are clear and you are still asking for more, or the right course is plain and you are still consulting, ask honestly what you are afraid it will cost you. Name that cost before God, and decide. This applies above all to the call of Christ. You do not need one more argument to believe him. You need to stop postponing.

Uncertain wording. “A rather accurate knowledge” renders a Greek comparative, literally “knowing more accurately”, with no comparison stated: more accurately than the accusers allowed, or simply “quite accurately”, as such comparatives often mean. Nor is it certain whether Felix adjourned because he knew the facts, or although he knew them. Either way, he knew enough to see through the charges.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked about faith in Christ, Paul reasons with a corrupt governor and the woman he had taken from her husband about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and Felix, frightened, sends him away.

Drusilla. Luke names her, and the name carries a history. She was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king who killed James with the sword and was struck down in this very city for accepting the shout that he was a god (12:1–23). Her brother was Agrippa II and her sister Bernice, and both will walk into this palace in the next chapter to hear this same prisoner. She was now about twenty. She had been married to Azizus, king of Emesa, and Josephus records that Felix, wanting her, used a Cypriot magician to persuade her to leave her husband and marry the governor instead.

Righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment. They sent for the prisoner perhaps out of curiosity, and few sermons in Acts are more precisely aimed. Righteousness, the character God requires and the justice a judge is meant to give: preached to a corrupt governor who was hoping the defendant would offer him a bribe (v. 26). Self-control, mastery of one’s appetites: preached to a couple in an adulterous marriage, the woman he had taken from another man sitting at his side. The coming judgment: preached to a man who judged others and had never seriously considered being judged. Paul preaches to Felix’s life, not just his mind.

Felix was alarmed. Filled with fear: not irritation or intellectual disagreement. No sign was given. A prisoner talked, and the word of God found the conscience of a man who had buried it, and he could not sit still under it. This is the work Jesus said the Spirit would do in the world, convicting it concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8), and Paul’s three subjects closely match the Lord’s three words.

Go away for the present. A convenient time, as older translations put it: few words spoken to the gospel are more dangerous. He was genuinely under conviction, and he postponed, and as far as Scripture records, the convenient time never came. The Bible’s word is always now: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:15); now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Faith in Christ Jesus, preached as judgment. Felix asked about faith in Christ Jesus, and Paul answered with righteousness, self-control and judgment. That is not a change of subject, for each leads to Christ. The righteousness God requires is found in no governor and no prisoner, only in Christ, whose righteousness is given to those who believe (Philippians 3:9). Self-control is beyond a slave of appetite until the Son sets him free. And the judgment belongs to Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22). The prisoner was telling Felix the name of his Judge, and offering him that Judge as his Saviour. Faith in Christ is more than knowing about him, which Felix already did (v. 22). It is trusting him, leaning your whole weight on him for pardon, as a drowning man takes hold of the rope thrown to him.

The Judge who bore the sentence. What frightened Felix was the holy God behind the prisoner’s words. Paul could preach judgment without fear, because the judgment to come holds no terror for those in Christ. The Judge has already borne the sentence for his people: the wrath Felix trembled at fell on the Son of God, so that all who trust him will stand on that day without condemnation.

Why did Paul begin with judgment, not with good news? It is how the New Testament habitually begins with the comfortable and the powerful: with God’s standard, our failure to meet it, and the day it will be assessed. There is no good news in a pardon until there is bad news in a verdict; a man who does not know he is condemned will not value a Saviour. That does not mean every conversation must start with hell; Paul began differently in Athens (17:22–31). It means the gospel always includes the truth about sin and judgment, and loving people means telling them, gently and plainly, before it is too late.

Is it not manipulative to frighten people with judgment? Only if the judgment were invented to control them. Paul gains nothing by frightening Felix; he is the one in chains, and his honesty will cost him two more years of them. A watchman who blows the trumpet when he sees the sword coming is not manipulating the city; he would be guilty if he kept quiet (Ezekiel 33:6). Fear of a real danger is the right response to it, and Jesus warned his friends plainly whom to fear (Luke 12:4–5). What would be manipulative is to frighten people and then sell them something. Paul offered Felix nothing to buy. He pointed him to a Saviour who gives himself freely to anyone who comes.

Why does self-control sound like a cage? We hear it as repression. Yet our culture is not short of control; it has simply handed it to someone else. Neil Postman, in Amusing Ourselves to Death, set two warnings side by side: George Orwell feared we would be ruined by what we hate, and Aldous Huxley that we would be ruined by what we love. Huxley has proved the better prophet. Whole industries now compete for our appetites, and most of us can feel them winning. Felix is the picture: the most powerful man in the province, and the one man in the room who could not govern himself, unable to say no to another man’s wife or to the hope of a bribe. The moralist’s answer is more willpower, and the libertine’s is surrender; both leave the self on the throne, and both lose. Paul offered Felix something else: a Lord to rule him who would first give himself for him, and a Spirit whose fruit, not whose effort, is self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

What should I do if I feel convicted but not ready? Do not wait to feel ready; you never will. Conviction is God’s mercy, the Spirit showing you your need of Christ, and it is meant to drive you to him now, not to be managed until it fades. You do not have to understand everything or fix your life first. Come to Christ as you are: confess your sin to him, ask him to forgive you for his death’s sake, and trust his promise that he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37). Then take the next step he shows you: talk to a pastor or a Christian friend, open the Bible, begin to obey. The only wrong response is Felix’s: later.
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Felix keeps Paul two years, hoping for a bribe, and leaves him in prison to please the Jewish leaders; yet not one day of the delay was outside God’s hand.

He hoped that money would be given him. Luke gives the real reason, and it is squalid. Taking bribes for releasing prisoners was illegal but common, and Felix had heard Paul mention that he had come bringing alms for his nation (v. 17); perhaps he thought Paul had wealthy friends. Paul never paid, though a payment would have been easy, arguably even reasonable, with two years of his life on the other side of the scale. There are things a servant of Christ cannot buy his way out of without ceasing to be one.

He sent for him often. Many conversations, no conversion. Felix heard the gospel repeatedly, over two years, from one of its ablest explainers, and it did him no good, because he was listening not for the answer but for the offer of a bribe. Hearing without heeding hardens. He kept coming back, interested, curious, even entertained, and each conversation left him a little less able to feel the fear he had felt the first time. It is possible to attend church for forty years the way Felix attended these conversations.

When two years had elapsed. Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in office about two years later. Felix was recalled to Rome after violent clashes in Caesarea between Jews and Gentiles, which he had put down brutally. Luke gives the two years a single clause: after the promise of Rome (23:11), no trial, no verdict and no release. One of the most fruitful missionaries in history, with churches round the Aegean needing him and a promise from the Lord in his pocket, sat in a provincial palace while a corrupt official waited for a payment that never came.

Felix left Paul in prison. On his way out of office, with no case to answer, he kept an innocent man in custody one last time, as a parting gift to people he had spent years mistreating. It did not work. Josephus records that the Jewish leaders of Caesarea went to Rome to accuse him anyway, and that he escaped punishment only through the influence of his brother Pallas at court. He sold his integrity and did not even get the price.

Never in a hurry and never late. Our God is never in a hurry and never late. He let Joseph sit in an Egyptian prison for years, forgotten by the cupbearer, until the day he was raised to save his family. He let his Son lie in the tomb until the third day, not a moment longer. Every hour of Paul’s two years was in his hand, and so is every hour of ours, and at the end of the waiting there is always a ship, and Rome, and the face of Christ.

Can I have heard the gospel too many times? You can have heard it many times without obeying it, and that is a dangerous place to be, because the heart grows used to what it resists (Hebrews 3:13). But as long as you still care about the question, the door is open. The cure for familiarity is not to stop listening but to start obeying: to ask, each time, what God is telling you to do, and then do it. If you have grown up hearing the gospel and it has never moved you, pray honestly for a new heart, which God alone can give (Ezekiel 36:26). He delights to answer that prayer.

Why does God let his people wait so long? These two years are in the Bible for everyone who has been given a word from God and then a long stretch of nothing. Paul did not know he had two years; he only knew he had today. Yet the promise had not weakened by a syllable. Delay is not decay. God is not slower than his word (2 Peter 3:9), and a promise apparently idle is not going stale; it is carried by someone who does not need to hurry and never forgets. What looked from the cell like silence was the Lord of history arranging a governor’s recall, a successor’s ambition, an appeal to Caesar, and a ship. Nor were the years wasted: perhaps Luke wrote his Gospel; certainly Paul prayed; and God was keeping him safe for Rome.
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
24.overview:
Where we are. Rescued from a murder plot, Paul has been sent under guard to Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, with the tribune’s letter finding no charge deserving death or imprisonment (23:12–35). The Lord has promised that he will testify in Rome (23:11). Now comes his first trial before a Roman governor.

The message. The gospel is put on trial and found innocent, and then it puts its judge on trial. The charges against Paul collapse, because his only real offence is believing that God will raise the dead and judge the world. The danger in the room is not to the prisoner but to the governor who hears the truth, is shaken by it, and puts it off. God is never late; a sinner can be.

Why it was said. Luke writes for readers like Theophilus, who needed to know whether the Christian faith was a threat to Roman order (see the introduction). Here a governor who knows the Way well finds no crime, yet keeps Paul for two years: the delay is the doing of a corrupt man, while God keeps his promise in his own time.

How the chapter makes its case. The high priest’s hired advocate flatters Felix and brings four charges: Paul is a plague, a stirrer of riots, a ringleader of the Nazarenes and a would-be profaner of the temple (vv. 1–9). Paul answers each with checkable facts and reduces the case to the hope of the resurrection (vv. 10–21). Felix, who knows the truth, adjourns without a verdict (vv. 22–23). In private Paul reasons with him and Drusilla about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and the governor, alarmed, sends him away (vv. 24–25). Hoping for a bribe, Felix keeps Paul two years and leaves him in prison to please the Jewish leaders (vv. 26–27).

Where it leads. Paul’s trial follows his Lord’s: an accusation that opens “we found this man”, a chorus of unproved charges, a governor who knows the prisoner is innocent and acts to please the accusers. But Jesus was condemned though innocent, bearing charges that were true of us, and he is the Judge of whom Paul spoke. The judgment that frightened Felix belongs to Christ, and the man in chains was offering the governor his Judge as his Saviour.

For us. Felix did not reject Christ in one dramatic moment; he kept saying “later”. If the Spirit is pressing the truth on you, come to Christ now, as you are. And if, like Paul, you are waiting long on a promise of God, take courage: delay is not decay, and every day of it is in his hands.

keyVerse.quote: And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.”
keyVerse.note: Here the chapter turns from Paul’s trial to Felix’s. A governor who knew the Way well heard the gospel aimed at his own life, felt its force, and chose delay, and as far as Scripture records the convenient time never came. The verse sets the same choice before every reader, while the Judge Paul preached is still offered as Saviour.

24.reflection:
Tertullus flatters Felix, while Paul offers one true courtesy and no more (vv. 2–4, 10). Where are you most tempted to flatter, or to enjoy being flattered, and what would honest respect look like there?

Paul could invite investigation because he took pains to keep a clear conscience toward both God and man (vv. 12–13, 16). Is there a wrong, toward God or toward a person, that you have left unsettled? What would putting it right involve this week?

Felix was alarmed by the truth and said, “Go away for the present” (v. 25). What “convenient times” do people tell themselves they are waiting for before they obey Christ, and why is postponing so attractive?

Paul spent two years in prison with the Lord’s promise of Rome apparently on hold (23:11; 24:27). How does it help you in a season of waiting to know that God is never late, and what might faithfulness look like in your own “two years”?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord’s promise of Rome is kept through the very men who are trying to prevent it. The chief priests renew their old ambush plot with a new governor, and Festus, guarding his own jurisdiction, bypasses it without knowing (vv. 1–5). The charges are many and unproven, and Paul answers in one sentence (vv. 6–8). When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus must grant it (vv. 9–12). Then King Agrippa arrives, and as Festus tells him the case the real issue comes out: a dispute about “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive” (vv. 13–21). The king asks to hear Paul himself (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

May a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had the risen Christ’s promise that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a lawful right to get there (see the note on vv. 11–12). Providence employs means, even unspiritual ones: a citizenship register, a governor’s ambition, a form to fill in.

Two cautions. That the means are lawful does not make the motives of those who supply them good: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did. And God’s certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime, and Paul stays in chains. Both are true.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment: a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.

Now: Anyone long in a pew can state the resurrection as accurately as Festus did (see the note on vv. 18–19). Say the sentence out loud, a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive, and if nothing moves, go to the living Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new governor arrives, and Paul’s old enemies are waiting for him; but the Lord who promised Rome has not lost sight of his prisoner either. Through every powerful man in this chapter, the risen Christ is moving his servant exactly where he said he would.

Three days. Paul has been in custody at Caesarea for two years (24:27). Felix has been recalled, and Porcius Festus has arrived, around AD 59. Within three days the new governor is on the road to Jerusalem, which suggests he had been told how close to revolt the province already was. He would die in office about two years later, and within about seven years the province would be in open revolt against Rome. He goes to introduce himself to the people who can make his term ungovernable, and they are ready for him.

Laid out their case against Paul. Two years have passed since the riot in the temple and the forty men’s oath. Governors and high priests have changed. And Paul is still the first item on the agenda: not one of several matters raised with the new governor, but the thing they came to say. The verb for what they do next, urged, means to press with insistence. They are lobbying on day three, before the man has unpacked.

The chief priests. Not quite the same as the high priest. The high priest was the one supreme religious officer of Israel, who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. The chief priests were the priestly aristocracy around him: the serving high priest, former high priests (who kept the title and influence after Rome deposed them, which is why Annas is still called high priest in Luke 3:2), the heads of the few wealthy families from whom high priests were chosen, and senior temple officers such as the captain of the temple and the treasurers. Mostly Sadducees (5:17), this ruling class appears again and again in the Gospels and Acts as the ringleaders against Jesus and his apostles.

Two years from two sides. For Paul, two years of nothing whatever happening; for his enemies, two years of unbroken attention. Hatred keeps long accounts; a grudge will run for years on nothing at all. But the Lord keeps longer accounts, and his are accounts of love. For two years the men in Jerusalem never lost sight of Paul, and for two years the Lord never lost sight of him either. The prisoner whom the chief priests remembered with malice was remembered by the risen Christ with a purpose, and the purpose was Rome.

The establishment that pressed Pilate. Nearly thirty years before, this same priestly establishment had stood before another Roman governor and pressed him about another prisoner, until their voices prevailed and Pilate granted their demand (Luke 23:23–24). The Lord had warned his disciples that if they persecuted him, they would persecute them too (John 15:20), and on the Damascus road he said that to strike his people was to strike him (9:4). So the lobbying of Festus is the old campaign against Jesus of Nazareth, still running against the man who preaches him alive. The first campaign ended at an empty tomb.

In everyday life. Is there anyone you have been carrying a grievance against for years, simply keeping it current? Bring it by name to the God who has forgiven you far more, and begin to pray for that person’s good.

Why was Paul left in prison for two years if he was innocent? Because Felix wanted money from him and favour from the Jewish leaders (24:26–27), and an untried prisoner cost him nothing. It was a real injustice, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. But the two years were not empty. Paul’s friends were allowed to visit and care for him (24:23), and it may well be that Luke, who seems to have been nearby, used the time to gather the eyewitness accounts behind his Gospel (Luke 1:1–4). God’s delays are never wasted time, even when they are someone else’s sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind a polite request lies a murder plot: two years on, the same men try the same ambush on a new governor.

Asking as a favor. A favour, a kindness (charis): the word for the grace of God, used here as the ordinary currency of Roman public life. You do this for me now, and I am in your debt. They invite the new governor to begin his term by doing them a kindness, which they will then owe him for.

An ambush. Luke cuts in with the truth in a subordinate clause. On its face the request is reasonable, and Festus cannot see what lies behind it; we can. Two years earlier the forty men asked for exactly this: a transfer to Jerusalem, with an ambush on the road (23:12–16). Two years of failure have produced not a rethink, only a fresh attempt on a fresh governor.

Respectable men. The men who wanted Paul dead were not monsters. They were religious, respected men, who over two years quietly kept a murder on the agenda and learned to think of it as the defence of God’s honour. Nobody arrives there in one step, but by a series of small permissions, each granted to yourself on the grounds that the cause is good. The Lord warned his disciples of exactly this: the hour would come when whoever killed them would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2).

An hour not yet come. The same leadership once sought how to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (Mark 14:1), and for a long while they could not, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). When it did come, it came not because the plotters had finally won, but because the Son laid down his life of his own accord, and their plot became the means of the world’s redemption by the definite plan of God (2:23). The ambush cannot succeed while Christ’s promise about Rome is unfulfilled, and when Paul’s own hour comes it will come as his Master’s did: at the appointed time, in the Lord’s hands, not the plotters’.

Does this mean the Jews as a people were against Paul? No. Luke is describing a particular group of leaders, the priestly establishment and those around them, not the Jewish people as a whole. Paul himself was a Jew, as were Jesus, all the apostles and thousands of believers in Jerusalem (21:20), and he loved his people so much that he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). Christians have sometimes read passages like this as permission for contempt toward Jews, and that is a grievous sin. The lesson is not one nation’s wickedness but what religious people of any nation can become when they decide that their cause justifies anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus says no for his own reasons, and without knowing it he kills the ambush: the Lord protects his servant through an ordinary Roman rule.

Kept at Caesarea. Festus refuses for entirely the wrong reason. He is not protecting Paul, whom he has never met, but his own jurisdiction: a new governor does not begin his term by handing over a prisoner as a personal favour.

Let the men of authority among you go down with me. The offer is fair, and inconvenient: if they want the case heard, they must travel some sixty miles to argue in a Roman hall on Roman terms. And with it the ambush is dead, not discovered but simply bypassed, because the road Paul was to be killed on is now a road he will not travel.

Providence through procedure. A tribune’s fear (22:29), a nephew’s ears (23:16), and now a Roman rule about where a case must be heard: three times Paul’s life has been saved by the most ordinary means. Providence is God’s ceaseless upholding and steering of all he has made, so that nothing happens by mere chance: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord (Proverbs 16:33). He can save by an angel opening a prison or by a governor who prefers his own courtroom, and he is as fully at work in the second as in the first.

A jurisdiction above the governor’s. Festus is defending his jurisdiction with no idea whose jurisdiction he lives under. The risen Christ told his disciples that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to him (Matthew 28:18), and that includes a Roman governor’s authority over a list of cases in Caesarea. Pilate heard the same truth from the prisoner in front of him: he would have had no authority at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). The governor’s rule about venues is a small thread in the hand of the King.

Should I pray for officials who are not Christians? Yes, and this passage shows why. Paul tells Timothy to pray for kings and all who are in high positions, so that believers may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and he wrote that when the emperor was Nero. God uses ordinary, unbelieving officials to restrain evil and protect his people, often without their knowing. Pray by name for your councillors, judges, police and national leaders: that they will be fair, honest and wise, and that they will come to know Christ.

Does providence mean I will always be kept safe? No, and Scripture is honest about it. The providence protecting Paul here is the same providence that did not protect Stephen, or James, whom Herod killed with the sword while Peter walked out of prison past the guards (12:1–11). God’s care is real, and it is not a guarantee of safety. What it guarantees is that nothing will cut short the work he has given you, and that whatever comes will be made to work for your good (Romans 8:28). Paul had been told that his work included Rome, so the road to Jerusalem could not be the end of it. Your times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15), whether long or short, and you are immortal until your work is done.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers pile up serious charges, hoping that their number will make up for their lack of proof.

Eight or ten days. Luke does not pretend to know exactly: the habit of a writer who sets down what he was told, vagueness included.

Stood around him. Luke’s verb means encircling, the way the mob did in the temple court. The setting has changed; the posture has not.

Many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. Many, serious, unproven, as before (24:13). Unable to establish a single count, they bring many, and make each one grave, hoping that twenty unproven things will feel heavier than one. The tactic often works, because we treat volume as evidence; “no smoke without fire” is precisely the error a courtroom exists to prevent. Many reputations are damaged this way: rarely by one provable offence, almost always by an accumulation of unprovable ones, none ever tested. Roman law’s answer is the whole of Paul’s defence: they could not prove it.

Many bore false witness against him. The tactic was used first on the Master (Mark 14:56). The charges failed there too, until the high priest asked him directly whether he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, and he answered, “I am” (Mark 14:61–62). He was condemned in the end for no crime, only for the truth about himself. The servant faces many charges that cannot be proved; his Lord, against whom nothing could be proved, accepted the sentence that the true charges against his people deserved. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?” (Romans 8:33). Rest there, in an innocence that is not your own and cannot be taken from you.

What should I do when someone tells me several bad things about another person? Ask the question Roman law asked: what can actually be shown? Do not let the number of stories stand in for evidence. Ask the speaker whether he has gone to the person himself (Matthew 18:15), and refuse to pass the stories on. If you have a responsibility in the matter, insist on hearing the person accused, face to face, before you form a view; Scripture requires two or three witnesses before a charge is accepted (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19). Many charges cannot make a lie true.

What if I am the one accused of many things I cannot disprove? Do what Paul did. Answer what can be answered, plainly and without bitterness, and leave the rest with God. You cannot chase down every rumour, and trying to will consume you. Keep doing what is right, so that those who speak against you are put to shame by your conduct (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Tell a trusted elder or friend, so that you are not alone with it. And remember that the Lord Jesus, when he was reviled, did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

Textual note. Many later manuscripts read “more than ten days” instead of “not more than eight or ten days”, which is why the King James Version says “more than ten days”. The difference does not affect the story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers every charge, religious and political, in one sentence: he has done nothing against the law, the temple or Caesar. He needs no more words, because nothing new has been alleged.

Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar. It is the shortest defence Paul makes in the whole book, and the brevity is itself an argument. The three headings cover religion and politics alike. The law: the charge that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses, which started the riot in chapter 21 and was never true. The temple: the charge that he brought a Gentile past the barrier, which has been shrinking since it was first shouted. Caesar: nobody had formally raised it today, and Paul names it deliberately. Tertullus had called him a plague who stirred up riots (24:5), and Paul knows that in a Roman court the charge that matters is the political one, so he denies it flatly.

His Master before him. The same three kinds of charges were brought against Jesus, who was said to be misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be a king (Luke 23:2), and against Stephen, who was accused of speaking against the holy place and the law (6:13). The servant is not greater than his master. Paul could stand clear before Festus because Christ had stood condemned before Pilate, bearing the offences of others. Glory to the spotless Lamb, whose innocence is now the robe of every guilty sinner who trusts him.

The shape of a clean answer. Paul does not argue that the charges are unkind, that his accusers are hypocrites, or that he has been badly treated, all of which were true and none of which is relevant. He addresses the actual counts, in the categories the court recognises, and stops. A man with a clear conscience can afford to be brief.

Did Paul still keep the law of Moses as a Christian? He kept it among Jews, freely, for the gospel’s sake, but not as the ground of his acceptance with God. He circumcised Timothy (16:3), took part in a temple vow (21:26) and kept the feasts, becoming as a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). He never taught Jews to abandon their customs. What he denied was that keeping the law could justify anyone (Galatians 2:16), or that Gentile believers had to become Jews to be saved (15:1–11). To justify is to declare a person right with God, and God gives that verdict only on the ground of Christ’s obedience, received by faith. So his denial here is entirely honest: he had broken neither the law nor the temple’s rules, and he had never been disloyal to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus tries to please Paul’s enemies with a harmless-sounding offer, and Paul refuses, respectfully and plainly: he is already in the right court, and the governor knows he is innocent.

Wishing to do the Jews a favor. Luke has used that phrase before. The last governor left office desiring to do the Jews a favour, and left Paul in prison to do it (24:27). Pilate before him, wishing to satisfy the crowd, handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:15). Festus is a better official by any ordinary measure, and within two weeks Luke describes him in the same words. So the problem was never just one lazy governor. A man whose position depends on the goodwill of people who want an innocent man dead will find a way to give them something, and he will not experience it as corruption, but as being reasonable.

Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me? The form is mild. Festus does not order Paul to Jerusalem, which would be indefensible; he asks. “Before me”: it will still be my court, my authority, my verdict. But the change of venue that sounds like a courtesy would put Paul on a road where men are waiting to kill him, and into a city where the Sanhedrin would in effect decide the case. Festus does not know about the ambush, but he does know he is offering to move a prisoner into the reach of people who have demanded him for two years, and he is doing it because it would be convenient. Paul knew what awaited him there.

I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal. Paul’s answer is legally exact, and it closes the door. A governor’s court was not an alternative to Caesar’s authority; it was Caesar’s authority, delegated. Paul is already in the correct court, and moving him to Jerusalem would abandon the very jurisdiction Festus is exercising.

As you yourself know very well. Literally, you know better. Paul tells a Roman governor, in open court, that he knows the truth and is manoeuvring anyway: bold, respectful and plain. Felix too had “a rather accurate knowledge of the Way” (24:22). Two governors knew, and neither did anything with the knowing. The danger is not ignorance but knowledge held without consequence: seeing clearly what is right and finding a way round it, politely, for reasons that sound sensible later.

Christ did not please himself. At Pilate’s judgment seat the favour-seeking of a governor fell on the one man in history who never once courted anyone’s favour at the cost of the truth. “Christ did not please himself,” Paul would write, but the reproaches of those who reproached God fell on him (Romans 15:3). He bore the cost of Pilate’s wish to please, and of every such wish in us, so that people-pleasers could be forgiven and set free to please God. Paul’s calm refusal to be managed is the freedom of a man bought by that Lord. Every earthly judge is under pressure to please someone; the Lord Jesus can be lobbied, flattered or bought by no one. How good it is to stand at last before a Judge who is also the Saviour.

Is it wrong to want to please people? Not in itself. Paul tried to please everyone in everything for the sake of their salvation (1 Corinthians 10:33), and we are told to please our neighbour for his good (Romans 15:2). The sin is pleasing people at the cost of truth or justice, when their approval matters more to us than God’s. Paul’s own test was sharp: if I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The question is never whether others are pleased, but whether, to please them, you are doing what you know to be wrong.

How do I speak truth to someone in authority over me? As Paul did here: respectfully, plainly and briefly. He did not insult Festus, raise his voice or accuse him of corruption; he stated the facts and named what Festus already knew. Give the honour due to the office (1 Peter 2:17), speak to the specific issue, avoid exaggeration, do not threaten, and leave the outcome with God. Courage and courtesy are not opposites; in the mouth of a Christian they belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not run from justice but refuses to be handed over to injustice, and his lawful appeal to Caesar becomes the road by which the Lord’s promise of Rome is kept.

I do not seek to escape death. Before the appeal comes the concession: Paul begins not by claiming his rights but by granting the court’s right to put him to death if the charge stands. Then he points out that no charge has been proved. He is not trying to escape justice but to stop an injustice.

No one can give me up to them. The verb is the verb for granting a favour: no one can make me a present to these men, not even the governor.

I appeal to Caesar. It was one of the oldest and most jealously guarded rights of Roman citizenship: the right to have a case lifted out of a provincial court and heard by the emperor himself. Once made, the appeal could not easily be refused, and the governor could no longer convict or, in practice, release. His remaining duty was to forward the prisoner to Rome with a written statement of the charges. This is why Agrippa will remark that this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:32).

Did Paul make a mistake? No, and the reason is not legal but theological. It was settled two years earlier in a dark barracks in Jerusalem, when the Lord stood by him and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Paul is not gambling. He is holding a promise, and he has just been handed the one legal mechanism in the Roman world that guarantees delivery: to Rome, at the state’s expense, under guard. Paul used his rights wisely, and God used them to send him where Jesus promised.

Which Caesar. Around AD 59 the emperor is Nero, still in the early years that Roman writers themselves regarded as good government, before the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and the persecution that followed, in which, as the early Christian writers report, Paul would die. He goes to Rome under the protection of the man under whose rule, by that same early testimony, he would be put to death.

To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go. The formula is final, and Festus means nothing by it beyond a legal duty. But it is the promise of the risen Christ (23:11) coming back to Paul out of a Roman governor’s mouth, with the full weight of the empire behind it; of the two speakers, only the Lord knows what is happening. The Lord said Rome, and the empire rose up to carry his servant there, with soldiers for an escort and Caesar paying the fare. This is how the Lord usually governs the world: not by miracles that interrupt its ordinary course, but by directing that course. The kings of the earth take counsel together, and their counsel is his instrument (Psalm 2:2–4; Acts 4:27–28).

His Lord made no appeal. Paul appealed to Caesar and lived. His Lord made no appeal and died. On the night he was betrayed he could have asked his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and he asked for nothing, because the Scriptures had to be fulfilled and sinners had to be saved. Because he made no appeal, the guilty may now make theirs, not to Caesar but to the throne of grace, where their sentence has already been borne. Blessed be the Lord who would not save himself, so that he might save us.

Using lawful rights. It is right for a Christian to use his lawful rights, and Paul does so without a flicker of guilt; earlier he invoked his citizenship to stop an illegal flogging (22:25–29) and refused a quiet, hushed-up release (16:37). This does not contradict the command to turn the other cheek, which forbids personal revenge (Matthew 5:39; Romans 12:19), not lawful appeal to the authority God ordained to do justice (Romans 13:4). Paul forgave his persecutors and used the courts; the two sit together. Nor does it clash with his warning in 1 Corinthians 6:1–8, which forbids believers to sue one another before unbelievers; here a believer accused by unbelievers appeals to a Roman court for justice. And lawful protections are a freedom, not always a duty: “Why not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). Use them without bitterness, for justice and not for getting even.

How do I know when to use a right and when to give it up? Ask what will serve the gospel and the good of others, not merely what will protect me. Paul insisted on his rights when silence would have let injustice stand, harmed others or hindered his mission (16:37; 22:25). He laid them down when insisting would have put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). If you are being wronged, and a lawful protection would stop the wrong without revenge, use it. If insisting would damage a brother or your witness for a small personal gain, let it go. When unsure, seek counsel from wise believers.
