Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong, often from a deep concern for mercy and for the risk of executing the innocent. This commentary’s view: Paul here accepts that some crimes deserve death and that the state may impose it, as he teaches in Romans 13:4 (the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain), grounded in Genesis 9:6. The state has the God-given right to punish grave crimes, including with death, though it must do so justly, with due process and certain guilt. Christians may disagree on when it is wise to use it.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king arrives from the family that had opposed Christ for four generations, and the forgotten prisoner is about to stand before him, as the Lord had said he would.

Agrippa the king and Bernice. They came, as client rulers did, to welcome the new governor, and the family name, Herod, would have carried a chill. Herod the Great tried to kill Jesus in the cradle and murdered the infants of Bethlehem to do it (Matthew 2:16). His son Herod Antipas beheaded John the Baptist to save face at a birthday party (Mark 6:26–27), and on the morning of the crucifixion treated Jesus with contempt, dressed him in splendid clothing as a joke, and sent him back (Luke 23:11). Herod Agrippa I killed James with the sword and was struck down for accepting the shout that his voice was a god’s (12:2, 23). Now comes his son, Agrippa II, the last of the line in the New Testament.

The right man to consult. Agrippa ruled territories to the north and east of Galilee, and Rome had given him an unusual set of duties: oversight of the temple, the keeping of the high priest’s vestments, and the right to appoint and depose the high priest himself. He was an expert in Jewish customs and questions (26:3).

Bernice. Bernice is his sister. She had been married to her uncle, was widowed young, and for long periods afterwards lived in her brother’s household, an arrangement that produced a persistent rumour of incest, reported by Josephus and openly mocked in Rome by the satirist Juvenal. She would later become the mistress of Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. Luke names her without comment and lets the reader supply what he knows.

A man left prisoner by Felix. Two years of a Roman citizen held without a verdict, compressed into one dismissive clause. Left, the way you leave a coat behind in a house you have moved out of. Such neglect is not usually malice; one man’s case is rarely anyone else’s priority. Yet at Paul’s conversion the Lord had said he would carry his name before Gentiles and kings (9:15), and the forgotten prisoner is about to stand before a king.

The true King of the Jews. The family’s quarrel was always, at bottom, with one person. Herod the Great slaughtered children because Magi came asking for him who had been born king of the Jews (Matthew 2:2). Each Herod ruled by Rome’s permission, and each was confronted by a King whose throne no emperor gave: the Son to whom God would give the throne of his father David, whose kingdom would have no end (Luke 1:32–33). The child Herod the Great tried to kill now sends his apostle in chains to preach to Herod’s great-grandson. Kings come and go, and dynasties end in a sentence; the Son of David reigns for ever, and his patience with the proud is as astonishing as his power over them.

Near the gospel and far from it. In four generations no Herod did anything with the gospel but try to destroy it, mock it, exploit it or find it interesting. Nearness to the gospel is not the same as receiving it, and it does not build up from one generation to the next. What people lack is not access but willingness, and that is the gift of God: left to ourselves we do not want him, and it is God who makes the unwilling willing, drawing them to his Son (John 6:44) and working in them both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). Parents grieving a wandering child should hear the other half of that truth: because willingness is God’s gift, no son or daughter is beyond his reach, and prayer for them is never wasted.

The forgotten file. When your own situation feels like an oversight rather than a plan, remember that Paul was a line item in a handover briefing, and he was exactly where the Lord had told him he would be.

If my family has no Christian history, am I at a disadvantage? No. Grace does not run in bloodlines, either for blessing or for doom. The Herods show that a family can be near the gospel for generations and never receive it; the rest of Scripture shows that God delights to call people from families with no faith at all, as he called Abraham out of a home of idol worshippers (Joshua 24:2). If you are the first believer in your family, you may be the beginning of a new line. Pray for your relatives by name; God saves whom he wills, and no family is too far from him.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus gives the king a flattering version of his week, but the principle he quotes, that no one may be condemned unheard, is the reason Paul is still alive.

Not the custom of the Romans. Every clause Festus tells Agrippa is true. But he does not mention that the priests asked for a transfer to Jerusalem as a favour (v. 3), and when he comes to his own offer of a Jerusalem trial (v. 20) he presents it as the puzzlement of a man out of his depth. In fact that offer would have handed Paul over to his accusers, against the very principle he is now quoting so proudly. Lysias did the same in his letter, rearranging one clause so that his rescue of Paul looked principled rather than accidental (23:27). Neither man invents a fact, and Luke sets the arrangement beside the events without comment, for a reader who already knows what really happened.

Face to face. Still, the principle Festus cites is magnificent. Roman practice held that a man could not be condemned unheard, and that accuser and accused must stand face to face. Scripture had said it long before: a single witness was not enough, and false witnesses were to be punished (Deuteronomy 19:15–19); even Nicodemus had to remind the Pharisees that the law does not judge a man without first hearing him (John 7:51). The right to face your accuser is still a foundation of a just court.

Rome’s custom and Israel’s law. The men entrusted with the law of God, who knew that a matter is established by two or three witnesses, asked for a sentence of condemnation on a man they had not allowed to speak, asked for it as a favour, and were planning an ambush on the road. The pagan governor said no, because it was not the custom. Rome’s custom was better kept than Israel’s law, not because Rome was righteous but because the men holding the law had stopped letting it govern them. They decided that this once the procedure could be set aside, and became the sort of people a pagan has to restrain.

By oppression and judgment. The principle Festus quotes saved Paul. It did not save Jesus, though he stood before a Roman governor bound by the same custom. Pilate heard him face to face, examined him, declared him innocent, and then delivered him over to their will (Luke 23:22–25). Isaiah had seen it long before: “By oppression and judgment he was taken away” (Isaiah 53:8). Every safeguard gave way in the case of the one truly innocent man, because the Father had purposed that he should bear the condemnation of the guilty. The servant is sheltered today by a rule his Master was denied. The God who commanded that no one be condemned unheard has himself provided that his people will never be condemned at all.

Can unbelievers sometimes act more justly than believers? Yes, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so. God has written the work of his law on every human heart (Romans 2:14–15), and by his common grace unbelievers often see and do what is fair. Abimelech rebuked Abraham for a lie (Genesis 20:9), and here Festus restrains the priests. That should humble the church, not unsettle it. Unbelievers are not saved by their fairness, but Christians have no excuse for being less honest, less just or less fair than the world around them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus is proud of his promptness, and rightly; but speed in procedure did not stop him nearly handing Paul over to please the powerful.

I made no delay. Festus wants the king to notice his efficiency, and he has earned it: Felix left the case for two years, and Festus had it on the tribunal within a fortnight. Competence in office is no small thing; a prompt hearing is a mercy to the man waiting for it.

Speed is not integrity. None of that stopped him doing the one thing that would have killed Paul. He was prompt, correct and as far as we know uncorrupt, and eight verses earlier he asked whether the prisoner would care to be tried in the city where men were waiting to kill him, because it would please the people he had to work with. You can be blameless in every procedure that can be audited and still make the decision that matters on the basis of who you need to keep happy.

Never early and never late. Set beside Festus the one whose timing was always perfect and never self-serving. Jesus told his brothers that his time had not yet come (John 7:6), and he would not be hurried by anyone’s agenda. Then, when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), toward the city where men were waiting to kill him, not to please anyone but to do his Father’s will. Festus was prompt in what gets inspected; Christ was prompt in obedience, and it took him to a cross for us.

How do I know whether my decisions are driven by fear of people? Ask three questions. Would I decide differently if no one important would ever find out? Am I avoiding the right course because of one person’s reaction rather than because it is wrong? Am I describing my choice to myself as sensible, realistic or not worth the trouble, when the honest word would be afraid? “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). Bring the decision to God in prayer, ask what he requires, and do that, however competent the alternative looks.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stripped of its accusations, the whole case comes down to one question, and a bored governor states it exactly: is Jesus, who was dead, alive?

No charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Festus had expected sedition, fraud or violence, the ordinary business of a troublesome province, and the prosecution had nothing. What remained were points of dispute about “their own religion” (see the box below).

A certain Jesus. A Roman governor summarises the entire Christian faith in half a sentence and treats it as a local religious quarrel. The phrase means some Jesus or other, a name you have no reason to remember, and he says it a few days’ journey from the place where Jesus died and rose. The name at which every knee will one day bow is, to Festus, a detail in a quarrel he is trying to get out of.

Who was dead. Nobody in the room, on either side, disputes that Jesus of Nazareth was executed and buried. The death of Christ is common ground between the apostle and the men trying to kill him.

Whom Paul asserted to be alive. The tense matters: Paul kept on asserting it. It was a claim he would not stop making, from Damascus to Rome. And Festus has got it exactly right: Christianity is, at bottom, a dispute about whether a particular dead man is alive. Paul said as much himself to people who claimed the dead are not raised: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Festus, who believed none of it, put his finger on the hinge of history.

Festus is dust. A certain Jesus, who was dead. He was dead: the centurion certified it and the tomb received him. And he is alive, in a body, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, holding the keys of Death and Hades. Festus is dust; Agrippa is dust; Nero is dust. The certain Jesus whose name the governor could not be bothered to learn is on the throne of the universe tonight, and every one of those men will bow the knee at his name. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, and who lives for ever and ever.

Accurate and untouched. So the gospel can be stated accurately by someone completely untouched by it. It never occurred to Festus that if the claim were true, it would concern him personally. Those who have been in church longest might ask whether it has cost them anything or moved anything in them lately. If not, the answer is not to know less but to come to the living Christ himself, who welcomes the long-time churchgoer as freely as the stranger, and who can still make an old truth burn.

How can we be sure Jesus really rose? The evidence is strong, and it begins with the fact this verse records: nobody disputed the death. Jesus was publicly executed by professionals and buried in a known tomb. Within weeks his followers were proclaiming in the same city that the tomb was empty, and his enemies never produced the body, though that would have ended the matter. More than five hundred people saw him alive, many still living when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), and that list is no late legend: Paul wrote it within about twenty-five years, passing on a summary he had himself received, probably within a few years of the events. Frightened disciples became fearless, and men like Paul, an enemy, and James, a sceptical brother, were transformed. Men do not die for what they know to be a lie. No argument compels belief, and honest people weigh this evidence differently; but alongside the evidence, the Spirit himself bears witness through the Word that it is true.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “religion” (deisidaimonia) can mean reverence for the gods or superstition, and which shade Festus intended cannot be known for certain. To a Jewish king he probably meant it neutrally, and the ESV’s “religion” fits that; but a Roman of his class could also hear contempt in it. Paul used a related word at Athens (“very religious”, 17:22), where it is likewise hard to tell how complimentary it is.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of his depth, Festus reached for the course that pleased the powerful; the question he could not investigate is one God has already answered by raising Jesus.

Being at a loss. The word pictures finding no way through. Festus is not being falsely modest: his training does not equip him to judge whether a crucified Galilean is alive.

I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem. He omits that it was to please the Jews (v. 9). Being at a loss, he did not adjourn or take advice; he proposed the one course that would have ended Paul’s life.

The decision of the emperor. The title is the Greek for Augustus, the revered one, with a hint of worship in it, and it meant Nero. Festus reports the appeal as an inconvenience, not knowing he is describing the promise of 23:11 moving one more stage down the road.

The question no tribunal could open. Festus was at a loss because the case had come down to a person, and the question about that person was one no Roman court could settle: is the crucified Jesus alive? God had already answered it. Paul had told the philosophers of Athens that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance of it to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). Festus, puzzling over how to investigate the risen man, is himself the one under investigation. The prisoner’s Lord is the governor’s appointed Judge, and the day is fixed.

Confusion is not neutral. When a man genuinely does not know what to do, he does not stop; he falls back on whatever pressure is strongest in the room. Festus’s bewilderment produced not caution but a proposal that pleased the people he needed. So the test is not whether you know what to do; often you will not. The test is what you reach for when you do not know. Festus reached for the course that would cause him least trouble, and it nearly killed the apostle to the Gentiles.

What should I do when I genuinely do not know what to do? Stop and pray before you act, and ask God for wisdom; he gives it generously to those who ask (James 1:5). Search the Scriptures for any principle that bears on the decision. Seek counsel from wise and godly people, not merely from those who will be pleased by one outcome (Proverbs 15:22). Do the right things you already know, even if the larger picture is unclear. And if your uncertainty keeps landing on the option that pleases the powerful, be suspicious of it. It is often wiser to wait than to reach for the easiest course.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Herod asks to hear Christ’s servant, as another Herod once wished to see Christ himself; and this time God answers curiosity with the gospel.

I would like to hear the man myself. Agrippa had probably heard of Paul for years (see the box below). And a Herod has said this before.

The Herod who wanted to see Jesus. Of Herod Antipas, when reports of Jesus reached the palace, Luke wrote that “he sought to see him” (Luke 9:9). On the morning of the crucifixion he finally got his wish, hoping to see some sign done by him; he questioned him at some length, but Jesus made no answer (Luke 23:8–9). Few silences in the Gospels are more terrible. Herod’s curiosity had had years to turn into faith and never had, and when the moment came there was nothing left to say to him.

Tomorrow you will hear him. Now the last Herod wants the same, and the outcome is different. Paul will preach to this king one of the fullest and most personal defences in the book (chapter 26), close enough, or stinging enough, that the king asks whether Paul thinks he can make him a Christian in so short a time (26:28). That is mercy. Antipas mocked, and got silence; to the merely curious Agrippa God sends one of the finest preachers of the age with a message shaped for his exact history and knowledge. How patient is our God with the curious and the proud. To a family that had tried to kill his Son, mocked him and murdered his apostle, he sends his servant once more, with the gospel in his mouth.

Curiosity is not conversion. But Luke goes on to record what Agrippa did with it, and the answer is nothing. He heard the whole thing, agreed it was harmless, remarked that the man could have been released, and went home unchanged (26:31–32). Curiosity about Christ can be a door, but some enjoy the subject for years and have never once been to Christ for mercy. Agrippa wanted to hear the man. He got exactly what he asked for, and it was not what he needed, because he never asked for what he needed.

How do I talk to a friend who is curious about Christianity? Welcome the curiosity and take it seriously. Answer honest questions honestly, and admit when you do not know. But do what Paul will do with Agrippa: move gently from the interesting to the personal. Ask what they make of Jesus himself, not only of the arguments; tell them what Christ has done for you; invite them to read one of the Gospels with you. And pray for them, because curiosity becomes faith only when God opens the heart (16:14). Do not be content to keep a curious friend interested for years; lovingly ask where they stand.

Uncertain wording. “I would like” translates a past tense (eboulomēn) that Greek often used for a polite present wish, but which can also mean “I have been wanting”. Both are possible. If the second is meant, Agrippa had wanted to meet Paul for some time, and Festus’s account gave him his opportunity.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God seats the ruling class of a province in front of a prisoner, and the man in chains is the only one who knows why he is there. Agrippa and Bernice enter with great pomp, with the tribunes and leading men of Caesarea, and Paul is brought in (v. 23). Festus tells them that the Jews have shouted for this man’s death, yet he has found nothing deserving death (vv. 24–25). He must send the prisoner to the emperor and has nothing to write, so he hopes the king’s examination will give him a charge (vv. 26–27). The scene is set for Paul’s defence in chapter 26, and for the Lord’s word that Paul would carry his name before kings (9:15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus said that being brought before kings and governors for his name’s sake would be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). The hostility of the council, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king and a problem with a covering letter together seat the ruling class of a province in front of a preacher. The opposition built the platform and handed the prisoner the floor.

This promises no easy victories and excuses no idleness. God often works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he uses the powers of this world, he needs neither its permission nor its goodwill.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. Paul had a chain and the floor, and within a day he had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to answer him.

Now: The principle shows up in smaller rooms: the meeting where you are the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the odd position. He used the floor he was given, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole power of the province gathers in splendour, and the one man in the hall who knows why he is there is the prisoner in chains.

With great pomp. A display put on to be looked at, the whole power structure of the province in one hall: Luke’s word (phantasia) gives us our word fantasy.

Paul was brought in. He does not enter; he is brought. And he is in chains: he says so himself before the hearing ends, in one of the most gracious sentences in Acts, when he tells this room he wishes every one of them were as he is, except for these chains (26:29). Festus is about to admit he cannot say why the prisoner is there; the one man in the room who knows exactly what is going on is the one in irons. At Paul’s conversion the Lord said he would carry his name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel (9:15), and here all three are in one hall.

The whole Jewish people. Festus is overstating; thousands of Jewish believers would have said otherwise. But he has just put on record, before the province’s assembled nobility, that they were “shouting that he ought not to live any longer”, and in the next breath he will say that he found no ground for it whatever.

The King of kings. The kings of this world come with a display that is gone by morning. The King of kings was laid in a manger, rode a donkey, wore a crown of thorns and was lifted up in shame, and he is clothed now in a majesty that will never be taken from him.

He ought not to live any longer. Paul is not the first prisoner over whom that was shouted. Before Pilate the crowd cried out together against Jesus, “Away with this man”, and then, “Crucify, crucify him!” (Luke 23:18, 21). Paul heard the same cry on the barracks steps (22:22). But the shout over Christ did not have the last word. Men said he ought not to live; God raised him, and he lives for ever. That is exactly why they want Paul silenced: the man in chains keeps saying that the one they shouted down is alive.

Is it wrong for Christians to enjoy ceremony, wealth or fine things? Not in itself. God made a world of beauty, and Scripture describes the splendour of Solomon’s temple and the glory of the new Jerusalem without embarrassment. The danger is what Luke’s word exposes: display for its own sake, splendour used to make ourselves look great, trust placed in what will fade. Enjoy good things with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4; 6:17), use them generously, and never confuse them with true greatness. The question is whether the things you have point others to God or to yourself.

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus is sending a man to the emperor and cannot say what he is accused of; and the title he gives Nero in passing belongs in truth to the prisoner’s Lord.

Nothing deserving death. A Roman governor is putting a prisoner on a ship to the imperial court, and the file is empty. Every authority that has examined Paul has found no crime: Gallio (18:14–15), Lysias (23:29), Festus twice, and soon Agrippa (26:31–32). Luke simply files the verdicts, and they echo another set in his first volume, when Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and sent him to the cross anyway.

Nothing definite to write to my lord. Sending a prisoner to the emperor with no charge would make Festus look foolish, so he hopes that after the king has examined Paul he will have something to write. Then comes the phrase a Christian reader should not walk past: my lord, kyrios. Festus uses it of Nero as the ordinary courtesy; within a generation Domitian would want to be addressed as lord and god.

Two lordships in one sentence. For the man in chains that word means somebody else entirely. Paul had written to Corinth that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6), and he would write to Philippi that God has given Jesus the name that is above every name, so that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:9–11). He is being shipped to Caesar’s court for the specific purpose of saying so, and the governor can see only one of the two lordships he has named. Nero was lord of the world for fourteen years and died by his own hand at thirty. Jesus Christ was lord of nothing anyone could see, and he is Lord tonight. The title Festus gives Nero in passing is a courtesy; the title Paul gives Jesus in chains is a fact, and every tongue will one day say so, to the glory of God the Father.

In everyday life. Let your life be so honest at work, so faithful at home and so clean in your dealings that anyone looking for something to accuse you of would come away with an empty file. You will not manage it perfectly, and before God you need not: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his clean record is counted as yours (Philippians 3:9), and his Spirit is making yours cleaner year by year.

Is it wrong for a Christian to call anyone lord or to honour rulers? No. Scripture tells us to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17) and to give respect and honour to whom they are owed (Romans 13:7), and Paul himself addresses Festus as most excellent (26:25). What a Christian cannot do is give any ruler the worship, absolute allegiance or final obedience that belongs to Christ alone. That is why believers in the early centuries would honour Caesar but would not say Caesar is lord in the sense that Caesar is god, and many died for it. When a ruler’s command contradicts God’s, we must obey God rather than men (5:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor admits that what he is doing is unreasonable and does it anyway; yet this injustice is exactly how God keeps his promise to bring Paul to Rome.

It seems to me unreasonable. The chapter ends on a bureaucrat’s complaint about paperwork. But hear what it concedes: he knows the thing is unreasonable, says so out loud, and does it anyway. Everyone with the power to judge knows Paul is innocent, and none of them sets him free. The system worked exactly as designed and still could not do the right thing, because at every stage somebody needed a favour.

And yet. Here is what the promise of Rome (23:11) looks like from ground level: a governor who cannot fill in a form. Not an angel or an acquittal, but a procedural embarrassment that will put Paul on a ship at imperial expense and carry him to the one city he had been promised. It is a real injustice and also the exact means by which a promise is kept. The Christian life is mostly lived in that overlap.

A charge written over the cross. Festus cannot find a charge to write against Paul. Over his Lord a charge was written and set up for all Jerusalem to read: “This is the King of the Jews” (Luke 23:38). Pilate meant it as the crime; God made it the truth. And Paul would later write that something else was nailed there with it: the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, which God set aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The servant goes to Rome with a blank charge sheet, because there is nothing to write. The sinner goes free before God with a cancelled one, because everything that could be written against him was written over Christ, and paid.

A governor’s embarrassment into a pulpit. Festus wanted something to write, and he will get chapter 26. God turns a governor’s embarrassment into a pulpit, an unjust chain into a passage to Rome, and a cross that every court agreed was unreasonable into the salvation of the world. Not one of his promises has ever failed. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, for ever and ever.

Why does God allow innocent believers to remain in chains? Scripture does not give us every reason, but it gives us enough to trust him. Paul’s chains carried the gospel where no free preacher could reach: the praetorian guard and Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:12–13; 4:22). Suffering for righteousness joins believers to Christ, who suffered unjustly first (1 Peter 2:19–23), and bears witness that he is worth more than freedom. God will one day judge every injustice openly (2 Thessalonians 1:6–8), and until then he does not waste a single day of his people’s suffering. Many Christians today are imprisoned for no crime but their faith, and they need our prayers, our letters and our advocacy.

In everyday life. Find out about one believer, or one church, imprisoned or persecuted for faith in Christ today, through a ministry that serves the persecuted church, and pray for them this week, remembering them as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3).

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”
25.overview:
Where we are. Paul has been held at Caesarea for two years, left in prison by Felix as a favour to the Jewish leaders (24:27). A new governor, Porcius Festus, now arrives, about AD 59. This chapter and the next belong together: Paul’s appeal to Caesar, then his defence before King Agrippa, the last hearing before he sails for Rome.

The message. The risen Lord keeps his promise through people who have no idea they are keeping it. He had told Paul, “you must testify also in Rome” (23:11), and here a murder plot, a governor’s wish to please, a citizen’s lawful appeal and an empty charge sheet each carry Paul a step nearer. And at the centre of the bewildered court stands the one question that matters: whether “a certain Jesus, who was dead,” is alive (v. 19).

Why it was said. Readers like Theophilus needed to know why the apostle was in chains and whether Christians were a threat to Roman order (see the introduction). Luke lets a Roman governor answer: the prosecution proved nothing, and the quarrel was about religion and a man said to be risen, not about crime (vv. 18–19, 25).

How the chapter makes its case. In Jerusalem the chief priests ask Festus, as a favour, to bring Paul there, meaning to ambush him on the road; Festus makes them come to Caesarea instead (vv. 1–5). Their charges are many and unproven, and Paul answers them in a single sentence (vv. 6–8). When Festus, to please the Jews, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and the appeal is granted (vv. 9–12). King Agrippa arrives, and as Festus tells him the case he admits he is at a loss (vv. 13–22). Before the assembled power of the province, Festus presents a prisoner he must send to the emperor and cannot charge (vv. 23–27).

Where it leads. Paul walks the road his Master walked: the same priestly lobby, a governor anxious to please, a Herod who wants to see the prisoner, verdict after verdict of innocence. The likeness shows the difference. Paul appeals and is protected; Jesus made no appeal, and was condemned in the place of the guilty. And the governor’s summary names the heart of the gospel without meaning to: Jesus was dead, and he is alive.

For us. God usually keeps his promises not by interrupting the ordinary course of things but by steering it, through officials, procedures and even other people’s sins. So use lawful means without fear, do not let anyone’s favour govern your decisions, and ask whether the fact Festus stated so coolly, that Jesus is alive, still moves you.

keyVerse.quote: Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.
keyVerse.note: Stripped of every charge, the case comes down to this, and a governor who believed none of it states the hinge of the gospel exactly. The plots, the appeal and the king’s curiosity all turn on whether this dead man is alive, and Paul will not stop saying that he is. The question Festus could not investigate is the one every reader must answer.

25.reflection:
The chief priests kept their case against Paul alive for two years, with a murder plot behind a polite request (vv. 1–3), and no doubt called it zeal for God. How can a good cause slowly come to justify wrong methods, and where might you be at risk of that?

Festus was a competent official who wanted to please the people he worked with, and it nearly cost an innocent man his life (vv. 9, 17, 20). In what situations are you most tempted to let someone’s approval decide what you do, and what would fearing God instead look like there?

Paul appealed to Caesar, and God used a lawful right to keep his promise of Rome (vv. 10–12; 23:11). When is it right for a Christian to insist on rights, and when is it better to lay them down?

Festus summed up the faith accurately, “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive” (v. 19), and was untouched by it. Has the resurrection become a fact you can state without being moved? What would help it become a living hope again?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prisoner in chains holds up the risen Christ before the rulers of a province, and by the end it is the court that has been examined. Paul shows that he is accused only for Israel’s own hope (vv. 1–8), tells how the persecutor was stopped and sent by the risen Jesus (vv. 9–18), and insists that his message adds nothing to Moses and the prophets: a suffering Messiah, the first to rise, bringing light to Jews and Gentiles (vv. 19–23). Festus calls it madness and Agrippa turns it aside, but Paul prays aloud that all who hear him might become what he is, except for the chains (vv. 24–29). The officials agree he is innocent, and the appeal carries him on to Rome (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The spine of this speech is that the Christian faith is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the question that would settle it: do you believe the prophets?

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isaiah 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Daniel 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish matter, which is what his opponents wanted and what he would not give them.

Underneath lies grace that is entirely from God's side. Paul was not seeking; he was in a raging fury, and he was stopped, named and commissioned. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness: performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20; on root and fruit, see the note on vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the gospel from the apostle to the Gentiles, in the language of his own Scriptures, from a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not refute a single point; he made a wry remark and stood up.

Now: Many decline Christ the way Agrippa did (see the note on vv. 29–30). If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa stated none. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way again and again. Christ still receives all who come to him (John 6:37), and Paul's one request at the start of the speech, that the king would hear him patiently, is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given a fair hearing at last, Paul counts himself fortunate, not because a king might free him but because a king can understand him about Jesus. The Lord’s word that Paul would carry his name before kings (9:15) is being kept.

Permission to speak. Paul has waited more than two years for this sentence. A mob, a brawling council, a governor hoping for a bribe and a second governor out of his depth: four hearings, and not one of them fair. Now a king who knows the Hebrew Scriptures says: speak. Paul stretches out his hand, the orator’s gesture, with a chain on it (v. 29).

I consider myself fortunate. Blessed, happy, well off: the word of the Beatitudes (makarios). On trial for his life, Paul calls himself fortunate, not because Agrippa is powerful but because he can follow the argument and will not hear the word “resurrection” as provincial nonsense. Paul is not counting his chances of acquittal. He is counting his chances of being understood about Jesus Christ.

The accusations of the Jews. “The Jews” is Luke’s shorthand in these chapters for the Jerusalem leadership who brought the case, not the Jewish people as such, and certainly not Jews as a race. The man speaking is himself a Jew arguing from the Hebrew prophets. This book has been misread down the centuries to justify appalling things; it does not say them.

Agrippa and Bernice. Herod Agrippa II, great-grandson of Herod the Great, ruled territories north and east of Galilee and held the Roman right to appoint the high priest, so Festus wanted his advice on a Jewish matter. Bernice was his sister. Festus had recently replaced Felix as governor (24:27).

Your opportunity to bear witness. The Lord had said his followers would be brought before kings and governors for his name’s sake, and that this would be their opportunity to bear witness. He added a promise: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict” (Luke 21:12–15). The speech before Agrippa is not Paul’s talent on display. It is the risen Christ, who once stood silent before Herod Antipas, now speaking through his servant to Antipas’s great-nephew.

A fortunate man in chains. Held two years on a charge the governor cannot put into writing (25:26–27), Paul calls himself fortunate because someone competent is finally going to hear about Christ. The Lord opens doors no one can shut, often in the places that look most closed. Measure your own least free places, the hospital bed, the difficult office, the family table where faith is mocked, by the same rule: someone there may hear about Jesus.

Why does Luke tell Paul’s conversion three times? Luke tells it first as narrator (9:1–19), then in Paul’s words to a Jewish crowd (22:3–21), and now to a king; ancient writers repeated what they most wanted remembered. The conversion of the church’s fiercest enemy proves that the gospel is God’s work and not man’s, explains why Paul went to the Gentiles, and shows that Christ can save anyone. Each telling is shaped for its hearers, but the heart is the same: the risen Jesus met Saul and sent him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the king for the one thing the gospel needs from any hearer: a patient hearing.

Customs and controversies. Agrippa knows the practices and, more useful still, the arguments, such as the old quarrel between Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection (23:6–8). He is competent to hear this case.

Patiently. Literally, with a long temper rather than a short one (makrothumōs), from the family of words used of God’s own longsuffering. Paul asks the king for a small share of it: do not grow irritated before I have finished. God bore with the persecutor Saul until the day he stopped him, and bears with us still; the Lord’s patience means salvation (2 Peter 3:15). Every day a sinner is given to hear the gospel is a day of that patience.

Beginning with Moses. Paul’s long speech follows a pattern set by the risen Lord. On the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Christ gave them not a slogan but an afternoon and a whole Bible, because all of it is about him, and Paul will do the same for a king (vv. 22–23).

An overlooked reason. What follows is not a legal defence but a story and an argument from Moses and the prophets, and that takes time. Impatience, not hostility, is a common reason people never deal with Christ: the subject gets a few minutes, and the verdict is reached on a case that was never heard. Paul is not asking Agrippa to agree, only to stay in the room long enough for the argument to be made.

What if I am the impatient one? Then give Christ a fair hearing, deliberately. Many Christians as well as unbelievers grant the Bible a few distracted minutes and then decide what they think. Read a whole Gospel, Mark or Luke, in two or three sittings, as you would any serious book, and ask what kind of person Jesus is. When a hard passage troubles you, stay with it until you understand it. God promises that those who seek him with all their heart will find him (Jeremiah 29:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s life before Christ was public, devout and exact: whatever turned him around, it was not ignorance of Judaism or a lack of religion.

Known by all the Jews. Paul opens with the public record. He was raised in Jerusalem, trained under Gamaliel, one of the most famous rabbis of the age (22:3), and made his reputation in front of witnesses who are still alive. They could testify, “if they are willing”: the prosecution has the evidence and will not produce it, because it helps the defendant. No one can say Paul left Judaism because he never understood it.

The strictest party. The most exact, with no margin of error (akribestatēn; compare 22:3). He belonged, thoroughly, to the most exacting school available, the Pharisees.

He does not disown it. He said the same to the council (23:6) and wrote it years later (Philippians 3:5). Paul never regarded following Jesus as leaving Israel, but as Israel’s hope arriving. His conversion was not from irreligion to religion, but from the best religion without Christ to Christ: the best of human religion is a dim lamp beside the rising sun.

The exactness he found in another. The strictest Pharisee in Jerusalem was chasing a righteousness measured to the last tithe of mint. On the Damascus road he found that someone had already kept the law with that exactness and more: not an iota, not a dot, left unfulfilled (Matthew 5:17–18). Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). The Pharisee did not abandon his longing for an exact righteousness. He found it, complete, in the obedience of Jesus, and received it as a gift: when a person trusts Christ, God counts Christ’s perfect obedience as his, so that he stands before God clothed in a righteousness he did not earn (Philippians 3:9).

Closing the exits. We reach for comfortable explanations of conversion: he was badly taught, unhappy, young, searching. Paul closes the exits. He had the best training in the nation, status and approval, and was riding a career hard in the opposite direction, and winning. God took the most exact Pharisee of his generation at the height of his zeal and turned him around with a word. No one is too religious for his grace to humble, and no one too far gone for it to reach.

Does a strict religious upbringing count for anything with God? It can be a great mercy, filling the mind with Scripture and the habits of worship, as Paul’s did. But it cannot save. Paul later listed every one of his religious advantages and counted them all as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:4–9). If you were raised in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you are trusting Christ himself and not your background.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is on trial for believing that God has kept the promise Israel prayed for through the centuries, above all the promise that he will raise the dead.

On trial because of my hope. Prosecuted by his own nation’s leaders, he is in chains for believing that what Israel has prayed for, morning and evening, for centuries, has been answered.

Night and day. “Our twelve tribes” means all Israel, as one people. Their worship was itself an act of hope, waiting for God to do what he had promised, and Paul grants his accusers’ piety warmly: the prayers are real.

The threads of the hope. The hope has three strands, all come true in Jesus. The resurrection of the dead is its heart (23:6; 24:15, 21): “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2; compare Job 19:25–27; Isaiah 26:19), and very probably by Paul’s day it was woven into daily Jewish prayer; the Amidah, the standing prayer, still praises God as the One who revives the dead. The promised Messiah is the promise to the fathers (13:23, 32–33): Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 22:18) and David’s everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16). And the redemption of Israel, the prophets’ great restoration hope (Isaiah 40–66; Ezekiel 36–37), is the hope for which Paul wears his chain (28:20).

Accused by Jews. That is what makes the charge so strange, and so sad: Jews accuse a Jew for believing the Jewish hope. A thing can be prayed for so long that the praying becomes the settled shape of life, and the answer feels less like fulfilment than disruption. They wanted the right thing, got it, and did not recognise it, because it came in a form that cost them something.

The centuries of prayer had a face. God was not deaf to one of those prayers. Luke has shown us where the waiting led: an old widow, Anna, worshipping in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, looked on an infant brought there by his parents and began to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:37–38). God gave more than Israel dared to ask, a King who has conquered death, so that the hope of the fathers is now the living hope of everyone who trusts him.

Can I pray for something for years and miss it when it comes? Yes, and these verses are a warning. God often answers in a form we did not expect, and if we have fixed exactly how the answer must look, we may resist it when it arrives. Many in Israel expected a Messiah who would conquer Rome; God sent one who conquered sin and death by dying. Pray humbly, holding your requests open to God’s wisdom, and search the Scriptures to learn what he has actually promised, so that you recognise his answer, which is always, in the end, more of Christ.

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God is God, raising the dead is not incredible; yet Paul himself once refused to believe it of Jesus, and fought his name with a sincere conscience that was pointing the wrong way.

Why is it thought incredible by any of you? Paul turns mid-speech and asks a question, and the Greek “you” is plural. He is no longer speaking only to the king but to the whole hall: the tribunes, the leading men of Caesarea, the governor, Jews and Gentiles alike. He does not wait for a reply; the question simply asks people to state their actual objection.

Not the hard part. If there is a God at all, the Creator who gives life and breath to all (17:25) and made the heavens and the earth out of nothing, then raising one dead man is not the hard part. A God who can start life from nothing can certainly restart it. So the question is not whether resurrection is possible, but whether God is God.

I myself was convinced. Paul admits he once thought it incredible too, at least of Jesus, and was convinced that opposing him was a duty. His conscience was fully engaged and pointing the wrong way. A man can be sincere, devout and at peace with himself, and be at war with God. Sincerity is no defence: Paul’s was total, and it made him more dangerous, not less.

God’s verdict on the name. Saul opposed the name because he was sure God had disowned the man: a Messiah does not die on a Roman cross. The resurrection reversed that verdict in public; Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). If God raised this man, the name Saul fought is the name God has vindicated, and the persecutor was fighting God. He spoke, and the worlds came to be; he called, and Lazarus came out of the tomb; on the third day he raised his own Son, never to die again. The God who did that will not lose one of his people to the grave.

What would follow if it were true. When someone says the resurrection is impossible, ask what would follow if it were true. If a dead man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then he is who he said he is, and everyone must one day answer to him. Honest people have real questions about the evidence, and they deserve real answers; Paul gives his own list of witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8. But for some the case against the resurrection is not really about evidence: they do not want what would follow. Paul knew that from the inside.

How do I know my own convictions are not wrong, as Paul’s were? By testing them against Scripture, not against the strength of your feelings. The Bereans checked even Paul’s preaching against the Scriptures daily (17:11). Ask whether your conviction exalts Christ or opposes him, whether it agrees with the plain teaching of God’s Word, and whether it produces love, humility and holiness or pride and harshness. Be willing to hear correction from mature believers, and pray with the psalmist that God would search you and see if there is any grievous way in you (Psalm 139:23–24). A conscience must be taught by God’s Word to be a safe guide.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unasked, Paul confesses to a king the worst thing about himself: he imprisoned, condemned and tortured Christ’s people in a raging fury. He tells it calmly, because the mercy that met him is greater than the sin.

Many of the saints. No prosecutor has raised his past; Paul volunteers it, in detail. And he calls his victims saints, God’s holy people. Back then he would have called them heretics.

I cast my vote. Literally “I cast down a pebble”, from the stone dropped into an urn to register a verdict. The plural, “when they were put to death”, suggests that Stephen was not the only one, though Luke tells us only of him.

Tried to make them blaspheme. The verb describes repeated action: he kept trying, as a method. This was persecution aimed at the soul, pain applied to force Christians to curse Christ. Some eighty years later the Roman governor Pliny wrote that he released anyone who would curse Christ, since none of the real Christians could be made to do it.

In raging fury. Exceedingly mad (perissōs emmainomenos), from the verb to rave (mainomai). Thirteen verses later Festus will shout that Paul is out of his mind, from the same root (v. 24), and Paul has already answered him. The madness in this story was not the preaching of a risen Christ. It was a brilliant, devout, exactingly trained man dragging women out of their houses in the name of God (8:3). He would call himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

Why say it to a king? His biography is the evidence in an argument: something turned that man into this one, and no education, disappointment or gradual softening did it. The risen Jesus did. That is not a story of human improvement; it is the triumph of sovereign mercy over the worst a sinner can do.

The name they would not curse. Saul tried to force the saints to call Jesus accursed, and very probably believed it himself: a man hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23), and to a Pharisee a crucified Messiah was a contradiction. The risen Lord taught him that the curse was real and that Jesus had borne it, not for any sin of his own: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The man who pressed Christians to curse Christ would later write that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says Jesus is accursed (1 Corinthians 12:3).

The Judge of all the earth dropped none. Saul dropped his pebble into the urn against the saints, and the Judge of all the earth dropped none against Saul. The verdict he deserved fell on the Christ he hated, who bore it and then met him on the road with a pardon. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). Blessed be the Lord whose love is stronger than our fury.

The freedom of the forgiven. Paul can say the worst about himself calmly, in public, to power, not because the sin was small but because the pardon is settled. People unsure of their forgiveness edit their story; someone who knows God has forgiven him no longer needs other people’s good opinion to feel safe, because it is God who justifies, and no one else can condemn (Romans 8:33–34).

Can God forgive someone who has done something truly terrible? Yes. Paul had helped to kill Christians, and Christ forgave him completely and made him an apostle. He received mercy precisely so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so great that the blood of Christ cannot cleanse it, for those who repent and believe. Forgiveness does not erase earthly consequences, and the forgiven should make things right where possible; but the guilt before God is gone. And if that seems unfair to those he hurt, remember that grace is always unfair in our favour: no one is forgiven because he deserved it, the respectable no more than the violent (Romans 3:22–24).

Should I tell other people about my past sins? Not everything to everyone. Paul told his story where it served the gospel and glorified Christ, not to dwell on the sin or to shock. Confess your sins fully to God, and to those you have wronged, seeking their forgiveness. Share more widely only when it will help others see the grace of Christ, with wisdom about who is listening. The aim is always to make much of the Saviour, never of the sin.

Uncertain wording. The idiom of casting a pebble was the ordinary language of voting, a dark pebble for condemnation. What it does not settle is whether Saul voted as a member of a council, perhaps the Sanhedrin itself, or simply that he gave his approval to the executions, as he did at Stephen’s death (8:1). Either way he shared the guilt.
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On an errand of persecution, at the brightest hour of the day, Saul was overwhelmed by a light from heaven brighter than the sun: the glory of the risen Christ.

Authority and commission. A commission is a delegated authority, a warrant (epitropē). This was no private vendetta: the prosecution’s own institution issued the warrants. Then he met a higher authority.

At midday … brighter than the sun. Midday, the hour when nothing looks mysterious (22:6); and, new here, brighter than the sun: under the fiercest natural light his world knew, something outshone it that did not belong to this created world. It was the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Those who journeyed with me. He argues like a witness, not a mystic: something objective happened on that road at noon, in front of company.

The third telling. The three tellings (9:1–19; 22:3–21; and here) differ in emphasis, not substance. To a Jewish crowd Paul gave Ananias a central place, because a devout man of good reputation in Damascus mattered to that audience. To a king, Ananias disappears, and the commission comes straight from the mouth of the risen Christ. Paul tells the same true story and brings forward the part the hearer most needs, and a king needs to know who gave the orders.

Its lamp is the Lamb. At noon, under a burning sky, the Lord of glory let a sliver of his brightness through, and it outshone the sun. John saw the same face on Patmos, like the sun shining in full strength (Revelation 1:16), and fell at his feet as though dead, as Saul fell in the dust. One day the city of God will need no sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The light that blinded the persecutor will be the everlasting day of the redeemed.

Does Jesus still appear to people like this today? Not in the way he appeared to Paul. That vision was part of his unique calling as an apostle, and he calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared in that way (1 Corinthians 15:8). God now speaks through his completed Word and brings people to faith through the preaching of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). Christians assess reports of people dreaming of Jesus charitably and differently, but any experience must be tested by Scripture and must lead a person to the Scriptures and the church. You do not need a light from heaven: in the gospel you have the same Christ who met Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord flattened his enemy, spoke to him by name in his own tongue, and told him that his resistance was only wounding himself.

We had all fallen. Only this telling has the whole party fall, the voice speak in Hebrew and the saying about the goads (at 9:7 the companions stood speechless; men knocked flat get up). The falling is the point: this is what happens when sinners meet the holy God, as Ezekiel fell on his face before the glory (Ezekiel 1:28) and Isaiah cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5).

In the Hebrew language. The detail Paul saved for a Jewish king: the glorified Christ, brighter than the Syrian noon, speaks the language of Galilean villages and Jerusalem streets. He did not shed his humanity at the resurrection: the Lord of all still speaks like a man from Nazareth.

Kick against the goads. A goad was a long pole tipped with iron, used to drive oxen. An ox that lashed back at it drove the point deeper. The proverb was well known in the Greek world for resisting the gods, so both halves of the room could follow. Its first meaning is that resisting God hurts only the one who resists. Many readers fairly hear more: an ox kicks only at a goad it has felt, so something was already pricking Saul.

What the goads were. Scripture does not say, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise. But in the chapters before Saul’s conversion Luke has laid things in front of us: a face like an angel’s in a courtroom (6:15); Stephen dying with a prayer for his killers, out loud, while Saul held the coats (7:58–60); people who would not curse the name however hard they were pressed; and behind it all the uncomfortable possibility, for a man trained to read Moses and the prophets exactly, that these people might be right. He would have called it noise; it was a goad.

The goad was the mercy. Some have argued for years with a verse that will not leave, or the memory of a Christian who was inexplicably kind. The kicking is what does the damage. The goad was never the injury; it was the mercy. Paul kicked, and Christ conquered him: he spoke his name twice, in his own language, and the war was over. Grace does not drag us in against our will. It is effectual, which means it always achieves what God intends: it changes the will itself, so that we come willingly (Philippians 2:13).

In everyday life. What has God been pressing on you for a long time: a sin to give up, a person to forgive, a truth you keep arguing with? Stop kicking. The hand on the goad belongs to the Saviour who bore your curse, and his Spirit makes the yielding possible: name it before him today.

If grace is effectual, why does God plead with people at all? Because his pleading is one of the means by which his grace works. He does not save people like stones but as persons, through his Word: he speaks, warns, invites and goads, and by his Spirit makes the heart willing to hear (John 6:44–45; 2 Timothy 2:25). The invitations of the gospel are sincere, and everyone who comes will be received (John 6:37); when someone does come, it is because God first drew him. That is why we pray for unbelievers and keep speaking to them: the goads are God’s, and he uses them.

Uncertain wording. Luke’s “Hebrew language” (Hebraïdi dialektō) may mean Hebrew itself, or, as most think, Aramaic, the everyday tongue of the Jews of Palestine, which Jewish writers in Greek also called “Hebrew”: the related word at John 19:13 is rendered “in Aramaic” by the ESV. Either way the point stands: the risen Lord spoke to Saul in the language of his own people.

Textual note. Readers of the King James or New King James Version will also find the saying about the goads at 9:5. It is there only in later manuscripts; the earliest have it only here, which is why modern Bibles print it only in this chapter.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice from heaven belongs to Jesus, alive, who counts every blow against his people as a blow against himself, and who lifts his enemy from the dust to make him his servant and witness.

Who are you, Lord? Saul asks the shortest and most important question a human being can ask, and gets a name in reply, as before (9:5). Not a title but the name of a man from a village in Galilee whom Saul knew perfectly well to be dead, and whose followers he was travelling to arrest.

Whom you are persecuting. Present tense, and not “whose people you are persecuting”: to lay hands on a believer in Damascus is to lay hands on him. Here is the seed of Paul’s teaching on the church as Christ’s body: the Head feels every blow struck at his members. The point for Agrippa is simpler and harder: the man you all agree was executed is speaking, and he takes the arrests personally.

Rise and stand upon your feet. The words echo the call of Ezekiel, flat on his face before the glory of God: “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you” (Ezekiel 2:1), before he is sent to a rebellious people. Paul is commissioned in the language of the prophets, and a king who knew his Scriptures would hear it.

Servant and witness. The two words define the rest of his life. A servant (hypēretēs) is an assistant, a man under orders; a witness (martys) testifies, and has no freedom to improve the account. It is the plainest description of a preacher, and the reason Paul decided to know nothing among the Corinthians except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). Here the commission comes as Jesus’ own words, since what Ananias told him came from Jesus (22:14–15; on why Ananias is left out, see vv. 12–13).

Those in which I will appear to you. The Damascus road was not the last of it: the night vision at Corinth (18:9), the Lord in the temple (22:17), the Lord standing by him in the barracks (23:11), and things he could not put into words (2 Corinthians 12:1–4). Christ did not commission him and leave him to it.

He answers persecution with a commission. The Lord who said to Saul, “Rise and stand upon your feet”, had himself lain in a tomb and risen from it. He lifts his fallen enemy from the dust and gives him work to do. Christ was himself the Servant of the LORD and the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), and he makes servants and witnesses out of rebels. What a Lord, who turns an enemy into a friend who will carry his name to the ends of the earth.

Am I a servant and witness too, if I am not an apostle? Yes, in your own measure. Paul’s commission was unique: he was an eyewitness of the risen Christ, sent with apostolic authority. But every Christian is called to serve Christ under orders and to bear witness to him (1 Peter 2:9; 3:15). You are asked not to be impressive but to tell the truth about Jesus as Scripture reveals him and as you have known him. A witness only reports, and that frees you from the pressure to persuade by your own cleverness.

When was Paul born again? Readers have long asked whether Paul was already regenerate as he answered “Who are you, Lord?” Scripture does not pin the moment. To be born again is to be given new spiritual life by the Holy Spirit, a new heart that loves God instead of resisting him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26). The marks of a heart already being turned are plainly present, and what is certain is not when it happened but who did it: whenever it was, it was God’s work from first to last (John 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ sends Paul to do what only Christ can do through him: open blind eyes and move people out of Satan’s dark kingdom into God’s light, where by faith in Jesus they receive forgiveness and a place among God’s people.

Delivering you. It is not the promise we would have written. The word (exairoumenos) means rescuing out of danger, which assumes he would first be in it, the kind of protection Jeremiah was promised (Jeremiah 1:8). That is how it went: stoned, flogged, shipwrecked, imprisoned and, as the early church remembered, executed in Rome. Every rescue happened, but Paul was delivered out of troubles, never spared them.

To open their eyes. The fullest statement of the commission in Acts begins not with informing people but with making the blind see. Paul had all the information and was blind; struck blind, he was sent to open eyes.

From darkness to light. A change of realm, not of opinion. Before, a person does not know God and does not want to; afterwards he knows him, loves him and begins to walk in his ways, not perfectly but truly. God has called his people out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).

From the power of Satan to God. Modern readers skip this clause, but people are not neutral. They are held, mostly by ordinary things: self-interest, appetite, fear of what people think, the settled conviction that one’s life is one’s own. It is a real dominion with a real ruler, and getting out is not a matter of trying harder. God has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13).

Receive forgiveness … a place among those who are sanctified. Receive: the posture of open hands, not of someone settling an account. A place (klēros) is a lot, an inheritance, a share, a seat at the table with the holy ones. And the ground of it all, stated last so nobody can mistake it, is not works or law but “faith in me”. It is a summary of the gospel from the lips of Jesus himself.

The Servant’s commission. “A light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon”: that is Isaiah, describing the task of the Servant of the LORD (Isaiah 42:6–7, 16). Christ takes the Servant’s own commission and hands it to Saul of Tarsus: what the Messiah was sent to do, he now sends this man to do in his name.

No other explanation for a single Christian. The risen Christ fetches people out of the dark, not by improving them but by moving them from Satan’s kingdom into God’s. He forgives the sort of man who had been dragging his followers out of their homes and gives him a share in the inheritance of the saints. The whole chain, from the opened eye to the place at the table, is his work upon people who were doing nothing but resisting him, and there is no other explanation for a single Christian who has ever lived.

Does being under Satan’s power excuse unbelievers? No. Scripture holds together two truths: people are held captive by the devil (2 Timothy 2:26), and they love the darkness and choose it (John 3:19). Satan’s rule is one people prefer, because it lets them keep their lives as their own. So no one is excused, and no one can free himself. Only Christ, the stronger man, can bind the strong man and set his captives free (Luke 11:21–22). That should make us humble about our own conversion and full of hope for others.

What does sanctified by faith mean here? Set apart as God’s own, made holy in status, at the moment of faith. In the New Testament sanctification has two sides: the once-for-all setting apart of the believer, so that every Christian is a saint (1 Corinthians 6:11), and the lifelong work of the Spirit making us actually more holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Here Jesus speaks of the first. The second follows, and the first is its foundation.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul simply obeyed the risen Lord, calling Jews and Gentiles everywhere to repent and turn to God, and to show it by how they live.

Not disobedient to the heavenly vision. A remarkable understatement, and the understatement is the point. Some twenty-five years of floggings, a stoning, three shipwrecks and daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), and he sums it up as “I was not disobedient”: no sense of achievement, no self-pity, just a man reporting that he did as he was told.

First to those in Damascus. The geography is the outline of Acts (1:8).
