One honest question: Paul tells the Galatians that in his early years the churches of Judea did not know him by sight (Galatians 1:22). The likeliest answer is that here he sums up his whole ministry, including later visits and the believers who heard him in Jerusalem (9:28–29; 15:3), rather than the first weeks after his conversion.

Deeds in keeping with their repentance. Repent: change your mind. Turn to God: change your direction. And then do things that match, as John the Baptist preached (Luke 3:8). Paul is not saying the deeds earn the turning; he spent whole letters demolishing that. Justification, God’s verdict that a sinner stands righteous before him, rests on Christ’s righteousness counted to the one who trusts him, never on the sinner’s own record (Romans 4:5). The deeds show that the repentance is real. By grace you have been saved through faith, not a result of works, and in the next breath, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10). The works are not the root but the fruit, and a tree with no fruit after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.

Obedience to a person. The heavenly vision was the risen Jesus, and what Paul preached is the commission he gave his disciples: that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). Repentance in Paul’s mouth is never a self-improvement scheme but turning to God through Christ, toward a forgiveness he has already purchased. And the Lord who gave the vision also gave the obedience: those years of floggings and sleepless nights were not the strength of a hero but the faithfulness of Christ in his servant.

Name one. Repentance in the New Testament is specific. A conversation you have been avoiding because you were in the wrong. Money that is not yours. A habit conducted privately. A person you have written off. What deed would be in keeping with the repentance you would say you have? If nothing comes to mind, ask God quietly to show you; and if a great deal comes to mind and you feel crushed by it, remember that wanting to turn is already his work in you.

What if I have repented but keep falling into the same sin? Then keep repenting, and do not despair. Repentance is not a single act at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life, and a believer may struggle with the same sin for years (Romans 7:15–25). The question is not whether you ever fall, but whether you hate the sin, confess it and fight it, using the means God gives: prayer, Scripture, accountability, and removing what feeds it (1 John 1:8–9). Fitting deeds include getting up again. And your standing with God rests on Christ’s obedience, not on your record of victory.

Where Christians differ: faith and works. Some think Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that we are justified by faith alone (Romans 3:28), and here, that true repentance produces fitting deeds. Works are not the root but the fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:18). Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was nearly killed for taking the gospel to the Gentiles, and he is still standing only because God has helped him; and everything he preaches was already in Moses and the prophets.

For this reason. This, the Gentile mission, the place among the sanctified given to outsiders by faith, is why they tried to kill him. It was not the resurrection as a doctrine that enraged them, but a risen Messiah who welcomes Gentiles on the same terms as Jews, by faith, without first making them Jews (15:9–11).

The help that comes from God. The word has a military flavour (epikouria, only here in the New Testament): reinforcements arriving for a position under pressure. Paul does not say he has been resilient; he says help arrived from outside. “To this day” gathers up a list: the basket over the Damascus wall, the stoning at Lystra, the prison at Philippi, the mob in the temple, the forty men and their oath. Every one should have ended the story.

Both to small and great. Before a king and the aristocracy of a Roman capital, he mentions the small first. He had said the same things to a jailer at midnight and to women at a riverside.

Nothing but what the prophets and Moses said. Here is the heart of his defence. Paul claims not to have added a syllable: everything he preaches was already in the books read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath (15:21), books Agrippa knew well. The charge is that he teaches something new; his answer is that he holds to the old Scriptures, and his accusers have stopped believing their own.

The ally who stood by him. The help had a name. Paul has just quoted the risen Christ’s promise on the road, “delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles” (v. 17), and every rescue was that promise kept (18:10; 23:11). The reinforcements were not luck or stamina but the risen Jesus keeping his word to the man he had sent.

The whole library was about him. They were all speaking of him. Moses at the burning bush and the Passover lamb; the seed of Abraham in whom the nations would be blessed; David’s son on a throne that would not end; the child born in Bethlehem, too small a town to matter; the Servant with no beauty that we should desire him, despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own, silent before his shearers, numbered with the transgressors, and afterwards seeing the light of life and being satisfied. Some thousand years of writing converge on one week in Jerusalem and one man walking out of a tomb.

Being kept. Perseverance does not feel like strength of character from the inside. It feels like being kept: arriving at the end of another week still believing, unable to name a single heroic decision that accounts for it.

How do I experience God’s help today? Usually not in dramatic rescues, though God can give them, but in being kept: strength for the day, grace to endure, wisdom when you need it, the encouragement of a friend, a promise from Scripture that comes alive, a door that opens or closes. God has promised never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5–6), and his grace is sufficient in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Ask for his help specifically, then look back regularly and notice where it came. Most believers, looking back honestly, can say what Paul said: to this day, I have had help from God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets foretold that the Christ must suffer and be the first to rise, and by rising bring God’s saving light to Israel and the nations; at the word resurrection, the governor decides Paul is mad.

That the Christ must suffer. The summit of the speech, and “must” carries great weight. For most first-century Jewish expectation a suffering Messiah came close to a contradiction in terms: the Messiah was the one who ended suffering, not the one who absorbed it. But the suffering was what God had appointed, and the Scriptures had foretold it (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22). The Lord made the same point on the Emmaus road: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26; see 24:46).

The first to rise from the dead. Others had been raised before, the widow’s son, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus, but every one of them died again. Christ is the first to rise and stay risen, out the far side of death in a body that cannot die. So Paul calls him the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23) and the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18): not the only sheaf, but the first of a harvest, and the guarantee that the rest is coming.

Proclaim light. Not a vague glow of enlightenment but God’s saving rescue dawning on a dark world. Paul is echoing the Servant Songs, the passages in Isaiah about the Lord’s chosen Servant: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6); a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners (Isaiah 42:6–7). In Isaiah light stands with salvation, sight for the blind and freedom for prisoners. Paul had already applied Isaiah 49:6 to his mission (13:47), and his commission was to turn people from darkness to light (v. 18).

Where did Moses and the prophets say this? Paul does not list the texts, but the apostles preached from them: the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and the sufferer of Psalm 22 for the death; Psalm 16:8–11 (compare 2:25–31; 13:35) and Isaiah 53:10–12 for the resurrection; and the promise to bless the nations through Abraham and to make the servant a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6; compare 13:47).

You are out of your mind. The governor loses his composure and interrupts a prisoner mid-sentence. The likeliest provocation is the resurrection, which most educated Greeks and Romans found absurd (17:32). His diagnosis is almost affectionate: “your great learning”, literally “your many letters”, is driving you mad. A scholar who has read himself into a delusion: it is the oldest way of not answering an argument: find a cause for the belief, and you need not examine the reasons for it. Jesus too was called mad (Mark 3:21; John 10:20).

The sunrise. Christ proclaims light by being the first to rise from the dead: the resurrection itself is the sunrise, new-creation life breaking over the grave (Isaiah 9:2; 60:1–3). The light of the world was put out on a Friday afternoon, when darkness covered the land from the sixth hour to the ninth; and on the third day, before dawn, the sun of righteousness rose with healing in its wings.

Simeon’s song. Luke opened his Gospel with old Simeon lifting the infant Jesus and calling him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32): again Isaiah 49, again light for Gentiles and Israel. What Simeon sang at the cradle, Paul declares at the climax of the mission. For everyone who has sat in a long inward darkness, this is the gospel: the Light has come, and his name is Jesus.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners: God’s justice required that sin be punished, his love purposed to save, and at the cross Christ bore in our place the penalty our sins deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6).

Is it not unjust for God to punish the innocent in place of the guilty? It would be, if Christ were an unwilling third party dragged in from outside. But he is God the Son, who came willingly and laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The Judge did not punish a stranger. God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins, the sacrifice that takes the full weight of his just anger and so removes it (1 John 4:10). And those who trust Christ are joined to him, so that his death really counts as theirs (Romans 6:5–8). The cross is not injustice; it is the holy God satisfying his own justice at his own cost.
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is not mad but sober: the gospel is true, reasonable and public, a matter of facts the king himself knows, not secrets whispered in a corner.

Most excellent Festus. Told in public that he is insane, Paul neither loses his temper nor grovels. He gives Festus his correct title, the formal style for a governor, and flatly denies the charge. He gives the office its honour and the accusation nothing at all.

True and rational words. True (alētheias): words of truth. Rational (sōphrosynēs): soundness of mind, sober judgment, the exact opposite of mania, madness, the word Festus has just thrown at him, and a virtue the room respects (on where the real madness lay, see vv. 10–11).

The king knows about these things. Agrippa is not being asked to accept a private experience he cannot assess, but recent, public, checkable history in his own region.

Not done in a corner. Christians defending the faith have leaned on this phrase ever since. The mystery religions of the ancient world did their business in corners: secret rites, private initiations, truths for insiders that could never be checked. The life, death and resurrection of Jesus happened in public, under a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, whose name is on record, before hostile witnesses who were still alive. Christianity stakes everything on a particular execution and a particular tomb, in a city you can still walk around, and Paul invites investigation.

He said nothing in secret. The Lord Jesus told the high priest that he had spoken openly to the world and said nothing in secret (John 18:20), and he saved the world the same way: on a hill outside the city, under a notice written, John tells us, in three languages for every passer-by to read (John 19:20). The last act will not be done in a corner either: he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

Is faith opposed to reason? No. Biblical faith is not believing without evidence or against it, but trusting God on the basis of what he has shown and said. Paul reasons here from history and Scripture, and the New Testament everywhere appeals to witnesses and facts (Luke 1:1–4; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; 1 John 1:1–3). Faith goes beyond what reason alone can reach, because it is personal trust in Christ worked by the Spirit, but it is never unreasonable. Christians are to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in them, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul presses the king to believe the prophets he already reveres, and Agrippa, cornered, turns the appeal aside with a question.

Do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe. Paul turns from the governor to the king, asks him directly, and supplies the answer himself: the boldest moment in the speech, and a trap, though not a cruel one. If Agrippa says yes, he has conceded the argument, because Paul has just shown that the prophets promised a suffering and rising Messiah who would bring light to the Gentiles. If he says no, he has publicly renounced the Scriptures before the Jewish subjects whose high priest he appoints, with Roman officers listening. He can neither affirm nor deny, so he turns the question aside.

Would you persuade me to be a Christian? Whatever the exact sense (see below), the tone is probably ironic or evasive. What is not in doubt is the word he reaches for. “Christian” appears only three times in the New Testament: coined as a nickname at Antioch (11:26), used by Peter of those who suffer under it (1 Peter 4:16), and here, on a king’s lips, almost certainly with an edge. Agrippa will not name Jesus; he names his followers. And he has changed the subject; a few sentences later he stands up and leaves.

Moses, the prophets and one risen from the dead. To believe the prophets is to be pointed at Jesus, who said that if they believed Moses they would believe him, for Moses wrote of him (John 5:46). The scene almost acts out the story of the rich man and Lazarus: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). Here a king who knows Moses and the Prophets hears a witness of the one who did rise, and deflects. The prophets and the risen Christ speak with one voice, and the heart that will not hear the one will not hear the other.

Almost persuaded. The old rendering may misread Agrippa, but it has fixed on a tragic place. To be almost persuaded, interested, moved, near the kingdom, is still to be on the wrong side of the line; almost saved is wholly lost. Many perish not as scoffers but as the almost. Do not mistake weak faith for almost: a trembling believer who clings to Christ, doubts and all, has crossed the line, and anyone who wants to come is welcome today (John 6:37). Christ was not almost obedient, almost crucified or almost raised. He does not almost save; he saves to the uttermost all who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

How should I respond when someone deflects the gospel with a joke? Gently, and without letting it close the door, as Paul does in the next verse. Take the humour in good part, then return kindly to the real question: but what do you actually think of Jesus? Humour is often a shield raised when a subject gets too close; do not attack it. Show that you care more about the person than about winning the exchange, leave the door open for another time, and pray, because only God can turn a deflection into a question.

Uncertain wording. “In a short time” (en oligō) is genuinely ambiguous. It can mean in a little time, or with little effort, by a little argument. The King James took it as degree and gave us the famous “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian”; most modern translations take it as time, and the ESV notes that the question can also be read “would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” The tone is not recoverable from the page: probably a courtroom deflection with a smile in it, conceivably the nearest a Herod ever came to faith. The old rendering became a famous hymn and sermon, but probably misreads him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers the king’s jibe with a prayer that everyone in the room might have what he has in Christ, everything except his chains; and the king answers by standing up.

Whether short or long. A king makes a joke, and the awkward moment should pass. Paul picks up the king’s phrase and refuses the exit: little or much, quickly or slowly, it does not matter to me; what I want is the thing itself.

I would to God. This is not a figure of speech but a wish addressed to God in the hearing of everyone present. In a Roman audience hall, on trial, Paul stops arguing and prays out loud for the man judging him.

Such as I am. He owns nothing, everyone in the room outranks him, and he is on his way to be tried by Nero. He looks at the king in his splendour and Bernice in her jewels, and what he feels is not envy but pity. He was richer than all of them: forgiven, free in soul, a child of God. By the grace of God he was what he was (1 Corinthians 15:10), and grace was the one thing in that room he could give away.

Except for these chains. A kind clause, with grace and a touch of wit; he may well have lifted his chained hands. He was asking not for sympathy or release but for Christ, and careful to say he wished them his Lord, not his suffering. The chains were on his mind, and he mentions them lightly, without complaint, as the one part of his life he would not pass on.

Christ took the chains himself. Paul wished them everything he had except his chains. Christ wished us everything he had and took the chains himself. He was bound in the garden and led bound to the high priest (John 18:12, 24), and he bore the sentence our sin had earned, so that his people might have all of him and none of what they deserved. Every throne in that hall was poorer than Paul’s cell, because Christ was in the cell.

Then the king rose. Nobody answers. The response to a direct appeal is not a refutation but an adjournment. That is how many people decline Christ, then and now: not with an objection, which at least takes the thing seriously, but by finding that the hour is late and the conversation has reached a natural close. Agrippa did not say no; the standing was the answer.

Is it proud to wish that others would become like me? It would be, if Paul meant his personality, achievements or opinions. He means his faith in Christ, his forgiveness, his standing as a child of God: gifts he did not earn. He could say, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), because what he wanted copied was his Saviour. To long for others to have what you have in Christ is not pride but love, and the test is whether you would gladly see them surpass you, as long as they have Christ.

Isn’t it disrespectful to try to change someone’s beliefs? The magician and outspoken atheist Penn Jillette once said that he did not respect Christians who never tried to share their faith: if they really believed what they said about heaven and hell, he asked, how much would they have to hate someone not to tell them? Indifference is not respect. Paul, the one in chains, compels no one. He does not flatter, threaten or trick; he reasons in public, takes a king’s joke in good part, and prays for his judges. That is the line Christians must never cross: persuasion, never coercion, and never the pressure that turns a person into a project. What Paul offers is not his culture or his opinions but a gift he did not earn, and to keep such a gift to yourself would not be humility but a strange kind of contempt.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every authority agrees that Paul is innocent, and he stays in chains; yet the appeal that seems to have cost him his freedom is the road the Lord promised him to Rome.

Doing nothing to deserve death. The verdict is given in the corridor, where it costs nothing and changes nothing. It is at least the fifth time officials have found no crime in Paul (18:14–15; 23:29; 25:18, 25–27): now a Jewish king, a Roman governor and the senior officers of the garrison agree. It was so with Jesus before Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:14–15). The faith was investigated repeatedly by the authorities best placed to convict it, and the file kept coming back empty.

Could have been set free. Legally Agrippa is very probably right. Once a citizen’s appeal to the emperor had been formally registered, releasing the prisoner would have been at least an affront to Caesar; the case belonged to Rome. So the natural reading is that Paul made a mistake, a few weeks too quick, and talked himself out of an acquittal.

The appeal was the road. Except that the reader knows what Agrippa does not. Two years earlier the Lord had stood by him in a barracks cell at night and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Released in Caesarea, Paul would have walked into a province where a conspiracy had sworn to kill him and the leadership had twice tried to have him moved within reach. What looked like a closing door was the route to the promised city, travelled at imperial expense, under armed guard. His chains would carry the gospel into the emperor’s own guard (Philippians 1:12–13, if, as most think, that letter was written from Rome). The chains do not stop the word; they carry it, as Acts ends with the gospel preached in Rome “without hindrance” (28:31).

Another prisoner who could have gone free. Luke’s readers had heard this before. Pilate too wanted to release a prisoner he knew to be innocent (Luke 23:20). Jesus could have gone free, by Pilate’s wish or by a single word in his own defence. He did not, and Barabbas walked out instead (Luke 23:25). Paul’s chains were laid on him; Christ took his of his own will: no one takes my life from me, he had said, I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The one who could have been set free stayed bound, so that the guilty could be released.

Right verdict, wrong question. Agrippa got the legal question right and the only question that mattered wrong. He pronounced the prisoner free and left as the one still bound. Luke does not tell us why, but a king had much to lose: a Herod who bowed to a crucified Jew would forfeit the favour of Rome and the respect of the priests he appointed in a single afternoon. Position, approval and comfort are strong chains, and they are invisible to the man who wears them.

What if a decision I made seems to have closed a good door? Bring it to God honestly, and remember Paul: a choice that looks like a mistake may be the very road God intends. If you acted in good faith and with prayer, trust that the Lord, who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11), has not been taken by surprise. If you acted wrongly, confess it, and know that God weaves even our failures into his purposes for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Either way, do not live in endless second-guessing. Ask what faithfulness looks like now, on the road you are actually on.
verseByVerse.note: Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent.

26.title: Paul Before Agrippa
26.text: <sup>1</sup>So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: <sup>2</sup>“I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews, <sup>3</sup>especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. <sup>4</sup>My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. <sup>5</sup>They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. <sup>6</sup>And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, <sup>7</sup>to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! <sup>8</sup>Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? <sup>9</sup>I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <sup>10</sup>And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. <sup>11</sup>And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. <sup>12</sup>In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. <sup>13</sup>At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me. <sup>14</sup>And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ <sup>15</sup>And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. <sup>16</sup>But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you, <sup>17</sup>delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles—to whom I am sending you <sup>18</sup>to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, <sup>20</sup>but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. <sup>21</sup>For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. <sup>22</sup>To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: <sup>23</sup>that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” <sup>24</sup>And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” <sup>25</sup>But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. <sup>26</sup>For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner. <sup>27</sup>King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” <sup>28</sup>And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” <sup>29</sup>And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.” <sup>30</sup>Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. <sup>31</sup>And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” <sup>32</sup>And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
26.overview:
Where we are. Paul has been held at Caesarea for over two years. Festus has granted his appeal to Caesar but has nothing to write to the emperor, so King Agrippa II is to hear the prisoner (25:23–27). This is Paul’s last and fullest defence in Acts, and the third telling of his conversion.

The message. The risen Jesus is the hope God promised Israel, and he is still turning his enemies into his witnesses. Paul does not plead for his freedom. He tells how the Lord he persecuted met him, forgave him and sent him to open blind eyes, and then presses the same Christ on the king judging him. The real question in the room is whether a dead man has risen, and what anyone will do about it.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers needed to be sure that the faith was neither a betrayal of Israel nor a threat to Rome (see the introduction). Here a Jewish king and a Roman governor hear it in full, and agree that Paul “is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment” (v. 31).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul begins with his record as a strict Pharisee, on trial only for Israel’s hope that God raises the dead (vv. 1–8). He confesses his fury against the saints (vv. 9–11), then tells how the risen Jesus stopped him at noon and sent him to turn Jews and Gentiles from darkness to light (vv. 12–18). He obeyed, and says nothing beyond Moses and the prophets: a suffering Christ, the first to rise, bringing light to the nations (vv. 19–23). Festus calls him mad; the king turns the question aside (vv. 24–28). Paul prays that all might become as he is, except for the chains, and the court rises agreeing he is innocent (vv. 29–32).

Where it leads. The whole speech is about Christ: the hope of the fathers fulfilled in him, his voice on the road, his commission in the words of Isaiah’s Servant, his suffering and rising foretold by the prophets. The scene echoes his own trial: a Herod, a Roman governor, a prisoner declared innocent and not released. But Paul’s chains were laid on him; Christ stayed bound of his own will, so that the guilty could go free.

For us. Every believer has Paul’s story in miniature: God met us while we were resisting him and moved us from darkness to light. Tell it plainly, and do not be the hearer who admires the argument and then stands up to leave. Christ still receives all who come, whether the persuading takes a short time or a long one.

keyVerse.quote: to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.
keyVerse.note: In one sentence from the lips of the risen Jesus stands the whole of what the gospel does: blind eyes opened, a change of realm and of master, sins forgiven, and a place among God’s people, all received by faith in him. It is the commission that turned the persecutor into the apostle, and it explains everything else in the chapter, from Paul’s chains to his prayer that the king might become such as he is.

26.reflection:
Paul was utterly sincere when he persecuted Christians (vv. 9–11), and utterly wrong. What does that teach us about trusting our own conscience, and how can we make sure our convictions are shaped by God’s Word?

Verse 18 describes conversion as eyes opened, a move from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, forgiveness, and a place among God’s people. Which of these pictures helps you most to understand what God has done for you, and why?

Festus explained Paul away as a scholar driven mad, and Agrippa deflected with a question and then stood up (vv. 24–30). What are the ways people today, ourselves included, avoid dealing with Christ without ever actually saying no?

Paul wished that everyone in the room might become such as he was, “except for these chains” (v. 29). Who in your life would you love to see come to Christ, and what would it look like to speak to them, and pray for them, with Paul’s mixture of boldness, respect and love?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Setting Sail and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prisoner who belongs to Christ sails against the wind toward the city the Lord has named, and when every human resource is exhausted, God’s word still stands. The voyage runs from Caesarea along the coast to Myra, where Paul’s party boards an Alexandrian grain ship (vv. 1–6), then slowly to Fair Havens on Crete, where Paul’s warning is outvoted (vv. 7–12). A gentle south wind lures them out into the northeaster, and they are driven for days until all hope is lost (vv. 13–20). Then Paul stands up among them with an angel’s promise: because he must stand before Caesar, the ship will be lost, but not one life (vv. 21–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Actually Promised

The angel's word had two halves: there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22), and we must run aground on some island (v. 26). God guaranteed every person. He did not guarantee the vessel, the cargo or a chosen port, and he said so in advance; all three were lost, and the promise was kept in full (on what God promises his people, see the note on v. 26).

Alongside that runs the chapter's second theme: providence works through means, never around them (see the note on vv. 31–32).

And not one of the instruments God employs is a believer: a centurion's kindness, a crew's seamanship, an officer's fear for his career.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The disaster began with a harbour that was safe and boring (see v. 8). So the professionals voted to run for somewhere better, and a gentle south wind seemed to confirm it.

Now: A following wind on the morning of a decision feels like a green light and is often just the weather (see vv. 13–14), and the dull harbour may be the safe one (see v. 8). And if you have already sailed and the storm has come, the God who kept every soul on that ship has not stopped keeping his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prisoner sets out for Rome under Roman guard, but the voyage belongs to Christ, who has promised that Paul will testify there and who does not send him alone.

We should sail for Italy. The we is back. Luke last used it on arrival in Jerusalem (21:18); the riot, the council, Felix, Festus and Agrippa have all been told from outside. Now the narrator is aboard again, which is why what follows is so detailed: the ports, the winds, the depths in fathoms, the sailors’ name for a gale.

The Augustan Cohort. An imperial regiment. Its centurion, Julius, treats Paul well throughout, and before the chapter is over he will save Paul’s life.

A ship of Adramyttium. A coastal trader heading home to a port in north-west Asia Minor, calling along the coast where a ship for Italy might be found.

Aristarchus. A mob in Ephesus once dragged him into the theatre because he travelled with Paul (19:29); he helped carry the collection to Jerusalem (20:4), and from prison in Rome Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner” (Colossians 4:10). Most likely he and Luke came aboard as Paul’s attendants, as prisoners of status were sometimes allowed, accepting a servant’s standing in order to go. The Lord who sent his servant to Rome did not send him alone, as he gave Elijah a widow and Jesus the women who stood by the cross.

In the flow. These last two chapters end the road Luke has built since 1:8, through 19:21, 23:11 and 25:11 (see the overview).

A prisoner for Christ Jesus. On paper Paul now belongs to Rome, but this voyage began with another word: in the Jerusalem barracks the risen Lord told him that he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Every soldier, ship and harbour in this chapter serves that word. That is why, writing from prison, Paul never calls himself Caesar’s prisoner, but “a prisoner for Christ Jesus” (Philemon 1; compare Ephesians 3:1). The chain belongs to the emperor; the man belongs to Christ. And the Lord who sends him into Gentile hands walked that road first, delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32) for the salvation of Jew and Gentile alike.

Who would get on the boat with you? Two men arranged their lives so as to be on that ship when Paul had nothing left to offer them. Aristarchus had already been mobbed once for the association; Luke could have practised medicine anywhere. After twenty-five years of pouring himself into people, Paul had two who would get on the boat. Not two hundred. Two, and that was riches. Ask it before the storm starts: who would get on the boat with you? And whose boat are you on?

Who was Luke, and how do we know he was there? Luke was a doctor (Colossians 4:14), a Gentile companion of Paul, and the author of both the Gospel and Acts (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). In several passages he slips from “they” to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), quietly telling us he was present. He was with Paul on this voyage and in Rome, and stayed with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11).
verseByVerse.note: “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. Aristarchus later shared Paul’s imprisonment.

parallels.desc: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner

verseByVerse.quote: "The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day a pagan officer lets the worn-out prisoner go ashore to be cared for by the believers at Sidon; God’s kindness reaches Paul through a centurion and a local church, while the wind is against them from the start.

Sidon. A Phoenician port about seventy miles up the coast from Caesarea: the first day of the voyage.

Julius treated Paul kindly. After two years in custody Paul is worn out, and the centurion lets him go ashore to be tended by the believers, probably under guard. He did not have to: letting a prisoner bound for Caesar out of sight was a professional risk. Keep an eye on this man. He will side against Paul at Fair Havens and be wrong; he will act on Paul’s word at the ship’s boat and be right; and he will overrule the soldiers who want the prisoners dead, because he wants Paul alive (v. 43). He is one of a long line of decent pagans in Acts whose ordinary kindnesses God uses without their knowing.

Under the lee of Cyprus. On its sheltered side, out of the wind. The prevailing north-westerlies of late summer are already dead against them, and the wind will stay contrary for the whole chapter.

I was in prison and you came to me. Jesus said that on the last day the King will tell his people that he was in prison and they came to him, and that whatever they did for one of the least of his brothers, they did for him (Matthew 25:36, 40). The church at Sidon was caring for Christ in the person of his worn-out servant. And the Lord who will say that made himself the needy one first: born where there was no room, provided for by the women who followed him (Luke 8:3), bound and led away. He counts every kindness to his chained servants as done to himself.

Letting himself be cared for. Paul has spent his life being the one who gives; here he is a tired man being looked after by friends, and he lets them. Some Christians cannot accept help and mistake that for strength. How tender the Lord is with his tired children: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

How can I care for Christians who are in prison or hardship? Do what the believers at Sidon did: receive them, feed them, rest them and encourage them. Remember those in prison as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3). That may mean writing to persecuted believers through organisations that serve them, supporting the families of the imprisoned, prison visiting through a chaplaincy, or caring for a worn-out pastor or missionary home on leave. Small kindnesses at the right moment can strengthen someone for the storm ahead.
verseByVerse.note: Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre. “Under the lee” means sheltered from the wind by the island.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sails past his home province in chains, without stopping, to the port where a ship for Rome will be found: the promise advances by the most ordinary means.

Along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia. Cilicia is Paul’s home province. Over the northern horizon lies Tarsus, the city he named to the tribune with a flash of pride (21:39). He sails past it in chains, and there is no record that he ever set foot there again. Luke does not remark on it, but it is one of the quiet costs of a life spent going where you are sent: the places that formed you slide past on the horizon, and you do not get to stop.

Myra in Lycia. A major stop for the grain ships from Egypt, which could rarely sail straight west to Rome against the prevailing winds and so went north to the Asian coast and then west along it. Myra is where you changed from a coastal vessel to an ocean-going one.

How ordinary the mechanism is. The promise of Rome (23:11) advances this afternoon because a centurion goes down to the harbour looking for a westbound ship, and finds one. It is also a threshold nobody notices: from Myra Paul is crossing open water. The safe part of the journey ends without a warning, as it usually does.

He set his face. In his Gospel Luke told how Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and from then on everything moves toward the cross. The Son of Man who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58) had left far more than a home province: the glory he shared with the Father. Paul at the rail, watching Cilicia slide past, follows a Master who never stopped to go home on the way to the place he was sent, and whatever Paul loses on this coast, he loses for a Lord who lost far more for him.

What about the costs of going where God sends? They are real, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. Following Christ may mean leaving home, family, familiar places and plans, sometimes for good (Luke 9:57–62). Jesus promised that no one who leaves such things for his sake will fail to receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life (Luke 18:29–30). It is not unspiritual to feel the loss; Paul surely did. But it is never wasted. The places that slide past are in God’s keeping, and the city he is taking you to is better.
verseByVerse.note: Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is put aboard a grain ship bound for Rome, and from the start the wind fights them, pushing them slowly toward a coast nobody chose.

A ship of Alexandria. That means a grain freighter, and it explains most of what goes wrong in this chapter. Rome’s bread depended on Egyptian wheat, shipped each year in enormous merchantmen, the largest perhaps 180 feet long, and the emperors treated the grain supply as a matter of state security. That is why there are 276 people aboard, and why she is at sea so late in the year with a cargo she cannot afford to hold over till spring.

Slowly and with difficulty. Cnidus is on the south-western tip of Asia Minor, and the intended route was west past it to Greece and Italy. Instead they turn south-west, round Crete’s eastern cape at Salmone, and creep along the island’s sheltered southern shore: a long detour that leaves them on the wrong coast as the sailing season closes.

Bread for Rome. Rome sent this ship for bread, and the empire’s machinery stood behind the cargo. Nobody in Rome had sent for the prisoner. Yet the wheat will end on the sea floor off Malta (v. 38), and the prisoner will reach Rome and spend two years teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ (28:31). It is the contrast Jesus drew between food that perishes and the bread of God, who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:27, 33). Emperors could keep Rome’s granaries full for a season. Only Christ could feed her for ever, and he was sending his word there in chains.

How disasters are assembled. Nothing dramatic has happened yet: just weeks of a wind that will not cooperate, a schedule quietly falling apart, and a ship pushed toward a place nobody chose. Many disasters are assembled like that, from small pressures none of which seemed worth stopping for. The moment to stop is usually long before it feels necessary, and stopping then rarely looks heroic.

Do contrary winds mean God is against my plan? Not necessarily. Paul was exactly where God wanted him, and the wind was against him from the first day. Difficulty is not proof of disobedience, and ease is not proof of blessing. Sometimes God closes a road to redirect us (16:6–7); sometimes he lets us struggle on the right road to teach patience. The question is not how hard the journey is but whether you are going where his Word and wise counsel point. If you are, keep going, slowly if need be.
verseByVerse.note: Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Cnidus lay at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; they turned south to shelter behind Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With difficulty they reach Fair Havens, a small, dull and safe harbour: the one genuinely safe place in the chapter, and they will leave it.

Fair Havens. Luke surely enjoyed writing the name: Kaloi Limenes, a small bay on the south coast of Crete that still bears it. There was nothing wrong with it except that it was small, exposed and dull, an open anchorage beside a minor town, Lasea. It would have kept them alive.

A safe place that was inconvenient. The whole disaster turns on that. The ship is not lost through recklessness or wickedness. Ruinous choices are easy to see; it is harder to notice when something safe and unglamorous was available, a job that was not exciting, a church that was ordinary, a routine that was working, and the only reason for leaving it was that it was dull. The northeaster is six verses away, and every soul aboard would give everything to be back in the boring harbour.

What safety looked like from inside. Be fair to them, though. Wintering there meant four months with a valuable cargo idle, an owner losing money daily, and 276 people confined beside a village that could barely feed them. On the morning of the decision the safe option looked merely irritating. The right decision rarely announces itself; usually it just looks like the dull one.

How do I know whether to stay or move? Begin with Scripture and prayer: would either option require you to disobey God? Then ask honest questions. Do I want to leave because something is wrong, or because it is dull? Is the new thing necessary, or only better? What would I lose if it went badly, and could I bear it? Seek the counsel of mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22), and weigh your responsibilities to family and church. If staying is faithful and safe, boredom alone is a poor reason to go. If you do move, go humbly, knowing that God can redirect you.
verseByVerse.note: Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, 'Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Late in the season Paul warns, from experience, that sailing on will bring disaster: wise judgment, right about the storm, but not a word from God.

The voyage was now dangerous. Sailing in the Mediterranean was thought dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether from mid-November to March. The season is about to close.

The Fast was already over. The Day of Atonement, in late September or October; in AD 59, the likeliest year, it probably fell on 5 October. Luke, very probably a Gentile, dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar, a small sign of the world he and Paul shared.

Paul advised them. A prisoner giving advice. But years before, he had written to Corinth, “Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea” (2 Corinthians 11:25). He had perhaps been in the water more often than most of the crew.

I perceive. The language of assessment, not revelation. Paul does not say “Thus says the Lord”, and Luke does not present it as a word from God. It is common sense from experience: the season is gone, the ship has fought a headwind for weeks, and open water lies ahead.

Right about the storm, wrong about the deaths. Paul foresaw loss of life, and not one person died, as the angel would tell him (v. 22) and the last verse records. Luke leaves the discrepancy standing, and that is a mercy: Scripture does not claim that a godly man’s seasoned judgment is divine revelation. Paul giving his best assessment was right about the storm and wrong about the deaths. Paul delivering a message from an angel twelve verses later was exactly right about everything.

Once for all. Once a year on the Fast the high priest went behind the veil with blood for the sins of the people, and the next year he went again; that very repetition, says Hebrews, showed those sacrifices could never take sins away (Hebrews 10:1–4). On this ship sailed the apostle of the High Priest who entered the holy places once for all by means of his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). The Fast was over for that year. In Christ it is over for good, and Paul is carrying that news to the heart of the world.

How do I tell a godly person’s opinion from a word from God? Ask where it comes from. A word from God for us today is what Scripture says, rightly understood, and it binds the conscience. Anything else, however wise or sincerely felt, is counsel: to be weighed, tested against Scripture, and received with gratitude or set aside. Be wary when anyone, yourself included, says God told them about a decision Scripture does not address. Better to say with Paul: I perceive, this is my judgment. That is honest, humble and often very helpful.

Where Christians differ: does God still give prophetic words today? Many brothers and sisters believe God still gives prophetic impressions, and they agree that every such word must be tested and may never bind another’s conscience (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21).

This commentary’s view. With many Reformed Christians, this commentary holds that now the canon of Scripture is complete, Scripture is the one word that binds us. But both sides can agree to call a judgment a judgment.
verseByVerse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether in winter.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion follows the experts and the majority votes to sail on: a reasonable decision, made by competent men for sound reasons, and wrong.

The pilot and the owner. Who would not have listened to them? A lazy reading has the worldly men ignore the man of God and get what they deserve. But consider the room. On one side, the kybernētēs, the sailing master who handles this ship for a living, and the nauklēros, the owner or charterer whose money is aboard. On the other, a prisoner in chains with a religious reputation, no nautical qualification and no standing to speak at all.

Not suitable to spend the winter in. Fair Havens was poor and exposed. Phoenix, some forty miles farther west, was a proper wintering port, and a single day’s easy sail away.

The majority decided. By every ordinary measure the majority’s choice was reasonable. It was still wrong; truth is not decided by vote. The heart likes a majority because the crowd feels safe and shared blame is lighter. That is the fear of man, which lays a snare, while whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

The competent men got it wrong. Resist the moral that expertise is not to be trusted; the crew’s skill is about to keep everyone alive for two weeks. The point is narrower: competent men deciding a matter squarely in their field got it wrong, because expertise and profit can blind, and the one man with no standing got it right by ordinary observation. Luke offers no method for knowing in advance which situation you are in; most days the pilot and the owner are right. The one protection he shows is small and available to anyone: the harbour was safe, and the move was an improvement, not a necessity. Forty miles of improvement seemed worth a day’s risk at the wrong time of year.

Their voices prevailed. At the trial of Jesus the chief priests and rulers, the religious experts of the nation, and a crowd with them, shouted against the one man in the room who was right, and Luke writes with terrible brevity that their voices prevailed (Luke 23:23). The majority was never more wrong than on the day it condemned the Son of God. Christ never let the crowd, or even a friend, overrule his Father’s word (Matthew 16:21–23), and his perfect obedience is counted as ours when we trust him. Yet even that vote could not overturn the counsel of God: the crowd’s verdict sent him to the cross, where he gave his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The vote at Fair Havens will serve his purpose too.

Should Christians defer to experts? Generally, yes, in their fields. God gives real skill to doctors, engineers, pilots and lawyers, and it is wise and humble to listen to them. But experts are fallible, they can be swayed by money or pressure (the owner had a cargo to sell), and they cannot speak with authority on moral questions or on what God has said. So listen, ask questions, seek a second opinion when much is at stake, and notice when someone with less standing but real experience raises a concern. And never let a majority, however expert, persuade you to do what Scripture forbids.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gentle south wind seems to confirm their decision, and then a hurricane-force wind falls on them from the very shore they were hugging for safety.

The south wind blew gently. Perhaps the most dangerous sentence in the chapter, and it describes perfect weather: exactly the wind you want to run west along Crete, arriving as if on cue. Luke’s word for their state of mind is precise: “supposing”. They only thought they had what they wanted.

The northeaster. Luke gives the sailors’ own name for it, Eurakylōn, a rough dockside hybrid of the Greek for the east wind and the Latin for the north: a landsman writing down the term he heard shouted on deck. (The KJV, following later manuscripts, calls it Euroclydon.) “Tempestuous” is typhōnikos, typhoon-like. And “struck down from the land” is exact: Crete’s mountains rise to some eight thousand feet, and its killing winds fall off the high ground without warning.

The house the stream could not shake. Jesus ended his great sermon in Luke’s Gospel with weather of this kind. The one who comes to him, hears his words and does them is like a man who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock, and when the flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it (Luke 6:47–49). The sailors’ foundation was a gentle south wind and a majority vote, and it lasted an afternoon. Christ does not promise that his people will miss the northeaster. He promises himself as the rock beneath them when it falls, and his word as the one forecast that never deceives.

Weather is not confirmation. A favourable circumstance after a decision feels like confirmation, and it is nothing of the kind. A door opens easily, a house sells, the money arrives just in time, and Christians take it as proof that God has blessed the decision. Sometimes he has. But the gentle south wind blew for the ship that was about to be destroyed, at precisely the moment that made the destruction possible. A headwind that morning would have kept them alive.

How do I tell whether an open door is God’s guidance? An open door alone tells you very little; it may be God’s provision, or simply the weather. Guidance comes first from Scripture: is the choice in line with what God has commanded and with his priorities for your life? Then pray, seek wise counsel, and weigh your gifts, responsibilities and motives honestly. Circumstances can confirm a decision made on those grounds, but cannot replace them. Be especially cautious when the circumstance gives you exactly what you already wanted, and hold every decision humbly, ready for God to redirect you.
verseByVerse.note: The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from the mountains of Crete.

parallels.desc: he raised the stormy wind

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship can no longer head into the wind, so they give way and are carried along: helpless, but carried by a wind that answers to Christ.

Could not face the wind. “Caught” is Luke’s word for a person seized or arrested. “Could not face” is antophthalmein, literally to look in the eye; ancient ships often had eyes painted on the bow, and this one could not look the wind in the eye. A ship survives heavy weather by keeping her head into it; turned broadside she rolls, and turned tail she runs wherever the wind sends her. So they stop trying. No longer sailing, they are cargo, and the storm carries them.

Even winds and water obey him. When a windstorm came down on the lake and the disciples cried out that they were perishing, Jesus rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they asked who this could be, who commands even winds and water, and they obey him (Luke 8:23–25). That Lord now reigned at the right hand of God, and the wind driving this ship answered to him; to be carried by a storm that obeys Christ is very different from being lost in one. When the storm on the lake stopped, the disciples were afraid of him instead: the holy fear that is the right response to Christ, and the one fear that drives out all the others.

There is a time to stop fighting. Sometimes the competent, faithful thing is to stop trying to make headway and keep the hull together while you go where you are being taken. Anyone who has lived through a serious diagnosis, a bereavement or a stretch of depression knows the phase where effort no longer moves you, and the instinct is to treat it as a lapse of faith. Luke does not; it was what the professionals did, and it was right. Keep the hull together with the simple means of grace, rest, prayer however feeble, the company of believers, and leave the direction to God. Being carried is not the same as being lost.

The storm that will not be managed. Modern life runs on the promise of control, and quietly assumes that a well-run life should meet no storm the right plan cannot steer round. So when the unmanageable arrives, a diagnosis, a redundancy, a child who walks away, it feels somehow illegitimate. One popular answer is borrowed from the Stoics: Epictetus taught that some things are in our power and others are not, and that peace comes from caring only about the first. There is wisdom in that, and the crew practised it. But the Stoic can only ask you to accept an indifferent universe with dignity. Luke’s ship was not adrift in fate. The wind had a Lord, and that Lord had once given up every scrap of control he possessed, crying, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46), so that his people could be carried where they could not steer. Christians are not promised a steering wheel. They are promised hands.

Why does God not calm every storm, as Jesus did on Galilee? Because he has more than one way of saving his people. Sometimes he stills the storm (Mark 4:39); sometimes he brings us through it, as here; and sometimes he takes us home through it. In every case he is equally sovereign and equally present. A calmed storm shows his power over creation; a storm endured shows his power to keep his people and fulfil his word in the worst conditions. If he has not calmed yours, it is not because he cannot or does not care, but because he is doing something through it that a calm would not do (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

verseByVerse.quote: "Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the brief shelter of a small island the crew do everything competent seamen can to keep the ship together and slow her drift toward the deadly sandbanks.

Cauda. A scrap of land about twenty-three miles south of Crete. Running past it buys a few minutes of calmer water, and Luke records, in order, what a competent crew did with them.

The ship’s boat. The dinghy, towed astern in fair weather, was by now swamped and battering the hull, and it was their only means of getting ashore. Luke’s “we” suggests the passengers, the doctor among them, were hauling on the ropes too.

Undergird the ship. A last resort to stop the timbers working apart (on this and “lowered the gear”, see below).

The Syrtis. Vast shifting sandbanks off Libya, unmarked and constantly moving, where a stranded ship was slowly broken up miles from anywhere: a Roman byword for hopeless destruction, directly downwind. So the strategy is not escape or progress, but time, in the hope that the wind changes before the sandbanks arrive. They never reached the Syrtis, because the God who sets the bounds of the sea had marked out a different shore.

Is it faithless to take precautions when God has promised to keep us? No. The crew did everything a competent crew should, and Paul never rebuked them; later he would insist that they stay and use their skills (v. 31). Faith does not neglect means. Nehemiah prayed and set a guard (Nehemiah 4:9). Take your medicine, buckle your seat belt, save for the future, lock your door, and trust God. Precautions become faithless only when we trust them instead of him, or when fear drives us to grasp for control he has not given us.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. The deepest answer was given in the wilderness. When the devil set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and quoted Psalm 91’s promise that angels would guard him, he was inviting the Son of God to prove his trust by throwing away every ordinary safeguard. Jesus answered, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test’” (Luke 4:9–12). True faith does not leap to force God’s hand; it hauls in the boat, passes the cables and leaves the outcome with him.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are sailors’ technical language that cannot be pinned down exactly. “Supports” is literally “helps”: most take it as cables passed under the hull and winched tight, like a belt round a barrel, though some think of cables run lengthwise or of bracing. “They lowered the gear” is vague in Greek and probably means they let out a drag or sea anchor, or lowered the mainsail, to slow the drift and keep the bow steady. Either way, the aim is to hold the ship together and buy time.
verseByVerse.note: The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind. Cables were passed under the hull to hold it together. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day by day the storm strips them: first the cargo goes over the side, then the ship’s own tackle.

Jettison the cargo. Day two: overboard goes the cargo, the entire purpose of the voyage; the last of the wheat will follow on the final night (v. 38).

With their own hands. Day three: the tackle, spare spars, rigging, perhaps the main yard, the equipment needed to sail the ship even if she survives. Throwing it away admits there may be no sailing left to do, and the sailors do it with their own hands.

Something greater than Jonah. Jonah’s sailors threw their wares into the sea too (Jonah 1:5), and their storm came because of one man running from God; it ended only when he was thrown overboard and went down into the deep. On Paul’s ship the one man is going where God sent him, and his presence will save everyone aboard without anyone being thrown in. Jesus said that something greater than Jonah had come (Luke 11:30–32). He had done nothing to deserve the storm, and he went down into the deep of death of his own will, so that the storm of God’s judgment falls silent for everyone who belongs to him.

Profit, tools, hope. The sequence of many serious troubles: first the profit goes, then the tools, then hope itself (v. 20). The question stops being “What is this worth?” and becomes “Will this keep me afloat?” People discover in a hospital corridor, in hours, that almost everything they had been carrying was cargo, valuable in itself but at the critical moment only weight. The ship that reached Malta arrived with nothing in the hold and every soul aboard alive.

How do I let go of things I have valued? Name them before God honestly: possessions, plans, reputation, comfort, a dream. Thank him for them, because they were gifts. Then ask which of them you are holding so tightly that they keep you from obedience or peace. A person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15), and Paul counted everything loss compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Letting go is often painful, and grief over what is lost is not unbelief. But what you lose for Christ, or in the storms he sends, is never the thing that keeps you afloat. He is.

parallels.desc: the mariners hurled the cargo into the sea

verseByVerse.quote: "When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, 'Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no sun or stars and no food, every hope of rescue dies, even for the believers aboard; and into that darkness Paul stands up to speak.

Neither sun nor stars. With no compass, position and heading were worked out from the sun and stars. Take them away for many days and nobody aboard knows where they are, how far they have run, or which way they are pointing.

All hope was at last abandoned. “No small tempest” is understatement; the phrase after it is not. The verb suggests hope stripped away day after day, and the word for saved is one Luke will sound again until the last verse (see v. 44). And Luke includes himself: “all hope of our being saved”.

Without food. No cooking fires in a pitching hull, stores soaked with seawater, men too frightened and sick to eat: they are starving as well as terrified.

Paul stood up among them. He is about to tell exhausted, hopeless people that an angel spoke to him and nobody will die, and they have no earthly reason to believe him. So he establishes the one credential he has: I told you before, and I was right; now listen. He is not scoring a point but buying a hearing, and he needs one badly.

While the sun’s light failed. As Jesus hung on the cross there was darkness over the whole land while the sun’s light failed, and in that darkness he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:44–46); Matthew and Mark add that he cried out in the words of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The Son of God went into a darkness deeper than any storm, to bear the judgment our sin had earned, and came out of it on the third day. A believer in the dark is never as alone as he feels. His Lord has been further into the night than he will ever go, and he is a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

Despair is not the same as unbelief. The man who wrote a Gospel gave up hope in a storm, God did not hold it against him, and the promise did not depend on his morale. Paul himself once despaired of life itself, so that he would rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Unbelief refuses to trust what God has said; despair is what a believer feels when he sees no way out and has not yet heard God speak into it. When the word came (vv. 22–25), they all took heart (v. 36).

What should I do when I have lost all hope? Tell God, honestly; the psalms are full of people doing exactly that (Psalm 88). Do not make big decisions alone in the dark. Eat, sleep and let others help you, as Paul is about to insist. Hold on to God’s promises even when you cannot feel them; your feelings do not change his faithfulness (Lamentations 3:21–24). Speak to your pastor or a trusted believer. If despair persists, seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if medicine is needed, taking it is not a failure of faith but a good use of God’s gifts. If you are thinking of harming yourself, get help the same day: call your doctor or emergency services. The promise did not depend on Luke’s morale. It does not depend on yours.
verseByVerse.note: Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul promises that not one life will be lost, only the ship, because an angel of the God to whom he belongs has told him so.

Take heart. “Yet now”: two words turning the chapter from loss to promise. Paul’s word is euthymein, be of good cheer, a different word from the Lord’s to Paul in the Jerusalem barracks, tharsei, take courage (23:11). The Lord’s word to Paul in the dark was courage; Paul’s word to a shipful of starving pagans is cheer.

Only of the ship. A promise of God, astonishingly precise: not one person will die, and the vessel will be smashed. Paul does not soften the second half to make the first more welcome. A lesser comfort would have promised everything and delivered part; this promises exactly what will happen.

The God to whom I belong. As short a description of a Christian as any in Acts: belonging, then serving (“whom I worship” is the language of religious service), because the second follows from the first. He says it without apology to men who most likely honoured Isis and Serapis, the gods of Alexandria, or the emperor, at the one moment they are all listening. God does not abandon his property to the sea. To belong to him is to be safer in a sinking ship than any king on his throne.

Everything the angel gave Paul, you already have. Paul got one “Do not be afraid”; you hold a whole Bible of them, and the promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5), and the pledge that nothing can separate you from the love of God (Romans 8:38–39). Paul had an angel beside him for a night; you have the Spirit of Christ within you for life, and the Son himself, greater than all angels (Hebrews 1:4). So do not pine for a vision. The God who would not let the sea swallow Paul reigns over every wave of yours.

In everyday life. Say Paul’s phrase to yourself whenever fear rises this week: “the God to whom I belong and whom I worship”. And look for a moment, as Paul did, when people are listening, to name your God plainly and without embarrassment.

Should believers expect an angel like this today? Angelic appearances were never everyday even in the Bible; they cluster at the great hinge-moments, and this is one, God steering his apostle on a once-for-all mission. Today God ordinarily guides and comforts by surer, settled means: his completed Word, his indwelling Spirit, prayer and unseen providence; “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). Angels are still ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen; what we must not do is expect or chase visible appearances (Colossians 2:18).

What does it mean to belong to God? You are his by creation, and if you are a Christian, his by redemption, bought with the precious blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20; 1 Peter 1:18–19). That is a claim on your whole life, and also the deepest security there is, because God does not lose what belongs to him (John 10:28–29). The Heidelberg Catechism begins here: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and he said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s purpose that Paul must stand before Caesar cannot fail, and in grace he has given Paul the lives of everyone aboard; Paul’s courage rests on nothing but God’s word.

Do not be afraid, Paul. Paul was very probably afraid too, and the angel begins with comfort for him. The man who would encourage 275 people had first to be encouraged.

You must stand before Caesar. “Must” is Luke’s word for the fixed purposes of God (dei; on its use of the Son of Man, see v. 26), the word of the Lord in the barracks: “you must testify also in Rome” (23:11). The storm has changed the route, not the destination. The angel does not say “you will survive” but “you must stand before Caesar”: survival is simply what God’s purpose requires between here and Rome.

God has granted you all. Given freely, as a favour (kecharistai, from charis, grace): God has given Paul the 275 others aboard, perhaps in answer to his prayers. He owed that ship nothing: a crew that would try to desert, soldiers who would propose killing the prisoners, Paul among them (v. 42), prisoners bound for judgment. The promise concerned one prisoner, and into it he swept every soul aboard, because it pleased him to give them to his servant. He gives more than was asked, to people who did not ask, and so quietly that 275 people walked up a beach on Malta without the faintest idea that they had been handed to somebody as a present.

Exactly as I have been told. Paul’s assurance is not about the weather, the ship or his own resilience; he does not say “I have a good feeling”. On a disintegrating ship, with nothing he can see to support it, the sole ground of his composure is that God is not a liar. That is faith: not wishful thinking, but trust in a promise.

The pattern of the righteous one. Scripture often shows God blessing or sparing many for the sake of one. Potiphar’s household was blessed for Joseph’s sake (Genesis 39:5); Abraham pleaded until God agreed that ten righteous men would have saved a city (Genesis 18:32). The ordinary Christian has no idea what his presence is worth to the people around him; Paul did not know until an angel told him.

Those whom you gave me. Behind this gift stands a greater one. On the night before the cross Jesus prayed to his Father about the people you gave me out of the world, and said that he had guarded them (John 17:6, 12). Paul’s gift reached no further than the beach; the Father’s gift to the Son is a people from every nation, secured at the cost of his own life. Scripture’s word for this is election: God’s free choice, made before any of them was born or had done anything good or bad, of those he would save, flowing from his love alone (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). No one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28).
