In everyday life. Pray by name for the unbelievers around you; you may be on their ship for a reason.

Were the 275 saved eternally because of Paul? No. They were spared from drowning because of Paul; that was the gift. Eternal salvation is never inherited from someone else’s faith or presence; each person must repent and believe in Christ (16:31; Romans 10:9–13). A believer’s presence can bring real blessing to unbelievers around him, above all the hearing of the gospel; but only Christ’s righteousness saves, received by each one through faith. Pray that those blessed by God’s kindness for your sake will come to know him for themselves.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Reformed Christians speak of definite or particular redemption: Christ died for those given to him, and his death was aimed at, and actually secures, the salvation of a particular people, the sheep for whom the good shepherd lays down his life (John 10:11, 15). Many faithful Christians believe instead that Christ died for everyone in the same way. All agree that the offer is free to all, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37).

This commentary’s view. This commentary holds the Reformed view: Christ’s death is sufficient for all and effective for those the Father has given him, and so the gospel can be offered to anyone without reservation.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we must run aground on some island.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel’s promise includes the wreck: God will rescue them not from the disaster but through it, and he tells them so in advance.

We must run aground. From the same angel, in the same breath: the ship will be destroyed. “Must” again: God’s plan included the shipwreck. Not rescue from the storm, but rescue through it.

The wreck is inside the promise. The shipwreck is not a failure of the promise, nor an exception to it. Our instincts treat catastrophe as evidence that a promise has failed, and the ship breaking up on the rocks would look, to anyone in the water, exactly like God not keeping his word. In fact it was exactly what he had said. Nor does he hide it: for the rest of the storm they know that the ship is doomed and that they are not. God often deals with his people so, not removing the wreck but telling the truth about it early enough that when the timbers go, it is not the end of the world. Jesus did the same: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Necessary that the Christ should suffer. Luke’s “must” is the small word he used of Jesus: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected and be killed, and on the third day be raised (Luke 9:22). On the Emmaus road the risen Lord asked whether it was not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26). The disciples had treated the cross as the end of every promise; it was the promise. The wreck of Christ’s body looked to everyone watching like God failing, and it was God keeping his word to the letter. Because of that one, every lesser wreck in a believer’s life is inside God’s promise too.

What exactly did God promise? Ask it slowly; many Christians need it more than another verse about victory. Think of what you have been treating as proof that God did not come through: the illness that was not healed, the marriage that ended anyway, the job that went, the prayer that got the answer you were not asking for. Then ask, not “Why did this happen?”, but: what exactly did God promise? He has never promised the ship. He has promised, to those who are his, that nothing will separate them from his love (Romans 8:38–39), that he works all things together for their good (Romans 8:28), that he will never leave them (Hebrews 13:5), and that he will bring them home. Comfort, property and the preservation of your circumstances are not on the list. The wreck may well be inside the promise.

How do we know Paul was not simply deluded? Scripture itself tells us to test such claims: a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken from the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:22). Paul named things no one aboard could arrange: the ship lost, every life kept, a landfall on an island. Any of those could have failed in front of 275 witnesses, and Luke, who was there, records that every one came true. A deluded man hopes; this man made a forecast the sea could check. A sceptic may answer that the record comes from Paul’s friend, written afterwards. True; but Luke wrote while soldiers, sailors and prisoners from that ship could still contradict him, and his account has held up well wherever it can be checked.

Does God promise that Christians will be spared suffering? No; what he does promise is listed above. Jesus warned that his followers would suffer (John 15:20), the apostles taught that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22), and Paul himself would die in Rome. Teaching that faithful Christians will always be healthy, prosperous and safe is not the gospel. But neither is despair. What God promises, he keeps entirely, and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed (Romans 8:18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his promise to the last soul, and he keeps it through the means he has appointed. On the fourteenth night the ship nears land in the dark, and the crew anchor and pray for day (vv. 27–29). Paul stops the sailors abandoning ship, because the promise is to be kept through their seamanship (vv. 30–32). He urges everyone to eat, gives thanks for bread in front of them all, and they take heart (vv. 33–38). At dawn they strike a reef and the stern breaks up; the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops the soldiers killing the prisoners, and on planks and pieces of the ship all 276 reach land (vv. 39–44).
verseByVerse.theology:
Certainty and Effort Are the Same Faith

Verse 31 is the hinge: after an unconditional promise that not one life would be lost, Paul says that unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved (see the note on vv. 31–32). The same logic governs the meal at dawn (vv. 33–34).

The section also shows how God's promises are usually fulfilled: not by suspending the ordinary world but by working through the wreckage of it, swimmers and planks.

And quietly at the centre: the prisoners live because the centurion wanted Paul (see the note on vv. 42–43).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An hour before the ship broke apart, Paul took a piece of bread and thanked God for it out loud where everyone could hear. A shipful of frightened people watched a man in chains be visibly grateful to God, and they were encouraged, and they ate.

Now: Paul's argument had been outvoted at Fair Havens; what reached them now was his steady confidence in God. The people around you may forget what you said about God when things were going well; they will remember what you did on the worst morning of your life. That steadiness is not a performance; it is what the God who keeps his word gives his people in the storm.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two weeks lost in the dark, the sailors sense land and their soundings show the shore is near; no one aboard knew where they were, but God did.

The fourteenth night. Two weeks in a gale, with no sun or stars, little food and no idea where they are. Yet for fourteen nights, while sailors guessed, the Lord who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isaiah 40:12) knew exactly where that hull was.

The Adriatic Sea. In ancient usage, the whole central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy, Sicily and North Africa, not the narrow sea that bears the name today.

The sailors suspected. Not “saw”. In the middle of the night they very probably heard it: surf on a shore carries a long way across water, and no experienced sailor mistakes it. And for now the sound of land is the sound of danger. Land is where ships die, and a gale is driving them onto it in the dark, with no chart. The thing they have longed for may destroy them.

Twenty fathoms, then fifteen. A fathom was about six feet: a hundred and twenty feet, then ninety. Two soundings give a rate as well as a depth: the sea floor is rising fast, and the shore is close.

Details that fit a witness. The depths Luke records, in that order and at that spacing, correspond closely to the approach to St Paul’s Bay on Malta as it has been surveyed, and sailors who have calculated the drift of a large ship from Cauda in such a wind reckon it would reach Malta in about fourteen days. This does not by itself prove the story, but it is just what we would expect from a writer who was aboard, as his “we” claims.

In everyday life. When you have no idea where you are in life, keep doing the simple, faithful things, the soundings: read, pray, worship, work, listen. God is bringing you somewhere, even in the dark.

Do these accurate details really matter for faith? Yes, in their place. Faith rests on Christ and his Word, not on nautical measurements. But Luke’s details, the winds, the ports, the depths, the titles of officials, have been confirmed again and again where they can be checked, and show a careful historian (Luke 1:1–4). Accuracy in small things does not prove a miracle, but if he is trustworthy about the soundings off Malta, there is good reason to take him seriously about the empty tomb. The Bible’s history is not a decorative frame around spiritual truths; it is the place where God has acted.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily. The ESV notes that twenty fathoms is about 120 feet and fifteen about 90 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship's boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fearing the rocks, the crew anchor and pray for daylight; then they try to save themselves by stealth in the only boat, abandoning everyone else.

Four anchors from the stern. A ship normally anchors by the bow. Anchoring by the stern holds her with the bow pointed at the shore, so that at first light they can cut the cables, hoist a sail and run her straight up the beach without turning in the surf. Admiral Nelson was said to have read this chapter before the Battle of Copenhagen, where his ships anchored by the stern.

Prayed for day to come. Most naturally the sailors praying: pagan seamen hanging on four cables in the dark with rocks somewhere ahead, praying for morning. Luke reports it without scorn and without pretending it was conversion. It is what men do when there is nothing left to do, and the God who was actually holding that ship gave them the morning anyway.

Under pretense. Then the ugliest thing in the chapter. With a plausible lie the crew lower the dinghy to abandon more than two hundred and fifty people on a breaking ship, taking the only boat and all the seamanship aboard. They had heard Paul’s promise that not one life would be lost, and their answer was to leave in the dark.

The hired hand flees. Jesus described exactly this: the hired hand sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, because he cares nothing for them. Against that he set himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11–13). On the night of his arrest Christ did not lower a boat. He stepped forward to the men with swords and said, “if you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8), and then went alone to the cross. Every Christian rests on a Saviour who stayed when staying cost him everything.

Assenting and resting. Do not merely condemn them. Under real pressure, people who have genuinely heard a promise of God still make private arrangements, believing it the way one believes a weather forecast: taken seriously, and hedged against. The difference between assenting to a promise and resting your weight on it does not show until it is dark and the boat is in the water.

Does God hear the prayers of unbelievers? God hears everything, and in kindness he often gives good things to people who do not know him: rain and fruitful seasons, food and gladness, and a morning after a terrible night (14:17; Matthew 5:45). But the promise that he will hear and answer as a Father is for those who come to him through Christ, the one mediator (John 14:6, 13–14; 1 Timothy 2:5). An unbeliever’s cry for help can be the first stirring of seeking God, and he invites all to call on him in truth. If you pray for morning, pray to the God who made it, through the Saviour he has sent.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “prayed” can mean either to pray or to wish, and some translations have “wished for the day”. Prayer fits sailors in mortal danger, and most modern versions take it so, but “longed for day to come” is possible. Either way, there was nothing left for them to do but wait.
verseByVerse.note: Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready for beaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.' Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s promise that all will live is certain, and it is to be kept through means: the seamen must stay aboard, so Paul speaks up, and the soldiers cut the boat away.

Unless these men stay. A key sentence on how God’s promises relate to human action. Nine verses earlier, on an angel’s authority, came an unconditional promise: “there will be no loss of life among you”. Now: “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” Read flatly, they contradict each other. Both are true.

The decree includes the means. A decree is God’s settled purpose, what he has determined will happen, which nothing can overturn (Isaiah 46:10; Ephesians 1:11). He does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means by which they arrive. When he determined that every soul on that ship would live, he determined the whole chain: a boat cut loose at midnight, the seamanship to beach a ship at dawn, and a prisoner who noticed what the crew were doing and said something. So Paul’s absolute confidence and his urgent intervention are the same faith. A man who thinks everything depends on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well, and a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither.

The soldiers cut away the ropes. Instantly, and perhaps too eagerly: with the boat gone, everyone will have to swim. But look who is giving orders. A chained prisoner speaks, and a centurion’s men reach for their swords. At Fair Havens nobody listened to Paul; a fortnight of storm later, his is the only voice on the ship that carries weight. In a crisis authority moves to whoever turns out to know what is actually happening.

The definite plan and lawless hands. The clearest case is the cross. Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and killed by the hands of lawless men (2:23). Nothing was ever more certainly decreed, and nothing was ever carried out through more human choices, a traitor’s bargain, a governor’s weakness, soldiers with nails, for which real people were answerable (Luke 22:22). At the cross God’s fixed plan and real human choices meet, and the world is saved.

If God has already decided, why bother? Because the bothering is part of what God decided: the sailors staying aboard was the promise arriving. If God has promised to keep you, then read your Bible, go to church, confess your sin and stay away from what will ruin you, not although he has promised, but because the keeping happens through exactly those things. Paul puts it plainly: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). The “for” is the whole doctrine: we work because God is at work in us.

Does this mean salvation is conditional and can be lost? No. “Saved” here means rescued from the sea, as in vv. 20 and 44. But there is a parallel: as God kept his promise to the ship through means, so he keeps his people to the end, and the warnings and commands of Scripture are among the means he uses.

Should I still evangelise if God has chosen his people? Yes, all the more. God’s choice is the reason evangelism will not be in vain. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10), and in Corinth the Lord told him to keep speaking because he had many people in that city (18:9–10). We do not know who the elect are; we are told to preach to everyone. God brings his chosen ones to faith through ordinary means: the gospel spoken, a book given, a friend’s invitation, a prayer. You may be the means he has decreed.

Where Christians differ: God’s decree and human action. Some reason that if God has determined an outcome, what we do cannot matter, and some in the church have used that reasoning to neglect prayer or evangelism. Others, to protect the reality of human choice, hold that God permits free choices but does not determine them.

This commentary’s view. This verse holds both truths together. God decreed the end (all saved) and the means (sailors staying, eating, swimming, planks), and Paul’s warning was one of them. His sovereignty does not make human action pointless; it makes it meaningful. So with salvation: God has chosen his people, and calls them through preaching (Romans 10:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, 'Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before dawn Paul urges everyone to eat: God’s promise of life does not excuse them from gathering the strength they will need to reach the shore; it is the reason to do it.

Paul urged them all to take some food. The most spiritual man aboard spends the last hour before the wreck telling everyone to have breakfast. He could preach. Instead he meets the most urgent need first, and it is a physical one.

In suspense and without food. Fourteen days keyed up and watching, with no relief and no proper meal. They are about to attempt perhaps the hardest thing any of them will ever do, beach a disintegrating ship and swim through surf to an unknown shore, in a state of near-collapse.

It will give you strength. Literally salvation, safety (sōtēria): eating is part of their rescue. The logic is the same as with the sailors, applied to the body: God has promised that you will live, so eat, because you will need the strength for the swim. There is a kind of piety that would have prayed instead of eating. Paul does both, and he is not confused about which one supplies calories.

Not a hair is to perish. An old Hebrew proverb of complete safety (1 Samuel 14:45), and almost exactly what Jesus promised his disciples facing persecution, “not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18), said, remarkably, in the same breath as “some of you they will put to death” (Luke 21:16). So the promise guarantees not that nothing will touch you, but that nothing will be lost. Men may take your life, but they cannot take you from Christ, and the body they kill he will raise (Luke 12:4–7; John 6:40). Paul, an hour from the rocks, is handing on his Lord’s own words.

Ordinary pastoral care. When Elijah wanted to die, God’s first provision was a meal and a sleep, twice, before a word of correction (1 Kings 19:5–8). Much that looks like spiritual crisis is a body that has not eaten or slept. The Bread of Life, who multiplied loaves for the hungry and cooked breakfast on the shore for his tired disciples, stands behind Paul’s plain “take some food”. He is not too lofty to care for our bodies, nor too small to keep our souls.

Is it unspiritual to care about food, sleep and medicine when I am struggling? No. God made us bodies as well as souls, and he cares for both. Jesus fed hungry crowds and told his tired disciples to come away and rest (Mark 6:31). Eating properly, sleeping, exercising and seeing a doctor when you need one are ways of receiving God’s good gifts, not signs of weak faith, and low mood is often made worse by exhaustion and hunger. Look after your body, and bring your soul to God as well.

In everyday life. If someone you know is in crisis, take them a meal before you take them advice.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul publicly thanks God for bread and eats, and one man’s visible confidence in God gives the whole ship courage.

He took bread. Four verbs: took, gave thanks, broke, began to eat. Luke has written that sequence before: in the upper room, “he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them” (Luke 22:19), and at Emmaus, where two disciples recognised the risen Christ in that very gesture (Luke 24:30). Now he writes it on the deck of a doomed grain ship.

Is this the Lord’s Supper? Almost certainly not. There is no cup, no “This is my body” and no gathered church; this is a shipload of pagans, and the Supper is not given to unbelievers. Paul is doing what any devout Jew did as head of a household before a meal: taking bread, blessing God for it and breaking it. But Luke does not use that sequence carelessly, and the echo says something true: the Lord who broke bread with his disciples on the night he was betrayed is present with his servant on this ship, and the ordinary act of thanking God for food is the sign of it.

In the presence of all. He does not mutter it or wait until he is alone. A chained prisoner, about to swim for his life, audibly thanks the God of Israel for a piece of bread: the habit of a man who gave thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

They all were encouraged. Luke uses Paul’s word from v. 22: they became of good cheer. Not because the danger had lessened; the rocks were still there. Because one man’s confidence in God was visible, and courage is contagious in a way that argument is not.

On the night he was betrayed. The echo also teaches how to face trouble. Jesus gave thanks in the upper room with the cross hours away (Luke 22:15–19). Paul, an hour from the wreck, has learned from his Master that the Father can be thanked before the rescue arrives, because the Master’s own thanksgiving was answered by an empty tomb. And he had not calmed this sea; for fourteen days he sent no light, no let-up, no sign. Yet the One who gathers the wind in his fists (Proverbs 30:4) is no less sovereign when he lets it blow, and not absent when the sky is shut.

Should I give thanks for meals in public, in a restaurant or at work? It is a good and natural habit, and it can be a quiet witness, as Paul’s was. A brief, sincere thanks is enough. Avoid display, which Jesus warned against (Matthew 6:5), but do not hide your gratitude out of embarrassment either. With unbelievers you might simply say, “I am just going to thank God for this”, and do it. Thanksgiving for daily bread is one of the simplest ways to show that you live before God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: "(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke counts the 276 people the promise covers, every one of them, and the wheat, the whole purpose of the voyage, goes into the sea.

276 persons. Luke drops the number into the action like a man checking a ledger. It is the figure the promise must be measured against: all 276 must reach the shore.

Throwing out the wheat. They need the hull riding high so she will run as far up the beach as possible. So the wheat goes, and with it the entire purpose of the voyage (see vv. 6–7).

Every one counted. God did not promise to save a shipload. He promised not to lose a person: soldiers, sailors, prisoners, the owner, a doctor, a Macedonian, an apostle, every one counted. That is the arithmetic of the Good Shepherd. It was the Father’s will, Jesus said, that he should lose nothing of all that had been given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). Luke’s 276 is a small picture of the count Christ will make at the end of all things.

Failed and succeeded. The voyage failed completely, by every measure it was undertaken for. And it succeeded entirely, because the one cargo God cared about was a prisoner he had promised to get to Rome, and 275 people he had thrown in as a gift.

Does God care about me as an individual, or only about his people as a whole? Both, and the one does not swallow the other. God loves his church as a whole, the bride of Christ, and he also knows each of his people by name (John 10:3). Jesus told of a shepherd who left ninety-nine to find the one, and said there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:4–7). Luke counted 276, and God counted each one. You are never lost in the crowd to him.

In everyday life. Look around your church this Sunday and notice someone you have never spoken to. God has counted them. Learn their name.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read seventy-six, as the ESV notes. The number 276 is far better attested, and the shorter reading probably arose from a copyist’s confusion of Greek numerals. A large grain ship could easily carry that many; Josephus tells of sailing in one with six hundred aboard.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At daylight, on a coast no one recognises, the crew make one skilful, all-or-nothing run for a beach.

They did not recognize the land. Not one man aboard, crew included, knows the coast. It is Malta, at the place traditionally called St Paul’s Bay, off the main shipping route; they will learn its name only ashore (28:1).

A bay with a beach. Luke is cautious: “if possible”. They can see one hopeful feature, a beach rather than cliffs, and the plan is to drive the ship straight at it.

They cast off the anchors. Not hauled up but cut loose: four anchors left on the bottom, a one-way manoeuvre with no second attempt. Ancient ships were steered by two great oars, or rudders, one each side of the stern, lashed up for a fortnight so the storm would not smash them. Now they are freed, because for the first time in two weeks the ship is to be steered somewhere on purpose, and a small foresail gives her enough drive. It is a good plan, executed correctly. Then it goes wrong, through something no seamanship on earth could have prevented.

All things were created through him. Every rope, timber and gust they worked with had been made through the Son: all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). And when the Son came into his own world, he came as a craftsman; Nazareth knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). The skill on that deck was his gift, though the sailors did not know him. Common grace means God’s goodness to all people, believers or not: sun and rain, food, skill and sense (Matthew 5:45). It is never faceless. It is the kindness of Christ to people who have not yet heard his name.

Is it right to admire unbelievers’ skill? Yes. Every good skill comes from God, the giver of every good and perfect gift (James 1:17), who gives them to believers and unbelievers alike. Bezalel’s craftsmanship was the gift of God’s Spirit (Exodus 31:1–5); the pagan sailors’ seamanship was his gift too. Thank God for the surgeon, the pilot, the engineer and the electrician, whether or not they know him. Honour their work, and pray that they will come to know the Giver.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An unseen reef wrecks the ship a short way from safety: the painful half of God’s promise arrives, and no one is yet safe.

Striking a reef. A shoal or bar they could not see (see below). Nothing in the crew’s handling was wrong, and that is not how we prefer disasters to work: the wreck comes not from the bad decision at Fair Havens, which produced the storm they survived, but from an unseen ridge a short distance from safety.

The bow stuck. Forward, the ship jammed solid; aft, the surf demolishing her plank by plank, with 276 people standing on her and no boat. It is the worst moment of the voyage.

Half the promise kept. The angel’s promise is now exactly half fulfilled (v. 22): the ship is lost, and no one is yet safe. That is very often the position of faith: the painful part of the promise arriving on schedule, and nothing yet to show for the good part but the character of the one who said it.

Remember how he told you. The disciples once stood exactly there. On the Friday the painful half of what Jesus had told them came true: he was delivered into the hands of sinful men and crucified. For two nights and a day they had nothing to show for the other half, that he would rise on the third day, except the word of the one who said it. Then the women found the stone rolled away and heard the angels say, “Remember how he told you” (Luke 24:6–7). Every believer standing on a breaking wreck stands where they stood on the Saturday, and the Saviour who kept the second half of his word for them will keep it for us.

Why do bad things happen when I have done everything right? Because we live in a fallen world where hidden reefs exist, and not every hardship is a punishment or the result of a mistake. Jesus said the man born blind was not suffering for his own sin or his parents’ (John 9:1–3), and that those killed when a tower fell were no worse than anyone else (Luke 13:4–5). God is sovereign over such things and has purposes in them, often hidden from us. Do not torment yourself searching for what you did wrong when Scripture gives you no reason to. Bring the pain to God, and hold on to what he has promised.

Uncertain wording. Luke’s phrase is literally “a place between two seas”, as the ESV notes. It probably means a shoal or spit with open water on both sides, where currents meet, or perhaps a channel between an island and the shore; a likely spot has been identified in St Paul’s Bay. The exact feature is uncertain; that the ship struck bottom short of the beach is not.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them: everyone is spared for the sake of one man.

The soldiers’ plan. Under Roman discipline a guard who let a prisoner escape could be made to suffer the prisoner’s penalty. Luke has shown this twice: Herod executed the sentries when Peter got out (12:19), and the Philippian jailer drew his sword on himself rather than face what was coming (16:27). These soldiers are coldly working out how to save their own necks.

Wishing to save Paul. Julius intervenes, and Luke tells us why: he wanted Paul alive. To save this one man he forbade the killing of any prisoner, and God’s promise was kept through a centurion’s will. It is the third time in the chapter that Paul’s presence has saved people who had no idea of it: the angel gave him all 275 lives (v. 24), his warning kept the crew aboard (v. 31), and now his value to a Roman officer turns aside the swords.

Those who could swim. The centurion sends the swimmers first, so the strongest are ashore to help the rest: decent leadership from a pagan officer, and the last thing he does in the book.

The shape of the gospel. Luke does not say so, but the shape of the gospel is unmistakable: people with nothing to commend them, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. And at the centre stands One who deliberately took the place of the condemned and let the sentence fall on himself; we live because the Father has accepted us for his Son’s sake. For the sake of one Man, a multitude no one can number walks out of the surf of judgment alive. The prisoners on that beach owed their lives to a man they had probably never spoken to. Every Christian owes rather more than that, to a Man who sought him out.

Should I stay in a workplace or family where I am the only believer? Usually, yes, unless you are being drawn into sin or are in danger. Paul taught that each believer should remain in the situation in which God called him, as far as it is right to do so (1 Corinthians 7:17–24), and that a believing husband or wife can be a blessing to an unbelieving household (1 Corinthians 7:12–16). Your presence may be doing more good than you know: restraining evil, showing kindness, earning trust, keeping the gospel within reach. If you are in danger, abused, or pressured to deny Christ, seek help and safety; God does not ask you to stay in harm’s way.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every one of the 276 reaches land, on planks and pieces of the wreck: God’s word is kept exactly, to the last soul.

On planks or on pieces of the ship. See how the promise is kept: not by a calmed sea or an angel, but by exhausted people thrashing through cold surf, and those who cannot swim clinging to bits of the ship. The wreckage is the lifeboat. We wait for God to keep his promises in a manner we would find impressive; he is far more likely to keep them by way of a plank, something splintered off the thing that fell apart, floating within reach as you go into the water.

All were brought safely to land. Luke’s last word on the voyage is the arithmetic, and it is perfect: 276 went aboard, and 276 came ashore. Paul’s own assessment had feared loss of life; the word of God promised better, and kept it. The verb is chosen with care: diasōthēnai, saved through, rescued completely. Luke has sounded “save” through the chapter, from hope of being saved abandoned (v. 20) to “you cannot be saved” (v. 31), and now all were saved through to land. A reader who knows that elsewhere in Acts this word means salvation from sin will hear the echo.

Not one of them perished. He said not one of them would perish, and not one perished. That is what his word is like. It does not arrive tidily or on anyone’s chosen schedule, but it arrives in full, down to the last person on the roll, because the One who gave it does not deal in approximations and has never yet mislaid a single thing entrusted to him. Most of those dripping on that foreign shore had no idea whose word had carried them in. Glory to the God who keeps his promises to the last soul.

Is the shipwreck a picture of salvation? Luke does not present it as an allegory, and we should not turn every plank into a symbol; it is history. But some have rightly seen in it a picture of how God saves: the ship of this world breaks apart, but all whom the Father has given to Christ are brought safely home, some swimming, some clinging to planks, all safe (John 6:39). The parallel lies in the faithfulness of God. He promised, and he lost no one, which is exactly what Jesus says of those the Father has given him.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.
27.overview:
Where we are. Paul has defended himself before Agrippa (ch. 26), and having appealed to Caesar he now sails for Rome, probably in the autumn of AD 59. The “we” returns: Luke is aboard, and this chapter is his eyewitness log of the voyage and the wreck. Chapter 28 brings the survivors to Malta and Paul at last to Rome.

The message. God keeps his word to the last soul, and he keeps it through ordinary means. The Lord had told Paul that he must testify in Rome (23:11), and neither a gale, a reef, a deserting crew nor soldiers with drawn swords can prevent it; God even gives Paul the lives of everyone sailing with him. The wreck itself is inside the promise: the ship is lost, and no one is.

Why it was said. Luke’s first readers needed to know that the apostle’s chains had not derailed the gospel (see the introduction). He gives the voyage more space than almost any other episode because it shows what his whole history has been proving: nothing, not councils, courts or the sea itself, can stop the word of the Lord from reaching the place he has said it will go.

How the chapter makes its case. Slowly, against the wind, they reach Fair Havens on Crete (vv. 1–8), where Paul’s warning is outvoted (vv. 9–12). A gentle south wind lures them out, and the northeaster drives them helpless until all hope is gone (vv. 13–20). Then the prisoner stands up with an angel’s promise: the ship will be lost, but not one life (vv. 21–26). On the fourteenth night Paul stops the sailors deserting and gives thanks for bread in front of them all (vv. 27–38). At dawn the ship strikes a reef; the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops the soldiers killing the prisoners, and all 276 reach land (vv. 39–44).

Where it leads. The voyage belongs to the Lord who once rebuked the wind and now reigns over this one. The “must” of Paul’s journey is the “must” of Christ’s own road to the cross, where what looked like God failing was God keeping his word to the letter. And as 275 people live for the sake of one man they hardly knew, so sinners live for the sake of the Son, who loses none of those the Father has given him (John 6:39).

For us. God has not promised his people the ship: comfort, property, the preservation of our circumstances. He has promised that nothing will separate us from his love and that he will bring us home. So take every ordinary precaution, give thanks in front of others, and rest your whole weight on what he has said.

keyVerse.quote: So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.
keyVerse.note: On a breaking ship, with no sun or stars, Paul’s courage rests on nothing he can see, only on what God has said. That is what faith is: not a good feeling about the weather but trust in a promise because of the one who made it. The rest of the chapter shows the promise kept to the last soul.

27.reflection:
Fair Havens was safe but dull, and the experts and the majority voted to leave it (vv. 8–12). When have you been tempted to leave something safe mainly because it was ordinary? How should we weigh expert advice, the majority view and a concern raised by someone with less standing?

A gentle south wind seemed to confirm the decision to sail, and it led straight into the storm (vv. 13–14). How can we tell God’s guidance from circumstances that simply give us what we already wanted?

God promised that no one would die, yet Paul insisted that the sailors stay and that everyone eat (vv. 22–24, 31–34). Why does God’s certain promise make our ordinary obedience more urgent rather than less? Where does that apply to you this week?

God promised the lives, not the ship (v. 22). Is there something in your life you have treated as proof that God did not come through? What has he actually promised you, and how does the cross show that he keeps his word?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brings his servant to Rome through the hands of people who never know they are serving him. Islanders who speak no Greek light a fire for the shipwrecked (vv. 1–2). A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the crowd judges him first a murderer and then a god, wrong both times (vv. 3–6). Paul prays for Publius’s father and many others and they are healed, and the island provisions the company (vv. 7–10). After three months a ship with a pagan figurehead and a kind south wind carry them to Puteoli, where believers are already waiting (vv. 11–14). Roman Christians walk out along the Appian Way to meet Paul, and the weary apostle thanks God and takes courage (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it by a believer: a fire lit by islanders, a Roman official's hospitality, a winter's provisions, a ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux, a favourable wind. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes, the ordinary people and events of the world, is not an abstraction in Acts: it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and were wrong twice, in opposite directions, within one evening (see the notes on vv. 3–4 and 5–6).

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15: God's provision for a discouraged apostle was a handful of ordinary Christians on the road (see the note on vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Believers in Rome heard that a prisoner they had never met was on the road. They walked as far as forty-three miles to wait at the side of the Appian Way. They did not free him or improve his legal position by a single clause. They turned up, and the apostle to the Gentiles thanked God and found he could go on.

Now: The strong Christian you know may need this more than he will say; Paul had faced down a mob, survived a shipwreck and shaken off a snake, and still arrived on that road with his courage low. Showing up rarely feels worth the trip; Luke thought it worth a verse, and it is the love Christ has first shown you that you carry down the road.

verseByVerse.quote: "After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the sea, God gives his servant a fire and a welcome, from strangers who have never heard of him.

Malta. They did not know where they were until somebody told them. Malta is a small island about sixty miles south of Sicily, well off the route to Italy; they have been blown some five hundred miles in a fortnight.

The native people. Luke’s word came into English as barbarians (barbaroi) and has picked up a sneer it does not carry here. To a Greek speaker it simply meant people who did not speak Greek; the Maltese spoke a Punic dialect. Luke is not calling them savage; he is telling you nobody on that beach could understand the locals.

Unusual kindness. Literally, love of human beings (philanthrōpia), the root of our philanthropy, and more than anyone had a right to expect: nearly three hundred strangers with nothing left, at the start of winter, every one of them needing to be fed.

They kindled a fire. No sermon, no miracle: wet wood, rain coming on, and people who did not have to light a blaze for foreigners who could not thank them in any language they knew. The God who brought 276 people out of the sea had a fire ready for them on the shore. A centurion’s courtesy at Sidon, a crew’s seamanship in the gale, and now a bonfire lit by people who had never heard his name: he uses what is there, and the people he uses generally never find out.

The kindness of God our Saviour. Luke’s word for the islanders’ kindness appears only once more in the New Testament, and Paul uses it: when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy (Titus 3:4–5). The Maltese lit a fire for strangers who had nothing to offer. That is a small, true picture of what God has done in Christ on an infinitely greater scale: he came to a world of wrecked people, strangers and enemies to him, and welcomed us when we had nothing to bring.

In everyday life. Think of the newcomers in your street or church this month, and light a fire for one of them: an invitation, a meal, a lift.

Should Christians accept help from people who do not share their faith? Yes, gratefully. Paul accepted the islanders’ fire, Publius’s hospitality and the provisions they loaded on board. All good things come from God, and he often gives them to his people through unbelievers. Receive such kindness with thanks, honour the givers, and let your gratitude be a witness. The obligation also runs the other way: Christians are to do good to everyone, not only to fellow believers (Galatians 6:10), and the islanders’ kindness is a standard the church should never fall below.
verseByVerse.note: Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect, not Greek, which is why Luke calls them “native people.”

verseByVerse.quote: "When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, 'No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The islanders read the viper as Justice catching up with a murderer, and they are wrong: you cannot tell how a person stands with God from what happens to him. The man with the snake on his hand is the one person on that beach whom God had promised to bring safely to Rome.

A bundle of sticks. Paul is the senior figure in this company by any spiritual measure, an ageing man just struggled ashore from a wreck, and he is collecting firewood: not directing the collection, not resting by the blaze. The man who wrote that Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7) had learned to serve from his Lord.

A viper came out. Exactly what happens when you throw a bundle of sticks on a fire: something cold-blooded sleeping in it, sluggish from the cold, wakes up in the heat.

No doubt this man is a murderer. Perhaps they saw his chains. Certainly they hold a belief, more common than its pagan form suggests, that bad things happen to bad people. Justice is Dikē, the goddess believed to hunt down the guilty. Their reasoning is tight: he survived a shipwreck, which looked like a reprieve; now a viper has him; so the reprieve was an illusion and the debt has been collected.

Half right. Half of that is right, and it is the half we are least comfortable with. There is a moral order; guilt is real and is not finally evaded. What is wrong is the assumption that you can read a person’s standing with God from what happens to him. It is the mistake of Job’s friends, alive in every sickroom where somebody wonders aloud what they did to deserve this.

Justice had already been satisfied. The islanders were wrong about where justice had fallen. The man with the viper on his hand had once persecuted the church, guilty of far more than they imagined (1 Timothy 1:13–15). But his sentence had already been carried out, on another man. Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and for Paul, as for everyone in Christ, Justice has nothing left to collect. The penalty has been paid once, and God does not demand it twice (Romans 8:33–34).

The religion that never went away. Plenty of people who would never call themselves religious hold the islanders’ creed under the name of karma: what goes around comes around, the universe keeps score. It is not a foolish belief; it is the conscience insisting that the world is moral. But notice what it does to a life: every good day is a wage you earned and every bad day an invoice, and you can never stop checking the books, your own or anyone else’s. The singer Bono once told an interviewer that karma lies at the heart of the world’s religions, and that the most startling idea he knew was grace, which interrupts it. That is what happened on this beach. By the islanders’ reckoning Paul had earned the viper, and by his own he had earned far worse, but his debt had been paid by another. Karma can only tell you what you are owed. Grace tells you what has been paid.

In everyday life. Since your Lord stooped to wash feet, look for the firewood job this week: the small, unglamorous task at home, church or work that nobody wants, and do it.

Does my suffering mean God is punishing me? Not necessarily, and for a Christian never in the sense of paying for your sins. Christ has borne the punishment for all the sins of his people (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, out of love, to train them (Hebrews 12:5–11), and sometimes suffering is the natural consequence of a particular sin, which should be confessed and forsaken. But much suffering has no direct link to any sin of ours; it comes from living in a fallen world, and God uses it for our good and his glory (John 9:3; Romans 8:28). If you are unsure, ask God to show you anything you need to repent of, and then rest in his love.

No snakes on Malta today? There are no venomous snakes on Malta now, and sceptics have made something of that. It is not much of an argument. Two thousand years of dense settlement on a small island, more wooded then, can easily wipe out snakes, and the islanders recognised the creature on sight and stood waiting for a specific and familiar death. Luke does not call it a miracle; he reports what they expected and that Paul came to no harm, and leaves the reader to weigh it.
verseByVerse.note: “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps the hand that must carry the gospel to Caesar, while the fickle crowd swings from calling Paul a murderer to calling him a god, wrong both times.

He shook off the creature. No drama, no speech, no gesture toward heaven: he shakes his hand over the flames and goes on with the evening. Paul must stand before Caesar (27:24), and no snake could stop that.

Waiting for him to swell up. Luke, a doctor, gives the two things the islanders were watching for, in words medical writers also used: swelling and inflammation, or sudden collapse. They knew the symptoms.

They said that he was a god. Within one evening, on exactly the same evidence, Paul goes from murderer to deity. Nothing about him has changed. The second verdict is as wrong as the first, and more dangerous. At Lystra it had happened in the opposite order: a healing brought out the priest of Zeus with oxen and garlands, Paul tore his clothes and insisted he was a man like them, and soon the same crowd stoned him (14:11–19). Luke records no protest here, but there is no cult of Paul on Malta; how he answered the compliment is told at vv. 7–8.

The serpent struck. The hand it bit was the hand God was keeping for Rome. On the cross the old serpent, the devil, struck the Son of God, and the Son of God crushed him.

Authority to tread on serpents. Sending out the seventy-two, Jesus gave them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and at once turned their eyes from the wonder: do not rejoice in this, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:19–20). Paul behaves on the beach like a man who has taken that lesson to heart: he makes no sermon out of the snake and no show of his safety.

Judged by the crowd. The people who decide you are wonderful and the people who decide you are worthless are often the same people, working from the same evidence, a fortnight apart. A man who needs the first verdict will be destroyed by the second. Paul appears to have taken no notice of either.

How should I respond to praise and to blame? With the same steadiness, because neither is the final verdict. Paul wrote that it was a very small thing to him to be judged by any human court; it is the Lord who judges him (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Receive praise graciously and pass the glory to God; receive criticism humbly, asking whether there is truth in it, and change if there is. But build your sense of worth on neither. Your standing rests on God’s verdict in Christ, and that does not swing with the crowd.

Where Christians differ: snake-handling. Some groups handle venomous snakes in worship, citing this passage and Mark 16:18.

This commentary’s view. Paul did not pick up the snake on purpose; it bit him by accident, and God protected him. Mark 16:9–20 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and is not a command. Deliberately testing God this way is forbidden (Matthew 4:7). God protects his servants in their work; he does not ask us to court danger.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leading man of Malta takes the castaways in, and the Lord answers Paul’s prayer by healing his host’s father.

Publius. Luke’s title for him is literally the first man (prōtos). Inscriptions found on Malta, in Greek and in Latin, show that “first man of the island” was the formal title of its leading official: a quiet mark of Luke’s accuracy.

Three days. Even if it is only the officers and their charges rather than all 276, feeding and sheltering the shipwrecked for three days is serious generosity at the beginning of winter.

Fever and dysentery. Luke the physician is precise. The Greek reads, literally, fevers and dysentery, a plural that medical writers used for fever coming in recurring bouts. Many have suggested Malta fever, a bacterial infection often carried in goat’s milk; that cannot be proved, but the description fits.

Visited him and prayed. Three verbs, and the order matters. He visited. He prayed, before he touched him, because the power was God’s (3:16). He laid his hands on him and healed him. Declared a god the night before, Paul sits with one sick man and prays for him, and that corrects the islanders: a man who has to pray is plainly not a god.

As at Capernaum. In Luke’s Gospel, Jesus entered Simon’s house, where Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and rebuked the fever; then, as the sun was setting, all who had any who were sick brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them (Luke 4:38–40). The pattern on Malta is the pattern of Capernaum. Luke is not saying Paul is a second Jesus; the islanders had just made that mistake. He is saying the risen Lord is still at work, through his servant, as he was in Galilee in person.

How should I pray for someone who is sick? Boldly and humbly together. Ask God plainly to heal, because he is able and he invites us to ask (James 5:14–16; Philippians 4:6). Ask also for what he has certainly promised: his presence, strength to endure, wisdom for the doctors, and the person’s spiritual good. Use medical help gratefully, as one of God’s means. Visit, as Paul did; sometimes the visit is the greatest comfort. And leave the outcome to God without guilt. If healing does not come, it is not because your faith was too small; God’s will is wiser than ours, and for his people the final healing is certain at the resurrection.

Where Christians differ: does the gift of healing continue? These healings confirmed Paul as an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12) as the gospel came to a new people. Yet Paul himself left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Many faithful Christians believe God still gives gifts of healing today.

This commentary’s view. With many Reformed Christians, this commentary holds that such sign gifts marked out the apostles and their message and ceased with them. Believers still pray for the sick, as James teaches (James 5:14–15), and God heals as he wills, but no one today holds the apostle’s gift. We gladly agree with those who differ that God heals in answer to prayer, and that every claim must be tested by Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman official on Malta, found in inscriptions there. Luke, a doctor, names the illness precisely.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole island comes to be healed: the kindness of God reaches Malta in the wake of a shipwreck.

The rest of the people. Malta comes to the door. Luke’s verb, etherapeuonto, gives us therapy; its tense suggests a stream of people over the weeks. Some suggest that Luke the doctor also treated them medically.

No sermon in the text. Three months on the island, and Luke records not one sermon. He is plainly not telling us everything: it is very hard to imagine Paul spending a winter among people who had watched God heal their sick and saying nothing about him. The silence is Luke’s, not Paul’s, and a church has existed on Malta from early times. What Luke does record is the gospel travelling by kindness received and returned: a fire lit by strangers, a house opened, a sick man prayed for, a queue of islanders healed, provisions loaded aboard at the end. God took a disaster and made it the door of mercy for a whole island.

Tell John what you have seen. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus pointed to what was happening around him: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them (Luke 7:22). The healings were never the whole message. They were the King’s signature on it, the signs Isaiah had promised, and the cures on Malta pointed past themselves to the Healer who will one day make all things new.

Mercy and the message. Mercy shown to a body is no substitute for telling people about Christ; a man can be cured of dysentery and still be lost for ever. But mercy is not less than a sermon either, and it is very often what gets a sermon listened to.

How do I hold together good deeds and gospel words? Do both, and do not let either crowd out the other. Jesus healed and preached; the early church fed widows and proclaimed Christ. Good deeds show the love of God and give credibility to the message (Matthew 5:16; 1 Peter 2:12). Words explain whose love it is and how a person can be saved, because faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). Serve people generously, and when the door opens, as it often will, gently tell them why you do it and about the Saviour who has done so much more for you.

verseByVerse.quote: "They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who stripped the company of everything in the storm sends them on fully provisioned, by the hands of people who worship other gods.

Whatever we needed. They arrived having thrown everything into the sea, and leave three months later with a provisioned ship. Every scrap came from people who had no notion that they were outfitting the apostle to the Gentiles for the last leg of his journey to Caesar.

After three months we set sail. Early in the spring, when sailing resumed, in another Alexandrian grain freighter, the same class of vessel that was wrecked three months earlier. They get on board anyway.

The twin gods. The Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus in the old stories and patron deities of sailors, who prayed to them for safe passage and took a glow at the masthead as the sign that the twins had come to rescue them. So the apostle of the living God completes his journey under their painted faces, and Luke notes it, perhaps with a smile.

The sons of Zeus and the Son of God. In the worst storm of all, no twin god came. The One who kept that ship was the God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose Son really did come down, not in sailors’ legend but in flesh, and who rescues not by a light at the masthead but by a cross and an empty tomb. Paul could sail under the painted twins without a flicker of anxiety because he knew the only Son of God, and the twins were wood: an idol has no real existence (1 Corinthians 8:4).

Should Christians avoid everything linked with other religions? Not everything. An idol is nothing and the earth is the Lord’s, so a Christian may eat food bought in the market, travel on a ship with a pagan figurehead, use days of the week named after Norse gods, or live in a city full of temples (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). What we must never do is take part in the worship of other gods, or lead a weaker believer to violate his conscience (1 Corinthians 8:9–13; 10:20–21). Ask: am I worshipping, or merely living in a world where others worship? Am I harming anyone’s faith? Then act with freedom and love.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus and protectors of sailors.

verseByVerse.quote: "Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the storm the Lord gives a following wind and brings his servant safely to harbour in Italy.

A south wind sprang up. Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy, on the Straits of Messina. From there, after everything, a following breeze: around two hundred miles in two days. Luke does not point out the contrast with the previous voyage; on the last stretch the wind simply gets behind them and they fly.

Puteoli. On the Bay of Naples, the main port for the Alexandrian grain ships, some 140 miles from Rome by road. Seneca describes the crowds of Puteoli turning out to watch the grain ships come over the horizon. This one is delivering a prisoner, and nobody in the port has any idea that he is the only cargo the voyage was ever really for.

He brought them to their desired haven. Psalm 107 sings of those who go down to the sea in ships: the Lord raises the storm, they are at their wits’ end, they cry to him, he makes the storm be still, and he brings them to their desired haven (Psalm 107:23–30). On Galilee the disciples watched Jesus do what that psalm says only the LORD does (Luke 8:24–25). Paul’s voyage reads like that psalm told at length, and this verse is its last line. The Lord who commands winds and water will bring all his people, after every storm, into the harbour he has prepared.

Should I be suspicious of easy times, after what happened with the south wind in chapter 27? No; be thankful, and humble. The lesson of the gentle south wind at Crete (27:13) was not that good weather is dangerous, but that it does not prove every decision right. Here the south wind is simply God’s kindness after the storm. Receive easy seasons as gifts, give thanks for them, and keep walking carefully; God is as much in the fair wind as in the gale.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain what Luke means by “we made a circuit”. The ship plainly went from Syracuse to Rhegium, but not plainly how. The phrase most likely describes tacking, working up the coast against an unhelpful wind, though it may simply mean following the curve of the coast. Either way, the wind did not favour them until it changed at Rhegium.
verseByVerse.note: Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy; Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the grain ships.

verseByVerse.quote: "There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s church is already waiting in Italy, and in one plain sentence the Lord’s promise is kept: Paul comes to Rome.

There we found brothers. Nobody sent them; Acts records no mission to Puteoli. The gospel had been moving all along, underneath the story Luke has been telling: along the trade routes, in the luggage of merchants and sailors and slaves whose names nobody wrote down.

Seven days. The centurion Julius must have agreed to the week’s stay: one last courtesy from a man who has been quietly decent to Paul since Sidon.

And so we came to Rome. A few words, dropped in without ceremony, and the entire book has been travelling toward them. Behind them stand Paul’s long desire to see Rome (19:21; Romans 1:10–15); the Lord’s own promise in the dark of a Jerusalem barracks that Paul must testify also in Rome (23:11); forty men sworn to prevent it; two years in a cell at Caesarea; a fortnight in a storm, a shipwreck, a viper. Not as Paul had planned, but as God had promised. The restraint is not coldness. The promise never needed decorating.

I will build my church. The brothers at Puteoli are the plainest evidence in the chapter of who has really been running the mission. The risen Christ, who said his disciples would be his witnesses to the end of the earth (1:8), had sent his word ahead along the shipping lanes through people whose names are lost, and when his apostle comes ashore in Italy, Christ’s church is waiting on the quay. Jesus said he would build his church (Matthew 16:18). At Puteoli he shows that he does not need his great apostle to do it, and still delights to use him.

Every word of God arrives like that. Plainly, at last, exactly as he said. He will bring all his people to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10), and one day the whole redeemed church will say it together in the new Jerusalem: and so we came home. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

Who founded the church in Rome? Not Paul, who wrote to it before he had visited (Romans 1:13; 15:22–24), and nothing in Scripture says Peter did. It most likely began with Jews and converts from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (2:10), and with believers who moved there.

Does a church need a famous founder to be real? No. The churches at Puteoli and Rome were real churches long before an apostle arrived. What makes a church is not a famous founder or an unbroken line of bishops, but the presence of Christ among believers gathered under his Word, with the preaching of the gospel and the ordinances he gave (Matthew 18:20; 28:19–20). Its foundation is the teaching of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). An ordinary congregation of faithful believers is as truly the church as the church at Rome.
verseByVerse.note: From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians Paul has never met walk miles to meet him, and the weary apostle thanks God and takes courage before he enters Rome a prisoner.

The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. Roman Christians who hear that Paul is on the road walk out to meet him, like citizens going out to meet a dignitary. Both places were stops on the Appian Way (see roads and travel), about forty-three and thirty-three miles from Rome: on foot, a long day or two out and as long again back.

They had never met him. Paul had written to this church perhaps three years earlier, the letter we call Romans (Romans 1:11–13). Its last chapter greets some twenty-six people by name, and some of them, in all likelihood, were standing on that road.

Paul thanked God and took courage. One of the tenderest sentences in Acts: “took courage” means he needed some. The man who faced down a mob and told a shipful of despairing men that not one would die is on the road into Rome with his courage running low, going to be tried before Nero. What God sends him this time is not an angel but a small crowd of Christians by the road who wanted to see him. Paul looks straight past them to the One who sent them, thanks God, and his courage comes back.

Allowed to stay by himself. House arrest, chained to a soldier: a mild form of custody, perhaps on the strength of Festus’s letter and Julius’s report.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. Paul greets strangers as family on sight, because they share one elder Brother. The Son is not ashamed to call his people brothers, and was made like them in every respect so that he could help those who are being tested (Hebrews 2:11, 17–18). The Christ who sympathises with a weary servant sends his body, the church (1 Corinthians 12:27), and the believers on the Appian Way were his own kindness walking down the road. And the Lord himself comes out to meet his weary people, like the father in Jesus’ parable who saw his son a long way off and ran. One day he will gather his whole church to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.

How do I take courage when mine is running low? Paul did not talk himself into courage; he received it, as Christ had given it to him before: “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome” (23:11). So when yours runs low, do what he did. First, go back to what Christ has said, because his promises are yours too: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Second, let other believers come out to meet you. Do not hide when you are low: tell one or two Christians, go to church on the Sunday you least feel like it, accept the visit or the call; Christ often sends his help with a human face. Third, thank God for the help he sends, because thanks turns your eyes from the size of the trial to the faithfulness of the One who sent it. Then take the next step. Paul still walked into Rome in chains. Courage is not the absence of fear but going on with Christ while afraid, because he has gone ahead: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

How can I encourage a mature Christian, such as my pastor? Simply, and specifically. Turn up: at the hospital, the hard meeting, the anniversary of a loss. Tell them in a short note one particular way God has used them in your life. Pray for them and let them know you do. Offer practical help without being asked. Often the people who give the most encouragement receive the least. Paul’s courage was renewed by people who did nothing but walk out to meet him.

Was Paul in prison? Not in a cell. He was in military custody, but in his own rented quarters and free to receive visitors (vv. 23, 30): a prisoner awaiting trial before Caesar, through whom the gospel still went out unhindered.

Textual note. Readers of the KJV or NKJV will find an extra clause in v. 16, that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the captain of the guard; it is in later manuscripts but not the earliest, so most modern Bibles leave it out.
verseByVerse.note: The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, roughly 40 and 30 miles from Rome. Paul was kept under house arrest, chained to a soldier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last scene shows the gospel offered to Israel first, divided over, and carried on to the nations without hindrance. Paul tells the Jewish leaders of Rome that he is innocent, brings no charge against his nation, and is chained for the hope of Israel; they agree to hear him (vv. 17–22). On an appointed day he spends morning till evening showing them the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Law and the Prophets, and some are persuaded while others refuse (vv. 23–24). Paul answers with Isaiah 6, the prophecy of dull hearts and a God ready to heal, and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (vv. 25–28). Acts ends with two years of bold, unhindered preaching in Paul’s lodging (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
