Why the Book Has No Ending

The abrupt close of Acts is a decision, not an accident. Luke could have written the death of Paul, as he wrote Stephen's and James's. Instead he stops with his hero alive, chained, and preaching (why, see the note on vv. 30–31).

Two things keep the final word, unhindered, from being read as a boast that the church always wins. First, unhindered does not mean unopposed; every hindrance in the book was real and several were lethal, and Paul himself would very probably die under Nero within a few years. Second, the man is still in chains as the book closes. Luke's claim is not that the church will have an easy time, but that the word of God cannot be stopped, which is a sturdier promise and the only one he offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last thing Luke shows us is a prisoner in a rented room, chained by the wrist to a soldier, unable to leave the building or visit a single church he had planted. And out of that room came letters and converts that reached further than his travels ever did (see vv. 30–31).

Now: The circumstance that looks like the end of a person's usefulness, illness, redundancy, years of caring that shrink the world to a few rooms, is often the beginning of the part that outlasts them. Paul's chain did not end his ministry; it relocated it. He simply welcomed whoever came through the door, every day, for two years, kept by the same Lord who had kept him through the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: "After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, 'Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul goes first to his own people in Rome, as a brother, and tells them plainly that he has done nothing against Israel and that Rome found him innocent.

The local leaders of the Jews. Chained to a soldier, he waits only three days, and sends first not for the Roman church but for the synagogue. Paul could not go to the synagogue, so he invited the synagogue to come to him. Jews had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion (18:2), and there were many synagogues in the city. He has reason to move quickly: a Jew who had appealed to Caesar against the Jerusalem authorities could easily be suspected of bringing Roman trouble on a community already expelled once, and Paul wants them to hear from him first that he comes with no accusation against them (v. 19).

In the flow. With verse 17 the last scene of Acts begins, in a pattern Luke has shown many times: the Jews first, the Scriptures opened, some persuaded and others refusing, and the gospel carried to the Gentiles (13:44–48; 18:5–6). Here it happens for the last time, in the capital.

Brothers. He calls them brothers, still, and speaks of “the customs of our fathers”. Before he defends himself at all, he plants himself inside the family.

I was delivered. His summary is scrupulously fair. He does not say the Jews of Jerusalem tried to murder him, though some did, or mention the forty men and their oath. He says only “I was delivered”, naming no one, and moves on.

They wished to set me at liberty. Acts has recorded one official finding of no crime after another, from Gallio at Corinth to Agrippa (18:14–15; 23:29; 25:25; 26:31–32). Paul states the cumulative verdict as simple fact, because by now it is.

Desiring to release him. Jesus too was handed over by the leaders of his own nation into the hands of the Romans; Pilate examined him, said three times that he found no guilt in him, and, Luke records, desired to release him (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 20–22). Pilate did not release him, because the innocent One had come to be numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37), to bear their sin and die in the place of the guilty. Paul walks his Master’s road because his Master walked it first, all the way to the cross.

To the Jew first. He had written the principle to these very people: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16). Driven out of synagogue after synagogue, he never changed the order in which he knocked on doors, because he loved them; his heart’s desire and prayer to God for them was that they might be saved (Romans 10:1).

Should Christians share the gospel with Jewish people today? Yes, with love, respect and humility, as Paul does here: as a brother, showing that Jesus is the fulfilment of Israel’s own hope, and never with contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul appealed to Caesar only to save his life, and with every reason to accuse his own nation, he refuses to bring a single charge.

Compelled to appeal to Caesar. The appeal was forced: Festus had proposed a trial in Jerusalem (25:9), very likely a death sentence, and the appeal was the only door left open.

No charge to bring against my nation. A remarkably gracious sentence. Paul could have brought counter-charges before the emperor’s court, with ample evidence: a mob in the temple court that beat him, a high priest who ordered him struck on the mouth, forty men under an oath to assassinate him, two years of his life in a cell at Caesarea. When he finally reaches the court with power to do something about all of it, he says: no charge.

He had written the reason. He had written it to this city: his great sorrow and unceasing anguish of heart, so that he could wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers, his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:1–3). That is not diplomacy. A man who could wish himself cut off for their sake is not going to sue them.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Paul learned this from Christ. Peter describes the Lord at his trial: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Like a lamb led to the slaughter he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Paul’s “no charge” before Caesar is a small echo of that silence. The Lord Jesus had every charge to bring against us, and instead of accusing us he interceded for us: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). A man who has been forgiven an infinite debt can let a lesser one go.

In everyday life. Paul let it go, not by pretending it had not happened, but by declining to use the leverage he had, because the people who wronged him were the people he most wanted saved. Is there a case you are still keeping ready to file, in your heart if not in court? Christ dropped every charge against you: name it before God today, and ask his Spirit for the grace to meet that person with nothing to file. When the grievance creeps back, as it will, your standing does not hang on how well you forgive; Christ forgave his enemies perfectly, in your place.

How do I forgive without pretending that nothing happened? Forgiveness is not saying the wrong was small or did not matter; Paul named exactly what had been done to him. It is releasing the debt: giving up the right to make the other person pay, and leaving judgment to God, who will judge justly (Romans 12:19). It does not always mean restoring full trust at once, especially where there has been abuse; trust is rebuilt over time, if repentance is real, and safety matters. But it does mean refusing revenge, praying for the person’s good, and, where you can, doing them good. Ask God for help; this is the work of grace, not willpower.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.' And they said to him, 'We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is chained not for abandoning Israel’s hope but for believing it has come in Jesus, and God’s providence gives him a fair hearing in Rome.

The hope of Israel. He has used the phrase at every stage of his trials (23:6; 24:15; 26:6–8), and it has always meant the resurrection of the dead, and the coming of the Messiah in whom the promise to the fathers is kept. He is chained not despite Israel’s hope but because of it: the chain is what believing it has arrived has cost him. Christianity is the fulfilment of Israel’s hope, not its rejection: the God Christians worship is the God of Abraham, the Bible Jesus preached from is Israel’s Bible, and the Messiah Christians trust is the one Israel’s prophets promised (Luke 24:44; Romans 15:8).

No letters from Judea. Nothing has come from Jerusalem, and Luke does not say why. Most likely the sea closed behind Paul in the autumn, so no ship could have carried a dispatch ahead of him through the winter. Or the Jerusalem leadership, having twice failed to get a conviction and more than once failed to get him killed, may have decided the case was not worth pursuing to Rome.

None of the brothers. For the first time in years Paul is speaking to a Jewish audience that has not been prepared against him. It is a small mercy, the kind that never looks like providence at the time: a winter storm closing the shipping lanes, and a prisoner in Rome getting a fair hearing because of it.

A horn of salvation in the house of David. Luke’s two volumes begin and end with this hope. Before Jesus was born, the priest Zechariah blessed the God of Israel for visiting and redeeming his people, raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and remembering the oath he swore to Abraham (Luke 1:68–73). Now Paul sits in Rome and says this is the hope he is chained for: the promise to the fathers kept in Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen. To be chained for the hope of Israel is to be chained for him.

Should a Christian be ashamed of suffering for the faith? No. If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:16). Suffering for doing wrong brings no credit; suffering for Christ is an honour (Acts 5:41; 1 Peter 2:19–20). Paul wore his chain without embarrassment because it was the badge of the hope he held. If you are mocked, passed over or opposed because you follow Jesus, you are in the company of the apostles and of Christ himself.
verseByVerse.note: “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish leaders know the Christians only by their bad name, but they are fair enough to hear Paul for themselves. The faith was spoken against everywhere because its Lord was spoken against first.

We desire to hear from you. An honest and rather appealing reply. They know nothing about Paul; about the movement they know only its bad reputation.

This sect. They call it a party or school of thought (hairesis). It gives us heresy, but did not yet carry that meaning; it is the word used of the Pharisees and Sadducees as parties within Judaism (5:17; 15:5). To a Roman synagogue the Christians are one more faction inside the Jewish world, and a disreputable one.

Everywhere it is spoken against. That was true, as Luke’s own book shows, from Pisidian Antioch to Jerusalem. It was what Simeon foretold over the infant Jesus: this child is appointed for a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34). Within about four years Nero would blame the Christians for the great fire of Rome, and the Roman historian Tacitus would call the faith a deadly superstition.

History in the room. Around AD 49 the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome, and the Roman historian Suetonius, writing decades later, says the expulsion followed disturbances stirred up over one Chrestus, probably a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Luke tells the consequence in passing (18:2). Some of these leaders may remember being put out of their homes over this sect. Their caution is earned.

Only fairness. Yet with a bad impression and real grievances, they ask him to explain himself and set a date: more than Paul got in most cities. It is only fairness, but Christianity has rarely asked for more as a starting point. A bad name is not a refutation. What matters about any message is whether it is true, and these men, to their credit, wanted to hear it for themselves.

On account of the Son of Man. Jesus told his disciples that a servant is not greater than his master, and that if they persecuted him they would persecute them too (John 15:20). He pronounced a blessing on exactly this: blessed are you when people hate you and exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man (Luke 6:22–23). The bad name that reached Rome ahead of Paul was a share in Christ’s own reproach (Hebrews 13:13), and Christ’s reproach has always ended in glory.

In everyday life. When you meet someone with a bad impression of Christianity, do what these men did for Paul: ask honestly what they have heard, and listen before you answer.

Should we try to make Christianity more acceptable, so that it is not spoken against? We should remove every unnecessary offence: harshness, hypocrisy, foolishness, unkindness, a bad reputation that we have earned (1 Peter 2:12; 3:15–16). But we must never remove the offence of the gospel itself. A crucified Messiah was a stumbling block and folly from the start (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus warned his followers that they would be hated for his name (Matthew 10:22). The aim is not to be spoken well of by everyone (Luke 6:26), but to be spoken against, if at all, only for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul spends a whole day showing from the entire Old Testament that Jesus is the promised King, and the same message persuades some and leaves others unmoved.

In greater numbers. Word has gone round the synagogues of Rome, and the room is full.

From morning till evening. Sunrise to sunset, one man teaching the Scriptures, in three verbs. He expounded (exetitheto): set out, laid open, the patient work of taking a text apart and showing what is inside it. This is exposition, not oratory. He was testifying, the courtroom word: not offering an opinion but reporting what he has seen. And he was trying to convince them, in a tense that means he kept at it, because he wanted these particular men to believe.

The kingdom of God and Jesus. These are the two great themes of Acts together. The book opens with the risen Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3) and closes with Paul preaching it in Rome (v. 31). The kingdom of God means God’s rule exercised through his King: Jesus reigning now at the Father’s right hand, bringing people under his gracious rule through the gospel, and one day returning to put every enemy under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–25). Readers differ graciously on how much of that is present now (see v. 28), but the kingdom was plainly Paul’s message to Jew and Roman alike, in this age.

The Law of Moses and the Prophets. As Jesus did on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27), Paul argues from the whole Old Testament: the Law and the Prophets was the everyday name for the entire Bible (Matthew 5:17; Romans 3:21). Luke gives the fuller form on Jesus’ own lips, “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44), and Paul’s sermon in Acts 13 reasons from Psalms 2 and 16 as freely as from Isaiah.

The whole Old Testament testifies to Jesus. From the first promise in Eden to the last prophet’s cry, every page bears witness to the Son. He is the true Passover Lamb, the greater Moses, the Son of David, the suffering Servant, the Lord our righteousness. Paul spent a whole day showing the kingdom and the King hidden in plain sight on every page Israel already revered.

Some were convinced. After a full day, the whole Old Testament and a willing audience, the outcome is split: Acts’ last word on how people respond to the gospel is not tidy. The same day, Scriptures and preacher left one man persuaded and the man beside him unmoved, so the difference was not in the preaching. Isaiah’s words in the next verses locate it in the heart (v. 27): what we do not want to be true, we find reasons not to see.

What if I share the gospel faithfully and people still reject it? Then you are in the company of Paul, of the prophets, and of Jesus himself. Your responsibility is to be faithful, clear and loving; the results belong to God, who alone gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Do not conclude that the message needs changing. Keep praying for those who said no; some who reject the gospel today will receive it later. And remember that in this very room some were convinced. God always has his people, and his word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: 'The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: "Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s parting word is Isaiah’s: the Holy Spirit foretold that Israel would hear without understanding, and such unbelief is God’s judgment on hardened hearts.

Disagreeing among themselves. They go out of the door still arguing, after Paul has made a single parting statement: a quotation.

The Holy Spirit was right. One of the clearest statements in the New Testament about what Scripture is. The speaker is God: the Holy Spirit said this. Yet it came “through Isaiah the prophet”, a real man, in his own way of speaking, in the eighth century BC, out of his own vision in the temple. That is the doctrine of inspiration in the form Scripture usually gives it: God speaking, and a real human being writing. Peter puts it the same way: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).

To your fathers. Said to Isaiah’s generation eight hundred years earlier, it is applied without apology to the men walking out of Paul’s lodging, as heirs of their unbelieving ancestors. Scripture is not a record of what God once said to other people; it is his address to whoever is in the room.

Hear but never understand. The quotation is Isaiah 6:9–10, the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning, when he saw the Lord high and lifted up in the temple. The New Testament quotes it more than any other text on unbelief: Jesus to explain why he taught in parables (Luke 8:10), John to explain why the miracles had not produced faith (John 12:40). Israel’s unbelief was foretold, and it is God’s judgment on hardened hearts. Paul does not soften it, but it is God’s verdict, not Paul’s grudge, and he quotes it in sorrow, about his own people, after a full day spent trying to persuade them. It must never become a weapon.

He saw his glory. John adds something that changes how the scene reads. Right after quoting Isaiah 6, he says that Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41), and the “him” is Jesus. The Lord high and lifted up, whose train filled the temple, was the Son. So the men walking out of Paul’s lodging were turning from the King of Isaiah’s vision, whom the seraphim hailed as holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3). That holiness undid Isaiah: Woe is me! For I am lost, for I am a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:5), until a burning coal from the altar touched his mouth and his guilt was taken away. The message of hardening came from that same holy throne. To walk away from Christ is not to decline a point of view; it is to turn one’s back on the Holy One who alone can take guilt away.

In everyday life. Before you open your Bible this week, pray the psalmist’s prayer: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18).

If God hardens hearts, is that unfair? No, though it is deeply sobering. God never hardens an innocent heart; he gives over to hardness those who have already closed their eyes to the light they have (Romans 1:21–24). Pharaoh repeatedly hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32), and God, as he had said he would, confirmed it in judgment (Exodus 4:21; 9:12). Hardening is judgment, and judgment is just. At the same time, no one who longs to see and hear and turn will ever be turned away; the desire itself is a sign of grace (John 6:37). If you are worried that you are hardened, the worry is good evidence that you are not. Come to Christ now.

parallels.desc: keep on hearing, but do not understand

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people have closed their own eyes and God confirms it in judgment, yet the verse ends with a God who would heal them. What shut eyes keep out is a Saviour wounded for sinners.

Grown dull. Grown fat, thickened, insensitive (epachynthē). Isaiah built the verse deliberately. Going in, the sequence runs heart, ears, eyes: the heart dulls first, then the hearing goes, then the eyes shut. Coming out, in the healing clause, it runs the other way: see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn. The way out is the way in, run backwards.

Their eyes they have closed. In the Greek Paul quotes, the shutting is something the people do to themselves, the deliberate refusal to look at something they suspect they will have to act on. And yet in Isaiah 6 the prophet is commissioned to produce this effect: make the heart of this people dull, lest they see with their eyes. God sends the message knowing, and in some sense intending, that it will harden. Hardening is both their choice and God’s judgment (Romans 1:24; 11:7–8).

Both sides held together. Scripture never gives up either truth for the other. Paul wrestled with it for three chapters to this city (Romans 9–11), and ended not with a formula but with worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). The hardened are genuinely responsible, and God is genuinely sovereign over the outcome. A reader who has to drop one to keep the other has stopped reading the Bible and started tidying it.

And I would heal them. The sentence does not end with judgment. It ends with a physician. The whole terrible mechanism of dulled hearts, stopped ears and shut eyes explains what is being kept out, and what is kept out is healing. That is the God being refused: not one casting about for an excuse to condemn, but one standing at the door of a nation with medicine in his hands, ready to heal if they would only look, listen, understand and turn, and grieving that they have shut their eyes. He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11).

With his wounds we are healed. The healing this sentence holds out has a name and a price. Jesus called himself a physician who came not for the well but for the sick, to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:31–32). And the prophet given this hardening commission went on to describe how the healing would be paid for: the Servant was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Shut eyes do not merely miss a doctrine. They miss a wounded Saviour.

How would I know if my own heart is growing dull? Watch for the signs Isaiah describes. Does God’s Word still move you, or do you hear it without being affected? Do you avoid passages or sermons that might require you to change? Has a known sin stopped troubling you? Are you more interested in arguing than in obeying? A dull heart rarely notices its own dullness, so ask a trusted friend too. The remedy is in the verse’s last words: look, listen, ask for understanding, and turn. He still says, “I would heal them.” If the very question troubles you, take that as a good sign (see vv. 25–26). Grief, depression and dry seasons are not the same thing as a dull heart, and the Spirit is at work in anyone who wants to see and hear.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The salvation many in Israel refused has been sent by God to the nations, and they will listen; it is not a sign that God has finished with Israel.

Sent to the Gentiles. Paul’s last words to a Jewish audience in Acts have been badly misused, and need careful handling. He says “this salvation of God”: the same salvation, not a substitute or a second-best. It “has been sent”: God sent it, so this is not Paul’s decision or Paul’s revenge. This is the third and final turning to the Gentiles in Acts (13:46; 18:6): in Asia Minor, in Greece, and now in Rome. And “they will listen”: most Christians reading this are Gentiles who listened, from Rome to the ends of the earth, in a thousand languages.

All flesh shall see the salvation of God. Luke chose an unusual word for salvation here, used only twice before, at the beginning of his Gospel. Old Simeon, holding the infant Jesus in the temple, said that his eyes had seen God’s salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:30–32). And John the Baptist’s ministry was introduced with Isaiah’s promise that all flesh shall see the salvation of God (Luke 3:6). Paul’s last word to Israel in Acts closes a circle Luke opened over a baby’s head: this salvation is the child Simeon held, now crucified, risen and preached, and carried to the nations exactly as Simeon said.

What it does not say. It does not say God has finished with Israel. Paul had already written to this city: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite” (Romans 11:1). Paul is himself the proof. On any reading, a Jew is saved exactly as a Gentile is, by faith in Jesus the Messiah. He goes on in that letter to speak of a remnant now, a hardening that is partial and temporary, and a future in which mercy comes round to Israel again (Romans 11:5, 25–26). And some Jews in Rome believed Paul that very day (v. 24).

In everyday life. Pray this week for Jewish friends, neighbours or people you know of, that God would graft them back into their own olive tree. And examine your heart for any trace of pride toward them.

Does this mean Gentile Christians have replaced the Jews? No, not in the sense of Gentiles taking Israel’s place while Jews are shut out. Paul’s picture is one olive tree: unbelieving branches broken off, Gentile branches grafted in by faith, and natural branches able to be grafted back if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:17–24). There is one people of God, made up of believing Jews and believing Gentiles, saved the same way, by grace through faith in the same Messiah. Gentile believers stand only by faith and must never boast; this verse should make them humble, grateful and eager to see Jewish people come to their Messiah.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the promises. Readers in our own congregations differ here, and should do so with respect. Many dear brothers and sisters hold that God’s promises to national Israel await a literal future fulfilment, because they take the promises seriously, and that instinct deserves respect; the same divide shapes how they read the kingdom’s presence now (v. 23). Among Reformed teachers, many expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, while others read all Israel (Romans 11:26) as the full number of God’s people, Jew and Gentile.

This commentary’s view. The Reformed reading emphasises that all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ and that Jew and Gentile are made one new man in him (2 Corinthians 1:20; Ephesians 2:14–16), and that is the more likely reading, because the New Testament itself declares the promises fulfilled in Christ and his one people. Within that one people, this commentary holds with humility that Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ. What both readings hold, and it is far more than what separates them, is that God has not finished with the Jewish people, that his covenant faithfulness does not fail, and that Romans 11 forbids any Gentile Christian the smallest trace of superiority: do not be arrogant toward the branches (Romans 11:18).

Textual note. Older Bibles have a verse 29 here: that when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves. The ESV prints it as a footnote, because the earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have it; a copyist most likely drew it from v. 25 to smooth the transition. Nothing hangs on it, and the manuscript record is so rich that we can see precisely where a later hand smoothed a seam.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: “And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.”

parallels.desc: your saving power among all nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke ends with the gospel preached openly for two years at the heart of the empire: the preacher is chained, but the word of God is not.

Two whole years. Around AD 60 to 62. Luke gives no verdict, no trial, no release. Paul is chained by the wrist to a rotating guard, in lodgings he pays for himself, perhaps with gifts from the churches (Philippians 4:10–18). He cannot go out, so everyone comes in.

Welcomed all. Jews and Gentiles, the curious and the convinced, slaves like Onesimus (Philemon 10), and, since the guard changed shift by shift, a steady procession of soldiers who had no choice but to stand there and listen. Paul mentions the result in a letter very likely written here: the gospel had become known throughout the whole imperial guard, and there were saints in Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:13; 4:22). On the traditional view, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon were written in this room: the chain that stopped him travelling produced letters that reached further than his travelling ever did.

The kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. On the kingdom of God, see vv. 23–24. Here Luke gives Paul’s subject its fullest name. At Pentecost Peter ended the church’s first sermon by declaring that God had made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ (2:36). The last sentence of the book has the same claim taught openly in the city of the emperor whom Festus called “my lord” (25:26). Caesar had the title. Jesus has the throne.

With all boldness and without hindrance. With all boldness: parrēsia, the frank, unguarded speech of a free man. It is what the church prayed for when first told to be quiet (4:29), and God has not withdrawn it. Without hindrance: akōlytōs, the very last word of the Greek text of Acts. Paul was in chains; the word of God was not (2 Timothy 2:9).

Why does it stop there? Every reader asks what happened to Paul, and Luke does not say. Some think he wrote before the case was decided; others suggest a third volume was intended. But the strongest reason is that Luke has finished the story he set out to tell. His subject was never Paul’s biography but the one announced in the first chapter: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). The gospel has reached the capital of the world and is preached there without restriction.

What happened to Paul. Early tradition, outside Scripture and held loosely, says he was released, travelled again, possibly to Spain as he had hoped (Romans 15:24), was re-arrested, and was beheaded at Rome under Nero, probably about AD 64–67; Scripture itself ends with him in prison expecting death (2 Timothy 4:6). But Luke ends on “without hindrance”. The book is unfinished because the story is unfinished, and we are in it.

What the word came through. Consider what the word came through before Luke could write that. The Sanhedrin ordered it silenced, and it spread. Its first martyr was stoned outside the city, and it spread. Herod put James to the sword and Peter in prison, the angel opened the door, and the word spread. It was flogged out of Philippi, laughed at in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, and dragged through four courts. The sea rose against it for fourteen days and put it on a beach, alive. A snake fastened on it, and it shook the snake into the fire. At the end, the emperor of the world has the preacher chained by the wrist in his own capital, and the word of God walks in and out of that room every day for two years, and no one on earth can lay a finger on it.

Frightened people on a hillside. Thirty years before that room, a handful of frightened people stood on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching a man go up out of their sight. They had nothing anyone would have funded: only his word that they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth, the promise of his Spirit, and the memory of an empty tomb. And he did it. He poured out the Spirit at Pentecost, and three thousand came in. He struck down his own worst enemy on the Damascus road and made him the apostle to the nations. He stood beside his servant in a barracks cell in the dark and told him he would see Rome, and then he held a ship’s company together for fourteen days to keep the appointment. Every mile was his doing, and every soul brought in was his. The Lord Jesus Christ is building his church, exactly as he said he would, and the gates of hell have not prevailed and will not. He is doing it still, through people whose names will never be written down, and he will not stop until the last of them is home. The chain was on the apostle’s wrist, never on the word of God.

In everyday life. Wherever your own limits are this year, illness, age, a small life, ask how the word can go out through you: to the people who come to your door, the letters you write, the child you teach, by the Spirit who gave the first believers their boldness (4:31).

If the story of Acts continues, are there still apostles and apostolic miracles today? The mission continues; the apostolic office does not. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him personally, who laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 15:8). Their teaching, now written in the New Testament, is complete and sufficient. What continues is the work they began: the word preached, the gospel spreading, the Spirit giving new birth, Christ building his church through ordinary believers and faithful pastors. You are not an apostle, but you are part of the story they started, and the same Lord is with you to the end of the age. On whether gifts such as healing continue, see vv. 7–8.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “at his own expense” (en idiō misthōmati) can also mean in his own rented lodging, and the KJV reads “in his own hired house”. The word normally refers to something hired or paid for, and whether Luke is stressing the cost or the place is not certain. Either way, Paul lived in quarters he paid for, not in a prison cell (compare v. 23).
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Luke ends with the gospel preached “without hindrance” at the heart of the empire.

parallels.desc: the word of God is not bound

28.title: Rome at Last
28.text: <sup>1</sup>After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. <sup>2</sup>The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. <sup>3</sup>When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <sup>4</sup>When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” <sup>5</sup>He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <sup>6</sup>They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <sup>7</sup>Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <sup>8</sup>It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <sup>9</sup>And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <sup>10</sup>They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. <sup>11</sup>After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. <sup>12</sup>Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. <sup>13</sup>And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <sup>14</sup>There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome. <sup>15</sup>And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. <sup>16</sup>And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. <sup>17</sup>After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <sup>18</sup>When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case. <sup>19</sup>But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—though I had no charge to bring against my nation. <sup>20</sup>For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” <sup>21</sup>And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. <sup>22</sup>But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.” <sup>23</sup>When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. <sup>24</sup>And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. <sup>25</sup>And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: <sup>26</sup>‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. <sup>27</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>28</sup>Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.” <sup>30</sup>He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, <sup>31</sup>proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
28.overview:
Where we are. The ship has broken up off an unknown coast, and all 276 on board have reached land safely, as God promised (27:24, 44). Paul is still a prisoner bound for Caesar, and in this last chapter of Acts the journey promised in a Jerusalem barracks (23:11) reaches its end.

The message. The risen Christ keeps his word, and his word cannot be chained. He brings his servant through shipwreck and snakebite to the capital of the world, and there the gospel is preached “with all boldness and without hindrance” (v. 31). People divide over Jesus to the last page, but God’s salvation goes on to the nations, and nothing can stop it.

Why it was said. Luke wrote to show that the faith was the fulfilment of Israel’s hope and no threat to Rome (see the introduction), and the last chapter gathers both threads: Paul, innocent by every official verdict, is chained “because of the hope of Israel” (v. 20), and Rome lets him preach for two years.

How the chapter makes its case. On Malta a viper fails to kill Paul, and the islanders who judged him a murderer call him a god (vv. 1–6). He heals Publius’s father and many others, and the island sends the company on provisioned (vv. 7–10). They sail to Puteoli, find believers, and come to Rome, where Christians walk out to meet Paul and he takes courage (vv. 11–16). He tells the Jewish leaders he is chained for Israel’s hope, and spends a whole day showing them Jesus from Moses and the Prophets (vv. 17–23). Some are convinced and some refuse; Paul quotes Isaiah 6 and announces that salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (vv. 24–28). Luke ends with two years of open preaching (vv. 30–31).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter points past Paul to his Lord. The Christ who promised his witnesses would reach the end of the earth (1:8) brings his word to Rome; the healings on Malta follow the pattern of his ministry at Capernaum; the hope of Israel is Jesus crucified and risen; and the Holy One of Isaiah’s vision, whom John says was Christ (John 12:41), stands behind both the hardening and the offer to heal. The book closes not on Paul’s verdict but on “the Lord Jesus Christ” taught openly in Caesar’s city. Caesar had the title; Jesus has the throne.

For us. Acts has no ending because the story has not ended, and every believer is in it. The Lord who sent brothers down the Appian Way still sends his people to one another when courage runs low, and the word preached in Paul’s room is now entrusted to us. Our lives may be small or confining; the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9).

keyVerse.quote: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
keyVerse.note: The last sentence of Acts gathers up the whole book: the kingdom the risen Jesus spoke about (1:3), Jesus proclaimed as Lord and Christ as Peter proclaimed him at Pentecost (2:36), and the boldness the church prayed for under threat (4:29). Its final word, without hindrance, is the verdict on thirty years of opposition: the preacher is chained, but the word of God runs free, and it is running still.

28.reflection:
The islanders judged Paul first a murderer and then a god, on the same evidence (vv. 3–6). Where are you tempted to read God’s verdict on a person, yourself included, from what happens to them, and what does the cross say instead?

Paul “thanked God and took courage” when believers he had never met walked out to meet him (v. 15). When has God renewed your courage through other Christians, and who might need you to walk out to meet them this week?

After a whole day of Scripture, some were convinced and others disbelieved (v. 24). How does Isaiah’s picture of hearts growing dull (v. 27) help us understand unbelief, and how should it shape the way we pray for and speak to people who say no?

Acts ends with a chained man preaching “with all boldness and without hindrance” (v. 31), and no account of his trial. What limits on your own life, like Paul’s chain, might be the very place where God wants his word to go out through you?
